Darkest Dungeon is a RPG with a whole lot of great ideas that are bogged down by some equally terrible and frustrating ones. Firstly, atmosphere is king here. Sound, visuals, all of it is fantastic though a bit basic in the animation department. Game play is thought provoking, and more geared towards thinking your actions through, planning ahead and making critical decisions which I enjoyed immensely.
Unfortunately, these positives are horribly outweighed by the over bearing negatives. At first the game will appear to be everything I just described but, before long, will turn into an infuriating grind that sucks all the fun out of it, topped off with an even more agonising RNG system that can feel like it's punishing you for even daring to think you can enjoy the game. The most infuriating example of this would be when my Crusader, with their 90% bleed resistance, was made to bleed three times in a row whilst the enemy managed to resist the same effective for six rounds despite only having 40% bleed resistance.
The characters, whilst it is made clear, are disposable, but that means little as far as the game goes. You become attached to them not because they are well thought out, attractive or charismatic. You become attached because you have sunk time and effort into them which leaves you with no real link to them. Their deaths are more infuriating than heartfelt because there is no real emotional investment which is a massive mis-step for any RPG, a style of game that is known for it's story and character building.
The worst part however, is that should RNG decide to mess you up for some inane reason, there is nothing you can do about it thanks to the incredibly terrible auto save system. You can't save any time you like and go back should you lose the hours and hours of work you put into a character to some bull♥♥♥♥♥♥the game decided to throw your way. What's that? The healer died because they got crit four times despite your tank having made themselves a target? Well tough, they are dead through no fault of you're own, guess you better train another up to level six, grind the gold to upgrade them fully, remove the neg stats they always come with and pray that RNG gives you the best pro quirks.
Again, this game could have been great. I really enjoyed the system at first but the second the game became unbearably annoying, I found it far to easy to put it down and walk away. Hopefully, the developers are still working on Darkest Dungeon and read the reviews pointing out the glaring flaws. This game has the potential to be a brilliant bright diamond, but until then, into the dark pit it goes.
Edit - On top of all that, the fandom for this game is terrible. Any criticism of the game is met with a "get gud", the irony of which seems to be entirely lost when you consider teh game itself is heavily RNG and grind based.
Has no purpose in being a game, and no right in having a price tag. Calling it nothing isn't reductive; it applies to it entirely. Not even worth your time.

First off, I have clicked the DO NOT RECOMMEND button at the bottom of this review. And that's only half true. See, I've been trying to beat the living hell out of this game ever since I bought it almost a week ago and I keep getting stopped by bugs. Below I'm going to list the four bugs I've encountered, and they're pretty catastrophic, but if you save often you'll be fine. Except that you can't save in dungeons. Luckily, none of these bugs took place in Dungeons.
The first bug I encountered: On leaving Castle Sasune I decided to go back to the starting village and see if I missed anything. When I talked to the Elder in town, the storyline restarted and I had to go back through gathering my party, whose levels had all reset to 3, 3, and 4, respectively, by going through all the cutscenes over again.
The Second bug I encountered: While on The Enterprise (Boat) I got into a battle, a lot of them, to try and level against the new monsters because YAAY DIVERSITY, only to come out of my 20th or so battle and realize I was standing in the ocean. There was no ship sprite, I was Luneth being followed by Desch.. standing on the ocean. The background music had stopped and I was unable to go back on land, and when I went past the first continent, the Big Rock that bars your passage before defeating Djinn was there again. Wee~ saved to an empty file and reloaded, bug not fixed.
The Third bug, and the funniest (in a cruel sort of way): After speaking with a friend about a treasure room just inside the crystal cave, I decided to head back there on The Enterprise (Save Often) and check it out, if only for the Achievement progress. I skipped the first village because I'd already dealt with that bug and I wasn't risking it. Go in to the cave, grab the loot and spot a hole in the floor. So I hop in, figuring the worst that could happen is that I'll have to walk through the crystal room again. NOPE. Game reverts Luneth and party to level 3, 3, 3, and 4 respectively and plays the opening cutscene again. And restarts the storyline, strips you of items and jobs unlocked. FUNNNN.
The last bug I found was upon restarting the game after the third bug: I loaded up my save and there I was in the middle fo the Ocean on The Enterprise. I decide to quickly get the hell off this boat before it glitches on me again. Got into a fight with 2 Hermits. Killed them quickly, was back on my boat, and two achievements popped up. Apparently I saved a lot of Gil, because I got both of the Gil-related achievements for nothing.
All in all, a great game but I have to play it in small chunks because of the ridiculous amount of bugs I've run into. Its frustrating, and I won't recommend the purchase of this game to any but the most stalwart of Final Fantasy fans.

Final Fantasy III (the original Japanese one, not FF6 which was unfortunately named "FF3" in its original western release)... There isn't much to say about the game itself that hasn't been said a million times during the decades. Solid early Square JRPG, originally for the NES. If you liked FF1 and 2, this is pretty much a sure bet. (This revamp of the game is also nice because the original FF3 was never exported back in the day, so not many people got to play it.)
The graphical upgrade is interesting. They could have gone the same route as with what they did with FF1 and FF2 when they remade them for the PSP and DS, iow. keep it 2D, just with modern graphics. Instead of that, they chose simplistic PlayStation1-style "retro-3D" graphics. This was an interesting choice, and it works. It brings the extra depth that 3D provides (in more senses than just the added third dimension), but still manages to keep a nostalgic "retro" feeling to it. They could have botched it up, but it works fine.
For someone who has never played JRPGs, and especially someone who has only played modern games, the visuals and gameplay may feel appalling at first. The game may feel extremely simplistic, even boring, both from a visual and a gameplay perspective. However, if you give it a chance, I'm sure that you'll end up loving it. (And of course if you are a long-time old gamer like me, you'll probably love it right away.)

This game is really good. It's a pretty engaging hacking sim that has you using a terminal for most functions in the game. Very few things in this game do you actually use a mouse for. This isn't hollowood style "click on this and it'll magically take control of the world." It isn't a "real" hack simulation either. What is it then? Kinda like the fisher-price version of a real life linux terminal. You use real life commands on a terminal in this game, with watered down versions of real life port work on servers. No, it won't teach you how to be an 3L1t3 HAX0R, but it will engage you enough to probably inspire you to go out in the real world and learn about programming and what real hacking is. Might even inspire you to enter into a CTF competition online, where you can legally practice hacking skills in real competitions with varying difficulty, which is what I did after running through this game and getting inspired to learn more about programming and real-world hacking. If you hate typing a lot, you'll probably hate this game. It's not a bad thing, it's just how this game is played. But otherwise, if you're looking for a casual hack sim, nothing beats hacknet. The story is okay, but simply doing contracts that feel realistic and are very engaging and immersive is, imo, where the game shines. I also believe on 3/31/17 there is an expansion coming out that will add an addtional 3-4 hours of single player, as well as a multiplayer function where you work as a team to solve contracts or something (Don't quote me on that). If you take the time to dig through other networks in the game, a lot of the files will make you laugh from time to time.
TL;DR: Very fun, realistic-ish hacking simulator. Certainly more than worth its price, but don't get it if you despise typing. Also, some files in the game are kinda funny.

I have played some of the XCOM series. All are very good games and I recommend XCom 2 as well.
This latest in the series has quite a few positive points but it has some issues as well.
Pro:
- the timer missions are manageable as long as you do not forget the main goal (which is not to kill all the enemies). Sometimes they are extremely difficult though.
- the variety/diversity of missions is very nice
- no more "hunt down the UFOs" thing... I do like much more the actual option of contacting different regions, building radio relays.
- a very good decision by the game creators:  the events "you may pick only one out of 3 missions". You block some of the obstacles, you cannot block all of them.
- very good game atmosphere, very good replayability.
The engineers and the scientists are very important, you may obtain them from missions or you may buy them from the black market or from your main region.
The soldier classes are different compare to the previous XCOMs.
There are 2 special missions by which you can unlock the mechs or some extremely powerfull beasts (as enemies), the "rulers". There are 3 rulers. Well... The rulers are extremely difficult to defeat: for every action of any soldier in your squad, they will get an action, and their power is devastating. If you are lucky (very lucky), a repeater might instantly destroy a ruler. If you have a repeater that is. And if the shot hits.
Killing enemies might get you item drops (only one drop by mission). Killing the enemies in explosions and fire will destroy the loot as well. The loot from dead enemies is timed: in 3 turns it will be lost if you don' t pick it up.
Cons:
- Central, the officer who informs you about the missions and so on, is annoying. I turned off the speach volume because of him and because of the soldier comments: they are ok for a while, but not in the long run.
- 80% chance to hit? Well, with 80% chance to hit for all your soldiers and you might fail to hit with all of them... It works the other way as well, you get a 15% chance to hit and you score a critical hit and save the day. If I would have to bet, I am betting on all your soldiers failing to hit with 80-90% chance to hit :D
- the mid game is extremely difficult. Early and late game are easy or acceptable. I simply stopped some campaigns and changed the research path the next patch campaign because of this. Having magnetic weapons is a huge differentiator.
- sometimes the enemies move much slower, their turn takes several minutes instead of a few seconds. Disabling XBOX DVR (I have Windows 10) seemed to solve the issue for at least 2 games (including War Thunder, where I have gone from unplayable 1 FPS to more than acceptable 100 FPS - I am not joking).
- the buildings... With all the great advantages of the higher elevation, the buildings seem to not offer any protection from the attacks from below. It is like being exposed.

Updated Review (11 JAN 2017):
NOTE: To be clear, the majority of my gameplay time on this game falls between initial release and the last patch, when I encountered no problems other than mod conflicts. As with most of my Steam games, I didn't bother with a review. Plenty of others were raving about the game so why should I say the same things? Lazy? Yeah.
That said I'm going to start this update by clearly stating that XCOM2 is one of my favourite games EVER. Its not the kind of game to give up on easily. Even though I was pretty angry when the last patch broke my install, and posted my initial review (below) as a result, I just couldn't let it go. It may be worth noting I didn't discover this right away as I'd been neck deep in other games prior to and after the patch. Stupid Orcs. Found out when game tanked while I was showing it off to a mate. Murphy's Law I guess.
This update is posted about a week into my latest clean install. And by clean, this time I mean both the Steam folder and the OS drive "My Games" folder - only my character pool was spared the axe. I then verified my game cache via Steam, and once the entire 29gb reinstall was done, I used steam to create a desktop icon.
As of right now, still getting red screen error on launch, but a simple tweak of launch options made that go away - seems to be for a multiplayer file or some such, so don't care. Tweaked graphics settings and then ran game. So far, it's running moderately well, but still a few crashes. Having sifted through several very long forum posts (one of which was 30 pages long) trying to get a handle on what causes the crashes I pretty much gave up. There seem to be multiple possibilities. Still, frustrating.
So... where does that leave this review? Hmmm... Well, I'm still leaving it as a thumbs down for the simple reason that I really prefer not to have to stuff around this much to get a great game running again after a patch. Nor can I ignore the fact it's still crashing sporadically for me. My comments re optimisation still stand. Frame rate is all over the place. It is just my opinion but I feel that a game this good should be able to reach as many players as possible - not everyone has a high end PC so a little more work to iron out performance on mid / upper-mid range machines would be in everyone's best interest. I cannot review this any other way as this is my experience and also that of others.
HOWEVER!!!! It would be unfair not to also add that this game is pretty frickin' awesome when it runs without crashing. The level of customisation of your characters is a 10/10 as are many  aspects of tactical gameplay. It is not an easy game to master, but rewarding as you slowly learn how to. Odds can feel like they're stacked against you and at times they are. Your grunts are going to miss a 90% shot chance on an enemy standing a tile away - that I think is a little overboard but your memorial wall is fairly large so... yeah. Enemy numbers and stats level with you - well, they can out-level you at times in fact - so you're never really going to rest easy. And just when you think things can’t get worse... they will.
Also not a huge fan of the timed missions (not all are timed however), mostly because I'm a turtle at heart and like to take my time - rushing to beat a timer detracts from the tactical aspect of the game for me. To a degree, this also holds true for the campaign map - there is a definite gearing towards pushing you ever onwards - a game design decision some will like and some will not. It certainly ramps up the tension and fits with the narrative. This is personal choice IMO, and as I say, I'm a slow poke. I don't see this aspect of the game as a negative as such, but perhaps an option to extend play time might be an idea. Oh, for days gone by and the Longwar mod...
Without Longwar Studios Toolbox, or another mod, your camera angles are only adjustable by 90 degrees - one of the few things I really didn't like control wise. There can also be some quirks with moving characters - one wrong click and a grunt can be toast. Not a game breaker, just need to be super careful.
Mod support is good but you do need to be careful as mod conflicts can cause issues and I found (regretfully) that the "more map" style mods may cause problems so I haven't used any of those in some time just to be safe. IMO, there are some mods that are must haves but I'd recommend playing vanilla at least once to get a feel for what you might want to tweak or improve. I'd also note here that if you're using certain combinations of mods, and with the way the XComEngine.ini file works, you may need to delete it (easier than editing) before starting the game to purge mod overwrite data - especially if you're using Longwar Toolbox in combination with certain other mods. Meh.
Conclusion: Great game with a few optimisation issues IMO - enough to keep it from a thumbs up. On sale, it is definitely worth buying. I pre-ordered my copy BTW - and ultimately I don't regret it but am frustrated with it at times. Could just do without the crashes. Can live with the rest. Despite issues, I'm not going to stop playing the game. That might not make sense to some people, but that's the way it is. I just can't give a thumbs up in it's current state.
TL:DR ...
* Gameplay / Features: 7/10
* Mods / Steam Workshop: 9/10
* Optimisation / Performance: 6/10 (on an pretty good but not super-beast PC); needs
work in that regard IMO
* Stability: 5/10 (harrumph!)
* Replayability / Map variety:  7/10 (map layout, while procedurally generated, does
feel limited and over time, repetitive).
* DLC: 5/10 - OK with what there is, but would like to see more content please
* Overall: 7/10 (pretty much excluding crashing issues)

This game has a great concept, but it unfortunately really falls short, almost feeling unfinished.  The game has huge potential in its mechanics and the idea of procedurally generated mystery in general, but it needs the story element (the mystery genre's strength) to be interesting.
The atmosphere is enjoyable (the soundtrack and art style are very nice), but the gameplay totally took me out of the mood.   At first, I completely didn't understand what I was supposed to be doing.  It is not intuitive, and there isn't a very good introduction/explanation of the controls.  You have to focus so much on figuring out how the game works that it's impossible to get immersed in it.
The story elements don't link up at all with the gameplay, which is a big part of why it's so confusing to figure out.  For example, you're no more likely to find a clue at the crime scene than in ANY other place in the game.  A lot of things feel very luck based, and it's frustrating to realize a lot of things you were trying to do were just a waste of time and resources.  The game does give you a lot of freedom in what you can do, but there aren't logical consequences for every type of action.
Everything you do in the game is done the same way (selectively spamming the interact button until you have enough data) and then solving a simple Guess Who logic puzzle.  Before you understand how it works, it's confusing and jarring, and once you do, it's overly easy.  There are a lot of interesting elements (like hunger meter and managing resources, factions, etc.) but without narrative to contextualize them, they feel empty.   It seems like the game is mostly figuring out how the game works, instead of actually playing the game.
The Dinner Party mode is a condensed version (1 night in a house vs. a week in the whole city), which I actually found a lot more enjoyable.  There's more of a real-time pressure, and it's easier to get immersed because the investigative style makes more sense on this scale.  The "madness" mechanic (essentially, the other characters will sometimes want to shoot you) makes you stay in the moment and keep moving throughout the house.  However, again, once you figure out how it works, it gets old quick.
If I'm a little harsh on this game, it's because it has such fantastic potential and concept that got me really excited, and it simply doesn't deliver.  I wish the devs kept it gestating a little longer, and spent as much time on integrating story as they did with coming up with (frankly really interesting) game mechanics.  Yes, you can play over and over.  Unfortunately, it doesn't really make you /want/ to.

Noir Syndrome is an interesting game. It tries to bring in something new to the Rogue-lite market, by putting you in the shoes of a private detective. From there, you have several places to visit to gather clues and suspects, while trying not to step on the wrong faction's toes.
While the concept is fantastic, the game's scope is much more modest. I was expecting much more from it, and it's not what it was trying to deliver.
Sessions last about 15 minutes.
There is a rampant murderer in the city (for cult reasons), and you can visit every landmark freely, spending one day to explore each area. I was expecting a bit more FTL or WeirdWorlds influence, with a deep lore that one could discover by playing it over and over again, but this is purely a mechanical game. Unfortunately, its mechanics are not robust enough to carry it, in my opinion.

The game's artstyle is not beautiful, nor unique. You can probably get that from the screenshots. But it's functional, and to be honest, it didn't prove very relevant in my enjoyment of the game. A great artstyle would certainly make it more enjoyable, but I could distinguish everything of important here, so it's fine.
The
, however, was pretty neat! As you would expect from a Noir game, it features a lot of
, with a bit of chiptune influences at times, and also Classical music in a couple of places (expensive hotels and the hunting club, for example). But for the most part, it's jazz. And it fits the detective vibe perfectly.
It's not something I'd listen to on my own time (it's simple, and not a lot of variety), but I didn't feel like turning it off while playing the game!

Now that this is out of their way, I'll explain how the game works.
You have 14 days to explore the city and find out who the culprit is, and bring him to justice. You have various different areas of the city to explore. You can explore one each day.
In those areas there are objects and people. In a restaurant, for example, you can speak to people there, and also explore the seats and tables for clues. Each area functions similarly. This exploration phase plays like a 2D side-scroller.
People can be either of 2: normal people, and sellers. Normal people can give you suspects (or give a very generic and not very convincing argument against them being a suspect... just flavour text), while vendors will try to sell you Food, Lockpicks or Bullets.
Examinable objects can also give you Locks, Bullets, Money, or Clues.
You'll need
to open doors or steal from vaults, and
to... well... kill people. More on that later.

Every clue is about the killer. This is very important (and also a big issue). No matter where you find it, the clue is always about the murderer. Also, the clues are

---
This is a very uninteresting way of making you a detective, isn't it? There's barely any brainwork from the player! It's just about running around the place, inspecting every random background object (because that's where you get clues), and then finding the right choices. It doesn't feel like you're playing a detective, and every game ends up playing too similarly.
Since every clue is about the killer, you don't really need to go to the crime scenes or follow leads to find anything about him(her). You can just explore any place that's convenient to you, and you'll easily succeed. This is probably the biggest issue I have with it. There's not a lot of thinking in this game, and it completely takes the "detective" part out of the game.
---
On the City, there are different possible events. There are Civillian Gatherings, Police/Mob takeovers, Crime Scenes, and fishy places. About he latter, I have no ideia... You get that information from the people, but there is nothing different in those areas.
The first 3 are areas dominated by said faction. This is relevant when you killed someone from the Police/Mob and left witnesses, or stole from either, as factions can then be hostile towards you, and shoot on sight. On Hard mode, there's always an hostile faction from the start.
CrimeScenes are areas without people, where you can look for clues, without the risk of getting murdered.

Other than that, one important aspect is the Hunger Meter. Yes. This has a ♥♥♥♥ing hunger meter.
I'm sorry, that's rude. But seriously... Why?!
The game has nothing to do with survival, except for the fact that you have to buy food not to die. Each time you examine something, or open doors, you'll lose 3 points. A piece of food can give you from 100 to 300, depending on the price. I guess this puts a stop to spamming Z constantly, but it doesn't feel necessary to have such a "feature".
---
This is a good segway!
The game is far too easy. There aren't too many suspects, and it's easy to find his attributes from the clues. Normal mode is not challenging at all. Hard Mode, can be fairly challenging, but for the wrong reasons. Food could be one of them, but you learn to play with it. The main reason is the factions that's trying to kill you. You have very limited bullets (1-2, usually), so you can't just kill everyone, which is good. However, while finding clues is very easy, finding all the suspects can take more effort, especially, when there's a faction that will kill you immediately, and there may also be hitmen on you, that seem to spawn randomly. You can literally enter an area and just die, because he was right in front of you, and you couldn't escape.
This helps the game having challenge, but still doesn't feel like being the detective was the focus. The detective part is a very thin layer, surrounded by all these other systems trying to keep you from examining it closely.
---
I think I've covered most of it. It's a purely mechanical game, of getting clues and suspects, and then arresting them. Killing them ends the game, but not with a victory. There are some special systems, like stealing from factions (that♥♥♥♥♥♥them off) or killing everyone in an area not to leave witnesses, but those play a very minor role in the overall game. This is because the game isn't hard at all! When you die, it's mostly out of your control.
The only narrative, is present in the murderers appartment, where there are random logs (6), with a passage of his Egypt-mythology related killing spree. Nothing substancial at all, though. There are no interesting plots throughout the city, no lore, no interesting random events, nothing of the sort. It was what I was mostly looking forward to, unfortunately...
Conclusion. It's not an awful game. It's actually pretty solid,
. If you're looking for a very simple game (perhaps a good first project), then go ahead. I enjoyed the game, but I don't consider it great at all. Lots of wasted potential, but an interesting effort nonetheless. Only higher from here!

First of all, let's get something out of the way: this game was QUITE CLEARLY made for a device such as a tablet. Now that that's out of the picture, Noir Syndrome is a very strange take on what one could call the detective games' genre.
Gameplay is a simple "look for clues" ritual, where you click the investigate button near a backdrop and have the potential of finding evidence that points you in the direction of one of the suspects or you click the same button near a person and talk to them, potentially adding someone to your suspects' list. The reason this is quirky is because at the end of a session you may not have had either enough evidence to point you to the real culprit (and thus force you to guess who the culprit is for the session) or, and this one's a real pain and somewhat usual phenomenon, you don't even have the culprit on your suspects' list yet; if this is the case, you have lost, period.
Other game mechanics are a hunger system, where you are forced to interact with salespeople to get food of various qualities for differing prices, a wanted system, where either or both the police and the mob are out to get you, and essentially a pressuring system where at some points during the game the culprit will send hitmen out to kill you. There's also a "quest" system so you can earn a little more money either by killing assigned targets or delivering mail to the intended recipient, but for both of those you need to have found the respective items to access the quest givers via the quirky random chance while inspecting the background, which is the main source of your character getting hungry by the way...
Noir Syndrome comes with three difficulty modes where the main factors are how awful are your starting conditions and how expensive every commodity in the game is. Yes, that steak isn't going to pay itself in Impossible Mode if you haven't been improving your money-hoarding skill that persists through different game sessions, so you'll have to start at Easy and work your way towards it.
...Which, after all, is Noir Syndrome's greatest sin. The game is awfully very much about strategy and luck, as you have to choose which areas you go into in order to get clues while taking into account if the police or the mob have a chance to be represented in the area, and also managing your scarce money to buy bullets, lockpicks and the ever-important food at different locations. But after you've raised your money-hoarding skills to the point of making money become just another number you casually look at while at the hardest of difficulties, it's almost like you're playing on Easy again if you have the right strategy, and the game becomes once again about how lucky you are to find the clues you need. This makes Noir Syndrome fit into the category of mindless fun: at some point, you'll be doing something mechanical, taking the same options as you play essentially the same game over and over again. And it can stop being fun to become boring.
As you've noticed, I don't recommend this game. The reason? It simply isn't worth the full cost, and it hinges on your willingness to continue grinding away until the game becomes "easy enough" at each of the difficulties you'll be playing in. If the game was somehow grander, most of the clues less redundant and/or less narrowing, or if the ideal strategy wasn't too mechanical to the point of almost making you shut out cognitive thought and forcing you to reacquire it when something immediate happens (such as a very innoportune hitman that once killed triggers the police/mob to want to gun you down), I would have recommended this game because it is, surprisingly, fun to go around poking random stuff for random clues which may or may not be enough to catch the culprit.

If you are a fan of RNG rogue-like games, then this one is a treat.
Darkest Dungeon is not an easy game.  At the same time, it's not that challenging either.  What I mean by this is you will have heroes die by the dozens, but you will always have more at your disposal.  Our heroes are essentially fodder that you throw at this world while trying to slowly crawl your way to wards the end.   You will have favorites of course, and you will be heartbroken when they die.  Maybe you take better care of them and sacrifice other characters to save the ones you love.  These are the kinds of choices you get to make in this game.  Do you cut loose a diseased hero because you have no money to heal them or do you spend the money and wait a week before they are usable.  In Darkest Dungeon, you manage your heroes as much as your gold.
The world of Darkest Dungeon is a savage place that even the strongest mind succumbs too.  Darkest Dungeon turns this idea into actual gameplay, in which you must manage the sanity of your heroes.  This system can have all kinds of effects on your heroes at any point.  You could be in the middle of battle, demolishing your foes when their sanity maxes and they get an adverse condition that causes you to lose control of the battle.  Your best hope is that you only lose that character and not your entire party.  Sometimes though your hero will fight through the darkness and become a beacon of hope.  In doing so they will be gifted a positive condition that you can then make permanent back in town.
Speaking of town, you have a variety of options here.  You vist the Hamlet after each battle to spend your gold.  You have a choice of upgrading weapons and armor, curing heroes of diseases and ailments and providing them with entertainment at the tavern or church; to lower their sanity.  Be careful though, treating sanity means that those heroes will be out of battle for exactly one quest.  You will have to make do with other heroes.  This is one of the greatest things about Darkest Dungeon.  You can't just rely  on 4 heroes You must manage many many more.  Some will die, some will get sick, some will go crazy, as you crawl your way towards the end.
When you are not in the Hamlet you are questing in one of the many areas in the game.  Each area has a vastly different feel with enemies that are varied.  Each area will also offer different diseases and challenges that your heroes will face.  Once you choose your quest, which comes in multiple varieties and difficulties, you choose your party of 4 from dozens of different classes.  These classes are incrediblly unique and offer a variety of ways to play.  You then get to outfit your party with provisions that can range from food and torches to other goodies that make your questing easier.  Keep in mind that they cost a fairly decent amount of gold.  Once outfitted, you enter your dungeon and proceed to make your way from room to room. You will spend most of you time disspatching any foes in your way and uncovering any treasure, until you complete the requrements for the quest.  Dugneons and enemies are at the wimsy of the RNG, so every game will be different and fresh.  Some quests will have you facing barely any enemies and then others you could end up fighting waves of them.
When you do engage in battle, you will be met with a very confusing screen that will take some getting use to.  There is a slight learning curve to the battle system, but it's nothing you wont have mastered in short time.  Essentially they play out in turn based fashion, but with an added twist.  Hero and enemy attacks are based on their postion in the party.  There are four postions for four characters.  Front, two middle, and back.  Attacks and buffs will depend on that postion.  You might have a really strong attack for a character in the front, but get pushed to the back where that character is useless.  You would then have to waste a turn or even two to get back up front.  Same can be said for the enemy.  Also in battle you will have to control your sanity and any diseases that you happen to be infilcted with.  Status effects like Blight, and Bleed are more dangerous here than in most games.  In Darkest Dungeon you will need to master these status changes more so than other RPG battle systems if you are to complete the game.  You won't be able to just blunt force your way through this game.
Darkest Dungeon  features some of the best  hand drawn artwork in this ever crowded landscape of indy games.  It truely does set itself apart, with its haunting voicework, soundtrack and overall look of the game.  You will spend dozens of hours looking and listening to it all and if your anything like me, you won't be tired of it by the end.  The atmosphere is amazing in this game.  Truley one of hte best we have seen in gaming in a long long time.
Darkest Dungeon manages to take the hugely popular and formulaic rogue-like genre and shake it up a bit.  In Darkest Dungeon we have something that manages to be extremely challenging, but also not if you willing to embrace loss and death in way that most games don't ask you too.

In general, I like this game, but I can really see why some people don't. I should probably mention before I get going that I haven't finished the game, but I know how it ends and I think I've played it long enough to get a good feel for the mechanics. I also don't have either of the current dlcs, so I can't comment on their quality or how they effect the main game. The combat is turn based and fairly simple, reminding me of some of the old school Final Fantasy games (which I love), but I still haven't figured out how the turns actually work since the game doesn't have any sort of timer bar that shows which character is up next. There's a good assortment of characters, and as long as you keep your roster filled out, it's pretty easy to construct a well balanced party, especially since most of the characters have some sort of healing move (though the tank and dps characters tend to only have self healing moves, but whatever helps). I think the most troubling thing about the game for me personally is how grind-y it gets, and how repetitive the game gets because of it. There are a couple different varieties of low level dungeons to level up your recruits on, which makes sense, but the frustrating part comes when you have a high level character die and you have to grind up a replacement for them. This is probably more my problem, but this would cause me to avoid longer and harder dungeons until I felt really confident in my heroes, so I'd stick to the lower level dungeons for a while, making the game more repetitive. Also, a slightly minor gripe, but gold quickly becomes kinda useless outside of de-stressing characters. Armor and weapon upgrades take a while to unlock (at least for me, I've had a ♥♥♥♥♥ of a time finding enough paintings), so I don't spend a lot of gold on those, and the trinket shop doesn't usually have great stuff, or at least not good enough to justify spending gold on most of the time.
Personally, I find this game best for fairly short play sessions, maybe 2-3 hours at the end of the day. It's really not something I'd recommend for long play sessions, and I can't stress this enough, you won't like it if you don't like turn based combat, and you REALLY won't like it if you can't stand grinding. I personally really like the atmosphere and lore of the game, and like I said, I like old school FF type games, so there's enough that I enjoy to make it so I can tolerate the flaws, and I only really recommend this game if you think similarly. If you're on the fence, wait til it goes on sale.

After having gotten a few hours in and having enjoyed the game a bit I have my first impressions.  For now, I would recommend this game and plan to keep an eye out on it and see how it unfolds.  It has a lot of potential and I would love to see it flourish.
First let's start with the good things.  It has a large variety of ships and they do have varying play styles.  With some feeling a little samey to other ships in how they play or handle.  The fact there's now way for a wallet warrior to quickly power boost himself and destroy others is also refreshing but at the same time, such things are innately hard with skill based games like MOBA's.  Unlike other MOBA's there are no creep waves and it's all ship on ship combat so keep that in mind when you try it.  As spaceship combat isn't for everyone and you won't have waves of minions to feed on or hide behind.  However, the game feels very competitive and the respawn timers are generous.  If a bit too much so.  There is quite a fair bit of customization as well with you being able to change out your crew members, loadouts, and the massive number of ships being split into 3 weight categories and 3 game roles.  Offensive, support, and defensive along with light, medium, and heavy.
Just like the ships, the maps are surprisingly varied given the environment of space.  The environments are rather awe inspiring and interesting to look at and the game has a decent enough story to it to explain the conflict ratinally.  Corporations fighting over sectors of space to get the resources and so they hire mercenaries like yourself to fight for them in this business war.  Obviously like many games of the Genre, you don't really come for the story.
As for things I dislike about the game we'll start with some of the obvious if not expected.  Due to the fact it's a free game, the grind is very apparant if you want to get things for free.  With the length of the matches and how expensive stuff is, you'll probably end up playing dozens of matches before you're able to get a new ship or get your favorite ship the loadout you desire.
The games do feel slow at times even though, compared to other MOBA's, the actual time isn't that bad.  The games realistically only last 10-25 minutes on average while other MOBA's tend to be closer to half an hour in my experience depending on the map and players skill.  This is largely due to the fact your flying a space ship I think as it gives the impression of this huge hulk blasting over huge distances.  Also, with the lack of other enemies besides the enemy commanded ships and whatever fighters/bombers/drones/buoy's they may dispatch that you could shoot down, the map feels almost too small for how long the match goes on and like there isn't enough happening.
Speaking of the loadouts, that's the next thing I dislike.  A lot of the ships currently lack loadout upgrades due to the game still being in development which is understandable.  The other issue I have with it however, is many of the loadout upgrades feel very similar to the base version.  Due to how hard they try to make everything of equivalent power, they don't look too different on paper.  This missile does a total of 180 damage when comparing DOT and initial impact.  Both upgrades simply change how much is in the DOT or how much is in the impact.  Making them feel far too similar.  The end result is the same after all.  Some loadouts do actually change it up however.  Say changing out your syphon drones for a spotter drone.  I do hope that the loadouts get a revision and that many of the abilities see loadout options that actually can change up your playstyle.

I like Final Fantasy. It's sort of like a virtual chicken nugget (I also like chicken nuggets). But I never really got to experience it's Golden Era as I was just a young little soul at the time (I wasn't actually even born yet). It's remakes like this that allow me to see what the first generation of Final Fantasy games were like. Heck, they were pretty good.
I am fully aware that this is a port of the DS version, but it is still great to play some of the older games in this new console generation, as the current generation of FF games have not lived up to their expectations. Except A Realm Reborn. Damn that was good.
Final Fantasy III was the only FF game that was not released in NA or Europe until the 2006 DS remake, and like said above this is esentially the same game. It was also the first FF game to introduce the Jobs system, a mechanic which allows you to choose and switch between different classes in-game, a system that has been used in many Final Fantasy games in the following years.
Final Fantasy III is pretty much your standard Final Fantasy game. Magic chrystal, mystical bossfights, cliché characters and damn hard boss fights. I can see any fan of the series enjoying this game, but it's not something for new comers. If you want to get yourself into the FF universe, start off with FF VII - which is widely regarded as the best Final Fantasy game (not in my opinion, but hey)
All in all, as a fan of the series I can say I have enjoyed the DS version and this PC port. I reccommend it to fans of the francise too.

Heat Signature is a game about breaking into spaceships and trying not to die. It's the most thrilling fun I've had in a game all year.
~~~~~
I'm stuck on a ship facing enemies I can't kill. You see, they all have shields equipped, and I don't have any tech left to take out said shield, so they're impervious to anything I can throw (or shoot) at them.
My target is already dead. The captain is also already dead. I'm not at risk of getting captured here, I can just leave. But there's an enigma clause on this contract, and I want the extra coin. After all, I'm fighting to save my friend Mercy, and losing these credits is going to be a setback I don't want to risk. The clause says no living witnesses, and I'm stuck here with seven of them. Seven guards who've seen me, whom I can't even hope to kill.
My very last hope on this ship is a lone room with a viewing window. If I can manage to corral all the remaining guards into that room and break the glass, it's game over for them and a perfect contract for me. That's...a big ask. I don't have much to work with here, and it's not as if the guards will kindly and helpfully congregate in front of the window if I ask nicely. No, there are going to be bullets flying everywhere, and if even one witness remains I'm screwed.
But - I've got a shotgun.
I can pull the guards to me by firing off shots from adjacent rooms. They'll come to investigate the noise, and I can lead them toward the viewing room. If I do it right, I can get them to bunch up. They'll cluster close enough for the vacuum to pull them all out at once, and if I go with them I can just remote pilot my ship and save myself. This could work!
I move methodically through the halls, firing shots to grab the attention of the guards. Mercifully, they act as I'd hoped! They investigate the noise, moving as a group, all ten remaining baddies clumped up like some kind of shielded-shooty amoeba pushing itself through a maze of spaceship corrdiors. Finally, we hit the room I want them in, but I have to dodge down a hallway first, lest the leader of the pack shoot prematurely and hit the glass. When they all enter the room and are in range, I push back - but I'm cut off by three guards. They've spotted me, they're close enough to shoot me with no chance of dodging. I've only got one choice...
I fire my shotgun.
In slow motion, I see myself get hit by one of their bullets and fall unconscious. I see my shotgun spray creep forward, hit the leader's shield, and ricochet toward into the viewing room. I hold my breath, praying for the sound of breaking glass. And CRASH - there it is. The viewing window breaks and all the remaining guards are pulled out into empty space. My body lay there bleeding as I wait for the recovery timer to finish counting down. I see the notification pop up saying SHIP CLEARED as the triumph sets in. I can't believe what I've just pulled off. I can't believe there's no achievement for this!
I fulfilled my enigma clause, and got my full pay. A couple missions later, I freed Mercy and regained her as a player character, then retired. I learned one very important lesson from this ordeal: when the♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan, it's time to open a window.

Interactions with the few NPC's such as shop keepers and the banker are done through hitting, "Enter" and typing out key words, such as "Quest, Train, Skill, Yes, Vault" etc. Selling items? Right click on item to drop it on ground in the shop, left clicking items on shops floor purchases them if you have the funds. If not, the Shopkeep will tell you how much it costs.
I personally like the game due to its pretty much bare bones old school approach. Yes, people can pick up loot you drop or are dropped from mobs, even if they didn't hit/tag the mob. Just like in real life, some people can be tools, walk up to you and take something that you dropped that or even type in "unfriendly" flag red and kill you. When you die from pvp or mobs you drop everything in your inventory that isn't "engraved".
Yes, you can engrave anything you have which will give it an 85% chance not to drop upon your death, so the danger of losing your nice long sword is still there. It just means you have to play smart, don't over extend and don't be a♥♥♥♥♥♥to other players by being a jerk or talking too much♥♥♥♥♥♥..because they can and will kill you. And if you are a murderous scum bag red, when you die (if you've killed one too many players) you get sent to jail and cannot leave until you time out. Which can take hours or days. At the end of the day Aberoth isn't for everyone. If you like high res graphics, 3d environments, tons of interactive UI and NPC's with wordy story lines...then no, this game's not for you. I decided to make an actual review of this game instead of making a witty comment.
Aberoth is a "hardcore" mmo with permadeath, minimalist graphics and a combat system as functional as the No man's sky multiplayer.
Aberoth has some pretty interesting ideas but fails miserable to execute them, i'll give credit to the dev for creating a java-based MMO on his own, and i assume this is one of his first project using java, which in that case, is pretty impressive.

I was pretty impressed at first. Being able to zoom out to see the entire galaxy to zooming in on a single tiny pod is pretty cool. The concept of hijacking ships and kicking♥♥♥♥♥is pretty fun too. The novelty of it all wears off after a few hours, unfortunately.
It's not a bad game, it's just pretty bare once you get into it. There's not a lot of depth to it; you just have to hijack ships, do an objective, and get better loot. Then you liberate colonies, and that's about it. The ships are cool at first but soon become very repetitive despite its randomized nature. I see a lot complain that the guards are a problem, because most of the time there's groups of guards in single rooms, and one might venture out and become isolated, then you can pick him off. Rinse, repeat.
I started to approach about every mission with a wrench because you can hit with it from afar and throw it, taking out two at once, initially. The game mixes it up a bit including shields and other things on enemies, which require specific weapons to deal with or some ingenuity. Like, you can lead these guards with impenetrable armor (again, unless you have a certain item) and shoot a window, sucking them out. Often times it's not the best choice, but it's there.
The retirement system seems cool at first but in the grand scheme of things doesn't really matter. The Defector missions are really fun and are probably the highlight of the game, but like a lot of things in this game, it simply doesn't matter. There's no benefit to defector missions other than fun; it doesn't contribute to your end goal in liberating the entire system.
The artwork is fine, I appreciate the little details thrown into the different factions but it (again) gets repetitive. Some of the textures when you move in become pixelized like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ jpeg. The game also has only two FPS options, 30 or 60, which is silly but maybe there's some constraint I'm not aware of.
If it looks like I hate the game, I don't. It's actually pretty addictive and I managed to put in ~14 hours into it. If the developer adds more to the game then I can see it becoming a really special game. At this point though, there's a sort of novelty to it that wears off way too fast. Still, for 15 bucks, it's not a bad deal, but it's not really something I personally see myself or many others spending a great deal of time on.

aerofly FS is a flight sim for beginners and more advanced pilots.
The glider and ultra-light flight simulation is really rather good.
The sim can be used for training approaches and landings with single-engine propeller aircraft as well.
There are plenty of airfields and nice scenery from Switzerland to fly in.
The simulation is not that good for fighter jets, you need to look at DCS for high-quality simulation of those.
However, jets in this can be fun still even if not most accurate flight simulation.
The developers of aerofly also have different product for RC-plane and helicopter simulation and training (hook up RC transmitter to PC for example), if you aim at improving RC skills then that might be better choice.
Depending on what you are after this does have good points and value for money.
For relaxing and training with glider or ultra-light this is a good choice.
For combat with modern jets you need to look at other choices.

A very good but basic Flight Sim. The flightmodels are absolutely magnificent a very close replica to the real world equivalents. That being said I think it is due to be added in the next version/ patch. The weather physics (e.g. Wind) is absolutely brilliant, it feels very much like real life especially through the valleys where there are updrafts and downdrafts & thermals etc, very good. The user interface is easy to use and looks decent. There is good controller detection support as well & the game in general is very easy to setup.
As im sure others have posted it's a great starter or casual sim experience. It is worth noting its simulation experience is probably not on the same level as some products such as FSX, P3D & X-Plane but it is still an excellent product in its own unique way. Would deffinetly recommend to others.

This has got to be one of the best procedural games I've seen in a very long time. You play a detective who is given a limited period of time to whittle down suspects through the elimination of possibilities. Three lifestyle categories, two genders, and several job descriptions are your means of getting there. By the way, hope you're fast on the draw-- the closer you get to solving the case, the more likely it is someone will show up with a gun.
Graphically the game is less than stellar-- and I love it. The game doesn't get fancy and allows you to focus on the task at hand. Obvious (and not obvious) locations of clues will have you thanking the designer for his art scheme later on. The soundtrack is perfect for the genre and evokes memories of gumshoes, mobsters, and private♥♥♥♥♥♥♥(that was a term for a generic male, people).
The recombines the clues to make for a really great game that can be replayed over and over. In the span of twenty minutes I was shot 4 times, solved 1 case (without getting killed), and shot 4 people (only some of which were actually shooting at me). It had me right at the edge of my seat the entire time. For the price of less than a movie ticket you could be in a trenchcoat saying 'Here's looking at you, kid.'
An easy 10 out of 10 for the price, the music, and the magic.

As I stood in my run down apartment, my mission became clear.
Noir Syndrome is agame that hits all the right targets: it's stylish, has a good story and is, most importantly, fun. The player's goal is to travel around various buildings in a 60s Chicago town, collecting clues and learning of possible suspects. However, you are only human, and in this mystery game hunger and hitmen sent by the culprit because you know too much are also your enemies. Anyone anywhere in this town is a suspect, but you need to find someone who's backstory fits the clues you have gathered. Then finally when the culprit is obvious, you locate them and apprehend them.
This game has certainly been worth 5 quid, maybe more (And that is NOT. repeat NOT a hint to raise the price, guys). The general rush of desperately trying to piece these vague clues together while deaths occur all around you is an experience not usually encountered in other games. Beside that, the way you execute justice is entirely up to you. Want some gun action? Go bounty hunting for the Hunt Club. Want a challenge? Rob a shop or kill a gangster and have the police and mob on your tail too! Hungry? Go to the diner and grab a ham and cheese plate. It's basically 8 bit, scaled down GTA.

reading all the reviews on this game i feel like i should write my own. People have commented on the RNG of the game, how the deck feels stacked against you and how your adventurers don't feel like 'heroes' but skittering madmen and how quickly things can get out of control and the grind of recovering your loses. Yes the game 'can' get grindy at times and yes there are times when an encounter will scale so far out of control and you lose some or all adventurers, but despite what some might think this is the minority and most times it is players gambling or pushing their luck.
Darkest dungeon is set almost like in a lovecraftian story, its not about heroes fighitng monsters and smiting their way to victory, it is about clawing and scrambling in an attempt to win a losing battle. The characters or adventures you hire aren't heroes, they are the dredges of the world who are either suicidal or mad enough to venture in. The first time you play you will be blind and as such you will be beaten many times, the bosses in particular are terrifying not so much because they hit hard or have a lot of health (though it doesn't help), but because the way they act or behave is so different to what you have expereinced previously in the game. You will lose characters in this game (it says it right on the box when the game loads), but you learn from your mistakes and you come back with the knowledge of your failed attempts and you succeed and that i think is one of the true enjoyments of the darkest dungeon. Its about surviving the dungeons long enough to find what holds and to exploit your foes with your new knowledge. Its like a combination of Dark souls and the game Risk, the game isn't unfair it's just not lenient and a large portion is simply knowing when to cut your losses and retreat from a dungeon instead of losing characters.
For those interested but concerend about the reviews concerning grinding or mechanics/difficulty, the game allows you to change and adjust many of its aspects. Radiant mode keeps the difficulty which speeds up adventurer XP gain, reduces gold costs and many other changes which act to reduce the grind as well as slaken some of their strict rules and in the options menu you can change other aspects as well and craft it to how you wish to play the game. Its only on the harder difficulty settings when you are forced to play by the designers rules and even then i find it more enjoyable because it adds a sense of urgency by placing you under a timer (limits how many adventures you can go on and how many adventurers can die) and makes you have to deal with unfavorable circumstances while in the other difficulty settings there is no timer and you simply need time to recover from ANY situation. This game is not for everyone and that is fine, but with the different modes, the ability to customise some mechanics you can tune it to how you wish to enjoy it. This game has always been a 10/10 for me and the Crimson Court DLC made it an easy 12/10.

Uuuuuuugh another one of those "Wish I could give a maybe" games.
Reviews are meant to be for reccomending games--not if you liked it or not. I think half of us don't read the "Do you recommend this game?" above the yes or no buttons.

To start off I got this game on day one cause the idea of space travel has always been my favorite. Most space travel games are really not the space travel I look for. I want to need to go exploring not the want.

TerraTech is a neat little idea. You're a little guy who pops down to a planet and steals, crafts, and/or buys bits to put onto yourself to become a DIY Frankenmobile. However, there's one significant problem with this system. Let me try to be short, even though this will probably end up not being as much: Your survival depends strictly on your weapons. Speed and medium of transportation can change, but in the end, your guns are your strength. So, no matter how small, big, fast, slow, etc. you are, the basis of "More gun = Win" stands true, right? This creates a paradox in which all crafts made to be more powerful follow three distinct designs that constantly show up in anything that isn't an NPC or a build made only to look good and not work well. I'll call them by the names I've given them, then explain what it means. The first and probably most common is the Stairs design. This is where a tech is built in steps, that can be anywhere from 1 block wide, to things above 5 blocks wide; and every block going up has a weapon on it, and every side of every block has a weapon on it, so in essence you have combat stairs. Then, there's the Wall design. Instead of building up, it builds to the sides or backwards, making a wall where every block across has weaponry on it, then the front/sides is/are either all lasers or drills. Similar in idea, only difference being shape and that it's more likely to melee. Then there's the biggest, ugliest, and generally worst of the designs, the Cube. It's literally a big block of hull with a ton of weapons, mostly arcing guns like the mortars, all over the top, then lasers and what not all over the sides, and the core is either on the front or in the middle. Unfortunately, this design is one of the most effective, as it allows the most weapons and an astounding amount of defense; meaning, with some shields and maybe a regen sphere, it's an unstoppable war machine, and if such a thing invades you, you can kiss goodbye to the land around it unless YOU build one, which is why these designs are so widespread. You have to conform to battle it; so this entire complex system of blocks and guns and thrusts comes down to the Cube, the Wall, or the Stairs. Until you throw efficiency out the window and build for design and accept death - as it becomes a common occurence - you're stuck with these choices, because nothing else works against these except these, and this will keep going until a wrench is thrown into the gears that makes other designs more powerful; i.e. things that work better with any build, and makes "lots of guns" strategy null. So yeah, you may get people playing the game; but in the end, all you've got are cubes, stairs, and walls. Don't let the trailers fool you. All those really cool looking techs won't save you from Invaders. Just trust me.

Honestly, I can only really fault the game on two things.
No. 1, The fact that a lot of your choices early on feel like they have little/no meaning.  However, as the story progresses, choices definitely feel like they have more impact, endgame especially.
and No. 2, the engine isn't perfect.  For instance, when the player has made several neutral-decisions... but the overall allignment balance may be either to one side or the other, some dialogue choices by the NPC can feel like they came out of nowhere.  This sometimes leads to the overall story feeling a little bit stilted and disingenuous.
However, these 2 drawbacks (at least for me) weren't dealbreakers; the story still flowed fairly well and the whole game I was constantly struggling with what was the "right" decision.  Emotions ran high during many of the major turning-points in the story, and I can't lie, my eyes did start swelling at the chapter 5 finale...

This is my first steam review. I decided to write one for this game due to a lot of the negative reviews and comments towards the game. I have 7.4 hours from playing non stop.
I feel like a lot of people (not all of them) only played this game maybe twenty to thirty minutes tops then gave up and quit. I feel like a lot of people put this game down due to the low quality 80's DOS/Atari-like graphics. However, this is a very unique MMO once you learn what you are doing. I, personally, am I a fan of the 80's DOS/Atari-like graphics so maybe that's another reason why I really enjoy this game. Let me get down to a lot of the things that make this MMO unique though.
The PvP system is unique. Everyone starts as friendly, and when you are friendly, everyone else that is friendly cannot hurt you. However, if you switch to unfriendly, then any friendly person can attack the unfriendly person, but the unfriendly person can attack the friendly people. Now, don't let this discourage you because it's not a PvP fest what-so-ever from what I saw during my 7.4 hours I spent so far on the game. Whenever you die, you love everything unless you have certain items engraved (which cost money) and even then, there's still a chance to lose them if I can remember correctly. I could be wrong on that. This might sound bad, but you got to remember, it's a challenge. This game is not for people who want there hands to be held the entire time and things to always be easy. There's also an infamous implement for the PvP. If you do happen to be a ruthless killer, you will be known for it and probably have to pay for it.
I have yet to see one mean person. 95 percent of the 7.4 hours I put towards this game so far have been spent communicating with other people and there's A LOT of people on the realm I am on (black, if you want to know). Not one person has been mean or hurtful. It's almost like the servers population, stranger or not, are one giant family or something. It's hard to explain.
The shop system. No NPC sells an item, only the players in the shop. This means, if you have a dagger and want to sell it, you can either go to the shop, right click it and it will fall on the ground and you get partial gold of what it's worth instantly, and the dagger will stay on the ground in the shop until another player comes along and buys it full store price, or you can try to sell it to another player personally. I felt the need to mention this because, it's pretty unique from any other MMO I have played and I like this system.
Now, there are some things that I do not like. The fact that I feel like there isn't a WHOLE LOT from what I haven't yet gotten to. Don't get me wrong though, there's still plenty, and PLENTY for me to explore and do. Afterall, I'm only 5 quests in and the description of the game says there's over 50. I guess it's more of a fear of mine right now and I fear that the game doesn't get a lot of expansions. If a dev reads this, please add expansions and continue adding on to make this game even greater and bigger.
Another thing I dislike is that while talking to the quest giver, she'll only talk to one person at a time. This means, if there's ten people standing around the quest giver, you have to keep trying until she finally talks to you. Also during peak hours, trying to kill certain things can be a pain sometimes.
In conclusion, I'm sure there's more pros and cons I could think of, but I haven't slept for a long time so I'm not going to put too much thought in it as I feel like I got a lot of the things I needed to out in this review. I highly recommend this game unless you know you hate older looking graphics. To just give up before you really learn how to play though could possibly be a shame. I almost quit my first twenty minutes but I forced myself to learn what I was doing. It's a different kind of MMO and holds a special charm that I can imagine being a love/hate sort of thing. I also could be wrong on certain things I noted, but I'm pretty positive I'm not. I only say this because I'm still a noob. I do pay close attention though to details. If I am wrong on something, please be sure to let me know and I'll fix it.
EDIT: If you want to find me, I'm Thefword on the black realm.

If you are an AC fan, you will love and hate this game.
First thing to consider is - What performance specs does your computer have? Second, have you been keeping up on your computer's maintenance?
This game requires a lot of performance from your computer. If you are not keeping up on the maintenance and have too many background processes running, you will run into drops in FPS and stickiness. You might even encounter issues with online connectivity. You have to be very careful to adjust your computer's settings to aid in a resolution in this issue.
(Keep in mind, Ubisoft is not a part of Steam. In their forums they give you a list of troubleshoot steps to follow to correct any online connection issues. Being they have nothing to do with Steam, follow their walkthrough verbatim. However, do not disable Steam or any Steam services.)
My Machine runs an AMD FX 9590. 24GB DDR3 Xfactor Self cooling RAM. A single GTX 970X GPU. Middle end Asus system board. ACX Cylinder Cooling. My computer runs this game without issues - in terms of FPS and standard performance. My computer is well over their System Requirements. Because my HDD is slowing and only a SATA2 3.5Gbs, the load screens take a little while to load. Which will be corrected when I load my SSD.
My son's computer is running an AMD A10 33xx(something). 8GB DDR3 standard RAM. An AMD Sapphire R9 270x. Stock MSI Jasmine System Board. Dual fan cooling (ACX in GPU). 6Gbs HDD. His computer will sometimes drop FPS or appear to slow down. He plays with low/medium graphics quality. His computer falls within range on their Minimum System Requirements. However, his load screens are quicker loading then mine. Though, we have tested his HDD to mine, and his is much faster.
I am a Computer Technician by trade. My son is learning. Both of our systems remain optimized and tuned up on a regular basis. I cannot stress this enough. Tuning up your computer and maintaining your background processes is essential to any game. Especially those that push your hardware to its limits.
Enough about systems. On to the game.
Ubisoft has a history of seemingly not knowing what is going on with their multiplayer engine. Either they will not admit to shutting it down or limiting it. They cannot find and fix an issue(s) with it. Or whatever the speculation is. The fact is that their multiplayer engine with the AC franchise... sucks. And it gets worst with each release (Unity was developed and released, Black Flag started having more and more issues. Black Flag was released and their previous releases became worst, repeat). If you carefully follow their support guide, you should be back in business. But DO NOT DISABLE STEAM!
This game, as all games, has some minor bugs, glitches. I have yet to experience any crashing. The bugs are minor. For example, in a Co-Op mission, the target to follow just stood there. All objectives were complete. Never ended the mission. If everyone was to die and de-synchronize, it would fix itself. However, simultaneous de-synchronization is not easy when you are playing with strangers. Better to exit the mission and try again.
The glitches are standard with AC. You are climbing up and you think this path is A the direction you are moving to, and B the direction that is best suitable. The game mechanics disagree. You might just find yourself jumping to the wrong ledge.... Like in all AC games, correct it as you go.
Or, again like in all AC games, you jump and land, stumble and catch yourself. The game thinks you fell off the edge. You might jump around a little.
Sometimes when you kill an NPC, their bodies appear to have a seizure. How many games have we seen this happen in?
Outside the standard bugs and glitches. The game itself.... I miss being able to pick up an enemy’s weapon and use it in a fight. I miss being able to pick up the body and hide it. They took a lot of things out of this game. In some ways, the mechanics of Black Flag were better. In other ways, Black Flag made the game too easy. Hide in a bush and whistle... Can't do that in Unity.
The AI has been adapted as well. When you drop a guard off the roof top, citizens would cry out. Guards would investigate. This was all standard with ALL the AC games. Well, not so much anymore. They will investigate, but are not as vigilant.
Multiplayer. Has awesome as it is. I was disappointed. I thought it was Co-Op through and through. My son corrected me. Apparently, I did not read all the way through. There are Co-Op missions and you can explore. You cannot do the single player missions when connected with a friend online. This does disappoint me. Fable allowed you to. Borderlands allowed you to. I wish ACUnity would allow it.
Past all the bad. There are tons of new things in this game that makes it unique. Makes it enjoyable for any AC fan! If you can get past all of this, it is of my opinion you would enjoy this game. Thus, I recommend it.
As for the other reviews:
Chests Require Companion App: They moved the mini games out of the game and placed them on an APP. This way you can play the mini games even when you are not at home and gain the rewards. They went modern.
4 Types of Currencies: They took out the mini missions and added them on apps and web browsers. You earn game money, level points in form of currency, style points in form of currency, and hack points. Which means you can spend real world money to get in-game currency. The latter is optional.
Micro transactions: You have to keep purchasing consumables or loot them from bodies, or steal them. You also have to purchase any weapons and armor. Multiplayer boosts. Skills. You also have to upgrade these items. Again, you can pay RWC if you are lazy or impatient, but it is not a requirement - outside DLC.
Gear has stats. They help boost your abilities or give you an edge. However, outfits (costumes) do not give stats. If you want to look like the guy in Black Flag, you will have no stat boost that I noticed. However, if you want to be unique, you will have stat boosts.
Bugs, glitches. I covered that already. Nothing out of the ordinary on my computer or my son's. Drops in FPS, again nothing here. Though, there is some lag when online. This will depend on your cables, modem, router, WiFi or LAN, and of course, the bandwidth.
This is as much information as I can offer without rambling (too much). Take this, along with the other reviews and make your choice. I say wait for a good sale and pull the trigger. But make sure you have the hardware first.

Coming from a guy who spent more than 200 hours on the game, a negative review is perhaps quite weird, but here's what I think as of now:
+map generation, you will never play the same map twice, altought you will see some identical areas on different maps
+mods, lots of mods available
-Performance, the game just looks like the old enemy unknown with somewhat sharper textures, but whereas the old game ran silky smooth on my machine, this one has a bad framerate on anything but lowest settings
-Bugs, in a game where iron man is pretty much is "the way it's meant to be played", there are way too many bugs. Enemy unknown did have some, but I never observed them in my 147 hours in that game. Various bugs in this one includes not being able to open a door, smoke grenades not working properly, an enemy visually appearing in the wrong location on the map compared to where he actually was, an enemy going under the map and making me unable to win the mission, an enemy attacking through a closed door, and two enemies who both "cloned" themselves upon death, so that they efffectively took no damage despite my soldiers hitting them and triggering a death animation on both
-You cannot develop a particular type of ammo/grenade/heavy weapon/armor vest, if you try to develop ammo you just get one out of 5 possible types at random, if you try to develop a grenade you get one out of 3 possible types at random etc.
-Concealment, where your soldiers start the map in a "stealth mode", it just makes the enemies extreme short-sighted, until you blow your cover and they magically gain long-sight. You can run almost right in front of them and they won't notice when you're in stealth mode.
-Assault class in EU, who relied on it's shotgun, has been replaced with this ninja class who has a shotgun, but also relies heavily on a sword, and can act as a scout. The sword in my opinion doesn't fit in the game. Having a scout is very useful, but also a very boring way to play
-Sniper class in EU has been replaced with a revolver cowboy class who also carries a sniper rifle. This class is designed to attack multiple enemies in the same turn, rather than focus on important enemies. Doesn't fit in the game.
-Panic, is better than EU, but still not good enough. Your soldiers won't start killing their friends at random like in EU, but they will run randomly towards the enemy, into a position with inferior cover. Makes no sense whatsoever.
-Psionic units are now a class of their own. You train them not by using them in combat, but by having them sit in a training room in your base. Boring.
-The combination of turn timer, some really dangerous enemies, and some really strong soldier abilities, makes the tactic of "destroy the enemy pods on the same turn the engage you" the only viable tactic. If you can pull it off properly the enemies won't even have the chance to attack you, which isn't much fun. Colonel rank soldiers are too strong. Lancers and shield bearers are a big pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ Sectoids may sometimes be easy to deal with, but in early game you may have bad luck and lose a soldier to mind control. You are forced into carrying flashbangs to counter this, as it is the only reliable counter. Turn timers are the least problem as they can be fixed with mods.
-Very armored enemies, like sectopods, force you to bring a heavy gunner on every mission, in order to deal with the armor, or alternatively equipping many soldiers with armor piercing rounds. Limits your options, not fun.
-Poor enemy design. The sectoids in EU have become humans with weird jaws, the thin men have become snakes with boobs, the floaters have become some sort of statue with a built-in jetback. The avatars are just humans with glasses and funky hairstyle. The advent troops are humans who speak in a different language. Codex is a yellow human. The andromedon and the gatekeeper are good and alien-like, but they are the only ones.
-The futuristic style of houses, vehicles, street lights, fences, etc, are uninspired, and doesn't give the game much of an atmosphere. It also lacks the mystery surrounding the aliens. Much unlike enemy unknown, that game had great atmosphere.
Overall: xcom 2 fixed the issues with enemy unknown, in that you don't have to replay maps, and that you can add and change a lot with mods. But they messed up almost everything else.
edit: actually I can think of another positive: the level destruction in the game is great. most objects, including floors/roofs, can be destroyed.
