I really wanted to like this game and there are a lot of elements from the game I do like. It just falls short in so many aspects that I constatnly have to put it down to the point where I've now given up on this title.
I'll start by mentioning the story. On the surface it seems sort of interesting, sort of like what Fallout New Vegas was trying to do with their story. The issue with Fallout 4 however is with how bluntly they try to execute this all. Dialoge is straight forward, most characters have a single or very few purposes that they clearly execute, and everything is practically spoon fed to you. Now I don't think a game should be overly complex to be enjoyable, but Fallout 4 simply insults your intellegence by putting the story on tracks so it doesn't get derailed going as far as to even making a good chunk of the characters you meet unkillable or "essential",
The story doesn't reward you, the most you'll get out of it is a few lines of dialog and the success sound effect. If anything it'll go as far as punish you for completing certain quests. For example, the best ending to Fallout 4 will require you to have limited contact with all the other factions. On the contrary, Fallout New Vegas and Fallout 3 implored you to meet every last character in the story. The two previous games would go as far as mention the ill fates that awaited all the characters you ignored if you chose to ignore them.
The game is just so linear it's painful. The most a speech check may do for you is get you to avoid a fight, but it would still give you the same (if not marginally better) reward regardless of your options and it would still give you the same quest progression. Fallout 4 only has a few pivitol moments where your choises actually matter or a few neat moments where things are tailored around the character you create. Not very much changes from playthrough to playthrough though.
The areas and locations will usually have some fairly cool story to them. I feel like all the optional story is even more interesting than the actual main story you're meant to follow. Unfortunately there's only so much exploring and piecing together you can do before you realize how two dimensional the game is and shut it down. I'd recommend watching some of Oxhorn's videos instead of going through the trouble of trying to get all the side stories instead.
I feel like there's a big problem with Immersion in Fallout 4. The biggest issue I take with this game is the countless endless quests you are given by characters, whether it's for the Minute Men with Preston Garvy, your settlements with your settlers, the gangs of Nuka World, Ryse and the Brotherhood of Steel, I could go on all day naming each and every one of these infinite quests. IT puts you off when you hear the same dialog over and over again from the same characters sending you on the same missions only in different places.
There's also a problem with balance. Unless you're playing survival mode, you may as well pick nearly everything up since every item is useful and with the weight you get you shouldn't have very many issues with being over the limit. Single shot weapons tree is the only way to go since it affects shotguns, snipers, and rifles. A good number of perks are actually detrimental to your playthrough should you use them or they have negligble effects like being able to breath underwater or in the case of negative perks canibalism.
Weapon modding is unbelievably boring. It's so painful that the weapon modifications are tiered with mods getting better and better as you go up. Of course there's only four tiers of weapon mods, so this whole "climbing the ladder" mentality for modifications that Tom Clancy's The Division went for doesn't work in this game. With limited mods, you'd think that they'd force you to make some hard decisions on what benefits you want to give your gun but the most you'd ever have to consider is what sort of sight you want or if you want a compensator or a supressor (which is a pretty simple choice to make when you take the sneak crits into consideration).
The story gets fun for the last hour of gameplay. I hope there is a hacknet 2 with more gameplay and upgrades!

This was an incredible experience and definitely worth the money. A lot of games that attempt to be that Uplink successor are either very basic (read: butt ugly and short, with little to actually do) or are ridiculously complex and not very fun. This meets perfectly in the middle; easy to get into, giving you a lot of tools to work with that you have to use at the right times, while offering a fair and surmountable challenge. I do wish the act of "covering your tracks" were a bit more fleshed out, as in the game currently, all it entails is typing a quick command to delete everything in a "log" folder, but besides that, I never felt like the game was playing itself. I did in fact mess up a few times and and got one gameover while playing, so it definitely wasn't a breeze.
The story itself was something of a page-turner; the characters felt real (given that your communications with people are through gramatically incorrect text interactions) and I felt genuine emotions towards and from the various characters you meet. Another small complaint was, when it was obvious that you were supposed to move on to a different "stage" of a game (i.e. wrap up the missions with one faction and go to the next one), that old faction more or less froze like a statue, their website never changed after that, and those characters (for the most part) were never seen nor heard from again. A bit of closure in that department would have been nice.
Anyway, very fun, not-too-long game, I'd but it again if I went back. Recommend for sure

The amount of randomness in this game hurts it. I have been in situations where I have all the clues and cannot find someone to give me proper suspects. Even worse is that you can be in a situation where there are two equally valid choices. The clues only narrow down gender, affiliation (police, civilian, or mobster), and potential job. I've had it where two characters had the exact same characteristics. The game is too heavily based on luck with the only option to actually figure out who the person might be is through spending a large amount of cash on the mobster tip option. Finding the culprit within a short amount of time is nearly impossible. The game also makes a big deal about "those who are dead, stay dead." What that means is that if there are a string of murders, you're suspect list might get shorter but in the multiple games I've played, has had almost no effect. Everything resets when you start a new case, so that means they don't really stay dead. They're just not there on that case.
Ultimately the main game is not worth much except maybe a few tries if this goes on a heavy sale. Even at the relatively cheap price, you're paying too much. I will admit the mansion minigame that gets unlocked once you luckily solve one case is a bit more fun. In that, you have the full suspect list and have to find the clues. You also have to worry about the people in the mansion temporarily going insane and trying to kill you. The same issue of multiple suspects meeting the exact sime criteria for the clues unfortunately hurts even this fun mode. You also have to worry about the failure state induced by killling the actual murderer rather than arresting them. So, the game is good in concept and maybe a couple playthroughs in concept but is not worth the full price they want.

* Started game and everything was zoomed in no matter what resolution was set.  Zoomed in so far that all you could see was the top, left quadrant of the actual image.  Game is so new that there was no troubleshooting help online.  I had to scan through 20 + reviews and forum pages just to find mention of this issue.
---------*** SOLUTION For those of you with the same experience***---------
*  Select the FF3.exe file in your steamapps folder.
* Right-Click on .exe and select 'Compatibilty'
* Now selct the compatibility tab from this window
* Toggle the 'disable DPI' setting.
.... The reason you are having this issue is because you are using a monitor that displays very high DPI.  I'm currently using Apple's Retna display and that is the highest DPI you can get right now besides 4k stuff.  But any monitor capiable of displaying over 1080p will most likley fall in this category.
* The only other problem I experienced was a slight gamepad issue where my character wouldn't stop traveling west no matter what I did on the gamepad.  Unfortunatley, travelling west on the world map made me bump into a few mobs that I wasn't geared or leveled for, I died and then was sent back to my original save point which was signicantly far back in my game play.  This really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off--- so I restarted and everything was fine.  If it happens again, I'll simply unplug the controller in hopes that will make it forget the error.
Besides those 2 experiences, I would say that I am loving the game.  I never played the DS version nor did have I ever played any ports besides those awful ones for psx from the late 90s.  The game looks so beautiful now that it has been upscaled for PC and looks even better on my 50" display (sitting 10 feet back of course).
I really wanted to give a good review since FF are my favorite games, but unfortunately this PC release came out in 2014 and none of these issues should even exisit in the first place.  High DPI monitors are the future and no game should ever make you have to troubleshoot to find out that it is something this simple.  This game should be patched to auto-detect high DPI displays and allow users first time experience to be a plug n play situation like advertized.

Before starting, I must state (because it seems many do not know this still) this is **NOT** the FFIII that was on the SNES (that was FFVI in Japan). FFIII was never released in NA until a few years back, when it was brough to the Nintendo DS & later Android (I assume iOS as well).
This brings back the job system established in the first FF, with a large variety of jobs to choose from. These include the standard jobs you expect, like white/black/red mage, dark knight, dragoon; and others not commonly found in the FF series, such as viking, onion knight, and scholar. This also brings back a large world to explore, where you are not hand held and running down a hallway for 80 hours, which recent iterations of FF have unfortunatly de-evolved into.
The graphics are bright, as to be expected of something ported from the DS. No, it has not been updated for the PC, but hey, it's not 8-bit graphics and high pitched MIDI sound killing your eardrums. Character design reminds me of a simple version of those seen in Bravely Default on the 3DS.
I have never been able to get into mobile gaming (the drain on battery murders my phone), and am glad this came over to Steam. If you still need to add this one to your FF collection, and have not played it yet, pick it up as you will not be disapointed.

This sure is Final Fantasy 3,
firstly i want to talk about the port, this is a bare bones cheap and nasty port from the mobile version straight to the PC, no bells, no whistles, and considering that the android and iOS version is itself a port from the DS remake what we have here is some butt ugly textures and models being displayed at a high resolution that does them no courtesy, the sound is straight from the DS is is everything else, the game doesnt even fit to the proper aspect ratio, be prepared for 2 black bars to run vertically down the sides of your screen, there are barely any options to toggle this game has trading cards and controller support and that is literally about it, not enough to justify the price for anyone familiar with FF3
The first three Final Fantasy games are very easy to group together, they are easilly the worst the franchise (with the exception of 13 and its iterations) but they are still important games that made mistakes that would only surface themselves through time.
3 has a class system in place that anyone familiar with 5 or 14 should feel comfortable with, you can select Jobs and level them individually as well as level your own characters base stats. 5 handles this better but this is the first FF game to bring in the system,
personally id argue 3's biggest flaws are the same as FF1 and FF2's flaws but on a larger scale, Heavy grinding, vague story and a large overworld easy to get lost in, this to some people sounds like hell while to others it probably sounds great, this is an NES era RPG and this port doesnt do much to change that for better or for worse.
its still a cracking game albeit one i feel that has aged the least well, with a very large difficulty curve (that frog tower...oh my god) that is showing its age. If your already familiar with FF3 and merely looking to see what this PC port brings to the table, i cant recommend that the price is worth your time, equally if your looking for a decent JRPG on the PC, the poor port quality and how harsh and aged this game really is means that i cant recommend this over say child of light or Recettear.
However if you are intruiged to see what FF3 brings to the table on its own, and dont have access to the mobile ports (which could likely be found cheaper for the exact same content) and the sounds of a tough as nails old school JRPG sound good to you, then id recommend jumping in, maybe during a sale, theres just no reason this game should cost this much, 50% off though and id say go for it,

This game is a classic. And anyone who ever played a Final Fantasy-game should probably get it. It really is a great remake of classic that took a very long time to come the rest of the world besides Japan.
Pro's:
+ They kept the charm of the orginal game (when making this they really kept an eye out to how the original game was made. And especially with the game mechanics, like the job-system and battle-system they kept very close to  the orignal)
+ Job System (The job system is a definent pro of this game, you can take on any job any time you want, as long as you have access to it. However you do need to make tactical choices for which character, you gonna lean more on magic, cause when switched you have to begin again)
+ Music (The music is one of the plusses of the game, great masterpieces that remind you that you are really playing a JRPG)
+ Hope for more to come (Though this might not be linked to the game, it is a pro. Seeing that they did port this game to the PC, who knows what is more to come. The library is still extensive)
Maybe's:
* Graphics (I personally am very charmed by the graphics. I like this kind of art-style. It's also why I liked a lot of the RPG's on the DS. Plus the fact that they are indeed more detailed then on the DS. But however I can understand that some people are turned of by it. Take a cllose look to the screenshots, cause this is what you gonna get)
* Story (The story is a standard RPG-one. World is in peril and you have to save it. It doesn't have any super crazy plot twists or points, but it's more fleshed out then the orginal NES-story.)
* Difficulty (The game has a definent steep difficulty curve at some points in the game. Sometimes you can cruise right through a dungeon, only to find out in the next one you are major underleveled. This however is easier then the orginal game. They had also a bit more severe penalties on job-switching. It is a challenge. But if you are up for it. You gonna enjoy this)
Con's
- None (Personally I don't think this game has any con's really. A few maybe's yes. But it doesn't need you to sign in to Square-Enix as Final Fantasy VII and Final Fantasy VIII did. It's a real loveletter to the old classic Final Fantasy's. So yeah, it's a good game)

Audacious quest: Rescue Zhaneta Gemini. Enigma clause (no living witnesses). Large ship. Warzone. 19 second timer once alarm sounds. How is this even possible?
Take the quest anyway. Fly to the ship and dock at an entrance. Target prisoner is on the other end of the ship, 9 or 10 rooms away plus locked doors. Once I dock, a countdown to a warship attack starts. That's about 15 seconds away. But what's this? The room the prisoner is in, is next to two rooms with windows.
I have a hunch, and pull out without stepping foot past the airlock, causing no alarms. Disengage my pod, and start inching my way over toward the windows from the outside of the ship. Not too close, because normally, windows also act as searchlights, and if you go in range you get seen and exploded. I hover around the side.
15 seconds pass. Enemy warship attacks my target ship. Just as I had hoped, a missile blows open the two windows, negating their searching capability and also turning them into dockable points for my pod. And also starting the 19 second panic alarm before mission failure.
But they're next to each other, and in the chaos of space, my pod latches onto the wrong one. This puts me two rooms away from my target, but with a wall between us. Nope. I back out and detach. A second after I detach, a missile smashes into the window I was in. That rips apart the entire ROOM from the ship, sending it spiralling away into space. Close call. 14 seconds left.
I nudge my pod along the side of the ship, and latch onto the correct window. Pause the game. 11 seconds left. But no guards around! I run in to the first room, then adjoining room, pluck Zhaneta from her bed, and carry her back to the pod. 8 seconds left. Detach. Fly off amidst a shower of missiles and head back to base.
Just another day in the life of a rebel fighter. And there are many more like that, tales of insane deeds performed by legendary heroes in subzero space with no living witnesses to corroborate their story.

Noir Syndrome is like single player Clue, but with a detective/noir feeling and a pixel art aeshthetic.
You are plopped into the life of a pixelated detective and must catch a serial killer in 15 days. You're presented with an array of locations to visit, where you'll collect clues and interview people in point-and-click adventure style. Once you leave an area, a day has passed. Any info you've collected is placed in a notebook you can access at any time. Gather enough clues about the gender, occupation, and civilian/mobster/police affiliation of the suspect and you'll be able to pinpoint them and arrest them before they can kill again. Behind all this is a hunger system, but most locations offer at least one food vendor. I've never gotten hungry enough to experience any ill effects, but I imagine if you reach full hunger you die.
That's only the core of the game. There are all kinds of side objectives and optional activities. You have a gun, and if you play on a harder difficulty, steal from the mob, or shoot an innocent civilian you'd better be quick with it or you'll be dead.
This isn't a health bar situation, this is one shot to kill.
Money is an important resource in Noir Syndrome, as you'll need it to buy lockpicks to investigate locked rooms, bullets to defend yourself, and food to sate your hunger. You start with an appropriate budget for a private investigator, about the price of one hotdog. In the course of your investigations you'll find more cash, and by earning badges (essentially in-game achievements) you can unlock better starting bonuses, including extra lockpicks and bullets.
There's a seperate Dinner Party mode, in which you've been invited to a Clue/Murder By Death style dinner party and must uncover the identity of a murderer. You already know all the suspects, but finding clues is complicated by the paranoia of the remaining guests who can become hostile with little warning.
A playthrough of either mode will likely take you less than half an hour, but since the clues and culprit are randomized each time you'll want to play repeatedly.
I love Noir Syndrome, if for no reason other than that it's the second game I've ever played that actually lets you use deductive reasoning to solve a mystery, the first being L.A. Noire.
The art is great, and gives you just enough information to know what you're seeing, but not enough to get you bogged down in details (insert GIF of Cole Phelps examining a beer bottle, mumbling "useless" to himself.)
The game's soundtrack is great, but gets a little repetitive after a few playthroughs.
The controls can take a few minutes to get used to, and I find myself clicking the wrong button to close the notebook often, but these are minor details, and I expect they'll be addressed.
This game is not in Early Access, but is being actively deveoped, and each patch I've seen has added significant content. The latest as of this review added randomized challenges for each playthrough, which I haven't tried yet.
My only real complaint about Noir Syndrome is that the hunger system feels inappropriate for the rest of the game, Like it was left over from some earlier iteration in which this was a survival rogue-like. But for the most part it's unobtrusive and doesn't detract from what is otherwise a birlliant game.
I highly recommend Noir Syndrome, and if you like solving mysteries it's an absolute must-have game.

Noir Syndrome is a procedurally generated Detective-Em-Up and it's a heck of a lot of fun.
The mechanics are fairly simple. you basically move from location to location hitting Z (to search) on everything to gather clues, suspects and various items.
The fun comes from taking these clues and trying to work out who the culprit is.
Your Notebook gathers all your clues together along with any suspects you've learnt about.
It's then about eliminating suspects who don't match the clues.
For example, one clue might belong to either a Poet or an Artist so you know the killer has to be someone with either of those hobbies.
The killer and the clues are randomised every game, although the locations are always the same.
You'll also find money, bullets and lockpicks as you search each location.
Although a playthrough might only take 20 minutes or so there's a lot to come back to.
Beyond simply trying to track down the killer there are various other side things to do.
For example, one area houses a vault that's been sealed shut for 100 years. Tempting, no?
There's also a more condensed mode called Dinner Party where you and all the suspects are locked in one location.
Here you already know all the suspects including their affiliation (Civilian, Mob or Police) and their hobbies so all you need to do is hunt down the clues and piece them together.
Although it seems being cooped up together does take it's toll on the guests, over time they go a little crazy and need to be avoided (or shot) until they cool down.
Aside from the two main modes there are also in game Badges to unlock for completing various objectives, such as closing five cases or visiting 100 crime scenes.
Each game also offers an individual challenge, fire 10 bullets for example.
Unlocking badges and completing challenges give the player permanent bonuses for future games, such as starting with an extra lockpick.
Oh and there are costumes to unlock too.
The soundtrack is superb as well.
On the downside, the gameplay is really simple. You talk, you search, you shoot and you unlock. That's it.
I think it helps that there are side objectives to do but if you're looking for something really deep you won't find it here.
Although each game technically is different there's not a lot that changes between playthroughs.
The clues, suspects and killer will be different yes but this doesn't really mean as much as you might think.
You'll still be doing the same things regardless. You choose a location to visit, you hit Z on everything and then you have a look at your Notebook before moving on.
There's also no real logic to the clues. You find them anywhere, regardless of whether it makes sense to do so or not. Sometimes murders happen as you play and an area is marked as a crime scene but all this means is the area will empty on that day. You won't necessarily find a lot of clues in that area for example.
The Hunger mechanic can be a bit of a pain too, you lose hunger every time you do something (even searching in an area you can't find anything in for example, or searching the same area twice). This has been improved now that the Notebook states hunger as a number though. Before that update it simply said "Hungry" or "Full" without giving any indication how much longer you could go without eating anything.
Also it's a really minor thing but it'd be nice to be able to score people off the suspect list.
Overall though, I'd recommend it for sure.

If you like logic puzzles, then you will like Noir Syndrome.
As in "Sam, David and Cindy are suspects. Sam's a cook, David's a poet, Cindy's a driver. You found glasses that could belong to a poet or driver and male fingerprints. Who did it?"
Except in Noir Syndrome you have to ask around for the suspects' names, find the evidence that gives you clues and work it all out from there.
Games themselves are fairly short, ranging from 30-45 minutes, and have infinite replayability, with the suspects/clues completely changing each time. There are three modes to gameplay, Normal, Hard and Impossible. In the Hard and Impossible modes there are actual antagonists who will try to shoot at you. There is a simple, if clunky, gun that comes in handy. Or you could go around killing NPCs for fun. That too.
There is an in-game badge system that encourages you to explore more elements of the game, like "Buy information from the mob"/"Kill 20 people in 1 game"/"Have a long conversation with Jasper".
When the regular game gets dull there is a "Dinner Party" option, which is set in one location, a mansion, and has you exploring for clues, whilst avoiding dinner guests that go in and out of gun-toting madness.
Despite not having the type of "mysterious" quality that Nancy Drew or other myster games have, I ended up liking Noir Syndrome for its simplicity and replayability. When I don't have time to get into a long, drawn-out game, I go to Noir Syndrome.

I played the heck out of this game way back in the day. This is a real-time strategy with two parts. The first is the campaign, which is pretty unremarkable. Second is where the game really shines - skirmishes. The big draw here is that you level up between games, which lets you unlock new and more powerful bonuses, which you can activate by doing things such as creating units or controlling train routes.
One huge plus for this game is that the countries play very, very differently. In the first two Age of Empires games, the civilizations were basically the same plus or minus a technology and one unit. Here, the difference is huge. Russians create units in "batches", the Dutch rely on gold instead of food and can build banks to create a flow of passive income. Those are just some examples - each civilization plays very differently and all of them are interesting. Except for Spain, but you can't win 'em all. I definitely recommend this to anyone who likes real-time strategy games!

The art, narration, music and sound fx are top notch. The atmosphere created is rich. Darkest Dungeon is at it’s heart more than just a rogue-like RPG. It’s a tale, a story, an epic if you will. Becoming attached to your characters cannot be helped and only makes those final blows much more painful to witness. You cannot go wrong with Darkest Dungeon! The game play gameplay is slow and methodical, but that does not make it stale. Oh no, the gameplay is as staunch as the droves of monsters you’ll slay. Blood II is simply abysmal. Don’t even buy it when discounted. And yes, I have played the game through and multiplayer.
Blood 1 was a fantastic 2.5 d shooter, and I had the pleasure of replaying it last year. It still stands up great. Blood II doesn’t live up to its predecessor.
I don’t blame Monolith for the quality of this game – it was rushed for a Halloween release date, along with development on Shogo happening simultaneously. It is kind of sad that a lot of promised features weren’t included – this game looked a lot more promising before release. The new patches fix a lot and add some stuff, but it doesn’t really save this game.
Let’s start with the cutscenes. They are unskippable, which is bad because the story is horrible. Cutscenes  start in random places. For example, while Caleb is standing on an escalator, he has a conversation with Gidgeon as the escalator slowly moves him away from Gideon until they are talking to each other through walls, and this is at the very beginning of the game.
The voice acting is absolutely HORRIBLE. Seriously. The NPCS are annoying, say very dumb and random things. Caleb has turned from a badass to a weirdo. When lit on fire, he will scream about long after the fire is gone. He will randomly laugh while killing. It seems that the developers also had no idea what voice or accent he should use, as it changes throughout the game.
He also randomly asks for the “Pain to go away” or something while he’s taking damage. It’s so weird and out of place that it breaks any immersion, not that you should have any, and it makes you feel all uncomfortable, like you’re playing an angsty teenager and not a hell raising badass.
If you’ve ever played Shogo, another game by Monolith, the blood and gibs look roughly the same. However, this really doesn’t fit the serious (I guess? The Life Seed and hearts look the same. What do they do? Whats the difference? I don’t like it when games hold your hand but this is just confusing/lazy. I mean yeah the wiki exists, but still.
A lot of the stuff in the environment is destructible. You can destroy washing machines, garbage cans and other junk. This is cool, but a Soda Machine will explode and take half your health. What gives?
Levels are linear and lame, and lack the interesting design and just interesting places of Blood 1. Grey and brown falling apart city. Woo. I’d rather play Kingpin if I wanted that.
Music. Like Shogo, Blood II attempted adaptive music, music that adjusts to situations. This results in annoying jingles playing randomly and no consistent atmosphere due to transitions between combat and walking stuff.

Darkest Dungeon is a game that I wish had a free demo version that you could try before you buy, because it is one of those games you will either love or completely hate. It is also seems to be updating constantly - the version I'm playing is Buld 21142, and I don't know whether that means there have been 21,142 seperate updates to the game or not. This unfortunately means that your enjoyment of the game may change dramatically for no reason at all as bugs are fixed, exploits closed and features added to make it more fun.. or not.
Darkest Dungeon is a HARD game. It is REALLY hard. It's one of the first games I've ever played in which my character died in the freaking tutorial, and he died not because of any bad action on my part, but due to a couple of bad dice rolls. Once you actually start playing the game, you feel like you are constantly only a hair's breath away from a total party kill. Once characters are dead, they stay dead and you have to start over with a fresh lot. The time, effort and resources you put into the dead character is wasted.
However, there are parts of the game that I really like. I have come to learn that the narrator of the game is a complete and total jerk, but he certainly has a way of making things seem much more epic and awesome, despite the one frame animations. In fact, I find the narrator my absolute favourite part of the whole game - I would LOVE to have him narrate my SatNav. The theme, plot and mood of the game is suitably dark and tense, if a bit depressing, and the music makes you feel like you're in a life or death struggle to survive. When, or if you triumph, you feel this awesome sense of accomplishment that makes all the hard work totally worth it.
Personally, I love the game and consider the money I spent on it to be well worth it. But your mileage will most definitely vary.

*This review is based on the game Final Fantasy III, not just this particular port*
The story is standard fare, you play as an orphan collecting crystals and saving the world. Obviously there are more nuances there, but this is where the game truly feels its age with each character essentially being a blank canvas. The writing is interesting enough to offset the generic overtones though, it's generally something that Square are very good at. I want to emphasize that the story itself isn't bad though, you just shouldn't go in expecting something incredible.
The gameplay is traditional turn based, using your agility stat to determine where you appear in a queue. Some abilities have higher priorities and will therefore be used first, if your agility equals someone elses.
The development system uses the Job system, and FFIII was the first Final Fantasy that let you freely change jobs outside of battle. You have jobs like White Mage (healer), Black Mage (nuker) and Knight (tank). There are lots of jobs to use, and you can make a party of your choosing. The development system is
shallow, but has enough depth to keep things interesting. This system was then perfected in Final Fantasy V. (steam release please)
The Magic system is a little bit iffy, instead of having a standard MP pool, you have a number of uses tacked on to each level of magic (which raises through levels) which means you could use nine level 1 spells and still use a level 2 spell after that, assuming you had charges for level 2 magic. You're also limited to only 3 slots per level of magic, meaning you have to make a decision on which magicks you want to use (especially if you use a red mage) I feel like they improved on this in subsequent titles. (MP pool, no choosing magicks)
The difficulty curve can make the game frustrating at points and too easy at other points, but it's never unfair or completely simple.
Visually the game looks OK. I've never personally been a fan of the DS esque chibi art though, so take that with a grain of salt. The game itself upscales pretty well, and looks nice on the PC unless you stare too intently and some of the textures.
The controls are ok, and very intuitive if you're using a controller and you've ever played another Final Fantasy game. The menus can be a bit sluggish sometimes, but it's never to the point of frustration. The zoom feature can be a pain sometimes too, but again it's never

The Walking Dead is a game made by Telltale Games. Well, maybe the word "game" doesn't fit it, someone called it more like an "interactive movie" which isn't far from truth.
We are Lee, a professor that is going in jail 'cause he murdered a senator that was having an affair with his wife. Not exactly a good start, right? Well, during our trip to prison, bad things happen: zombie everywhere. We save (and are saved by) a little girl, Clementine. With her, we start a journey to find her parents in a world where maybe the true enemies aren't the zombies here, but the humans left alive ("Homo homini lupus" which means "A man is a wolf to another man").
The gameplay is pretty simple and straightforward, the puzzles here are really simple with some action events. What makes the game so special from others is the possibility to select the dialogues during the game and changing the story on how we play. On the paper sounds good, but all that glitters is not gold. The story will go anyway on the same route, making our choices a bit meaningless. Anyway, beside that is still a game worth of playing. Someone could say "Go on youtube and watch a gameplay serie of Walking Dead then it's like you've played the game". Here we return at starting point, where that's why game isn't exactly the word doesn't fit in. One reviewer on IGN said that playing "Walking Dead is like a coloring book where everyone have the same books with black and white sketch but it's up to us to fill it as we see fit".

UPDATE:  2014/06/11
The game starts!  Square must have patched it up, so here's my initial thoughts:  it's still a lackluster port.  If you have never played FFIII and love JRPGs, then you will really enjoy it, and the PC version has the most potenial.  The menu lay-out is spot on the mobile version (which I played on my Androids, GS2 and GS4) and the controls NEED to be changed to make sense.  Otherwise, I'm keeping my eye out for the numerous reported launch glitches.
Overall, I do not recommend this game.  Final Fantasy 3 is possibly the hardest in the franchise and compared to later games, it's a bit weird.  The characters (who didn't exist in the original NES version) are all card-board cut outs, and they don't even have basic architypes applied to them, so they're uninteresting, and the game's overall plot--while unique--is predictable and cliched (cliched due to setting the bar, not jumping on existing cliches).  Combat is basic, and character leveling and skill management is difficult to understand and never feels like it's making an impact, so grinding levels and items is always a chore in FFIII, plus you're in constant fear that a character may faint and you'll have to rush to a town with a revive fountain because Phoenix Downs are scarce.
If you are a fan of JRPGs or Old School RPGs, then I can't recommend playing this game overall, and this should be the best version of this classic, but I strongly feel most gamers will get upset or frustrated with this title.  I loved the Nintendo DS version, but I've played every game in the series (at least the main series) and understand that this one is black-sheep-ish compared to the styles and gameplay of the later games.
This game totally isn't worth $16 by the way.  The genre and indsutry changing classic, Final Fantasy VII is only $12, but that even seems too high for 3, considering it brings nothing new to the table.  It's just the iPhone/Android version, which was a single-screen DS version.  There's no update to the aesthetics and no content that improves the game, and 2006 DS graphics do not look good on a PC monitor made in the last ten years.
tldr, JRPG fans will like it, but it is a more advanced JRPG, so general gamers won't get into it.

Final Fantasy III was initially a mystery to gamers outside of Japan, having only been released on the Famicom in 1990. Since then, Final Fantasy III has been re-released several times; Nintendo DS, Playstation Portable, Wii’s Virtual Console, iOS, Android, and most recently making its way here to Steam. The game’s format and mechanics may feel a bit dated/unusual to those familiar with newer Final Fantasy titles, but I believe that the game still provides a worthwhile playing experience.
My first exposure to this game was the Nintendo DS version, which I picked up used for quite a bargain. That version is a 3D remake of the original Famicom game, and it appears that this PC version stayed loyal to that style. Due to the limited specifications on the Nintendo DS, I always felt that the game was a bit held back in the graphics and sound department. This PC version seems to have given the artwork better treatment, and appears to resemble the PSP version of the game more closely. I was concerned that the graphics would be overly pixelated due to the small resolution on handhelds, but was pleasantly surprised to see that the graphics felt right for PC.
The music, as usual in Final Fantasy titles, is superb. As a remake, they stayed very true to the themes present on the Famicom release. Many of the musical themes fit the mood of the game quite well, allowing the player to enjoy a calm stroll through a town or a hectic boss battle at the end of a dungeon. The sound quality is superb, as well, and doesn’t have the muffled sounds that the DS version provided.
Final Fantasy III’s combat system strays far from the system of its predecessor, and attempts to advance the system that was originally present in the original Final Fantasy. The player has the option to choose from a variety of jobs. As the player advances through the game and completes various quest “checkpoints” (for lack of a better word), additional jobs open up. Some of these jobs which offer a brand new range of healing, magic and utility, while some are simply upgrades to existing jobs. There are over two dozen jobs in total, giving players many chances to experiment. Along with jobs, this is the first Final Fantasy game to introduce summons. So if you’re familiar with summons in later titles such as Shiva and Bahamut, you’ll be right at home.
An immersing story has been an important part of the Final Fantasy franchise in recent years. Going back in time, however, it wasn’t always this way. In Final Fantasy III, the story is notably flat compared to the extended stories present in modern RPG titles. It’s easy to understand, rarely sees plot twists, and has a relatively small cast of characters. It’s nothing spectacular, but it was a step ahead from the two previous entries in the series. Unlike the Famicom Final Fantasy III, however, the characters in this version are given formal names. Despite the limited storytelling, I still feel it’s pleasant; just don't go in expecting a 50 hour long legendary tale.
The difficulty of this game is a bit jarring. The early game starts off quite bearable, giving players the ability to simply auto attack their way through many of the fiends. As the game progresses, the difficulty spikes up considerably. The final dungeons are notoriously difficult due to lack of save points and insufficient materials provided throughout the game. Compared to the difficulty of some modern Final Fantasy titles, the harsh difficulty in this game might turn some people away. But if you can fight through the barrage of random encounters and somehow make it through the dungeon, you’ll be rewarded with quite a sense of accomplishment.
In conclusion, I feel that Final Fantasy III is a worthy purchase for those who wish to revisit the roots of the Final Fantasy franchise, and JRPGs in general. It’s difficult, but rewarding. A worthy game for the name “Final Fantasy.”

Audacious quest: Rescue Zhaneta Gemini. Enigma clause (no living witnesses). Large ship. Warzone. 19 second timer once alarm sounds. How is this even possible?
Take the quest anyway. Fly to the ship and dock at an entrance. Target prisoner is on the other end of the ship, 9 or 10 rooms away plus locked doors. Once I dock, a countdown to a warship attack starts. That's about 15 seconds away. But what's this? The room the prisoner is in, is next to two rooms with windows.
I have a hunch, and pull out without stepping foot past the airlock, causing no alarms. Disengage my pod, and start inching my way over toward the windows from the outside of the ship. Not too close, because normally, windows also act as searchlights, and if you go in range you get seen and exploded. I hover around the side.
15 seconds pass. Enemy warship attacks my target ship. Just as I had hoped, a missile blows open the two windows, negating their searching capability and also turning them into dockable points for my pod. And also starting the 19 second panic alarm before mission failure.
But they're next to each other, and in the chaos of space, my pod latches onto the wrong one. This puts me two rooms away from my target, but with a wall between us. Nope. I back out and detach. A second after I detach, a missile smashes into the window I was in. That rips apart the entire ROOM from the ship, sending it spiralling away into space. Close call. 14 seconds left.
I nudge my pod along the side of the ship, and latch onto the correct window. Pause the game. 11 seconds left. But no guards around! I run in to the first room, then adjoining room, pluck Zhaneta from her bed, and carry her back to the pod. 8 seconds left. Detach. Fly off amidst a shower of missiles and head back to base.
Just another day in the life of a rebel fighter. And there are many more like that, tales of insane deeds performed by legendary heroes in subzero space with no living witnesses to corroborate their story.

I picked this up because I thought it was an interesting concept. After playing for a bit, I realized that it really doesn't live up to the idea in its current form. However, I think there is potentially a very fun game here after some modest rework on the part of the developer. Since I don't like to leave a negative review without some suggestions of how to improve something, here's some thoughts --
1. Classic detective fiction is about the meticulous and patient building of a case. Here, you visit random, unrelated locations and hit the Z button a bunch of times. If a person is murdered, I would expect to be able to visit the crime scene and search for clues there, as well as interrogate potential suspects. I'm curious about the evidence, too. Why would I randomly find fingerprints in a random building? Let's just say that I find a gun at the murder scene. I should be able to take that to a gun shop, and ask the gun shop owner about it. He could say "I think the customer was female." There should also be some red herrings and false leads.
2. I stole from the mob by accident while searching for clues. No warning dialog?
3. In detective fiction, there is also an interplay during interrogations. A well-designed dialog based minigame here would be great. In other words, give the player options of "What do you know about person X..." when talking to people and so on.
4. Everything felt kinda "generic" about the game and case. It would be interesting to have a bunch of different case types, such as finding a missing person, investigating a jewel theft, and so on.
5. Ditch the hunger system. It's a modern city, not a post-apocalyptic battle for survival. Or, optionally, use food as buffs. Likewise, lose the bullet count and add gameplay-based consequences for gun use (wanted level, penalty for killing an innocent, antipathy from people). Lockpicking seems irrelevant, because you can get money and buy more lockpicks. It would be more relevant to have certain areas be off-limits and be opened via dialog with characters, finding a key, or as progression in an investigation.
I think there is a lot of potential here, and I really like the idea of another game in what is really an under-represented genre. It just comes off feeling very hollow and unfinished in its current state, but could be turned into something great with some rethinking of the design. I hope the developer takes some of the other critical reviews to heart and considers incorporating those ideas as well.

TL;DR: One of the worst flight simulators I've every played.
I've been a fan of Flight Simulators ever since I played Microsoft Flight Simulator X back in 2007, and have been playing various simulators ever since.
Aerofly looks decent, has neat graphics, and looked promising. I managed to fly (and land) the Cessna quite easily.
So what's my problem with this game?
I guess my standards are too high. Flight Simulator X had dozens of planes, and allowed me to fly anywhere in the world. aerofly has a much smaller selection of planes and airport, which was disappointing.
The fact that you can break various parts of your plane (mostly the wings) when crashing looks visually good, but it usually makes no sense: if I slam on the ground too hard, my wings shouldn't fall off. I'd expect an explosion, or my plane stopping to work, but having my wings fall off and the rest of my plane rolling around makes no sense at all.
While we're at the subject of crashing, crashing planes is where the physics engine of this game really shows how bad it is: I don't know if you watched Air Crash Investigation or saw footage from real plane crashes, if you would you would see crashing in this game is nothing like that. when I crash in game, my plane is thrown back into the air upside down, falls again and then the game restarts.
The planes in game were too easy to manouver and did not feel right. The controls are extremely senetive and the planes react so quickly as if they are unaffected by gravity, wind or drag. Calling this a simulation is like calling Just Cause 2's flight mechanics a simulation: it's a balant lie.
On the subject of simulation, there's no Air Traffic Control, no failure simulation, no ability to start in a parking lot and drive your plane there, no control over most of the detailed plane subsystems (Compared to other simulators which allowed me to turn off the engine, or cut off one of the fuel tanks, enable navigation radios, or set trim...).
So my bottom line: not really worth 40$ (and I'm starting to think it wasn't worth the 20$ I paid for it when it was on sale).

I always wanted to fly, and I bought aerofly FS a few months before starting real life flying lessons. The idea was to be in a Visual Flight Rules (VFR) airplane and familiarize myself with flying, but skip (unknown) procedural parts. aerofly FS isn’t a full flight simulator like MFSX or X-plane, but to my opinion, it succeeds very well in introducing VFR flying. Flight dynamics are accurate; I spent most in-game time in the Cessna 172 Skyhawk, flying VFR over Switzerland, and landing/taking off at all airstrips. I use real VFR circuit patterns and airspace classification information to add to the experience, and just fly VFR flights from one place to the other. I also do a bit of airwork, e.g. maneuvers (stall recovery, steep turns, slow flight, crosswind landings) and procedures (emergency, circuits), but lack of resistance of joystick/pedals and lack of G-force loadings are not making the experience very close to the real deal. But none of these is the game's fault. In that regard, I miss other AI traffic, radio telephony with ATC, simple procedures (e.g. start the engine, turn on landing lights, VOR navigation), and maybe recording capacities. Few additions are planned, but it is still unclear when and how they will be released. Nevertheless, I love flying & I love aerofly FS. Out.

Hacknet is a pretty entertaining hacking game for those that have an interest to stay long enough or of the genre.
To start, hacknet has a nice flow of events. The story is rather compelling and starts off fast. You are literally thrown into the events right away. The hacking is also somewhat similar to how the events would go in real life (to a degree of course) as some of this stuff is also what real life hackers employ from what I know. There are also interesting and funny parts of this game. At a certain point I remember hacking into a certain system and reading the logs. One of the logs was the top searched terms, and they were all like "Boobs" "Big Boobs" and stuff like that. The music for this game is also pretty good and fitting.
There are bad parts of this game as well. The biggest bad part is when you get hacked and are thrown into a screen without any directions to do anything. I was so confused at that point that I had to look at a guide to know what the hell was going on. Another bad part of this game is that its hard to get back into if you stop playing, as in it's hard to pick back up since some of the things are rather specific and easy to forget if you drop it for some time. Additionally, the game starts off really fast and you will be confused for a bit with all the different commands. I don't know how many times I had to bring up the help and notes. The game really doesn't have a particularly good transition from tutorial to game mode as well. Although you get to practice it a lot because there are a ton of hacking missions.
Overall, pretty good hacking game, but it is more meant for those interested in this genre.
Rating: 7.8/10

(You can also shoot people, pick locks to gain access to more areas, buy things, steal things...) Talking adds suspects to your list and sometimes gives other hints; searching finds equipment, cash and clues. Suspects and clues are randomly generated and are added to your notebook; when you think you have figured out who is the murderer is, track them down and arrest them.
Its very rogue-like-like; each playthrough may last only 5-10 minutes, but you learn more about the game as you play and can level your character up by earning achievement "badges" to get more starting gear and better drops on later games. You don't have to "win" a game to get credit towards levelling up. Over time you learn more about the town and where to find food, gear, best places to talk to people or search for clues etc. Some locations are definitely more useful than others.
Combat can be entirely avoided (you won't be attacked unprovoked unless on hard mode, even then its avoidable) but is frantic and fun when it happens despite the simple interface. Its definitely NOT the focus of the game, you should be talking to people to get a list of suspects and search for clues. There is other stuff to do in the town too - gamble with the mob or steal their loot, raid the vault in the old fort, etc.
The difficulty is entirely player controlled, once you start to level up and figure out where things are, you can start tackling some of the harder achievements and give hard mode a try.
One warning: You should remap the default controls and change X for shoot to another key that you can get to quickly, but not press by accident. S works well. I've killed people by accident when trying to press Z.

Me and my friends got Trove because it was a free game that looked decent and something that we could mess around together on. We're now well and truly addicted. Trove is a game all about grinding, leveling up your character basically the definition of a good MMORPG with other things that you can mess around with. The combat system is great and easy to use also upgrading your character and suchlike is extremely simple (other than gems which may need a little bit of time to figure out) making it accessible to all types of players. There is also a variety of character customisation like mounts, allies, costumes, styles, auras etc. Furthermore now that Mantle of Power has been released Trove has a lot more content and playability meaning that you can spend a long time on this game. The community, trading system and market are also really great allowing you to join/make clubs with your friends and make flux (the ingame currency) by trading or grinding.
However
Although I think that the game is great it does have some cons. For example you have to put A LOT of time into the game to get good unless you spend some money which most people end up doing. The things you can buy are very overpriced for what you can get with them eg. I can make around 300k flux (sounds a lot but in the scheme of things it's decent) by spending £20 on the store by buying some costumes and selling them or make 1,000,000 by trading things with other people. Also the servers are very faulty for example on the reset of shadow towers day it can take up to 5 minutes just to get through a portal angering everybody in game and seeing as Trion/Glyph has enough money I really don't understand why they don't upgrade them because it's a pain for everybody.
All in all, I think Trove is a really good game with a few faults that anybody can get into if they just put enough time into it and although you may stop for a couple of weeks when the grinding gets too much you'll (or me anyway) will always find yourself falling back into it and having even more fun than before.

So, I decided to dress up my review to make it easier to read as its a bit cluttered. As a long time fan of the Final Fantasy Series, I didn't get a chance to play FFIII till way later on an Emulator program on my PC. While I liked it immediately I lost interest after a few days because of the NES styled graphics.  With THIS release, however, the modern player will have a more enjoyable experience than with previous installments. It has improved graphics (well, DS level but definitely better than the NES), monsters are animated, music is a bit less annoying than the .midi's use to be and the way the cutscenes play out are vastly improved over their original versions.
FFIII is the story of the Onion Knight, the reimergance of the Warriors of Light and the birth of Final Fantasy's Job Class System. The story is good, although the cast seems a bit "thrown together", it's really the mechanics and nostalgia that makes FFIII worth the buy. Random battles, old fashioned grinding (yes, it was popular before WoW and EQ) and FF canon like Moogles (Complete with a lackluster MogNet), Chocobo's, everyones favorite Mechanic / Airship Captain; Cid and the oddest overworld map on any FF game, ever.
Overall, even as a slight fan of Mystic Quest (loved the dungeon music) and with my distaste with FFII and XI, FIII still maintains its place HIGH on my list of favoritsm for the FF Franchise. Although, FFIV will always be my favorite of the older series and XIII for the later series. If you've never played it yet but are a fan of the series, a young'un wanting a taste of nostalgic old school gaming or just someone with $15 to blow; come and relive a classic and get ready to have the level up theme stuck in your head for weeks!

Final Fantasy III has seen many make-overs, and this one is pretty much a port of the one on the DS with just a bigger resolution. But still, if you're a fan of Final Fantasy or love JRPG's, then you should still pick this up, especially if you haven't played this game already.
Here's a quick look video so you can see for yourself what this game is like. But if you'd rather have a simple pros/cons/unmentionables list of the game, continue below.
As promised, the pros and cons breakdown.
+Good, relaxing music. FF has always been good about this.
+The ability to customize your party to your playstyle with the flexible job system. Anybody can be anything. Why not girl warriors and guy white mages? Break those stereotypes!
+Strategic, turn-based combat. Some may prefer action, but I count this as a plus because you play at your own pace and the battles can be close sometimes.
+Great exploration. There's hidden passages to treasure, optional dungeons, and mazes to loot littered everywhere, even at the beginning of the game. Did I mention you get an airship early on?
+You can quick save anywhere. Super handy for any RPG and a person always on the go.
?Because of the exploration, you can wander into places you're grossly unprepared for and get stomped into the ground.
?The story is your typical "you're the chosen one to save the world and help people along the way." I'm not really bothered by it, but some people who want something different may be turned off by it.
-No options menu besides changing resolution. Square-Enix actually makes really good option menus for PC, so I was a little sad to see that there wasn't even AA to get rid of some of the jaggies.
-Because this is an old port, though a good one, the graphics aren't exactly breath-taking like the opening CG cutsceen. Personally I don't care since the good gameplay matters to me over graphics, but a lot of people get turned off by dated graphics unfortunately, even more so when they expect more from Square-enix.
-It's pricey for what it is. But that's the FF brand for you.
-No voice acting. While not the end of the world, it certainly does help immerse you into the world.
Overall, it's a really good game, and it's nice to have an old-school RPG every now and again. Remember that childhood, my friends. Remember it.

You would think that such a peaceful game would be less exciting than one filled with epic battles, but farming and socializing have never been so engaging.  Indeed, what little combat this game has is simplistic, which allows one to focus on what really matters: getting to know the people of Pelican Town.  Aside from the social aspect, which sees the player interact with all manner of likeable and multi-layered characters, you must also make a living by farming, mining, foraging, and fishing in a world filled with magic.  It becomes important to keep track of the seasons and plan ahead.
Among the best things about the farming in Stardew Valley is that it's all done by hand, as opposed to the automation you'll find in many such games.  I've never really liked making automated farms in games unless the automation mechanics are exceptionally well-designed, and this game's hands-on farming is not only refreshing, but also brilliantly thought out.
I'd love to say more, but you really should experience Stardew Valley for yourself; the Overwhelmingly Positive reviews aren't lying.  Stardew Valley is a game I can recommend to almost anyone.

For a free game, it's not that bad. I only recommend it because it's free, otherwise I woudln't even bother. It used to be owned by a different group, but it was bought out by Kabam, which is known for for their terrible mobile phone games. Since then, they have brought their typical "free game" money making tactics into the game to try and make a profit. While I believe you can still find everything via drop, there is no telling what alterations they may have made to the game to hamper that ability. The previous group had something similar, but not to the same extent. But let's talk about the game itself.
The game is rendered in nice animated pixil art. Makes the game playable on low end machines, so if you are limted by a games requirements, this is a good thing. It has a retro feel, so nothing to argue about there.
The gameplay is based off a permadeath system and features several classes to pick from, all of which have their own special ability and equipment that they can use. The game requires that certain classes reach a certain level before you can unlock others, which is neat. However, the classes are unbalanced, some being a lot better than others. Luckly it's not a PvP game, otherwise this would be a problem. As fate would have it, you need to pay to be able to have more than one character at a time, and in order to make a new one, your old character has to die. Annoying, but since characters reach LV. 20 (LV. Cap) rather quickly (matter of a few hours), it's not a big deal.
The in-game currency is fame, which you attain every time a character dies, and you  only get a good amount by having a character last a long time, and it gathers over time. Unfortunately, you can hardly buy jack with fame, as the only items anyone cares about are the ones that require actual money to purchase.
The game can be a little difficult later on because there are plenty of mobs that'll require you to have friends, which ups the ante for taking them on. The lower level stuff is a cake walk even for a child, and basically stays that way till nearly the end of your leveling, but later on, the mobs can be overwhelming if you've yet to find good gear.  The goal of the game is basically for everyone to kill a specific list of monsters, and once done, everyone is transfered to the boss dungeon. Lots of people die here, but it's fun to raid a boss dungeon with 30 other people at once. Often more.
Other than that, it's not much more. It's something I would play if I were bored and had nothing to do, which I do. So, do as you please. Free is free.

This game got a lot of bad press, but at this point (as of Patch 5), I can finally recommend it. Patch 5 finally fixed the remaining issues I had (SLI issues with water flickering and a few crash bugs). Game is running fine for me at this point, and, overall, it's a fun addition to the franchise.
Pros:
-The new movement system is much smoother than in previous editions, once you get used to it you can scale buildings, up, down, sideways, and diagonal, and make some impressive leaps, very fluidly
-Graphis are pretty impressive
-The main story mission is of a decent length, and draws you in
-Player equipment customization (armor) is back to affecting stats, plus you can wear an outfit over the top
-Reasonably interesting final boss fight, but you can cheese it
-Additional game modes are interesting
-Progress in companion app is finally not required to access chests (some chests would have taken forever to get)
-The (too few) cities are interesting and well mapped
-There's only one property you can buy and improve
Cons:
-The ending to the main story sucks and is a letdown on so many levels, the Dead Kings DLC helps with that somewhat, but, avoiding spoilers, the biggest thing that made the ending suck doesn't change (and can't change as it's pretty final what happens)
-No ships, hunting, crafting ?!?!
-Most of the armors, and the pants, look pretty cheesy, even if themed according to the period; prowler armor is decent though
-No recruiting and training up Assassin's in-game, it's all handled through the companion app; which means you can't access them in-game to help with missions
-Feels like a much smaller world than previous titles
All in all it's a good addition, if there would have been naval combat, assassins in-game, crafting, and more opportunity to explore (and no bugs at launch), and to own property, it would have been one of the best, as it is, I put it somewhere around Assassin's Creed 2. Black Flag is still the best game in the series to me, but I haven't played Rogue yet.

Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like turn-based RPG featuring perma-death. Throughout the game you will send a party of four into randomly generated dungeons where they will hunt for treasure, slay monsters and complete objectives. From a first glance each unit looks rather simple to understand, only having 8 potential abilities and only 4 abilities usable in a battle, however, with the inclusion of positioning and class-restrictive skills the complexity lies in how you set up your party. Each class feels viable and figuring out how to synergise your party leads to very satisfying gameplay.
This game is by no means easy, with the inclusion of perma-death and the RNG inherent in all RPGs you are bound to lose many heroes through your adventure, often leaving you with a bitter feeling as a lot of the time what happens is out of your control. Unlucky crits and status affects will claim many lives before you can do anything and with the low health-pool compared to the high damage output of the enemy if a hero is focused they can die within a single round of combat.
The art style is beautiful and fitting with the tone of this game, everything looks ugly or corrupt and the music keeps to this concept. The narrartor who is present throughout the game creates a cinematic atmosphere whilst you play, often spouting dramatic quotes whenever something significant happens in battle. Together these aspects are really what raise Darkest Dungeon above other turn-based RPGs.
Finally I must discuss the modding community, there are plenty of mods to keep you playing this game, from hero reskins and new classes to overhall mods like Pitch Black Dungeon. Many of these mods are so well made that they are indistinguishable from the base game and result in endless stream of content to play.
Overall I would recommend this game, whilst the gameplay may seem unfair at times, once you understand how each class functions both alone and with the party the game becomes infinitely more enjoyable.

The game is extremely simplistic and, despite being part of the "community choice: roguelike" bundle, it is not a roguelike by any stretch of the imagination (if this is a roguelike, then Pitfall! is a roguelike).
You basically click locations on a static map and walk across the screen mashing the Z key like a little monkey (well, okay, mashing it will make your character get "hungry" but whatever, food is easily acquired from the same three or four locations and money flows like rain). You are rewarded with either "suspects" (if you mash the Z key on top of a NPC and get lucky) or "clues" (if you mash the Z key on top of a background element and get lucky). There's really no rhyme or reason to the "clues", each one exists as a mere token to narrow down which suspect is the killer - those expecting to piece together a mystery-puzzle on their own will be gravely disappointed. For instance, finding a leather wallet will mean the crook is either a civilian or a cop, but not a mobster. Each new game picks a random culprit and random list of suspects with random professions / affiliations, and some games are going to be unsolvable save through luck (there may be two Male Artists with the Mob, for instance).
I was pretty disappointed by how formulaic and - moreover - simplistic the game turned out to be, but for some reason it's strangely addictive - possibly because it doesn't really demand too much of the player. There's no small text to squint over, it doesn't demand lightning reactions or pinpoint hand-eye precision. Games resolve themselves in about ten minutes or so, so it's hardly a timesink either (well, unless you want to unlock the costumes and badges (costumes are self-explanatory, badges give you boosts to ammo/lockpicks/money/hunger-level when starting out). These unlocks are retar­dedly "priced", requiring literal DAYS of constant Z-mashing to earn enough stats to eventually unlock).
It's definitely not worth full-price, hence the "no" recommendation, but for $2 or so you could do a lot worse. Just don't pay $7.00 for it, because at that rate it really is a total ripoff.

This is an amazing game that is very similar to Hotline Miami in terms of the actual gameplay. Where it differentiates itself, however, is in the tactics department. At any moment in Heat Signature you can pause the live gameplay and make an educated decision regarding your next move or action. This take on game tactics is further improved by the vast amount of options at your disposal during that pause in gameplay.
For example you could find yourself assaulted by two guards, one of which has just fired a shot at you. You could: 1) Use an item that swaps places with that guard, which will kill him with his own bullet and then dispose of the second guard while he is confused. 2) Teleport behind the shooting guard and knock him out with a wrench then fire a shot at the second guard before he figures out what is happening. 3) Use an item to slow down time then side step the bullet and dispose of each of the guards with your own gun. These are just three options which come to mind, but there are countless other ways to handle this specific situation.
The vast amount of variables and options create an amazing science fiction themed toy box for you to play around in for countless hours. I was a participant in a beta for this game and have clocked many hours in addition to my current steam counter.
This game has a ton of content for the value and if you're a fan of the gameplay of Hotline Miami, you should not be disappointed.

Noir Syndrome isn't a terrible game, but it lacks in-depth gameplay. In this game, you solve cases by asking questions and finding clues, but the way you do so is redundant. How do you find clues? Rather than actually looking for a clue, you just press the 'Z' button whenever you stand near something interactable and hope you get lucky enough to get a clue. In other words, you don't find clues in this game; you just wait until the game decides to hand you a clue. How do you get information out of people? The same exact way. Press 'Z' and hope they give you information. No story, no dialogue options, just a 'Z' button. A successful detective game needs to make the player feel like they are actually solving the case themselves. Make them find the clues; make them interrogate suspects. Don't reduce everything a good detective game needs to one simple button. This game is playable, but the shallow gameplay will ultimately lead you to let the game sit in your library untouched for a long time.

It is hard to tell whether Blood II is good or bad at all. It is a little of both, with respect to the time it was created. It would not be fair to compare it to current games, of course, but even in comparison to games of the same era it stands back a little. There is no other game I can remember where the opponents are
stupid. One can hardly call that "AI". Even a Pacman ghost has more AI than the Cabalco zombies. Rendered cutscenes are embarrassing at best, and the storyline is more than questionable. On the other hand, the game features nice graphics and effects, and has some funny moments. Somehow, once in a while, playing it again is actually quite fun. But eventually I "grew" up with that game and it brings back memories. That is the only reason to replay at all.
I certainly would not recommend the game to anyone who isn't already familiar with the Blood gameset. And now for the main reason why I cannot recommend the game at all: it is technically close to unusable.
Blood II used to become unstable even back in the old days if you owned a PC "too powerful". Apparently the developers have put their engine timing a little on the cheap side, and nothing has been changed about this at all to make it more compatible to current platforms. Actually you will buy the same binaries that were on the original game CD back in 1998! The Steam client does not even have to be running so the binaries obviously literally weren't changed a bit. And you better don't use the Steam client to launch the game at all becuase it is usually not running in an Admin context, so it will not apply compatibility mode which is a mere joke... the game will crash almost instantly.
While on some machines (including mine) there is still a chance to get it working (e.g. by setting the compatibility mode to XP SP3 and running the game as Administrator directly from the installation folder), you should anticipate at least one crash in 10 minutes of gameplay at random times, so remember to save frequently...
frequently.
So this is a really bad strategy for remarketing. I would expect a software provider to do what is necessary to restore compatibility to current hardware before a game goes for sale. If I had known in advance, I could just have used the Blood II CD that I already owned (purchased 1999!).
Steam did a nice job getting Duke3D running thanks to excellent DosBox integration. The Blood I package is already a bit screwed up because no link is created to run the setup.exe you need to map keys, set video resolution etc... if you are not familiar with DosBox, you won't get very happy. Seems to me they are just squeezing some dollars out of reminiscent fools like me without actually caring much about the quality delivered. Too bad. So the best experience for these old games is running them on the machine they were built for, if you still have one that works.

Noir Syndrome is a simple crime-solving game, but a successfully addicting one.  One game takes roughly 10 minutes to play, so you'll find yourself playing a lot and saying, "Just one more time."  Admittedly there isn't much variability in the clues you find, but you still need to gather a majority of them in order to nail down the culprit.  There are a number of locations to visit in the city, each with a different 2-D atmosphere of its own.
The bonus challenges in each case provide an extra level of depth, and you may sometimes find yourself completely abandoning the main task just to get it done.  The openness of the game is refreshing.  For something short and simple, you never feel hemmed in by restrictions.  If you want to be a criminal instead of solving the case, go ahead.
For additional replay value, there are 30 in-game badges earned by accomplishing certain tasks.  Every 3 badges increases your Detective Level which confers permanent bonuses on future playthroughs.  Additionally, you can collect clothing scraps to unlock new costumes.  The costumes themselves are purely cosmetic with no actual benefits, and many of them aren't very impressive, but completionists will want to get them all.
One last note: If you are a "graphics snob" then stay away.  The game is meant to harken back to 2-D pixelated games of yesteryear, so some modern gamers may be put off by that.

The Walking Dead is an excellent interactive story with believable characters, beautiful artwork, voice acting and music, and a powerful emotional impact.
There are some puzzles to solve and zombies to kill, but mostly the game involves deciding what to do or say to the other characters during time-limited interactions that are often filled with tension. These decisions make the story feel like it is your own, allowing you to shape Lee and his relationship with Clementine and the other characters, and I felt this resulted in it having more of an impact on me than if I had watched it on TV.
The characters are well developed and felt real, many becoming people for whom I cared (and still think about) and it hurt to see them suffer during what were intense and sometimes devastating scenes. Oftentimes I found myself questioning my decisions, regardless of how justifiable they seemed. But while the story is pretty grim at times, there are touching moments as well, particularly during the interactions with Clementine, who is the heart and soul of the game.
Expect to get around 2-4 hours per episode depending if you inspect everything and exhaust all dialogue options. I enjoyed The Walking Dead, and it is easily one of the best games I have played.

First off:  if you're looking for a game with action... or direct control of anything, really, then please find a different game - this one is not for you.  In fact - don't consider Dinner Date to be a game - instead, it's a work of short fiction.
With that out of the way:  Dinner Date is a short story (~20 minute) consisting of a single plot thread that you seemingly have little (no?) control over.  Instead, which the story plays out you play the part of the characters conciousness, and exert minor control of what he does while he waits for his date to show up to dinner.  It's all a bit 'Being John Malkovich', which is pretty neat.
The game - sort of like 'Gone Home' - is an interesting experiment in how a story can be told in an interactive medium, and for that it should be applauded.  If you're a fan of experiemntal game development, and especially of story-driven experiences, then it's well worth a few dollars to see what has been created here.
