It's not a horrible game so don't take anything that I write as harsh, only as my observations.  Unfortunately to write the review, one has to pick either 'recommend' or 'not recommend' so I have to choose 'not recommend' at this time.
The missions are mundane and unchallenging.  Once a vehicle has shields/regen/batteries (as well as weapons of course), I don't think I ever took any damage.
The construction is glitchy.  When attempting to attach an item onto a vehicle, it can go through the vehicle and attach to the bottom.  Then, the vehicle starts 'hopping around' making it difficult to retrieve the last item place.
I also hope you like disassembling/reassembling the same vehicle repeatedly to charge batteries (until you can level enough to get the remote recharging items), and then I hope you like setting idle waiting for the batteries to recharge.
If you don't play full screen, then you may be missing some vital information to gameplay... like how much currency you currently have.
What I would like to see:
1) Give the player access to the parts collector (USB?) and paintbrush utility from the beginning of the game.
2) Allow players to 'snapshot' a base to deploy them.  Even if this requires a secondary item storage pool to reserve the items...   or even the snapshot can be considered a separate item with all the items already combined.
3) Better resource pickup.  I found that it was often faster for me to manually grab the resource with the mouse and drop it onto the vehicle than wait for it to realize the resource was there.
4) Why am I seeing pop-up advertisements in a game for which I paid?  No.  You can put that on the start page if you want, but don't have it popping up in the game.
5) How about a 'map'?  The radar has 'N' on it  but the user needs the map coordinates to get back to that location.  It could be your base if you have driven a large distance, but it could be something like a geyser that has no markings on the radar.

Sadly, this is a game that is pretty fun at first, but I can tell that it's going to quickly slip away into complete irrelevance.
Main issue is the matchmaking. Every player has their own MMR or MatchMaking Rating tied to how well they do, generally increasing for wins and/or good performance and decreasing for losses and/or poor performance in matches. I guess it's vaguely similar to the ELO ratings of Chess or something, but applied to a 5v5 system (and that has never, EVER worked)
The major problem is that the player pool is just not big enough for their MMR system ... at peak hours you're hitting some 1.2k players, which is okay, but at all other times maybe 250 players max. In such situations, you're unlikely to find players even remotely close to your rating. Up to the 800s, I was generally being matched to players in the 400-900 range, but once I went over 800 I started getting consistently matched vs players with 1,500 - 2,000 ratings. There simply are not enough players to find opponents and teammates who are close to my own rating, I guess.
I had quite a few friends who were willing to give this game a chance at my recommendation, but it turned into a disaster because of MMR. Being brand new to the game, they fell to the 400s of MMR (starting base value is 500), while I was in the 800s. Result: they were being consistently put in games with players who were way more experienced and skilled in the game, and it killed it for them. Combine that with the incredibly slow rate at which you unlock new ships, and they quickly lost interest, and I found myself just playing this game alone.
What's especially sad is that the team values are often not even close. Often times I'd see values like Team A MMR: 4,000, Team B MMR: 4,600. What?
Speaking of unlocks, someone had the idea that crew unlocks should be entirely based on chance. As in, you pay something like 135,000 credits (which is more than some of the actual ships in the game) to get a RANDOM SPIN at a crew unlock for your ship ... however, you routinely land on characters you already have. Getting a redundant roll like this gives you 1,500 DNA. If you have 18,000 DNA, you can unlock a specific character for use. Go back and look at those numbers, and factor in that for an average 20-30 minute game that you win, you're going to make something like 10,000-15,000 credits. The math sucks, especially since it's random chance.
Feel free to look at 'how to build your crew' guides in the steam guides section for this game, and it will become obvious that this is pretty important. There are crew combinations that are just flat-out superior to the basic stuff you start with.
A quick list of other problems:
- typical moba community. Have fun with that.
- Certain ships that are completely obsolete and useless.
- Snails pace at reworking said obsolete ships.
- Very slow unlocking process. Unlocking all the alternate weapons on some ships costs 2x the cost of buying the ship in the first place. Also the crew problems.
- Typical obscene prices for paid content, though I will say some of the starter packs are good.
- I have had team matchmaking take 30 mins to NOT find us a game, at which point my friends gave up and quit.
Too bad, it coulda been a contender.

This is an amazing game that is very similar to Hotline Miami in terms of the actual gameplay. Where it differentiates itself, however, is in the tactics department. At any moment in Heat Signature you can pause the live gameplay and make an educated decision regarding your next move or action. This take on game tactics is further improved by the vast amount of options at your disposal during that pause in gameplay.
For example you could find yourself assaulted by two guards, one of which has just fired a shot at you. You could: 1) Use an item that swaps places with that guard, which will kill him with his own bullet and then dispose of the second guard while he is confused. 2) Teleport behind the shooting guard and knock him out with a wrench then fire a shot at the second guard before he figures out what is happening. 3) Use an item to slow down time then side step the bullet and dispose of each of the guards with your own gun. These are just three options which come to mind, but there are countless other ways to handle this specific situation.
The vast amount of variables and options create an amazing science fiction themed toy box for you to play around in for countless hours. I was a participant in a beta for this game and have clocked many hours in addition to my current steam counter.
This game has a ton of content for the value and if you're a fan of the gameplay of Hotline Miami, you should not be disappointed.

Darkest Dungeon is a rogue-like turn-based RPG featuring perma-death. Throughout the game you will send a party of four into randomly generated dungeons where they will hunt for treasure, slay monsters and complete objectives. From a first glance each unit looks rather simple to understand, only having 8 potential abilities and only 4 abilities usable in a battle, however, with the inclusion of positioning and class-restrictive skills the complexity lies in how you set up your party. Each class feels viable and figuring out how to synergise your party leads to very satisfying gameplay.
This game is by no means easy, with the inclusion of perma-death and the RNG inherent in all RPGs you are bound to lose many heroes through your adventure, often leaving you with a bitter feeling as a lot of the time what happens is out of your control. Unlucky crits and status affects will claim many lives before you can do anything and with the low health-pool compared to the high damage output of the enemy if a hero is focused they can die within a single round of combat.
The art style is beautiful and fitting with the tone of this game, everything looks ugly or corrupt and the music keeps to this concept. The narrartor who is present throughout the game creates a cinematic atmosphere whilst you play, often spouting dramatic quotes whenever something significant happens in battle. Together these aspects are really what raise Darkest Dungeon above other turn-based RPGs.
Finally I must discuss the modding community, there are plenty of mods to keep you playing this game, from hero reskins and new classes to overhall mods like Pitch Black Dungeon. Many of these mods are so well made that they are indistinguishable from the base game and result in endless stream of content to play.
Overall I would recommend this game, whilst the gameplay may seem unfair at times, once you understand how each class functions both alone and with the party the game becomes infinitely more enjoyable.

Good. Difficult. Good.
Seriously though, it has great atmosphere, and it is an interesting game to play, but it can snowball into a serious problem if you let it. It's incredibly easy not to buy the correct things in the provisioning stage of the quest and end up with several severly disadvantaged characters. If you don't wish to play a game that is going to occasionally (read: frequently) bone your characters and take your money, ensuring that you never have anything to progress further in the game... is it obvious I haven't beaten this? All of its difficulty just contributes to the theme of despair and grimness. Its what happens when you step in to the kind of world like you might find in H.P. Lovecraft or gothic fantasy, and the rng dice here do exactly what I expect them to do to me in real life, which is to say screw me and you every which way. It's difficulty that is generated by dice rolls, so if you can't stand weighted dice rolling against you, sorry bro, there's not a lot of gud that you can get to.
Gameplay is interesting in that it comes off a bit like a D&D where you choose 4 characters who line up and go through a dungeon, encountering hazards, obstacles and random/staged encounters. Combat is made up of trying to arrange your 4 people in optimum placement so they can use the 4 abilities that you can choose for each character, which can only be used in certain positions in the lineup, (put the arbalest in the back, put the tank in front, find a place for the other two you take.) Your abilities are abilities: there is no specific "basic attack" but one of your abilities will probably do damage. There are abilities that buff, debuff, heal, damage, and relocate certain things you fight in their lineup. If you want advice for combat, quoting the game itself (or paraphrasing, i could be getting some words wrong,) "great is the weapon that cuts on its own." Disease and bleed effects are DOT attacks and you should use them. Always. As often as possible. Always.
While adventuring, it is possible to recieve perks and flaws that can be gotten rid of through buildings in town; you upgrade these with items you collect while adventuring. You will also collect items to equip to your character, but the rub is none of these are weapons or armor, you have to upgrade those in the afore-mentioned buildings in town. You also train abilities, and upgrade your roster. I may have just been bad, but I had a LOT of difficulty doing a very good job upgrading these in to any real use sometimes, so if you play I will suggest you not expect to upgrade fast or well, this is a journey, and the destination is one you crawl through hell (possibly literally) for.
Finally I would like to say a few words about the classes: they are all fitting and well constructed. The abomonation, the leper, the occultist, the grave robber are all amazing. The other classes all have their functions and fulfill them admirably. Just for the love of god do not play the antiquarian, I cannot say enough bad things about it, a buffer that cannot even do that one job it was created for.
All in all it's a fun game to journey through, but if you can't handle some lost time put into a now dead character, I'd suggest going somewhere else.

"Hotline Miami in the ships from FTL with the pause mechanic from Transistor." -- not my words, but a solid nutshell description of what to expect from Heat Signature.
I'd put Heat Signature firmly in the Roguelite bucket - your inventory, loot, missions, and targets are all procedurally generated, but it does a great job of letting you play a roguelike in a larger metagame that still retains and rewards your progress.
When you first start playing Heat Signature, it can feel a little plain. You have your silent melee attacks, your loud ranged attacks, and maybe a Key Cloner to help you get through locked doors. Your primary goal on a given ship is often just to find and murder (ok, or knock out) the Pilot so that damn alarm will go off. You may spend a good chunk of time in space, remote-controlling your pod to come rescue you after some goon tossed you out an airlock. You learn the value of the Offworld Angel custom pod.
The middle of the game gets weird and a little challenging -- you find tools like Swappers and Subverters and you're not sure quite how to use them. Guards start showing up with personal shields and heat sensors and teleporters - not to mention there are four or five of them in one room. It's here, though, that one of the persistent-progress mechanics comes in super handy: Liberations and their accompanying Defector Missions. These are one-off, retryable missions that task you with accomplishing an objective in a large, well-populated ship with a very limited set of equipment. When you start a map with nothing but a shortblade and a self-recharging Visitor, things get interesting and you learn a whole lot very quickly.
And that leads you into the end game, where I'm just arriving. The first time you unlock one of your four mercenaries' personal missions, there's a good chance you won't be ready for it - you won't have the gear, or the experience, or simply the confidence to take it on. So you switch to a new merc and do it again - liberating more stations, unlocking new items at the shop, and learning more about how the game works and what you can get away with. You figure out guard behavior. You're swapping equipment mid-fight to maximize your moment-to-moment effectiveness. You learn that sometimes, blowing out a window or blowing up a compartment is something to do intentionally, not just by accident.
And maybe, just maybe, you'll finally rescue your idiot partner who got captured by Sovereign in your first hour of playing.

I bought this game not really knowing what to expect of it but it seemed interesting enough to pick up on a sale.
It's definitely one of the most unique games I have ever played.
I assume that some people won't really enjoy this game because of the gameplay mechanics, the amount of reading and lack of visual content, but I highly enjoyed it.
In case you are worried about it being complicated due to the use of UNIX commands as the main playing tool, I can assure you that there is no reason for that.
I had absolutely 0 prior knowledge of any commands, but the game explains it in an easy to follow way and it doesn't take long to figure it out and get used to it. If you forget commands again, after a longer pause of not playing the game for example, you can always type in help and get a list of the most essential commands again.
While definitely an unusual gameplay mechanic it serves this game really well, as it makes you feel like a "real hacker", typing away on your keyboard and cracking those firewalls and proxys and ports and...
The story is interesting and captivating as well and on top of that there are a lot of funny things hidden on the computers you're hacking. It's definitely worth looking around a little bit instead of just focusing on finding the information needed to progress in the main story.
So summed up, a very unique and enjoyable game, but probably not for everyone.

Well If read this, then you properbly already know Xcom series and how to play this turnbased strategy game.
But be aware this game work in a little different way.
On the big world map you now have a flying base from start-end in the game. You fly from country to country setting up radio towers to earn funds for your operation of xcom. What is pretty cool is that everytime you start a new game then everything is random so the replay value is fantastic, also the battles never play out excactly like last time, since the enemys are also random selected depending on your tech level and how far you are in the campaign.
You will without a doubt encounter enemys you already know from the series, but there are also some new ones that you love or hate.  ( properbly hate since they kill your men he he )
All in all you will fly arround the map all the time completing random missions that variate from capture vip, to protect resistance HQ against enemy raid..  Sometimes you also get special missions that can alter the course of the campaign. Example you get 3 missions to choose from that all effect what you get out of it different.
Example do you want a scientist in reward, you want money, or maybe you want that a hidden event will not happen.
Be aware the game take a little time to understand how the new features work and how you move arround on the tactical world map, but once you learn the rules of the game and so on then it is actual pretty good if not excellent.
The game AI i think is pretty good and is indeed a challenge. They will assult/run away or maybe flank you.
The shooting animation and detail of the graphics are excellent as well.
As you know the game is all about research and getting better gear to combat the aliens, and well you are in for a long journey.. There are allot of tech, and in this new xcom game you can even put extra gadjets on your weapons so they become more powerfull or precise.. Why not give you soldiers some armour that if enemy try to thouch you set them on fire... quite handy when one of the anoying snake aliens want to cuddle with you.
I recommend that your first campaign will be the most easy level, even if you are experienced.. The game is quite tough, and there it take a little time to learn how the new game work.
Well what are you waiting for, BUY IT..... 10/10.

The Most Important achievements in Video Game History
Wolfenstein and Doom Created the basic of the first person gaming experience.
Opening doors and searching for key became the standard for the genre it self. (Quake, Duke 3d, Shadow warrior ect)
But on November 8, 1998 Half Life Change everything. It was no longer about searching for keys it became more about A First Person Narrative that didn't exist before in the gaming industry. There was no cut sceen only direct contact whit the environment and caracters that you encounterd. It was a personal story about crowbars, jumping, crawling in vent and survival. The user/player was Gordon freeman, you have a PHD in theoretical physics, you blew up the microwave of you colleague and  yes you brought chaos at Black Mesa, before the even began.
It was a Daring Aproache but one that paid off, it was a changing point in the FPS genre and viewed by many has one of the Best Video Game ever made.
In this day and age The FPS Genre is the Cow Milk of the industry and game like Half Life are Rare and are not the standart of the Gaming industry but they should be.
10/10: Verdict: A MasterPiece
There is no reason for me to convice you to play this game in 2015 but if you like First person shooters and you did not play this game, then Grab your Crowbars and enjoy this Masterpiece.
Ps: If you think that the Graphics are Outdated then you are in Luck there are excellent mods that update the visuals.
Mod DB will be your friend.

Pro's:
+Amazing character personalites.
+Amazing amount of choices you can make.
+Very emotional at times.
+Good music and background sounds and sound effects in general.
+Good amount of interactivity.
+Combat system, for the game that it is, is good.
+The way the series are played out, except for Episode 1, I will get into more detail about that at the bottom of this review.
+The artstyle is amazing, it does not really play that big of a role in this game considering what it is, but when you do reflect of the look on the game, you wont say anything negative on it.
+Amazing ending.
+Very good story.
Con's:
-Horrible menu, both graphics and how limited it is.
-Can't skip end credits of each episode.
-Many bugs during cut scenes/when you're having a conversation, for example people talk over each other the captions lap over or are not correct. This does not happen often but... often enough for it to be noticed.
-Horrible graphics of the faces of zombies, very pixelated, seems to be one of the things the developers spent the least amount of attention on, which is kind of weird.
-DLC is not worth the money for the amount of content you get, I only recommend the DLC to anyone who is a die hard fan of this game.
-Text in the menu and when you start the game is quite clearly pixalted in the edges, could've been smoother.
-Extremely limited options menu. Extremely limited.
But, for the me the pros outweigh the cons heavily, very heavily which is why I give the game 10/10.
Okay, about the Episode 1 thing, it's good, of course, but it doesn't.. I don't know how to explain it but it is not as good as any of the other Episodes, far from it. But you have to of course remember it is a lead up to the rest of the game.
Comparing this game to Life is Strange, I like Life is Strange better simply because of the impact(emotionally) of that game.
Life is Strange made me cry where tears would run down my face every Episode, this game did not.
I am a very emotional person and this game made me only cry during the ending of Episode 5.
Of course it made me feel sad and emotional throughout the whole game but only tears during Episode 5.
A lot of people, including myself, seek tears and emotion out of games like these, this one of course holds up to the that but maybe not up to the standard of some people, but that does not hold the game back.

I would really like to recommend this game but I cannot. For a few reasons. I will start with the pros and end with the cons.
Pros.
Great gameplay in regards to battles and using tactics to push, pull or defend positions and take bases.
Artwork is pretty nice.
Its a space game with ships you can chose from and pilot.
Its multiplayer.
Its free.
I have not noticed anything that you can only get with real money that influences stats or gameplay.
You have a decent choice of starting ships to learn from and pilot.
Cons.
Severely lacks in ship customization and item choices to retrofit your ships with.
Severely lacks in mission rewards.
Severely lacks in entertainment value over a long period of time.
RNG loot chests for your daily mission reward. This could mean if you have bad luck, it will take you forever to get something even remotely useful. For instance, I have only gotten DNA and some credits from chests... numerous chests.
Huge grindfest and unbalanced match maker.
Leveling seems to take exponentially longer with each level up.
Lacks players and battles seem to always be mostly similar.
FPS is pretty bad even on lowest graphics, but this is probably due to my CPU. I am getting constant 15 fps in this game.
I will update my review if things change and or I decide to play more and get further revelations.

Great idea, let down by poor A.I, lack of long term vision, and heavy reliance on team play (people do not help/support each other enough).
Matchmaking is terrible (partially due to lack of player base), often pitting you against much higher ranked players with better ships/weapons ( if you actually ever get to find a match without someone disconnecting )
Most annoying was the downtime when you are killed, it starts with about 20 seconds, but quickly increases to 1 minute as the game progresses, leaving me to ponder about other games, which did not punish me for being cannon fodder for the higher ranks.
Graphics are great, and the designs well thought out, with the ship design variants a big plus.
Map designs are ok (only a couple in PVP) but quickly become dull as you rinse and repeat your way up the grind ladder.
Background music and weapon noises are on par with other space games, but I quickly became annoyed with my crews constant background chatter, only to end up turning voice levels to zero.
Controls are great, I was expertly moving my ship behind cover within minutes, floating like a butterfly around my chosen targets.
Sadly, the bones of the game are solid, but left me thinking about all its potential.
5/10

I played this a game quite a bit years ago i.e. when it first came in 1998. I actually started off with the demo. Yes I did play it today and it still the same I've clocked multiple times so I know the game well. The game is okay but nothing special, it disappointing unfortunately.
Okay yes it is sequel to Blood. However I really don't think the game is as good. I think that because of the standard of 3D games at the time i.e. low poly models that sort of thing, making the transition to 3D didn't really benefit the blood series of games. In fact if you don't count 'Nightmare levels' expansion for this. This was the last blood game. And personally I think it that's they tried to do it in 3D to early on. The first game in 2D actually looks better than this. Just compare the first level of game to each. The first Blood had Caleb rising from the  grave in a cool mortuary and traversing through a funeral parlour. Blood II has you walking down the carriages of a train. It cannot get more corridor like and linear, and that level only goes for about one minute if you just run down it. Yes the textures in the first game are pixelly but you actually see the detail such as text clearly. In blood II textures look like a painting whose colours have run because the canvas was soaked in water; everything is a blurred smear. The models in Blood II look so much worse than the 2D sprites in the original game. Compare the Tchernobog 3D model in Blood II you find in the museum to the 2D version you find at the end of Blood. The sprites had so much more detail in them including their animations. I mean blow an enemy up in Blood and you witness them being torn asunder in an animation formed by a series of sprites. But blood II they will just be replaced by the crappy low poly gibs and blurry blood spatters. The first Blood game has so much more detail; finer detail. Environments in that game looked like they had a lot of effort into them. Maybe it in Blood 2 it is not so much that effort wasn't put into the game, more that PCs that people had at the time weren't that powerful so higher detailed 3D models and detailed levels weren't really feasible yet let alone the standard.
Even the one liners from Caleb and other player characters are not the same. Yes it sound like Caleb. I think it is actually a different voice actor maybe. But the lines are less black humour and more just sadistic.
Anyway it's not all bad. Some of the gun play is actually satisfying, then again some is pretty lame and it's hard to control fine control your character movement. Years ago, not now lol I played the demo over and over again. Using the assault rifle felt pretty good. I'm recommending that people can enjoy this but it's just an inferior substitute for the original game which is also now available on steam. If you have to choose between them play that instead.

I had high hopes for this game, and while it might possibly be worth it's sale price, I don't recommend it at the full cost.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There isn't really any mystery to solve. People are dying, but the clues you can find are rather meaningless, and in the end you need to just guess who is the murderer, (and with as many suspects as there are, it is nearly impossible to correctly choose your suspect). The idea of there being a new "mystery" every time is entirely laughable, since it takes place in the same town with what might as well be the same people. While I wouldn't mind this normally, they advertise it as one of their main selling points. On the postive side, the pixel graphics fit the noir style nicely. The music, (however basic is is), also helps set the tone.
Basically, in the end, what we have here is a game of "Clue" or possibly even "Mafia", just without any deduction or the fun of other people being there to enjoy it with you. I do not recommend it at full price, I'm simply glad that I got it on sale.

Well If read this, then you properbly already know Xcom series and how to play this turnbased strategy game.
But be aware this game work in a little different way.
On the big world map you now have a flying base from start-end in the game. You fly from country to country setting up radio towers to earn funds for your operation of xcom. What is pretty cool is that everytime you start a new game then everything is random so the replay value is fantastic, also the battles never play out excactly like last time, since the enemys are also random selected depending on your tech level and how far you are in the campaign.
You will without a doubt encounter enemys you already know from the series, but there are also some new ones that you love or hate.  ( properbly hate since they kill your men he he )
All in all you will fly arround the map all the time completing random missions that variate from capture vip, to protect resistance HQ against enemy raid..  Sometimes you also get special missions that can alter the course of the campaign. Example you get 3 missions to choose from that all effect what you get out of it different.
Example do you want a scientist in reward, you want money, or maybe you want that a hidden event will not happen.
Be aware the game take a little time to understand how the new features work and how you move arround on the tactical world map, but once you learn the rules of the game and so on then it is actual pretty good if not excellent.
The game AI i think is pretty good and is indeed a challenge. They will assult/run away or maybe flank you.
The shooting animation and detail of the graphics are excellent as well.
As you know the game is all about research and getting better gear to combat the aliens, and well you are in for a long journey.. There are allot of tech, and in this new xcom game you can even put extra gadjets on your weapons so they become more powerfull or precise.. Why not give you soldiers some armour that if enemy try to thouch you set them on fire... quite handy when one of the anoying snake aliens want to cuddle with you.
I recommend that your first campaign will be the most easy level, even if you are experienced.. The game is quite tough, and there it take a little time to learn how the new game work.
Well what are you waiting for, BUY IT..... 10/10.

Noir Syndrome is a detective game analog to Noir cinema. Its simple graphics and music don't harm the game in anyway, in fact it suits it just fine, but the excessive simplicity of its core mechanics prevent it from being a better game.
In the main game mode you have to find who the murder is on a limited set of days. You do this by visiting various places on the city map, going from place to place as you collect evidence and questioning suspects, until you'r ready to point who's the culprit and arrest him. If in paper this sounds interesting, truth is that the gameplay fails to establish any significant connection between you and the game. You basically side-scroll your way through the levels constantly pushing "Z" hoping to find any clue or money randomly hidden on the set.
Also, the fact that this is a rougelike does little for the game. It doesn't offers enough replay value and, in any way, it compensates for the lack of narrative depth.
Still the biggest problem the game faces it's being on PC. If you get it for a portable platform then I think it might be more worth it, but if you plan to play it on PC I say to stay away from it.

If you are at all interested in hacking simulation games this is by far one of the best. The fact that it is worked predominantly on a terminal using actual unix commands may seem like a barrier to entry but is infact one of the games greatest assets when you get used to it. It allows much faster hacking than a visual click based game like say uplink (not to say uplink is a bad game).
For me coming from using linux ditros for university picking up on the commands in the terminal was very easy. The tutorial works very well at explaining what the different programs do and how to use them without explaining all of them or over explaining anything.
It still allows for the feeling of discovery that comes from finding software on a machine and trying it out. Especially given that some software can be found before it is technically needed if you keep an eye out.
As an extra bonus too some of the commands you will learn and use frequently will allow you to do basic stuff on a unix terminal in the real world as they are built in commands.
To sum up i would absolutely recommend this game to anyone interested in playing a good hacking sim especially if you have any experience on a terminal already.

A heady and thematic concoction of punky, grimy rebellion and the seedy underbelly of a space opera, with prominent notes of bedlam and intensity.

Half-Life.  Where Valve started.  This is the game that put them on the map and the game that eventually spawned the entire engine and framework that is used for all of Valves games (Team Fortress 2, Half-Life 2, Garry's Mod, etc...).
Half-Life tells the story of science gone wrong, likely caused by some odd organizational force, as you'll discover through playing.  It tells the story through the eyes of Gordon Freeman, a scientist at the Black Mesa Research Facility.  The game essentially begins with a very interesting explosion, and from there on out, you are met with otherworldly creatures, and humans that only share the desire to kill you.  You must escape.  Save as many people as you can.  Stop the spread of these creatures that seem only hell-bent on destroying life as you know it.
Did I forget to mention the crowbar?

There's a crowbar.  Use it, live it, love it.

LEGO The Hobbit is on one hand a great improvement over LEGO Lord of the Rings, and on the other it is by far the buggiest LEGO game I have played.
TT Games addressed three of my main complaints with LEGO LOTR: lack of a mini-map (this was introduced in LEGO Marvel) and lack of the ability to summon a horse to travel faster.  Both of these things help immensely with navigating the game world.  The other major fix is game performance.  Both LEGO LOTR and LEGO Marvel stuttered badly moving around the game world.  They finally seem to have fixed the problem with this game so it runs nice and smoothly like it should.  Otherwise, the game is very similar to LEGO LOTR as expected, though some new character abilities were introduced.  One of the main complaints I have read about the game is that the dwarves, who have many different abilities, are difficult to tell apart but I didn't have much trouble after the first hour or so.
If you've played other LEGO games, you should understand how they play and this one isn't really any different.  What is different is the bugs.  While I haven't played many LEGO games, the bugs have been pretty minimal.  In this one however, I ran into numerous game-breaking bugs that required quitting and reloading my save.  I had the fast travel system stall so I was stuck in midair, I've randomly lost the ability to open the map, and I even had the blacksmithing minigame freeze up on me.  At one point I managed to get a character stuck during a combat QTE sequence in a position where the sequence wouldn't complete, so it kept repeating endlessly.  All of these things happened several times throughout my playthrough and were quite frustrating.
Despite the bugs, the game is still enjoyable and is definitely recommended for LEGO and LOTR fans.

Heat Signature has been a fantastic experience so far. You really can approach an objective from any angle, and the game actively encourages experimentation and diversity of playstyles. The stealth feels tense and rewarding, the action over the top and thrilling, the space travel a delicious wrapper around the whole package. Your character is powerful--very powerful--which feels super fun, but one small slip up and you're liable to be thrown out into space, so the game is not easy; its balanced perfectly I'd say. Optional mission criteria (like completing objectives without killing anyone) and the constant creation of new characters keeps the game from feeling too repetitive most of the time. My only complaint is on high-difficulty missions, they generally challenge you by having guards with lots of shields and ships with lots of turrets. So far I only know one way to counter these foes, and its more of a slog then giving me a thrilling choice of tools.
But overall, I love this game. Great for a long play session or a quick pop-in to your space station. Plus, you can flee a space ship by shattering a window and hopping out into space. Or you can kill a target that way. Smashing windows is great.

The game play is lot of features from the previous game including a feature which you build a big Lego object out of bits of broken down objects that you have smashed up in the world. Each of the characters which you play have their own unique ability or weapon that gives them there on use and key element to you finishing each level or finding all of the hidden items in the game.  The game is split into sixteen chapters, each of which are connected by a huge map which you are able to explore in a free roam sort of mode. Between each main chapter's story, you are able to carry out side quests for other Lego characters throughout the world.
Story wise, it basically follows the story lines from the books/films. There are some small modification to fit events into a suitable number of chapters, as well as adding the increasingly well known Lego humor that we all love.  Sadly according to a number of sources across the net, there were plans to bring out some DLC for the final chapter in the story, but the idea appears to have been scraped so we won't get to see the final book/film in this series.
All of the audio in Lego The Hobbit is taken directly out of the film it self. Christopher Lee has the role of the narrator throughout the whole game as well.
This game does not carry any difficulty what-so-ever. You have unlimited lives so dying is not an issue. The main aim, apart from finishing the story of course, is to collect Lego bricks on each level in order to be the "Master Builder" along with lots of other little collectibles such as special building kits, which can all be used to unlock hidden characters in the game.
A playthrough the story mode of this game as well as a good portion of side quests took me twelve hours to complete. Once you finish the game you have the option to go back and finish the remaining quests, as well as free roam around all the levels replaying them to find the remaining hidden items and collectibles. This will probably add on another four or five hours worth of game play if you are the completionist sort.
All in all, Lego: The Hobbit is a brilliant game and is certainly worth the low regular price on Steam of £14,99 - saying that the Lego Games do go on sale quite regularly too, so if you get it for less than that, this is an absolute bargain. I would really recommend anyone who is a fan of the Lego series or The Hobbit to pick this up as I failed to find any real issues with this game.

I like this game, and it gave me hours of solid fun, but there are three things that dishearten me and make me want to stop playing altogether.
1. Limited Multiplayer.  If I want to play with my friends, I'm going to want to do more than race through a gauntlet or wrestle each other out of a ring.  Almost 2 years of development and Sumo and Gauntlet are the only multiplayer modes available?  Weak.
2. No Block Rotation.  To rotate a block, it depends on a. where you are facing/pointing and b. the position of the blocks next to where you want to put a block.  So, if I want to take an armored half two block (The names of these blocks aren't that great, I know.), which is a 1x2x1 sloped block, and if I want the slope to face the way I want it to, I have to put other blocks down to get the armored half two block in the right orientation BEFORE I can place it.  Not having a simple way to rotate a block makes it needlessly difficult and tedious to build, you'd think there'd be something done about at least a few months after release, but no.
3.  Death Cube.  As some of you may know, the GeoCorp Tech Gangs that you are quested to destroy can be massive, like the useless GeoTech or the hulking Rolling Fortress.  As big and slightly lag inducing as these two were, I enjoyed trying to work around them, using long range weapons to steadily weaken the Rolling Fortress, working my way to it's core from a distance, until it collapses.  I've been getting these for hours, with very little variety.  "Okay, so these must be the only GeoCorp models that were accepted for GeoCorp tech gangs." I tell myself. "Maybe no other models could compare".  I hit GSO Rank five, and the next GeoCorp tech gang has two gargantuan techs called "Bricky".  It is literally a giant cube with wheels all over the underside, plasma cutters spamming the top with a ring of 3 pound cannons, and nothing but diamond drills on the other 4 faces of the cube.  Needless to say, their collapse is a lag fest, but that's not what bothers me.  What I'm getting at is: YOU DON'T HAVE TO BE CREATIVE IN THIS GAME.  You don't have to worry about how heavy you are, you don't need to worry about shields or power supplies, you don't need to worry about balancing your weapons with your harvesting tools, you don't need to worry about fuel and booster jets.  All you need to do is make a giant frickin' cube, slap some guns on it, save it, and *BAM!* your boring cube-tech can be sent to every other player to either spam them, bore them, lag them out, or all three.  So, in a game that emphasizes creativity, why is there a lack of variety?  Why do we have to put up with lag inducing "Bricky" spawns because some half-wit thought he was funny?
Nevertheless, I'm done playing.  On one hand, I'd like to see an update with these issues addressed, and maybe I'd play some more.  On the other hand, it's been almost two years since this game was released, and it's STILL in "early access", and I'm willing to bet that the game will never leave early access.  The fact that the issues I've mentioned are still prominent in the game after all this time says a lot about the nature of the developers, which from what I can gather is either "slow and lazy" or "keep it in early access so we can lure players in and take their money without doing much about the game".
If you want a game that has survival elements, block based building and vehicle combat, and some actual multiplayer, I suggest Empyrion: Galactic survival, their developers are fast, hard working, actually listen to the player's concerns and kill bugs faster than pesticide.  Not to mention they have been able to do far more with Empyrion in a year and a quarter than TerraTech's has been able to do in two.

Well, it's no Overwatch, but it's fun for me at least.
Fractured Space is a Free-to-Play Multiplayer Online Battle Arena(MOBA) where two teams of 3 or 5 battle in grid-like maps for control of the sectors.
It has a wide variety of ships, roughly 30+ ships, controlled by three different factions.
Each ship has weapons and abilities designed to counter other ships.
It has diverse crewmembers that improve a variety of stats for each ship they operate.
Each map has beautiful graphics that truly display the untold mysteries of the galaxy.
Despite these features, it has a couple glaring problems.
Problem #01: It's too repetitive
Right now, there are only two modes players can select, Conquest and Frontline.
Conquest pits two teams where the goal is to defeat the enemy team and capture their base.
Frontline pits two teams where the goal is to defeat the enemy team and capture their base.
The only difference is that Frontline is faster in pace due to being on such a small map while Conquest uses Gamma, a timed event that gives powerful buffs to the team that captures it.
To simplify, the game's modes lack in variation, which leads me to the second problem.
Problem #02: It has no diversity
Having 30+ ships is an amazing feature, but it's not enough to maintain my interest.
Since it's a MOBA, there's really no need for any originality like a story or universal lore but it does help the game in the long-run.
In addition, every sector almost always has a planet in view, so why not try ground battles?
The idea of invading space stations with said ground units is also an idea to consider.
Think about it, what keeps blowing up the stations in Conquest Mode if it's not the ships?
Overall, It's a fun game, but it's going to lose out to bigger titles like League of Legends and Dota 2 unless it can bring something to the field that helps it stand out from the others.
Fortunately, it's got a lot of potential so all it needs is some inspiration and the right touch.

This game is what happens when Ubisoft listens to its fans.
Wait, wait. Hear me out.
For years, "fans" of the AC series have asked for certain things: dedicated stealth buttons, more stealth gameplay, better variation in mission types, extra things to do, collectibles, achievements, better combat... and AC: Unity represents an attempt to give fans what they want.
There's a reason fans aren't game designers, however. Ask a kid what he wants for dinner every night, and you're liable to get ice cream as a response. But you know, as I do, that ice cream is not an acceptable dinner food.
AC: Unity, representing a "crowdsourced" AC game, is ice cream for dinner. It's things you think you want, things that in moderation may be great, but when thrown together, end up just being bad for you.
Which is not to say that the game is bad, per se. The game is mediocre. Arno is a mediocre protagonist, akin to Connor or Altair. He lacks Ezio's roguish charm or Edward's roguish roguery. He doesn't have the personality of Shay or Aveline. In that regard, he's much more of a "blank slate," easy to step into the shoes of, but ultimately, a little flat.
The game also features very little bleed-in from the modern day story line, again something "fans" have been clamoring for, and again, something that doesn't feel right for the series. The series' more annoying moments (tail missions, instant fail missions, anything with Desmond, etc.) served to highlight its truly bright points. The series has never been a "stealth" game series. It's historical tourism with a side of stabbing simulator. It's a third person action game with wonky, yet familiar, controls. AC: Unity tries to change that, and in what ends up feeling the most like a video game, also feels like a shift away from what made the series popular, even if it wasn't always the toast of aficionados on gaming forums.
What good can be said about the game? It's beautiful. Obviously, Ubisoft put a lot of work into the new engine, but the edges are rough. This is a craftsperson's first try with new tools, and it shows. However, it's plain enough to see that as the engine matures and the technical bugs get ironed out, it will produce some simply stunning graphics and gameplay.
The game also has some innovative features: the murder mysteries, for example, are great. We've been master assassins and soldiers long enough. Let's have a Great Detective Assassin character, a rollicking mix of Holmes and Batman. The gear customization is also a nice change.
But what are we missing? Series mainstays like Assassin Tombs, variation in mission types (a problem with ACIII and AC:U, it seems). Rewarding combat (AC:U penalizes you for getting into combat. I suppose this is supposed to make you play more stealthily, but see above: stealth is not a strong suit of a game with janky controls and odd rules about line of sight). A well-written premise. I feel like we were cheated out of our Pere Dumas-inspired storyline for some crap about a murder we don't get to care about because we hardly know any of the characters. Even the star-crossed Templar/Assassin lovers storyline is downplayed for, what, the 30th time we've seen a bildungsroman about a young protagonist who totally doesn't want to follow Mom and Dad's creed, yo, only to realize by the end of the game that the Creed is worthwhile and the evil Templars must be stopped? It was cool when Ezio did it. It wore thin with Connor. Matt Ryan's performance as Edward saved that storyline, and now again we've got flat-voiced Arno learning that the world is a bigger place than he thought when he was young? Yawn. Yawn yawn yawn.
I think Ubisoft's heart was in the right place, but the execution fell flat. If AC:U is nothing more than a game hastily constructed around a tech demo for the next-gen AC engine, then it makes sense. If they meant this to be a full game, it's a sour note in the AC symphony. Still, there's enough good elements here to work with that I think the series still has a bright future.

I have a laptop with a Geforce 960M in it and the game runs beautifully with 60 fps and ZERO lag spikes.
Now onto the gameplay. It is a big improvement from all of the nba 2k games so far. The most noticeable change is the defense. In older versions of the 2k series, I remember i was able to run around until the AI backs off enough where I can drive it in or shoot a 3. Now the AI tends to adapt to how you play, making you learn how to be more of an all-around player and change my strategies. The defense is more aggressive and it makes you have to use acutal plays and utilize the pick-and-roll a lot more than I ever did in any other 2k game. A lot of the animations run a lot smoother and flow much better than its predecessor.
The biggest concern so far for me is the MyCareer. Now don't get me wrong. Spike Lee put an interesting approach to the MyCareer series and it was well done. Was it the best way to do it? I personally do not think so. In the very beginning, Spike Lee introduces the game mode and how it will give you many options from choosing your previous college and how well you played in college, which makes you feel like you will have a lot more option to broaden the game experience to come. It gives you about 7 colleges to choose from, which isn't much, but this isnt NCAA march madness. Anyways, that's basically the only decision you make in the MyCareer during the "Living the Dream" story by Spike Lee. They choose your agent for you and make the decisions for you, making the story very linear. Instead of boasting the options in the game with the hlp of Spike Lee, they should've promoted the emotional aspect of it, because he delivered on that end. With Spike Lee controlling the story it added a side to NBA that wasn't shown as much as the others, but falls short with what it could have been if you were more in control.
With that in mind. The game is actually really great if you have the computer power to control it. If you're like me and buy the game despite all of the negative feedback its been getting, you will not be disappointed.

This is a really fun, interesting game. When you first get it you will dump a lot of time into it, at least I did. It is early access but a lot of the core features are complete enough for you to get in the game and have fun. It feels really great exploring the galaxy, finding new worlds and killing their inhabitants. Building is well executed and you can go all the way down to the core of a planet or build a tower to space. I have not engaged in multiplayer and the game is light on story.
I am not surprised by all the negative reviews, but what you need to understand as someone considering purchasing the game is that most of these people are frustrated with the decision by the developers to release updates through a parallel beta. They did this because updating this game involves frequent character wipes. One segment of the community complains about lack of updates and the other complains about character wipes. All of these people were chomping at the bit to buy this game and play it and most of them had a good time with it. The negative reviews are mostly the result of frustration with the beta program and the fact that Chucklefish moved their entire operation over to the UK last year, slowing development.
It is definitely frustrating that development on this game has been somewhat slow, but it is progressing every day and you can see that with the "nightly build" beta program if you choose to opt in. This will not satisfy many, as you can see. The bottom line is this: Starbound is an excellent early access game that set the bar very high and they are taking their time with development in order to really do it right. If you want a totally bug free, feature complete game you might be waiting until 2016. But if you want a fun, intuitive game like this you will find a lot of fun here and now, just be mindful that some of it will be rough around the edges.
If you do purchase this game, be prepared for the long haul. You won't want to quit when you first get the hang of it. Eventually you will burn out on it, but it took me 230 hours and that is without any online play. I would say that is pretty good for early access.

A very good 2D sandbox game. It has one of the most atmospheric game-soundtracks I ever heard. As an example, the music changes to be more dramatic in fights, sounds adventurous while mining and is relaxing while exploring the planet.
I like the idea of having multiple planets with different resources. Playing offline is not that fun for me, but when playing with friends/my family the time goes away extremely quick as it is extremely fun. The game also has very interesting physics. Sand and gravel rolls around, water, lava and poison can flow away as they are not endless water-sources. The graphics are extremely good and change from planet to planet. There are interesting dungeons on every planet and you alway want to take everything with you. One "slot" in the inventory can handle 1000 items of the same kind.

Every single mission amounts to repeating the same simple steps over and over, while praying to the RNG.
1. Go to social gatherings. Talk to everyone to fill up your suspect list, examine everything else for resources. Buy stuff if you're low on resoucres. (All of these actions can be done by basically holding down right+z)
2. Go to crime scenes and suspicious areas. Examine everything to fill up your clue list.
3. Cross-refence to see if the clue-list and suspect list match up with only one possible action.
4. Repeat until game is over, either through victory by getting the right information in time.
That is literally everything to the game. The rest of the mechanics are near worthless.
Starvation? Eating once gives you enough food to survive until the final day.
Factions? Literally just "don't go to this area right now or you will die".
Combat? If you need to use combat, you've already lost. It's basically impossible to recover from, and it causes your score to plummet so far that there's nearly no reason in continiung.
Story? Literally completely nonexistent. All character names are completely random, and every single killer has the motivation of "I'm doing it for Anubis. Don't ask why."
You don't get to examine bodies, you don't get to examine clues.

It's overall better than XCOM:Enemy Within. Maintains the general design, but refines it a lot and addresses a big chunk of the criticism. Plus it's moddable! There's quite a few interesting mods out there.
It's less stable, still has quite a few bugs, but mostly related to animations and the interface. I haven't encountered anything game breaking.
It's a lot more balanced, with difficulty that is coming from the high amount of alien types and their special abilities, as opposed to being able to one-shot your guys like in the previous installment. The game feels challenging, but fair, on a Veteran playthrough (difficulty 2 of 4). For comparison, the original XCOM difficulty 2 of 4 was very easy, while 3 of 4 had a very big difficulty spike due to aliens one-shotting XCOM soldiers easily in the first one third of the campaign.
In my oppinion it's the best squad-focused turn-based tactical strategy game out there at the moment.
My only complaint is that the end game is pretty short and you don't get that much of a chance to use the shiney last tier equipment or the most powerful abilities at your soldier's disposal. But there's a long war mod for that :P (the Partisan War mod).
EDIT: A Long War 2 mod made by the original team behind the XCOM1 LW mod and backed officially by Firaxis has been launched. It's really good, brings a lot of new content (missions, research tree options, utility items, 2 whole new weapon tiers, maps, aliens, etc.) and an overhaul of the strategic (geoscape) layer. Two thumbs up for XCOM2 just because of this mod - it increases the replay value of the game hugely.

I want to be able to recommend Dinner Date - it's definitely one of the more unique game experiences to be found on Steam - but too early into it, you realize that you've experienced just about all the game has to offer, and you're left slogging through monologue after monologue waiting for things to move on.
I went into this game knowing absolutely nothing about it. I received it as a gift, and had not heard of it prior. I expected it to be a lame dating simulator, and it's probably the best praise I can give to say that it is not that. Instead, you play as the inner subconscious mind of young-ish man who's set up his small kitchen for a date. As he sits at the table and waits for his date arrive, you can influence his actions by focusing on different parts of the scene, all while listening to the man's thoughts as the night grows later and later.
Unfortunately, this gets monotonous very quickly, and you're stuck following a very linear path as you pick your way through all the interactive parts of the scene. It also becomes very obvious early into the experience what will happen, which doesn't help the game feel more like work than play.
It's too bad, because the premise is interesting, and it could have been enjoyable, even if only as an art piece. As it stands however, Dinner Date is too slow and predictable to be any fun, in my opinion.

Xcom: Enemy Unknown was my first turn based strategy game that I really put any time into. I thoroughly enjoyed the first one which was a surprise since I'm usually not too fond of turn based anything. So to keep it short, if you liked the first one you will definitely enjoy the second. If you haven't played the first one I'd highly recommend it, it will make your experience with xcom 2 a whooooole lot less frustrating. There's a lot of innovative enhancements to the original gameplay to keep it fresh and interesting but still has the core Xcom feel. I really like the new skills they added and the more in depth class system. Also the character customization is awesome, I thought I wouldn't give a damn about character appearance in a game like this but there's a lot of options and it makes you that much more inclined to try and keep your favorite soldiers alive. Another thing, I've seen quite a few reviews complaining about bugs and glitches interfering with gameplay. There are definitely some AI bug issues, but in my case nothing interfered with my gameplay other than the occasional pause because the game gets stuck on the enemy turn for a few seconds. The rest were pretty small and easily ignorable bugs. (Again, this was my personal experience) I don't have too much negative feedback to give on this game other than certain missions feeling way too hard for your current progress and some lag and pauses during the enemy turn. NOTE TO NEW PLAYERS: PERSONAL SUGGESTION, DON'T DO IRON MAN ON YOUR FIRST PLAY THROUGH. I WOULD HAVE SMASHED MY WHOLE COMPUTER TO PIECES.
The good:

The bad:

-some of the countdown missions feel way too rushed and next to impossible to come out with a success and a full crew. Then again that may have been the intention. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.

It's difficult to really describe Dinner Date without ruining a decent chunk of what makes it worthwhile, but I can safely say it is by far the hipsterest video game the world has ever seen. If you should choose to give it a try, expect an extremely brief (20 minutes or so per my Steam clock), vaguely interactive story-telling exercise, akin to Dear Esther but radically different in scale and style. Also, watch a few dozen britcoms first to attune yourself to British accents (I strongly recommend Black Books), and turn down the music volume a bit while cranking up the dialogue if you intend to have any idea of what's being said. It's by no means a tear-jerker that'll yank at the heart strings, but there's something poignant and sad and empathetic here all the same.
Stand proud, Dinner Date; you will be forever remembered. Perhaps not as the most enjoyable game, and perhaps barely as a game at all, but you've gone and done something Weird and Different, and I can certainly appreciate that.

Heat signature is a delirious romp through space. You get a random set of equipment and a breacher pod and then wreak havoc across an unsuspecting galaxy.
All the gadgets have uses and synergize together for all kinds of crazy problem solving.
Sneak around stealthily or go brash. Non-lethal take downs or copious bloodletting. The choice is yours and they are all satisfying.
It's a game that fosters implicit story telling. One example is the story of Chantel Fury. A woman out for blood. But then an opportunity to save lives arose. If she could free a faction stronghold, the galaxy would be one step closer to peace. So she set aside her quest for vengeance to tread a gentler path. She made it to the bridge of the siege ship without knowing she'd have a scant few seconds to escape the impending blast. She had no teleport, shield, or stealth gadgets, but she did have a slipstream. She was certain she would die, and yet she couldn't leave this life without a fight. And so she ran. She dodged bullets and guards and streaked across the ship at breakneck speed. She couldn't believe her eyes as she watched the siege ship's end from the cockpit of her pod milliseconds before she'd have joined it's fate.
And this is but a small part of Fury's tale.
Seriously. Buy the game. You won't regret it.

Half-Life
Run, Think, Shoot, Live.
Developed by Valve and released in 1998, Half-Life was, at the time, considered the finest first person shooter (fps) of its generation and still remains today one of the best games of all time.
When a mysterious alien artifact is tested at the Black Mesa Research Facility, a Resonance Cascade occurs ripping holes in the fabric of space and allowing aliens from another dimension to pass through to Earth. Awaking in the test chamber Dr. Gordon Freeman must fight his way through Headcrabs, Bullsquids and the powerful Vortigaunts as well as the U.S. Army who has been sent dispose of the Aliens and witnesses.
Half-Life’s plot, although not readily apparent, is extremely complex and dense. It does explain clearly why you need to go from point A to B, however the backstory can be very confusing and still, some of it, remains unresolved to this day. It’s this complexity and mysteriousness that makes the game so much more effective.
Gameplay is one amazing aspect in Half-Life. Being both a puzzle game and an fps, Valve has equally weighted these two genres with lots of little puzzles throughout the game, (some hard and some not), as well as lots of fun alien and solider blasting in-between, using a large range of cool weapons. Your signature weapon that is now an iconic symbol for the Half-Life franchise is your crowbar, which although not as lethal as a rocket launcher or crossbow, is useful to complete small tasks like breaking a window or the entrance to a ventilation shaft.
The soundtracks in this game always suit the environment and never fail to add to or significantly change the atmosphere of some scenes. The soundtracks consisting of electrical and techno sounds go extremely well with the chapters played in the Border world Xen, The creepy number played at the start of the game, while in the tram, blew the suspense factors through the roof and nothing goes better with the satisfaction of completing Half-Life than the iconic end credit soundtrack. Unfortunately, after most of the “feel good” soundtracks start you will pass a checkpoint that will que the next sequence and stop the song.
The level design in this game was truly ahead of its time. There is not only significant attention to detail and lots of optional interactivity with the environment, but the game is constantly catching you off guard with jump scares from Headcrabs or collapsing bridges. The graphics are quit dated however, and might affect your level of enjoyment, which is why Valve released an updated version of Half-Life where they improved the graphics significantly.
Overall this game is an artwork. The storyline is great and only gets better in later games, the gameplay is exciting and this is all made exceedingly better with the incredible soundtracks and level design. I would recommend this game to anyone but in particular fps gamers as it is a classic and arguably one of the best fps’ of all time. If you buy this game...

Hacknet is the lone developer's pet project, and it saddens me to give it a negative rating. Honestly, though, I just didn't enjoy the game at all. It is extraordinarily repetitive, and after a while, it feels that you're doing nothing except waiting for hacking animations to finish. With only 2 exceptions,
mission can be beaten by typing the same 6-7 commands in a predetermined order. After 2-3 hours of gameplay, I kept asking myself, "why is every mission the same, and why am I being forced to do it again and again?"
I did enjoy the jokes hidden in the IRC chat logs, but even then, they repeated themselves. If you read every IRC log in the game, you'd run across the same exact joke (literally) 4-5 times. It's a bit disappointing that the developer couldn't even populate the IRC logs with unique jokes.
As an alternative criticism... the UI has some definite issues. For example, the node map gets so cluttered that it becomes completely unusable. You're constantly forced to backtrack and look at the mission statement in order to remind yourself which nodes should be broken into. It's very frustrating, and definitely killed my sense of immersion.
All in all, I can't recommend this game. I understand that others love it, but honestly, it just wasn't for me.

There are very few free-to-play games that I like. Most of them end up being a pay-to-win game if you actually want to stand a chance against other players. This game allows you to purchase new ships in a reasonable amount of play time with the in game currency that you earn at the end of each match. A rookie player can defeat an higher level player if they're wise in their tactics. This is definitely a game where a team of lower level players working together can easily lay waste to advanced players who aren't communicating. Teamwork is KEY to winning a game and defending your team's territory. This is not a game for lone wolves or anti-social players.
There are a few upgrades for each ship that can be bought with that same currency that upgrade certain ship abilities. That said, the ship abilities that come as default are more than enough to stand up to upgraded versions (which usually just modify the way a specific ability works, not make it overpowered).
The game shows off a gorgeous vision of space combat thanks to the power of the Unreal 4 Engine. The amount of details on each ship are staggaring with the graphics turned all the way up. Light shafts stream through clusters of asteroids as you navigate your ship to capture enemy territory. The weapon impacts and particle effects look particularly great. When ships are hit, chunks of armor, metal and depressurized atmosphere fly off the vessels into the black of space. Massive spherical shockwaves issue from ships as their reactors go critical as they're destroyed. The end of each match is highlighted by a cinematic view of the enemy (or your own) home base space station blowing up in spectacular fashion as the victiorious team's ships fly past the camera in formation.
If you like space combat, especially giant capital ship space combat, then this is definitely the game for you. It's easy to pick up and start and looks fantastic. I would recommend this game to anyone looking to play a slower paced but occasionally frantic multiplayer game. Happy hunting.

Plus, given that you can choose the difficulty of the dungeon you take on each time, you can always play it slower and safer and build up your town upgrades to make your heroes stronger. After the sensational Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, I did not anticipate that a successor could be any better. But the show must go on, so Assassin's Creed Unity hit stores.
First of all: Black Flag was designed on the old console generation (PS3 & XBoX360) and exceeded the Assassin's Creed (1) tale by far (sailing and swashbuckling pirates are not very stealthy). Now, with the new instalment, the makers could have preceded with sea fights and stuff and completely alienate their franchise OR do something completely different. And so they did, by erasing all ships and going back to solid land. Paris sets a wonderful and big stage to explore. Though it’s not as big as the Caribbean Sea it certainly has more than enough to explore to make both games even. However, the new console generations demanded new graphics and therefore a lot more -all from scratch- programming. The game, its DLC Dead Kings as well as the App and Assassin's Creed Initiates
were buggy to the point of being unplayable. Most of the issues are fixed by now, but it is a disappointment to by a AAA-title and get crapware.
However, Unity does a lot of things right by going some steps backwards. Everything that made the franchise memorable has been redone: parkouring, inventory, people, fighting and multiplayer are all brand new and -though not perfect- gives a solid feeling. That promises more and even better instalments in the future.
My creed: It's pure Assassin's Creed and bugs free. Don't expect another Black Flag but enjoy the revolutionary Paris. And for those who like the franchise it's a must-play anyway.

Well isn't this a nice little game, a creative idea executed fairly well.
The idea behind it is you're a private investigator in a violent town, trying to arrest an assassin. As a result, you investigate this filthy town while trying to stay alive.
The clues are randomly placed in the environment and you have to investigate every nook and cranny to get the clues that will reveal who the true culprit is. Some clues are more decisive than others, for example, a bullet casing may indicate the culprit is a Mobster or a member of the Police, while a Police ID precisely tells you the culprit affiliation.
You have to figure out 3 things : Affiliation (Civilian, Mobster, Policeman), Job (Driver, Chef, etc.) and Sex (Male or Female).
Of course you can just guess and try an arrest but if you get it wrong you fail.
As to how gather suspects, you have to talk to the people in various places, crime scenes don't have people lingering about but have generally more clues and some events make people amass in a place, particularly if they're from one affiliation.
Anyway, this becomes quite important when playing a higher difficulty than normal, because either the police or the mob want you dead, so the investigation becomes much harder with shootouts, especially since bullets are limited and costly, that's why it's wise to avoid places where the affiliation that wants you dead hangs out.
Bullets aren't the only thing that can kill you however, hunger can as well, you have to manage your money to buy the right resources like lockpicks, bullets or food to survive, everytime you investigate or talk with someone you get hungrier until you die.
Some places need lockpicks to explore fully and you can even rob some places where hopefully you don't get spotted or you make another faction your enemy.
Everytime you start a new game, the culprit and the clues are randomized, as is the faction that hunts you down, the events of course are randomized too, as is the place you can find clues.
The gameplay is free and you can go whenever you want mostly, but you have a time limit in days to catch the culprit... or you might just go on a murder spree.
All in all this is a repeatable noir detective story with a great soundtrack and a great feel to it. Recommended, but might get old pretty fast.

Compared to the first XCOM game, there are some new twists but the same (great) core game is there.
The game has wonderful character and weapons detail, you can really customize everything about your squads.  As usual, it's fun to rename your team with names of friends, family, or in my case celebrities (a soldier with the name Sean Connery with a british accent is hilarious to play with - also try Queen Latifah or Oprah Winfrey - YMMV).
From the original game, I missed shooting down and then exploring UFO's, there really isn't any aspect of that in this game.  But they've added some neat new mission modes and base defense opportunities that were fun to experience.
The campaign story itself was very engaging, it took a good pace, but has a short research tree.  If you like to research a lot of things, you'll feel a bit let down here.  Ultimately, though, the game's mission to save the world is an enjoyable one.
Tons of great voice acting throughout really gets you into the game, as well as awesome sounds.  Best of all I think the music tied it all together very well.  You really get that JUST ONE MORE TURN thing going, especially when the music is going in the thick of combat.
I found the graphics great at 1440p.  There are some odd occurrences with the camera angle sometimes, if it's doing an action view of a character shooting, but they are adjacent to the wall.  You get a real good close up of the wall and that's it.  But overall this happens rarely and the action shots and sound make the BAM of the weapon firing and hitting quite satisfying.
When I finished up with this game I was at 45.7 hours, with a single campaign playthrough, with all DLC's.  I'd be happy to start another run through, so the game has great replay value and I'm sure I'll open it up again at some point in the future to do it again.
If you like squad based combat like the first XCOM game, Xenonauts, UFO:Aftermath, Aftershock, Afterlight, or the original UFO/XCOM games, you'll have great fun with this one.  It's a very modern version of the same awesome core gameplay style.

Dinner Date is a very short indie title about a man waiting for his date to arrive and I ♥♥♥♥ing hated it.
The main reason I hated this game was mainly due to the usual false expectations scenario. Rather than just completely rip this game apart let me explain what I thought the game was going to be, and then what the game actually is.
What I thought Dinner Date was going to be:
Everything I thought this game was going to be came from what people posted about on the internet. Nothing I am writing in this section is what I hoped the game would be, this is what I expected based on others experiences with it. Like I mentioned above, this is a game about a man waiting for his date to arrive at his house. However, I was under the assumption that this would be 1st person, without any narration, and you are completely free to do whatever you want while you wait for the date. You do not know who the date is, or why this man is possibly being stood up. Maybe this is him being dumped, maybe he murdered her, maybe he doesn’t have a date and he’s lonely, we just don’t know. While waiting for your possible date to arrive, you are free to do whatever you want in your apartment. Doing actions will affect the outcome of “The Date”. Maybe you could eat your entire meal before he/she shows up, would that have an effect? Maybe if you drink the whole bottle of wine you will pass out and miss the date entirely, never knowing if the person came by or not. Maybe you could just sit there and wait the entire time, twiddling your thumbs, eagerly watching the clock. Maybe you could just ♥♥♥♥ing kill yourself, the point is what sold me on this game was mystery. Every time I looked into this game online, for whatever reason, the game was completely shrouded in mystery, and this made me want to play the game so badly. I was honestly expecting to play this game multiple times just to see what else I could make happen. There could’ve been so many possibilities, so many outcomes, but as you can guess I ended up being tremendously disappointed.
What Dinner Date actually is:
A monologue. The game is literally just a monologue disguised as a video game. If there are any David Cage fanboys reading this, buy this game right now. NOTHING you do while you “wait” for you date matters. I only played this game once and I went in with the intention of killing my character through alcohol abuse, but even though I am drinking down a glass of wine every 5 seconds, the character doesn’t shut up…even while he is drinking. You are forced to listen to this guy whine and complain and there’s nothing you can do about it. Yeah, there are actions, but they are ♥♥♥♥ing meaningless. I’m pretty sure if someone smoked 47 cigarettes in a row he would maybe cough a few times in the middle of his ♥♥♥♥♥ing. The game kept giving me hope that something good would happen. Oh look! He’s getting up! Can I jump out the window? Nope. Can I open my fridge? Nope. Well, can I grab that endless bottle of wine again? Not right now, nope. When I realized that I could just sit back and the game would play itself I decided to stick through to the end, with the hope that maybe something interesting would happen, but of course not. You listen to this guy whine and complain about life for awhile and then that’s it, it just ends. He doesn’t kill himself (sadly), the date never shows up, nothing ♥♥♥♥ing happens. The best part about the uh experience is the torture is short. My game time for this is 23 minutes and I waiting till the credits ended.
So that’s it, I can’t even recommend this game to people who enjoy monologues, or hearing sad..ish life stories. Rather that waste your time listening to this guys issue’s you could go hang out with your friends, and maybe help them with their problems. I can promise in that situation different outcomes and functionality that makes an impact, I dare you to try and drink as much wine as I did in this game while hearing your friend talk. In other words, real life is more of a video game than Dinner Date.
