TL;DR, I like the idea of paid mods, but they implemented it HORRIBLY.
I'm not actually opposed to paid mods. Similar to other things, hobbies can become jobs. The route that most people say you should take is working on a game after building a reputation in the modding community, or joining an existing studio.
I disagree that this is the only option. Paid mods, if handled correctly, could add massive amounts of longetivity to many, many games. Incentivizing skilled developers can cause far better mods to come to games. In addition, if properly implemented, paid mods could ensure that more mods are cross-compatible, mods remain up to date, and mods get better quality control and bugfixing.
The problem here is that Bethesda's idea was to have some people make some shoddy skins and sell them at absurd prices. To my knowledge, there are no paid mods available that offer any unique, in-depth content. Few that even come close to this are also available for free, and two of these notably are BETTER in the free version. So here we are in 2015 and I FINALLY played Half Life. What took me so long? I don't know for sure but I'm mainly a console gamer.
This game lived up to its reputation and for a game made in 1998 it still packs a punch today. Even the AI is acceptable by todays standards. The guns are fantastic and have a great weighty feel to them.
When you consider that the brilliant Goldeneye 007 on Nintendo 64 came out in 1997 and Half Life just one year later this game has aged far far better. I now can't wait to start playing Half Life 2 and everybody knows that 3 is due only any day right...right?

It's overall better than XCOM:Enemy Within. Maintains the general design, but refines it a lot and addresses a big chunk of the criticism. Plus it's moddable! There's quite a few interesting mods out there.
It's less stable, still has quite a few bugs, but mostly related to animations and the interface. I haven't encountered anything game breaking.
It's a lot more balanced, with difficulty that is coming from the high amount of alien types and their special abilities, as opposed to being able to one-shot your guys like in the previous installment. The game feels challenging, but fair, on a Veteran playthrough (difficulty 2 of 4). For comparison, the original XCOM difficulty 2 of 4 was very easy, while 3 of 4 had a very big difficulty spike due to aliens one-shotting XCOM soldiers easily in the first one third of the campaign.
In my oppinion it's the best squad-focused turn-based tactical strategy game out there at the moment.
My only complaint is that the end game is pretty short and you don't get that much of a chance to use the shiney last tier equipment or the most powerful abilities at your soldier's disposal. But there's a long war mod for that :P (the Partisan War mod).
EDIT: A Long War 2 mod made by the original team behind the XCOM1 LW mod and backed officially by Firaxis has been launched. It's really good, brings a lot of new content (missions, research tree options, utility items, 2 whole new weapon tiers, maps, aliens, etc.) and an overhaul of the strategic (geoscape) layer. Two thumbs up for XCOM2 just because of this mod - it increases the replay value of the game hugely.

Half-Life
Run, Think, Shoot, Live.
Developed by Valve and released in 1998, Half-Life was, at the time, considered the finest first person shooter (fps) of its generation and still remains today one of the best games of all time.
When a mysterious alien artifact is tested at the Black Mesa Research Facility, a Resonance Cascade occurs ripping holes in the fabric of space and allowing aliens from another dimension to pass through to Earth. Awaking in the test chamber Dr. Gordon Freeman must fight his way through Headcrabs, Bullsquids and the powerful Vortigaunts as well as the U.S. Army who has been sent dispose of the Aliens and witnesses.
Half-Life’s plot, although not readily apparent, is extremely complex and dense. It does explain clearly why you need to go from point A to B, however the backstory can be very confusing and still, some of it, remains unresolved to this day. It’s this complexity and mysteriousness that makes the game so much more effective.
Gameplay is one amazing aspect in Half-Life. Being both a puzzle game and an fps, Valve has equally weighted these two genres with lots of little puzzles throughout the game, (some hard and some not), as well as lots of fun alien and solider blasting in-between, using a large range of cool weapons. Your signature weapon that is now an iconic symbol for the Half-Life franchise is your crowbar, which although not as lethal as a rocket launcher or crossbow, is useful to complete small tasks like breaking a window or the entrance to a ventilation shaft.
The soundtracks in this game always suit the environment and never fail to add to or significantly change the atmosphere of some scenes. The soundtracks consisting of electrical and techno sounds go extremely well with the chapters played in the Border world Xen, The creepy number played at the start of the game, while in the tram, blew the suspense factors through the roof and nothing goes better with the satisfaction of completing Half-Life than the iconic end credit soundtrack. Unfortunately, after most of the “feel good” soundtracks start you will pass a checkpoint that will que the next sequence and stop the song.
The level design in this game was truly ahead of its time. There is not only significant attention to detail and lots of optional interactivity with the environment, but the game is constantly catching you off guard with jump scares from Headcrabs or collapsing bridges. The graphics are quit dated however, and might affect your level of enjoyment, which is why Valve released an updated version of Half-Life where they improved the graphics significantly.
Overall this game is an artwork. The storyline is great and only gets better in later games, the gameplay is exciting and this is all made exceedingly better with the incredible soundtracks and level design. I would recommend this game to anyone but in particular fps gamers as it is a classic and arguably one of the best fps’ of all time. If you buy this game...

I enjoy writing joke reviews with a real rating. I can't joke about this game. This is functionally one of the best games I've ever played. It's wonderfully balanced, constantly worked on and improved upon, perfectly paced, and original. In many regards it functions as a MOBA. You push down lanes to approach and destroy the enemy's base and level up based on your team's progress. However, the lanes are not contiguous sections, you need to jump in and out which requires forethought as there's always a cooldown afterward and a spool up time within which you are 400% more vulnerable to enemy fire. The game forces you to commit to fights all over the map, ensuring frequent engagements that make use of it's spectacular art style.
There are something like 30 ships in the game and each is unique, but the gameplay itself is consistent enough for the variety to not be super overwhelmin to a new player. I've watched this game grow from a handful of ships fighting it out in blocky environments (and even then it was fun as hell) to practically a fleet of warships purging environments from icy asteroid fields to the orbit of a star of each other's presence.
This is a ♥♥♥♥ing excellent game.
PS - all components of the game that you can pay for are skins or are available with currency achievable in game at a fairly quick rate.

Great Moba inspired game with the added touch of 3 dimensional space to traverse.
Although I generally avoid F2P games due to the developer or publisher introducing cash shops which often lead to a Pay-2-Win scenario Edge Case Games has so far managed to keep the shop of a purely cosmetic transaction.
While players can opt to purchase all the ships to gain early access to the more expensive ships or skins, the same can be said about many of the other popular F2P mobas available. I have never felt at a disadvantage at any point in time, thanks to the well balanced gameplay mechanics and ships abilities and designs.
Asthetically the game is very impressive, the scale of the ships and the detail each and everyone posses truely adds to the atmosphere and lends it's self perfectly to the sense of scale the developers are trying to achieve in terms of massive space based conflict. It really does feel as if you are commanding a massive capital/corvert/support ship which has hundreds if not thousands of crew onboard. The game natively supports 21:9 which is always a plus.
The sound enginering and ambient music is well suited and balanced throughout.
For anyone that loves the idea of massive space battles this is a great, not to mention free, way to expeirence intense interstellar combat on a grand scale. I often forget I'm actually playing a moba.

The problem though is how the game works.
Games should provide a challenge as games are just problemsolving puzzles. But at this point i can no longer recommend this game. The frustration is just through the roof. You may believe what you like about me being salty but i think we can all agree most of us plays games to just relax and have fun and not brag to your friends that you are a hardcore elititst who needs confirmation and acknowledgement for your low self esteem and selfdestructive behaviour.
I am fine with heroes dying, i am fine with failing. What i am not fine with is failing just for the sake of failing and this game holds no threads bared in doing so. Entering a dungeon already gave my heroes 20 stress. For just walking through a door. I am fine with random encounters and dying because every hall has big encounters and dying to being outnumbered.
But what drives me to just shut down the game is how the game goes well out of its way to just ruin everything.
The stress build up is laughable. When a hero reaches 100/200 stress their resolve is tested. The nice thing is you have a chance of your hero getting more determined and getting a powerful trait. But most of the time your hero will become a raving lunatic spreading his cancer to the other heroes.
Now i am fine with this whole thing until this point; If your hero gets a positive resolve, that vaporizes the moment you complete the mission, but if he gets a bad resolve, that remains until you either cure it or the hero dies. And this is what i mean with going out of its way to ruin your game.
The negative sides have a far greater impact than the positive ones. I know that adventuring in real life would be close to this because most people view dungeons and dragons for example as a single dwarf slaying a dragon though were it real the dragon would just devour it. But we don't play D and D to get our characters just plain out mauled to death, because we want some enjoyment. And this game just takes every single shred away.
Crimson court with the blood makes it even more tedious. I used to play this game, the stress mechanic is something i always found a nice incentive but poorly executed. But now with these other things piling on top, i started to loathe the game. I just feels like every single thing is RNG. If a hero gets a positive resolve it does nothing for me, i don't feel great, relieved or excited. I just think, woohoo now at least i do not need to spend coins to get rid of it.
Also after every mission the heroes get quirks. More often than not ofcourse only negative ones. Again a nice incentive but there is one thing i really hate about em. How can my hero get a fear of filthy things, if we did not encounter anything related to being filthy or encountering enemies using blight attacks?
How can a hero gain the negative quirk: Morbid curiousity if he did not interact with anything. Give the quirk to a hero that opens too many things, that makes sense and sounds reasonable.
But again all these mechanics just get thrown in a bingo wheel and no matter what, the negative will always outbalance the positive. And even if things, on the slim odds, work out for you, by the end of the mission most of it will be gone.

I have 70 hours in this game, so it's a review with some meat on its bones.
You've probably noticed the "mixed" or "negative" review listing for this game.  I'm sure that was absolutely true before Patch 5, but not anymore (for the most part).
The game runs with a small amount of hitching on my higher end computer.  Sure, it causes a few issues now and then... sometimes I end up facing the wrong direction when running down a street, or I end up jumping oddly onto another roof I wasn't planning on.  But, for the most part the game killing stutters and freezes don't seem to be something I'm seeing.  Granted, I never played before Patch 5 (by design), so I can't speak to the increase in playability as a percentage.
That being said, I'd like to talk about a few of the positives and negatives of this game:
Positives -
-  PACKED streets.  You actually feel like it's a live city, and that it's alive.  People go to the tavern, they carry their dead friends away from violent street battles, pr0stitutes (cuz that word is blocked, even though I used it in a legit manner...) attempt to ply their goods to passerbys, and so much more!
- Murder Mysteries!  They've added a new type of mission (since I played last in Black Flag) that allows you to solve crimes by talking to people and investigating (multiple) crime areas.  These are EASILY my favorite new missions.
- Customization system.  You can make your character look just about any way you want to with gear you gain from in-game missions, chests, and (not real) money purchases.  It's not just for asthetics, though; your character's gear denotes your stats.
- Multiplayer.  It's pretty fun, and can be engaging, or competitive... depending on who you end up with.
- Side Characters.  There are a lot of interesting characters you run across in the game (like de Sade, Bonaparte, and Robespierre) that add a lot of spice to the game.
- Paris.  It's just an absolutely gorgeous map.  A LOT of the buildings are open, too, so you can run through the streets, on the rooves, or inside the houses.
Negatives -
- Hitching.  The game hitches a little every now and then.  It's not game killing.  I understand why, though, considering the amount of stuff they pack into each screenful.
- Janky Combat.  Sometimes my character won't engage the next enemy, or pull out my sword unless I'm pointed RIGHT at them.  Also, using a secondary (F key secondary) can sometimes be hit or miss... when you're counting on a smoke bomb and it won't go off, then goes off twice in a row (wasting one) you get a little peeved.
- Lock Picking.  It's a bit boring with the new "line bobbing up and down, press space when it gets into the blue zone" sort of mini game.
Post Script -
There are a lot of elitist snobs out there who think a game is 50gb is going to release out the door with the middle name Perfection.  What a bunch of garbage.  Yeah, the game could have been released with better stability and FPS playability, but besides that... it's a PHENOMENAL game.
Whining about no horses?  You don't freaking need them.   It's freaking Paris.  Whining about ONLY getting 60 FPS?  The HDTV you use to watch TV is most likely only 1080p50 (50 fps)... so stop being a snob.  The game isn't perfect!  So?  The last perfect game was pong (which you can write in 30 lines of code).  Frankly, I can't find any fun in a game like that.
Stop being such a snob and enjoy the game for what it is.  A fun time, a great, beautiful map, a hitchy, little janky assassin combat sim with a hint at historical context wrapped into an RPG.  You want it to be more than that?  Make your own.

You have two weeks before the mysterious killer known as Anubis assassinates the mayor. Ask around to find suspects, and narrow down your list by finding clues to the muderer's identity. Try to avoid the wrath of the police and the mob, because they'll kill you on sight. Or play the dinner party mode, where you're locked in with the killer, and the other guests occasionally go mad and kill you. Collect badges to level up your subsequent characters, and play on three difficulty modes, all of them challenging. Noir Syndrome is great fun with procedurally generated mysteries that usually don't last longer than ten minutes, but there are some obvious flaws.
Controls are fully rebindable, as they always should be in a PC game. There are only five action keys, but a couple would have been helpful. The "investigate" key handles all actions except shooting, which is quite annoying when someone is standing in front of an object you want to investigate or a door you want to enter, but the game insists on making you talk instead.
The interface is a bit clunky as well. Using multiple screens to try to manage a very small amount of information on the suspects is rather ridiculous. The game doesn't let you cross off suspects who don't match the clues you've gathered, and you can't un-designate a culprit once you've selected one (though you can change which one you'll arrest if you talk to him or her).
The tutorial is bare-bones; some will appreciate learning the mechanics on their own, but it would have been nice to learn more before being thrown into the game. On the whole, though, there's a lot of pixelly fun to be had here.

Starbound is a game that shows what AAA title games are lacking.  As a gamer I want a few thing out of a game that I buy:
1: A goodstory/concept that encourages playing through it.
2: Graphics that follow a specific art style and aren't random .PNG's found on the internet. (Not neccesarily High quality)
3: A concept in the game that makes playing it rewarding and fun to play overall.
These three concept are what I was looking for and found either in a early stage of or implemented enough to make the game fun!
So your story begining starts "Slightly" different with each race you choose. I'm a big fan of games that make your choices matter right from the get-go. (The Dragon Age series is a good example.) At the current stage fo development, this is worked upon very much but was implemented to give the impression that it will (Hopefully) be expanded upon.
You next are greated by a ship that is different in design dependent on your race and so far as I've only played three of the races (IE: The Nova-Kid race has a steampunk train engine ship that makes sense if you read the data log on the race.)
There is plenty of ores to mine and a unique system of the more dangerous the planet the more dense and rae of ores you will find.

The performance in some area's of the game are attrocious... Like 10 FPS on my sytem that is decent. (Its a know problem that their working on.){A simple way to double your FPS is to turn on fullbright btw}

Update: I've decided to rewriten my review as I may have slipped in a bunch of bias on it. I promise that this one (While still negative) will provide a legit standpoint as why I think this game isn't enjoyable.
The Short Review: Questionable design choices, the effort of a web-browser game and it's super unfriendlieness towards it's users at the start make Aberoth a hard recommendation.
When originally writing this review, I wanted to give the developr the benefit of the doubt and that for his first MMO it was an OK effort. But when I was writing the review, I was feeling agitated and incredibly mad at the game for it's rightful action to place a super strong enemy next to the starting area where newbies start out.
So let's start out with the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
-For probably a first-time effort, it's clear that the developer "tried". I'm quoting this because I think the developer could had put more effort towards making the game at least present itself better and help players understand the core gameplay mechanics and objectives before sending them off to do whatever they please.
-I honestly hate how the graphics look, seeing as how unappealing that kind of "Retro" style has gotten after playing so many "Hey, our game has retro graphics. Buy it!" indie titles. How ever, it's not a bad look and had a bit more effort been put into the game it would had reasonably been decent overall.
Cons:
-
It's very anti-user friendly UI and it's idea of restarting that of a roguelike doesn't make the game challenging, but more frustrating. The thing is, this isn't your typical roguelike, it's a MMO. There's nothing wrong with trying to implement permenant death in a MMO, (See Realm of the Mad God before it got screwed over by microtransactions) but it's definitely not right when players lose 20 minutes to hours of progress because they couldn't figure out how certain things work and when trying to experiment themselves get killed instantly.
-Shops are so lazily done. Come on, what shop has you buy items by picking them up on the floor? It looks lazy. So lazy.
--The UI doesn't need to be streamlined aka WOW and GW,
This UI is text-based and for a MMO that takes lots of pleasure in wasting your time for grinding, it makes these actions absolutely painful to do.
-There is no want for monetization as it's membership perks while sound devasatating are absolutely useless. Why not spend money on cosmetics, are other things that don't make the player OP but gives them something to improve their experience.
-Seriously, what is up with this text-based UI? Quest Givers give out their messages below their nametag on the NPC and it's a bother when your own character is blocking the text. There is no window to view the quest message nor can you see it in some form of a chat window. So many things in the game are bound by the UI, and it's ridiculous.
-PVP. And the fact that trolls can freely kill others for the sake of it. This is a big problem when it's happening in the earlier areas.
-Like the infamous Sonic 06, this game loves taking pleasure in wasting people's time. I'm not saying this as a good thing, you spend your first few minutes of the game grinding by hunting rabbits and bees for gold.
First off, I'd like to let others know that just because I spent 20 minutes on Steam doesn't mean I played it on browser earlier (With hours logged in and with multiple attempts at trying to enjoy the game, which all ended abruptly by poor design choices). I've been told off by many that my complaints are unjustified because I'm the many that just logged in and bashed on it for the sake of circle jerking. Those reviews bring up legitimate concerns and it's ♥♥♥♥ing toxic when the community tells others who do have experience in the game to get out and play something else. What a joke of a community to see people saying that.
I'm being told that this game isn't supposed to hold my hand and that I'm spoiled by modern games for easy tutorials. There is a difference between a game with poor design choices preventing the player from making their own indidvidual decisions and a difference where the game is not holding your hand. Games that leave you to yourself are games that don't leave out basic and unhelpful tutorials, or unitutive UI, or poor shops, or cheap enemies. They're games that start you off with basic knowledge and let you free with the tools to play well. Aberoth demands players to figure out tons of things for themselves without properly teaching how combaat works, or how the basic mechanics of the game work. It can let the player off after teaching that but this is the difference between character action games and MMORPGs. MMORPGs usually ease the player into the tutorial so they can later learn how to create divisive builds and handle combat tactically when they get towards the end game and throughout that journey has learned new skills and faced new challenges.
First impressions are everything. If a game doesn't somewhat hook you or want you to play the game after 5-20 minutes, then you know something is wrong.
This game isn't what I consider good. It's not worthy of being on Steam, espicially since that Steam games have a bit higher standards. The quality of games that go on the store can be a bit low (Get out of here, Digital Homicide) but users on here demand for good quality games and Aberoth's poor effort towards presentation and questionable design decisions brings the negative reviews on here. For those who enjoy the game, it's better you know that Steam isn't a good place for games of this quality. This should had stayed Browser-based. This shouldn't had been released in a public storefront that was created by the people that defined PC games and video games as a whole in the 2000s.
I find it hard to recommend this game to anybody. I'm sorry, but that's the case for me, and a lot of others.

Noir Syndrome is one of those games that falls into the quirky category of "For its price, it's pretty good." In spite of the claims of the developer, to say that each playthrough of Noir Syndrome generates a new and unique procedurally generated Murder Mystery story is a bit of a stretch. That being said, it's still a fun puzzler that mixes in enough demand for quick reflexes, gut instincts, and the ability to bluff with confidence to make it a very worthwhile experience.
In Noir Syndrome, you play an anonymous flatfoot who wakes up one day to a city under siege from the mysterious murderer Anubis. You are given 14 days to explore the city, interviewing citizens for tips and suspects, searching through garbage cans and police desks for clues, and avoiding the bullets of the police and the mob (assuming you were rude enough to tick off either party somehow). Over time, Anubis will strike again and again, reducing your score but also helping weed out suspects. Visiting crime scenes burns through your valuable time, but searching for clues and chatting with citizens burns calories, so between the actual detective work you'll need to scrounge up funds and get a bite to eat. You can also spend cash on tips from the mob, lockpicks to aid in your more "thorough" investigations, and bullets for taking out those who take offense at your methods.
Once you have enough clues and suspects, you'll be able to narrow down the names and know for certain who your man is. Of course, if time's running short, you might be forced to make an educated guess and hope for the best; given the choice between walking into a nest of furious gunmen and placing your faith in a coinflip, sometimes half-baked detective work is really your best bet. Each game takes about 20 minutes to complete, so it's not like you aren't committed to success, but at the same time losing isn't exactly the end of the world.
Eventually, the game will get a touch dull; there's only one city layout, and the number of variables they can flip around really isn't that huge. Fortunately, there are three difficulty settings which drastically affect the experience, 30 in-game Achievements to acquire that provide you with bonuses for future cases, and an alternate Dinner Party play mode that forces you to find your man in a fraction of the time of a normal game, and which unlocks a variety of goofy costumes (always a solid selling point).
Noir Syndrome accomplishes all this with a presentation better suited for an NES than a radio serial broadcast. It might not scratch any authentic murder-mystery itches, but it's a clever little puzzler that's well worth the price of admission.

This game gets a 5/5 from me for eternity.
This game is easily better than Starcraft 2 and any other RTS out there right now I couldn't think of.
The materials you gather makes sense, the units you use to fight are diverse and balanced, the nations you can play are balanced.
In depth (sorta lazy) review:
-Food, gold, wood. In the napoleonic era that covers proper material costs, no random crystal to produce troops.
-You have like 13? nations to choose from (I'm not going to count), but they have very diverse units and the later expansions bring 100% diverse unit regiments to the game.
-These units are diverse, but they share the same categories in game so you can easily learn your armies quickly.
-The maps are randomly generated each map, but depending on the map you choose it does have its theme you remember. Orinoco... 55 trty... ugh, so gay, plays out the same way each time.
-The card system ingame brings out an even more diverse strategy that absolutely comes into play whether you play a treaty, deathmatch, or rush game.
-I've never really played single 1v1 matches because I had so much fun playing with friends against others, but my highest rank was Captain in treaty.... only sargeant at best in rush. Never really played deathmatch.
-You can easily learn and play any nation, and its not like the other side is going to pick the same enemy nations each time or play the same way each time, so it really brings out game immersion and keeps the game fun.
-Playing against AI can be fun and a way to train yourself a bit.... AI is insanely good at rushing but is overall dumb and predictable. And they suck at upgrading their units besides their cannons. AI could use a upgrade or re-work, but still fun to fight.
Cons:
- the game has been out so long that its community has shrunk, but you can still get a game with 2000 ppl on at one time.
- people finally found out how to hack the game, so those P.O.S.s can ruin it. Luckily there are still many that play fair, but god, hackers are such huge P.O.S.s. Any multiplayer game hacked... ugh.

Her name was Orchard.  Yeah, odd name but does that really matter especially after you pull the sort of stunt she did?  I don't think so and if you ask me, others wouldn't either.
What does matter is that stunt; her's was an interesting story, what with a daughter who fell into the wrong crowd and wounded up being a prisoner to the Glitchers.  Never did find out why but she wasn't the first person I've heard of ending up in a cell with those tech crazy freaks.
Orchard's a good mom so she does what any decent parent does, she digs.  She gets the info she needed but it ended up being costly--200 credits if I recall right and to get all of them required a lot of work, most of it pretty damn sloppy truth be told.
She started the job with a wrench and a three charged swapper--given the lack of lethal weapons, she probably preferred to get around folk than kill them so she did that to the best she could.  She got shot at least five times in those early days but she did amass the credits and a lot of expensive and well-to-do gear--the sort of stuff that would get you shot five more times over if the wrong sort of person learned you had any of it.
Well, after enough close calls she finally finds the ship where her baby girl is being kept.  She breaks in and wouldn't you know it? Every damn guard on that ship is carrying a personal shield that blocks even her graviton hammer from whisking them to la la land. Does she have anything to bring down those shield? Yeah she does but it only has three charges and there's at least twenty or so of those sheltered ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
So, what does a mom do? She abuses what she found--it was a five charge slipstream, lets you move faster then a man could blink an eye, all she appeared to these folks was an odd blur moving from room to room, stopping to malfunction a door that was in her way until finally, she's carrying her daughter over her shoulder--exhausted but relieved to finally have her baby back, flesh and blood whole at that.
Charge on the slipstream is gone.  Her swapper? One person at a time--she's not leaving without what she's come so far to get.  There is one little idea but its risky--the room, the one and only way into the cell where she's at has a panel that when damaged will take away a whole section of the ship.
She had found a grenade in her second mission--kept it for a special ocassion.  It wasn't going to get more special than this.
She throws it, waits for the shake and the blaring sound of alarms echoing in the place along with a warning that they were heading to a station some fifteen seconds away.  There's no turning back here...
Her and her daughter go jetting through the black, nothing but a fast ship and a prayer standing between the two of them and a cold death.
When she arrives on the station she takes her daughter and vanishes.  She didn't want this kind of life and now that she got what she wanted she could leave it behind--her graviton hammer was left behind though, folks have gotten around to calling it "Orchard's Lullaby" in honor of one crazy, truly caring mom.
If you happen upon it...well, who knows? Maybe something of Orchard will get passed along with it.  A person in this line of work could always use a little hope and a lot of luck.

This review originally written on May 14, 2012 on GameFAQs
"The best FPS ever made, simply a must play."
Half-Life is the story of Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist at the Black Mesa Research Facility. Something goes terribly wrong during an experiment and aliens invade our realm. As if that wasn't bad enough military men have been sent in to kill everything, including you! The game is played in first person the entire time with no cutscenes or cinematics. There is a wide variety of weapons, and enemies to kill them with. Unlike most modern FPSs you can carry as many guns as you can find and your health does not regenerate. While the game itself is technically linear, the various areas you pass through aren't as simple as walking down a corridor and shooting whatever along the way.
I've played this game (and its expansions) many times over the course of the 7 years I've had them. They never get old and are still wonderful to play even as time goes on and games continue to evolve. Although there is a deathmatch multiplayer option I will be reviewing the single player only. The game was played on hard difficulty.
STORY: 10/10
The story is done differently than most games. Rather than give you a cinematic or a cutscene of you talking to someone, characters will talk to you and you are free to move around and do what you will. You, Gordon, never ever speak. This is what's called a silent protagonist. As you play, the scientists will be the main characters who tell you what you need to do and why. There is also a mysterious man who, if you're observant, seems to be following you around. What does he have to do with this catastrophe? There isn't as much dialogue explaining the story as some games. This is not a bad thing as the area you are in and its state tells its own story. Wait until you get to the very end, it's really cool!
GRAPHICS: 10/10
This score is not based on current standards of graphics, but rather what they were at the time and my own appeal for them. The vanilla graphics from the disc version has large blurry pixels. It's honestly kind of hard to look at, but for its time they were very good. The release of the second and final expansion, Blue Shift, came with HD graphics for Half-Life and its two expansions. These made the graphics look far better. With the release of Half-Life on Steam the graphics have been cleaned up even further.
The animations are actually pretty well done for it's time. The environments are very nice looking, not bland or overly reused. The character models are else very nice, especially for the aliens. My only complaint is that there are only about 4 scientist models reused throughout the whole game, and only 1 or 2 security guard models.
SOUND: 10/10
The sound effects are really great, even by today's standards. What little dialogue the game has is done reasonably well. At certain points in the game a short music track will activate. The music, when it appears, is really nice. The rest of the time you are left to the sounds of the aliens as they lie in wait, the chatter of the soldiers, or the environmental sound effects. The same problem of the reused models occurs with the reused voices for scientists and soldiers.
WEAPONS: 10/10
There is a wide selection of weapons to choose from, and best of all you can carry them all around at once! All the weapons have their use and unless you're really bad at aiming you shouldn't have to worry about running out of ammo.
ENEMIES: 10/10
This game has a wide variety of alien creatures from the slight annoyance to the super deadly. There are also a few human soldiers to fight. I feel the human soldiers could have used a little more variance because even though the different types use different weapons they all basically fight the same. Though there is a certain class of human enemy that are very different from the rest and quite deadly. The aliens all vary and require different tactics to most effectively kill them. The bosses, especially at the end of the game, are fun and challenging to fight. It doesn't happen often but soldiers and aliens will fight each other and even a certain type of alien doesn't like another.
LEVEL DESIGN: 10/10
The level design is more akin to old school FPSs where it's not a straight corridor to the next room to fight more enemies. Instead there are often little hidden areas you can access if you explore a bit which contain useful health and ammo. It is quite common to have to climb and jump around to progress where you need to go. Sometimes you get small puzzles which generally aren't a big deal to figure out. The level environments are very well done and do what they're supposed to. The last level is my favorite, but I can't reveal why without giving spoilers.
LENGTH AND REPLAYABILITY
The game is fairly long for an FPS being about 10 hours plus especially if you take your time. I've replayed this game over 5 times over the 7 years I've owned it so I'd say it has lots of replay value. Whenever I'm in the mood for an old school FPS I check out this game.
FINAL SCORE: 10/10
It should be noted that I'm using my own slight variation of a scoring system where 10/10 does not necessarily mean flawless and perfect in every way, though this game gets pretty close to that impossible goal. If you have even a passing interest in FPSs you should check out this game on Steam and at least give it a shot. Although there are FPSs that are slightly better in certain regards, this game still holds the title of best FPS ever made because it was here so long ago and is the one that set the bar for fully 3D FPSs.

Finally, we come to the head of the saga in Episode IV: Sol.
This is the one we've been waiting for. The culmination of all of the games before it.
Sol introduces new features such as choice, meaning that the ending will depend on the choices that you make throughout the game. I'm not spoiling anything, but this is one game that I advise making multiple saves for. It also takes away the map screen "hub spots" of its predecessor. The story and character development has remained solid throughout the game series as a whole, which many games do not accomplish. The ending of this one has a couple of twists to it, so don't take too much at face value.
All in all I've really enjoyed this simple Space RPG. This one, being my favorite in the series, might leave you with mixed emotions depending on the ending you get.
I'm a bit sad that I'm reviewing the last game, but eventually all good things come to an end. I rate Sol 10/10, and the series as a whole, 8/10.
Please keep up the good work, Devs.

My wife and I are always looking for games to play together. This is a really fun co-op opportunity for couple-gamers like us. Fractured Space is our first MOBA-style game and I highly recommend it.  The squad matchmaking interface is easy and works well. If you find a friend or two to play with you, even better! Teams of 3-5 (the max) can do really well. The ships to choose from are not 'better' than each other - they represent different playstyles and tactics which complement each other.  Unlocking new content is a bit slow, each match lasts 20-30 minutes, and it will take about 7-10 matches to earn a new ship. The ship prices are listed in order of newest-release (most expensive) to oldest (cheapest). Don’t be fooled though, old ships are extremely fun to play and compliment any team well. When you start the game, you are given wide variety of fun ships to try. Gameplay itself is fast and very satisfying. There are plenty of tips and tricks to learn along the way – I would say one of the most important is to use the cover the environments offer. The maps are beautiful, but they offer more than just a visual, they are places to hide and tactical opportunities! Know when to run, ‘death’ has a high penalty and will put you out of the game for at most 60 seconds (which can turn the tide of a battle for your allies). Each ship has a unique armor rating, and armor can be destroyed in combat with either weapons or abilities. If you shoot the damaged, unarmored sections of a ship, it will do about triple damage, so aiming and timing is important. This applies to your own ship too, so turn your broken side away from the oncoming fire. Try it out, it’s co-op experience is worth the time!

I see that you've stumbled upon my very own review.  Here I will give my personal opinion about the game and why I recommended it.
Let's start with the pros of the game:
Firstly, you must know that this game will test your limits. It will inevitably make you rage more than once, (Because you decided to do something you'd probably regret later). That being said, the RNG is real in this game. Yet, the unique mechanic it presents is truly amazing. You'd be more focused on your heroes mental status equally to their physical. This has a lot of ups and downs for your heroes. Will they be courageous against the horrors of the dungeon? Or will they fall to their hopelessness? Who knows? Only your actions will tell.
Second, the wide range of characters and their own unique quirks, stories, and personalities show a lot of variety for everyone. Do you like taking a noble leper on your journey? Or maybe a skilled bounty Hunter. The choice is yours. And with the workshop community adding more. You'll be happy to hear that you'll always find someone new.
Third, the ancestor. The ancestor who is the narrator of your journey. Gives you various amounts of comments during your adventures. Such one could be "A moment of clarity in the eye of the storm."  Or "Anger is power unleash it!" These little comments adds flavor to the dark and foreboding atmosphere, and seems to be suited right for it.
Fourth, the music. The darkest dungeon soundtrack has a handful of music for you to enjoy whilst slaying the monsters of the dungeon. The music can gain intensity when fighting bosses or stalking in the shadows. That being said, the music shows you the danger you're in and how dark it can get. And with each region having it's own soundtrack. You'll find yourself  not only enjoying the victory screen, but enjoying the sound of it as well.
And finally, the art style. The art style is very dark and gritty looking. Luckily if you're not into that. The mods from the community will give more of a lighter look. I digress, the art style of the enivornment, enemies, and heroes make the player feel like they are indeed in some dark world. And that they must relinquish the evil they're in. This shows they did a well job setting the mood of the world for the players.
Now on to the bad:
RNG.
You hear all the time in the review section. "The RNG! It's the RNG!"
And yes, the game is RNG. You will rage because you lost a hero to some b******t RNG. And that's why this game is getting negative reviews. The RNG. And of course it's to no surprise. Can you imagine having a full party then losing it to wilbur because he stun locked you? Yeah, RNG.
Repetition.
There's no surprise that this pops up. You grind, grind, and grind... Just so you can get to the darkest dungeon and (maybe) lose your heroes. In which you will try again and again.  Yada, yada, yada. You can see where this is going.
Difficulty?
Yup it's hard. The game punishes the player severely, having no quarter giving what so ever. Heart attacks, blights, bleeds. There so many things in the players way. And of course, the RNG makes it worse. It takes a while until the player can get more experienced with the game. And until that happens. The player will most likely suffer.
The end.
What do you think? Is this game to your taste? Will you be one of many who traverse the darkest dungeon? If so, I wish you the best of luck on your journey.
Personally, I love this game. It has great art and unique mechanics. But the endless complaints of RNG will sadly be this games downfall. No matter. I'd still consider this game my favorite. I wonder if anyone of you will too.

Note: Obviously, all info is only as up to date as this review's posted/last edit date.
TerraTech is a simple and cartoonish sandbox game, one of many created during the sandbox fever that gripped Steam so recently. You build vehicles from parts you get by killing other vehicles, and the campaign is one giant endless gladiator match where you shoot enemies, steal stuff, do missions, level up, rinse and repeat. Each part belongs to one of four corporate factions, with most of them having one particular aspect of the game they do very well:
GSO - Starter faction, very balanced with a bit of everything
Venture Company - Exploration and mobility
GeoCorp - Heavy mining and industrial processing equipment
Hawkeye Private Military Company - Advanced weapons and combat
The faction a part belongs to only influences its paint job and which missions you might unlock it by doing. Every part can be used on every vehicle, and not even the AI enemies tend to stick to one faction's parts when spawning in. I have found that the best build results from mixing all factions in approximately equal numbers, though for specific jobs I'll go with the company that does it best.
You wander around an infinitely procedurally generated, and honestly extremely bland and boring world full of resources, enemies and treasure scattered in such a uniform manner that exploration for fun is almost completely pointless. If you've seen one square mile of this world, you've seen the whole thing.
This leaves the main fun aspect of this game on building and fighting. I play this game fairly frequently because I rather enjoy the freedom of mixing and matching parts and fighting my own way. I consider this to be the game's one redeeming quality, as without the construction system TerraTech would be insufferably dull. However, even this gets tedious after a while, because though there are lots of parts, most of them are redundant. For example, Payload Studios seems to think that the one thing us gamers have a raging hard-on for is headlights. To wit, there are about 12 different light blocks in the game, across all factions, and pretty much all of them are just "shine in a cone in one direction" deals. I could almost forgive them for this if lights had ANY BEARING ON GAMEPLAY, but not only are nights never, EVER dark enough to require you to use lights, they're all so damned short-ranged you couldn't possibly make any constructive use of them anyway.
Missions are as grindy as they get, and reek of extremely basic random generation. Go here, shoot a guy, get a crate drop of♥♥♥♥♥♥you don't ♥♥♥♥ing need because you've already got 3000 max-tier GeoCorp heavy armor blocks from shooting the useless hulking masses of free resource this game calls enemies.
There is exactly one point in the game I felt that I accomplished something major, that I had truly advanced, and that was when I got the Megaton Cannon for the first time. A Megaton cannon is a weapon from the GSO that takes up a 2x2x2 cube of space and inflicts psychotic damage in a game full of mediocre pea-shooting lasers and mortars with 20 feet of range that never hit. Once I had them, I was never again challenged in a fight. I've made all my kills with them since then, and have never had any need to change my craft to do anything better.
The fact that weapons aim themselves, and you can't control them manually even if you wanted to, is cancerous in a game that already lacks combat depth.
Despite being overpowered and able to one-shot most enemy techs (the name for vehicles in this game), I still had to spend hours grinding through boring missions to very slowly earn XP and unlock higher-tier parts. In addition, the order in which you unlock parts is completely arbitrary and often rage-inducing. Sure, it's good the best weapons are difficult to unlock, but why in the hell do we have to wait until we've killed 500 GSO techs before we unlock basic flight gear. Venture Co actually won't give you hover plates until you've maxed out your xp on them. Hover plates. For hovercraft. Things that might be useful 10 minutes after you start the game, but have no damned business taking 10 hours to unlock.
To unlock a faction, you first have to have an encounter with them, which gives you the Tier 1 license. These encounters are incredibly rare and the game gives you no indication as to how you can work toward getting that faction faster. You're just halfheartedly slapped in the face and told to go grind for a few hours while the RNG decides when you get to have fun doing what you want to do.
That's probably one of the biggest problems I have with this game. No matter how good you are or how hard you try to do one particular thing, the game forces you along an awkward and random progression path if you ever hope to build big techs. The combat is some of the weakest I've ever seen, with auto-aiming weapons missing constantly if the enemy has the good sense to move half an inch per second. None of the weapons have tactical niches that make them better in some situations over others, the exact depth of weapon strategy in this game is "melee weapons are strong, ranged weapons have range." And again, post-Megaton cannon, forget about trying ever again.
Before anyone thinks that I'm raging off because I haven't given the game enough of a chance, I say to you that 20+ hours is plenty. I've fully unlocked all factions except Hawkeye, which I have only one tier left to unlock. This game is simply not ready to be called a full game yet.
This is to the developers. I can admit that I had fun with it, but this game needs a LOT more work before it's ready, so I can't recommend it at the moment.Retool your old factions to make them actually interesting. Give us the chance to decide what path we want to take, so if we want airplanes before factories we can damn well have them. Overhaul the combat so it's actually interesting to fight enemies. Stop filling the world with gigantic wimp enemies that give you thousands of dollars of resource after a one-shot kill. Optimization is also dreadfully necessary as the framerate declines rapidly after playing for a time. Make terrain generation interesting so we can explore and actually enjoy the experience.
You've created such a broad foundation for what could be one of the most interesting and creative video games ever made, but after all the time you've put into it it would seem that you haven't focused on depth, which is what it really needs.
EDIT 1 | March 9, 2017
A handful of updates have been released and I noticed the game's running better on my computer. There's also some new mission variety, and the massive oversaturation of parts from giant enemies has been mitigated by making parts less likely to survive being part of a craft that is destroyed. The dev team shows no sign of slowing down, so though I'm not ready to recommend I think it's worth mentioning that the game is constantly improving. If they follow through with their vision, I can't imagine I won't change to a positive review.
EDIT 2 | April 17, 2017
Creative mode has been added, and I'm officially ready to recommend this game. The old paid-for sandbox mode is still there and, in most ways, still worth checking out for those who want to support the devs. But allowing people who bought just the normal game to experience creative fun is, in my eyes, an overdue but still greatly welcome addition that proves Payload studios didn't actually intend to lock content behind a paywall, instead providing early experimental weapons to people willing to give more financial support, a move I believe to be in good faith. Excellent to know the devs still care, and despite being far from perfect I now heartily recommend the game to anyone who likes creative, under-development games with developers who don't give up on their ideas and loads of great things to come.

This is a very good game, i found it by watching a youtuber, and since i am a big fan of "building" and creative games, i decided to give it a chance.. I was not left dissapointed.
The game is basicly a cube-based game where you build land and eventually, air vehicles. After a little while it will through tutorials show you exactly how to build a base, which allow you to craft your own parts.
Thers factions in the game too, at the moment not even half have been implemented, and one lacks quest, but they are working. You have the basic one, GSO, which revolves around some rather basic designs, guns, more guns, blocky designs and it has most of the items used for factories.
Geocorp is the industrial faction, revolving around melee, giant builds, and harvesting resources.. As well as enemies. They tend to be FAR bigger than everybody else. Venture is basicly the "racing" faction. Fast, lightly armored vehicles. Nuff said.
Hawkeye, i think they're called, are the "hunters". They build some rather interesting things, use railguns, bikes, cannons. If it works in their favor, they probally use it.
The gameplay is pretty enjoyable, wonky at the right times, smoot where it needs to be, and punishing you for mistakes when it is prudent. Yet it never truly takes it all away.
So, lets look at pro's and cons:
Pros:
You can basicly design ANYTHING you want, ofcourse withind the limits of the game. Want a solid brick with mortars? What about a flying falic co(ck)pter? Well, go ahead, the game will allow it, with a bit of work.
No such thing as perfect aim. All shots are auto-aimed, at center of enemies cockpit, which make for some really solid fights.
Positioning is key, certain weapons handle a certain design better than others. Some need range, or speed to work.
Limits are basicly not there, but they are still implemented in a way, you dont want to build a oversized machine, you have no reason to.
Amazing devs who listen and cares about the community and player base, want proof? Look at the steam discussions.
Cons: Under development, it has bugs, some balance issues, but nothing truly game breaking.
So all in all, do i recommend the game? Yes, and i will probally be playing it for a long time to come.

Quite a great game. Unforunately, even after months of patching, many bugs still exist that can hamper the experience: the game is prone to lock-ups, animations (doors opening, windows shattering, etc) often break, and so on. Despite the many technical foibles, the tactical gameplay remains engaging and addictive.
From the beginning, every encounter is volatile. Enemies are immediately more dangerous than in the previous installment and engagements are decided by hard advantage swings; a battle will rarely last more than a couple of turns due to how both XCOM and the aliens are tuned to be overpowered. This is in contrast to the first game and, from what I've read, it has resulted in mixed opinions but I found myself enjoying it. Unlike the first game, XCOM 2 often gives players the initiative: the concealment mechanic and mission timers force players to be more aggressive by punishing the popular overwatch-turtling that EU rewarded. This need for aggressive positioning, combined with the overpowered balancing, provides tension to each mission by asking the player to make hard in-the-moment decisions. The fun of XCOM 2 is walking this tightrope between a well-oiled machine that does everything as planned and being totally blindsided and in tatters in a matter of one or two bad moves.
I have minor gripes with the gameplay (like how XCOM units in concealment can't have their overwatch set off unless that concealment is broken whyyyyyy did you just watch your friends die you had a shotgun you could have done something nooooo) and the number of bugs is inexcusable (many of the most popular reviews on here are centered solely around how the bugs hamper the experience and I can 100% understand where they are coming from) but it's still probably my favorite game to come out this year. The character customization, the procedurally generated maps, the mission variety...it's all very good.

Age of Empires IV is coming out and after the disappointment of Dawn of War III I feel it's important for me to get my thoughts out in time for Relic to change their formula before destroying this franchise too.
This game was a gem if you started with it like I did. I prefer it to AoE II, but had I started with AoE II my preference would probably be different. The general consensus seems to be that AoE II felt more dynamic. The maps were larger allowing different tactics such as flanks and the battles needed more micromanagment which could make a difference between victory and defeat even when you were outnumbered. AoE III automated a lot of the game and made it simpler for new people to manage armies, economies and upgrades. This could have been seen as a good thing had they increased the population cap and let you do more complicated war tactics, however it instead streamlined the game mostly into rushing in the second age. All of that said I have spent over 300 hours in this game before I bought it on steam and continued playing it here. The enjoyable part of this game that most of the AoE II players feel like they lost out on was the feeling that they created an empire and went to war with competing empires. They don't feel like a little skirmish, they feel like all-out war (AoE II moreso than AoE III) and that's what brings me back to this game. As soon as you join a league or go online people will rush and that removes most of the fun of building and maintaining your empire in the midst of a war you are intent on winning.
Relic is making Age of Empires IV, which I would be excited about 10 years or so ago. Dawn of War was amazing and Company of Heroes was pretty good too. DoW II and CoH II however were not quite as enjoyable and DoW III (which promised a return to basebuilding) was unfortunately more disappointing than both of them. I am nervous about AoE IV so I am writing this as a list about what you have done well and what you could improve on for AoE IV hopefully people agree:
Overall Relic has made a lot of games that I have enjoyed countless hours in, but the older stuff has always been what I go back to. Please let AoE IV break your streak and be a really large, slow-paced, empire building game.

This game has some of the chilliest guitar songs ever; it’s almost worth the buy for the soundtrack. The game is an action RPG on paper, but plays more like an old Legend of Zelda game sans the free roaming world map. You continually discover new weapons you can pay to upgrade. There is a leveling system, but all gaining a level does is grant a few hitpoints and give you a new potion slot. These “potions” are your upgraded stats. You can mix and match different passive effects depending on which potion you have equipped.
The plot stars "The Kid" who finds himself displaced after a word ending event know as "The Calamity." All known survivors from his homeland are dead save one old man who serves as the narrator from the beginning to the end. The BRILLIANT narration of the old man adds a whole new level to the nuanced plot.
The game difficulty can be catered to the individual player by adding "idols" to each level. Each of the 10 idols make the game harder in some distinct way. Activating all 10 at once can make the game brutally hard if you feel yourself becoming bored.
Overall, a super enjoying experience, and an obvious classic.

There are a few good things about Trove as well as a few bad things. Let's start off with the good news.
•
- You can easily lose track of time with this game.
•
- Styles—basically skins for your gear—are almost entirely made by the players of Trove
•
- the mechanics in Trove are solid and they work as they should.
•
- Three of Trove's developers are also members of the largest club in the game, Voxel Busters, and they won't hesitate to participate in chat and such, making them easy to talk to.
•
- Sounds are clear and distinctive, nothing wrong there.
•
- The game LOOKS nice, which is always a plus.
•
- This game isn't finished—things are always being moved around, so patches roll in every Tuesday morning. Only hotfixes occur on days other than Tuesday.
They do a lot right, huh? In constrast, there are a fair amount of things that Trove does wrong. If an item has
on it, that means the item isn't specific to Trove, but to all games that Trion manages (Defiance, Trove, ArcheAge, RIFT, Devilian, etc.).
•
- Trove isn't easy on the FPS, especially when it comes to having a lot of players in a small area. I remember a few streamers with some godlike machines being astonished that they were getting only 5-15 FPS when throwing a pinata party.
•
- Tying back into the first point, there is not much flexibility when it comes to video settings. You can't configure a lot of video settings.
•
- Let's face it; the servers running Trove are bad. I have never gotten a ping below 70 in Trove, and I have over 1.5k hours spent on the game (I switched to the Glyph launcher some time ago instead of running from Steam). The servers are laggy and I'm just used to it now. Actually, it might not even be the servers. It could be how players are connected. Whatever it is, getting a low ping is not possible.
•
- This one's not pertaining to lag, but to general server issues. Sometimes, when you go to enter another world, you get disconnected immediately. Maybe your actions are either delayed or completely dropped.
•
- Especially with this new Mantle of Power expansion, the game has become pretty dependent on RNG, or random number generator. The problem with such a high about of RNG is the lack of guaranteed progress. You can spend hours grinding and have it wasted simply because RNG wasn't in your favor. You could spend minutes grinding and have it boost your level significantly simply because RNG was in your favor. There's no correlation between effort and results when it comes to RNG.
•
- The Trove developers seem to focus on adding new content a lot. That's great and all, but all of this new stuff bogs down the game and its performance. It feels like the need for optimization is growing while the occurrence of optimization is shrinking.
•
- I get that these games are not easy to maintain. They are complex games that need a lot of attention. Developers are the only ones who can give Trove the attention it needs. They also need to fund themselves, be it putting food on the table, paying bills, or whatever use they have for money. Even with all that, this game seems very eager and obnoxious when promoting its goods that cost money. For example, take a look at the new Gems system. You can use a Booster to increase the chances of a Gem being upgraded (RNG). The best non-premium booster gives you a 3x level up chance. The only premium booster gives you a 40x level up chance. That is a HUGE advantage.
Is this game worth your time? I'd say it is. It is very fun. It's got strengths and it's got weaknesses.

Assassins Creed Unity. Well, what can we expect? After finishing it after almost 50 hrs, i can safely say, it is another Assassins Creed game.
If you like the gameplay mechanics of the previous games, you will find in Unity another great game of the Series.
The graphics are astonishing. Yes, you need quite a good rig to really run that game on Ultra settings, but if you can, it just looks beautiful. Only downer is the 30 fps lock (thanks to the consoles and the laziness of the devs) and the fact that the "borderless window resolution" for gamers with 2 Screens seems to be broken. But both is managable and the beatiful look of the game conceals those problems.
As i said, the gameplay is the usual Assassins Creed formula. Which isn't necessary a bad thing. I myself always liked the free running and climbing, the hidden kills and the stealth. It is up to your personal decision.
A shame that the devs put no naval warfare in the game and the critic the devs earned was well deserved. The naval warfare was the highlight of Black Flag. It was really well executed. But how could the devs add Naval Warfare to a game that basically only plays in Paris? I think it is quite impossible. Instead of the Naval Warfare, the developers put a lof of effort into the scenery and the city Paris itself.
The city feels very authentic and if we can believe what the developers said, Paris should be very accurate to its real counterpart.
In no other Assassins Creed game the city and the citizens felt so alive and real. I have to say that i was really impressed. The citizens do so many different things and don't just run through the streets like in the previous games. They paint, they play violin, couples run hand in hand through the streets and watch theatre. So many different things can be seen if you just run through streets. For the first time you really feel like you are in a real city and not in a computer program that puts people on the streets because they are needed for gameplay.
Many people that do a lot of things cause, of course, some problems :) Since the last patch the "floating" of people through the air is almost gone. Here and there you sure see some tho.
Just like the people and city, the audio and sounds are good as well. The soundtrack of Jesper Kyd is really missed since AC: Revelations. The soundtrack was never as good as when Jesper Kyd made the music. Nontheless the music is OK and the ingame sounds are pretty good. They enhance the already good flair of a lively Paris.
What really annoyed me on the sound is ever repeating of said lines. You go through the streets and hear ever 50 meters the same line in french. It is really annoying. Some goes to the accent of the english spoken textes, Somehow they have British accent. It is very annoying since we are in France and not in Britain. It really killed the flair a bit. It wasn't necessary to let them all speak with french accent, but the British accent doesn't really fit into the game one bit.
The characters are kinda bland. Like in every AC game you meet a huge variety of historc persons and you interact with them and sadly, like in most games they are kinda bland. Devsprobably did it to♥♥♥♥♥♥nobody off? I don't know. Except of Napoleon, who had a bit fire in him and some good lines, the rest were not that great.
The main characters aren't bad, but they aren't very good either. In the end Arno is a normal guy that you can easily identify yourself with. Elize, well. I can't really say what's up with her. She kinda annoyey me. She isn't really like the usual Damsel in distress. But somehow her thickheaded behaviour annoyed me quite a bit. Maybe i can't cope with strong willed women xD
The content is huge. Like, really huge. Many, many sidequests. A lot of chests and collectibles to open and find. So if you are up to collect em all, you will have a lot of fun. A lot of districts to explore. Which you have to explore the usual AC style. Climb up the biggest building around and synchronize with it :) It was fun climbing up the Pantheon or the Louvre.
The combat is like always. Very good. Finally you don't feel like a killing machine anymore. Every group of enemies beyond 3 or 4 guys bring you in big trouble. The counter system is still there but it isn't as easy to counter every attack and so you will get a lot of hits. Needless to say that Arno won't survive as long and as many hits before he dies. So the fleeing and vanishing plays a way bigger role in this game. And for me it feels good.
The weapons come in a huge variety which all influence your gameplay style. Sword and pistol, rifle, heavy weapon or long weapon. All have their own arsenal (which is huge btw) and their own attacks and pros and cons. With a gue axe you hit harder but you are also slower and so on and so forth.
Overall i really liked the combat. It feels more challenging now without sacrificing the usual AC finishers and overall sword fights.
The climbing is the usual AC. It is really well executed. With the usual confusing moves arno does once in a while. How many times did i sprint over the streets and all of a sudden Arno just jumped on the wall and then into the Seine while i screamed "NO NOT THERE!" In the end you deal with it after some time. The easy climbing down is a nice addition btw.
The story itself is meh. It isn't really that great. The "road of redemption" sort of story. Wasn't really that good, but at least easy to follow. It never got really tense or a dramatic plot twist. So there is a lot of improvement in that department.
Thank god, the devs but as less as possible of the modern world plot in there. It is still there, but it is really a minimum. They should finally cut that crap out at all. It is annoying.
The Multiplayer.... yea it is there, but it doesn't feel very good or necessary at all.
The before i finish that review, i, of course, have to say something about the state the game once was. The horrible graphic bugs and bad performance issues are a no go. So are the app you need to get some bonuses. To throw the game out in a buggy state like it was is a no go and after the ♥♥♥♥♥torm Ubisoft got for that fact (and some others) they hopefully listen. The fact that they granted us the first DLC won't conceal the fact that the game sucked at the start.
So despite the "mixed" user reviews of this game, i personally recommend the game. If you liked the previous AC games, it will give you 40 or more good hours of gameplay.
I don't regret that i bought the game. I had a lot of fun.

So I just beat XCOM 2 recently.
Second serious attempt.
Ironman Commander.
And the more I think about it, the less I can recommend this game to everyone in general, especially at 50-60$.
I don't recall if I played the Enemy Within/Unknown on Impossible, but I know I didn't Ironman it, so this one seems easier from the start, at least when it doesn't outright cheat.
Unless you go Legend difficulty, then the game gets real hard real quick (Like, the very first mission has twice as many enemies and you are running in to sectoids like 5 missions earlier than you should).
Overall it's solid and remains one of the best turn-based tactical games on the market, but it has its fair share of flaws, annoyances and bugs.
But before reading further, know that it is overall an enjoyable game if you like the genre, and I recommend checking it out if you liked Enemy Within / Unknown, especially if it's on sale for 20 or 30$.
Just be prepared for some bullpoop.
If you didn't play the previous game, I'd suggest checking that one out first, since it's less expensive and probably more enjoyable and stable.
Getting into why I can't recommend this game to people not already interested / invested in the recent XCOM franchise...
The last 2 or 3 cinematics would freeze the video (though audio was fine, and the game would advance) and the last mission crashed on me once.  Nothing major, a minor annoyance, but the cinematic is youtube-able, and the crash didn't wipe my data, so I'm not upset about that.
The DLC is fun but lacks clarity.
The content is great, but if you don't know what the DLC missions are, and that they are the only missions that are not time-sensitive, they can end your ironman run when they pop up, especially if it's your first game of XCOM 2 - which happened to me.
They are balanced well enough for an early game party, until you get to the last fight, when it's nothing but unbalanced bullpoo.  Having a squad of 3 +2 special NPCs, all with lowest-tier gear go up against a sectopod is what ended my first ironman run, and I had an even better start then the one I completed the game with (there was some cheating targeting bull that didn't help too, see the next 2 issues).
One of the more uncommon bugs I ran into that is potentially game-breaking in an ironman run is enemies having vision and LoS through walls.
Yes windows and doors exist and most walls can be shot through and destroyed, but some structures are invulnerable and windowless, and when the enemy can see and shoot you through those walls and you are unable plan for that or even return fire, that is plain cheating and can cause you to lose squad members.  I had one Viper shoot a poison cloud through an indestructable wall that poisoned 4 of my squaddies and a VIP pretty early in the game.
On a related note, on missions where additional enemies are added to a fight (which is many of them), they are allowed an immediate move, but not an action.
Which is fine.  But they are added to a fight, and move, as the first part of the enemy turn, before the existing enemies you made your tactical decisions for, have their action.  So all those guys you have on overwatch covering themselves, or an overextended squadmate, against the low health hostile aiming his shot, will be wasted on enemies that are not an immediate threat to your squad, and you will lose squadmates to that issue.
Certain ability usage uses a completely different input scheme than the most common inputs, so it is very likely when you are looking to pick a different target, or change targeting, you will give a command for a character to run in and take a melee swing, or other action, you did not intend to take.  VERY dangerous on ironman runs.
Wounds seem arbitrary.
I've had squaddies with 15+ health finish a mission having taken only 2 points of damage and needing to sit out 15 days to heal, while squadmates on the same missions with 13 health finish 2 pips left and are ready to go again in 3-5 days.
Pacing is weird (I didn't like it)
Almost every mission is time-limited (to one or two days) and super-mandatory to attempt (and succeed at).
There's no balance of "Is this mission worth it?  Do I really need the reward it gives?" and letting the player take a moment to not have to do a mission immediately and finish his upgrade that needs half a day to complete.
And the time spent in the overworld researching and contacting countries and building is shorter than it should be in between those missions.
Early game shortly after you start scanning something, you will have to take care of a mission.  And it only gets worse in the mid-game.
You can't enjoy the fruits of your labor as much, since you have to sit there putting out 5 missions worth of fires before you can finally finish anything and start new research (which you have to do to advance the story).
What's more, if you have a good start, you can research end-game weapons before you're even in the mid-game.  But if you have a bad start, you are missing so much that you can never catch up as the mission failures start cascading hard.
The end game conversely has almost no missions pop up, so if you need something you are sitting at HQ scanning for it.  And considering how rare Elerium cores can be, if you need to farm a few, you're going to be waiting a long time.  (Though you should probably have just enough to cover needs by end game, thankfully).
The pricing of Crew members via HQ is prohibitive until mid game and impractical until end game.
Supplies are immensely valuable, and needing to drop 100+ on a scientist, engineer or squad member is a waste early game when you actually need them, but can't afford them and need to upgrade your gear.  Especially when, for 80 intel you can get them from the black market (though that is somewhat of a waste too, but less of one).
The variety of mission styles is woefully small.  It's adequate enough, but misses out on some good opportunities.
Basically the missions you will run into are:
-Protect something
-Extract the VIP
-Blow something up
-Hack Something
-Protect the resistance base personnel
That's it.  And most of those missions have the secondary objective of "Kill all hostiles" for a proper reward.
On top of that, due to the way concealment and vision works in the game along with the prcedural generation of maps (which is alright but not that special), the few missions where you don't have to kill everything, don't encourage smaller squads or allow for stealth missions or assassination missions or a multitude of better designed missions, so you end up killing everything anyway.

Mixed review for a game I have played kind of a lot since I can't play Terraria on my Apple desktop (but that is material for another review).
I am a big fan of this genre for the possibilities it can/could offer, there's a lot you can do, quests, surprising environments, tools and interesting crafting ideas.
Now this is where I believe Starbound has not hit the target (yet) in my honest opinion.
It has good starts of ideas, but in order to get some of the features offered by the game, you gotta watch a walkthrough or look it up online, or you're gonna be clicking and tapping all the keys of your keyboard for several minutes like an idiot.
It is not totally intuitive in that regard.
There's a try at a tutorial in the first hours of gaming, on your "Journal", which I assume is where the developpers want the source of information/quests/guidebook for moving forward to be, and I get that this is an early access release but I've had the game for almost a year now I reckon. I find it kind of a letdown to not include what could be the motivator here after so long. It brings a "Now what?" feeling.
Given, once you have looked up online that there are different sectors which have different levels of difficulty (monsters, ore distribution, weapons and objects, etc.), you can go for it and craft the required items to summon the boss which allows you access to more ore/weapons/armor/planets, and that can take a lil while and put your head in the game for a few more hours.
After doing all this exploration, you kinda start stumbling across planets that look similar to that one you already visited like 4 planets ago, or, if you're like me and you did use the set as a home feature, looking like your home-planet, and the only thing remaining is collecting, maxing up your vines to make bandages, your coal for fuel, collecting all the fruit/tree seeds existing, crafting, farming etc.
And again, if you're like me and you don't play in Multi-player mode, it gets meh after a while.
Because it has been on Early access for so long, exploring new planets is not always as exciting, especially if you've already seen all the biomes and dungeons available for now, you can easily notice their pattern and/or easily cheat by digging a way in closer to things to loot or digging around to avoid it etc., ditto for boss monsters or villages/houses/camps.
It just gets a tiiiiiny bit repetitive.
One big positive point that I would like to stress on the music though. I have a sweet spot for Story/Quest/Chara dev and games OSTs and to be honest, I could listen to the soundtrack all day long.
And a silly positive point: the Frog merchant with a buncha dogs in his/her house (wish I could've adopted one as a pet).
All in all, I guess if/when the official game is released, there should be improvement coming our way.
Or so I hope, because I do like sandbox modes, but right now, this version lacks a spark of interest, of novelty, to make me recommend it.
