I picked this game up on sale purely due to the nostalgia I had toward previous lego games (mainly Lego Star Wars). Those games were great in two ways. They had a lot of replayability for guy like me who likes to unlock all the characters. They also had a great sense of humor in regard to the source material.
Let me explain that sense of humor a little. None of the characters ever spoke. They made sounds and displayed various cute animations thus showing the plot of the movie rather than telling us anything. As a result, those old games were great.
While Lego the Hobbit does maintain its replayability, it lacks any of the sense of humor of the original games. Long cutscenes clutter the entire beginning of the game (That's all I've played), all of which are narrated. The narration takes away from the original style and replaces the feel of the original games with something that very clearly feels like I'm just being shown a worse version of the film.
Furthermore, the old Star Wars games cost less than this and covered three movies (and 6 if you got the complete pack).  So if you do the math, $19.99 for a bad game covering 1 movie? Not a good deal.
In conclusion, I give this 3/10. If you really enjoyed the movie and either read or don't want to read the book, this may be a not awful way for you to get some more out of the franchise maybe? But only if you really must have more. Otherwise, avoid this purchase.

Truly groundshattering. Though I beat the game in 20 minutes, I could easily see myself playing this game for more than 300 hours. The game has amazing replay value, and though your decisions do not change the ending, every playthrough will leave you wondering what you could have done differently.
The game confidently struts into morally gray areas and makes you question your own ethics. The challenge is in deciding whether you should continue, or simply end your miserable evening. Should you have another glass of wine? A seemingly mundane decision, but one that carries world-altering repercussions in this game. Can you resist the temptation of double-dipping your bread, and potentially contaminating your soup? Could you handle the thought of lying to your date about your double dipping habits, should you choose to travel down the path of ultimate sauce corruption? Such maddening thoughts would bring dread to the most stalwart of dinner-havers.
The horrific potential consequences of your actions are bound to keep you up for many nights. Did you do the right thing? Maybe you gazed at the clock one too many times, causing irreparable damage to your neck. Perhaps you chose to forego cooling your soup slightly and burned the roof of your mouth. Maybe you even did that on purpose; the masochistic behavior of a true non-conforming renegade. Yes, it's true, that you knew the whole time you were shoving piece of bread after piece of bread into your mouth that you were dancing with death. Like a marionette, swaying to the symphony of the all-powerful carbohydrates; their promise of deliciousness cleverly luring your naive and all-too-trusting mind into a false sense of security. Little did you know the grossly unhealthy nutritional value of these baked goods would chaperone you to an early grave.
There is no end to the madness. I strongly recommend you buy this game and experience its haunting story-telling on your own. If you think you have a good understanding of how your subconscious mind works, and feel that you are in complete control over your actions and its consequences, then prepare to have your illusory world of make-believe completely ♥♥♥♥ing shattered.

I had a lot of fun playing this game in co-op, just like I mostly enjoyed LEGO Lord of the Rings. Unfortunately, I'm mostly left with negatives.
The story of LEGO The Hobbit is told like in LLOTR - original movie dialogue is used to voice the characters, while their mostly ridiculous animated behaviour makes for a humorous parody. I found that LEGO the Hobbit can't quite keep up with LOTR in that respect tough, just like the Hobbit movies seemed not quite able to capture what made the LOTR movies great. Luckily, the gameplay holds up just the same.
Compared to LLOTR, this game has some additonal character special abilities. Small characters now buddy up -- or dwarf up if you like -- with a second small party member to destroy particularly tough walls or deal damage to stunned bosses. With the slingshot, there is now another type of ranged weapon to be used in puzzles. Instead of pushing large blocks slows over checkered floors, Dwahlin, your Dwarven heavyweight, will now instead smash boulders along slides. That skill, just like the ability to mine ores, is curiously exclusive to one character throughout the whole story. And while all Dwarves can buddy up, most of them have abilities that only they possess. Combined with the fact that that the character selection wheel now accesses your inventory, you'll spend most of your time in this game swapping around the party. Even tough it's clear from some of the unique animation of the characters, that the developers wanted to give them meaning, some, just like in the movies, are left with a secondary role. One tends to wonder why the three dwarves whose sole special ability is that they can stand on top of each other, cannot fill the role of a second miner, shooter or rope-carrier.
Like in LLOTR, you'll need to make use of these abilities not just during the story missions but also when replaying a mission in free play and when attempting side-quests in the overworld. Compared to LLOTR, your access to the world until the end of the game is even more restricted, as there are seldom more than 5 characters available for you to use. This means you pretty much have to finish the story before attempting the side quests. This means that there are rarely opportunities where you can finish stuff around the world on your way to another mission and basically restricts you to exploring the world after the story is over.
The last and probably most damning point is, as other user reviews have mentioned, that the game is unfinished. It plays fine until you get to the part which is the end of the second movie and the game does not go on from there. The publisher, Warner Bros., stated that it intended to release an expansion to the game for the third movie. But this expansion is no longer forthcoming. The story ends at a cliffhanger and even though I'm sure most people know the cliffhanger is resolved, (the game being based on a children's book, it's not exaclty difficult) the player is still left with a feeling of incompleteness that will probably keep most people from going into free play mode. The hardcore collectors, however, will find lots of quests and things to do to keep them interested after the story has reached the apparent end.
Bottom line, if you're looking for more LEGO game action, just like the LEGO titles you've played before, you probably will get some enjoyment from this title. Otherwise, this game will probably miss the mark for you.

Most of this review can be summed up one way, and that's by saying this is a 1C game.
1C are Russian game publishers characteristically known for how alien their games feel. They've gotten better in recent years, but this is an old school 1C game from 2003, back when you wondered if they were from another planet. If you want to play RC Cars, you're going to have to work for it.
To get this game to work correctly, you primarily have to do two things:
- Manually set the game's framerate (otherwise it won't run properly). I suggest 60fps.
- Manually set your controller's analog senstivity AND the analog deadzone (otherwise, you won't be able to control your vehicle).
Once you do this, you'll be able to navigate the game's confusing menu system and eventually compete in a race. The game itself is pretty difficult; the cars themselves seem to almost have sort of a simulation feel to them. What this means is that any little bump in the road will often fling you wildly out of control, just like a real RC car. But, with enough finesse, you'll eventually come to grips with it.
Tracks are laid out in obtuse patterns. Early tracks follow the typical racing game format of circuits, but it's not long until 1C takes the "checkpoint race" concept in more esoteric directions, leading you down narrow dead ends and back out again. Tracks themselves take you across beaches, deserted ghost towns, mines, busy highways and active military bases.
Vehicles can be customized, but not much. Each of the four or five available vehicles have several different paint jobs, and can be upgraded in three categories: boost, engine, and tires. Upgrades cost money, which can be won by completing championship races. What you might not realize at first is that you also have to pay to enter championship races; on one occasion I spent so much on vehicle upgrades that I had grind for more money just to do the next race.
Would I recommend the game? Given that it's only $5, sure. It's not going to blow your socks off, and you might actually end up getting annoyed eventually, but it's just different enough from the norm that I think it's probably worth it.

RC Cars is a simple little racer originally released in the PS2 era. Unlike similar games, there are no weapons, it's just pure racing. There are various obstacles around the tracks to hamper your progress, and jumps and bumps to fly over.
Driving the cars is fairly easy as it's an arcade racer through and through. Most of the vehicles seem to grip well and aren't affected too much by rough terrain as in some other RC racers. The AI isn't too bad either, of course the other drivers will bash and shove you but your car isn't affected that much by this so they don't push you into a spin causing you to lost the race in the last 100 yards.
Graphically it's pretty good for a game of it's age with nicely detailed cars and tracks. It looks a little sparse compared to a modern game and some of the textures seem fairly low quality, but as I said it's and older game, so probably looked OK at the time.
Sound is decent to with the main engine sounding like a tiny engine should and plenty of ambient sounds such as waves crashing on the beach or the sound of gulls. Music however is not so good. It's not especially bad, just more of a background noise while you race.
Problems? Well when I first loaded it up I experienced the same annoying slow menus as everyone else, then when I eventually managed to get into the game my car just bounced around uncontrollably. This was the cause of much swearing and I nearly wrote this review based on that, but then I adjusted the graphics and now everything seems fine. The menus are snappy and the cars control well.
All in all this game is sort of average. Once you sort out the problems it's fun for a while. Having said that I'm not sure I'd want to pay 4.99 for it, but if you get it on sale it's fine.
BTW. I don't know if this will help anyone, but since it is and old game I  ran CPU  Killer to limit the speed of my system. The game was jerky, but the menus were more responsive and the when I got into the game the physics seemed OK. Then I just adjusted the graphics to 1920x1080, maxed everything and set frame limited to 60 rather than unlimited. I've ran it a couple of times since (without CPU Killer) and it seems fine with nice snappy menus and cars that stay on the road.

Stardew Valley is one of those games where.. if you give it an inch it'll take you a mile. There's something so incredibly relaxing about the game. Even though I've walked away from it several times I keep coming back after a while, but those times when I DO play it I go a long ways. Instead of playing a little here or a little there, if I start it up I just get sucked in and can't get away from it for at least a week or longer. It's so easy to find yourself going "just one more day, just one more day..." and the next thing you know it's now 3am and you have work in 6 hours!
People will obviously compare it to Harvest Moon or Rune Factory, and that's okay because it does have elements of both. You are doing the whole "running a farm" thing, but you also a deep mine that allows for mining (obviously) and combat with various mobs such as bats or slimes. There's also a fishing minigame that, while fun, also feels a teensy bit unfair or difficult to get the hang of for some people. If that's the case for you, there's an easy to obtain mod wish makes the fish a little (or a lot, if you want) easier to manage. Speaking of mods, since this is the PC version that is most certainly a thing that you can do! The game is fun enough in vanilla state, but there's so much modding potential, even if it's just little visual changes.
On my game, I've got a couple of small graphics replacement files to change up things like the horse or your pets. While setting the mods up for the latest version of the game, I also came upon a really cute one that swaps out the scarecrows for owls! If I'm gone from the game for a few months (which happens easily when you have a backlog in the hundreds), I like to switch up how the game looks a little. Previously, my scarecrows were cats and my horse was a dragon; now they're owls and a velociraptor! (And my cat is Carbunkle from FFXI.) However, there's also mods for changing the gameplay, as well. Including one to improve sprinklers, expand your refrigerator, and even give you a new cooking skill to level up.
Aside from growing crops or harvesting fish, you can also befriend a lively town full of people. They all feel pretty interesting, and there's now 12 available spouses for you to woo! From your stereotypical cute nerd and rude jock to a depressed drunk and reclusive writer. Most people are polite-yet-distant and a couple are downright unfriendly, but they'll gradually open up to you and it's nice to see their personalities change over time. Some people, depending on their friendship level, will also have little scenes or events you can come upon if you're in the right place at the right time. Usually, but not always, there is a chance to influence how they feel about you by making a choice when prompted. Unfortunately, this brings me to one of the game's weak spots...
A few characters, like the children or the barkeeper, don't have a lot of growth even as they become friendlier. Considering both kids are related to marriage candidates, you'd think they'd be more interested in your involvement with their lives. I think one of the best examples is Maru, whose father initially does not like you getting close to his daughter. Another issue the game can have is a feeling of stagnation the further in you get. Working towards making your farm functional and self-sustaining is one of the funner parts of the game, to me, and once you can plant a whole grove of strawberries without huring financially, or setting up a dozen brewing kegs, it can start to slow down a little.
For me, that tends to start around the third year, provided I don't go too fast and take my time. Of course, if you tire with the farm you have, you can always start up a new one. But it is certainly true that, at least in my opinion, the funnest part of the game is the first 2/3 of it. There's not an ending, per se, so it's entirely possible to keep going for upwards of 10 years. Pity your kids never grow up... or help on the farm.... or talk to you.....
Clearly, there's room for the game to improve, and late game content has been a part of the last few updates the game seen to be sure. Personally, I'm looking forwards to multiplayer so me and my ex can run a farm together! She's got almost as much time logged in this game as I have.

W.O.W. Monster grind combat meets Minecraft building and exploration.
Pros: Intriguing game world with a great co-op focus. Cons: Difficult to play solo; monsters can be repetitive to battle.

I do reccommend this game, but with two caveats: 1.) Play this game with friends, or you'll get frustrated really quickly. 2.) Don't get fixated on wiki'ing items or monsters, because the surprise of discovering them is half the fun, and you'll have loads of time to see them and possibly get sick of them.
Basic overview:
This game is the most fun when you have someone to play with, otherwise it's really difficult to progress at lower levels and getting good loot can be tantilizingly close and frustratingly difficult to get. (On this same point, it is a positively gleaming moment when you do.) This is certainly one of those games that it wouldn't hurt to be grandfathered into, or if you're the friendly type, it's pleasantly easy to ask for already online players to come to your aid and assist you in dungeon crawls.
Also, keep in mind that this game is W.O.W meets Minecraft, which means that you'll be fighting a lot of similar enemies and grinding, so this gameplay can be grating for when you are looking for a specific drop in a specific area. Don't bother trying to wiki monsters and other items, because it belittles the world and exploration is a huge part of what makes this game deep. The fighting resembles W.O.W in many ways -the party assembles and coordinates to take on bosses, etc-  but the discovery and map expansion elements were what kept me playing after I met the basic bosses and underling types.
Minor Critique(s):
The building mechanic that the game provides would be better implemented if you were allowed to have a larger Cornerstone. These are squares of material which serves as your spawn point in world, but is fully customizable and placable anywhere in the world map. It has this great little touch where decoration recipes you pick up in the Uber world stage can be placed anywhere, including club worlds, the overworld, or Cornerstones but they are only permanate in clubs and Cornerstones. The Cornerstone is the only area in which you really have meaningful building room that you can come back to, but it's so narrow that there's very few forms of architecture that are both practical and unique.
Positive Points:
Firstly, this game is gorgeous. It's a striking sight when you first open up the tutorial, and the graphics quality remains constant all through the game. The game uses a full range of colors and different "3D Pixel" sillhouttes for each class, so the visual style is simple, bright and fun.
The world gives you a minimap filled out with different biome types. When hunting for challenge missions or crafting, the biome distinctions cleverly keep the world organized and straightforward. The enemy types change with each terrain and are fun to discover. Loot is varied from territory to territory, too, which gives you some real incentives to keep looking around in every biome.
Lastly, loot is really smartly handled here too, with the game spawning a drop set for each player involved in the take down of recipe dungeons and other boss monsters.
Final Thoughts:
In summery, this game is 100% worth your time to investigate. It's free, so there's no reason not to test it out and see if you like it. There's plenty to do, at least in the first 50 hours or so, and I'd say even more so onward. There's a decent amount of play for everyone that's implemented nicely: pretty well made melee classes and casters, challenging crafting, expansive exploration, lovely sight-seeing, monster grinding, trophy collecting, and free-form building. The game can be a lot of fun in groups and with mental adjustment for grind, this can be a highly addictive and rewarding time sink. Grab some buddies and open Skype, it's time you paid this game a visit.

Realm of the Mad God is a top down free to play MMO mouse aim shooter with a simple art style. It has been around for a few years as a Flash game. You start the game easy enough, by selecting from unlocked classes such as rogue, warrior, priest, archer and so on. Each class plays the same, you fire projectiles. Have a sword? You shoot projectiles. The only difference between the classes are the stats and the equipment they can use. You can unlock more classes when you reach certain levels with the base classes. Each enemy gives you some minimal experience and leveling up will only improve your stats. There are no new spells and no choice of improvement. It all feels very dull and too simple for a MMO.
The controls are like every other mouse aim shooter, arrows to move with mouse aim and click to shoot. You have a special ability and potions too, but for the most part you can just use your normal attacks. Speaking of the mouse aim, it feels very inaccurate. I can stand still, fire the projectile and the projectile will miss even when I shouldn't. Maybe there is an accuracy stat or something. It feels odd when enemies very accurate. Luckily you are quick enough to dodge projectiles. Again, maybe its a stat and I need to have better gear, but there is nothing on the equipment that shows accuracy, just range and attack power.
There are a lot of enemies, each with different stats and attack patterns. For the most part they have enemies simply shoot at you. Most have single shots, others have double and triple spreading shots. Still some fire a sort of 360 degree bullet shield preventing anything from getting close. The bosses aren't that different from normal enemies. They just have larger sprites with other creatures swarmed around them.
There are quests in the game, but I mean that in the vaguest sense of the word. All quests seem to be kill the big monster. No one tells you to. You just do it. The game points out the direction of the big monster when you enter the location.
The maps feel a bit jumbled randomly with trees and foliage with a path drawn through the map. It just feels like lazy or quick map design and not 'randomly generated.' Some enemies will drop portals to different areas which is a fun feature, but since the areas look just thrown together its always just another randomly thrown together area. You have a mini map that will reveal more as you explore, but if you leave an area and return, you need to explore it again to show it on your mini map. At any time out in the wilderness, you can instantly warp back to the town / nexus with the click of a button.
The locations might look like a jumbled mess, but the town / nexus looks great, but its all just a big store to sell you stuff. All of the stores have items visibly showing you everything so you need to walk over them instead of having an easy to use menu. Another problem is to see the stats of the item you need to hover your mouse over the 'buy it' button. Don't accidentally click that button though. You cannot sell equipment, so you're forced to drop it or trade it with other players, but for the most part the equipment feels useless when enemies drop it all. Plus players are kind enough to just give stuff for free since everything is so abundant.
Normal games would have you kill enemies for gold, but in Realm of the Mad God, you need to buy gold with real money of course. Everything is right there in town / nexus for you to buy after a brief tutorial area. What do you buy with gold? Name changes, more characters, armor, weapons, rings, boxes with random items, keys, pets, extra storage, building materials and everything. Did I mention that when you die you lose all progress and items? So if you spend real life money into a free game and you die, you've just lost everything. Do you need gold to have fun? No. The town / nexus has plenty of people selling gold via their website for real money and it floods the chat for some servers drowning out any real discussion.
This feels like a really dull game that is out for your money. Not just that, but it seems hastily thrown together. The quick simple art style, the slow grind for experience, the awful map design, no real quests, the laggy input, and the inaccurate aiming, all makes me not want to be in the game let alone buy anything in the game with real money.

Heat Signature feels like a crazy hybrid of Hotline Miami and FTL.  The Hotline Miami comparison should be clear, but the similarities with FTL go further than the sci-fi setting.  The game features a time-slow mechanic whenever you are being spotted, and has a pause feature that allows the planning of your next action while simultaniously opening the inventory.  It feels much more like a tactics game than an action game because of this.  Mix in some strange, strategy changing loot and some rogue-lite mechanics, and you have a really exceptional package.
Music is evocative of HotMiam, but HeatSig's most impressive artistic direction is the universe scale.  I realize that the graphics are not so taxing that it would make these effects a technical marvel, but the lack of loading screens really goes a long way to depicting the scale.

Addicting, still updated, almost endless, Starbound is like Terraria, but uhh... way better. Don't get me wrong, I definately don't hate Terraria, but you can "end game" Terraria a hundred times and not even get close to the level of variety and fun you experience on a character in Starbound. I first heard about Starbound years ago, and I expected a lot from it once it was finally released. The missions were sort of bad at first, but everything else was still pretty awesome.
The new update being released soon changes many aspects of the game and adds many more as well. As of right now, there's an unstable version out that I've been playing with/without friends, and I've only found Multiplayer to be the  thing with any problems, and that's only been the game waiting a second or two after the beaming animation to actually teleport you, but that could easily have been the server for all I know.
On to unstable itself, the UI, ships, missions, crafting, ores... almost everything has changed for the better, although mining tools have almost been rendered useless, but I'm glad the Matter Manipulator has finally been given a use, and many upgrades that will probably make pickaxes obsolete anyways.
And keep in mind this is only early access. :0
Overall, uhhh… buy it.

It's more of a thought experiment than a game,  focusing on largely irrelevant actions such as eating bread or looking at your watch in order to get a feel for the character. Playing Dinner Date feels very much like acting in a play, trying to fit yourself into a predetermined role rather than letting your choices determine who your character is. It's a manner of roleplaying you don't usually see in games, and if it that sounds interesting, this might be worth a look.
Buyer beware, though; it clocks in at about twenty minutes of gameplay, and I find it to have little to no replay value, so I wouldn't recommend picking it up at full price.

Telltale's "The Walking Dead" suffers from the same weakness that most other games made by Telltale suffer: it's linear, and somewhat boring. The Walking Dead is set in a world cursed by the demons, "Screen Tearing" and "Poor FPS", in one of the several universes of this franchise. Despite how good this game looks, it is surprisingly linear: your making a decision, be it good or evil - kill Sally Lou, or leave her be - has no meaning: for if you decide to go for the Good option, someone else in the group will do whatever they need to do to make sure that the Bad option is undergone shortly before chastising you for being a ♥♥♥♥♥-less♥♥♥♥♥♥- or on the other end, where you'll choose the evil option, the exact same person from scenario 1 will chastise you for being a pussly-less, murdering♥♥♥♥♥♥
The game tries to sell itself by facading as a "Choose your own Adventure Game", when what's really offered is more along the lines of "Choose what you want to say to (x) to make them feel gooey inside, or tell them that you don't like them as a person, but offer them a lolipop so they feel all gooey inside about being hated by the One Black-Man to survive the apocalypse.
Ultimately, this game lies to your face: it hints that it has tonnes of replay value, when in reality, it does nothing to draw you into the game after buying it - you'd get a better service for your dollar by hiring a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and asking her to hug you for half of her purchased hour, and asking her to leave shortly thereafter.
If this review seems long, then that is because I'm an angry Australian♥♥♥♥♥♥who can't quite be ♥♥♥♥ed to reread his writing, but just isn't lazy enough to leave this game review-less.

Believable charterers and an excellent story that will suck you in from the minute you start playing, Telltale are very good at setting the scene for a story right from the get go, its like a choose your own adventure book, remember them? :)
You will grow VERY attached to the charterers as you play, your choices have real weight to them spamming through the dialogue to get to the action is not recommended as most of this games appeal comes from its excellently written story that brings the game alive.
Most of the action is played out through quick time events, but there is some walking around rather large areas solving puzzles, collecting items and talking to people.
Again you will grow attached to the charterers as you play, the voice acting in this game is done really well and definitely helps set the scene, it can get quite emotional at times, seriously.
I would recommend having this game in your library as it is one of those great games that will have you coming back for more, I did not play games like this till a friend gifted it to me for my birthday, now I have played most of Telltale's games and loved every one of them, would highly recommend the second series of this if you have played the first, I'm getting through it now and is just as good as the first one was :)

PARTICLE MACE looks and plays like a great arcade game from the early 80's.  As it clearly appears to be inspired by Asteroids that isn't too surprising.  However, instead of shooting the asteroids you have to smash them with a set of spheres (I'm assuming they're are the "particle mace" the game's title refers to).  Like Asteroids, the larger rocks, break into smaller ones and so on until they're finally destroyed.
The game changes things up as well by making the game arena change sizes and shapes so that at times your ship has less room to maneuver.  There are also a variety of enemy ships that attempt to kill you.  Some being tricky and others just heading straight for you.  Like Asteroids, one hit from a rock or ship kills you.  Except you only get one life (unless you're playing multiplayer) or a certain ship.
There are a variety of ships to unlock snd the ships vary by the manner in which the "mace" tags along or how the ship handles.  The ships don't play the same so  picking a different ship can make playing the game feel completely different.
There is also a bonus system in that the more of the alien ships you destroy the points you get for smashing/killing multiply.  You have to destory another alien ship within a certain amount of time or the bonus resets.  That also adds a bit of pressure attempting to maximize the bonus or hunting that alien ship to keep the bonus going.
The music is well done.  The music will start to pick up as the map shrinks and that helps ramp up the tension.
While it is enjoyable solo, it also has the option of allowing 2-4  player couch co-op (which is always a welcomed feature).  The multiplayer is set up in a way to play with friends regardless of skill level.  If one of your partners die their "spirit" passes randomly across the map and if a survior passes their "mace" through the spirit the dead player comes back to life.  That dead players don't have to sit around and wait for the game to end takes the tedium from players who may not be as skilled.  If you're looking to play something to waste a little time and have some laughs with some friends you can't do wrong by giving this game a try.
The game also offers a mission mode in which you have to complete different tasks like staying in a limited area for a certain amount of time or destroy a number of enemies before the bonus runs out.  There is also a deathmatch mode, but I have never tried it.

SUMMARY: Like the arcade games of old, this game's entire appeal comes from its gameplay and it does that very well.

It's worth the $5.99 I paid for it.  I don't think I'd pay full retail price on it though.
I didn't think the combat was as slow as a lot of people are saying.  I started as a rogue, which means light armor + fast weapons, and I didn't have any problems.  I will say that the heavier weapons are slow as hell, and good luck hitting anything with them.
I don't think some people really understand what 'slow' combat means in an ARPG.  Slow, clunky combat is games like Monster Hunter.  This isn't anywhere near that bad.
Something else people need to understand about this game is that rolling isn't that good.  It's not your best defensive and offensive counter option like it is in Dark Souls games.  Blocking is objectively better in this game, because blocking recovers faster than rolling does, allowing for superior counter attacking capabilities.  It's insanely easy to hold block and circle => backstab mobs in this game.  Easier than it is in any of the Dark Souls games.  You can also parry fish a lot of enemies for a oneshot.  Even those otherwise extremely OP 'big shield dudes', just parry their running attack.  So my suggestion to anyone not looking for 'slow' combat, to play as a rogue, and be a backstab/parry fisherman.
FYI, this game kinda is a poor man's Dark Souls, but that doesn't mean it's not a decent game for the price.  I don't think the game is terrible, it's just not very balanced.  My recommendation for this game is at a price around $10 or less.  Much more than that, and I wouldn't recommend it.

Trove is a 3d voxel-based, role playing, mmorpg. It's a game that feels like a combination of my two favourite things, crafting and looting (minecraft + torchlight 2). Now previously, my review was negative because of a few things I had noticed early on as a returning 'veteran' player. However I realize that a lot of the issues that other reviewers complain about, are actually not as bad as they may seem, and some have been and are being worked on as we speak.
Actual gameplay review will be below the upcoming section.
A major complaint you'll see when browsing these reviews is that the game was less P2W than now. I can tell you that when I rejoined the game almost 2 weeks ago, I noticed immediately that a lot of things were
locked behind paywalls, and a new gem system that was crazy expensive at very high tiers also began to deter me. But let me tell you why my mind was changed.
Classes being locked behind a paywall is indeed a bad thing in my opinion, however the current state of the game makes it quite easy to make the money to buy new classes. In fact, I was personally very surprised when I was able to buy 2 of them in like 2-3 days of regular gameplay. I didn't prioritize any particular farming method or try to manipulate the marketplace, I simply played the game, and over time I got items that people wanted, in high quantities. Thanks to the addition of the marketplace, it's now very easy to sell items and track their prices, and even without it, the trade chat exists.
Some of you may know of Warframe? One of the most sucessful F2P games of this generation? I know there's no 'perfect' F2P game, but in terms of the marketplace, Warframe is highly efficient and allows F2P players to obtain items that could only be purchased with real money. In other words, F2P and paying players can obtain the same things, both in reasonable amounts of time. Trove is VERY similar, and the more I looked at the trade chat, the more I realized the massive similarities between the two. Paid costumes, rare items, etc being bought and sold without a problem.
So in reality, F2P players in Trove can access most of the content that paid players can, however they must be able to put in the time for whatever they want. The exception to this of course, is the exclusive items that come from various paid packs.
So you might be wondering to yourself, but isn't this going to take months upon months to get to the point that a paying player would get? Not at all. Each day there are bonuses for a particular aspect of the game. Knowing this, you can utilize those bonuses to advance quickly in a particular aspect of the game. In my 11 day spree I was able to to obtain 4 extra classes, 95% of rare fishes, tons of allies, skins, etc. In all honesty, the things I obtained were things that can't be just paid for with real money. Paying players still have to grind, and at times, buy & sell items.
I need to finish this section before it becomes a rant. Is Trove P2W? No. You cannot pay to win this game as almost everything revolves around RNG (random number generation). You can however, pay to recieve some very nice bonuses which can speed up your progress to a particular item or level, or give you exclusive items.
With the most troublesome issue out of the way, you find a brilliant, colourful game that is bursting at the seams with simple, yet immensely fun gameplay with complex nuances. Classes are varied and unique, with each having a unique playstyle to cater to everyone. From doing dungeons, to shadow towers to the sky realm, each environment is complex and well designed, some bright and beautiful, others dark and gloomy; each carries its theme perfectly.
There is a lot of grinding to do especially as a totally F2P player, so keep that in mind. The gem system, while not perfect, is getting better, and I have hope that Trion will bring it to a state where players can have fairly deep progression without spending too much time grinding for no results. The recent addition of a gem upgrade karma bar is a meaningful step towards this.
Sadly this game suffers from some pretty laggy servers and it can really get annoying, as well as an under-optimized HUD which really needs to be dealt with. Framerates and ping in large groups can go from okay to horrible in a matter of seconds. On top of this, there are many classes that are either outrightly bugged or perform horribly due to server lag (mainly ranged/projectile users) so keep this in mind. However despite this, when Trove runs well, it shines.
I am amazed that I even spent this much time in the game in such a short space of time. This reminds me of Warframe in many aspects, and with how good that game is, it only speaks highly of Trove. This game is not perfect, not by a long shot, and not everyone will have the time or money to commit to this, but if you can appreciate a game that gives a challenging grind for an oh so satisfying result, look no further than Trove.
8/10 -

Had this on my wish list for a long time and finally purchased it. Firstly, this game is not for everyone. Even if you THINK you would find it fun to play a hacking game, you will become frustrated quick when you realize it takes some work to get it right. You will be given a quick introduction, some references to read (I recommend reading them) and then tested to solve problems like your own terminal being hacked. The community is helpful, but don't expect to have your hand held with "How to do it" advice. Expect only nudges to point you in the right direction.
Thus far, the game has been intense for me and I look forward to more self induced stress lol. There is something giddy about being where your not supposed to be. Then getting out before anyone knows you where there, or running out before you get caught. I like the feel of the terminal interface and the requirement that you need to be (or willing to be) comfortable with a command prompt. I have not encountered any bugs as of yet and the game is very stable on my Win10 system. The only gripe I have is some of the documentation on the in game archive servers is hard to read do to grammar/typos. Like it was translated to English from some other language. This was fine and added to the realism when reading IRC logs and stuff but detracted from my experience when I was trying to learn a little more.
I'm only 6 hrs in, as of this writing, but I am hooked enough to know that I would recommend HackNet.
It's stellar.

Strange as it may sound, especially due to all the problems this title had at launch, it's close to being my favourite Assassin's Creed of all times!

If you enjoy big open world games, definitely check this game out.

Starbound is a game that shows what AAA title games are lacking.  As a gamer I want a few thing out of a game that I buy:
1: A goodstory/concept that encourages playing through it.
2: Graphics that follow a specific art style and aren't random .PNG's found on the internet. (Not neccesarily High quality)
3: A concept in the game that makes playing it rewarding and fun to play overall.
These three concept are what I was looking for and found either in a early stage of or implemented enough to make the game fun!
So your story begining starts "Slightly" different with each race you choose. I'm a big fan of games that make your choices matter right from the get-go. (The Dragon Age series is a good example.) At the current stage fo development, this is worked upon very much but was implemented to give the impression that it will (Hopefully) be expanded upon.
You next are greated by a ship that is different in design dependent on your race and so far as I've only played three of the races (IE: The Nova-Kid race has a steampunk train engine ship that makes sense if you read the data log on the race.)
There is plenty of ores to mine and a unique system of the more dangerous the planet the more dense and rae of ores you will find.
The game also has a "Decent" tech tree design that branches out at the 5th & 6th teir. As it stands now though they have said that they are expanding upon armor and weapons.
As the developers said: “We were at a point in Starbound's development where it was already pretty fun, so we decided to release the game in beta through early access to ensure the community has a chance to help us shape the game.”
I can't agree more with this statement. Their is plenty to explore and build in the game currently and is deffinetlly worth the $14.99 listing price as I feel it is a good point to join the games development.
Now... Some of the things that need work/are broken.
The performance in some area's of the game are attrocious... Like 10 FPS on my sytem that is decent. (Its a know problem that their working on.){A simple way to double your FPS is to turn on fullbright btw}
The AI pathfinding is even worse but usually just funny and helpful as many enemies in the game can and will kill you in 2-4 hits depending on your armor.
Multiplayer is bandwidth hungry but I feel since its only in beta that getting the game to work in SP first should be priority.
Crash wise its rare and every time it has crashed it saved ALL my data and I lost zero progress/items.

This review will be in three parts: (1) The patches/how to get the game running, (2) my thoughts on the game overall, and (3) 5 reasons why or why not you should get AC: Unity.
Update: I'm not sure why some people haven't found my review useful, but I suppose keep that in mind. I would like to point out that my PC specs are as follows: FX-8350 with 16GB ram and an HD 7970
Part I:
As of patch 1.5 the game is more or less* running extremely well. Practically all bugs regarding quests/missions/co-op gameplay have been fixed. Microtransactions/Companion app walls have been almost entirely removed: You don't need to pay extra money, download something, or sign up for anything to be able to experience the full game anymore.  I believe the Dead Kings DLC is now free and included in the purchase of AC: Unity.
*Patch 1.4 forced low quality distant environment textures, and Read: For compatiblity 1-3
For compatiblity:
1. DO NOT USE MSAA! This game is poorly optimized for MSAA, seriously don't use it. (I get better FPS at 2160p no AA than 1080p 2x MSAA)
2. If you're glitching through floors, and sticking on objects then you need to lower your graphic settings.
3. Ultra-high texture quality is amazing, but it's the biggest FPS hog next to MSAA (I think it's because it's linked to the hair physics)
4. Start the game with your desktop resolution as low as you can set it, for some reason this can give a huge performance increase.
5. If you're using an AMD GPU, DO NOT try to use any custom AMD game settings (if you do you can cause the game to crash on start up.)
6. If your game won't start up read 5. then verify game cache, if that doesn't work re-install.
7. DO NOT USE MSAA! (They might fix this, but I wouldn't hold my breath)
Graphic optimization:
1. Hair looks really good, but also bad if you play on a high-ish resolution with no AA. I recommend using 1080-1440p with FXAA. I honestly think this game looks worse in 2160p than 1080p (buildings look nice though.)
2. Shadow texture quality on Low is a must, if you need extra FPS, and looks very simlar to High.
3. I think Ultra-high texture quality is worth it, but a few times I had to lower it to get OK FPS. Evironmental quality looks pretty good even on low.
Part II:
Main-Story(ies):
1. This game probably has the best personal historical story out of all of the AC games to date.
2. The assasin's brotherhood story is garbage.
3. The modern outside-of-the-animus story doesn't exist.
Minigames/Side-missions:
1. Assasination missions finally have decent plots now, If you pay attention to dialog and the database entries they can be really enjoyable.
2. Murder mysteries, these are awesome. I found myself getting out a notebook and jotting things down to remember what clues I found, or who said what.
3. There a few others, all puzzle orientated.
Co-op:
1. Co-op missions have unique stories which are a lot of fun. They are playable solo, with friends or strangers. They get repetative quickly, but there are a lot of different ones to chose from.
Graphics:
1.Graphically this game is amazing. It's really hard to comprehend the scope of this game's world. I would really compare this game's world to GTA:V, but more compact and with detailed interiors and exteriors.
2. The faces, hair, facial movements are stupid good.
Gameplay:
1. Very fluid, being able to freerun down things makes the game so much more enjoyable. Before if you ran onto a small ledge you would have to do an awkward jump off, now you move how you want to.
2. The fighting mechanic is a bit different than previous AC games, since you're camera is much more personal. You now actually have to rotate you're camera to be able to see if someone is about to attack you. I feel like this mechanic is much more engaging and feels less like an impersonal button masher.
Part III:
Reasons to get AC: Unity:
1. Tons of historical locations, with tons of detail. Videos on YouTube do not do the buidlings justice.
2. Very solid personal Story
3. Good Story based side-activities that make you think
4. 20+ hours of gameplay (I ended up doing about 45-ish hours for the main story + dead kings DLC)
5. You're addicted to the assassin's creed series.
Reasons not to get AC: Unity:
1. Huge let down in terms of modern storyline progression.
2. Garbage assassin's Brotherhood storyline
3. You have a need for MSAA
4. Lots of listening and reading to get the full story
5. You still haven't recovered from AC:III

At first Aberoth seemed clunky, bland and unpolished. I gave it a negative review and was ready to be done with it. But I went back for some reason, and given some time it grew on me.
Part of it might be nostalgia. I'm a veteran gamer, and Aberoth strongly reminds me of the very early days of one of my first MMOs: Runescape. In 2001, Runescape was fresh and chaotic. Players dropped all their items on death, for all to grab; You could duel to the death anywhere in the game world. The game was still being very actively developed (membership wasn't even an option yet), and there was still some mystery left in the world, as the playerbase was still very new.
Aberoth is just that: a new, open-world PvP-optional game, with full looting (until you learn how to protect yourself from it). Aberoth does not hold your hand, which feels initially frustrating, but can also be refreshing.
My biggest gripe at this point is that it does seem to be a bit grindy, but for now this simple, low-poly anarchic world has its hooks in me.
It's also worth noting, I guess, that there are some lag issues, and some funkiness like not being able to make the window full screen. If you can forgive these things, and enjoy a raw, retro-feeling, and challenging game - then Aberoth might be for you.

Dinner Date is not a game. That is to say, loading it up and playing it doesn't expose you to anything you might consider gameplay. It is an intellectual experiment, trying to create art from a gaming perspective. Unfortunately what comes out is something that is so pretentious it seems to have been sucked through it's own rear end and into a completely different reality.
Now, if this was a free to download and try experiment at merging gaming and art I probably would be more positive towards it. But this is a priced experience, you don't simply get to try something new, you have to pay for it. And you don't get much for your money.
You play as Julian Luxemburg, or rather, as his subconscious as he sits around, nervously waiting for his date to arrive, you get to hear his inner monologue, fidget with the various items on the table and drum your fingers a bit. And that's really it, that's the entire experience. The subtle differences that can occur from taking different actions are so minute that it's hardly worth a second playthrough.
Only bright side to this experience is the above average voice acting of Julian but that alone doesn't add much.
All in all, this is quite simply a travesty. I am all for game developers experimenting and trying new things but when you are charging me money for 10 minutes of listening to someone worry about life that's just attempting to cash in on the bizarreness of your creation. Do not buy this, it is not worth your time and even if you're into this sort of art, there are much better experiences outside of the gaming medium.

The origin of everyone's favourite crowbar-wielding, vent-crawling theoretical physicist.
This game is amazing, in nearly every way. The level design is clever and intuitive, cleverly directing you between objectives without the use of floating arrows or map markers. Every level feels visually distinct, and the difficulty curve is well-balanced and ramps up steadily throughout the game.
Half-Life's story is simple but engrossing, and is told without ever taking away player control. The pacing is extremely well-done, striking a good balance between firefights, exploring, and environmental puzzles.
Jumping physics are solid, and the platforming sections are never frustrating (don't forget to quick-save before a tricky jump!). Guns and weapons handle well and feel powerful. Health and ammo pick-ups are well-spaced, providing enough tension caused by resource scarcity, but avoiding frustratingly long stretches of having low health or no ammo.
The sound design is incredible, whether it's the sound of Gordon's footsteps on a metal grate, the moans of a headcrab zombie, or the resounding "BOOM!" of a shotgun.

Heat Signature is an extremely well executed interstellar stealth game. The random ships are different enough to provide countless enjoyable experiences but also similar enough to allow for the player to create their own strategies that work in many scenarios. Death is punishing, forcing you to start as a new character, but the game makes beginning again an exciting experience, so you never feel like the game is enragingly hard.
PROS:
-Massive replayability
-Lots of items to unlock and collect
-Random levels
-Player can decide their own way to play (Sneaky or forceful? Kill everyone or only the target?)
-Mixes strategy with luck (where will the guard go?) very well
-Any mission can be done with starting items, if you are good enough
CONS:
-Some may find that the ships are repetitive.
BUY IF YOU LIKE: Gunpoint (same devs), Binding of Isaac (random adventures w/ dodging and skill), Hotline Miami (top-down shooter)

It's impossible to talk about Stardew Valley without mentioning Harvest Moon (Unless you don't know Harvest moon lol)
Stardew pretty much copies/mimics all the basic features from classic Harvest Moon games, you play as a young man/woman that inherits a farm from your grandfather and has to work in the farm, planting , taking care of animals, building and upgrading stuff, building relationships with the villagers, getting married and so on.. Stardew use all those elements from Harvest Moon and adds more to it , like crafting items, combat and more.
So Stardew is a 'fresh new' kind of Harvest Moon, that has updates every now and then.
So if you really enjoyed playing Harvest Moon in the past (or in the present) and wants to play something similar and refreshing at the same time Stardew Valley is definitively the way to go.

Not sure if this game is even pretending to be fair, but.... it already fails at being fair at the very first boss fight. Roll too early and it will still hit you. Don't roll far enough and it will still hit you. Think a boss's sword can't reach further than a single roll backwards? Think again, it will still hit you. It sometimes vaguely seems to take into account the blade did not get a full hit, but you can never make an educated guess whether taking one hit would mean your next swing will still be enough for a kill. Added to that is how at least the guy with the axe has a teeeeeerrribly slow attack. Even with a perfect dodge, you won't really get enough time to land a single hit, let alone the even slower heavy attack.
Even worse, bosses generally never get stunned. But if you stand too close, you will find you do get stunned, only to get hit at least one and a half times if not more. I wouldn't go into this game thinking it is as fair as Dark Souls, where a well timed roll prevents a hit.
So nope, in this game you're going to almost die constantly with every boss or if you do not succeed... die a LOT. Can't say that feels very good, because it simply does not feel very fair and balanced most of the time. This means you could run into even the weakest of foes 'getting lucky' on you, cutting your health in half. Yes, half. Tough luck if that happens twice or you will likely have to start over from the last checkpoint.
And then I haven't talked about how the game sometimes seems to fail to register key presses or indeed counts a player hit before a boss hit in how it calculates damage. This means you could technically have killed a boss, but die anyway because their hit is calculated first. It's again the problem of a boss not getting stunned upon a hit.
It also doesn't help the camera movement isn't great in tight corridors. The game tells you to 'watch out' for foes 'using the mouse' to look around, but in reality the camera in such cases is such a struggle it is hardly fair.
I love the overall aesthetic of this game. The designs are top-notch. People can have different tastes, so that's alright and all. But the game does look better than any of the Dark Souls games (yes, including Dark Souls 3). It did not bother me to basically play within the castle setting at all. I personally don't think the outdated visuals of Dark Souls are that great in terms of levels anyway.
So yeah, now the tough part... should I recommend this game? Probably not. But for it's current discount it's worth a shot. Getting better at the game does help in making the experience a bit better, but not by much really. I kind of hope they would make a sequel and fix the combat and weapon balance. Because in some ways we can't have enough games that focus more on skillbased gameplay. But to say this game does a great job at that is unfortunately untrue. It's a 65/100, 70/100 for those who are able to get past the flaws of combat and learn to deal with it (for example; never get within range of the shield of a boss, increase distance even more when bosses do their spinning attacks and when you get a feel for when EXACTLY to start a dodge roll without a boss readjusting where to hit in the last second because you dodged too early). Whatever you do though, do NOT get this at full price.

I can review this game with pure numbers. Here is a list of my play times with the last three AC games.
ACIII: 90+ hours
ACIV (Black Flag): 110+ hours
ACUnity: 50 hours
So it's been entertaining for half as long. So I judge it about half as good as the last two.
Good stuff: Oh sure, it's pretty at street level and inside buildings. Sometimes very much so. And the combat (which many hate) for me is interestingly varied and the swordfighting feels appropriately hard, especially when you're surrounded.
Mediocre stuff: The plot isn't great. The voice acting is sub par (for a series which has usually been great this is a big miss). And the collection stuff feels -- for the first time, IMO -- very much like a chore.
Bad stuff: The parkour -- one of the keys of the franchise -- doesn't feel anywhere near as breathtaking and dangerous as it once did. Maybe this is because we're "used to it". But maybe it's also the awkward way that every roof in Paris seems to "stop" your movement; those long flowing runs are mostly gone. Gaining viewpoints used to be an absolute highlight for me in previous versions. But every swoopy synchronization in *this* iteration is just a sea of blue-grey roofing tiles. Yawntastic.
Conclusion: Skip it. You're not missing anything "important" in the overarching plot. Wait for the next one, and hope it's good.

I am a big fan of this genre for the possibilities it can/could offer, there's a lot you can do, quests, surprising environments, tools and interesting crafting ideas.
Now this is where I believe Starbound has not hit the target (yet) in my honest opinion.
It has good starts of ideas, but in order to get some of the features offered by the game, you gotta watch a walkthrough or look it up online, or you're gonna be clicking and tapping all the keys of your keyboard for several minutes like an idiot.
It is not totally intuitive in that regard.
There's a try at a tutorial in the first hours of gaming, on your "Journal", which I assume is where the developpers want the source of information/quests/guidebook for moving forward to be, and I get that this is an early access release but I've had the game for almost a year now I reckon. I find it kind of a letdown to not include what could be the motivator here after so long. It brings a "Now what?" feeling.
Given, once you have looked up online that there are different sectors which have different levels of difficulty (monsters, ore distribution, weapons and objects, etc.), you can go for it and craft the required items to summon the boss which allows you access to more ore/weapons/armor/planets, and that can take a lil while and put your head in the game for a few more hours.
After doing all this exploration, you kinda start stumbling across planets that look similar to that one you already visited like 4 planets ago, or, if you're like me and you did use the set as a home feature, looking like your home-planet, and the only thing remaining is collecting, maxing up your vines to make bandages, your coal for fuel, collecting all the fruit/tree seeds existing, crafting, farming etc.
And again, if you're like me and you don't play in Multi-player mode, it gets meh after a while.
Because it has been on Early access for so long, exploring new planets is not always as exciting, especially if you've already seen all the biomes and dungeons available for now, you can easily notice their pattern and/or easily cheat by digging a way in closer to things to loot or digging around to avoid it etc., ditto for boss monsters or villages/houses/camps.
It just gets a tiiiiiny bit repetitive.
One big positive point that I would like to stress on the music though. I have a sweet spot for Story/Quest/Chara dev and games OSTs and to be honest, I could listen to the soundtrack all day long.
And a silly positive point: the Frog merchant with a buncha dogs in his/her house (wish I could've adopted one as a pet).
All in all, I guess if/when the official game is released, there should be improvement coming our way.
Or so I hope, because I do like sandbox modes, but right now, this version lacks a spark of interest, of novelty, to make me recommend it.

Pros and Cons
pros. Everything

10/10 Masterpicece
STORYLINE
A mysterious Alien Artifact has been recovered and brought to a top-secret research facility in the Black Mesa. When newcomer Dr. Gordon Freeman is assigned to physically test the artifact, things go very wrong when the artifact opens a destructive and unstable portal to Xen, a planet in a different dimension. Gordon blacks out, and awakes in a now crippled and ruined research facility. When Freeman and the survivors of this ordeal discover the portal has allowed its inhabitants-deadly alien creatures-to enter the facility, they realise that they must call the government for help. The government, however, already has plans to contain this incident by silencing the witnesses. 
Half life's story is a very diverse and confusing one, but is still executed brilliantly. since Half Life does not rely on cut scenes, there are moments when subtle important plot references are hinted towards key features of the story, but these references can be left unnoticed especially on a first play-through. This really depends on the player and their play style if you are to notice these references. Therefore this game mechanic should not be seen as a flaw rather as an attempt to try something new that valve knew very well wouldn’t mix with everyone.
GAMEPLAY
Half life is the most influential First Person Game Ever Made. This is best exemplified through its game play mechanics. Let me explain. 
Growing up as a young grommet the only fps game I was familiar with was DOOM. At the time DOOM was piratically seen as the best pc game of all time. All fps games two follow copied the DOOM formula, all except half life. You see Doom had 
.NO Apparent storyline
.NO Interesting characters 
.NO Absorbing atmosphere [It felt very arcade like]
.And no real apparent goal
The game was really a stress reviler where you just shoot s.hit and blow c.unts up. Not saying DOOM is a bad game. DOOM is one of my favourite games its just that Half life beat DOOM at the fps formula in all ways by Half Life having 
.A fantastic and engaging story.
.A scary immersive atmosphere.
.A roster of witty and interesting characters.
.A simplified moving mechanic
.A mechanic where you could look up and down.{ thank F.UCK for that }
.A Mixture of action and Puzzles
.And a game with an apparent goal from the very start.
You see Half Life wasn’t one of those games where you would just shoot s.hit and blows c.unts up. Half Life was the first real fps game to feel like a immersive gaming experience. Therefore we have half life to thank for saving and changing what was commonly thought of as the First Person Shooter Genre.
PACING
Half Life Pacing is Executed very well. The game has the whole survival horror game feel to it and the game really exemplifies this through a sense of dread. At the start of the game it is apparent that you need to escape the black mesa facility but only an hour down the track you start to lose recognition of that thought and just have the mindset of surviving, and that is why this games pacing is so good. You never quite feel like you have an objective to do rather you just feel you have to survive. and coupling this with the fine selection of jump-scares and mind blowing scripted events it truly holds up.
LEVEL DESIGN
Valve has a name for level design in their games. Its hard to describe on paper but no gaming developer team does it like valve, you just have to see it for yourself, I mean talk about attention to detail. Before Half Life level design in fps video games were very simplistic and felt like an arcade experience. Half Life's level design was truly ahead of its time. Structures would collapse, you could interact with all most everything from the environment, and the game used a clever use of scripted events through the level design. It is very hard to explain on paper but you can tell a lot of work was put into this category of game design for half life.
IMMERSION
Immersion, Probably The Fundamental Aspect Of Game Design That Every Game Director Should Take Seriously, Gabe Newell Certainty Did With Half-Life. You See Half-Life Never Breaks The Immersion Because The Game Never Allows The Player To Stop Playing. This Is Because The Game Doesn't Consist Of Cut-Scenes Or Any Other Immersion Breakers. The Game Never Says, ''Hey Maybe You Should Take A Break''. The Only Thing Controlling Your Will To Stop Or Keep Playing Is The Player's Own Demanding Ambition.
SOUNDTRACK
Half-Life soundtrack consists of a techno and ambience like tracks. One of Half Life's key elements two its atmosphere is said soundtrack. Half Life's soundtrack always seems to change conveniently creating a completely different mood and atmosphere to the last segment of the game. The use of ambience like tracks for the more creepy, mysterious moments through out the game coupled with the techno prodigy like tracks for the scripted action moments through out the game really create an experience like no other. Space Pilgrim Episode IV: Sol is an adventure game about a bunch of fugitives who fight against the authorities. Although both ending won't affect the core story, it will affect some minor parts which might interest you. In this game, you'll mostly interacting with objects and reading through the story.
The game itself is pretty simple. You basically have to interact with everything you see and try to use it to achieve whatever you need. Whenever you are stuck, you'll just have to interact with everything or try to combine and use everything in your bag.
I always feel impressed with the writings of this story; how the devs put their time and effort in the NPCs dialogue and how the devs made them sound like having different personalities. The story itself takes in more different places than usual, mainly because the main characters have to move to places.
To be honest, this game is the most satisfying compared to the other series, probably because of how good the ending is conveyed. Actually, i want to know more about the story, but seeing it to be wrapped up so well, i don't think that it deserves more.
There are 2 slightly different endings, which will only affect certain part of the story. However, seeing that the ending will only affect a little part, being not able to skip or fast forward the dialogues can be a pain in the.
Just like the other series, the mappings in this game are awesome. There are a lot of new maps introduced in this game and the planet cutscenes are beautiful as usual. I like how the devs show the fact that the main characters' appearance are changing from episode 1 to the last episode.
The music is awesome as how the other series are. It really blends well with the environment.
All in All

This game is comparable to those times when there is a blockbuster movie in the theaters and you go on to a streaming service to suddenly find a low budget movie trying to capitalize on the theater movie's coattails. Overall this game is not really horrible for say. It can be enjoyable for a sitting or two. It just a tad on the forgettable and slow side in the end.
It tries to capitalize on the Demon/Dark soul's formula a little too much. Which is not overtly bad as that is how we get new game genres. Leading to us getting more games we love in the future. Honestly, even the Souls games take a lot of ideas from much older games.
This game's combat is frankly snail mode even compared to a Souls game. They took the Souls idea of forcing the player to use tactical combat: you know watching for telegraphed openings to exploit but took it too far. In this game, you rush in to attack the enemy for a hit, then run out of its range and wait for an opening or get 1-hit KOed. Unlike Souls, you really can't dance with the monster, while waiting for the openings as dodge is utterly worthless. So it's either post out of the enemies range or stay in melee range to die.
To make matters worse for this game, all the difficulty balancing appears to have been from the designer perspective of: Let's just make everything damage sponges. With the added bonus, we also give the player really slow attack animations. So it'll take forever to kill anything even trash monsters. Then we'll make everything do 1-shot attacks. Now that will make our game hard. So in the end, deaths are not a fun challenge, they're just flat out chores.
Still what really hurt this game for me was where they actually tried to be different. Unlike Darks Souls atmospheric storytelling. This game has a very linear in your face story that presents the player with defined main character. You'll either be indifferent to him or outright dislike him. The story itself is honestly forgettable. I lost interest in the story rather quickly and it kind of killed my desire to continue playing. Had they did a strong interesting story. It would probably make the game far better.
Between the agonizing slow damage sponge combat and the yawn storyline. I found myself never feeling the desire to come back and finish this game past my initial sitting. Thankfully for the developers, this game was an excellent game design "learning lesson" for them. So when they release their next game "The Surge". It came out to be fun and I would really recommend you go look at that game instead.

Pros:
- nice to look at, nice to listen to
- nice to play like a simulation
- nice to laugh with (or at) Shaq and Kenny
- nice to play with your friends (most of the time)
Cons:
- absolutely terrible Spike Lee story for MyCareer mode (completely linear with no choices at all, and terribly written "drama")
- MyCareer starts at 2016-2017 - good luck with retiring of your favourite old guys
- some lagging (he he) issues with online play, although it is improved over 2k15
- no protection from people who cheat online - you have to beat guys who are quicker, stronger, taller, more precise than you will ever be just using your gaming skills
- virtual currency isn't balanced well enough - some things are too easy to acquire, some are too hard, and some things just shouldn't be available to purchase with real money - this is an issue that's only going to be worse as years go by
- a bug here and there, like sudden silence from the commentators' booth (for some gamers it's game-breaking, for me not so much) or unskippable cut-scenes mid-game. However, we've already had two patches and it seems that this year the developers are actually caring a bit more!
Overall:
- if you're a basketball fan(atic) and an avid gamer, then you already have this game
- if you're looking at a high price and wondering if it's worth it, the answer is yes - just look for a discount somewhere and you will find it
- if you want to know why there are more cons than pros up top, read on - this game is really good, but has a few annoying things that really shouldn't have been like this
Thanks, Spike Lee. You've managed to write the story for MyCareer mode that wouldn't get a 3 on IMDb if it was a movie. What did I expect? A branching and immersive story. What did I get? My career starts in 2016/2017. No relation to real world anymore. Trades going on. MVPs happen. And I missed all of that.
As you could have guessed, this is the game mode I play most. When this awful part of the game ends (the story), the game really becomes something much better. Many improvements have been made. Many opportunities have been missed, too, but you can't expect every single item on your wishlist to come true.
The game is really challenging (on Hall of Fame level) and sometimes brutally unforgiving (your teammates just can't sink a shot or defend anyone sometimes, even if you're on fire on both ends of the floor), but I would say that it is a feature, not a bug.
Online experience has been somewhat improved regarding MyPark from the last iteration, and I haven't really played much of other game modes.

Trove is easily one of my favorite games on steam.
Most of the gameplay is spent roaming procedurally generated areas to enter dungeons, clear them of enemies, and collect rewards. As long as you don't enter areas that are too high for you, the gameplay is simple but entertaining. Soloing is totally viable, but the ad-hoc cooperation is a big plus of this game.
Being a voxel based game, you can also use blocks and crafted items to decorate you own house (which is portable in that you can place it on any empty plot) or guild world.
The interesting dungeons and fun of collecting mounts and dragons make this game appealing to most people I think.
My only complaint about the game is the fact things created in you home or guild world are untimately decorative. Of course, this would be very difficult to add to the game, so I understand why it isn't part of the game and I'm not saying it is a reason not to play.

I will admit, sometimes the chosen diolouge can be confusing to pick, and you'll end up saying the wrong thing. It still is an upgrade, adds much more life to the game.
The map is impressive! It is certianly smaller than the earlier games, but it's so jam packed full of city buildings to explore.
I love the companions interactions, and I feel it's an improvement. I like how there is a romance system. Only thing I don't like, is most of the companions like someone who is good all the time. I personally like to play it bad, that's why I liked the karma system so much.
The building system is such a great mechanic. It adds so much fun to the game.
Biggest problem I have with it; is it starts out with a bang, gets boring, then you start to have fun once you pick it up after a while. I think of it like Saints Row 4. Which had an amazing start that caught my attention, but then it was VERY boring right after. Plan on playing a few solid hours before it finally picks up and gets interesting. It is very worth it though.
As for the creation club, that is trash, and Bethesda needs to seriously stop. Though I personally am not too hurt over it, since I prefer vanilla games. I still think they need to get rid of it. I'm sick of them being a cash grab lately, especially with Elder Scrolls Online. I always valued Bethesda, and thought of them as a very wholesome company. They have great content, but lately they've been acting odd.
Overall, it's a great game. It is very much worth playing. My heart belongs to New Vegas, but I still absolutely LOVE this game.
Please don't, if you want more dark souls, this is not it. Just buy Nioh
