If you've never heard of Fallout, it's a game franchise that plays in the devastated world after an earth-spanning nuclear holocaust. Every game starts with a new character in a new setting and can be played without needing to know the others. But if you do of course there's the bonus of recognizing a few of the things that other characters reference.
Setting:
In this part, you play as the (male or female) eyewitness and survivor of said nuclear holocaust. On the day the bombs fall, you enter a vault and get cryogenically frozen to wake up many, many years in the future. And right off the bat, you are driven to explore the strange world outside: While you were trapped inside your cryopod, someone killed your spouse and kidnapped your infant son. Who are they and what did they do it for?
The world of Fallout 4 is vast. Set in and around (former) Boston, in an area now called "the Commonwealth", you will meet several larger factions all of which have their own plans and ... yeah, i didn't really count, but their number may approach the three digits - many individual NPCs. Along your way, you will also encounter several companions to assist you on your quest which, by the way, will likely sooner or later take kiiiind of a backseat as there is so much to explore and the game doesn't rush you.
When you work on the main quest, you will soon have to pick one of the larger factions to support. They don't all play nicely with each other, so be prepared to become enemies with part of this world. By the way, at this point I've sunk way more hours into this game than shows on this review (playing offline a lot), and I couldn't bring myself to finish the main quest yet. I still have so many other things I want to do, also because I bought the two story DLCs. Yet it has to be said that after the main game's ending, you can continue playing at your leisure, so the order in which you tackle things doesn't really matter unless there's something that comes tied to a certain faction or that requires certain events to not yet have taken place.
Gameplay:
At its core, FO4 is an RPG with a focus on gunplay (or melee, if that's your thing).
The gunplay part shows when you fight enemies (well, duh) with one of your preferred weapons most of which are customizable. You can fight either using VATS, a game feature that's supposedly an approximation to the turn-based combat in RPGs of yore, meaning time will slow down massively and you can then use action points to pick which enemies to hit where and in which order. Alternatively, you can fight in real-time like in any shooter. I'm using both styles in different situations, e.g. with small or fast enemies, VATS is pretty useful, and if you want to snipe over a long distance, real-time is better.
The RPG part shows in the hundreds of quests, the hours of dialogue and the fact that when you level up, you can pick or improve certain character skills/perks and thus shape your character for your preferred style of play: Good with heavy weapons, pistols, rifles, melee? Very efficient when wearing power armour? Using VATS to its full efficiency? Or rather someone who gets bonuses when doing combat in real time? Better when standing still in combat, or when moving? Great at modding weapons or armour? Charming the socks off of everyone they meet? Good lockpick because you must have every last treasure? Able to carry tons and tons of loot (good when you said yes to the previous question)? Able to breathe underwater for full exploration? Can consume tons of "chems" (drugs with useful gameplay effects) without getting addicted? etc.
Settlement building is another feature of the game. You will have to build at least a few barebones settlements with resources you find while playing. If you want, you can go above and beyond and spend hours and hours with that. Personally, I don't care too much for it, but there is a certain siren call to it, like a casual game on your mobile phone: "Those trees need to go. Huh, I could build some shops. And while I'm at it, the settlers could have nicer rooms. And then I'll quickly..."
What I liked
The world. I'm actually not a fan of post-apocalyptic stories with their grimdark settings, but the Commonwealth has something fascinating about it. I like exploring the sun-lit* ruins of the past to find out about their previous and present inhabitants in oh so many little stories that are waiting to be discovered. Some criticise the main story of FO4, and at least I have lost all sense of urgency to resolve it while playing, if only because it's patiently waiting for me. But FO4 does shine in the small stories: Reading old logs in still-working computers tells stories e.g. about corporate recklessness or personal loss, pre-war remains that are scattered all over give clues as to how these people died. Or you lend a helping hand to the still-alive citizen and will break into a safe, help a mourning father find closure, get a very old acquaintance back on his feet, learn how your companions really tick, become the embodiment of a pre-war radioplay hero etc. All this serves to establish a tone of heartbreak, hope and ironic humour.
*There really are all kinds of weather in FO4, but as you will see from my screenshots, I do like the sunny days best, maybe because they make the setting less grimdark, see above.
Mods. Bethesda games are known for their huge modding communities, and you will find that whatever it is that bugs you may  already have been fixed by a modder. Or you take your pick among mods that add new aspects into the game, change small things and more.
Now, there has been a recent uproar when Bethesda announced additional mods published by them and for money. Some people (you know who you are) even give this game a thumb down for that very reason because they think mods should always be free. Seriously, I don't see the issue: The free mods are still there, nobody's taking them away. And if Bethesda wants to make money with a franchise they own, that's very much their right. But no matter what your stance is on that issue, this game can be played perfectly fine without the payable mods.
What I didn't like
Repetitiveness. Since Fallout is made to be played for hundreds of hours, you may do just that and find the same gameplay patterns repeating: Explore, read/talk, shoot, loot.
And by now I know the game's assets by heart (let's loot another mop, scalpel, shopping basket, baseball ... just like the 10,000 before).
It wouldn't be as obvious with a game designed for a shorter playtime, but here we are. So ... expect to maybe not want to play this for days and days on end, at least after you've played for a few weeks in real time.
Graphics issues. I didn't experience any game-breaking bugs. There was one single time where a character I needed to talk to had gone for a swim and couldn't be talked to underwater, but that was solvable by making my character sleep for an hour. This bug-free experience may be because I installed the unofficial patch mod. But many times the game would suddenly drop to very low framerates and become unplayable for maybe 20 seconds. It could be due to my no longer new computer, but apparently people with newer hardware have the same problem. It was nearly gone after a few tweaks but reoccured after the update that introduced the Bethesda-made mods.
Achievements. I stopped getting achievements after I installed the first mod (which was pretty early in the game). Assumedly it's to stop people from cheating their way to glory, but then, if I really wanted, I could just enable the in-game console and cheat without mods. So it's just annoying to not be able to show off as usual.
(Well, there's apparently a mod to undo this effect, but I've always been too lazy to read my way through the how to of its installation ...)

This is what happens when you milk a once good series. The following reasons are why I will not purchase another Assassin's Creed title. These are the things that make me put the game down, giving me no interest to pick it up again.
Combat - After killing someone, Arno seems to stay focused on his dead enemy as if he's shocked by what he's done. Really annoying especially when trying to walk away. Indoor combat is annoying as the camera goes all over the place other than the enemy. The combat is boring and feels unrewarding. Seems everytime you kill an enemy, it shows a mini cut scene of Arno slitting his throat, stabbing him, snapping his neck, etc... all while you can be shot at and stabbed. Even while fighting a group. I just want them to die so I can kill again.
Hyperactive detection - Guards will sense Arno even while hiding in a bush or behind curtains for no reason at all. When I'm walking through town, a random enemy will detect me. Not brutes which do this as intended Just now, a sniper detected me when I as going to open a gold chest that was nowhere near a restricted area. I was even walking, not running which can catch a guards attention.
Parkour - Sometimes Arno will jump the opposite direction  of where your heading, sometimes he won't jump at all. Sometimes he will jump off a roof instead of the beam straight ahead. Sometimes he will jump through that beam and die. Sometimes when on a wall trying to jump down, Arno will just turn around instead of jump in the ground. In other words, the parkour is tedious and anoying, especially if you're around enemies just sitting on the wall waiting for them to detect you.  Sometines while running, Arno will get stuck on a random object (stool, barrel in the ground..etc) This can turn you into a pinata if it happens in combat. Some walls and ledges which look like they can be climbed are not, and vice versa. Even small things like stools are climbable, complete with a climbing animation. When trying to climb through windows, I will run up the side of it or even across the window entrance.
The app - Noone wants it. Really a shame to lock things in game behind a phone app. Atleast they could have cleaned up the map clutter by removing the app objects if we don't use / want the app... How long has initiates been down for now since December 24th, 2014 "during the holiday period"? It is reported that it takes about a month to unlock Altair's outfit.
Sync points - Although you do get a fair amount of these from completing the storyline quests, the remaining points are locked behind multiplayer. Although you can solo some of the MP maps (I haven't tried them all), I feel that sync points should have been provided in the singleplayer only.Some of the gear is locked behind this and club competitions also.
Hiding - Sometimes haystacks and curtains don't function. You can't enter them, even while out of combat. Its like trying to jump into a wall. And that silhouette feature can bug out even if youre hiding in one. The silhouette "feature" seems undercooked. When hiding they can constantly appear and reappear. Or sometimes not at all.
In game vendors -  After buying anytyhing from one of the ingame vendoes (comsumables, gear, etc... after purchase, you need to wait 4 seconds before buying another item.
The storyline and Arno's personality are really bland. I won't delve into spoilers here, but these 2 things help shape the game. If Arno had an interesting personality instead of chasing a girl around. You're also confined to the city. I loved the exploration in ACIII and ACIV.  This game does not feature it. It feels like a rehash of ACI & II. Only with weaker features.  I'm sure I missed other things, like the cash shop where you buy helix points and temporary boosters, which I think have no place in such a game.
I guess the graphics make up for it, right?

Mixed review for a game I have played kind of a lot since I can't play Terraria on my Apple desktop (but that is material for another review).
I am a big fan of this genre for the possibilities it can/could offer, there's a lot you can do, quests, surprising environments, tools and interesting crafting ideas.
Now this is where I believe Starbound has not hit the target (yet) in my honest opinion.
It has good starts of ideas, but in order to get some of the features offered by the game, you gotta watch a walkthrough or look it up online, or you're gonna be clicking and tapping all the keys of your keyboard for several minutes like an idiot.
It is not totally intuitive in that regard.
There's a try at a tutorial in the first hours of gaming, on your "Journal", which I assume is where the developpers want the source of information/quests/guidebook for moving forward to be, and I get that this is an early access release but I've had the game for almost a year now I reckon. I find it kind of a letdown to not include what could be the motivator here after so long. It brings a "Now what?" feeling.
Given, once you have looked up online that there are different sectors which have different levels of difficulty (monsters, ore distribution, weapons and objects, etc.), you can go for it and craft the required items to summon the boss which allows you access to more ore/weapons/armor/planets, and that can take a lil while and put your head in the game for a few more hours.
After doing all this exploration, you kinda start stumbling across planets that look similar to that one you already visited like 4 planets ago, or, if you're like me and you did use the set as a home feature, looking like your home-planet, and the only thing remaining is collecting, maxing up your vines to make bandages, your coal for fuel, collecting all the fruit/tree seeds existing, crafting, farming etc.
And again, if you're like me and you don't play in Multi-player mode, it gets meh after a while.
Because it has been on Early access for so long, exploring new planets is not always as exciting, especially if you've already seen all the biomes and dungeons available for now, you can easily notice their pattern and/or easily cheat by digging a way in closer to things to loot or digging around to avoid it etc., ditto for boss monsters or villages/houses/camps.
It just gets a tiiiiiny bit repetitive.
One big positive point that I would like to stress on the music though. I have a sweet spot for Story/Quest/Chara dev and games OSTs and to be honest, I could listen to the soundtrack all day long.
And a silly positive point: the Frog merchant with a buncha dogs in his/her house (wish I could've adopted one as a pet).
All in all, I guess if/when the official game is released, there should be improvement coming our way.
Or so I hope, because I do like sandbox modes, but right now, this version lacks a spark of interest, of novelty, to make me recommend it.

A mission game in space built around the ability to pause and prepare actions whenever you like. This lends itself to some really crazy gameplay, and taking out entire rooms of guards in a quick flurry of pausing, shooting, dashing, and throwing feels amazing. Teleporters, hacking guns, and stealth shields add another layer alongside special mission conditions such as no alarms or no killed guards to offer a surprising amount of replayability.
The progression system of retiring mercenaries and slowly unlocking more equipment is also pretty cool, and I love that you can see the items your steam friends have retired, and get the chance to save their captured mercs.
My only real complaint is that certain guard traits like shields or armor can be really daunting to deal with unless you've unlocked some subverters or other equipment, but even that's pretty minor, given that you can always beat them with grenades, depressurizing rooms, and stealth.
The game is a bit sparse with instructions at times, and knowing things like F to speed up space travel or the fact that you can pilot hijacked ships and use their rockets to attack other ships (and create a new opening to dock with) would be good information to tell the player more directly, but if you like discovering new tactics or interactions and becoming a space-badass that slashes and warps through a ship in effortless, fluid motion, definitely give Heat Signature a try

I understand why this game recieves so much hate. It most definetely has it's flaws. BUT, I enjoy this game, so I will give it a far review.
First off, there ARE US servers, as well as European and Russian. There are 3 classes: Sniper, Assault, and Support. The Sniper scope is absoulutely TERRIBLE, but it's pretty much a one-hit KO to the head, so I guess it evens out. Support comes with a shotgun, not really sure how that's supporting. Assault is self-explanatory.
There is definetely a good deal of lag on some servers, but I usually get servers that areen't as laggy.
The music at the title screen is amazing, so you may just want to install it for that :P (kidding, but the music really is awesome. At least, in my opinion it is.)
Everything you buy is real life money, but it's not really a pay-2-win game. You can survive without buying anything. Also, some stuff in the shop is pretty cheap. I'm not one to buy things for a game, but some things are 40 cents, which I guess isn' that big of a deal.
There are a variety of game modes. There's Versus, tanks, capture, and a whole bunch of other stuff.
You can build and destroy the landscape. You can only build with one block, though, and that's a bunch of bricks that are the color of your team. Kind of like Ace of Spades, I guess. (Haven't played that game in a while though, so don't judge me if I'm wrong.)
As you level up you gain more stuff, but the leveling up process is tedious. It's pretty darn slow, but once you get to level 2 you can start to really have fun. You get an RPG-kind of-thing and it's pretty cool. 1 hit KO, but you only get 1 rocket. You also get 10 blocks of TNT, which doesn't really have a use unless the enemy is stupid enough to shoot it. You get a couple of grenades. Unfortunately, I think my character forgets to pull the ring on the grenade, because I never hear/see any explosion.
All in all , fun game to try. If you don't like it, uninstall. It's worth at least a few seconds of trying :P

Hands down the best small game I've played in ages. Incredibly unique in all the ways that count nowadays, simple design with huge potential and a ton of love put into it. Oozes that 'open' spirit missing from developement post big money gaming, keeps the spirit alive. Charming art design, simple sound that delivers and doesn't try too hard. Music is cute and beepy boopy but gets you in that space operator feel. The creativity possible with the game elements at its base is extremely wide open and situational; I don't think there is another game of it's kind that does everything this does so tactfully without a single hint of ugly DLC moneygrabbing or content choking, my hat is firmly off.
The combat mechanics are clean and simple, delivering a very uncluttered experience. The pause menu system is useful and spartan like I feel they should be. No consolization Y-wheel bologna, opens alot of possibilities and creates a puzzle system feel. The space piloting element of the pod feels just like how you think space would be in 2D like those old flash games that turned into infinite space etc- clunky but not for the sake of bad controls.
Docking in motion is fun at its base and when♥♥♥♥♥♥gets hectic you invoke the COME ON TARS in yourself and dock with that floating chunk of wreckage holding your rescue target (bless you warzone rescues with tight limits). The pods are all quite different and I gotta say, the Brick is a hoot to just smash♥♥♥♥♥♥with boy howdy. Window diving and catching yourself with your pod always feels just so godamn fun, the vacuum element is sweet. There is so much to discover in such a tightly packaged GAME that I can't say enough good things.
This game has invoked a feeling of early 2000s, dreamer game design with big universes done simply- space feels like space. The dev doesn't squeeze your♥♥♥♥♥for every dollar, the game is priced very nicely. It is just, good. Please play this and get the experience, it's one of those gems.

That would about sum it up. It's really not so much a game as it is a kind of neat gimmick (i.e. the voice over) tacked on to the most mediocre ARPG ever created. Of course the typical formula for an indie game these days is "retro gameplay + a gimmick = success" and there are much worse games (and, indeed, much worse gimmicks) out there than "Bastion." But I really can't think of another game that is more grossly overrated than "Bastion" is. Once the novelty of the voice over wears off it really doesn't have much which would distinguish it from the literally scores of free-to-play, browser based, ARPGs out there (except, maybe, the backstory which is, by turns, both half baked and over wrought). Don't see what the fuss was about with this one.

Great game. I am not sure why it got panned as a ♥♥♥♥♥ier Dark Souls. The feel/aesthetic is a bit different: a little slower, and more rugged and real. The biggest gameplay difference is that rolling is mostly worthless in this game - even the fastest movement speed encumberance tier only rolls at a speed equivalent to something like a Dark Souls mid-roll - simply not good enough for anything other than an emergency. So instead of spamming rolls, you will mostly be walking in and out of enemy range, baiting their attack, stepping out, then stepping in and punishing (or use the running attack to leap in on them - this move is typically really good in this game). You can also circle to backstab, stay back and fire off magic or a ranged weapon that you get a bit into the game, etc. There are weapons of all kinds, heavy slow♥♥♥♥♥ones, fast, dual wield, two hand, etc. Bucklers that you can parry with, heavier shields, light/med/heavy armors, etc. Basically everything you'd expect in a game like this is in there. Absoluely gorgeous graphics, though I have everything maxed out (I saved this game in my backlog for years until I finally put together a new and powerful system). The story is alright.

Tip: Don't spread your points too thin as every weapon in the game only scales with only exactly one stat (STR, AGI, or FTH), so there is no quality style build where you mix both STR/AGI. You can mix one of those two with some FTH for magic purposes if you want. Blue magic is kind of convenient because the Shelter spell regens a lot of HP, basically giving you a downtime heal so you can save your potions. Don't be afraid of the starter class weapons i.e. the rogue ones have daggers which doesn't appeal to me, but you will pick up new gear as you go pretty quickly (and for example with those AGI rogues, there are things like AGI based monk staffs), so you can meld yourself to be whatever soon enough (though again, keep to only one of either STR or AGI (you can maybe mix some FTH with that if you want depending on what you are going for). Bucklers (which can parry) are AGI based, heavier shields STR based, STR is mostly swords, greatswords, some hammers, AGI is daggers, swords, staves (like monk staff, it's cool),♥♥♥♥♥♥like that, FTH is mostly hammers, staves, etc.  FTH was slightly disappointing weapon wise (many of their better weapons are like Drake Sword style i.e. you meet the minimum requirement to wield it and then further scaling is not added or not much so it doesn't pay to keep pumping FTH super far, even for magic or your ranged attack which both use it) - there are some solid FTH options but not as much variety or volume of drops compared to STR or AGI. END is good for equipment burden (use lighter stuff to move faster to make it more like Dark Souls, or you can tank up and go slow -- green color is the fastest movement tier, gray is middle, yellow is fat, red is can't move -- keep to green or gray) and some energy. VIT gives you some HP but you don't need much extra. LUCK isn't great and apparently bugged so don't bother.

I recommend Fractured Space since it's free to play and you have nothing to lose.

Fractured Space, due to it being free, falls in the middle of recommend/not recommend. It’s free, if you don’t like it you lost nothing. However, I did not experience anything game breaking that would place it into the not recommend category. Are there game balancing issues? Sure, it’s an online adversarial game. World of Tanks has been around for ages and they are still tweaking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it. That is the nature of the beast, can’t fault the game for that.
Pay to win? I don’t have a gazillion hours on the game, but I can’t see how it could be. Nothing is unattainable to free players other than ship skins. What I find odd is the lack of a premium account found in many similar games. Not sure why, this game would be perfect for such a system.
You can test fly every ship to see how it handles and works on a gunnery range. Spawn in what you want to shoot at and blast away. Being a free game you could get your money’s worth just playing around with each ship. The matches are above average in length when compared to other adversarial games. However, once again if you don’t like it you lose nothing by trying.
I do have a couple of issues with the ships. One being the omnidirectional fire arcs. Accuracy matters and distance matters, but not direction. Performing a broadside or a frontal/aft attack, all guns hit. Just point and shoot. The other issue I have is there is no up in space and there is in Fractured Space. For lack of a better explanation, all ships are aligned along a Galactic Plane as if it was water. Don’t confuse this with not being in three dimensions because the game is. The ships themselves do not behave as though they are. They cannot tumble or roll. Why does this matter? It matters because one major tactical element of the game is armor and breaking it. Once a ship's armor is broken, that side becomes very acceptable to damage. If this was a real, as if there is such a thing, space fight the ship could roll over to its undamaged side.
Like I said in the beginning, there is nothing I could find as a deal breaker that’s why I give it a recommend. One more time, it’s free to play so you lose nothing by trying.

Having been told that Lords of the Fallen is Dark Souls lite, and having not played Dark Souls I didn’t quite know what to expect when I started my run through this. I was pleasantly surprised at how much I liked this game (I was expecting something much more rage inducing).
You play as Harkyn, a convict who is forced to fight extra-planer entities of the fallen god Adyr to stop then from wiping out the humans in the fortress monastery where you were jailed. Depending on what class you pick (pick warrior), you will power your way through mobs of Rhogar (daemons), to eventually kill the Rhogar lords.
Gameplay wise, this is a game about maxing stats into your chosen class and timing. Don’t try and make a balanced character – you will be able to finish the first play through, but will be destroyed in the next. It will also stop you from being able to use your classes most damaging weapons. Usually I play a very defensive style, so it was very different to think that it’s all about attack (on the harder difficulties 1-2 hits will kill you and bosses will kill you no matter what if your timing isn’t good). I was expecting this to be very unforgiving, but once you get into the hang of things its actually quite easy. Even on a second and third run (each run lets you select one of the other classes to be able to use) the difficultly isn’t so bad, until you get to the final boss. I’m not sure if the developers were trying to be cruel, but that fight ramps up to stupid levels of hard. The DLC features a new boss that has a instant kill attack (you have to know how to dodge it)- it broke the pattern of the other bosses but was still enjoyable. There are plenty of lore scrolls around if you know where to look, which builds up the world fantastically.
Visually the game is dark and foreboding, which given its setting works very well (graveyards, catacombs, monastery grounds, Rhogar plane ect). I don’t remember any monsters other than spiders in the catacombs) that jump out at you, and you can usually hear most enemies before you see them, which builds to the suspense along with the low haunting music
You will need a few runs if you are chasing a 100%, but it’s worth it. I think I finally hit my stride at the end, and wanted to do another run where I was the boss, and not getting owed in most fights.

Whilst I long for a faithful recreation of the original XCOM or UFO from the 90's, with its seemingly endless campaigns, huge tech trees, full environmental damage and sprawling bases, this will more than do.
The world is under alien occupation and, as the resistance, it is your job to quell the alien threat.
The game has two halves. Firstly, there is the planet-wide base building and mission finder, where you plan your global strategy, build up your base, choose missions, find resources and research new technologies. Secondly, there is the strategic combat element, which occurs when you send the troops in on missions and focuses on moving individual soldiers around a finite area. This works a bit like a game of chess - albeit over multiple levels and scenarios, with various targets or objectives and, of course, aliens to seek and destroy or humans to find and protect.
One negative for me is the timers on missions; some are quite strict. I understand they are there to induce a sense of threat - which works if you like that - but I prefer to play slowly and methodically, coving all corners and such. With such strict turn time limits, you can't play like this as you are up against the clock! But the timer can be patched out with a mod if you so choose.
With that minor gripe out the way - this is strategic and unforgiving. Just the way it should be.

This game encourages thinking outside the box. Literally. In any other space based game, decompression would be fatal, or incredibly dangerous. In Heat Signature it is merely another tool in your toolbox... did I say toolbox? I should really have said your massive wheeled toolchest. The solutions to problems in this game are plentiful, and many obstacles can be overcome in multiple ways, allowing for a wide range of creativity.
The combination between frantic top down action and tactical gameplay is fantastic. The gadgetry is often as hilarious as it is useful, especially when you start bringing about teleporters that all function in different ways, time dilation devices etc. The enemies commit the fatal sin of letting the vacuum of space decide your fate, if they manage to hit you, which means that with a little skill, a death is not necessarily going to be a death, though it will get harder to survive next time.
The persistence of characters in the universe is very well done and the game actively encourages changing characters often, sending others to the hall of fame, or letting newer blood continue unlocking gear, until you can return to them, and tool them up with the kit necessary to do their own personal mission.
The game will, eventually get a little repetitive, however I've put close to 4 hours in so far and I'm not even close to having explored every possible route. I have however discovered my favorite, which involves wrenches and decking everyone in the face with them.
I did not expect this game to be so charming and so addicting.

It's an underpriced gem. Unique and engaging blend of game concepts (but still focused on clear ideas), with a high level of polish hinting at a lot of developer passion. First "roguelike" that really clicked for me - the core mechanics and player freedom are balanced just right to create memorable experiences and unexpected twists without relying on a scripted story. Intense but not stressful, thanks to the ability to pause anytime to plan the next move; almost gives it a turn-based feel. Can be played on easier missions for a while, but for some of the later progress you have to go through at least a few harder missions. I hit a wall early on, but luckily didn't give up until my skill finally improved. There are many items/gadgets that can help, but over time I've also started enjoying playing with minimal items (e.g. whatever comes with a fresh character) for an even more focused experience. It can absolutely be possible to pick the hardest available mission with a completely fresh character with no fancy items, and still beat it because there are so many ways to achieve your goal - immense satisfaction. Even though there's no real story, the game's mini-universe actually feels pretty immersive - there are no transitions between screens, it's all seamlessly mousewheel-zoomable from a close-up of your character all the way to a map of the entire universe. Music is great and adds to immersion as well. The concept is new, but other games came to mind for certain aspects - "hotline miami in space" is probably the closest, but it can also be more stealthy/tactical almost like the old "commandos" games.

.  Anything you build...kiss it goodbye should you roll up to someone with a few of these game breakers on their tech and you don't have one to shoot them with first.   It was at this point I changed my formerly positive review to a negative one.

The Good: Unique narrative, visual, and beautiful soundtrack, combat is deep, responsive, and fun, enemies are challenging and vary greatly, lots of things to do
The Bad: Can be very difficult in spots, some proving grounds are nearly impossible to beat, only lasts about 7 hours
One thing that Bastion does differently from most games is the strong and unique narrative. A man narrates the boy’s every step and action in Bastion and this is a very interesting way of telling a story. It’s like you’re playing an interactive story book especially since it looks like one too. You are trying to re-build The Bastion which is a safe spot to run from The Calamity and throughout the story you find out what this is and why this boy is trying to find these shards to build this thing. Rucks (the narrator) guides you through the story as it unfolds, so you don’t know anything until it actually happens like a story book, but it’s happening while you’re doing it.
With the excellent narrative aside the combat is top notch and responsive. You can use a regular attack, special attack, block, and a projectile weapon. There are plenty of weapons and you can upgrade them to add different attributes and bonuses. As you progress through the game you unlock six different areas which include an arsenal to swap weapons,  a forge to upgrade your weapons, a shop to buy upgrades and special powers, a shrine to make the game harder, and an “achievement” area where you can meet requirements for extra shards (in game currency). The customization and upgrades are deep and will keep you busy for a long while thanks to the proving grounds which are unique challenges for each weapon. If you meet certain criteria you get prizes based on your performance. These are not easy by any means and a few were almost impossible to beat for me.
Combat is very responsive and challenging. The enemies are quick, smart, and vary from stationary, fast moving, slow moving, heavily armored etc. I should probably say that the balance is perfect and you slowly get introduced to tougher enemies as the game progresses. You really have to use a combo of everything to stay alive because you will gulp health tonics constantly if you don’t use block and dodge a lot so stay on your feet. The action gets hectic and you start realizing this game is for hardcore action fans and not the casual gaming crowd that the visuals might seem to cater to.
There are a lot of levels and the length varies from 5 minutes to 15, but one thing I can’t get over are the visuals. As you run through the levels the walkways appear under you and seem to float in the air. The levels vary so much and not a single one looks the same. The hand drawn visuals are just gorgeous, plus you can’t forget about the amazing soundtrack that is something you stick on your MP3 player and listen too. This feels like a high budget game, but only an indie game can deliver something on this side of creativity and originality. Bastion is a unique game and nothing is quite like it in terms of narrative and visual deliverance. Every action fan should own this, because it’s $15 well spend.

I always feel impressed with the writings of this story; how the devs put their time and effort in the NPCs dialogue and how the devs made them sound like having different personalities. Unfortunately I have to give this game a thumbs down after a long pause and fresh start after I really enjoyed the demo of The Surge, a similiar game of the same developers. Although Lords of the Fallen is visually stunning and I enjoy the difficulty and challenging gamedesign, I think the frustration levels are still too high in the end.
Depending what class you are picking you are either gonna start as a heavy armored but slow knight, a fast but weak rogue or an average armored and moving cleric with magic advantages. And although you are looking similiar to Kratos from God of War, you will feel desperately underpowered sooner or later, no matter what class you pick. You are becoming better though while you progress. You need to be carefully chipping the HP from all the ghastly enemies away and learn their moving and attacking patters to kill them and to advance forward. To go through this progress with the impressive level bosses is especially challenging and might take some time. But it feels great to finally beat those big basterds.
I enjoyed to explore the levels and to feel the dangerous and scary environment, however the frequent respawning of the same enemies again and again made me drop my enthusiasm. As soon you are leaving an area or were dying (what could happen at that difficulty easily if you are not careful), every enemy you just chipped down bit by bit, will be there  at the same spot to annoy you again. And this is where I get bored the most and only would want to skip more of what I just already were working hard for. But rushing is not supposed to be in this game and so you could end up being punished even more, because you die again from enemies, who were actually not so hard to beat when you were careful.
At least the bosses are not respawning if you come across their area later again.
So, if you are into these kind of challenging games (Dark Souls etc.) and don't mind to rinse and repeat maybe even a large chunk of the game, then go for this one, it is actually really well designed. If you get frustrated or bored by repeatition easily as me, then look for something else. I think I am not going to continue playing it. If I made a long way through challenging and time consuming enemies and am dying on the long road, it's not enough fun to me to need to be chipping through everyone of them again.
Btw, but you could try the developers futuristic The Surge if my concerns sound familiar to you, there is even a large demo to play for free. I think it's way better designed regarding my criticism, I never felt that annoyed by the respawning enemies as it's in Lords of the Fallen. Also, I like the improved combat mechanics of The Surge. In Lords of the Fallen I either felt slow like fighting under water as Knight or way too weak as Rogue and I am missing more customisation options to compensate that, even as Cleric. In the Surge I found more ways to customise my character, even though you got only two starting classes to chose. I am looking forward to buy it at the upcoming christmas sale and to continue playing it over the holidays.

*Updated for 1.0(.5) release*
*Skip to bullet version for tl;dr*
Game's wiki:
Terraria in space. 4 years in the making with few stable builds, but they did it. Over the course of four years, I've seen it go from a poor Terraria (in space!) clone to what it is now - a proper Terraria-in-space clone. True, there's some changes compared to it's older brother. Combat for instance is small scale, 1-3 monsters at a time (10 if you just zip in one direction and they're still able to keep up with your running) instead of feeling like a Dynasty Warriors side scroller where several hundred zombies are kicking down your door. But for the most part, it's like a Terraria (in space! Did I mention that already?) clone with a storyline.
The tutorial is now pretty minimalistic (as compared to beta where it gave you a set of quests to basically hold your damn hand until endgame) and leaves you to your own devices early on. In fact, after the prologue, it more or less leaves you to your own devices except for the one time popups from your ship's AI, telling you the bare basics really quickly in a small chat box that doesn't pop up in your face demanding you to do anything. Also, it's a humorous little bugger that gets the point across while making light of your situation.
Storyline is similar to Terraria in that there's a big threat, but if you like you can completely ignore it and just do your own damn thing and sandbox around. There's no progression blocking - no need to defeat the Wall of Flesh to unlock hardmode ores, it's all technically available from the start. Technically. You'd still need to craft certain things to survive (you don't really expect to be magically breathing on a moon without atmosphere without an Environmental Protection Pack, do you?) on the worlds that have the ores you're after, but that's life.
Progression is similar to Terraria (minus the non-optional Wall of Flesh for the good stuff) but instead of going deeper (insert Inception meme here) you go further. Going deeper into a planet yields better deposits of ore than simply scraping the surface (geology 101) but ores are restricted to certain planet types and/or are richer on higher tier types. In that sense, planet types are Starbound's version of depth, but you can get more, faster by going deeper.
Bullet version:
Positives
+ Combat is now decently balanced. It's more focused on 1-3 at a time unlike Terraria's 50 at a time.
+ For the OCD builder who likes to create entire towns, this is heaven.
+ For the explorer, this is also heaven.
+ Procedurally generated content. Entire planets and systems! In the event you're on one end of the universe and your friend is on the other end, can share co-ordinates, kick up the FTL drive and meet up!
+ OH MY GOD FURNITURE IS USABLE! I won't lie, this made me interested in Starbound before anything else. Just like the screenshots show, you can sit your♥♥♥♥♥down on a frickin chair or go to sleep in a bed. That always annoyed me about Terraria - can't simply just knock out and wait for dawn. You still can't interfere with the day-night cycle, but at least you can put your character's head down for a bit! xD
+ There's a similar amout of block types to Terraria, so you can put together a basic wooden hut or a futuristic science complex. It's also more simplified - you just right click with the block selected to make a wall. No more weeping at having to carry Obsidian Bricks and Obsidian Walls in your inventory!
++++++ YOU. CAN. MOD. THIS. Not quite TES level modding, but the game supports modding. Entire new races! New decorations, ships, loot! Don't like the sprinkler being on the floor? There's a roof mounted sprinkler!
+ They fixed the AI. It's a lot less silly than it was in Early Access.
+ Haven't tested it yet, but there's an option to allow/disable mismatched assets (IE mod checking) which I assume is the answer to the client side based mods that allowed people to walk into a random server and start shooting meteors with their troll weapon, killing everyone and destroying hours of work in an instant.
+ Colony system is fully functional now. Build a house, decorate it, buy a colony deed, stick that in the house. Tada, you're a landlord/lady/attack helicopter! Colonists will be generated based on the furniture tags detected in the dwelling - as well as the walls I suspect. I've seen some Apex beaming into a Glitch themed house before. Still, you can just knock the deed off the wall and replace it until you get the tenant you're after.
+ Hunger's back. 3 modes of gameplay as usual. Casual where dying costs you nothing (filthy casuals!) and there's no hunger, Survival where there's hunger and dying will cost you 30% of your current Pixels (money - which can be mitigated via Voxel Printing in 1k, 5k and 10k stacks to be banked) and your usual Hardcore where dying is permanent. For the (filthy) casuals that still want hunger but don't want to lose money, there's a mod for that. Ahhh, I love that line. "There's a mod for that."
Negatives:
- Variants (eg tree saplings) aren't named. Be prepared for a MASSIVE headache when searching for that palm tree sapling you were gonna transplant to your home base.
I'll leave it to you
+/- Shop inventory never changes. Good if you backtrack for something, not so good when you think about your own merchant colonists. Or it could be, if you keep changing out the merchant until they sell a specific item, such as Raw Fish or Ribs which are otherwise annoying to get in bulk.
+/- Wiring (yeah, equivalent to Terraria's wire/wrench stuff) is HILARIOUSLY COMPLICATED. In it's simplest form, you can hook up lights to motion sensors or switches. In it's most complicated form, you can do all sorts of nutcase things, such as one-use switches that can be used ONCE to open a gate and never close the gate again. Thing is, you can't spawn monsters. Still, in it's simplest form, you can do stuff like rigging a klaxon to go off when you sit down in your Captain Chair to jump to a new system. Your inner nerd may squee. That said, unlike Terraria, there's no three-colored-wires. Instead it's just one wire that you can hook up to things at will. I never really go past the bare basics of sensors, doors and lights, so if you're into the whole logic circuitry, you'll have to consider this yourself. On the bright side, there's no range to the wire - feel free to wire something on your ship's bridge to the rear of it if you like.
+/- Decorations and furniture (chandeliers, beds, couches, etc) are mostly 3D printed with the game's currency - Pixels. That means you can go kill a ton of enemies, scan a copy of what you want to mass produce (not everything can be scanned, some are special stuff like rare art or boss combat specific things) and go wild. Sure, you can still be conventional - chop down a few trees, make wooden planks, build a wooden bed. Thing is, most of the really fancy stuff you wanna decorate with (fancy data panels, maybe medieval themed items courtesy of the Glitch) is unproduceable. So short of raiding a few (dozen) villages (the guards will be hostile if you do this a lot), you're gonna have to turn to Pixel Printing. Pixel Printing is also a mid-endgame ability now since the printer requires mid tier materials to obtain. So expect to be raiding villages a lot early on I suppose.
+/- Your basic multitool (the Matter Manipulator - Pickaxe, Axe, Hammer, Bucket Wire AND Wrench, all in one!) starts out entry level, but subsequent upgrades will make it better than anything you will ever find. Take that how you will. Still, you're able to obtain other tools (pickaxe, drill - both function as axes and hammers too) but those are rare finds and fairly costly early on from the shop at the Outpost. They break too after using them enough (I don't bother with these, but the hp stat on them can be found at the wiki on
).

Whilst I long for a faithful recreation of the original XCOM or UFO from the 90's, with its seemingly endless campaigns, huge tech trees, full environmental damage and sprawling bases, this will more than do.
The world is under alien occupation and, as the resistance, it is your job to quell the alien threat.
The game has two halves. Firstly, there is the planet-wide base building and mission finder, where you plan your global strategy, build up your base, choose missions, find resources and research new technologies. Secondly, there is the strategic combat element, which occurs when you send the troops in on missions and focuses on moving individual soldiers around a finite area. This works a bit like a game of chess - albeit over multiple levels and scenarios, with various targets or objectives and, of course, aliens to seek and destroy or humans to find and protect.
One negative for me is the timers on missions; some are quite strict. I understand they are there to induce a sense of threat - which works if you like that - but I prefer to play slowly and methodically, coving all corners and such. With such strict turn time limits, you can't play like this as you are up against the clock! But the timer can be patched out with a mod if you so choose.
With that minor gripe out the way - this is strategic and unforgiving. Just the way it should be.

If you've never heard of Fallout, it's a game franchise that plays in the devastated world after an earth-spanning nuclear holocaust. Every game starts with a new character in a new setting and can be played without needing to know the others. But if you do of course there's the bonus of recognizing a few of the things that other characters reference.
Setting:
In this part, you play as the (male or female) eyewitness and survivor of said nuclear holocaust. On the day the bombs fall, you enter a vault and get cryogenically frozen to wake up many, many years in the future. And right off the bat, you are driven to explore the strange world outside: While you were trapped inside your cryopod, someone killed your spouse and kidnapped your infant son. Who are they and what did they do it for?
The world of Fallout 4 is vast. Set in and around (former) Boston, in an area now called "the Commonwealth", you will meet several larger factions all of which have their own plans and ... yeah, i didn't really count, but their number may approach the three digits - many individual NPCs. Along your way, you will also encounter several companions to assist you on your quest which, by the way, will likely sooner or later take kiiiind of a backseat as there is so much to explore and the game doesn't rush you.
When you work on the main quest, you will soon have to pick one of the larger factions to support. They don't all play nicely with each other, so be prepared to become enemies with part of this world. By the way, at this point I've sunk way more hours into this game than shows on this review (playing offline a lot), and I couldn't bring myself to finish the main quest yet. I still have so many other things I want to do, also because I bought the two story DLCs. Yet it has to be said that after the main game's ending, you can continue playing at your leisure, so the order in which you tackle things doesn't really matter unless there's something that comes tied to a certain faction or that requires certain events to not yet have taken place.
Gameplay:
At its core, FO4 is an RPG with a focus on gunplay (or melee, if that's your thing).
The gunplay part shows when you fight enemies (well, duh) with one of your preferred weapons most of which are customizable. You can fight either using VATS, a game feature that's supposedly an approximation to the turn-based combat in RPGs of yore, meaning time will slow down massively and you can then use action points to pick which enemies to hit where and in which order. Alternatively, you can fight in real-time like in any shooter. I'm using both styles in different situations, e.g. with small or fast enemies, VATS is pretty useful, and if you want to snipe over a long distance, real-time is better.
The RPG part shows in the hundreds of quests, the hours of dialogue and the fact that when you level up, you can pick or improve certain character skills/perks and thus shape your character for your preferred style of play: Good with heavy weapons, pistols, rifles, melee? Very efficient when wearing power armour? Using VATS to its full efficiency? Or rather someone who gets bonuses when doing combat in real time? Better when standing still in combat, or when moving? Great at modding weapons or armour? Charming the socks off of everyone they meet? Good lockpick because you must have every last treasure? Able to carry tons and tons of loot (good when you said yes to the previous question)? Able to breathe underwater for full exploration? Can consume tons of "chems" (drugs with useful gameplay effects) without getting addicted? etc.
Settlement building is another feature of the game. You will have to build at least a few barebones settlements with resources you find while playing. If you want, you can go above and beyond and spend hours and hours with that. Personally, I don't care too much for it, but there is a certain siren call to it, like a casual game on your mobile phone: "Those trees need to go. Huh, I could build some shops. And while I'm at it, the settlers could have nicer rooms. And then I'll quickly..."
What I liked
The world. I'm actually not a fan of post-apocalyptic stories with their grimdark settings, but the Commonwealth has something fascinating about it. I like exploring the sun-lit* ruins of the past to find out about their previous and present inhabitants in oh so many little stories that are waiting to be discovered. Some criticise the main story of FO4, and at least I have lost all sense of urgency to resolve it while playing, if only because it's patiently waiting for me. But FO4 does shine in the small stories: Reading old logs in still-working computers tells stories e.g. about corporate recklessness or personal loss, pre-war remains that are scattered all over give clues as to how these people died. Or you lend a helping hand to the still-alive citizen and will break into a safe, help a mourning father find closure, get a very old acquaintance back on his feet, learn how your companions really tick, become the embodiment of a pre-war radioplay hero etc. All this serves to establish a tone of heartbreak, hope and ironic humour.
*There really are all kinds of weather in FO4, but as you will see from my screenshots, I do like the sunny days best, maybe because they make the setting less grimdark, see above.
Mods. Bethesda games are known for their huge modding communities, and you will find that whatever it is that bugs you may  already have been fixed by a modder. Or you take your pick among mods that add new aspects into the game, change small things and more.
Now, there has been a recent uproar when Bethesda announced additional mods published by them and for money. Some people (you know who you are) even give this game a thumb down for that very reason because they think mods should always be free. Seriously, I don't see the issue: The free mods are still there, nobody's taking them away. And if Bethesda wants to make money with a franchise they own, that's very much their right. But no matter what your stance is on that issue, this game can be played perfectly fine without the payable mods.
What I didn't like
Repetitiveness. Since Fallout is made to be played for hundreds of hours, you may do just that and find the same gameplay patterns repeating: Explore, read/talk, shoot, loot.
And by now I know the game's assets by heart (let's loot another mop, scalpel, shopping basket, baseball ... just like the 10,000 before).
It wouldn't be as obvious with a game designed for a shorter playtime, but here we are. So ... expect to maybe not want to play this for days and days on end, at least after you've played for a few weeks in real time.
Graphics issues. I didn't experience any game-breaking bugs. There was one single time where a character I needed to talk to had gone for a swim and couldn't be talked to underwater, but that was solvable by making my character sleep for an hour. This bug-free experience may be because I installed the unofficial patch mod. But many times the game would suddenly drop to very low framerates and become unplayable for maybe 20 seconds. It could be due to my no longer new computer, but apparently people with newer hardware have the same problem. It was nearly gone after a few tweaks but reoccured after the update that introduced the Bethesda-made mods.
Achievements. I stopped getting achievements after I installed the first mod (which was pretty early in the game). Assumedly it's to stop people from cheating their way to glory, but then, if I really wanted, I could just enable the in-game console and cheat without mods. So it's just annoying to not be able to show off as usual.
(Well, there's apparently a mod to undo this effect, but I've always been too lazy to read my way through the how to of its installation ...)

This game encourages thinking outside the box. Literally. In any other space based game, decompression would be fatal, or incredibly dangerous. In Heat Signature it is merely another tool in your toolbox... did I say toolbox? I should really have said your massive wheeled toolchest. The solutions to problems in this game are plentiful, and many obstacles can be overcome in multiple ways, allowing for a wide range of creativity.
The combination between frantic top down action and tactical gameplay is fantastic. The gadgetry is often as hilarious as it is useful, especially when you start bringing about teleporters that all function in different ways, time dilation devices etc. The enemies commit the fatal sin of letting the vacuum of space decide your fate, if they manage to hit you, which means that with a little skill, a death is not necessarily going to be a death, though it will get harder to survive next time.
The persistence of characters in the universe is very well done and the game actively encourages changing characters often, sending others to the hall of fame, or letting newer blood continue unlocking gear, until you can return to them, and tool them up with the kit necessary to do their own personal mission.
The game will, eventually get a little repetitive, however I've put close to 4 hours in so far and I'm not even close to having explored every possible route. I have however discovered my favorite, which involves wrenches and decking everyone in the face with them.

It's an underpriced gem. Unique and engaging blend of game concepts (but still focused on clear ideas), with a high level of polish hinting at a lot of developer passion. First "roguelike" that really clicked for me - the core mechanics and player freedom are balanced just right to create memorable experiences and unexpected twists without relying on a scripted story. Intense but not stressful, thanks to the ability to pause anytime to plan the next move; almost gives it a turn-based feel. Can be played on easier missions for a while, but for some of the later progress you have to go through at least a few harder missions. I hit a wall early on, but luckily didn't give up until my skill finally improved. There are many items/gadgets that can help, but over time I've also started enjoying playing with minimal items (e.g. whatever comes with a fresh character) for an even more focused experience. It can absolutely be possible to pick the hardest available mission with a completely fresh character with no fancy items, and still beat it because there are so many ways to achieve your goal - immense satisfaction. Even though there's no real story, the game's mini-universe actually feels pretty immersive - there are no transitions between screens, it's all seamlessly mousewheel-zoomable from a close-up of your character all the way to a map of the entire universe. Music is great and adds to immersion as well. The concept is new, but other games came to mind for certain aspects - "hotline miami in space" is probably the closest, but it can also be more stealthy/tactical almost like the old "commandos" games.

A must for any LEGO/ Tolkien fan!
Content:
The game takes you through the Hobbit movies. On your journey you will meet interesting characters with brilliant abilities and visit beautiful places. Once you finish the game there are many other things to do in Middle-Earth...
You can:
Explore the entire journey  ( and a few places from LOTR like Moria and Lorien ) again in Free Roam.
Accept quests from the people scattered across the land for resources.
Trade unwanted rescources for better ones.
Forge items of Mithril in Bree.
Customize a character in Lake Town.
Unlock and buy extra characters like Gollum, Saruman and Sauron (  to unlock Sauron at any time use the following code: oara3d )
Jump on the back of an eagle for a fast way around the kingdom.
Replay completed levels.
Jump forward or back in time using campsites.
Gameplay:
Good with a fairly fast computer, amazing with a gaming one. Each level features different puzzles and funny cutscenes with real audio and dialogue from the movies. Each of the 13 dwarves have unique abilities like:
Using a bow and arrow to shoot targets ( Kili )
Eating food on special picnic mats and allowing the rest of the company to jump on him like a trampoline ( Bombur )
Mining rare resources like gold and ruby ( Bofur )
Using his staff to dwarf stack ( Gloin )
Using his flail to attach to gold hooks and bring down high items ( Dori )
Using his warhammer to push items ( Dwalin )
Pros:
Free Roam
Long levels that pack lots of puzzles in
Many characters to collect
The barrel scene from Desolation of Smaug ( available at all good Thranduil's Kingdoms )
Eagle Flying
Horse/ warg riding
Boat using
Beorn the shape changer's special ability - turning into a fast and strong bear!
Cons:
No Battle Of The Five Armies gameplay yet ( coming soon as DLC )
Middle-Earth is dangerous at night ( orcs come out!)
Had a few problems with shutting computer down in game after saving at a save point - don't do that if you get it!
Conclusion:
I would rate this 9/10 at the moment because there is no Battle Of Five Armies gameplay yet!

Overall, I had to say that I enjoyed playing this game. When I first started it, I was encountering some crashes but someone's suggestion on the forum quickly cleared up anything and I never saw a crash since. Regarding the gameplay, I enjoyed it. The combat did feel grittier than a Souls game, and I like how the magic in this game was much more 'supportive' rather than primary, as it can be in a Souls game (as an aside, I feel like magic ruined Dark Souls 2, but that's just an aside).
The boss designs were decent--they could use improvement, but I did enjoy some of them. I also did enjoy all of the little details they put in the game, like different ways to defeat bosses, different ending paths based on choices (which did seem a little hardboiled at times but was still a nice effort none the less). The only thing that frustrated me from time to time was the level design, which seemed labyrinthine.
There's lots of weapons in this game, and plenty of loot. The armor and weapon design were all decent.
All in all, is it "Souls-like"? Yes, it is. Do I care? No. It's not like Dark Souls was the first Action RPG. Is it a fun game? Yes, yes it is. Do I hope they make another one and improve upon the first? Yes.
I think what sometimes people forget, especially with original titles is that to criticize it needlessly and blast it with negative reviews, and to make statements such as "don't support this publisher", will ultimately lead to less variety, innovation, and entertainment. This is not a defense of bad games, but it is a defense of "improvement". If they make another, and I hope they do, I hope they can improve the formula, add some additional features that make it interesting and continue to innovate on this extremely fun genre. The more the merrier, I say.

This will probably be my first ever review of any game and I have a lot of games that I've played.
Fractured Space came off of early access recently and it reignited my love for space combat.
Let's hit this off with segmented sections.
Graphics: 9/10 Unreal Engine 4 has always looked good, but the amount of detail in the ship models is insane, the lighting, the beams, the rockets each ship has it's own distince style with each manufacturer having a different theme.
Sound: 7/10 The Crew say interesting things and the sound is very good but there's nothing worth noting about it, it serves its job well enough to not be a nuisance.
Gameplay: 8/10
Balance: It's definitely not pay-to-win, the ships are well balanced and there are no sure win strategies as this is also a game of deception, it's slow-paced and you will find yourselves dying by a decision you made 30 seconds ago. That means every warp in and warp out you decide cas consequences that can have an impact in the game, early deaths are less punishing and an early lead can easily be over taken with the right coordination and being at the right place at the right time.
Ships: Each ship design is vibrant and no two ships are alike with different roles even if both can do heals. Support craft and attack craft do have their counters but certain strategies can subvert that counter and the map often makes for interesting encounters that you won't feel unfair to either team.
Payment Model: 8/10 Nothing is unfair and it's very much like LoL, I do feel the Crew could have more methods of acquisition, but overall it's not unfair
TL;DR 8/10 Addictive, Fun and full of moments of wow. Please please if you are undecided, Try this game first before doling out judgement. I made this review because that's how much I love it.

Fun game, some major faults but still worth free download 100%.
TLDR
Pros
-Fun ships
-Mostly the combat is satisfying
-Good ship variety
-Can buy ships with/without money
-Lots of skins (pay money)
Cons
-Incredibly boring map endings/lane phases.
-Only 1 map.
-Unforgiving with recalling.
-Pay to win crew?
-Awful win conditions often leads to unsatisfying outcomes.
The combat, ships, abilities and playstyles of the ships are pretty cool, I enjoy the combat for the most part. Its like a mix of moba and team shooter, but it is a mixed bag and not always the best mix.
The main faults I have are the endings and the pay to win aspect. This will never be a fair fight like league etc because you need to spend money to upgrade crew as far as I know and you can only do that with real money. I.e pay to win. The other faults I have are with the map endings and the victory conditions.
I think people complained they didnt like the way the games ended so they put a cinematic. This didn't address the issue, its like putting fireworks on the last page of a boring book thinking it will fix the boring book.
The issues for me is : the way you win is to occupy the enemy base with more players than they have. Which completely ruins the assault aspect and removes the feeling of a final fight... imagine winning league of legends because you have 4 people in their base area and they only had 3 (with no fight required).
You can literally lose the match because people were just not spawning in time. In league/dota etc you need to finish a base to win... in this it just ends in the most ridiculous push with no fight. It is odd because there actually is a base there with destroyable turret shields, but it just lowers the damage you take while you cap. It needs a health bar on the base or something, would make the game way more interesting. You can lose the whole match because you were 10 metres outside your bases area bubble trying to rush back into it. Its so unfun.
I feel the map is dull though with not enough pve aspect.. put some base at the end of each lane with turrets or something.. its so boring. The lanes have cover in the form of asteroids which leads to cool tactical battles. But sometimes not so much. You just push an empty lane into the base and win sometimes... its not good.
I don't focus on the positives, there are many, but they need no attention from me, theres plenty of praise singers out there. I feel if you fix these things you could have a real contender. Its recommended based on the free pricetage but I do not recommend parts of the pay model. Buy the ship pack (unlocks all ships really cheap too) if you want to support the devs but I strongly disagree with the crew packs.
Make your money from skins and other stuff... getting better crew from paying only hurts the game if you cannot unlock it without money. Find another way to make your bank.
p.s Good game apart from those things.

Aberoth, oh Aberoth.
Aberoth is 8bit style MMORPG, which will not hold your hand. Not even if you ask it kindly.
The game is a niche that is definitely not for everyone, featuring a full loot death system. That is, if you do not protect your items, you can engrave your items making them belong to you. If you die with an engraved item there is a 90%+ chance to keep that item. If somebody else happens to pickup your dropped engraved item. This is seen as a act of thievery, until they either decide to return it to you directly... or alternatively deliver it at the inn, The regular player the item belongs to then can go and pickup their item for no fee what so ever.
Overall I think I have fallen in love with the game, and it definitely is a game for me. Having said that the game has flaws, which do hurt the game overall.
Pros
- Full loot
- Enemies pick up dropped loot and start fighting with it
- Criminal system
- Bunch of skills to level up... including drinking!
- A world which is great if you have imagination
Cons
- PvP everywhere (given that somebody marks them self as /unfriendly) might scare off new players. Stagnating growth.
- The graphics style is not for everyone and can be inconsistent in places
- The game lacks UI for the most part
- Quests take leaps and bounds in power, grinding will be necesarry at one point or the other.
The go further into the cons,
PvP everywhere is awesome... but a curse. There is currently as of writing this an♥♥♥♥♥in Realm Green just killing people in the Noob fields. Even while we epically teamed up with 6 people at once, we had no chance to hit enough through his defence to murder him. When later proper criminal hunters arise, this will be lmited. But for the moment people who grinded the hardest at launch and got some good weapon/armor have free game... until they are jailed ;D
The UI is... well it isn't there. Other then seeing the items in your imediate backpack on the right, your health on the right... There is no UI whatsoever. This... is probably my biggest problem with the game.
To equip a weapon from your inventory you need to. Throw your mainhand weapon on the ground, throw the weapon form your inventory on the ground, then pickup the inventory weapon and then pickup the mainhand weapon. While you doing this and you are dropping stuff on the ground anyone can come by and just steal your item.
-------------------------------------------------------
My score on a general level will be a "Try it out for yourself"/10.
This game is such a niche that you either hate it or love it. So the only way to truly find out is for you to boot up the game and try it out ;D

Pixel/text-based MMORPG.
The 1x scale resolution is 640x480, except that the main viewport is already scaled x4 (i.e. a pixel is really 16 pixels), for an effective resolution of 160x120, or half that of VGA (320x240). The original gameboy had (slightly) more pixels than this! Zelda never ran on a system with that few pixels (the NES had 3x as many).
There's no GUI, the commands are text-based. Head on over to
and check out the "help" - might as well check out the "champions" and the "store", while you're at it.  I don't think you can find out an opponent's strength without attacking them, or even find out what's lying on the ground without picking it up. Gameplay is grind, try to hit the pixels that is a bee with the pixels that is your hand, or a club, or a knife - you can't tell what it is anyway.
Because the game is PvP everywhere, i.e. you can get killed anytime, anyplace, by anyone, the only way to avoid having to start back at square one seems to be to have items in your vault and money in the bank. You can also pay to have items engraved, that gives you a 90% chance to retain them upon death.
I recommend this game for the vision-impaired: set the font size to 30pt, and then you'll be on the same footing with anyone who still has 20/20 vision and a 4k monitor. Everyone else, this is definitely
going to be the next WoW.

If you're reading this, you probably already know what the game is: An interactive story in which your choices keep the events going further. It's a story, where you actually care about the characters, you sometimes have to decide about life and death of your companions – and not always is there a clear “best solution”.
It may be clear at this point, the story makes or breaks the game. And let me tell you, the story is written in an excellent way. There is also gameplay (duh!), but it often breaks down to quick-time-events, press button “A” as fast as you can, or: search this room, while every item you could find or event you could trigger gets highlighted, when you aim closely to it. You may die a few times, but generally the game is not very hard to beat. But that's not negative, because a “hard” game would distract you from the scenery; the dire atmosphere, the danger hovering over the characters, even when at rest...
If you'd like getting a story told, where you can influence the direction it's heading and where you actually focus on story rather than gameplay – buy the game! While I'm writing this, the game is rated “overwhelmingly positive”. And I have to agree: It's worth every cent!
