A while ago I started writing some "10 hours in" reviews, under the premise that if 10 hours of experiencing a game could not convince me whether or not a game was worth buying, it was not worth buying as anything that takes more than 10 hours of learning/grinding to get enjoyable I'd simply consider a bad product. Gaming isn't supposed to be an acquired taste.
Lords of the Fallen managed to invert that concept by being a game you could, even on a first playthrough, complete within those 10 hours, having seen all it has to offer, and in my case still be sorely disappointed. Half of my recorded (20h) gametime was wasted AFKing or faffing.
It doesn't start out badly. It has a good trailer/introduction. Sadly the awesome power displayed in the cinematics is never actually reached in-game. Some hint is given towards defying gods, which sounds awesome, but during gameplay that balloon is pretty much deflated, leaving us with naught but a flubby object and a disappointing *pft* noise.
One is introduced to this game through a nice but vague cutscene following the introduction. You play as Harkin, a convicted criminal, freed by an unknown wizard/monk guy, and arriving at a monastery entrance in order to find the "saviour of mankind" before he gets murdered by the demon army assaulting the monastery and its attached citadel. The game does a good job of introducing you to its core concepts, giving you a brief tutorial about how to fight your first enemy. Lords of the Fallen's core combat system, which is actually fairly decent (if not for everyone) is revealed in this tutorial.
Before this tutorial moment I was a little in the dark about the game's mechanics. I had to select who my Harkin was, and the game gives you a choice of 9 "classes". To be more precise, you have 3 armour types to start with (light, medium, heavy) and 3 magic groups to combine your armour choice with. Your magic choice is permanent and you can learn the other magic types in subsequent playthroughs, though why you would is still beyond me. Your gear choice is fairly irrelevant, other than starting gear you can equip whatever you like depending on how you advance your character. I had no idea what I was doing, so I chose a medium armoured Solace magic character and ended up with a "Cleric".
I never felt like a Cleric. The combat tutorial taught me how to beat a guy down with my hammer, which in itself would be okay except this is pretty much all the game turned out to be. Beat guys down with your weapon. Equipment has different effects, weapons have different attack speeds and stats so you kinda get to play how you like... assuming you find a weapon corresponding to what playstyle you chose. Armour is more straightforward, you have a carry weight and armour has a weight value, if you burden yourself more with heavier gear types you have more damage reduction overall and more "poise" (a stat which helps you to not get your animations interrupted), if you stick to lighter armours you maintain maximum avoidance through dodgerolling distance and speed. All of this took me a bit to figure out as the explanation about these mechanics is completely absent.
After beating the first guy with my hammer in the tutorial, I was set loose into a pretty linear game environment which, while pretty well designed, was dull. Opponents had some variation but not much, and I just beat them down with my hammer. They felt like filler till my inevitable first bossfight, which ended up also feeling like filler. Moreover, combat animations are very slow. The game obviously sought a type of gameplay of fighting in a rhythm rather than button-bashing, which is in itself totally fine but the implementation leaves something to be desired. I died the first fight because I was unaware of this, once I'd become aware of this, I hammered down everything in my path.
And then I found the gauntlet. And magic.
The stupid thing is that this game doesn't really have magic. I did select the Solace magic school at the start, which eventually granted me access to 4 whopping spells, showing me clearly that this game wasn't about magic but about swinging your weapon and avoiding the attacks of the enemy. Except it really isn't.
The Gauntlet is an artifact found close to the start of the game, and is used in lieu of your shield, or in lieu of swinging your weapon twohanded, a style choice you can freely swap between (which is good). The Gauntlet fires magical projectiles, or a magical grenade, or a close-range magical blast. All of this uses magical power, same as your spells do. Meanwhile your spells are either useless or overpowered. Solace school had 4 spells: Prayer, Shelter, and two others that I forgot the name of because they ended up being useless. They don't work on bosses. Who the hell cares about spells that only work on opponents that don't matter? Of course if these spells DID work on bosses (the first being a slow-aura from point of casting which made any opponent caught in it hilariously incompetent, the second being a retributive spell that stunned anyone that hit you) they'd be stupidly overpowered. Prayer was rarely worth using (it creates a simulacrum that distracts enemies till it runs out or dies, an effect useless on trash, and nearly useless on bosses which kill it quickly), but Shelter was outright godly... IF you could cast it.
The Shelter spell gave me increased defenses, constant healing while it was up, AND reflective damage. The only problem was getting it cast, the animation of spells in this game is so stupidly lengthy and easily interruptable it was a drag using it consistently, but if you could time it right you simply could not die. The design is so stupidly ridiculous it's mind-boggling. Add to that that going for a magic build as I did let me fire magical projectiles at bosses consistently in a way that completely negated their obvious melee-based tactics, as the game had made it clear in the tutorial I was supposed to be swinging my melee weapon to kill stuff, and what is left is a game that has such grievous design flaws it ends up utterly boring.
So I tried doing what the game wanted me to, swinging my weapon some more. Even using a Faith (read: magic) based weapon, I did less damage than I did spamming my Gauntlet missiles, and the only difference was which boss animation I avoided. Bossfights were inevitably similar: either avoid the attack, swing till I run out of energy, avoid more attacks until I have energy to attack again, rinse and repeat, or alternatively going for magic: Spam Q while avoiding damage till boss dies.
The main problem of Lords of the Fallen ends being that they have some very nice design ideas, but the developers had no idea how to translate these into decent gameplay. The game's style is good, environment looks well-designed, the equipment is arguably over-designed, the opponents though lacking variation do look like scary extraplanar warriors. The combat system, while feeling slow, could be a good system except that resource management is trivial. If you take the magic route like I did resources are less trivial, but spells are either overpowerd or useless and the Gauntlet trivialises combat tactics. The world and the characters have potential, there is some lore available during gameplay which sounds like there could really be an interesting story going on in the background but it's like the developers thought they better not introduce too much story, or the action-hungry gamers could get bored. The resulting story is so vague it never has any impact.
Long story short, Lords of the Fallen tries to cater to too many audiences and in doing so fails to cater to any. It is dull, decent-looking, repetitive and ultimately, thankfully brief.

Following right after the cliffhanger ending of the previous episode Sol concludes the Space Pilgrim saga and ties up many plot points left open in the preceding games: I won't spoil anything, let's just say you'll have to find a way out of your predicament and will then take part in a mission that might have serious political consequences in the game's world.
This time you'll find a pretty engaging story, decent puzzles and a quite captivating final section: it's still a simple game at its heart but one that functions well.
-decent soundtrack
-while not winning any points for originality the story is interesting and enjoyable
-the final mission is well done, sees many characters taking an active part in it and provides a good closure
-there's finally a pretty competent attempt at giving the characters some depth
-fairly good puzzles
-good length at 2,5/3 hours
-I honestly fail to see any "key decisions" as stated in the store, the only decision I was faced with only
affected two minor characters and, even then, there was little difference overall
-the overall narrative works well enough, but there's really nothing new and you'll find quite a few cliches
-one of the romance options feels ham-fisted at best
The whole saga finally comes at an end with Episode IV, and does so quite well: considering the overall simplicity of the game I can safely say there's still quite much to enjoy and a good amount of content to be found.
The story is still quite straightforward and nothing you havn't seen before, but it works and the situations you and your allies will face give a good amount of momentum to the whole story. The puzzles are decent and generally not too challenging, but they all make sense in their context. The final closure wass good and satisfying, both for Pilgrim as a character and the whole universe the game is set in.
The game is still linear though, and the flaunted "decisions" aren't really there or make much difference: at least this time we get a bit of character depth though.
There's alot to like both in Episode IV and the saga as a whole if you're ok with its simplicity both in story and gameplay: for its price it's a good amount of fun.

I pre-purchased this game on Steam and even bought the Gold Edition since I'm a huge Assassin's Creed fan. But I'm very disappointed with this game. Here are some reasons why (Warning: light spoilers ahead!)
1. Story and Character Development
The story of Assassin's Creed always intruiged me since it incorporates real historical time periods with a twist. Sometimes it would get a little boring but usually its very good. In Unity, there was a real chance for the story to be different by showing the gray area between Assassins and Templars and coming to the conclusion where both Assassins and Templars have their strengths and weaknesses in their belief. The character of Arno and Elise who are Assassin and Templar respectively further provide the means to tell a unique story different from the previous Assassin's Creed titles. But, it ultimately fails! Personally, I would have liked for Arno and Elise to both realize the faults within their respective orders and break away from their orders or something. Or even uniting to bring down the "bad guys". Rather than what happened in the story. The characters themselves are merely functional and don't go beyond that which is a damn shame.
****Spoilers******
I find it extremely annoying with most Assassins Creed killing off female characters, just so that the male characters have a different view on life and are able to become more mature. Christina (Ezio's first love interest), Lucy Stillman, Mary Read just to name a few. (This game is no different too which angers me more!) The ending of Unity is more agitating since it merely sets up DLC! The Dead Kings dlc to be exact. This is unexceptable for me. It's as if they had to change the story just to accomodate the DLC later....
****End of Spoilers*******
2. Modern day story (Abstergo and the Assassins)
This has also been unique and mostly interesting aspect of AC. However, the modern day story in this game is a JOKE! It's barely there and I have no idea what happened.
3. Loot System
Loot system is terrible in the game since only one loot is given for each mission. Thus to get all the loot, we would have to replay the same mission three times, which ends up being a chore since there is little to no variation in the mission itself. Furthermore, the "Legendary Equipment" are locked and can only be obtained via Club Competitions which are extermely buggy and frustrating in general.
4. Combat
Not many agree with me but I liked the combat in previous games where you could counter kill an enemy and even combo kill them by pressing the right button. It made for more fun combat. Here, combat is brutal and punishing. Although I don't mind sticking to stealth, I would have liked the previous combat system to also be there. This combat feels sluggish and makes Arno look far inferior compared to previous Assassins such as Ezio, Edward, etc.
5. Microtransactions
This is ABSOLUTELY unforgivable in a triple A game such as this one. I cannot believe this exists in this game and it makes me very sad. Even though it isn't necessary to spend real money, I still can't believe that the in game economy hasn't been tampered with no matter what others may say.
6. Poor Optimization
The game is a technical marvel when it comes to the environment with Paris looking beautiful! However, this is marred due to poor optimization with terrible texture issues, insanely low framerates for using Eagle Vision and various other issues that make the game more frustrating to play. (My rig is a high end rig so I don't expect this to happen, but this is the only game where this happens) Oh! And there are plenty of bugs and glitches that still plague the game, even after four major patches.
There are various other things that I don't like about the game but there is no way of telling it without spoiling the story partly. In conclusion, I think this game is not worth at $60 at all, but if there's a sale then I think this game should be bought, if only to see the beautifully rendered Paris. There are plenty of games out there worth much less but allow for more fun while playing. I myself don't hate the game since I'm and AC fan but I'm not going to play it as much as I did with Black Flag. I would recommend Black Flag instead! It is much more fun compared to this game.

This is probably the worst thing that has ever come out of a game development studio.  They've taken a game and meticulously balanced it (well, they tried to), set up a plethora of rules and conditions that the player and AI has to abide by, set up a world where all of your actions and decisions are difficult, consequential, and permanent...
Then they give you an enemy that cheats.
You and the enemy AI can only move during your turn, can only attack during your turn, can only perform any actions during your turn.  Except the rulers who can move any time.  And attack you any time.  And outrun all of your soldiers.  And can do devastating area attacks when you have zero options to avoid them.  And can kill your soldiers with one attack.  And can stun or disable many of your soldiers with one ability.  And can show up from the very first mission with your most basic rookies.  And can appear in missions that you can't EVAC from.  And can completely end your campaign in just a few seconds.
I cannot recommend this.  If you don't have this, don't buy it.  If you have this, don't enable it until you're well through the tech-tree.  If you enabled it by mistake, or just not fully knowing what it is like me, or haven't gotten far into your campaign, find a mod that disables or nerfs the rulers.
This isn't the kind of game you can pull these kinds of tricks in.  This isn't like DayZ where I go in expecting to have all my progress wiped in a moment.

Nothing gives such easy and simple joy like a Lego game; we all remember the feeling of smashing bricks with Mario to get coins, and that mindless amusement is what I have loved about the Lego games.  But mindless is definitely a word I would use to describe both the Lord of the Rings and Hobbit installments of the Lego franchise.  While creative block-building and humor were the charm of Batman and Indiana Jones, the LOTR themed games seem overly focused on "sticking to the script" of Peter Jackson's oh-so-serious films by recreating the movie in Lego form.  You will sit through about as much cut scene as you will active game time, and the cut scenes chop up the game world in a frustrating way.  The Hobbit, in particular, seemed to have a lot of annoying repetition in its side quests, since Middle Earth is apparently made up of helpless trolls and orcs who want you to ease their way with more tedious mini games than you have patience to complete.  Oh, and those helpless inquisitors NEVER. STOP. TALKING.  You will want to leave the room instead of sitting through their speech on why they need a Mithril Potato Gun.  Boss Battles are just as mindless, as the screen tells you which buttons to pulse in order to defeat them.  It's worth playing if you like Lego games, but I would recommend Indiana Jones or Batman if you enjoy fun over tedium.

Oh my gracious sauce, it is time to review Bastion.
Let's first begin by talking about the gameplay. While it is not extraordinary, it is very solid and I enjoyed it like I enjoy a rich potato salad.  You can carry two weapons in your main loadout as well as one special move or skill. As you progress through the game you will find more weapons and your options will increase dramatically.  Experimenting with the different weapons to find the playstyle you like best is great fun. There is also an upgrade system for these weapons which allows you to experiment even further. All super sauce.
You play through many different levels as you defeat enemies and collect shards.  This is where the great visuals are shown off.  They are crazy delicious. Ridiculously good. They did great work on the art style of this game and it pays off.  The music is also fantastic.
The biggest flaw of Bastion is that the main game is shorter than most. However, the replay value is boosted by optional challenges and endurance tests.  The difficulty level is also quite tame, but they allow the player to make the game harder and recieve more EXP by playing on harder difficulties.  It is up to the player to add more pasta sauce to the game if the length and difficulty do not satisfy.
What I believe to be the most defining part of Bastion is the narrator who narrates all that the main character does in the game as you control him.  It is a very unique and fresh idea that made me say "Holy iguana lungs, this idea is pretty sauce!". The voice actor for the narrator is also excellent and his voice is quite godlike and very fitting.
Overall, this game is definitely a slam dunk worthy of a top 10 special on ESPN.  The music, the art style, the narration, the story, and the gameplay are all as professional as a broadway musical.
I have awarded Bastion a rating of "5/5 top notch godlike".  Thank you for reading my review.

IMO, XCOM2 is far better than XCOM EU/EW. Its hard to explain without playing how it differs from XCOM 1, but its really nothing alike other than the basic mechanics. the style of play is NOT the same. I would almost say that unless the player really accepts these differences, that they are in for a real supprise.
Most of the missions are different with the exception of retaliation/terror. In XCOM 2, all the missions feel neccessary rather than tedious, and have real lasting consequences other than just making the terror level increase in other countries like XCOM1. The missions DEMAND that you not only complete the mission, but ALSO manage to extract your team. I cant put enough emphasis on EXTRACT because thats your real mission most of the time. the mission is NOT to stay around and kill all enemies. Its to do what you need to and get out as soon as literally possible to do so! The game will PUNISH you severely if you fail to understand this. this might seem like a no-brainer, but if you leave a soldier behind, all his/her gear is lost. i HAVE carried unconcious soldiers to the extract, and would do again. If he says intercepters inbound, sprint your asses off to get OUT, or be left behind to be captured! Many missions MAY have a nonstop supply of enemy reinforcements! this is not something that breaks the game, it rather makes it more exiting/difficult. You are playing as a small team in ememy occupied territory. not expecting to get flooded by ememies is delusional. RUN RUN RUN! i HAVE been in quite a few situations where i literally had to disengage under fire to get to the extract point. I would say, dont force a mission if it goes sour. call the skyranger and get your troops out before they all die. the potential mission rewards are never going to help you recover from a squad wipe.
the soldiers now have a rich set of customization, and each have their own look and personality. you WILL get attached to them, and you will be genuinly upset if they die.
I LOVE to play, and prob will do some more complete play thoughs, but the game isn't without its flaws. the 2 issues i found were missing soldier actions, and a glitch in the avatar mission carrying the body resulting in failure. these are not game breaking, but could have ended my Ironman playthough abruptly. i managed to recover, but i was deeply upset about it.
would recommend! get it on sale when you can!

Often described as "Hotline Miami in space", I thought I would really like this game. I did at first, but after playing for awhile I found that the lack of cohesive story line (at least that I could discern) and lack of purposeful level design really set it apart from HM. Which isn't to say that there is no story line, it just seems split up among 100 random characters you play. I didn't play so many of those characters that I could see if they were repetitious or not, but ultimately the mission they send you on to complete your story line is one of the 3 kinds available. Those 4 were assassinate, capture, steal or hijack. There might be different stipulations with those sure, like don't sound the alarm or don't kill anyone, but really you're doing all the same things.  The small amount of weapons, enemies and mission types quickly make the game boring. I enjoyed the simple graphics, they felt right at home with the gameplay. And the gameplay was what really shined in this game. The use of pause, slow mo and teleporting lets you solve scenarios in creative ways. Unfortunately you start to see those same scenarios over and over again very quickly.
It isn't that I don't think this game can be fun, it can be! But there really isn't a lot of depth to it, and once you reach the bottom of that very shallow pond you may find yourself feeling disappointed like I did. On the other hand, I really wouldn't blame anyone for loving this game, and if the developer adds some content I feel like it could be a really great game.

Alright, I had a sort of joke review for this game before, but I think I should give it a bit more of a genuine response.
Let me start by saying that I have a few friends (who shall remain nameless) who really like the game. They played it way back when they were younger and they still play once and a while to this day.
However I didn't find out about this game 'till I was much older. So, as a new player, I found the game very easy to understand, and the gameplay is very straight forward. It's basically Rogue-like, MMO, Bullet-hell. Simple concept, interesting idea, and in a lot of ways, I can respect that.
Now, as for my experience with the game, it was actually sort of fun just starting out. However once you start getting to the late-game, it just becomes a really stressful chore. At that point the game becomes significantly less enjoyable (at least for me anyway). But as I said before there are rogue-like elements to the game, you can save equipment between deaths if you store it in your bank before you die. Unfortunately though there aren't any traditional rogue-like elements to give you any form of permanent upgrades between lives. So unless you've stashed away equipment, every single death starts you back at square one, no matter what. Which (again, for me) creates a very unenjoyable experience as it can be so stressful and frustrating to have so much progress undone with a single mistake, or to have absolutely nothing to show for all of your playtime.
One more thing I'd like to mention on the more objective side of things. I have noticed that even on some more beefed up computers, the game still chugs from time to time, which makes the game that much more unenjoyable to play.
Once more I'd like to reiterate, this review is mostly my own personal problems with the game, but my final consensus would be that this game is really dated, and most of the people who actually like the game just have nostalgia goggles for it.
Basically, it's not outright the worst game ever, but if you didn't grow up with this game, you're probably going to have a hard time getting into it, just as with something like say, Runescape.
So, I would give this game a positive review. But bethesda has ruined all of my trust as a company. Paid mods on a full priced single player RPG? complete BS.

Groundbreaking. ♥
Story:
If you haven't played Half-Life, truth is - You're missing out on a very awesome story! Playing the role of Gordon Freeman, you must fight your way through numerous creatures from a planet named Xen, such as the Headcrab, Alien Controller, Alien Grunt, and many more! The atmosphere changes a-lot from time to time, bone-chilling, heart-wrenching, or just plain intense!You've got two enemies hopping onto your back in this game, The HECU & Xen, think about that. Getting shot at while having a Headcrab trying to jump on your head! There is also one giant mystery to this whole series, and that is - The G-Man, nothing is really known about this character, not even till this day! Countless theories have been made upon trying to crack the code as to why he's even there.
Gameplay:
For 1998, the gameplay is steady! Keep in mind that there are other games with steady game-play that came out in 1998, but this is Half-Life we're talking about! A wide variety of arsenal, Smg, Shotgun, Pistol, RPG, who CAN'T love that? I do admit, some of the physics are a bit off, such as sliding a box or jumping onto a box that has physics, it could throw you off! This game features moments where you could be caught or not, such as a helicopter flying over you while you're in a sewer tunnel, you could shoot & trigger enemies early or sneak past - It's the players choice and how they want to see the story as.
Voice Acting:
Let's be honest, most games around this time didn't have amazing voice acting, but I would give the Voice Acting in Half-Life 1 a pass. All the scientists sound the same, along with the security guards. But I could see why they'd re-use the same voice actor, budget-wise, etc. No further analysis needed for this section!
Soundtrack:
Oh boy, the soundtrack is very intense! Every track played during sequences definitely fit the tone of that particular scenery/scene! One of my favorites is "Drums and Riffs". The soundtrack is a mix between Ambient & Dark Industrial!
Conclusion:
All in all, this was my one of my first FPS's I've ever played, and I've played it on the PC & PS2! I love both versions equally, thank you so much VALVe for providing us with such an amazing series!

Darkest Dungeon is a rough game that expects a lot out of you. Unlike most RPGs, your characters have flaws, and I don't just mean bad stats. Some characters are thieves, and will steal loot from dungeons right in front of you; some characters are obsessed with pain and will pop open a torture device and hurt themselves; still other characters are drunks, who will only wind down after a mission with a stiff drink. Not only that, but the dungeons wear on your heroes. They get stressed, and when pushed too far, they can break. Panic, cruelty, and madness set in.
Enemies are rough, and they will not only harm your characters physical, but mentally, forcing their stress up faster than you're ready for. Bosses hit hard and take hard hits better than any other enemies in the game. One bad team matchup could mean the end of a hero or more in any given run.
All of that said, Darkest Dungeon isn't just a hard RPG. Yes, it has moments where RNG gets you, yes there are times where things just feel stacked against you despite your best efforts, yes, the game can be unfair. However, like many other lauded hard games, the power of Darkest Dungeon is in your sense of accomplishment when defeating a hard enemy or finishing a rough mission. YOU overcame the obstacle. Rarely does a single crit save the day; it's your planning and strategy that led you to victory, and that just feels good.
Pros:
+Amazing visuals and audio, leading to a wonderfully cohesive and at times unsettling experience
+Great lore and a narrator with a seeming endless array of sweet quotes
+Unique mechanics and interesting dungeons
+A diverse roster of heroes, each of them viable in their own way
Cons:
-Longer missions and time between important missions can feel like a grind
-The start of the game can be slow as you gather your early game resources
-Bouncing back from a particularly painful team loss can take time, adding to the grind
Overall: The game can lapse into a grind of doing similar dungeon missions over and over again, but the monotony is broken up constantly and consistently as you work through the game, and each adversity can be overcome with simple planning. The RNG can turn the tides, but it rarely makes or breaks any expedition. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a unique or challenging RPG.

Great game, one of the spiritual successors to Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay.
Initially I was a bit down on the game until I started listening to some "how to play" videos on Youtube and foud that I'd been playing it entirely wrong.
I think much of people's frustration with the game is they go the usual route of trying to keep your same heroes strong, and invest in buildings that will help fix their maladies. In truth you're supposed to play the game as "the world's most brutal HR rep" by dismissing heroes who become too insane or diseased to be of good, and invest your points into the buildings that let you recruit already powerful adventurers straight off the wagon to replace them. I actually had to watch that video just to know that you can kick them out in the first place, the button is underneath the option to rename and recolor heroes! The buildings that fix up heroes are more for endgame, or for a hero you're particularly fond of. Furthermore there's an anti-frustration feature in allowing you to resurrect one of a random three of your fallen heroes from time to time, so by keeping your graveyard somewhat empty of trash you may get to bring back a favorite.
Once I found that out I made the painstaking effort of fixing my past mistake, and now its rare for there to be frustration. Its still hard mind you, adventurers I invest in will die or become useless and I lose hard won items, but I don't feel like I'm hitting my head against a brick wall anymore.
Also, many bad reviews seem to mention the RNG. This is because buffs and debuffs are very important in this game, and planning for having a character who's sole job is to manage that is the way to go. Another solution is to utilize excessive abilities like bleed and blight, so you only need to hit once to continue to deal damage. Buffs, damage over time abilities, and debuffs all stack to an extent so a monster that debuffs every turn will cripple your party and cause you frustration, while using your own debuffs on your enemies or buffing your heroes every turn will allow you to flip the RNG against them. Using Herbal Remedy will remove most debuffs on your heroes instantly even during combat, so plan to bring extras to any delve to have a more enjoyable experience.
There's also the problem that the DLC content, Crimson Curse, activates the moment you do the first quest from it with little warning about what that will actually do. It is a HUGE noobie trap since it causes a very debilitating status effect on your heroes and causes a very difficult boss to begin randomly appearing, and shouldn't be started until you're able to kick adventurers out of your roster at will.
All in all, a wonderful game that I love, but it REALLY needs a better tutorial.

I honestly would prefer to give XCOM 2 a neutral rating. I enjoy much of it, but certain facets turn me off completely.
Pros:
Customization of soldiers/weapons/ship - They took the last XCOM and just improved.
New engineer/scientist system - Makes engineers and scientist seriously worthwile especially early game.
Ship vs base mechanic - I prefer the ship in XCOM 2 to the base in XCOM: Enemy Within by far.
Concealment - Adds a whole new emphasis on strategic placement in the beginning of most battles.
Specialists - By far my favorite class. Adds a new emphasis on support that is also a highly capable combat unit.
Carry mechanic - The ability to carry wounded/dead troops off the field is absolutley awesome.
Cons:
Bugs - Lost multiple soldiers to stupid bugs. Nothing game crashing so far.
Forced retreat mechanic - I like to play out missions and use tactics etc, but in XCOM 2 the majority of missions force you to get somewhere within a certain amount of turns severely limiting most tactics and turns most games into a rush.
Avatar Project - I don't dislike the story line. I dislike the speed at which the Avatar Project gains progress. I like to run around and do as much as I can, but with this I'm constantly being forced to gain new sectors and find their bases, not support my allies and my own soldier development.
Dr. Tygan - He just bugs me.
Things I'm on the fence about:
Accuracy - If I have a machine gun and I'm standing 5 feet from you...I'm not going to miss, yet somehow XCOM soldiers only have a 70-80% chance of hitting you.
Accuracy - If I have any gun and I'm 5 feet from you. I'm still going to hit you. 100% of the time.
All in all the speed of the game really turns me away from playing through more than once. I want to have time to build a resistance force and fight an occupying power. Not run after individual bases constantly. Other than that I think they took a lot of input from the previous XCOM and improved a lot of systems and game mechanics.

Oh my gracious sauce, it is time to review Bastion.
Let's first begin by talking about the gameplay. While it is not extraordinary, it is very solid and I enjoyed it like I enjoy a rich potato salad.  You can carry two weapons in your main loadout as well as one special move or skill. As you progress through the game you will find more weapons and your options will increase dramatically.  Experimenting with the different weapons to find the playstyle you like best is great fun. There is also an upgrade system for these weapons which allows you to experiment even further. All super sauce.
You play through many different levels as you defeat enemies and collect shards.  This is where the great visuals are shown off.  They are crazy delicious. Ridiculously good. They did great work on the art style of this game and it pays off.  The music is also fantastic.
The biggest flaw of Bastion is that the main game is shorter than most. However, the replay value is boosted by optional challenges and endurance tests.  The difficulty level is also quite tame, but they allow the player to make the game harder and recieve more EXP by playing on harder difficulties.  It is up to the player to add more pasta sauce to the game if the length and difficulty do not satisfy.
What I believe to be the most defining part of Bastion is the narrator who narrates all that the main character does in the game as you control him.  It is a very unique and fresh idea that made me say "Holy iguana lungs, this idea is pretty sauce!". The voice actor for the narrator is also excellent and his voice is quite godlike and very fitting.
Overall, this game is definitely a slam dunk worthy of a top 10 special on ESPN.  The music, the art style, the narration, the story, and the gameplay are all as professional as a broadway musical.
I have awarded Bastion a rating of "5/5 top notch godlike".  Thank you for reading my review.

Without listing many many pros/cons lets just say a few things. The game is a massive improvement and many of the new features are to give you the player options. This means every play though is unique on the minor choices. Such as every region bonus is now randomized from a pool about 3x more than needed so many bonuses you wont even see every game. Also you have the freedom/liability to have more impactful choices. Such as base building is now some what smaller but more important to what you build first and there is not a 100% best option on many of these choices. Primary weapons have mods such as scopes, mags, stocks, barrels and more which buff it and you can only have so many so yayaya choices...Classes can be respeceted if you dont like the perks you got. The classic abduction mission which is 3 identical missions with differant rewards is replaced by uhm more choices. Now its 3 differant missions with differant objectives out of the handful of possible mission types. Each has differant rewards. Also each is a counter to 1 of the 3 alien current missions which are things as for the next month aliens have more ammor, poison ammo, you get 1/2 money or they send a UFO to hunt you down! So each has 3 very meaningful decisions independent of the map its on or how many enemies or which enemies which are also indepent of each other. You collect your resources by spending time at that location which besides your main $ are randomized. Such as pick up a soldier some where or varies resources but you dont know exactly how much. Now you really need to choose since you can only be at one place at a time so do I unlock region x or y? Do I build building x or y first with real reasons to do both at the same time. Choices is the number 1 thing the game gives you. You dont feel like o many an other missions x I just did like 2 of those in a row. Combat maps are like puzzle peices with differant peices being allowed to connect to differant ones in logical ways. Such as besides a few preset story mission maps which are partially randomized still every map is unique. It takes a whole play through to realize hay ive seen that "part" of this map befor. Parts are small like say 10-20% of the map. Its no longer "ive played this map 100 times and there are 20 possible maps for the city/forest so I know exactly what is the best strategy for this map and location". No its now this is a custom map for you to explore. Even the last mission has several versions of it with the only one being the same being the first and last room. In other xcom games enemies dont really scale but you just encounter differant ones. In xcom 2 all enemies scale so that sectoid late game is still a threat. Its not as much a threat as in the begining of the game but its still a threat. An example would be the weakest enemy a Advent Trooper starts with a mighty 3hp and grenades do 3 so bam dead. Late game they have 8. Which means you should be able to 1 shot kill with primary weapons but not always. On higher settings they start with 4 and end with 11 which means its a risk to 1 shot kill without crits. Unlike say enemy unknown where sectoids start with the same hp they end with which is 3-4 depending on setting which means late game they are a joke you poke and kill. That trooper though not gaining new abilties is always low risk but does increase in damage on their gear and some enemies gain more armor as game goes.  The game always feels fresh.

Now even though this game didn't start on the right foot, as time passed and the patches came in, the game did acheive the state it was supposed to be in. Overall, AC Unity is a great addition to the franchise. Arno's story was an interesting one that included lots of interaction between the Assassins and Templars and good character build. The new parkour mechanics felt great and fluid, the increased difficulty in combat promoted stealth, the way AC games are supposed to be played (Even though I believe a true Master Assassins should be able to take out a bunch of guards with ease anyway), and the new RPG-like character customization definitely played out better than I expected. Paris is huge with tons of content and places to explore! I have over 50 hours played and I think I still haven't visited every section of the metropolis. The only thing I didn't like about this chapter of the series is that it had almost no Modern Day Story. I felt like Arno's story, even though interesting and important in itself, had no connection to the modern day problems; Juno's ultimate goal, the remaining Assassin camps, and Abstergo Industries' next step. Maybe we'll just have to see if any of Arno's story actually is connected to the modern day through a sequel (*cough* AC Victory *cough*). In conclusion, I definitely recommend this game to any AC fan and even newcomers (since there really isn't much of a modern day story that you would've needed to know about details from previous games in order to understand).

Pros:
-Amazing stealth mechanics.

Cons:

-Forgettable story and campaign (*Dead Kings DLC not tried yet*).
-Dumb argument.
-Combat is, indeed, more challenging, but still easy.
-Phone app forced up your♥♥♥♥♥
-“Initiates”.
The game itself is NOT good. Please, remember this if you’re planning on buying it. It’s bad, ok?
The memorable yet confusing AC story that we all appreciate is a mayor disappointment in Unity. ONE CAN’T EVEN UNDERSTAND THE GOD DAMN ENDING!!! I’m serious here, by the end it feels like the story never actually moved forward as NOTHING INTERESTING HAPPENS.
Co-op is entertaining, but gets old really fast, even with friends. To prolong your experience try doing them solo in stealth, that’s when a real challenge kicks in. Therefore, if you’re not into stealth… be ready to be disappointed as the new combat system also gets old quick, 2 hits with whatever last tier weapon you have, that ALSO you’ll have quite early in your gameplay, and you got yourself a kill.
Nevertheless… if you’re a hardcore stealth gamers, like me, you’ll have tons of fun. Unity like no other AC before makes you feel like an actual assassin, allowing you to approach your targets the way you see fit without risking desynchronization. While the AI is not clever enough to feel immersed in the game, they still possess a challenge. Some situations, specially doing a co-op mission by yourself, will look impossible, BUT THERE’S ALWAYS A WAY AROUND IT, you just have to use your brain and all your gadgets. And parkour? Is not only better, is encouraged!
My advice? Buy the game… when uncle Gave puts it on sale.

From playing and completing this game I can tell how this was a masterpiece in 1998. However, I'm reviewing this for the people like me who never played this game when they were younger. So I want to answer the question. Is this game still worth a buy and a play in 2015?
So, a problem I seemed to have from the outset is that this game just assumes you know things, or you know the games concepts and mechanics already. There is never a tutorial of any type and in fact I got stuck for a solid 10 minutes at the very start of the game because I simply didn't know you could press "e" on people to make them follow you. Like, really? The game never told me I could do that. That is just one example of the game just assuming you know how to play.
Secondly, if you really look at this game. In essence, it is a very repetitive shooter. You pretty much do the same thing throughout the whole game from the first hour to the tenth hour. It didn't make me bored, but I can imagine it might make some people very bored.
Let me just add, THIS GAME IS HARD. Like, really really hard. I played on normal, and, oh my god. Just expect to die a lot. Over and over again to the same section, and throughout many sections in the entire game. It was at some points frustratingly difficult as I would find myself saving progress every 30 seconds at some points just because this try I did a little better and didn't lose too much health.
HOWEVER, that is the gem in this game. Because it was so difficult. It made me so happy to finally get past sections and eventually complete the game. I actually felt a sense of achievement beating this. Like a "I beat half life!!!" That is what gaming should be all about and it's a shame most AAA games lack that these days.
So, although this game has aged a lot, and elements are very outdated and in some circumstances, quite frankly, pretty awful. That doesn't take away from this game. This is a good game. I believe this game was enjoyable enough to still be worth a buy and play even in 2015.

Honestly I'm only doing this for the badge, but I've been super hyped about this game for so long so I nominated it first. Due to depression I haven't gotten around to playing it, though. I only played a bit when it came out, it seemed really cool.

The game is certainly addicting, and although it is a fairly simple concept I've found myself playing for hours.  It's simple to learn with an entertaining storyline, and the graphics are novel.  I do enjoy a good challenge, and Darkest Dungeon certainly provides that.
The main issue though is unlike a game like Dark Souls, the challenge mainly comes from blind luck rather than something that can be player controlled.  The most frustrating aspect of the game for me is the stress/thirst/quirks condundrums, where your peeps do ridiculous things beyond your control with devestating results.  A prime example is them constanly needing to "touch" things despite it being an obviously negative outcome.  Yes, even the biggest moron may be "curious", but after he's touched the same plant 5 times and gotten poisoned every time he probably wouldn't feel the need to touch it a 6th time.  Nor would he be like "oh hey here's a pile of old bleached bones.  Maybe there is some blood in this.  I think I'll touch it!"  (zap)  "Oh no!  I'm cursed now and have too much stress!" (Heart attack) "Agh!  Now I'm dead!  Time to spend hours and hours again leveling up from 1..."
Another fun thing is when you are waiting on a peep to take a critical action and for whatever reason they decide not to.  So say your healer badly needs to heal the crusader.  The crusader decides on his turn to control himself and attack your own and hits the healer, taking her hp down to dangerous levels as well.  Then on the healers turn, she decides to do nothing at all because she's craving blood or stressed or whatever.  The mobs go, and just like that they kill both of those idiots since you couldn't control thier actions.  Then it's time to grind once more  and hours later you finally have two new heroes up at lvl 6 only to have it happen all over again.  Very frustrating.  The game is hard enough without your party hurting itself without the gamer being able to control it.
Overall I must admit I've had a lot of fun with Darkest Dungeon.  Certainly a fun game to try and I think most people will enjoy it.  In the end though I've grown tired of the perma-death aspect of the game because the ways to die are too many and too cheap.  It would be one thing if I could raise these heroes back from the dead, even if it was quite expensive to do so, in order to counter the "100 Ways To Die In The Dungeon" angle here.  But having to keep doing the grind, over and over, gets old.

I honestly would prefer to give XCOM 2 a neutral rating. I enjoy much of it, but certain facets turn me off completely.
Pros:
Customization of soldiers/weapons/ship - They took the last XCOM and just improved.
New engineer/scientist system - Makes engineers and scientist seriously worthwile especially early game.
Ship vs base mechanic - I prefer the ship in XCOM 2 to the base in XCOM: Enemy Within by far.
Concealment - Adds a whole new emphasis on strategic placement in the beginning of most battles.
Specialists - By far my favorite class. Adds a new emphasis on support that is also a highly capable combat unit.
Carry mechanic - The ability to carry wounded/dead troops off the field is absolutley awesome.
Cons:
Bugs - Lost multiple soldiers to stupid bugs. Nothing game crashing so far.
Forced retreat mechanic - I like to play out missions and use tactics etc, but in XCOM 2 the majority of missions force you to get somewhere within a certain amount of turns severely limiting most tactics and turns most games into a rush.
Avatar Project - I don't dislike the story line. I dislike the speed at which the Avatar Project gains progress. I like to run around and do as much as I can, but with this I'm constantly being forced to gain new sectors and find their bases, not support my allies and my own soldier development.
Dr. Tygan - He just bugs me.
Things I'm on the fence about:
Accuracy - If I have a machine gun and I'm standing 5 feet from you...I'm not going to miss, yet somehow XCOM soldiers only have a 70-80% chance of hitting you.
Accuracy - If I have any gun and I'm 5 feet from you. I'm still going to hit you. 100% of the time.
All in all the speed of the game really turns me away from playing through more than once. I want to have time to build a resistance force and fight an occupying power. Not run after individual bases constantly. Other than that I think they took a lot of input from the previous XCOM and improved a lot of systems and game mechanics.

THIS IS NOT A GAME. I loved it, you'll likely hate it.
Pros: Artistic concept. Realistic tale.
Cons: This "game" takes all of 15-20 minutes to "play" and has zero replay value. F-bombs, etc., make the story realistic but means that it shouldn't be played by anyone under 12. (Which is a shame as the interface and game concept is excellent for all ages.)
Rather than a game, Dinner Date is akin to a story being read aloud to you. You have no control over the protagonist nor can you change the outcome of the tale. Instead, while the narration occurs, you get to add ambiance via gestures and actions.
If your mood is to experience 20 minutes of "narrative art" and you can buy this for $2, then I recommend it. If you're looking for a "game" or the price is more than a couple dollars, give this a pass.

Without listing many many pros/cons lets just say a few things. The game is a massive improvement and many of the new features are to give you the player options. This means every play though is unique on the minor choices. Such as every region bonus is now randomized from a pool about 3x more than needed so many bonuses you wont even see every game. Also you have the freedom/liability to have more impactful choices. Such as base building is now some what smaller but more important to what you build first and there is not a 100% best option on many of these choices. Primary weapons have mods such as scopes, mags, stocks, barrels and more which buff it and you can only have so many so yayaya choices...Classes can be respeceted if you dont like the perks you got. The classic abduction mission which is 3 identical missions with differant rewards is replaced by uhm more choices. Now its 3 differant missions with differant objectives out of the handful of possible mission types. Each has differant rewards. Also each is a counter to 1 of the 3 alien current missions which are things as for the next month aliens have more ammor, poison ammo, you get 1/2 money or they send a UFO to hunt you down! So each has 3 very meaningful decisions independent of the map its on or how many enemies or which enemies which are also indepent of each other. You collect your resources by spending time at that location which besides your main $ are randomized. Such as pick up a soldier some where or varies resources but you dont know exactly how much. Now you really need to choose since you can only be at one place at a time so do I unlock region x or y? Do I build building x or y first with real reasons to do both at the same time. Choices is the number 1 thing the game gives you. You dont feel like o many an other missions x I just did like 2 of those in a row. Combat maps are like puzzle peices with differant peices being allowed to connect to differant ones in logical ways. Such as besides a few preset story mission maps which are partially randomized still every map is unique. It takes a whole play through to realize hay ive seen that "part" of this map befor. Parts are small like say 10-20% of the map. Its no longer "ive played this map 100 times and there are 20 possible maps for the city/forest so I know exactly what is the best strategy for this map and location". No its now this is a custom map for you to explore. Even the last mission has several versions of it with the only one being the same being the first and last room. In other xcom games enemies dont really scale but you just encounter differant ones. In xcom 2 all enemies scale so that sectoid late game is still a threat. Its not as much a threat as in the begining of the game but its still a threat. An example would be the weakest enemy a Advent Trooper starts with a mighty 3hp and grenades do 3 so bam dead. Late game they have 8. Which means you should be able to 1 shot kill with primary weapons but not always. On higher settings they start with 4 and end with 11 which means its a risk to 1 shot kill without crits. Unlike say enemy unknown where sectoids start with the same hp they end with which is 3-4 depending on setting which means late game they are a joke you poke and kill. That trooper though not gaining new abilties is always low risk but does increase in damage on their gear and some enemies gain more armor as game goes.  The game always feels fresh.

Dinner Date is not a game, nor should it to be expected to be one. Rather its more of a story with visual accompniment and mild interactivity.
For what it was intended, it does a fairly decent job. It showcases the different mental stages a believable character goes through. You are privy to the neurotic ramblings of a socially-awkward nerdy would-be intellectual who seems to believe the only thing impoartant in life is "getting shagged", and is confused as to why this is difficult for someone who doesn't like to go out.
You can tell he is in a circle of friends whom all have more fun than him, and works in a place where nobody respects himself, and the only way he can justify his own behavior is through the guise of being a poetry-loving intellectual.
In many ways it was more educational than fun. You see him go through stages of denial, self-pity, anger, exasperation, and discontent. But if you don't understand the significance of it all, you won't get anything from this "game".

A roguelike Hotline Miami in space.
Basically, you're a member of the Guardians of the Galaxy.
This is a fun game, with ~20 hours of play if you want to see everything. It can feel a bit repetitive at the outset, then as you start to understand how to best customize kits you can really get into it. At a certian point your team has so many resources that it starts to feel repetitive again, and that's probably between the 10-20 hour mark depending on how quickly you push through it.
In the game, you have a team of characters. Each character starts out new, with basically nothing, and must be upgraded with new and better equipment, earned through missions. The more missions  you do, the more equipment and notoriety you earn. If you don't do something stupid and get your character killed or captured, there are personal missions. With high noteriety, you start to see diminishing returns on mission rewards, which does a good job of pushing you to complete your personal mission. Once the personal mission is complete, your character retires and a newbie takes his/her place. If, as previously mentioned, your character is killed or captured, one of his/her family members will often take his/her place. Their personal missions are to avenge or rescue (allowing you to play as that character again) the character you got killed or captured.
There is plenty of replayability, if you enjoy the format. You can even start a completely new galaxy if you want to begin from scratch.
My biggest gripe is that there seem to be plenty of missed oppertunities with mission variance. There are essentially 5 missions: Steal, Rescue, Capture, Hijack, and Assassinate. Each mission follows the same pattern: fly to ship, board, take something, go back home. For a game with so much procedural content, it would be nice to have seen procedural missions, as well. Multi-stage missions, involving multiple ships, could virtually eliminate much of the feeling of repetition. How about a mission where you steal explosives from one ship, use them to destroy another ship, then plant evidence of the crime on a third ship? Or perhaps you rescue a sick man from one ship, smuggle him through enemy territory on a second ship, capture an enemy doctor on a third ship and bring him back to ship #2, take a cure off a 4th medical transport ship, then deliver everyone to a 5th hospital ship? There are limitless possibilities with the current mission variants; if a few more variants were added in addition to multi-stage missions, that feeling of repetition might go away.
In spite of the flaws, I really love this game. I hope Suspicious Developments continues with it and expands upon its already fantastic foundation. But, even if they don't, I still enjoyed my time with Heat Signature.

Great game, one of the spiritual successors to Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay.
Initially I was a bit down on the game until I started listening to some "how to play" videos on Youtube and foud that I'd been playing it entirely wrong.
I think much of people's frustration with the game is they go the usual route of trying to keep your same heroes strong, and invest in buildings that will help fix their maladies. In truth you're supposed to play the game as "the world's most brutal HR rep" by dismissing heroes who become too insane or diseased to be of good, and invest your points into the buildings that let you recruit already powerful adventurers straight off the wagon to replace them. I actually had to watch that video just to know that you can kick them out in the first place, the button is underneath the option to rename and recolor heroes! The buildings that fix up heroes are more for endgame, or for a hero you're particularly fond of. Furthermore there's an anti-frustration feature in allowing you to resurrect one of a random three of your fallen heroes from time to time, so by keeping your graveyard somewhat empty of trash you may get to bring back a favorite.
Once I found that out I made the painstaking effort of fixing my past mistake, and now its rare for there to be frustration. Its still hard mind you, adventurers I invest in will die or become useless and I lose hard won items, but I don't feel like I'm hitting my head against a brick wall anymore.
Also, many bad reviews seem to mention the RNG. This is because buffs and debuffs are very important in this game, and planning for having a character who's sole job is to manage that is the way to go. Another solution is to utilize excessive abilities like bleed and blight, so you only need to hit once to continue to deal damage. Buffs, damage over time abilities, and debuffs all stack to an extent so a monster that debuffs every turn will cripple your party and cause you frustration, while using your own debuffs on your enemies or buffing your heroes every turn will allow you to flip the RNG against them. Using Herbal Remedy will remove most debuffs on your heroes instantly even during combat, so plan to bring extras to any delve to have a more enjoyable experience.
There's also the problem that the DLC content, Crimson Curse, activates the moment you do the first quest from it with little warning about what that will actually do. It is a HUGE noobie trap since it causes a very debilitating status effect on your heroes and causes a very difficult boss to begin randomly appearing, and shouldn't be started until you're able to kick adventurers out of your roster at will.
All in all, a wonderful game that I love, but it REALLY needs a better tutorial.

Hacknet is such a unique experience - it is designed well, and continues to throw the player curveballs. Often, the game is able to do much more with such a simple interface than you can imagine. The game did a good job of capturing my imagination, despite the vast majority of the game looking like an MS Dos prompt. You may steal files from other servers, delete files that were acquired illegally, alter school records or those of death row inmates, and (in what was the highlight of the game to me) even hack a pacemaker. The only issue I had with the game was when one particular server would not accept a password that I had right in front of me. The password explicitly referenced the server I was attempting to access, but something was lost in my ability to transcribe it. An N looked like an M, and the numbers 1 and 2 appeared to be of different heights. The game doesn't allow you to copy and paste, and I could never quite figure out what the password was supposed to be. I ended up looking up a separate password that I needed (that I was to find on the first server in question) to continue the game. Otherwise, the game is quite clever, and at times requires some lateral thinking. If you want a unique gaming experience, you should give it a try.

This is probably going to be long, so let me tl;dr it for you: BUY THIS GAME.
Okay, now that that's out of the way, let me tell you why you should get this game.
1. As you can see, I have almost 400 hours in this game as of writing this review. While the main storyline of the game is rather short (if you don't waste your time and take three years to do it like I did), it's actually endless. Even if you somehow manage to exhaust all the millions of things you can do in this game, there's still so much charm and peace and enjoyability that it's just endlessly playable. Not to mention that the wonderful ConcernedApe, the incredibly talented mastermind behind this masterpiece of a game, is about to release another update to add more to the game. Don't expect that to happen often, though, I'll warn you. He's stated that it's a mostly finished game (save for the multiplayer feature) but as I said, there's so much here plus so many mods that it's not that bad that he doesn't want to add much more content. He's constantly working on bugs anyways.
2. OOOOOOoooooOOOOOOooooOOOh the MUUUUuuuuuuUUUUUuuuuUuuuuuUuuuuuuuuUUUSIC. It's absolutely fantastic. There's a seemingly endless amount of music in the game, each song suited to the scene or season. A deep, droning, funky beat for the fiery hellpits of the mine. A floaty, bright tune for a spring morning. Apparently, they even released the soundtrack on some very colorful vinyl records for a while. Don't think it's still going on, but it was pretty cool.
3. THIS IS A ONE-MAN LABOR OF LOVE. Or, originally, it was. There are beta testers and everything now, but the creator of the game had to essentially teach himself coding, teach himself how to do pixel art, and survive off tea and determination for a very long time to get this game out there. I really think that alone makes the price worth it (even if we exclude just how great the game is and all that).
4. Okay, yeah, it wouldn't be a Stardew Valley review without mentioning Harvest Moon. Honestly? It takes the Harvest Moon formula and gives it a fantastic makeover. You can be gay, for one thing, which is fantastic and should have been a glaringly obvious necessity for previous games of this type. There's no animal slaughter AT ALL, unless you count catching fish or killing monsters in the mines. Speaking of, there are MINES. COMBAT. BEING A BADA*S. SWORDS. SLINGSHOTS. HAMMERS. You can even speak softly and carry a lead rod.
5. There's really no rush at all in this game if you don't want there to be. Yeah, the story lasts about two years in-game, but even if you don't reach the end properly then, you can push an ending at your own pace.
6. MODS. THERE ARE SO MANY MODS. Honestly, there are endless mods you can use, like one to diversify the town and one to make the world pastel. The people behind these mods are amazingly talented and are doing this all for FREE. Even if you do somehow get bored with the way the world is after the story ends, you've got endless modifications to work with. Good luck installing SMAPI though...
In all, this game is incredible. Please play it. Buy it at full price. It's worth it.

Telltale's spin on The Walking Dead is in many ways a success. The graphics on the game are pretty good. The story line, though extremely linear, is one that you can definitely enjoy in a single playthrough. The characters are, for the most part, well thought out, and engaging. Lee and Clem are both easy characters to love, along with their entertwining story. **Spoiler Alert** From this point on there will be portions of the game that will give away some of the storyline.
I almost freaked out when they had me dream that she became a walker. O.o
Some of the things that I think would have really pushed this game over the top if they had been better are as follows. The ability to TRULY choose my own story, I've played through many of the episodes 2-3 times trying to gain different outcomes, but it always ends up the same. Even when you choose between saving different people Telltale takes the choice away from you later on so that you have to follow the story line they've laid out.  Take for instance saving Carly or Doug. It doesnt matter because they both die later due to Lilly going insane, and there's NO WAY to stop it from happening. I replayed the episode 3 times before finally googling it to see if there was any way to stop Lilly and found that there wasn't. This to me is the major flaw to this, and all of the other Telltale games. They're not truly unique stories, and you can't truly change the way things happen in the end no matter what you choose. My biggest gripe with this series, as well as the other games I've played of theirs is that I can't really change the story, just a few minor plot points. If you're going to sell a game as a "Choose your own Adventure" type game, then please make it actually be able to be played through multiple times with different outcomes each time based on choices of the player.
In closing, I absolutely love the idea behind TWD, and the GoT series by Telltale, however they've sold us majorly short in my opinion on the whole "Choose" part of the adventure, it is nothing more than smoke and mirrors while they push the linear game that they wrote on you as a player. The games at face value are fun to play through once for sure, maybe even twice if you want to change the persona your character has, but not much more than that as the story never really changes.  Would I recommend this game? Yes when it's on sale. Just don't expect as much as I did when buying it.

The game is certainly addicting, and although it is a fairly simple concept I've found myself playing for hours.  It's simple to learn with an entertaining storyline, and the graphics are novel.  I do enjoy a good challenge, and Darkest Dungeon certainly provides that.
The main issue though is unlike a game like Dark Souls, the challenge mainly comes from blind luck rather than something that can be player controlled.  The most frustrating aspect of the game for me is the stress/thirst/quirks condundrums, where your peeps do ridiculous things beyond your control with devestating results.  A prime example is them constanly needing to "touch" things despite it being an obviously negative outcome.  Yes, even the biggest moron may be "curious", but after he's touched the same plant 5 times and gotten poisoned every time he probably wouldn't feel the need to touch it a 6th time.  Nor would he be like "oh hey here's a pile of old bleached bones.  Maybe there is some blood in this.  I think I'll touch it!"  (zap)  "Oh no!  I'm cursed now and have too much stress!" (Heart attack) "Agh!  Now I'm dead!  Time to spend hours and hours again leveling up from 1..."
Another fun thing is when you are waiting on a peep to take a critical action and for whatever reason they decide not to.  So say your healer badly needs to heal the crusader.  The crusader decides on his turn to control himself and attack your own and hits the healer, taking her hp down to dangerous levels as well.  Then on the healers turn, she decides to do nothing at all because she's craving blood or stressed or whatever.  The mobs go, and just like that they kill both of those idiots since you couldn't control thier actions.  Then it's time to grind once more  and hours later you finally have two new heroes up at lvl 6 only to have it happen all over again.  Very frustrating.  The game is hard enough without your party hurting itself without the gamer being able to control it.
Overall I must admit I've had a lot of fun with Darkest Dungeon.  Certainly a fun game to try and I think most people will enjoy it.  In the end though I've grown tired of the perma-death aspect of the game because the ways to die are too many and too cheap.  It would be one thing if I could raise these heroes back from the dead, even if it was quite expensive to do so, in order to counter the "100 Ways To Die In The Dungeon" angle here.  But having to keep doing the grind, over and over, gets old.

FX3 adds several key features that make it a unique experience over FX2, which was perfectly fine the way it was.
More voice clips on the main menu, hope you enjoy hearing "My Collection" over and over while browsing tables. That got annoying really fast. Why would anyone want this? The only use I can think of is for blind players, but the pinball wizard was also deaf so I don't think it'd help him.
Progression. Oh great, levels and powerups for the tables, complete with annoying popups every ten seconds saying you got exp for doing something. I don't want this and I'm sure the powerups will be mandatory for wizard mode on future tables, this is bad. Also, a nagging "Are you sure you want to play without them?" message to click through when I choose to start a table without slotting in the upgrades. Fortunately there's a "Classic Mode" for people who play pinball because they want to play pinball. This still has quite a few distracting pop-ups but nowhere near as many as the new standard single player.
Long load screens after every game. The last thing I want to do after my final ball drains is wait half a minute for a summary menu to load that compares my score to my previous best. I want to get back in and play another game. It's even worse on the new "standard" mode, another screen to click through showing unlocks. I just want to keep playing.
Then there's the licensing issues. Tables people paid good money for in the FX2 days are gone from the game because the license ran out and the tables won't transfer over to FX3.
Stick with FX2 even though it's unlikely any new tables will be backported to it.

Geometry Wars Melee
Plays best with a controller, but unfortunately the game will not accept a Steam controller.
Your typical top-down twin-stick shooter, except that it's not typical because it's not a shooter and it only uses one stick.
Move your ship around and use the inertia to swing your tetherballs at enemies and asteroids. Your own tetherballs can't hurt you, but contact with anything else will destroy your ship. The asteroids float around slowly like the asteroids in the game Asteroids. They also divide similarly. Enemies have different movement patterns, but they all come for you eventually.
The arcade mode is fine: survive as long as you can and try for a high score (and by extension a couple achievements).
I had a lot more fun playing through Mission Mode: There are 150 tasks for you to accomplish (things like "beat 10 enemies" or "pass through the checkpoints without breaking any asteroids"), and you're assigned 3 at a time. The round ends either when you crash your ship or when all three active tasks have either been passed or failed. Successfully completing a task crosses it off the list, and when the round ends you're dealt a new one to replace it. For the most part, they're delivered to you in increasing difficulty. An early mission may challenge you to survive for 20 seconds in a limited radius, while a later mission may demand 60 seconds within the outer pull radius of a black hole
I'm not sure if the 150 tasks are always delivered in the same order, but they make for some interesting combinations. Unfortunately, some of the combinations are infuriating. I had a round wherein I was expected to:
Any two of those tasks would've been fine, but having all 3 active at the same time meant I was trapped in a fairly small level choked with gigantic asteroids all getting pulled toward a black hole faster than I could repeatedly break them down with my single particle. After dozens of failed attempts, I finally got an asteroid configuration that allowed me to carefully sneak around and pick off the 10 enemies, so that when I died, the next round wouldn't be the claustrophobic black hole stage.
There are multiple ships to unlock, offering varying top speeds and particle options. You can change ships between each round of Mission mode, giving you an advantage against certain types of challenges.
Glad I dug out a 360 controller to give this one another try.

This game is absolutely amazing. There's literally no pressure to get things done because of the continuing years, so if you miss an event or in-season item, no worries. The ambiance is super chill. It somehow combined a ton of different subgenres (dating sim, farming sim, survival, fighting, RPG) and made it work flawlessly without becoming too much of one or too oversaturated with content. You don't even have to farm. You can raise animals or crops, you can fish and forage, or you can mine ore and fight monters for the guild. There's even little bits of the supernatural in there with the restoration of the community center (should you choose to), the wizard, fairies blessing your harvest, and witches cursing your chickens. There are holiday events and backstories to create three dimensional characters in a real feeling community. You'll grind away creating the best farm you can every year and want to keep doing it. You'll enjoy buying rounds at the bar. You'll care about getting all of the character cutscenes. I regret not being able to play as much recently, but with the new updates and multiplayer coming up, I'll be sure to pick it up again and devote way too much of my life to it. The fact that the devs continue to nourish this game and give it the potential it deserves makes it all the better.

Fun game but be very careful when buying tables if you already bought some for FX2.  It is possible to buy some tables twice because the steam interface doesn't recognize that you have them even though they might show up in game as unlocked.
Pros for FX3: Still the same fun and addicting pinball action from FX2 with better graphics, more game play elements to keep you engaged, and some new tables to play on. The menu has also been overhauled and is easier to navigate without a mouse. Most of the tables you purchased for FX2 are brought over to FX3.
Cons: Loading takes longer, especially when returning to the menu after a game.  The pop-ups during gameplay are a little excessive, but luckily they aren't intrusive.  As mentioned above, you can potentially rebuy tables you already own.  You can't buy individual tables anymore, only bundles.  There is no discount for the bundle if you already own some of the tables in it.  FX2 veterans will have to start from scratch for  achievements and high scores in FX3.  If you want to stick with FX2, you can no longer buy more tables for it if you hadn't purchased them already.  Tables purchased in FX3 don't transfer to XF2.  5 of the tables from FX2 are missing from FX3 and won't transfer even if you own them already: (South Park: Super Sweet Pinball, South Park: Butter's Very Own Pinball Game, Super League - Zen Studios F.C., Planst vs Zombies, and Ms. Splosion Man).
If you want to continue to play the tables missing from FX3, you will need to keep FX2 around.  I recomend backing it up as well just in case.

Jordan Hampton groaned as a cellphone vibration woke her from much wanted slumber. Her sweet slumber was disturbed by an urgent case.

If you enjoyed Enemy Uknown/Within, you're going to like this. It's more of the same but tweaked and changed so it keeps the best while improving on weakness and trimming the fat. It also introduces new elements into the old formula to spice it up, so being experienced with EU/EW is a false sense of security. It took me 58 hours and 3 failed games to finally win on normal difficulty.
Familiar enemies have progressed and improved in the wake of the alien victory, presenting new challenges.
World/base management has also stepped up consideradbly- where EU/EW boiled down to "bum rush your satellite production, win game", here you are more engaged by active counters, lurking UFOs and a doomsday countdown that will WRECK you until you've learned from your failures (more on that in a bit)
Character customization and generation is more in depth than ever, so you'll feel even more aguish when your soldiers get critted by some jack-off Muton WHICH IS ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T BTW
So in my personal experience, I would reccomend it.
BUT SOME THINGS TO CONSIDER:
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
-  I find the new soundtrack somewhat lacking. It's not that it's bad,  I just think it lost some of the personality that Michael McCann (guy who did the Deus Ex HR soundtrack) brought to EU/EW. Mods can and will remedy this though.
- The game can be buggy. For me it's mostly been inexplicable pauses that slow the pace, but some people report some serious issues with LOS. Your mileage may vary.
- If you hate time limits...I got some bad news for you. Mods will remove these if they transcend 'challenging' and wind up just ruining the game for you, though.
- BEWARE THE "ALIEN HUNTERS" DLC. This is my only objective complaint. This DLC is nonsense that at best will put a new player against an even more uphill battle, and at worst will render your game unplayable through game crashes. Save your 10$, you've been warned.
