Great game! Enjoyed it alot. The only disadvantage is - the game is quite short comparing to DS series.
What I like:
- Graphics - it is amazing and making very grim dark atmosphere you can dive in. IMO this game looks much better, than even DS3 which came out 2 years later.
- Artwork - artsts did a great job drawing weapons, characters and locations.
- Checkpoint system. It is really cool that enemies won't respawn when you use checkpoint. Only your bonus exp rating is reset.
- Physics. Character move and strikes are much more natural than in DS. And that heavy breath under helmet at low stamina - I love it! )
- Great DLC labyrint.
What could be better:
- The game is quite short IMO. I've completed it with dlc in 3 days (played alot a day though)
- The game could be harder. Maybe it is due to my DS experience. Some bosses are rediculously easy.

Strength:
-Creative crafting: The crafting system not only let's you create things, it lets you explore the boundaries of pertinence and viability. You create a tech, go out and experiment it, you like it or not, find a new part, think of a better way, off you go with a new project.  Dynamic and stimulating.
-Diversity of choices: Whether you want a big or small base, one or many, what use you make of it/them, build one multi-purpose or many single-purpose tech, the size of anything... The game successfully makes you feel every choice is pertinent and has potential.
-Open-ended: You understand very early that everything is doable everywhere. You might start off somewhere, but soon realise that this place sucks and would like to try this mountainside or this flat dryland a try. Nothing is going to prevent you from anything. Empowering.
-Playable: That might come as a weird strength, but it's worth noting given the alpha status of the game. Whatever you might not like about it, the developers managed to make this game balanced and content-rich enough to be enjoyable.
Weaknesses:
Alpha stage: Despite what i just said, everything that is NOT likable is probably because it's unfinished/unpolished. Most notably, given you like the game and play it through, the later phases leaves you bored with obvious lack of goals and repetitiveness. You come to think that there isn't lacking that much that would make you stick longer.
-Lack of content: Whether it is variety of mission types, variety of landscape, variety of anything, you've got to be forgiving to an extent. That's where the genius of the developers shines most: They've been able to make it enjoyable despite broad lack of content. Magic is there.
-Very poor AI: They talked about it and have a plan for it, but it's worth noting it currently barely deserves its name.
-Performance issues: Mostly when too many guns fire at once and when resources accumulate in large quantity in silos. Nothing optimization won't fix but that kind of break the parts-crafting system, so long as you're an industrial-size type. You won't see that until late-game.
-Everything else: You could wish for a bunch of smaller things such as component stats to be available, better specific tuning for some components, and whatever else, but they're not there yet.
Overall:
This game successfully captures the crafting spirit we have seen a lot lately and deepens it by combining base building, vehicle building, parts crafting and resources gathering from a vehicle perspective. It blends so well you barely notice the inherent challenges and possible failures of such an attempt. The developers deserve a fair share of congratulation for that. Making it definitely playable and enjoyable despite the lack of content also underlines talent. Unfortunately, its lack of development will prevent you to play as long as you would otherwise.
This game is actual gold. Singleplayer's fun, but grab a couple of controllers and you've got yourself an awesome way to kill an afternoon.

If you like exploring an endlessly vast universe, then play starbound. This game has the largest map of any game that i've ever played. You can spend hours just digging to the core of a planet or exploring the surfaces of worlds, hoping to find any semblance of life(sometimes you do). When you do talk to them, they usually give you witty or strange remarks.
Also, checking with the search button provides many interesting commentary on everyday objects. Each race has their own commentary which is pretty great given that there are 5 races(6th one to come).
Nitty-gritty details of Starbound:
Currently, Starbound is quite limited in terms of what you can do. Starbound is designed to be a game that allows you to do anything you want. But developers haven't got there yet. In a while, version 1.0 will finally be complete. This means that currently, the game is still undergoing development and the last stable development was like 8 months ago. That's not good.
*Note: As of this review, the current release is Enraged Koala (update 8)
There are no quests currently after the few quests given when you start off. Every other world has about the same design as the rest of the worlds:
1) There is usually a surface. You go around the surface trying to find life or rare materials.
2) When you get bored of doing this, you go deep underground. Trying to drill to the core of every planet.
3) When you get bored of drilling, you build a staircase to space, trying to see how far into the atmosphere you can go.
4) When you are satisfied after reaching for the heavens, you either fight bosses or NPC enemies.
5) When you've done all exploration on a planet or maybe in various planets, you try to go to a different galaxy and explore different surfaces(you collect items as you explore different surfaces).
6) Since each galaxy has harder and stronger lifeforms, you try to get the highest tier weaponry and armory to stay alive.
And after all that, you get bored. Because there simply isn't much content else. You do get to generate NPC characters though. I haven't tried that yet. But, in about 70 hours of gameplay, I managed to get to the highest tier of equipment and explore a decent number of worlds.
That's kinda boring. I want a quest I could do as a wanderer in space. You know, be a mercenary like Cowboy Bebop. Or I want to explore specially designed dungeons, the ones made to destroy me. I want to be able to smith more types of weaponry. There is a hard material called obsidian that's a pain to drill through but I can't make obsidian weaponry. Kinda disappointing really.
The Starbound now simply has a lot of potential. The developers work hard everyday and constantly post updates on what they're doing. You can check this out on the official Starbound website:
If you buy this game, know that it's worth it in the long run. Know that it's pretty interesting too now. But it's not interesting enough to be worth every single dollar you bought this for. Not yet. It's worth half of that now.
If you like exploring however, you WILL be addicted to this game. You WILL spend hours searching for any interesting planets and jotting them down just so you could visit them again.
All in all, Starbound is a game for those who have wanderlust in virtual reality. Those who wish to see various worlds, each with their own intricacies and sub-planet environments. But for those seeking a challenge or worlds with complex interactions with NPC, Starbound is not that game. At least, as of now.

This was the first FPS game I ever played. There is an immense history to this game, and in many respects I still believe it to be one of the base games ever created. The puzzle-based first-person shooter is definitely a bit of an odd one, but HL1 manages that quite well with plenty of little mini-puzzles that you need to solve to advance. The HD graphics supplied by both the Black Mesa update and the HD models pack both make the game fabulously modern, despite being released in 1998. There is still the charm in the pixelated baddies, though, and I still play this game on disc from time to time for the more retro feel. I recommend that you play this game if you have not already... The storyline is fantastic, especially for an FPS, the gameplay is interesting, and the history of how Half-Life *made* the FPS genre what it is today is absolutely worth it.
And if you get bored, there is always the plethora of mods to be installed!

I was waiting to finish this game before I gave a review but I just about had it with this game.
The game itself is not bad. The story is still intriguing but falls short of it's predecessors. I think they could have been far more creative with the script, but I am no writer so I do not fully understand the creative mind of writers. The game does have some repeatative sections but so have all the other AC games. You do not have to complete them if you do not want to. I usually hit about 80%-90% and I give up and replay the game, as I do not want to do missions that grant little reward or fail to have a meaningful story/point (i.e. the collection of the cockades in the game for silly color schemes).
The gameplay is still fun. Fighting off hordes of enemy with a sword and handgun (or whatever is your preference) is still exciting every time. They did away with some of the good features from past games, which I was a bit upset about. The human shield was an excellent addition that, for some reason, they decided to get rid of on this one. Until you have a fast pistol towards the middle/end of the game, enemies firing their handguns while you are fending off others with sword can be quite difficult. The first pistols you can own are rather slow and by the time you can quick shoot an enemy (look towards the respective enemy and double click) they have already let off their round. The human shield is almost a necessity in some cases when you are swarmed. The vast amounts of weapons and armor are a welcome addition. You can have a mixture of whatever you please and create an outfit that most fits your wants and needs. The whole ensmemble outfits are useless. They provide no additional stats but I guess you can aquire them for the nostalgia of past AC games. Overall I have enjoyed playing this game, when it works. This gives way as to why I do not recommend the game.
This game has been out for months and it still has a lot of glitches. They have released patches to no avail. Gameplay is almost impossible at times due to some of these problems. Ubisoft serioulsy needs to work on releasing games when they are ready, not when they feel they can make the most money. They have gotten progressively worse with every AC release as to how glitchy the game is. Here are some of the problems: randomly freezes for a few seconds, which is a huge problem when you are fighting as the screen will suddenly catch again and you are in serious trouble or dead at that point; the loading times are ridiculous, it used to be faster to switch to fast travel point but now the loading screen is on for so long that I have just resorted to running to the location; and the most frustrating thing is that the game will just crash at points, making you have to wait forever to load the damn game again. Ubisoft recommends that you disconnect from the internet to avoid all the catching and glitches, but it is an integral part in order to save the game and purchase items.
I do not have the best computer in the world, but I have never had so many problems with one game as long as I have owned it. It is very, very frustrating trying to play this damn game and I love the AC series. I have played it since the first one came out because of the history, story telling, and gameplay that it offered. Now I am starting to question if Ubisoft is just sending this series down the drain simply for profit. I really hope that the next series gets released COMPLETED and with far less issues. I still have hope for this series, but even fans like myself are having their doubts.

I've really enjoyed playing Darkest Dungeon and I recommend it with one caveat: If you like building up a squad of heroes with virtually no chance of your beloved adventurers perishing, then perhaps look elsewhere. In Darkest Dungeon you are at the mercy of random series of misfortune, which for some players makes it interesting and for others infuriating. The key is to go in with the mindset that your adventurers are expendable and have replacements in training ready to take over for when a cataclysmic series of unfortunate events leads to the death of a key member of your party because your near death man at arms gets belligerent and refuses healing just before being smashed to death. You can always choose to try and exit an engagement and then leave the dungeon. But that's down to 50/50 chance and comes with the penalty of stressing your party out, meaning they will need to rest and recover before heading back in. Darkest Dungeon does not reward failure.
The game plays out like an animated turn based board game with invisible die rolls. You'll need to equip and upgrade your characters and make strategic trade offs - more hit points at the cost of dodge, range or melee, that nice self heal or maybe a stun? You have 4 character slots to fill each time you enter a dungeon. Do you take a healer or mix character classes that you've chosen self heals for. Poison, bleed, melee or range?
With a limited inventory you'll need to make decisions about what to haul out with you and what to leave behind. Do you take those heirlooms you need to expand your base at the expense of the cash you need to buff out your party? What about that cool rare trinket that you can't use now but could be very useful later down the track?
There's a cool base building element up top in town where you must decide how to spend your limited haul of heirlooms you've taken as plunder from 5 or so different dungeons. Do you upgrade treatment facilities for the various afflictions your party suffers? Or improve the blacksmith for better weapons and armour? What about the stage coach for better recruits or the guild for training new abilities or improving existing ones? Random events in town can grant free use of medical facilities or halve your available provisions or perhaps allow you to raise one of your dead heores from the graveyard to fight again.
Each of the dungeons presents different types of challenges from the way the enemies fight to the sorts of buffs and debuffs used. You'll need to choose what provisions you take with you. More bandages to take care of bleeds? Spades for clearing obstacles? How much food and how many torches can you afford? Missions vary in length and difficulty with a neat camping mini game on the medium and long journeys. When do you strategically decide to use your limited number of camps? Do you heal one character at the expense of stressing out the others? Set up traps to prevent an ambush or buff your party for improved melee?
Your heroes are susceptible to various afflictions and quirks, both positive and negative. Some are downright funny, like getting snarky with other party members and telling them how poorly they are performing, or taking all the teasure from a chest for themselves. Positive ones could be a bonus to a certain enemy type or improved combat in a particular dungeon. The negative ones can be treated in the right facility but at a cost of time and gold.
There are interesting boss and mini boss fights that you need to figure out the mechanics of and take a party that can deal with it. Light itself, or rather the lack of it, is also your enemy. Keeping your torches lit reduces the chance of being suprised by the enemy and of scouting ahead. Lack of light increases stress, which you'll need to mange least someone freak out and have a heart attack. But you can only take so many torches in your precious inventory slots so you need to choose wisely when to use them.
In summary, if you don't mind a good deal of random events that can quickly change the situation either to your advantage or your doom, and you like a game where every decision you make has consequences with tradeoffs galore, then Darkest Dungeon is worth investigating.

Good to see pinball still lives.
Pinball FX2 was probably my comfort game. If I needed to just purely video game, practice some reflexes, and make a score get big, PFX2 was my go-to game. While not every table Zen Studios has put out has been brilliant, they're varied and creative in ways that often call back real pinball tables, or in new ways you can only really do in a videogame. Though they can be punishing, overall the difficulty is lighter than in actual pinball, since a game like Pinball FX has no need to swallow your quarters if it doesn't have to. Granted, it's still born out of the 3-balls and you're out genre, but it's friendlier than something like Pinball Arcade, complete with a more generous ability to bump the table.
Pinball FX3's real changes are nods to the "level, upgrade, and unlock" notions that have become standard in most other genres of videogames. There are bonuses to different types of scoring you can assign to a table, as well as the ability to increase your scoring temporarily, reverse a short period of time, or slow down the ball. There are also new challenge modes like a five minute time limit, being limited to only one ball, or a "survival" mode where you have a time limit that's gets increased as your score goes up. There also now competitive modes where you try and beat people's scores in short three-minute games, but my experience with those is probably the most negative of the new features - it mostly just tests your ability to grind your competitive score and requires too much of a time sink. I love competing on the scoreboards, but even that was too much for me.
The free table that comes with the game, Sorcerer's Lair, is a decent taste and has been improved from the original version in some subtle inside-pinball ways where it's a bit easier to score on than it used to be. Most of the old tables from Pinball FX2 have returned - delightfully, for free if you already owned them - and almost all of them have seen minor lighting, engine, and texture improvements. Others have seen subtle improvements to their rules or layout. It's a real testament to Zen Studios really servicing their fans, especially when it seems like big publishers are trying to desperately wring money out of players ad infinitum.
Overall, it's a very solid platform, allowing you to buy what tables you like and leave the rest behind if you want. It's tough to recommend specific packs, as Zen - for better or worse - seems to include both their greater and lesser tables in the same pack, so you're likely to get an A-side and B-side to whatever your buy. My personal favorite tables would be Epic Quest, Spider-Man, Venom, Starfighter Assault, Han Solo, and Champions... while my least favorite are Fantastic Four, V12, Shaman, Iron Man, and Masters of the Force. YMMV, though, and you'll probably be able to find something you like, particularly if you're a fan of Star Wars or Marvel. As a warning, though, with some modern movie licenses Zen either has trouble getting the plot, soundtrack, or voices right. These kind of tables are done on a budget and restricted timetable compared to the movies they're based on, and sometimes it unfortunately shows.
In general, though, it's a great new platform for pinball, and a lot of hard work has gone into it. Looking forward to seeing Zen keeping pinball coming out for the forseeable future. If you have any interest in pinball, it's worth a flip.

Not exactly a review, but a straight thumbs up instead:
Pinball FX3 is
! If you like pinball, you need to play this game!
There's a completely free table (Sorcerer's Lair) and you can test all other tables for a limited time, prioritizing to buy first the tables you liked the most. The prices for the table packs are very generous, and on sale they receive a large discount (and also, there are bundles on Humble Bundle from time to time), so you won't spend too much to complete your collection if you be patient.
For those who are not familiar, the Pinball FX series is focused on arcade gameplay instead of simulation - all tables have crazy things that wouldn't be possible to do on a real table with real physics. Also, this third iteration is very focused on friendly competitions, with multiple leaderboards, diverse game modes, tournaments, weekly challenges, etc. There is also a local multiplayer mode, with its own local leaderboards. It's also worth mentioning that there's a very dedicated pinball community on Steam if you want to compete in a more serious way.
Overall, you can't go wrong with
. There's still some issues here and there, but the developers (Zen Studios) are working hard to bring the best experience to the players.

This Game is amazing xcom 2 for me is a ton of fun even if you haven't played XCOM enemy unknown. firstly when you play the first time turn on the tutorial because alot of the opening story and opening cutsences are linked to it and will not play without doing the tutorial.
You will be a bit lost without it that said I found the tutorial to be entertaining I will not be spoiling anything in this review though at the time of writing this I haven't even completed the game because I was so drawn into the side missions.
which are all unique and have randomly generated maps I never saw the same one twice. when starting a game I do recomend playing on one of the higher difficultys verteran is a great start for new players but don't play on anything easyer and turning on iron man which means you can't relod saves (WARNING THIS WILL BE VERY ANOYYING EARLY) this makes every new enemy and situation shock you as you start to care about the soldiers in your team and if they die you lose all the abilitys they have and if you don't extract there body you lose all the gear you equiped them with. The way most things are introduced to you are by suprise which I found great because you have to adapt on the fly having  new enemys have cool new abilitys you weren;t expecting makes things incredible tense even though its turn by turn. also you can customise all you soldiers with a suprising amount of stuff faces armour hats facail hair you can make them look like almost anyone or thing you want and the mod support for this game only adds to that (NOTE: adding a mod will not disable achevments no matter what the mod does or affects so don't worry about disabling achevments because you REALLY want your favorite water gun that shoots apple pie to be in the game). There are also voice packs, texture mods, AI improvments, new weapons, all for free on the the steam workshop really helping alot with the replay ablity of the game. When I played it however I never saw the need for mods as the game runs amazingly and has a ton of detail but thats just me. it should be notied that there are some BS things in the game that can make it feel cheap like early game if a soldier gets hit by anything they are wounded for 28 DAYS (in game time not IRL time) this means that they fall WAY behind the rest of your squad. Also many soldiers early game will miss like point blank shots or 95% hit chances which can be very frusterating but for me I felt it was just part of the game but for some people this can be very anoyying as one wrong move if your not carful can snowball into a disater going as far as losing the whole mission (while this has not happened to me I have seen clips of it happening and its almost heartbreaking that said its INSANLY uncommon).
XCOM 2 also has a timer mechanic where if ADVENT gets to complete a certain project (don't worry no spoilers) you lose the game however this never felt like a problem to me for me it kept the game feeling very tense like I was pressed for time and every desision I make was important and while you can't mold you own story like in mass effect they have arguably more of an effect on the game  here because you choose what to reserch and build for your soldiers what weapons to get and not this means if you want to focus on armour reserch you will have to account for working with weaker weapons untill you can get better guns that said you can switch directives for reserch anytime and you willnever block one reserch option if you do a different one you can get all techs in the game. onto the DLC's for XCOM 2
I recommend getting them shens gift and alien hunters add alot of cool stuff to the game and shen's gift has an AWSOME mission which reqires alot of thinking and planning and adds deployable mechs called SPARKS to your team that said the cosmetic DLC is not personaly worth it as it breaks imersion and makes many soldiers look goofy but thats all my opinion many people may like that kind of stuff but mods add better cosmetics so theres no real reason to buy it i have it because I bought the game if the year equvent of XCOM 2 so for me it was free but its not needed at all. anywho thats all for this review if you have any questions about the game I would be happy to answer them over all I would say for me this game is a 9/10 its amazing great controls never had a problem great graphics its well optomised and I haven't had one crash or even a frame rate drop.

So this game is fun if you learn how to use the different weapons. All the weapon classes work differently, and more importantly, use different COMBO TIMING. On my first playthrough (using staffs) I couldn't image why you'd want to dual wield a weapon--two handed can still block and some shields are useful. Then I read about combos and built a character that can make use of daggers and holy c--p is dual wielding fun.
But even then you have to practice. Fist weapons have a different timing than daggers (and shortswords). If you watch your energy bar when swinging, if you timed the next swing right a circle shows up and you use less energy. The third swing is the super combo move (animation). You can do this in an empty room, you don't have to do it while fighting an enemy. You also have to get used to engaging an enemy without being able to hold LB; ie. you have to use spells more and the gauntlet differently.
Point being it takes about 30 hours of play to really get a feel for all aspects of the game (runes) and even more to master it. Now if you don't want to do that, that's fine, but it doesn't make the game crap. Plus it goes on sale for $5-$10 all the time, DLC included. If you like fighting games but can't seem to get a hang of this one, read some tips and watch some vids and try again, you'll be rewarded.
Just to add some cons: shield charge to find hidden rooms is dumb and all bosses are masters in all methods of combat (ranged and local stun) so you basically have to tank up and whittle them away before you're allowed to continue to the fun parts of the game.
This game gets pretty boring after a while but still fun while it last...

Stuff like dodging, shield bashing and counters technically exist, but in practice the enemies recover from a bash faster than you can use it, and almost every non-boss enemy will chain attacks faster than you can roll. So melee combat boils down to hiding behind your shield, while circling the enemy to get behind theirs and sneaking in an attack every now and then. This is tedious as hell, because many enemies have a ♥♥♥♥ton of hitpoints. It doesn't help that even heavy weapons don't seem to stagger enemies, but the lightest touch from any basic enemy will interrupt your attack, even in heavy armor.
Magic is overpowered in some cases (1 hitting an enemy you'd have to hit about 20 times with a heavy weapon), but randomly ineffective. For example "Stab" sends an illusion towards an enemy that deals ridiculous damage, but sometimes if the enemy is moving, it will run up to it, swing at empty air and disappear.
I quit after making it to a boss that took practically no damage from my melee weapons and about 5-7% of his HP if the "Stab" managed to hit. Meaning I would have to circle it for something like 10 minutes (magic has a cooldown), just dodging attacks and hitting the spell button every once in a while.
I almost liked this game, but that only makes me hate it harder, because I wasted time on it.

This was the first FPS game I ever played. There is an immense history to this game, and in many respects I still believe it to be one of the base games ever created. The puzzle-based first-person shooter is definitely a bit of an odd one, but HL1 manages that quite well with plenty of little mini-puzzles that you need to solve to advance. The HD graphics supplied by both the Black Mesa update and the HD models pack both make the game fabulously modern, despite being released in 1998. There is still the charm in the pixelated baddies, though, and I still play this game on disc from time to time for the more retro feel. I recommend that you play this game if you have not already... The storyline is fantastic, especially for an FPS, the gameplay is interesting, and the history of how Half-Life *made* the FPS genre what it is today is absolutely worth it.
And if you get bored, there is always the plethora of mods to be installed!

Go into ubisoft settings and tick (Start in offline Mode).
Then Find your Ubisoft folder
Computer/:C/Program Files x86/Ubisoft/Ubisoft Game Launcher
Go into your savegames
If one folder) = Open the folder and search for 857
If mutiple folders) = Open all folders and look for 857
From there you Delete all you're saves
Than In steam  Go to the Library tab in Steam and select the game (DONT RUN IT)
Right Click on the game and click on Properties
Select the Local Files tab
Click on Verify Integrity of Game Cache
Wait for Steam to validate your game’s install if it finds anything wrong with it those files will be re-downloaded and installed.
Click play and Steam will re-install and launch ACU with (Hopefully) No problem!

I would have liked to say how good this game is, as it had many great features, but, at the end, I can't recommend it, at least to people who play like me.
Indeed, I do not like to rely on wikis/cheat ♥♥♥♥♥ when I play games. I prefer to discover things myself. Problem with Darkest Dungeons is that the cost of experimentation is far too high.
For example, when I meet a new boss, the game does not give me any hint about what this boss can do. I end up sending my best characters, hoping that I have the good skills/abilities. Half the time, it is not the case and some of them die, while the other ones have to flee (a very expensive process).
As a result, I must level up new characters, which means even more (boring) grinding. This is what frustrates me and made me give up this game. In the game, time invested in levelling up characters is just too high when they can die so easily. Indeed, not only unknown bosses can kill your main characters, but also regular enemies when they start focusing on one of you characters and get some crits.
As a result, I do not recommend this game.
Pros:
-	Great graphics
-	Great sound, voice and music
-	Variety of characters
-	Interesting combat system
-	As a whole, great ambiance
Cons:
-	Too much randomness in fights, considering the cost of levelling up characters
-	Missing information, such as boss description (before embarking) or the results of not defending the hamlet against raiders (before sending anyone to treatment buildings). The information eventually comes in, but too late.
-	Again, too much grinding.

Defend the Highlands mixes elements from both the RTS and Tower Defense genre. The core gameplay is pretty simple and straightforward, especially if you’r eused to playing these types of games. What really sets Defend the Highlands apart from other titles is its Scottish theme along with some pretty funny dialogue and scenarios, as well as one of the most fitting theme songs I’ve ever listened to in a videogame of this type. The game starts off with you attempting to free Scotland from invading hordes of irish, british and welsh people and from there forward it is up to you to strike back at the enemy.
The game features a skirmish offline mode and a 20 level single player campaign. I must admit that I was surprised with the fact that each level was very unique and different from one another. You play on varied scenarios such as porridge factories, villages, caverns, fortresses, hills, subway stations, beaches or lowlands in which the enemy has the higher ground. There was this level in which cows kept running horizontally through the field and if they ran into an unit or construction, it would get obliterated.
There are some levels in which you can build some pretty neat looking fortifications by using all your available constructions, such as tables, that act as cover, porridge cannons, turnip machine gun turrets, among others. That said, the variety of weapons that you can use, combined with the renowned heroes you’ll get to control, open alot of possibilites for each level. Either build a wall along the frontline or deploy “scottish snipers” (units with golf clubs) in the back to kill your enemies from afar, it is up to you.
After completing a level you will be presented with some sort of skill tree, where you can upgrade your units or reduce the amount of time it takes to harvest porridge or to summon new recruits.
The most basic mechanic of the game envolves sending an unit to farm porridge, which acts as food to keep spawning units. Since you play as fellow scottish people, what better way to spawn more troops than by playing bagpipe? If you select a scotsman and order him to play his bagpipe, units will start spawning from one edge of the map and head towards you. It also adds music to the game and I found this to be a nice little touch which I thoroughly enjoy. I enjoyed so much the song that the Scotsman played with their bagpipes that I always found myself stepping on the floor at the rhythm of the song. Other than that they are the bulk of your army and attack by throwing bowls at the enemies.
As I mentioned before, you have hero units. As you progress through the campaign you’ll unlock more. However, your main hero, Alfredo, is the only one that can’t die during a mission. Failure to save him from death will result in a mission restart. That said, all heroes have their unique role to play in battle and it is important to keep them behind cover.
If you’re a fan of RTS or Tower Defense games, or if you’re interested in trying a nice mix of both, with a nice set of characters, funny dialogue and strategic gameplay, I’d recommend checking this one out.

Fractured Space has a lot in common with two other combat games I enjoy: World of Warships and Shattered Horizon. The game gives the player a single ship to command with differing attributes depending on class. Movement includes the Z-Axis and depends on the keyboard, turret and some special ability direction depends on the mouse.
Aesthetically the sounds, sights, and feel of the universe makes it very distinct. It really does feel like a few of the popular science fiction tropes are thrown in a blender to make a new universe. There's sparse information about the story of Fractured Space, but this game is more about the arena play over the one (or two, haven't tried the other) styles of objective play.
For a ship simulator like this, and with so many vehicles, it's easy to be eager to grind through games to get credits to buy those other ships for how they look... regardless of the "difficulty" or not. Fortunately the game allows you to try any ship in the game in a specialized shooting range that may not  be very exciting, but it gives you a place to practice the handling of those ships and learn a little more about how they handle and function. It can help new players better figure out which ships match thier play styles and target how far they want to grind.
The basic capture game mode is simple: You win by capturing the enemy base. To do this, there are two sectors with gatway outposts to each base that need to be captured. Between this is a time-unlocked outpost that provides bonuses to the team that has captured it, and the bonuses rotate every five minutes or so. There's enough here to give strategic significance to a player's part in the entire scenario, which can last about 20 minutes.
The game also allows for solo, PvE, and PvP games. I have done most of my gaming in PvE to get credits, but for new ships or practice I run Solo. Credits and exprience are handed to players in PvE and PvP.
For now this game has replaced World of Warships for me as my go-to ship battle game, because it's set in space. More than that, the sights and sounds of Fractured Space draw me in almost as much as they drew me in for Relic Entertainment's Homeworld. In fact, in some ways this does feel like a ship-driver version of Homeworld, which isn't a bad thing.
The only criticism I can level against the game so far is how long the game makes you wait on things. In PvE matches there are something like three different countdown timers forcing you to wait: You wait in the lobby for ship selections, you wait a second time for all players to make their final selections, and then you are waiting in the game, before the match, where you can pilot your ship and mess with your teammates before the game re-sets and you begin the scenario.
Even in the scenario though, depending on where you are when you die, you can have a wait time between 20-30 seconds to an entire minute if you die in the enemy base or in the Gamma capture zone (I think). It can be particularly frustrating when you rush to the defense of say, Alpha Base, only to be countered by the enemy team and die quickly to sit out for another half minute after about 10 seconds of combat. It's a minor irritant that does make me quit the game for a time, but it doesn't anger me enough to stop me from coming back again and enjoying another round.
I would give it an 8/10. I would like to see the game continue to expand and would recommend it easily to other ship simulator fans.

Alright, Fallout 4 review, here goes..
I should start by saying I was such a skeptic of this game, I did not buy it on release. In fact, I waited until about August 2017 before I got it on a steam sale. There are some pros and cons, I'll try and keep it short. (HA!)
The game is far better than I expected. I might almost go as far as saying that Fallout 4 was the post apocalyptic RPG I had been wanting to play for years. Fallout 3 was close, State of decay and other Zombie apocalypse games almost had it.. but none of them were quite right.
I wanted a game where I could play first person (or third but mostly first), use a system like VATS to strategically plan my moves or have some sort of break from 100% FPS, and I wanted to collect junk and turn it into cool stuff.
I heard a lot of complaints about the dialogue system, but I found it completely satisfactory. Instead of 2-10 scripted options where I read what the character is going to say and select one, I ussually have 4 options that denote tone or attitude. While past fallout games have rubbed me the wrong way by a character saying something nasty when I thought I was saying something nice, this new system surprisingly eliminates a lot of that confusion. Your character will say a line based on the intent you want to convey, which in my opinion was actually slightly superior to the old way. One could argue you technically have "less options" numerically speaking, but I find I have more options in the dialogues overall because the intent of my responses open up more paths or causes a character to have a certain disposition towards me, and I haven't felt at all restricted (thus far) in terms of dialogue options. Part of this could be because I favor charisma high characters who are good at the RP dialogues, but it was one thing I was very worried about heading into Fallout 4 that turned out to work really well, at least for me.
Some of the complaints I have heard involve the sole survivor (you) and their scripted dialogues. For me, I spent a long long time making the character as similar to myself as possible, and I proceeded to play as if I were the character (ie acting how I would act, doing what I would do, etc.) and I have not yet heard my character say something that makes me dislike them or the system. I have not had any of the problems other reviewers mentioned with the scripted dialogues being anything other than enjoyable.
I love love love the junk system. In every fallout game before this one, selective looting was the order of the day. Pick up what is useful and leave behind what is not. In this game, all the junk you collect gets turned into scrap that you use to build bases, walls, forts, guns, generators, water pumps, and pretty much anything else you see in settlements across the wasteland. While the system in place to doing the building can be finicky (hard to place items the way you want, or get them to snap together just right) I considered this to be perhaps the greatest achievement in Fallout. Yes, carrying around all those extra toilets and typewriters and coffee pots does become a pain in terms of carry weight, but the restriction felt fair and natural (IE I could usually collect all the crap in a spot, head back to my workshop, dump crap, and then do it for the next spot) and turning those typewriters into gunmods or those coffee pots into power armor feels incredibly rewarding.
I loved the power armor system, how it functions as a seperate suit of armor you get into and wear and walk around and have to fuel up with fusion cores, takes it's own damage, protects you from rads, etc etc etc. I loved building and customizing all my own power armor (hot rod flames are the best paint job xD) and I even made a base specifically for spare suits of power armor (yes I built all of this out of scrap coffee pots and toilet tanks) just so I could walk past the rows of suits and I loved the change in hud when you get into a suit, feeling like you're really in a suit and not just walking around with power armor on.
I loved the stories, the factions, the combat, the building, pretty much everything. They really did a good job on this one. And while I have some complaints, most of them involve limitations of games in general.
Dogmeat. Are there words to describe how much I love this pixelated little mutt? Alright he looks pretty purebred german shepherd but honestly, BEST COMPANION EVER. There's only been 1 or 2 points where I let him go so I could take another companion for the sake of quest flavor or whatever.
This leads us into the Cons... And while the list is shorter, the few things that I disliked were EXTREMELY distasteful to me. If I hadn't liked the game so much, these cons would have kept me from enjoying the game COMPLETELY. They are as follows..
Let's start with companions. Dogmeat should be able to follow you around everywhere, all the time. He's the best. He doesn't judge you, doesn't die, finds crap for you all the time, and IMO is the best companion. For some reason, Bethesda decided at the last minute that you would only be able to have 1 companion at a time INCLUDING dogmeat, instead of being able to have your dog +1 companion. Lots of things have been written about this online, mods have been made to allow you to carry dogmeat, etc. (mods are another gripe we have to get into in a moment) but in general, the decision to limit you to 1 companion including dogmeat ticked me off bigtime. For me personally, I eventually fixed this with a series of console commands to access the native programming that had dogmeat set to his own companion (ie dogmeatcompanion) while setting another companion to be the main companion (ie companion). The reason I had to use console commands is...
The mods disable the achievements. So if I want to update the textures and improve the visuals of the game you are going to DISABLE MY ACHIEVEMENTS to punish me? I tried to enable the dogmeat companion mod (so I could take another companion with me without having to lose my beloved canine companion whom I could not bear to part with) and it warned me my achievements would all be disabled. SO disrespectful, the developer has no f***ing right to tell me how to play when I am just trying to patch up mistakes in their game. If I hadn't found the console commands to fix most of my problems, I might have quit the game right then and there because of this. Bethesda have NO RIGHT to try and 'punish us' by disabling achievements or telling us how we can enjoy a single player adventure. Grrrr.
There are complaints about not being able to build settlements more, and while I came up against this and got pretty peeved that I had barely put up the wall and 2 stories of a place before I hit the cap, I did come to realize that the reason for this is limitations in the programming. This goes hand in hand with the arguments people have made about the AI not being better. Well, if you have 21 settlers in each settlement and each of them is doing something unique on/with things you personally built into the game haphazardly out of collected junk, it isn't a mystery to me why there is a cap on settlements and on the ai.
The truth is the bugs and problems with this game could have ruined my experience completely. But a few console commands patched up or fixed the problems and I was able to enjoy the game PROFUSELY. I'd say it's a good game but you will have to do some tinkering with the console to tailor it into a TRULY enjoyable experience FOR YOU. Maybe having to troubleshoot like that makes it a bad game, but for the sale price I paid and the enjoyment I have gotten from it, I say it was worth it.
TL;DR

My earliest and most enduring experiences of gaming can be drawn back to the old 'Command and Conquer' and 'Age of Empires' days, where real-time strategy games were a dominant market that was seeing constant expansion and inovation. However as the years went on newer and fresher takes on strategy began to take influence and MOBAs or days-long grand strategy games took over.
Yet after over a decade of gaming I find myself coming back to my roots, and in particular the third and "final" installment of the core 'Age of Empires' franchise. Why? Well I'll tell you.
For many the original 'Age of Empires' is the epitome of antiquity, static and janky movements of soldiers, a low population cap and a small, unimpactful variety of Civs to play. Taking command of a unique civ means little to the gameplay, meerly a change of aesthetic and a neat way to warp events of history in your image.
'Age of Empires II' and its expansions are by a substantial margin the best heralded of the franchise, with changes to civs now supporting unique and more potent traits, unique units, tech trees, appearances and of course the dozens of languages spoken by your loyal subjects. Its true I still come back to 'Age of Empires II' for an honest and lengthy game of good-old-fashioned strategy, games lasting anywhere between 1 to 4 hours.
That brings me to this game, 'Age of Empires 3'. In my mind it is the best Age of Empires, that has adapted to the previous real-time strategy market with a plethora of units, buildings, cards and civ traits that change up the experience even more. Many my criticise the card system, wherein your chosen civ has a deck of cards you unlock at each age in-game, allowing you to improve your economic power, bring in fresh and rare units, unlock new technologies, or even start a revolution.
The variety and adaptability of gameplay is what draws me to this game, a sense of real immersion in my civilization as I level it with each victory, and watch the homecity grow to further my colonial conquests. Both expansions offer new stories for singleplayer and a handful more civs to play as, however I believe the Dynasties expansion to be the stronger effort.
Balance has never been a huge issue for me, however I would like to see a Workshop brought into effect for this game as it could use the love of its community to keep it alive.

I have 272 hours played in-game. I enjoyed playing through it, modding it, and seeing the wacky, interesting, and downright fun stuff modders created. Now, it's fair to say I would have spent around 25-30 hours on this game without the fantastic modding community and their vast improvements to nearly every aspect of the game.
So, after so much time with the game..why the negative review..you may ask? Well, this negative review is for the base game, mod-free. It's lacking everything that made the prior Fallout games fun - such as meaningful dialog choices, meaningful perks (the streamlined perk system now is...boring, to say the least) and exciting quests. It runs mediocre even on a beefy system, and the main story is extraordinarily short.
Character creation is awful - your character will always, without mods, look like some oddly deranged individual because the creation sliders are...weird and terrible in every way. Not to mention the hairstyles, body types et al., are extraordinarily lacking. Further, it seems even after several years, Bethesda remains incapable of determining how to fix mismatched skin textures and neck seams - but the community, of people who are not paid by the company, are capable of doing so almost on release date. You know, the people who create FREE MODS for the community to enjoy...some of which have actually become borderline NECESSARY to enjoy the game. The subpar, insultingly buggy vanilla game.
Settlement building is tedious. Contrary to what Bethesda may want players to believe, it is obnoxiously difficult getting walls to snap into where you want them to go. It is tedious making sure the settlers are happy - mostly because their happiness is inhuman, and makes no sense. They could have all the food and water, entertainment and lights, that their misery-harboring hearts could handle...and still be unhappy. Oh, and may all the gods in existence have mercy if you are foolish enough to attempt building on uneven terrain. Good luck trying to get the walls to snap together without your base floating above the ground as if suspended by invisible strings. Apparently it's too difficult to have them snap to the ground. Additionally, the options regarding furniture, decorations, etc., are also fairly limited without mods.
The AI is relatively terrible. You could snipe a super mutant's head off and the other mutants will either (1) magically know where you are and descend upon you like a green wall of death, or (2) hide for 5 minutes before deciding the person who sniped good ol' Grok's head off must've scampered off into the wasteland.
While we are discussing AI - Companions are, to put it bluntly, morons. They are more of a liability than a help..and unless wasting time picking up one of the very few select dim-witted companions who stand out in the open because he/she decided to try and absorb all the plasma being shot  your way sounds like fun - the game is more enjoyable being a solo adventurer.
Loot is underwhelming, and as has been said in a significant portion of other reviews - you receive power armor somewhere around 30 minutes into the game. You can keep that power armor and have a ball waltzing through the relatively barren wasteland (again, without any mods whatsoever the wasteland is rather barren regarding open spaces..unless you go to one of the static locations..of which there are, actually, quite a few - though they run fairly similar to one another in aesthetic and layout) as an overpowered hulk of metal. If no challenge is your thing - by all means, go for it. Also, armor variety is quite limited.
Textures are...mediocre. They're passable but this isn't a gorgeous looking game. It's passable. I remember the heralded "wow look at the fur on dogmeat" stuff they promoted the game with. I'm sorry to say, it looks idiotic without mods.
Quests are...sadly, quite dull..as are a significant portion of the in-game locations. There's nothing that makes them stand out as memorable. Nothing at all.
The weapon attachments system is OK, except...if you want to use a melee weapon you're essentially stuck with a Super Sledge unless you want your brains kicked in by Super Sledge wielding Super Mutants..and the Super Sledge, and most melee weapons, have a grotesquely small amount of modifications available. So, pick up some guns or be satisfied with never picking up a cool, viable melee weapon. That being said, the amount of weapon attachments for guns is still extraordinarily limited. We're talking a few attachments, most of which you won't bother with because there's only one top-tier attachment for each of the 3-4 attachment categories. Essentially, attachments mean nothing because, if you want to be "hardcore super mutant killing awesomeness personified," there is only one option to pick - the others, like faster firing rate...are meaningless when compared to the damage attachments.
As a side note, I thought I would mention that character movement, and weight, feels awkward. I'm not sure why, it's as if the player character is gliding...something about the movement feels unnatural. Bethesda also, still, has not figured out hair physics or body physics as well. As with Skyrim, if you kill someone in the vanilla game - they may launch into the sky like someone stuck a bottle rocket up their..behind..into the distant cosmos. Hope you didn't want any of the loot on that super mutant, or bandit raider.
Bethesda also added the garbage gun (I do not recall the name after such a long hiatus - if anyone wishes to comment it I will edit this review :D), which shoots...garbage. I mean, that's kind of fun for about 5 minutes until you realize it does almost no damage when compared to the other heavy weapons in the game, or realize it's basically just like every other heavy gun in effect (meaning it shoots the same, has the same damage effects etc.,)..except it shoots garbage. Modders have added wackier guns that are more fun to use and more viable - but we aren't talking about those because Bethesda wants to put mods behind a pa-, I mean..they want us to join in on the diamond studded (for Bethesda CEOs, at least), unicorn prancingly wonderful, rainbow-graced land of the Creation Club. Well, this was a pretty good game. It isn't the best in my library in my opinion but it was good.
Half-Life is about a physician who has to take on both the forces of the US Military and the an alien race. This physicain isn't any ordinary physician, this physicain is Gordon Freeman. This is the beginning of a saga that is still remembered to this day as one of the best first person shooters ever made, but does it live up to that title? Let's take a look.
Unlike most first person shooters that give you the ability to look in all directions Half-Life takes the Doom movement route. Meaning that Gordon Freeman is constantly sprinting every where even when it would be safer to walk or go at a leisurely jogging pace. This both makes and breaks the game. The game is full of platfoming sections where the default super speed will constantly throw you off. The last eighth of the game would be much easier and it would make me grind my teeth a whole lot less during these portions. Where it makes this game is when you have to be constantly running from one side of the level to another, there are a couple of levels like this and they do get annoying, but if you're used to back tracking in games (like myself) you won't have too much trouble dealing with this.
Now let's talk about the enemies in this game, well they aren't bad. The game is very dark and gritty and the enemies are pretty much the same. They don't have too much color to them but which makes them feel like they belong in this world. So here's a noob tip, the first time I saw a Vortigaunt, you know those guys that will charge your armor in Half-Life 2 and are generally friendly towards you, I walked up to it and pressed e, don't do that. If you do that it'll get two or three cheap shots in on you and leave you nearly dead on the easy setting (which is what I played on). Other than that the other enemies are well designed and suited for their purposes, some of which make up entire levels on their own. I especially found it interesting how you had to fight a giant ball sack called Gonarch though three different boss level stages. I don't understand why Gonarch hasn't become a meme yet, I mean it's two of the things that people on the internet obsess about, balls and Half-Life. Why was Gonarch not brought back as a synthasized being in Half-Life 2? And we have the final boss, whom I can't remember the name of but he was well designed and looked like some sort of Alien Overlord. The head crab zombies in this game also look a whole lot more threatening than in Half-Life 2. Having those mouths in their stomachs was a good idea.
Next on the menu to talk about is the music, which is decent at best. It's kind of like Doom as it just kind of suits the mood of what's happening at any moment. Though the songs don't loop, so if you're stuck at a part of the game then you're stuck with just the sounds of the enemies.
The story wasn't bad, but it wasn't really anything compared to Half-Life 2's story. I guess it's a good story for a first try and the usage of portals as a plot point was a pretty good idea.
Age Rating: M for Blood and Gore, Intense Violence, Explicit Language, and Disturbing Content.
Overall Rating: 8/10

Defend The Highlands is a first game made by studio Kilted Camel, and published by KISS ltd (who you may know for games like Uriel's Chasm or Lifeless Planet).
It's a strategy game where you control a group of Scottish people who want to keep their independence and want to show the proof who is the boss there, as you'll be facing Irish potato farmers, English cricket players, Posh englishmen and more similarly silly enemies.
Your heroic group prefer throwing bottles in fights, and covering up behind their barricades. They have to eat something, so you'll have to feed them with porridge. And for that, you'll need to farm oat. But don't expect much complex stuff, most things are done automatically, keeping you with simple tasks like "choose who'll be the farmer". To get more people to help you in fight, you don't use any barracks or typical strategy requirement building. You just let your people play on bagpipes and people will gladly come to help you!
There's nothing extraordinary to say about sound effects, though it was a nice surprise to find it has a voice-acted tutor in your game progress. The graphics are more on the "meh" side, though it really depends on your taste.
What's really sad is the fact the game isn't much polished on the design part. All the menus and interface feels similarly to Air Control (if you don't know that game, you must be a happy person), as all you'll see are basic Unity buttons without any proper designing work. It feels rushed and amateurish, and makes a terrible impression.
Another huge con of the game is the optimalization, as it, for how it looks, runs bad. You can expect getting pretty low FPS if you decide to buy the game. But will you? I can't recommend this game, there are so many better strategy games and this can get attention only because of the humor about Scotland and others. And that's not enough for a game that feels like it shouts to every player "Hey, I'm their first game made in Unity engine!".

Defend The Highlands isn’t your typical Tower Defense or Real Time Strategy game. There is no mazing you need to do; it is just a matter of strategically locating your towers. Just setting down a tower isn’t enough though, you still need to place a unit in it for it to function. This adds up to an interesting twist in the standard Tower Defense genre. The individual towers and the worker units can all be skilled up by spending the skill points earned during each mission. While it isn’t the best Tower Defense games I have ever played, it is one of the more unique ones.
This game pokes fun at the various stereotypes of the British people. You play as the Scots… the drunken, porridge eating, haggis loving, golf playing, bagpipers. Are you low on units? Start belting out a tune on your bagpipes and the Scots for miles around will come join your cause to push back the evil British forces. You can then give the Brits what for with golfing snipers, haggis catapults, porridge shotgun cannons, turnip machine gun turrets and don’t forget the Bagpipe artillery. Alternatively you can poison them with the drunken haze surrounding your pub or crush them with a well rolled wheel of cheese. As you can see, the towers in this game are all quite hilarious. You also attract allied heroes to join you in your quest to overthrow the rest of Britain.
The enemy forces are just as amusing and stereotypical! I don’t want to spoil the fun by giving too much detail about the enemy so I’ll describe just a few to give you an idea. There are the posh British people who throw tea pots at you from great distances, the quick Welsh sheep riders and the Irish Potato farmers just to name a few. They tend to come at you in waves until you have killed every last one of them much like other tower defense games.
The game is not without its faults though. Unit pathing can be quite an issue. Often you place a tower down and tell a unit to go control it just to find the unit hung up on something and unable to reach the controls of the tower. It would be nice if the unit could teleport into the correct positon to control the tower if it is able to touch the tower, but sadly it does not which leads you to have to destroy the tower losing all the gold it took to make it. Sometimes the battlefield’s uneven surface can cause you to miss position your tower causing it to hit the ground despite looking like it should have a clear shot. The units will automatically run to any open tower or cover location when they first enter the field, unfortunately if there is something in their way they may end up caught on it and just infinitely run into a wall rather than trying to find a new path. Another issue I found was in the last mission. After playing for a while, my towers were randomly building way up in the sky where I could not control them. This led me to have to finish the battle with just my units which luckily I had skilled up throughout the game.
Pros:
Cons:
Overall, Defend The Highlands is a humorous take on the Tower Defense and Real Time Strategy genres. If you are able to look past the bugs and pathing issues then you should definitely consider Defend The Highlands.

Hotline Miami was incredibly hard, especially if you didn't take things slowly and carefully or if you weren't just good at the game. This game takes a small while to get used to, but once you DO get used to it and your characters get geared up, well, it becomes mind-numbingly easy. The slow-motion mechanics make dodging bullets a breeze unless they come from a turret or shotgun, and even then the game is very generous with loot it throws at you, giving you teleporters and items that let you dodge these things anyway.
It feels very rinse and repeat even with the game's style. You pick a mission, you check the guards' gear (there are a lot of variations, but not much in terms of quantity. There are five things guards can have: heat sensors, emergency shielding, actual shielding, armor and a teleport that makes them rush towards you. This really isn't very much, all things considered, and there often isn't enough variety.
Moving on, once you're prepared, you go to your pod, then fly towards the ship. After bumping into it a few times, you get to the dock and you land. You walk through, you rush towards the pilot and you kill or knock him out. Then you kill everyone inside via the easymode slow motion, you do your job, you go back to your pod. If you get KO'd or shot? Doesn't matter, you can just go right back in because the pilot's dead and apparently nobody onboard knows how to copilot.
So far, I have liberated three out of four strongholds of the four factions in missions that are supposed to be difficult as hell. It was a legitimate breeze. All I had to do was use my Visitor (a personal teleporter that teleports you to one place for two seconds before returning you to the original position), find and takedown the pilot of the ship then just breeze my way through. Shot? No problem, my Angel pod negates all consequences of that. Knocked unconcious? Again, Angel pod (or I could just catch myself, which really isn't hard, either).
Everything is just repetitive. Everything is boring. It was fun for the first two hours, and I mildly reget not refunding it. Oh well! I can't wait for the dev to release a 'BOILING HOT' edition or 'EXTREME' edition that will make the game more difficult for the low, low price of $12.

Great game right now, and lots of potential for the future.
I originally got the game before Venture was fully implemented and have seen this game gain potential throughout. The introduction of the Hawkeye Corporation firmly cemented that belief in my mind.
Pros:
Unending world- awesome to explore and find new enemies, bases, biomes, etc.
Near unlimited building possibilities- even though there is a limit on how big you can build techs (64x64x64 blocks I think), there are still literally millions of different combinations. I have never had two techs that are the same, even though their purpose may be the same.
Immense potential- this game can and hopefully will do great in the future. The game developers have confirmed multiplayer, and that will be huge. They also have at least two more unique corporations in mind. They have also expanded the game so much since the first time I played it, that I can't see why the game would bog down now.
Flying!- Ok, this is more of my personal thing, but flying in the game is really fun. Only thing is I wish is more effective air-to-ground weapons (other than the over powered Hawkeye Seeker Missiles :D ).
Cons:
Still in Early Access- this means the game still has quite a few bugs in it. I myself have experienced everything from corrupted save files to glitches techs. However many of these bugs have been fixed, and are being fixed right now.
Can rush through corporation grades quite quickly- I have nearly always maxed out 3/4 of the corporations in less than a week of playing (about 2 hours of gaming each night). Once you max the corporations out, the game becomes relatively boring since you no longer need to hunt for new blocks; they all unlock automatically.
Limited types of enemies (even with Twitter)- I have encountered all enemies over and over again (some a lot more than others). This is bad when you are trying to find new blocks, especially those just implemented into the game (Hawkeye). Invaders are really the only ways to gain those new blocks, but invaders are quite rare.
All in all I have enjoyed the game, and hope to see it gain more steam (no pun intended) in the future. ;)

I like the game, but gawd do the developers make it hard to enjoy it. Call this a neutral review with words of warning.
Imho Fractured Space can barely be called F2P. You can buy all ships for 36€ - which is fair for basically the whole game. Yet, if you don't buy the ships the grind is
.
A little mean about that grind is that any form of customization (Loadout & Crew) costs the same credits you need for ships. And what even worse: There are no Free-Rotations like in every other F2P.
That means two things: 1. You need to buy new ships almost blind (the shooting range is worthless to judge a ship) and 2. you can't play most roles till you saved up enough credits till you bought e.g. a healer.
I got ~8.000 Credits per match. Which lasted 20 Minutes on average. My favorite healer (Paladin) costs 600.000 which means...
. And I couldn't customize any ship while grinding for the Paladin.
Yes I like the core of the game but yet it had it's downsides. The game feels sluggish with most ships. The you hardly notice that the slower ships move at all. Positively speaking this leads to tactical gameplay. Realistically speaking: It's freaking sluggish. Turn speeds are even slower. Combined this leads to situations where you see your end coming but can't do anything about it because you can't turn arround and run.
But not only movement is sluggish. Cooldown on many skills is very long e.g. more than 70s for a simple 2 second speed boost. Once you spend your cooldown skills the game kind of plays itself. Aiming is so easy your granny would hit everything. And well then you slowly move while slowly aiming and shooting waiting for your cooldown to come up again...
One of the most questionable design choices is the teleport home command. You need to get to a base for any level up to take place. You got a home call with 60s cooldown. Yet... it spawns you several ship lenths away and facing in the wrong direction. So you need to sloooowly turn by 180° and slooowly fly toward the home base if you want repairs or want to get your next level up.

The ship selection is always blind pick. Which can result in unfun matches. Enemies have 2 Stealth ships but you have zero stealth detection? Not fun.
You got a bulky team of heavies? Sorry enemies picked a sniper heavy team and you are sitting ducks.
The tutorial covers only the absolute minimum you need to play the game. Even utterly important informations as that you take 6 times as much damage while prepering for warp aren't mentioned. Almost none of the stats are explained and you need to look for guides that explain you whether "cooldown" or "weapon cooldown" reduces the cooldown of missiles. Some mechanics are even only discovered by the players like what the upgrades at level3/6/9 actually do.
Considering how important all the stats and effects are the information politics leaves a lot to be desired.

This game isn't officialy out of Early Access - the quality of several aspects of the game speaks a different language.
- Connections problems or a crash during any moment during the matchmaking or ship selection screen results in a Leaver Mark without any chance to reconnect.
- I can't set up the controls I wan't because the game doesn't accepts them - no response yet from technical support.
- Kill/Assist counts "lag". You can do major damage to an enemy but sometimes you get no assist for it. Why care? Because you get only get credits for Kill/Assist/Support/Capture. This system also means you could capture a point for 99% > die > someone else get's the last percent and... you get nothing for it.
Most customization is homeopathic because it makes you think you are doing something meaningful but...
... at all.
: Often you get the choice between slow firing weapons that do more damage or quick firing weapons that deal less. The dps is always exactly the same. Which actually wouldn't be bad. But the differences for most of these customizations are so minimal you hardly notice them. And again they cost quite much credit and you can't try them before. And they are specific to a single ship. So you will be unlocking quick firing weapons on every ship... hurray!
is where it's getting silly. While small the loadouts have some impact. Crew is a different story.
Crew is locked behind several layers to unlock. You can buy lottery tickets for credits. These contain random blueprints for crew. You need DNA to Unlock Crew. DNA is very rare or you get a bit of it for duplicate bluebrints.
If you managed to get the best crew for your Ship the differences are laughable: 2% more turning speed for 1% less max speed? The changes are never more than a few percent.
Your daily quests are always the same Win 2 / 4 / 6 matches.
For every 2nd finished game you get a random small reward. The random rewards get better for the 4 games played and even better for the the 6 matches played.
The progress resets every 48 hours. Which wouldn't be so bad  if the rewards weren't so much better for 6 wins. 2 Wins gives 3000-6000 credits. 6 Wins gives 15000-35000 credits. Beside credits you can also get DNA and premium credits (Platin) which have similar differences for 2vs6 wins.
For me this means if I can't play 6 Matches (2+ hours) I feel less reason to play at all.
Surrenders before 15 minute mark or VS Ai/Coop matches don't count for dailies.
Why would you surrender so early? Because of leavers! Which brings me to:
Leavers are a major reason to not even start this game. If someone on your team leaves or disconnects you are basically playing 4vs5 in a MOBA. You get... 30% faster respawn as "compensation". Which means you feed the enemy team even faster. In big battles you don't have a chance with one player less. So even 30% more damage would be more helpful.
And there is little you can do if you got a leaver. I have seen only one concede vote to get accepted. If I understand it correctly the game even count's the leaver as abstention/anti-concede vote meaning one player who still want's to play means you are forced to endure the game till the end if you don't want to leave yourself.
And matchmaking is your typical moba: You can get a team of 5 randoms vs 4+1 Teamspeak using friends. Have fun when they instantkill you with 2 stealth ships the second you want to warp.
Overall Fractured Space is a nice game that loses most of it's appeal because of several minor issues.
I would be glad to give this game a thumb up once at least a few issues are fixed.

My earliest and most enduring experiences of gaming can be drawn back to the old 'Command and Conquer' and 'Age of Empires' days, where real-time strategy games were a dominant market that was seeing constant expansion and inovation. However as the years went on newer and fresher takes on strategy began to take influence and MOBAs or days-long grand strategy games took over.
Yet after over a decade of gaming I find myself coming back to my roots, and in particular the third and "final" installment of the core 'Age of Empires' franchise. Why? Well I'll tell you.
For many the original 'Age of Empires' is the epitome of antiquity, static and janky movements of soldiers, a low population cap and a small, unimpactful variety of Civs to play. Taking command of a unique civ means little to the gameplay, meerly a change of aesthetic and a neat way to warp events of history in your image.
'Age of Empires II' and its expansions are by a substantial margin the best heralded of the franchise, with changes to civs now supporting unique and more potent traits, unique units, tech trees, appearances and of course the dozens of languages spoken by your loyal subjects. Its true I still come back to 'Age of Empires II' for an honest and lengthy game of good-old-fashioned strategy, games lasting anywhere between 1 to 4 hours.
That brings me to this game, 'Age of Empires 3'. In my mind it is the best Age of Empires, that has adapted to the previous real-time strategy market with a plethora of units, buildings, cards and civ traits that change up the experience even more. Many my criticise the card system, wherein your chosen civ has a deck of cards you unlock at each age in-game, allowing you to improve your economic power, bring in fresh and rare units, unlock new technologies, or even start a revolution.
The variety and adaptability of gameplay is what draws me to this game, a sense of real immersion in my civilization as I level it with each victory, and watch the homecity grow to further my colonial conquests. Both expansions offer new stories for singleplayer and a handful more civs to play as, however I believe the Dynasties expansion to be the stronger effort.
Balance has never been a huge issue for me, however I would like to see a Workshop brought into effect for this game as it could use the love of its community to keep it alive.

Fractured Space nails the full 3D axis MOBA perfectly.
23 hours in and I'm looking for more. For a game barely rising out of early access the level of polish here is on par with any other  in a time when we see certain titles leave early access barely improved or half delivering on the promises that were made during early development.
Pros:
The graphics are spot on, ships are elegantly and lovingly detailed. Each ship faction has its own VERY unique visual style with regards to ships. I found myself just staring at some of the Zarek ships, honestly surprised at how well and thoughtfully they were designed.  While there is currently only one map available it is large enough to not feel repetitive even after several matches.
Capital ship combat feels great. Every ship plays in a unique way and a robust tutorial system works for even the greenest of noobs. The game holds your hand effectively and makes sure you understand how to play.
The sounds of the game are fantastic. It feels good to blast the enemy with lazers and on the flip side, it creates a sense of urgency when you are receiving a lot of fire and your crew members are yelling at you to "do something!".
Not too much MOBA. I have a love/hate relationship with MOBA style games but this one aces it with a simple levelling system that doesn't require me literally studying third party websites to devise tactics. Yet the depth still remains and each ship controls very differently from it's peers and the objectives are intelligently placed and non-threatening. No more running to the tower when you fail to gank someone, its all or nothing unless you can hide behind some asteroids and jump out of harms' way in time!
Not at all P2W! Cash shop is limited to cosmetics only!
Cons:
I had trouble picking out cons really... and I am a glass half empty sort of person! I must be losing my cynic edge.
But truthfully, the only con is that after a lot of matches you might be hungry for some variation. In the capital ships, in the backgrounds. Even if the map is 100% cosmetic give me a new backdrop, new asteroids to hide behind and I'll be happy. That's how I feel about multiple maps and the penchant for MOBAs to include just one or two maps for play.
The game locks complexity behind a paywall. Simply put, the capital ships that are harder to use tend to be the ones that are not available right away. They give you a
nice well rounded set of beginner ships and the rest you're going to have to grind for or open your wallet for.
Overall: Fractured Space deserves a lot more love than it has received and I look forward to playing more in the future and hope my review might sway somebody who is on the fence for one reason or another to give this well polished MOBA a chance.

2/7 days the servers are overloaded...
1/7 days the launcher may break your game causing you to have to download the WHOLE (cache verification does not work) game again...
2/7 days are ok but the servers are still junk..
