This is how Space RPG/Adventure games SHOULD be designed. You've got your starship, which works decently as a home (though you need a mod to change/replace your ship, ie get a bigger house) AND takes you to other planets which you can then beam down to. The worlds are all randomly generated with their position in space acting as their Seed.
There are currently over a dozen baseline biomes, and even more sub-biomes. That, combined with randomly generated trees types(Wood, leaves and colors), various types of plantlife, animals, etc, all means that there are a very wide variety of worlds you can land on, or things you can discover. Even if you've landed on planets of a specific biome type dozens of times before you could still discover something new/unique, like a metal-plated tree with eyes for leaves.
There are also structures generated on many planets, such as settlements, or even airships. Currently there are only a handfull of non-settlement type structures for each race, so discovering new types of buildings does become rare.
Overall, this is a very good game. There are still some things that could use more content(Types of Generated Structures, Ship Customization, and hopefully more pet or weapon-type options), but for early access there is definately a lot of great content, and it's fairly stable. What really makes this game good, in my opinion, is wonderfully exectured basic concept behind it. You pilot a starship between planets, land on them, do whatever you want, and explore. This game is ultimately more like Star Trek than most of it's own games. If you were to add some real ship customization, a space combat type system and maybe some random space anomolies which you can explore... this would be the quintessential space exploration game.

Half-Life is about a physician who has to take on both the forces of the US Military and the an alien race. This physicain isn't any ordinary physician, this physicain is Gordon Freeman. This is the beginning of a saga that is still remembered to this day as one of the best first person shooters ever made, but does it live up to that title? Let's take a look.
Unlike most first person shooters that give you the ability to look in all directions Half-Life takes the Doom movement route. Meaning that Gordon Freeman is constantly sprinting every where even when it would be safer to walk or go at a leisurely jogging pace. This both makes and breaks the game. The game is full of platfoming sections where the default super speed will constantly throw you off. The last eighth of the game would be much easier and it would make me grind my teeth a whole lot less during these portions. Where it makes this game is when you have to be constantly running from one side of the level to another, there are a couple of levels like this and they do get annoying, but if you're used to back tracking in games (like myself) you won't have too much trouble dealing with this.
Now let's talk about the enemies in this game, well they aren't bad. The game is very dark and gritty and the enemies are pretty much the same. They don't have too much color to them but which makes them feel like they belong in this world. So here's a noob tip, the first time I saw a Vortigaunt, you know those guys that will charge your armor in Half-Life 2 and are generally friendly towards you, I walked up to it and pressed e, don't do that. If you do that it'll get two or three cheap shots in on you and leave you nearly dead on the easy setting (which is what I played on). Other than that the other enemies are well designed and suited for their purposes, some of which make up entire levels on their own. I especially found it interesting how you had to fight a giant ball sack called Gonarch though three different boss level stages. I don't understand why Gonarch hasn't become a meme yet, I mean it's two of the things that people on the internet obsess about, balls and Half-Life. Why was Gonarch not brought back as a synthasized being in Half-Life 2? And we have the final boss, whom I can't remember the name of but he was well designed and looked like some sort of Alien Overlord. The head crab zombies in this game also look a whole lot more threatening than in Half-Life 2. Having those mouths in their stomachs was a good idea.
Next on the menu to talk about is the music, which is decent at best. It's kind of like Doom as it just kind of suits the mood of what's happening at any moment. Though the songs don't loop, so if you're stuck at a part of the game then you're stuck with just the sounds of the enemies.
The story wasn't bad, but it wasn't really anything compared to Half-Life 2's story. I guess it's a good story for a first try and the usage of portals as a plot point was a pretty good idea.

Well, where do I start off with this game.
Well, this game features a variety of things to do, making it overwhelmingly fun and there is always something new. First off, this game features a wide amount of crafting recipes, lootable items, and randomly generated biomes and planets. Most people at first would say, "Oh no, it's just another rip-off of Terraria". To that I say, think again my good friend. This game features around 4-5 playable races with their own unique starter "Home" planet. You may set a new home planet in the future, but I stuck with mine for a good while. I still have a base on it. In this game, you may craft weapons, armor, and a large amount of Vanity items to wear/equip. Then the in-game currency/crafting material "Pixels". With Pixels, you can buy new things at Shopkeepers, which can be found anywhere on a planet or a space station. This game, to my knowledge has these biomes. "Arid, Savahnna, Desert, Snow, and forest". Also, there are asteroid fields you may land on.
Also, mining can be quite difficult. With all kinds of monsters under the ground, to traps, to sand trapping you in. But, I digress, mining can be quite the pay-off. It may take a while when you start out on this game, because beleive me it took me quite a while to get the hang of things the first time I played. I died quite a few times, and it was just a bad start. But I kind of got the hang of things after a while. Once I got my ship fueled up, which you may use coal, I saw that it had a star map in my cockpit. Now, this star map was HUGE! I mean, it was so big just for one sector. You see, you can click on a orbital system and then click on any range of planets and then set your ship for their orbit. It is so big, and that was just one Mark of the star map. Your ship can be fitted with custom upgrades, and cool stuff like that. I HIGHLY reccomend this game to any user who has the 15$ on them. To me, this game is well worth over 15$. This is NOT Terraria. This is Starbound.

The biggest problem I have with this game is how hidden everything is. I have so far played this entire game 42 hours without looking up anything online and just learning as I play. It's been a gruelling experience. Your characters can suffer from negative attributes such as "Paranoid" or "Masochistic", but do you think there would be an explanation of what that is? Nope. They can get postive attributes like "Courageous" or "Powerful", but you will never know what that actually is, just that it makes them better in some way.  You will learn through experience that most of the negative stuff makes your characters randomly stab other characters or themselves, pass their turns, bring down party morale, or switch positions randomly. But there's no way in game to actually see what their affliction means.
Another example is individual characters have stats such as speed, which presumably means they get first attack in a sequence, but do you think you can ever see what the attack sequence is? No you can't. You can't plan because you can't see whose turn is next, you just finish your character's turn and maybe it's the enemy's turn next and maybe it's one of your guys, you will never know until the next turn comes up.
Different "curiousities" require you to offer different items in order to plunder them, but the game gives no clues as to what these are. You waste a bunch of supply items from your inventory in different places until something has an effect, and then you remember it for next time because it's pretty much the same after that. I guess I could just look in a wiki, or you know, they could just provide a tool tip. I still have no idea what to do with dog treats or laudunum, using them doesn't seem to be a thing, maybe I have to put them somewhere.
You can't see how much damage can be expected from an attack with one of your characters. You don't even get to see how much health an enemy has left unless you click on them. This game has an obsession of hiding basic statistics from the player, and it doesn't contribute anything positive to the experience.
Ideally you would hover your cursor over an enemy with a proposed attack and it would give you values of hit % and expected damage range, but you get no such feedback here. I really don't know if it's an oversight or a design decision, but either way it makes the game less appealing. I give this game a thumbs up just because it's compelling for me to play and I enjoy a challenge, but a couple friends I have tested on this game have rejected it. I give it a thumbs up with caveats.
There is a lot expected from the player as far as learning how the game works, probably too much,  which can become a balance issue when you encounter certain bosses that require certain loadout of characters. Again, I *could* just google it, but that seems cheap and I don't want to have to study a wiki just to understand a game properly. Or I could just go in with my party and risk death or insanity and fail a mission for nothing just because I wanted to see what fighting a particular boss is like. And then do it all over again with a next party and hope I got it right. There's isn't a lot of allowance in this game for making mistakes and "trying things out", you always need to bring your "A" game or you will eventually be forced to restart due to losing too many characters and resources. Don't trust the dungeon difficulty indicator either, it lies.
I hope to finish the game on normal difficulty and learn the story, as a personal quest and challenge. I really like how the torch system works with balancing light and darkness with the Health & Sanity of your characters vs the amount of Loot & Toughness of monsters you encounter. I like the idea of having a limited inventory and having to make tough choices as to what to carry with you. This game has a lot going on, if you dare devote the time to learn about it.

The game is often compared to the likes of Hotline Miami, but this is strictly untrue. Hotline Miami was incredibly hard, especially if you didn't take things slowly and carefully or if you weren't just good at the game. This game takes a small while to get used to, but once you DO get used to it and your characters get geared up, well, it becomes mind-numbingly easy. The slow-motion mechanics make dodging bullets a breeze unless they come from a turret or shotgun, and even then the game is very generous with loot it throws at you, giving you teleporters and items that let you dodge these things anyway.
It feels very rinse and repeat even with the game's style. You pick a mission, you check the guards' gear (there are a lot of variations, but not much in terms of quantity. There are five things guards can have: heat sensors, emergency shielding, actual shielding, armor and a teleport that makes them rush towards you. This really isn't very much, all things considered, and there often isn't enough variety.
Moving on, once you're prepared, you go to your pod, then fly towards the ship. After bumping into it a few times, you get to the dock and you land. You walk through, you rush towards the pilot and you kill or knock him out. Then you kill everyone inside via the easymode slow motion, you do your job, you go back to your pod. If you get KO'd or shot? Doesn't matter, you can just go right back in because the pilot's dead and apparently nobody onboard knows how to copilot.
So far, I have liberated three out of four strongholds of the four factions in missions that are supposed to be difficult as hell. It was a legitimate breeze. All I had to do was use my Visitor (a personal teleporter that teleports you to one place for two seconds before returning you to the original position), find and takedown the pilot of the ship then just breeze my way through. Shot? No problem, my Angel pod negates all consequences of that. Knocked unconcious? Again, Angel pod (or I could just catch myself, which really isn't hard, either).
Everything is just repetitive. Everything is boring. It was fun for the first two hours, and I mildly reget not refunding it. Oh well! I can't wait for the dev to release a 'BOILING HOT' edition or 'EXTREME' edition that will make the game more difficult for the low, low price of $12.

And this really is a strategy game, with some rougelite elements. There is permadeath, though it's not at all unavoidable. In fact, only one character has died so far, and it was only because he got shot so many times he could no longer take any more shots and go into incapacitation instead of just dying. Your characters can get captured and you can resuce them with another character; or you can reach a point where your current character can no longer truly benefit to progressing through the overall goal of liberating the entire procedurally-generated astroid belt-thing, at which point you can retire the character and name a weapon or otherwise piece of equipment they have in the off-chance it turns up again in future playthroughs with another character, or maybe in one of your steam friends' games. I named an armour-piercing sword the "Chastity Penetrator", by the way.
Back to strategy though, there is a lot of ways to deal with any given situation without needing specialized equipment. Need to knock out a guy wearing armor but don't have any weapons that can penetrate armor without also killing the target? Wait for him to walk past a window, shoot it out to catapult the guy into space and pick him up in your little space pod. Need to deal with a little cluster of guards but don't want to alert anyone? Grab a bunch of wrenches lying around the place, teleport in there, and pause to switch wrenches everytime you swing one and it goes into cooldown. The "pause, plan and play" style you develop as you get a feel for how to do things is somewhat similar to Doorkickers, another good game, but its more open with a ton of more choices of equipment. Or you could, you know, load up on a bunch of guns and Slipstreams - which are basically steroids without the downsides - and Rambo your way through the entire ship. It's a valid strategy if the alarm is already sounded and you need to finish your objective pronto.
And in terms of the equipment, it's quite similar to Borderlands. There are a variety of traits and equipment types, and the stuff you find are randomly created from those possible choices. I found an automatic silenced pistol that regenerated ammo over time once, and it was glorious.
Also, again, you dont neccesarily need specialized equipment to deal with a given situation. You COULD wait next to a terminal and whack the guards one by one as they come to do...stuff...on it. But there could be a time limit and you need to deal with them fast. Also that's boring. So instead you teleport into the room and throw wrenches at everyone because you don't need the alarm to trigger and you dont have any silenced weapons. Moments where things go wrong are when this game shines the brightest, as long as you don't mess up getting yourself out. You can theorhetically deal with any difficulty with the starter gear, even if that entails bugging out by throwing a sword at a window to vent yourself to space once you inevitably get spotted and picking yourself up with your pod by controling it remotely.

This game is definitely fun to play, even though it looks fairly basic at first, and probably won't last you more than 8-15 hours (depending on whether you want to do one playthrough or more).
Your role is that of... yourself, hacker extraordinaire—or something, because in the beginning, your character is probably just fiddling around with their computer. Until they receive an e-mail from Bit, late hacker who's posthumously trying to accomplish what they couldn't do when alive. Armed with a couple of commands and utilities, it's time to jump into the game, a game that may turn out to be bigger than you'd think.
Through a series of e-mails and missions, you get introduced gradually to other hackers, become part of hacking groups, and discover what's hiding behind the Bit case. The game is fairly straightforward in that regard (get a mission, hack ports, hack your way in, steal/delete data, delete logs, disconnect), and getting the tools you need isn't hard, however most of the computers you discover along the way also contain other files you can read, such as IRC logs, and part of the fun I had came from exploring. You also have to make a few choices that may affect which missions are available to you—for instance, accepting missions from another hacker will prevent you from taking another hacker's contracts—as well as a couple of other choices about more ethically-challenged assignments.
The interface is simple enough, in a "minimalist OS" way, with a few animations when running hacking utilities; I quite liked that, as seeing more "Holywood hacking animations" wouldn't have been very believable (but not displaying anything would, on the other hand, be a bit boring). I didn't really like the window with nodes representing all the computers you could access, though: it was nice in the beginning, then became seriously cluttered (in the end, I'd just type the IP addresses directly in the terminal, it was faster).
Interestingly, if you've never worked with Unix-based workstations, or Linux, this can actually be a nice little introduction to that kind of OS. Very basic, obviously, with commands that don't even need any arguments; still, since a lot of what you have to do in game is terminal-based, be ready to type fast and work with commands much more than with just clicking on buttons (being used to TABbing my way both in bash and on IOS, I was totally fine with that, and most often I would be faster this way). Getting the hang of this isn't very difficult, and even if you know nothing to running commands, the game will easily make you feel like you do.
Sounds and music: mostly music, with one voiceover at a given point, and alerts when you're getting traced. At first, I feared the audio tracks would become repetitive; in the long run, they fit pretty well, with appropriate change of tracks when you get into a new hacking group or attempt a new kind of operation, and provided good background music without being intrusive.
Problems I noticed: the game runs in full-screen and would crash when I alt-tabbed out of it. Not sure if it's just my computer, or systematic. It didn't detract from my enjoyment, so I admit I didn't pay much attention (and didn't exactly *have to* alt-tab out of it anyway, since the immersion is much better if you don't).
Awaiting the next DLC now? I also wouldn't mind multiplayer possibilities, like hacking each other, or having to form alliances. That would be fun as well.
Conclusion: Recommended.

If you're interested in simulation basketball, this game runs a mean fast break on all previous iterations -- I'm talking New Jersy Nets Gerald Green head above the rim alley oop windmill dunk. Gone are the days of the ubiquitous jack-of-all-trades superstars. More than ever, the basketball IQ of the person behind the controller matters, and I welcome that. Sure, some cheaters still exist, but, if you learn at least part of the art of basketball, it's not a forgone conclusion that you'll lose.
Despite the backlash against MyCareer mode this year, it's an enjoyable mode with a storyline that can be forgotten entirely after your rookie season. In fact, from the second season forward, this mode is probably the most in-depth and satisfying career mode in any sports game. If you're considering buying this game, don't listen to those who wished for the moon and were delivered a game rooted in great basketball mechanics.
There are so many modes in this game (I'll let you read about them elsewhere) that any basketball fan should be able to find something they like.

Huge personal victory, but the game didn't get any better. If I didn't pass my limted time before asking for a refund at that time I would have requested one. This game is hard, mainly because of poor camera control and enemies hiding behind corners and below EXP game mechanic:
-You gain experience by killing enemies (duh).
-You can store the EXP at a save point, allowing you to level up, gain stats, etc
-Or you can 'carry' the EXP with you. The more experience you carry, the more EXP you net from a fight. When you die, you 'drop' the EXP and can recollect it, until you die again.
-In and of itself that's a great system, but when you die, all enemies get reset, so if you fought 10 enemies before you died, you will have to fight 11 (incl. the one that killed you) to recollect your EXP.
That last item makes it a bit frustrating.
For the rest of the games, no complaints, so if you like punishing yourself A LOT, you should by this game.

Review of the 1.0 release.
Fractured Space is a 5v5 multiplayer game about territorial control. You control a capital ship in 3rd person, and each has a handful of abilities.
The team coordination required is similar to Dota and as a result it is not properly played alone or with a group of random pubbers. If you are looking for a single player game or a casual pick-up multiplayer experience this is NOT your title. The game does not contain built-in voice communication so I suggest that you join the official Discord server to find players. Once you have a few people willing to talk tactics on voice comms the game takes on a totally different character, which I highly recommend.
The combat is not terribly fast paced and it gives you time to think about your placement and objectives, so those adverse to twitch-gaming need not be deterred.

This game is not pay to play...You can get everything in the game by simply playing the game. By paying for patron or for packs/credits you are only taking a shortcut. It's that simple. You are not locked out of ANY portion of the game. What do you expect, the developers have bills to pay.
THAT being said... there is WAY too much RNG, even if you pay it's not a guarantee... To be honest I have spent over $100 dollars in this game and it has gotten me nowhere due to RNG and crazy market fluctuations. A key part of the game is time-gated so many players only play once a week to get what they can then leave...
That causes huge server loads on Mondays... Tuesdays are when the updates are applied so you have to wait to play... Wednesday is when the launcher is updated, more waiting...
So,
2/7 days the servers are overloaded...
1/7 days the launcher may break your game causing you to have to download the WHOLE (cache verification does not work) game again...
2/7 days are ok but the servers are still junk..
The last 2 days of the week you get bombarded with request to help people get their weekly time-gate items/power level for contest..
I would avoid this game until the developers find a REASONABLE way to reward players that are willing to pay a bit to speed up progress. As it is, the players that are at the top get the best rewards, that in turn, keep them at the top... It's very hard for new players to get going in this game...
I already logged in and gave all of my stuff (that was tradeable) away just to be sure i would not be tempted to come back so dont bother asking for any of it...
Now I'm going to go play Warframe, where at least I GET WHAT I PAY FOR! Not some random chance at something that is worthless because the market is already flooded with said rewards..

Gameplay itself is fun and addicting, constantly taking out baddies to earn more 'fragments' so you can upgrade your weapons and take out MORE baddies.
Yet, the thing that throws Bastion over the edge of greatness, is it's story. The story itself is one of hope in a time of despair. The plot itself has several minor twists, but avoids Bioshock-level revelations, still leading to something interesting.
So the story is what makes it great, right? Well there's something about the story that makes it great: The storyTELLING. The entire game is accompanied with a narrator (Who sounds amazing), who constantly provides insight on things going on.

Set within Paris during the French Revolution and follows the story of Arno Dorian in his efforts to expose the true powers behind the Revolution. Assassin's Creed Unity retains the series' third-person open world exploration as well as introducing a revamped combat, parkour and stealth system. The game also introduces cooperative multiplayer to the Assassin's Creed franchise, letting up to four players engage in narrative-driven missions and explore the open-world map.
Combat for the game was rebuilt, with fencing being used as an inspiration for the new system. In addition to a few returning weapons in previous games, Assassin's Creed Unity now introduces a Phantom Blade. The Phantom Blade uses the mechanics of a crossbow to fire a silent projectile to a great distance, while it still serves the same role as the Hidden Blade from previous Assassin's Creed games. Navigation for the game was also overhauled: new "Free-run up" and "Free-run down" commands were added to make it much easier for you to scale buildings that are in either direction.
Assassin's Creed Unity also introduces cooperative multiplayer to the series. Players can enter taverns, which act as social hubs in the game, where you are able to see if any of you're friends are playing the game at the current time. If they are currently in a mission, they will then appear as a "ghost" version of their player, allowing you to approach to request to join their mission. If your accepted, you are then transitioned to their game and the both of you reset to the most recent checkpoint, and continue on from there.
Four players max can join in together in this fashion. Overall I'll give Assassin's Creed Unity 7.5/10 the story and Co-Op are excellent with few bugs and glitches ruining all the fun. So I would say if you do see this game on for sale definitely pick it up, it's worth the price, but I would not recommend you buy it full price as it still has the bugs and glitches still crawling about in the game. So I definitely recommend this game allot and I absolutely suggest you go and pick it up because I am sure (If there weren't much bugs or glitches) it would just absolutely blow you away!.

Fractured Space is an incredibly fun and simple MOBA that gains surprising depth once you delve into the impressive collection of ships to learn and master. Each ship brings with it different tactics and different playstyles that you can tweak and change to match how you want to play.
Each battle can be turned in a moment's notice by a good play from either team, so no 'thrown' games that you would experience in League.
Some things to note :
-This game IS a MOBA, meaning it is a repetitive game mode
-There will be times where you get frustrated
-Learning new ships is sometimes a hard experience
However, these points are countered by the positives I have to say about this game :
-Very forgiving to new players : You will earn frequent rewards during your early play sessions. Surprisingly, this doesn't stop the further you advance and players are constantly rewarded for time and effort.
-Solo Queueing is actually a valid and viable option
-AI Takes over if a player goes AFK, so no risk of totally one-sided matches
-Massive variety of ships mean you can stick to your comfort zone, or try to become a Jack-Of-All-Trades; it's entirely up to you
Is the game repetitive? After long periods of play, yes. However each time I come back I find myself having just as much fun as before.
The game is beautiful and I can see it becoming much more impressive in scale and variety as time goes by.
Is it the perfect game? No. But it is an incredibly fun, versatile, 3rd person space combat game; with a great reward system and lots of replay value. I'd definitely recommend picking it up, especially at such a low price (Free).

-THIS REVIEW IS FOR THE GAME IN IT'S CURRENT STATE, I'M NOT GOING TO DISCUSS HOW THE GAME WAS ON RELEASE AS SEVERAL PATCHES HAVE COME OUT THE FIX LOTS OF ISSUES THE GAME HAD TO START WITH-
So far I really enjoy this game. The multiplayer bits are extremely fun when played with a full group. Some of the controls are a bit different from the previous games and you really need to get used to those before expecting to be great at this game. Free running takes a bit more effort as it's been divided into a free run up and free run down catagory by pressing spacebar and E respectively. The graphics are really good when you have the hardware to support them, the recent patches by Ubisoft have cleared up most of the glitches and frame lags that have been present in the earlier editions, I haven't stuttered once in the time I've played it.
The Companion app which you need to open blue chests really isn't a huge deterrent from the real game, it's very similar to Kenway's fleet and other minigames of that sort in the other AC games and if you have windows 8 you can use the app for free or put it on your smartphone.
As for people complaining about microtransactions in the game, there are relatively few. You can unlock things quicker by paying for "Helix Credits" but the only things unlockable soley through Helix Credits are timesaver packs which are wholly unnecessary. Skills must be purchased with sync points which aren't extremely difficult to earn and I feel like it adds a new angle to the game as you have to prioritize your skills and aren't immediately thrown into the game knowing everything.
TL;DR This is a really good game, it takes some getting used to and if you have a low grade system you probably won't be able to run it extremely well but if you have the hardware to support this game and the patience to learn the intricacies of it, it's certainly worth picking up (Especially on sale).

Alright, Fallout 4 review, here goes..
I should start by saying I was such a skeptic of this game, I did not buy it on release. In fact, I waited until about August 2017 before I got it on a steam sale. There are some pros and cons, I'll try and keep it short. (HA!)
The game is far better than I expected. I might almost go as far as saying that Fallout 4 was the post apocalyptic RPG I had been wanting to play for years. Fallout 3 was close, State of decay and other Zombie apocalypse games almost had it.. but none of them were quite right.
I wanted a game where I could play first person (or third but mostly first), use a system like VATS to strategically plan my moves or have some sort of break from 100% FPS, and I wanted to collect junk and turn it into cool stuff.
I heard a lot of complaints about the dialogue system, but I found it completely satisfactory. Instead of 2-10 scripted options where I read what the character is going to say and select one, I ussually have 4 options that denote tone or attitude. While past fallout games have rubbed me the wrong way by a character saying something nasty when I thought I was saying something nice, this new system surprisingly eliminates a lot of that confusion. Your character will say a line based on the intent you want to convey, which in my opinion was actually slightly superior to the old way. One could argue you technically have "less options" numerically speaking, but I find I have more options in the dialogues overall because the intent of my responses open up more paths or causes a character to have a certain disposition towards me, and I haven't felt at all restricted (thus far) in terms of dialogue options. Part of this could be because I favor charisma high characters who are good at the RP dialogues, but it was one thing I was very worried about heading into Fallout 4 that turned out to work really well, at least for me.
Some of the complaints I have heard involve the sole survivor (you) and their scripted dialogues. For me, I spent a long long time making the character as similar to myself as possible, and I proceeded to play as if I were the character (ie acting how I would act, doing what I would do, etc.) and I have not yet heard my character say something that makes me dislike them or the system. I have not had any of the problems other reviewers mentioned with the scripted dialogues being anything other than enjoyable.
I love love love the junk system. In every fallout game before this one, selective looting was the order of the day. Pick up what is useful and leave behind what is not. In this game, all the junk you collect gets turned into scrap that you use to build bases, walls, forts, guns, generators, water pumps, and pretty much anything else you see in settlements across the wasteland. While the system in place to doing the building can be finicky (hard to place items the way you want, or get them to snap together just right) I considered this to be perhaps the greatest achievement in Fallout. Yes, carrying around all those extra toilets and typewriters and coffee pots does become a pain in terms of carry weight, but the restriction felt fair and natural (IE I could usually collect all the crap in a spot, head back to my workshop, dump crap, and then do it for the next spot) and turning those typewriters into gunmods or those coffee pots into power armor feels incredibly rewarding.
I loved the power armor system, how it functions as a seperate suit of armor you get into and wear and walk around and have to fuel up with fusion cores, takes it's own damage, protects you from rads, etc etc etc. I loved building and customizing all my own power armor (hot rod flames are the best paint job xD) and I even made a base specifically for spare suits of power armor (yes I built all of this out of scrap coffee pots and toilet tanks) just so I could walk past the rows of suits and I loved the change in hud when you get into a suit, feeling like you're really in a suit and not just walking around with power armor on.
I loved the stories, the factions, the combat, the building, pretty much everything. They really did a good job on this one. And while I have some complaints, most of them involve limitations of games in general.
Dogmeat. Are there words to describe how much I love this pixelated little mutt? Alright he looks pretty purebred german shepherd but honestly, BEST COMPANION EVER. There's only been 1 or 2 points where I let him go so I could take another companion for the sake of quest flavor or whatever.
This leads us into the Cons... And while the list is shorter, the few things that I disliked were EXTREMELY distasteful to me. If I hadn't liked the game so much, these cons would have kept me from enjoying the game COMPLETELY. They are as follows..
Let's start with companions. Dogmeat should be able to follow you around everywhere, all the time. He's the best. He doesn't judge you, doesn't die, finds crap for you all the time, and IMO is the best companion. For some reason, Bethesda decided at the last minute that you would only be able to have 1 companion at a time INCLUDING dogmeat, instead of being able to have your dog +1 companion. Lots of things have been written about this online, mods have been made to allow you to carry dogmeat, etc. (mods are another gripe we have to get into in a moment) but in general, the decision to limit you to 1 companion including dogmeat ticked me off bigtime. For me personally, I eventually fixed this with a series of console commands to access the native programming that had dogmeat set to his own companion (ie dogmeatcompanion) while setting another companion to be the main companion (ie companion). The reason I had to use console commands is...
The mods disable the achievements. So if I want to update the textures and improve the visuals of the game you are going to DISABLE MY ACHIEVEMENTS to punish me? I tried to enable the dogmeat companion mod (so I could take another companion with me without having to lose my beloved canine companion whom I could not bear to part with) and it warned me my achievements would all be disabled. SO disrespectful, the developer has no f***ing right to tell me how to play when I am just trying to patch up mistakes in their game. If I hadn't found the console commands to fix most of my problems, I might have quit the game right then and there because of this. Bethesda have NO RIGHT to try and 'punish us' by disabling achievements or telling us how we can enjoy a single player adventure. Grrrr.
There are complaints about not being able to build settlements more, and while I came up against this and got pretty peeved that I had barely put up the wall and 2 stories of a place before I hit the cap, I did come to realize that the reason for this is limitations in the programming. This goes hand in hand with the arguments people have made about the AI not being better. Well, if you have 21 settlers in each settlement and each of them is doing something unique on/with things you personally built into the game haphazardly out of collected junk, it isn't a mystery to me why there is a cap on settlements and on the ai.
The truth is the bugs and problems with this game could have ruined my experience completely. But a few console commands patched up or fixed the problems and I was able to enjoy the game PROFUSELY. I'd say it's a good game but you will have to do some tinkering with the console to tailor it into a TRULY enjoyable experience FOR YOU. Maybe having to troubleshoot like that makes it a bad game, but for the sale price I paid and the enjoyment I have gotten from it, I say it was worth it.

I have 272 hours played in-game. I enjoyed playing through it, modding it, and seeing the wacky, interesting, and downright fun stuff modders created. Now, it's fair to say I would have spent around 25-30 hours on this game without the fantastic modding community and their vast improvements to nearly every aspect of the game.
So, after so much time with the game..why the negative review..you may ask? Well, this negative review is for the base game, mod-free. It's lacking everything that made the prior Fallout games fun - such as meaningful dialog choices, meaningful perks (the streamlined perk system now is...boring, to say the least) and exciting quests. It runs mediocre even on a beefy system, and the main story is extraordinarily short.
Character creation is awful - your character will always, without mods, look like some oddly deranged individual because the creation sliders are...weird and terrible in every way. Not to mention the hairstyles, body types et al., are extraordinarily lacking. Further, it seems even after several years, Bethesda remains incapable of determining how to fix mismatched skin textures and neck seams - but the community, of people who are not paid by the company, are capable of doing so almost on release date. You know, the people who create FREE MODS for the community to enjoy...some of which have actually become borderline NECESSARY to enjoy the game. The subpar, insultingly buggy vanilla game.
Settlement building is tedious. Contrary to what Bethesda may want players to believe, it is obnoxiously difficult getting walls to snap into where you want them to go. It is tedious making sure the settlers are happy - mostly because their happiness is inhuman, and makes no sense. They could have all the food and water, entertainment and lights, that their misery-harboring hearts could handle...and still be unhappy. Oh, and may all the gods in existence have mercy if you are foolish enough to attempt building on uneven terrain. Good luck trying to get the walls to snap together without your base floating above the ground as if suspended by invisible strings. Apparently it's too difficult to have them snap to the ground. Additionally, the options regarding furniture, decorations, etc., are also fairly limited without mods.
The AI is relatively terrible. You could snipe a super mutant's head off and the other mutants will either (1) magically know where you are and descend upon you like a green wall of death, or (2) hide for 5 minutes before deciding the person who sniped good ol' Grok's head off must've scampered off into the wasteland.
While we are discussing AI - Companions are, to put it bluntly, morons. They are more of a liability than a help..and unless wasting time picking up one of the very few select dim-witted companions who stand out in the open because he/she decided to try and absorb all the plasma being shot  your way sounds like fun - the game is more enjoyable being a solo adventurer.
Loot is underwhelming, and as has been said in a significant portion of other reviews - you receive power armor somewhere around 30 minutes into the game. You can keep that power armor and have a ball waltzing through the relatively barren wasteland (again, without any mods whatsoever the wasteland is rather barren regarding open spaces..unless you go to one of the static locations..of which there are, actually, quite a few - though they run fairly similar to one another in aesthetic and layout) as an overpowered hulk of metal. If no challenge is your thing - by all means, go for it. Also, armor variety is quite limited.
Textures are...mediocre. They're passable but this isn't a gorgeous looking game. It's passable. I remember the heralded "wow look at the fur on dogmeat" stuff they promoted the game with. I'm sorry to say, it looks idiotic without mods.
Quests are...sadly, quite dull..as are a significant portion of the in-game locations. There's nothing that makes them stand out as memorable. Nothing at all.
The weapon attachments system is OK, except...if you want to use a melee weapon you're essentially stuck with a Super Sledge unless you want your brains kicked in by Super Sledge wielding Super Mutants..and the Super Sledge, and most melee weapons, have a grotesquely small amount of modifications available. So, pick up some guns or be satisfied with never picking up a cool, viable melee weapon. That being said, the amount of weapon attachments for guns is still extraordinarily limited. We're talking a few attachments, most of which you won't bother with because there's only one top-tier attachment for each of the 3-4 attachment categories. Essentially, attachments mean nothing because, if you want to be "hardcore super mutant killing awesomeness personified," there is only one option to pick - the others, like faster firing rate...are meaningless when compared to the damage attachments.
As a side note, I thought I would mention that character movement, and weight, feels awkward. I'm not sure why, it's as if the player character is gliding...something about the movement feels unnatural. Bethesda also, still, has not figured out hair physics or body physics as well. As with Skyrim, if you kill someone in the vanilla game - they may launch into the sky like someone stuck a bottle rocket up their..behind..into the distant cosmos. Hope you didn't want any of the loot on that super mutant, or bandit raider.
Bethesda also added the garbage gun (I do not recall the name after such a long hiatus - if anyone wishes to comment it I will edit this review :D), which shoots...garbage. I mean, that's kind of fun for about 5 minutes until you realize it does almost no damage when compared to the other heavy weapons in the game, or realize it's basically just like every other heavy gun in effect (meaning it shoots the same, has the same damage effects etc.,)..except it shoots garbage. Modders have added wackier guns that are more fun to use and more viable - but we aren't talking about those because Bethesda wants to put mods behind a pa-, I mean..they want us to join in on the diamond studded (for Bethesda CEOs, at least), unicorn prancingly wonderful, rainbow-graced land of the Creation Club. We can all get royally #@%!ed together, as a community - no, a CLUB! Doesn't that warm your heart?
Additionally, I bought the borderline price gougingly expensive Season Pass and was given vastly underwhelming content barring Far Harbor. Content that is far surpassed, many times over, by free mods created by a passionate community who love the game and want to see others having fun...who create their mods out of love, not the desire to profit. I am a firm believer that such a motivation for creation is why so many of the free mods far surpass the mods on the Creation Club.
Ah, and thus, we come to the primary reason behind my negative review(before the Creation Club stuff, I would have given the game a 6/7 out of 10 without mods - the Creation Club lowered my rating to about a 3/10). They're pulling out the paid mods bludgeon and smacking everyone over the head with it relentlessly, again! Now, to add insult to injury, they're bludgeoning us while resorting to insultingly childish semantics such as, "well, it's not paid mods because we pay the mod authors...they're REALLY actually totally contractors. But..uh...you still pay for the mods." That..is insultingly dishonest.
I was about to download Fallout 4 again and try out some of the FREE MODS, but hearing about the Creation Club (cute, misleading name by the way...attempting to make people feel included by calling it a "club") has turned me off. I don't want to play Fallout 4 anymore. I don't want to play any Bethesda game after this.
They tried this with Skyrim, were met with extreme backlash..only to try it again. Greed is a slow and insidious killer...and I, as a consumer..am sick of developers exploiting us.
**Edited for grammatical consistency, and minor content additions.

A turn-based combat simulator in a Lovecraftian setting. You manage your roster of heroes, upgrade their weapons and skills, and form 4-man parties from this pool to clear missions of increasing difficulty. The random factor is certainly present, but quite manageable at first. Your heroes are seized by madness with increasing exposition, which develops quirks in them that are usually counterproductive. Send them to pray or drink it off between missions. This part is almost frighteningly realistic.
Darkest Dungeon is not graphically impressive, but it derives no small amount of charme from the narration, dark soundtrack and the insane dialogue of your "stressed" party. This is a fun little game with high replay value that is easy to pause or quit. After reading the other reviews here, I expect it to become repetitive and rng-dependent at some point, but the different classes, the increasingly difficult missions and the three difficulty modes for the entire game promise a lot of value before that point is reached. This was a good buy for 9€.

I've been following this game through from the start, and while I have fond memories of the heat signature mechanic, I think this game has changed into what it needed to be.
The random flyabout missions for each character are great, but I'm particularly enjoying the Defector missions - you get given a fixed starting kit and an objective on a ship and have to work it out from there.  It's both an interesting challenge, and a great way to learn the different tools.
As the sales blurb says, it's also a game about trying to get out of your mistakes.  Just had a great mission where I was a bit gung ho and set off an alarm, with over half the ship to still traverse to my goal.  With the seconds counting down until the ship docked and I was to be captured I evaluated my options.  I could try to head for the pilot to kill him, stop the countdown, then sweep the ship clean at my leisure, but that was risky with large clusters of guards in between me and him.  I wasn't convinced I could do it in time.  Instead I started making a beeline for my assassination target.  First hurdle: a turret directly in my path.  Whipping out my crashbeam, I shut down the turret, legged it across a tunnel opening before a patrolling guard could see me, and rounded the corner straight into a locked door.  With no key weilding guards in sight, I thought all was lost, until I spotted another patrolling guard on the other side of the door.  He was just in range of my swapper teleporter, so soon enough I was through the door, with a puzzled guard standing where I had been moments before.  With 10s on the clock I rounded the corner into a large room and lunged at the nearest guard, slicing him open before throwing my longblade at his nearby friend.  I then sprinted at my target, picking up my longblade en route, and ended him.  At this point I had 4s on the clock, and my escape pod was all the way at the other end of the ship.  I thought it was game over, until I realised I was near the hull.  Pausing and looking around I spied a nearby window and headed towards it.  With no guns available to me, and 1s left on the clock, I hurled my longblade at the window, shattering it and yanking me out into space.  Quickly taking remote control of my pod, I flew it around to pick me up and headed home, heart racing.  Marvellous.

Heat Signature is a game developed by Scott Francis who previously developed games such as Morphblade (2017) and Gunpoint (2013). Heat Signature is as Scott says in his own words "[A game] where you break into spaceships, make terrible mistakes, and think of clever ways out of them." Honestly, I think that's the best way to put it.
Heat Signature's gameplay boils down to what Scott says plus a little more - You break into a spaceship one way or another, probably screw it up somehow and then try to become a magician in an escape act. The things Scott
tell you in this summary of the game is though; is how you'll be spending 1/3rd of your time flying to and from your faction's (which you for what I can tell - cannot choose which for some may not be ideal) base, getting missions and then spamming "F" to speed up the downtime between choosing a mission and doing the mission.
Now for the missions themselves? They're fine. It's usually just a "steal this" or "kill this person" but there's certain ways you can do it which make them fun. For instance, I had to kill a person who (along with everyone else in the massive ship) had armor. Now you can't shoot through or really damage armor with anything that isnt explosives or an expensive gun with rare ammo. So I thought to myself "well It doesn't matter if I kill everyone else, because this mission isn't bloodless or anything." And then lightning strikes - what if I hijack a different ship, and use the missles to blow up the ship with my target in it?
It worked. And that's only the simpliest way I could think of to do the mission without killing myself. Now you might be asking though - "Why do you do the missions?" Well I'm getting there you slow, slow, child; you get to liberate more stations for your faction, now these stations could either just be nothing but another blip on the map to make you feel good about yourself, or they might actually be useful, for example some stations will allow you to buy that certain faction's pod, some pods can destroy ships by ramming themselves into it at the cost of health, and others can go into stealth. There is also the fact that to completely "destroy" a faction, you must liberate that faction's stronghold, which requires you personally, to go in and fly the ship into the stronghold, and destroy it (although you could put it on autopilot and run, where's the fun in that?)
Heat Signature's atmosphere is what you would expect for a space game, it'd big,vast, and mostly empty. but once you scroll back a bit and see the giant gas clouds that cover the solar system sized war that your milita is currently fighting for, you just sit there for a moment, and realize how beautiful it is; or atleast I did.
Heat Signature is a rouge-lite, as in there is not much story outside of generic "I want to [Kill,Capture,Steal] the [Randomly Generated Name for Valuable item,Man,Woman,Officer,Liutennant] [Who,So I can] [Killed,Tortured,Pay off my debt] My [Relative/Loved one.]" As for the writing of the game? If you played Gunpoint, the dialouge is a bit more toned down, but still there, and still obviously Scott's humor.
Heat Signature is a fun,funny,gameplay focused,beautiful indie game by the developer of Gunpoint which (as of writing this) is on sale - so why not buy it now?

Well what can I say about Unity. Unity in short is a "potentially" brilliant game that Ubisoft have once again screwed up. It depicts Arno Dorian, a posh French Assassin who led the way through the French Revolution. So this SHOULD have been a great game. But It's not, and there are many reasons why. But despite this, I have had fun playing it, but not so much as last years Black Flag. So heres why:
1) The Glitches
There are enough glitches and bugs in this game to give even the toughest gamer nightmares. Many are relevant to the new Parcore system, and also the combat system. One such glitch included running across a wall and then getting stuck in mid air.
2) The Graphics
Graphics ingame have a impossibly high requirement. Short of a military computer, you won't be able to run this game at it's peak. I have a good gaming PC, which handled last years AC4 Black Flag with ease. But this game ran so badly, I could barely move without lag. And one of the best way to improve FPS was to "Go Offline" on Ubisoft. When I tried this, the framerate doubled, which shows just how crap Ubisoft really are. If you have anything lower than a PROPER gaming PC then this game ain't for you.
3) The Storyline
Once I got the game running at an ACCEPTABLE framerate (cough cough) I then payed attention to the storyline. The storyline follows Arno Dorian, a boy whose Dad got killed by a guy who I still don't know who he was. You follow him through his youth, and on the way become an Assassin (Well duh) and grow more into a badass. But before all that, the game is slow to get into. And before then you can't do Co-op. So....
4) Co-op
Co-op is actually very good for the game (the one bit about the game that I like), which involves serious parcore & introduces multiplayer missions. You can have fun rescueing people or something like that. Co-op is also suited to various playstyles, such as playing as a "Mid/Long Range Sniper Assassin" or maybe a "Close Range axe Assassin", which means that players can accept various roles. This is the one good part about the game.
Overall, this is a "not brilliant but potentially good" game that Ubisoft have once again screwed up & let their customers down with. £30 on this doesn't feel justified, I actually think that the price should be approx £15 at most. Such a pity Ubisoft...

O Game Lego: The Hobbit veio com a proposta de trazer a história do livro de J. R. R. Tolkien para o universo de peças de LEGO , oq eu tenho a dizer... Bem a adaptação dicou Boa. O jeito que foi contada , detalhes , claro que faltou algumas coisas que não podem ser recriadas com a peçinhas , mais no geral o jogo está bom , e agora uma análise minha sobre o game:
Enredo: 9.0/10 (O enredo foi focado nos dois primeiros filme do universo de ''O Hobbit'' sendo eles: ''Uma Jornada Inesperada'' e ''A Desolação de Smaug'', foram bem adaptados e são mostradas as partes mais importantes de ambos os filmes , mais ai me vem a pergunta: Agora com o lançamento do filme ''A Batalha Dos Cinco Exécitos'' como iremos fazer para jogar o terceiro filme no game?, quem já possui o jogo irá ganha-lo como uma DLC gratuita ou teremos que pagar para joga-lo?).
Gráficos: 8.5/10 (Os Gráficos estão praticamente os mesmos de outros jogos da LEGO, o game LEGO: The Hobbit é um dos games mais recentes da LEGO, e os gráficos dele são facilmente comparados aos do game LEGO: The Lord of The Rings (Antecessor do game, que conta a história dos 3 filmes do de ''O Senhor dos Anéis''), Houve pouca Melhora Gráfica, mais não posso deixar de falar que houve uma melhora...Porém...muito pequena).
Trilha Sonora: 9.5/10 (Foram Usadas Musicas de ambas as Franquias Tanto as de ''O Senhor dos Anéis'' como a de ''O Hobbit'', e para quem é Fã e já viu os Filmes, Não preciso nem dizer que é uma Trilha Sonora Epica...).
Efeitos Sonoros: 8.0/10 (São bons, como peças de LEGO quebrando e de armas como espadas e arcos... mais nada demais...).
Quantidade de Personagens Jogaveis: 10/10 (Eu zerei primeiro o LEGO: The Hobbit antes de o LEGO: The Lord of The Rings, isso pq aidna estou no comecinho do game sobre ''O Senhor dos Anéis'', e a quantidade de personagens joveis é imensamente superior, em termo de textura, não ha uma diferença muito grande mais ainda assim é um pouco melhor em LEGO: The Hobbit... Oque já era esperado).
LEGO: The Hobbit cumpre com oque promete, traz os dois primeiros filmes ao mundo de peças de LEGO de uma forma muito criativa e inteligente... e sim tem potencial para agradar fãs dos filmes e do livro... Tanto Crianças como adultos.
Minha nota final para: LEGO: The Hobbit: 9.0/10

This is what happens when you have an appreciation for something to the point that you get inspired by it..but you don't fully understand what made the thing you loved so good.
It is not hard hitting combat that makes Dark Souls awesome, it's not the difficulty, or the rpg elements..
those are all important elements, but are only ingredients: but the sorely missing part of the souls formula that Lords of the fallen misses (just like Deck13's next game: "the surge") is something that i've seen replicated only in a couple of other souls like games (Salt & sanctuary, Shrouded in sanity, and to some extent Nioh) which is having a world that feels cohesive visually, mechanically and narratively.
i've played this game from beginning to end and i liked it quite a bit...but it definitely misses the point of what it was supposed to do since by practically it's own admission it is a souls derivative...and i fear that more and more developers, thinking to be inspired by the souls games, are going to focus on the lesser aspects of such formula.
I would overall reccomend it. It is still a fun game with an awesome amount of content for it's price (i paid 15 euro near release for a physical copy, but i think that 30 euro is still a decent price for it)

I enjoy it a lot.  it's a sort of action puzzle game, where you have to figure out the best way to handle the mounting threats against you.  The best moments for me are when things go pear-shaped and create an unexpected opportunity.  One event I'm thinking of is when I was breaking into a ship that had just a few too many keylocks than I had ability to steal keys based on my current build.  I snuck in an attack on a keyholder, but I used the wrong weapon (oops) and ended up tossing a grenade instead.  It knocked them out, but also alerted most of the ship.  Alert started, and I had 22 seconds to make it out (mission complete or not) OR get to the pilot and take them out.  Pilot was out of the question, and the pod was a very far run away.  No windows to jump out of...
Then I noticed the security guards were chasing to the point of my explosion, and there was a brief moment when the high security doors were open thanks to all the guards.  I had 2 high capacity sidewinders, so with the doors open I teleported at record speed through the ship, stole my objective, then made it back out to a window on the far side of the ship before anyone went far enough to let a single door shut.  Iw as out of the ship in seconds, completing a mission I thought I'd surely failed.
That's what makes the game the most fun.  Forewarning, there's a slow burn at the start, but they begin adding more and more mission types as you liberate more stations.

Nice game but not without some issues. The artwork, atmosphere, and voice overs are all great. The battle system is good, and the town upgrading system is nice. This is a game where your party is always imperiled, you will always suffer from multiple forms of insanity and different diseases at any given time across all your characters. It's like a machine that's ready to fly apart but you keep tapping the loose parts back into place, just enough that it still works. You never have a "good" machine, just a less broken one.
Pros
- Great artwork
- Compelling story
- Hardcore, no saving / reloading
- Large variety of characters and enemies
Cons
- No explanations for many things
- Trial and error pursuit of game mechanics
- Questionable game balance
The biggest problem I have with this game is how hidden everything is. I have so far played this entire game 42 hours without looking up anything online and just learning as I play. It's been a gruelling experience. Your characters can suffer from negative attributes such as "Paranoid" or "Masochistic", but do you think there would be an explanation of what that is? Nope. They can get postive attributes like "Courageous" or "Powerful", but you will never know what that actually is, just that it makes them better in some way.  You will learn through experience that most of the negative stuff makes your characters randomly stab other characters or themselves, pass their turns, bring down party morale, or switch positions randomly. But there's no way in game to actually see what their affliction means.
Another example is individual characters have stats such as speed, which presumably means they get first attack in a sequence, but do you think you can ever see what the attack sequence is? No you can't. You can't plan because you can't see whose turn is next, you just finish your character's turn and maybe it's the enemy's turn next and maybe it's one of your guys, you will never know until the next turn comes up.
Different "curiousities" require you to offer different items in order to plunder them, but the game gives no clues as to what these are. You waste a bunch of supply items from your inventory in different places until something has an effect, and then you remember it for next time because it's pretty much the same after that. I guess I could just look in a wiki, or you know, they could just provide a tool tip. I still have no idea what to do with dog treats or laudunum, using them doesn't seem to be a thing, maybe I have to put them somewhere.
You can't see how much damage can be expected from an attack with one of your characters. You don't even get to see how much health an enemy has left unless you click on them. This game has an obsession of hiding basic statistics from the player, and it doesn't contribute anything positive to the experience.
Ideally you would hover your cursor over an enemy with a proposed attack and it would give you values of hit % and expected damage range, but you get no such feedback here. I really don't know if it's an oversight or a design decision, but either way it makes the game less appealing. I give this game a thumbs up just because it's compelling for me to play and I enjoy a challenge, but a couple friends I have tested on this game have rejected it. I give it a thumbs up with caveats.
There is a lot expected from the player as far as learning how the game works, probably too much,  which can become a balance issue when you encounter certain bosses that require certain loadout of characters. Again, I *could* just google it, but that seems cheap and I don't want to have to study a wiki just to understand a game properly. Or I could just go in with my party and risk death or insanity and fail a mission for nothing just because I wanted to see what fighting a particular boss is like. And then do it all over again with a next party and hope I got it right. There's isn't a lot of allowance in this game for making mistakes and "trying things out", you always need to bring your "A" game or you will eventually be forced to restart due to losing too many characters and resources. Don't trust the dungeon difficulty indicator either, it lies.
I hope to finish the game on normal difficulty and learn the story, as a personal quest and challenge. I really like how the torch system works with balancing light and darkness with the Health & Sanity of your characters vs the amount of Loot & Toughness of monsters you encounter. I like the idea of having a limited inventory and having to make tough choices as to what to carry with you. This game has a lot going on, if you dare devote the time to learn about it.

This is a game I was not expecting to buy to be perfectly honest.
Hacknet is exactly what it sounds like:  It's a game where you hack computers, get some info, maybe some new software, and repeat.  You do this with the main objective of uncovering what happened to a hacker named Bit (1 or 0 I wonder).  As the story progresses, hacking becomes much more difficult due to higher levels of security and of course forgetting where the computer that you need to hack is on the net map (it is very cluttered by the end of the game).
The game does a fairly good job of making you care about the story in the beginning, the part where Bit is actually guiding you and talking to you, and then kind of forgets about it until the very end.  Don't be deceived though:  Everything you do in the main part of the game is absolutely necessary in order to complete the game.  You learn new tricks, get new software, and discover more organizations linked to Bit in some way or another.  It isn't the most compelling story, but the gameplay and story are very much intertwined.
Speaking of, the actual game itself is very engaging.  No cutscenes, no voice overs (save for one), no fancy bloom effects or explosions.  Just you and your computer.  You can watch the trailer on the game's store page to get a feel for what it looks like.  You get four different screens:  a RAM screen where you can see which programs/notes are actively running, a net map showing active nodes that you can connect to, a GUI, and a terminal.  The terminal is a nice touch and is very UNIX like, if you like that sort of thing.  However, I resorted to the GUI more often than not when I was on the clock due to a trace program, but having both options is a must when you need to copy some files or the like since the GUI is limited in what it can do.
Hacking becomes second nature after doing it a few times, and it runs the risk of becoming a bit too repetitive at some points.  Generally, there are four ports (five or six for computers later in the game) and sometimes a proxy, firewall, or both.  You can hack multiple ports at once, and sometimes it is required, but keep an eye on the RAM screen.  Run out of memory and your hack will take longer.  Once done, enjoy the files on that computer.  Sometimes there are new programs to download and there are almost always files in the home folder to give you some laughs.
You can beat the game in under 10 hours once you get the hang of it.  That would not appeal to most people, but there is so many files in the game that you can go through and quite a few programs that you can probably get another 10 hours out of it.  Add that to the number of computers in the game that you have access to and that's probably another 3 hours or so.  I am actually playing through it again because I missed out on some computers from my last playthrough.  "Highly addicting" is the best way to describe it.
Whether you're into computers or not, you should give this game a go.  Also, type "openCDtray" once you are in the game.  You'll thank me later.

This game is Xcom, but in my opinion is better than base game Enemy Unknown (Unknown w/ Within is better). Most of my thoughts on this series basics are already mentioned in my review for Enemy Unknown, so this review will focus on the changes.
and in my opinion better than the ones from Unknown. Most of the base enemies from Unknown return to kill your soldiers in this game, while the different variations from Unknown are integrated into their original counterparts from the start. Not to mention, there are still some new enemies with some lethal new abilities.
and (also) in my opinion better than the ones from Unknown. Most of the classes are similar to Unknown, but each now carries a new tool. Your Assault, or now Ranger, carries a melee sword ability which can cut down enemies with suprisingly effective results. Your Heavy, or now Grenadier, replaced their rocket launcher with a more effective grenade launcher, which can shoot over cover, be used after moving, and can shoot a varaity of different grenades. Your Sniper, or now Sharpshooter, carries a revolver and has several new skills revolving aroung said revolver. Finally, your Support, or now Specialist, scraps the smoke grenade for a nifty new flying drone, which can be used for healing allies from a distance or sabotaging the enemy (more specifically, their robots).
The item system received quite a large change as well. Some ability-only items, such as the smoke grenade, is now a craftable and usuable item for all classes instead of just the support. The flashbang grenade is now more effective, has a MUCH larger range, but also affects allies. The best change to this system is weapons and armors are now considered SQUAD upgrades, meaning once you craft one you have infinite amounts of said item. You're also on the run now, so special evac missions won't grant you all of the loot from the dead aliens or dead allies, so if a soldier with your rare frost bomb dies, better pick up and drag them to an emergency evac zone.
One final note is there's a new system to health called Armor. Armor are additional hitpoints you need to punch through every attack to deal damage to the units actual health. Luckily, with some weapons and new abilities, some attacks can remove this armor and allow your allies to pick off that healthbar.
This game is Xcom. Its long, difficult, rewarding and fun, and is a great way to kill off a few hours.
10/10 would uninstall again.

I bought this app 7 months before this review and I've already used it quite a bit off-steam for altering and changing textures to use on various 3D assets, it is very useful for tweaking or creating normal and specular maps to harmonise the skinning of various assets from different sources, it also has a built in feature to make textures seamless if you need to, which is going to be extremely useful to a lot of people who already make textures in paint programmes and then have to run them all through yet another 3rd party app to create a seamless version.
The developer is well known in the 3D game assets community and he also makes 3D game assets, so Normalizator seems to have been written from the ground up for this type of thing.
I have had no real issues or problems with the app once I got used to the layout, and while it's been in early access before steam it has been updated and tweaked, and it's turned into a very handy tool well worth checking out, and very good value.
Yes, a lot of this stuff you can do in photoshop (other softwares are available), with the right plugins and tutorials, and many of you will already be using photoshop to make  diffuse, normal, specular, illumination and height maps.  I used to use Paint-dot-net but find the whole process far simpler in Normalizator.  If you are comfortable with photoshop etc you may not need an app like this, but it is so easy to use that it's still worth thinking about even then.
A good feature is being able to view the lighting effect on various texture maps in the editor itself.
Its a small app, with low overheads and modest system requirements. There are some sample projects included and plenty of help available from the developer (whose english is very good) and as it is in early access you can expect more improvements as time goes on.
No hesitation in recommending you try this out, it will take you a little time figuring things out, but once it clicks it becomes quite intuitive and the workflow is quite logical and easy to follow.

This game is absolutely amazing, I cannot stress how good it is. It does involve grinding, but it has enough variation to keep things fresh and enjoyable, and brings in enough of a profit with each mission to make you feel like you're making a significant difference. The enemies share some similar attacks, but all of those are simple things, like increasing stress on a target, or a straight up damaging attack. One of the parts of this game I enjoy the most is realizing new strategies to use, to take down certain enemies, or combos of enemies. It's very rewarding, and I highly recommend you purchase it. You've likely heard many people complain about RNG, but keep in mind that the times where a 90% chance to hit misses, or the time a heal fails, are the exception, not the rule. Remember to always prepare for the worst, and use what you have wisely. A ration costs 75g, and not having that one extra could be the difference between a hero being on death's door, and having 1 hp. a shovel costs 250g, but not having one could mean your path is blocked by rubble, and your heroes suffer stress and minor damage. Expect the worst, and you'll never be surprised.

This game is Xcom, but in my opinion is better than base game Enemy Unknown (Unknown w/ Within is better). Most of my thoughts on this series basics are already mentioned in my review for Enemy Unknown, so this review will focus on the changes.
and in my opinion better than the ones from Unknown. Most of the base enemies from Unknown return to kill your soldiers in this game, while the different variations from Unknown are integrated into their original counterparts from the start. Not to mention, there are still some new enemies with some lethal new abilities.
and (also) in my opinion better than the ones from Unknown. Most of the classes are similar to Unknown, but each now carries a new tool. Your Assault, or now Ranger, carries a melee sword ability which can cut down enemies with suprisingly effective results. Your Heavy, or now Grenadier, replaced their rocket launcher with a more effective grenade launcher, which can shoot over cover, be used after moving, and can shoot a varaity of different grenades. Your Sniper, or now Sharpshooter, carries a revolver and has several new skills revolving aroung said revolver. Finally, your Support, or now Specialist, scraps the smoke grenade for a nifty new flying drone, which can be used for healing allies from a distance or sabotaging the enemy (more specifically, their robots).
The item system received quite a large change as well. Some ability-only items, such as the smoke grenade, is now a craftable and usuable item for all classes instead of just the support. The flashbang grenade is now more effective, has a MUCH larger range, but also affects allies. The best change to this system is weapons and armors are now considered SQUAD upgrades, meaning once you craft one you have infinite amounts of said item. You're also on the run now, so special evac missions won't grant you all of the loot from the dead aliens or dead allies, so if a soldier with your rare frost bomb dies, better pick up and drag them to an emergency evac zone.
One final note is there's a new system to health called Armor. Armor are additional hitpoints you need to punch through every attack to deal damage to the units actual health. Luckily, with some weapons and new abilities, some attacks can remove this armor and allow your allies to pick off that healthbar.

Review of the singleplayer campaign (not interested in multiplayer):
I have to say, I am honestly surprised. In a good way. The Black Ops 3 campaign is way longer than what we are used to in this franchise. I think it took me about 12 hours, which is a good length for a shooter, even by normal standards - but especially compared to other Call of Duty games.
The story was pretty boring in the beginning. But it got better and better, to the point where I was honestly interested in how it all would play out. The acting was pretty good (real actors, digitalized). And the ending - well, the ending was great. It left me sitting in front of my monitor and wondering what the hell just happened. I ended up reading explanations and theories about the story for another 20 minutes. It is a surprisingly complex story for this kind of action game. Not quite on the same level as Bioshock Infinite or To the Moon, but way above your usual CoD story. I have to say, I really liked it (despite the boring start).
The gameplay is CoD standard. Nothing special here. You have some abilities to unlock and upgrade. But I rarely used them. You have a wall-run, but only a few opportunities to use it in the levels. It felt unnecessary. And that was a shame, because it's a cool mechanic and should have been integrated better in the level design. Most of your enemies are the typical noname soldiers. There are also certain types of mechs. Some are soldier-like, and a few bigger ones, which require the use of a rocket launcher. So there is some variety here, but in the end it is typical CoD shooter gameplay. Which is not brilliant, but alright.
The graphics are ok. The game looks quite good sometimes, but overall dated. They really make the most out of the old engine. But the game cannot compete with modern titles like Battlefront or Witcher 3.
If you want a number - I guess I would give it a 7.5/10 for the campaign. And it could have been more, had they improved the gameplay a little more. I really didn't think it would be that good.

Fallout 4 takes many key gameplay features from Fallout 3, New Vegas, and even the Elder Scrolls and improves them(while also opening a fat can of worms other installments lacked) in addition to adding entirely new customization options. You now have much more control over player creation, weapon and armor customization, and even an entirely new feature: Settlement Building. The game world is rich full of characters with more depth than any previous fallout installment. The voice acting is superb (although I'd love for the next game or possibly a mod that allows voice customization of the PC) However, if you're playing an evil character, the voice acting comes off as too friendly. Fallout 4's characters are better done compared to other installments, I personally find it difficult to murder them because they seem more human.(Although it's advisable to get a mod like "STFU followers" as most followers in the game will glitch and repeat the same old lines over, and over, and over...and it's much worse when you've more than one. SO limiting their lines is a good idea.) The game certainly has very high replay value, and NEXUS is your friend.
EDIT: Player choice in the endgame and results are illogical...If you work towards peace the whole game, you will just be given an ultimatum anyway where it's like "Hey!
