My feelings over the last couple of months have changed. So I thought it would be good to update this review for one last time. For people who may see this, the state of this game right now is pretty good. There are less people playing on the PC so if multiplayer is your thing look to the console counter part. However the single player and playing with a friend online is fantastic.
The amount of content this game has and offers is insane for basketball fans. So as a "too long, don't read" part of the review I will say this:
IF YOU ARE A BIG FAN OF THE NBA/BASKETBALL BUY THIS GAME. it will be worth it for you. If you are a casual sports fan or want to get into the NBA and learn more BUY IT.
About 10 years ago I knew little about the NBA and wanted to get into it. My brother was really into it and I wanted to share a common love for a sport I have long over looked. I bought a copy of NBA 2k7 and Since then I have bought this series every year. Some years disapointed with the lack of difference or changes, some years amazed by the level of detail they put into a yearly series with the same core gameplay experience. The one thing I got from this series was a love for basketball. I want to thank 2K for doing this for me.
Everything below is what I orginally wrote on the game a few weeks or so after it came out. I played this game almost everyday since its release. One of the best game investments I have ever bought. Mainly because I have someone to play with me online. It can be frustrating at times with connection issues and unrealistic things, but overall a great game for basketball lovers.
Pros:
+Great Animations. Best in any sports game for sure.
+Good Singleplayer experience. MyCareer Mode is better then ever this year. Some problems with it (See Below)
+Sound is decent. Crowd noise is great, Commentary is top notch (when it works)
+Tons of Features and Gamemodes. You can spend a lot of time with this game.
+Gameplay is top notch.
+Graphics and lighting are superb.
Cons:
-Online on the PC has its problems mainly if you have sub-par connection
-Spike Lee is a hack who made a really bad B level movie story mode. Luckly it only lasts for a short time.
-Bugs here and there nothing to bad.
Lets talk about the "Spike Lee Joint"
So basically this year instead of the normal MyCareer mode like past years, you start out in High School and you are the "NBAs next big star"
Right at the start you are thrust into this family from New York. The Bronx to be specific. You're a ghetto kid who has one chance to make it out of the hard life and make something of yourself and help your family. You have the typical bad boy best friend who is always getting in trouble and acting a fool. You have the over caring, over protective sister. Who by the way is your twin.
Typical B level story, no big deal right? Well this is suppose to be YOUR GAME. You are suppose to make yourself and experience what it would be like to be a NBA player. Well there is one big problem from the start.... Your family is Black and you have a Black twin sister. I know that sounds super racist, but hear me out. You are probably going to make a character that is close to what you look like. So lets say I'm White. Now I have a Black twin sister and a black family. It takes you right out of the immersion of the game and story. It's like you aren't apart of whats going on. I think this is a big problem. Now I'm not one to make this comparison. But what if everyone who played this game was forced to have a white family and a white twin sister. People have cried racism for much less. There would be blogs complaining about it. People online ♥♥♥♥♥ing about how the game is racist.  It's not a super big deal to me, but I just don't see how this can just be overlooked.
After the first year in the NBA (only get to play 8 games) The story ends. It's a really bad story and is so full of cliches. However It was a nice change of pace from former NBA2K games. After that year you go into the normal MyCareer mode like from years past. There are a few new things that keep it fresh. Which is great. I like it a lot.
MyTeam is fun, not much changed from last year though. It also is a huge money sink. GM mode is cool and very in-depth. All in all this game is full of things to do, aslong as you really like Basketball.
In conclusion the simplest way to say it: If you like Sports games this game is great. If you have a PS4 or Xbox1 buy it on there instead. You will get faster updates, better online play. It will look worse graphics wise, but atleast you wont have to deal with the crashing and lag online.
Every year it takes months for them to patch the PC version of the game. Why do I still buy it every year you ask? Well because I'm a bored idiot who likes Basketball and I don't have much choice. If there is any game in the world I would rather play on a console its this game. That's a sad sad fact, since I truely believe that this game could be great if the Dev team were able to spend some time play testing the PC version. I know for a fact they aren't allowed to. A close friend worked for them and he told me the stories on how they aren't allowed to test the PC version for bugs. Console is main priority. That's a sad sad standard to have. I don't blame the dev team because like I said they are basically following orders from above.
So I guess if you REALLY REALLY REALLY REALLY INSANLY LIKE BASKETBALL BUY IT.

Although I do not think this game is worth full price, I would give it a strong recommendation. It has a great atmosphere, but as that is generally acknowledged by everyone, I will focus this review on the gameplay.
The gameplay of Darkest Dungeon centers around resource management. During your playthrough, you will have to manage gold, heirlooms, stress, town upgrades, character weapons & skills, and more. Juggling these factors creates both constant worry, and constant fun.
To get resources, you will have to compose parties to quest in dungeons. It is important to realize that the combat of Darkest Dungeon is more about the composition of your party and what skills they have. This is where many people start to complain about the game being "unfair". Many people will take four low stress heroes and throw them in a dungeon, when they should create their party in such a way that they exploit the enemies' weaknesses, and synergize with eachother. If you bring a good party for each dungeon, and know when to use the 'abandon quest' button, you should have an enjoyable time.
Of course, nothing is perfect, the game does have flaws. I will list this flaws in order from least to most annoying:
1.) Static Bosses: Each region as two bosses that you will fight three times each (apprentice, veteran, champion). The bosses don't gain any new skills as you fight them at higher levels, the only change is in their stats.
2.) Horrible hunger system: In DD, hunger is a tile system (when your heroes walk over a hunger tile, they will have to eat). Hunger tiles seem to have a high chance to spawn BEHIND you, which can lead to many failed expeditions.
3.) Abysmal Quirk System: Your heroes get quirks and diseases upon completing dungeon runs. Unfortunately, the quirks and diseases are completely random, and aren't based at all on what happened while you were in the dungeon (Your hero could take no damage, not interact with any curios, and he can get The Black Death + Kleptomania on the same run).
Overall, I would say Darkest Dungeon is worth 10 - 15 USD. Some aspects of the game are lacking, whereas others are superb.

Although I'm still halfway though the game, I must say it:
This is a must-buy for anyone who enjoyed Hotline Miami or SuperHot, and also for those who enjoy games that feature boarding enemy ships, or tactical action.
Heat Signature is a small gem of a roguelite game in which you fly around in a boarding assault pod, breaching enemy ships and killing them from the inside. You do this to further the rebellion against all the factions in the 'galaxy' (the game's region of space).
After "docking" uninvited on an enemy ship, you will
disable it by
cautiously knocking out the ship's crew - non-lethally,
.
The game allows (and encourages) you to press SPACE for a quick, tactical pause, that allows you to switch gear and do crazy amounts of cool moves. Like hacking a turret, disabling enemies' shields, teleporting/switching places with an enemy, murdering the pilot and blowing up a hole that sucks a squad of unsuspecting crew members out into space in a few seconds.
Having randomly generated characters with personal missions is also very neat. If you're a roleplayer (as in, you set rules, morals and/or goals for characters) you can create pretty cool stories.
If you're not into that, by losing a character you'll only lose its gear, which is pretty light when compared to roguelites/roguelikes by which you lose all of it's skills, experience and unlockables. Losing is Fun.
Mind that if you're not into roguelites, the lack of an overarching story and the expected repetitive nature of the game might get to you.
That said, the only thing I'd wish to have more of, is equipment/customization for your pod. Sensors, EMP, hacking capabilities, would make it a much more lively part of the game.
In conclusion, Heat Signature is an amazing surprise. I've only heard about it yesterday, saw 3 minutes of video and that's all it took to guarantee my purchase.
It is by no means a perfect game - much could be further improved or added. But for its price, even if you're not familiar with the related games, it's worth checking out.

It's fun going from Zaccaria to Pinball FX, the direct opposite in Pinball gaming. One is a hard as nails realistic simulation, the other is what video game pinball was even going back nearly 30 years to the like of Devil Crash or Crüe Ball: Unrealistic everything goes Pinball.
What Pinball FX3 has in common is all the insanity on the playfields: You have vikings walking down toward your flippers and you have to shoot them (which is kinda like a mode in Crüe Ball on Mega Drive) or you have Super Heroes fight it out on the side, like Iron Man versus Captain America or you just have Lee and Clementine play some football.
That is the big appeal of Pinball FX: It's unrealistic, it's over the top, it's loud, scores flashing everywhere, you have missions to the point where some tables actually feel more like video games than pinball, like the Bethesda Tables (and hate on me all you want, the Skyrim Table was a ton more fun than vanilla Skyrim)
As with the other Pinball games, you get one table for free which is Magicians Lair which is a fun table that somewhat reminds me of Williams' Cirqus Voltaire (a real life table i really like a lot) with some mini games and fun stuff. There are other tables the developers made, though the quality varies, some are from Pinball FX 1 and 2 after all and you can tell that they learned a lot from the likes of V8 and Paranormal to Epic Quest to the later licensed tables which are mostly Marvel (all your superheroes are there), the Alien franchise or some cartoons like Archer or the newest Universal tables (which are a let down because they lack the movie, Back to the Future without its theme is no fun)
PFX3 added some new stuff like having different passive and active skills you have to aquire by playing a table or do challenges like 1-ball and survival (add more time by doing missions). There are 6 Bonuses like a point bonus on the miles your ball travels, bumper bonus, multiball bonus and active skills like a rewind, so you can undo a massive mistake.
Of course there's also a regular no skills, no nonsense mode which is all about the pinball itself but sadly it seems like the majority of people just play the new mode with skills and stuff.
Considering the experience of the devs the ball and table physics are really good overall as well as the graphics and sounds being really great.
As for online there is sadly no head to head multiplayer but you can have tournaments and there are leaderboards to fight for scores which is good enough.
I really like this one, it's a great upgrade for the already fun Pinball FX2

The original version on Steam, Pinball FX2, was incredible. This is effectively a refresh of that, adding perks that upgrade themselves when you meet the criteria. This adds a very satisfying new layer to the existing tables. The physics are the most reliable yet, and  I say this as a player who began his relationship with this product on the XBox 360 back in late 2012: they are the most faithful to the (presumably) intended physics I've yet found in Zen's various versions of this game. Thus I must note that this is an absolutely fantastic game on that front. There are leaderboards for both classic and the new perk system, so you are not forced into playing either way on your tables of choise.
Edit: In the interest of honesty I wish to denote that a previous version of this review said the online matchup play was at best dodgy for submission. Online features are now properly working. Aside from the ocassional "failed to connect to servers" error which never seems to affect submission, this issue I was having with score submission seems to have been completely resolved with a recent patch.
The game has made a few interesting features to justify its release as compared to PFX2. Online simultaneous play (a thing you could seldom find matches for online in the first place in PFX2 on PC) has been replaced with a tournament score-style matchup play. How this works is as follows: four tables are changing weekly. There's a random score set (based loosely off your scoring ability for said tables), offering you 20, 30, or 40 points before bonuses applicable (you can get up to 15 points extra for having played one or more of the tables that week), and you have 3 minutes to score as high as you can. Due to the nature of the system it requires you have at least one of the tables to even participate, and needless to say the more tables you have, the better your potential to go up the tiers (3 ranks of Bronze, Silver, Gold, and Platinum). Doing so requires you to be in the top percentage of points. (as far as I've seen 20% in the bronze and 15% in the silver, can't confirm anything beyond that). This is a system designed to favor older players, but is not impossible for new players to enter into, so long as you're willing to dole out the cash for more than a few of the packs.
Some have made much ado on the fact that not every table has transferred from PFX2. Licensing is a tricky thing to deal with and it's worth bearing in mind that this is hardly a new issue. Every version of Zen Pinball (otherwise known as Pinball FX) and its various iterations has had access to a slightly different set of tables, but rest assured the 55 that made the jump from the PC version of PFX2 to PFX3 remain mostly faithful (they seem to have adjusted a few things in recent patches, but the structure, far as I've ever been able to tell, has always been the same). Zen is iterative in their designs- it wouldn't be the first time they've modified things to increase or decrease difficulty/scoring based on player feedback. It's great that Zen is willing to do this, and quite frankly, it makes this game a better overall experience that they do. These tables don't exist in the wild anywhere, so there's no reason for them to stick to "this is the way it is" logic if there's a way the community sees things could be improved. Maybe someday they'll add online multiplayer back again, but for now this is more than adequate, and a worthy successor to the Zen Pinball line of games.

This is a fun little game.  The graphics aren't much to look at but it draws from one of the greatest arcade games of all time: Asteroids.  So imagine you're playing asteroids, except that instead of giving you a weapon that goes "pew pew pew" you get a bunch of small projectiles on some kind of leash that you can whip around your ship as you fly.  That's basically the "Particle Mace" from the title.
So You're placed in a small area and these rather regularly sized asteroids come in around you.  They're not the main focus of the game though...they're more like extra obstacles.  The enemy ships ARE the main focus though.  They come in, darting at you, sweeping past you, flying all around.  You have to destroy these for big points, and for even bigger points you have to kill several in quick succession.   The way to a big score is not just killing enemies but combos.
You do get points for destroying the asteroids as well but it's a mere fraction of the points you get for destroying the ships.  However, there are some asteroid only rounds to clear so don't think you can ignore them totally.  Also, there's mission mode where each round has some objectives to complete The mission mode seems to be a collection of objectives you have to achieve before you can go to the next level. e.g. don't hit any asteroids for 20 seconds, don't hit any ships for 20 seconds, kill x number of ships in a certain time limit, destroy x number of asteroids completely (because hitting them only splits them in two and halves their size until they get really small).

I didn't enjoy this game much at all. I like the idea of playing a hacking simulator, but the execution really fell flat. The challenges are monotonous and uninteresting. The files added in for flavor are tired-old jokes. There's not much in the way of story. And the interface is awful. The worst part is the network map where you connect to hosts, which is a crowded bunch of unlabeled dots that you just have to remember, (I eventually gave up and put the list of hosts/IPs into a text document on a second monitor so that I could at least hide the ones I thought I was done with) but the terminal and RAM screens are both pretty bad too. The RAM screen is a combination of an arbitrary hurdle and an excuse to add silly hacker media trope animations, and I want to know what program spends 300MB of ram displaying a short text file. The terminal doesn't scroll or even have history, so once some output goes off the top of the screen it's lost. Did you cat a file and not bother to read it until after rm /log/*; dc;? Have fun breaking back in to get the file again since a bunch of "Deleting file" messages pushed it off the screen? Did you want to !solve because you didn't get everything you wanted the first time you broke in? Too bad.
Definitely not worth the price or your time.

I'm conflicted. A part of me, especially during the end segments of my stygian run, kind of wants to call this game wasted potential; it's beautiful, it's harrowing, and so many elements of the battle system and leveling system are great, fun ideas, but the rest of the time I find this game to be a chore, even when I tried radiant for a bit. The hamlet upgrading system and leveling system is so tedious, especially when coupled with the repeated and often annoying slog to sit through dungeons or repeated boss fights, that the game feels more like a manager simulator. I don't mind that, I'd still probably play the game if it were just that and I sent adventurers in without controlling them, but it's too much for a game when its selling features are its stunning visuals and inventive battle system. They are both appealing to me, but one felt too saturated and didn't belong.
It's the little moments, though, that really keep me going and falling in love with this game. Sure, the intro dungeon was just ok, but I cannot remember playing a game where I wanted to plan things out so hard when I tried my first medium and long dungeon. I'd think about whether I should have just chosen a short dungeon since I started on stygian and wanted to be super careful about heroes and time. I was afraid of the crimson court but mustered up the nerve to play it. Even after countless cleared dungeons that bothered me with its repetitiveness, the DDs offered a fresh new experience. Sometimes frustrating, but still fresh and entertaining. When I got those rare early crits to save my life or against me that made me cry out "NOOOO", I was really into it. The stress system fascinated me until I broke it into another management system that worked really well but ultimately was not fun. The lovecraftian themes were great. The designs were great. I could go on all day!
Ultimately, my verdict is probably somewhere down the middle. I value the difficulty of the game, since I'm a person who loves to maximize challenges and I seek to do the most with the least; because of this, the game is less pure RNG like for some people and only partly RNG to have those moments of sadness and pain or glory when a crit or a speed roll didn't or did go in my favour. This game really suits my taste and playing style/skill with RPGs and it is a huge boon for me, but I could very well understand that it's relatively niche, even with radiant making things a bit easier and quicker for others. The difficulty is also well-implemented, offering time and death deadlines that make you plan more, enemies that do things a bit differently, and a few other things that require a workaround instead of just beating your head with a handicap against you.
If you aren't someone like me, I can get the dislike. I'd dislike it too, but style and character is huge for me and this game's got both in spades.

Fun game, technical and requires a lot of adaptability. Every encounter, no matter how small or weak the enemy might seem has the potential to be lethal to any character. Now it has a slow build up but once the wheels get rolling, it is very fun once you learn your own strategies and applying them to your battles perfectly feels very satisfying. The stress system is interesting but it gets out of hand very quickly. You have very few ways to manage or remove stress as the 'stress heal' potions only remove the 'horror' debuff which is otherwise useless; you'll need a character class that can remove stress (there's only 2 classes that can remove stress from others and a handful that remove stress from themselves outside of getting criticals on your foes and carefully navigated curios).
My gripes with the game consist of the RNG factor that can♥♥♥♥♥♥on you at any time. Expect to hit for your minimum damage and be critted in return. This game will do that for at least one fight in every dungeon or two so plan ahead and make recovery strats. Expect to put in an hour or two to get past the initial 3 weeks and open the game up.
Gameplay wise the UI looks very neat, is easy to navigate and is accompanied by the narrator that will share tidbits of the story in a way that fits the overall 'lovecraftian' tone of the game. 10/10 to him.
Now if you are starting this game new, I reccommend not getting the Crimson Court DLC on your first time through unless you're looking forward to getting plagued by bloodsuckers, infected with vampirism and then subsequently hunted down by one of the more painstaking (no pun intended) minibosses of the game that can cut down the damage you deal to him by 50%, has deceptively high resistances and binds one of your characters to boot. The difficulty with the DLC climbs very fast and even with very rare trinkets and leveled characters will you be able to defeat a miniboss like this without taking a casualty.
If you intend on beating this game, be prepared to put in at least 80+ hours to learn and develop a playstyle and even then the game can get harder. Remember the RNG factor, characters WILL die (I've lost plenty of hamlets) and things will not go your way very often. Overcoming that hurdle is however, euphoric after the worst battles.
Back to the DLC; It's very unforgiving if you do not know what you're getting into but expands upon the story in a way that feels like it was always meant to be there. A new area (Courtyard) and one new character (Flagellant) are included alongside a host of bosses, minibosses and the bloodsucker enemy class. A worthy addition to the game.
I'll rate the game an 8/10 due to some minor balancing issues near the beginning such as insect class enemies having a base of 7-8 speed which makes it near impossible for characters of that rank to move first (with the odd exception that can happen vice versa, a 4 speed enemy might move before someone with 11 speed which seems kind of silly). NG+ does not offer anything new sadly except now you're on a time limit. Finally the stress system is as stressful as it sounds, rarely will it go in your favour should an adventurer reach their limit. I personally think if the stress potions did more than remove horror (which doesn't appear at level 1 quests) and removed say.. 10 stress and they increased the price while lowering the quantity in stock you might have more flexibility and fun with the game instead of feeling forced to always bring a certain character class and such.
Save yourself some grief by getting a feel for the game before getting the DLC and I really wouldn't bother with NG+ again unless you're just being masochistic.. but enjoy the best and worst that this game can bring out of you.

FRACTURED SPACE REVIEW/IMPRESSIONS:
Video Version:
GAMEPLAY: MOBA, over-the-shoulder shooter, with abilities, different types of ship, WASD+space+ctrl to move, mouse to aim and shoot.
CREW: Tactical, Comms, Captain, Engineer, A.I., Navigation Officer.
INTRO:
Fractured Space is, first and foremost, a free-to-play game. It was developed and published by Edge Case Games, and was released on September 22nd 2016. Winner of the PAX West award for Best MOBA in 2016, Fractured Space is a game where you are assigned with badass spaceships to take over the other team’s facilities and enemy base with the help of your fellow comrades and ship crew.
GAMEPLAY:
For starters, this game is hard even while playing against an AI. The difficulty of controlling the ships is as hard as if you were controlling an actual big♥♥♥♥♥ship. Your team consists of 4 other ships that go against 5 enemy ships. Your crew includes a tactical, a captain, an AI, a comms, am engineer and a navigation officer that will communicate via “radio”, alerting you to system destruction, facilities taken, new enemies in sight or allies down.
Your team must create a strategy in order to take down the enemy ships and use their respawn time to take over the facilities in each location to follow until you can get access to the enemy base and win the game.
While needing to pay attention to the enemy ships that spawn, you also need to control your facilities, capture new ones, beware ships that are shooting you, take cover and make sure you’re not destroying the ship by hitting meteorites on your way. Phew! Seems like a lot to do just in one go? Just wait till you see the minimaps! There are 5 locations in each round, these being the home base, beta 1 and 2, alpha 1 and 2, gamma and enemy base. On the minimap, you can see how many facilities are in each location, how many are under your team’s control, how many under the enemy’s and how many teammates are there, as well as the number of enemy ships.
BATTLESHIPS:
There are different kinds of ship, such as Attack, Defense and Utility. Even though you can relate to most MOBA that these types are the usual DPS/TANK/HEALER system, each ship has their own way of handling, shooting and gameplay. Attack ships are, as expected, specialised in ship destruction, but they can go from Sniper to Bruiser ships. Defensive are the ones that hold the front line and have their own squadron of fighters to help them, some even have repair drones that surround them during the combat, making them tougher to deal with. And Utility are ships that focus on supporting their comrades, not just by healing, but with abilities that buffs and clean debuffs. Their speed and attack effectiveness also change depending on your ship of choice and abilities vary according to the ship you choose. You can give the ships a try and see how each of the abilities work, I strongly recommend trying them, because on the Firing Range there are tips of how to play correctly with each ship.
PRESENTATION:
The ship’s design looks great, specially with the various skins for each. Their texture and color palette turned out really good, and you can appreciate them from each side and detail shown in the ships. The scenery is amazing, some locations seem to have been taken from a sci-fi film production, though it doesn’t seem to vary that much. I felt specially satisfied with the jump sequence, since it has been well planned for the game and reminded me of the Millennium Falcon Hyperdrive or the Enterprise warp jumps. The game’s sound effects are flawless and well-explored, though the voice acting for the crew seems a bit too robotic and a quite stereotyped. The epic soundtrack brings you the feeling of being in a real sci-fi space war.
CONCLUSION:
Considering that I played this game for nearly 5 hours and I plan to play more of it in the near FU-TU-RE, the amount of 25 dollars worth 5 hours were definitely worth the hours spent playing for free.
Seeing the final product, it's easy to notice that a lot of time and effort have been invested in this production. Since it’s a free game, our real question here is whether it is or isn't worth wasting your time to play it. Well, I’ve played this game for 4 hours and was getting as excited as a child to see my ranks and stats going up. I got impressed with it’s visual art and gameplay, even if it was a bit hard at the beginning. You may get a bit bored from some repetitions in scenery (sometimes, it may be just a bunch of asteroids on the way and that’s it) and your crew’s orders and reports. It is a fun game to play with friends, though! Teamwork is important here in order to create a strategy and make sure someone don’t just pop into a location and gets killed because they were alone.
Well, seing the overall, it is a very fun and beautiful game that you can enjoy playing non-stop for hours. It’s cost for the buyers is lower that the cost of production, and even if they wanted to establish a price of, say, 20 dollars for the game, it would be worth it. Since it’s free, I don’t see a single reason why you shouldn’t spend the next 5+ hours having an amazing time with this game! What are you waiting for? Go download it! Live long and prosper, y’all!

I really enjoyed the hell out of this game. It has just enough randomness that I never felt safe even with my A teams fully upgraded and trinketed but only rarely did it feel cheap. I started with a lot of gripes when I first played through Radiant mode but a lot of them went away as I learned more about the game. Here are some of my thoughts about the game, I'd like to see if my experience was similar to others':
The good:
* Itemization: Trinket selection was fun and reflective of the game as a whole. Sometimes even the best trinkets can really screw you by adding too much stress or reducing speed and/or dodge on a character that needs them.
* Randomness: As I said I hated the massive amount of RNG at first because it felt like I was just pulling on a slot machine rather than having the opportunity to make decisions. As I learned more of the game's mechanics I realized that mastering team comps and being flexible with my strategies overcame about 85% of the randomness, which was a really satisfying feeling.
* Party comps: Wow, there is so much to be said about how great this aspect of the game is. Obviously not all comps are completely viable but the game is balanced delicately enough that sometimes you can put an under optimized build into a party in order to enable another extremely powerful one. When I started I fumbled around and made terrible parties. Later I looked up builds to try to make it easier on myself. By Bloodmoon I was using all self-constructed parties that I felt were optimal in each of the four zones.
* Stress: Not much to say on this one. Stress damage is unique enough that I got frustrated with it in an entirely different way from when I'd lose health. I could feel myself getting stressed as the little white bar crept up toward 200. Ultimately it's just another health bar but I think Red Hook implemented it very well and it's a mechanic I'll probably never forget (or see again for that matter).
* SOME bosses: Many of the bosses in this game were a blast to learn. I wish there were more opportunities for intuitive mechanics but in a game where you expect to die sometimes I guess experimentation isn't so bad. Additionally it was fun to find ways to break encounters, which allowed me to try them at lower levels to challenge myself. I had to say just some though because there were a few encounters that could be broken so harshly that the boss could hardly damage you and they had no way to recover, such as shuffling the Anchorman.
The bad:
* Crimson Courtyard maps: The idea of a map that you could spend more time exploring was amusing at first but quickly became very tedious. There are simply far too few connecting hallways in the interest of making fun shapes (I think?) out of the maps. In particular, in the Countess's dungeon if you choose to go down (or mistakenly pick) a side path that doesn't lead to her, you'll find yourself having to return via the same path, cleared of enemies and anything interesting. Once the stress of proper preparation for these dungeons was handled, the Courtyard maps simply became very tedious to plow through if I was exploring them for the first time or trying to find trinket chests.
* A handful of abilities: There are so many classes in this game that I really can't complain too much that not every ability has a use. Some that come to mind are Bola, Hound's Harry (yes, even vs. Flesh it's mediocre), Caltrops, many of the -ACC skills.
* Diseases: Certainly not the worst thing that can happen to you in this game but for some reason receiving a disease was by far the most keyboard smashing part of the game for me. In a late game Champion Weald I had The Worries applied to two characters and Rabies to another before I had a turn. Diseases can be extremely punishing, essentially deleting the effects of your carefully chosen trinkets and giving you almost zero options for removal mid-dungeon. I realize that there are two classes that can remove them from others but it simply wasn't enough to keep diseases from being far more obnoxious than fun for me.
The UGLY:
* Barks: In the base game barks are handled reasonably well. If your character is afflicted then you've made mistakes or are the victim of very bad luck and your characters will understandably freak out. Barks became truly awful when your characters all had the Crimson Curse. Getting the Curse is not awful, it has ups and downs but it IS inevitable and long-lasting unlike afflictions. Cursed characters constantly yell unremarkable things randomly even when not in combat or in danger of any kind. They'll start screaming at you about Blood AS YOU ARE ADMINISTERING IT, which stops the game and prevents you from clicking. The only thing I can equate it to is when you are using a touch screen and an ad loads in front of the thing you're pressing as you've pressed it except it can happen 2 to 4 times in a row. In order to avoid the game missing my inputs I was often spamming left click on the UI to speed through the barks. I truly hated this part of the game.
* Game speed: Not much to say here, it's simply far too slow. I had to mod the animation times to make the game more enjoyable in this respect and that should not be necessary with how easy it was to change. RPGs have had Battle Speed settings since NES so it's a shame that this is not implemented.
* Invitations: The invite mechanic for the Courtyard felt poorly implemented. The purpose of it is to gate some of the content while you level up. Unfortunately the ideal way to start the game is to ignore the Courtyard for a while and this will screw up the court pacing for the rest of your run. Infestations inject enemies into other areas that can drop more invitations but they're rare enough that you could hunt them and still not receive an invite for 20 weeks. Red Hook was trying to make an alternative to the boss progression bars but this simply did not work for me and as a result I found more success ignoring the content.
* Trinket sets: A friend of mine commented that he thought trinket slots should unlock at higher Resolve levels (starting with 1 and ending with 3) and I agree with him. There simply isn't room for most of these sets. In many cases your characters will be nearly unusable without some form of +ACC. However, almost none of the trinket sets give you this stat. I liked the idea of the sets - enabling builds that were less than ideal in the base game. I tried all of the sets in Darkest mode - even the terrible Dagger Plague Doctor. I found uses for at least one item from each set and ended up using a lot of them in my Champion runs on Bloodmoon difficulty but I rarely ever paired up the set and couldn't help wondering how much more fun it would have been to have that third slot.
Hopefully you guys all enjoy it as much as I did. I would love to come back and play again if there's another DLC, especially if RH makes some quality of life changes to the game.

First off I would like to state that this is a good game. Several reviewers lately have posted negative comments and "would not recommend" reviews lately. I have noticed a trend with many of those reviewers. A large number of these reviewers have upwards of 30+ hours invested in the game. A good number of these have 60 to 90+ hours invested in the game. I would like to state that you received the game for $24.99 (or less if you received it for free or on sale). You received your money's worth. I would also like to iterate that if the game was bad, I doubt you would have invested this much time into it. Your overall time investment in Darkest Dungeon speaks loudly about your frustration with the game. This is understandable. Darkest Dungeon can be a frustrating. Does this merit a negative review? I don't believe that it does. You would not have placed this much time into it if the game was bad or broken
Now for the review portion of this little rant. Frustration is a good starting point. Darkest Dungeon is very frustrating at times. On the occasion it will feel as if there is nothing you can do to win. The game is unforgiving and harsh in many instances. This may drive the average or casual gamer away from the game. By all means, if you are looking for a game to play stress free and easily, you may wish to look else where. Just as your party in the game gains stress, you might as well. The game is harsh and unforgiving, but I would call it fair in all regards.
When I began the game, I played like a typical dungeon crawler. The first few available characters that you encounter are what you would normally find in a dungeon crawler. You have your tank (crusader), healer (vestal) and DPR (highwayman). You put your tank at the front of the group, your dps in the middle and your healer in the back. This works well for lower level dungeons. However, after the first fifteen hours, I found that thinking outside the box was rewarded. Just as the game appears to find ways to "screw you over," as it has been put so eloquently in other reviews, it makes it so much sweeter when you find combinations that work reliably in your favor.
The adventurers you are provided with are not just cookie cutter. It is very apparent that a lot of thought was put into their design. Just because the Highwayman has a pistol does not mean he is only good for ranged attacks. He also works very well as a second rank melee combatant. Lunging to the front with Fencer's Lunge and then returning to the second rank with your Point Blank Shot is formidable combination. Your greatest healing will come from an Occultist, not from a Vestal. Front lining with a Hellion, instead of a crusader. Repeatedly stun locking the back two ranks of your opposition with a Plague Doctor so as not to become over run. I could go on for ages about the diversity in roles each character could fill. Take your time with this game. Try new options. New combinations.
Also, you must know your enemy. Some enemies will be highly resistant to Blight. The Plague Doctor class may suffer in these dungeons. Others, such as Unholy enemies, may be especially resistant to bleed effects. A Houndmaster may suffer here because many of their attacks are supposed to apply a bleed effect. If your current party relies heavily on stun locking the opposition but the dungeon is populated by many adversaries with a high stun resist, switch out party members. Upgrade your roster size if you have a favorite of the class. Place gear that focuses on certain kinds of attacks or defenses on one and a different set on another to keep your class of choice relevant even in the most difficult situations.
However, no matter how good your ability is, you will fail. The difficulty of the game is something that I found refreshing. The permanent deaths of your party members is a fair response for succumbing to the fell advances of your enemies. The stress system is solid and I find appreciation for the game mechanic, even though it often causes me stress in return. As for glitches, bugs and the sort. As of this posting I have invested 37.6 hours into Darkest Dungeon and have found none. I purchased this game on sale for $10 and, knowing what I know now, would happily have invested $24.99 for the full game.
Darkest Dungeon is a solid dungeon crawler that will leave you with a sense of accomplishment when bosses are defeated and amazing rewards are received. I recommend this game to anyone who likes a challenge.

I was happy to see that we were automatically given all of the tables we had from Pinball FX2.  I always thought that FX2 had great graphics, but FX3 tables are clearly sharper and look better.  As far as I can tell there's no downside to FX3 compared to FX2.  The allegations that you need windows 10 and a beefy video card are untrue.  I have Windows 7 and a mid-range video card and it plays perfectly.  There's sometimes about a slight (under 0.5 seconds) freeze when an upgrade pops up, and I hope they can smooth that out, but I don't find it a significant problem.
Should they have left FX2 on the store?  Sure, maybe.  But most companies would leave the old game on the store, and then make you buy everything again if you want the new version.  If those are the two options, then I strongly prefer the way they did it.  Of course I'd be ok if they let you buy the old FX2 tables and then automatically gave you the tables in both games, but this would perhaps be hard to implement.
Some people strongly criticize the leveling up mechanic, but I don't really see why.  Is it realistic compared to physical pinball?  Of course not, but the whole game isn't, and the mechanic doesn't really hurt anything.  The upgrades mainly just give you scoring bonuses, its not like they change the way the tables play.  If you're really into tournament play maybe this is a significant thing for you, but for normal players it certainly doesn't make the game any worse.  People generally like to feel like they progress in games, and this gives them an incentive to keep playing to unlock things.  Look at achievements generally, many people will play a game for much longer than they normally would have to get them.  This is also why "rogue lite" games tend to be more popular these days than "rogue-like" games, since people like to feel that they progress when playing multiple times.
I do hope they continue to put table packs in bundle sites, and on good sales, to make them more reasonable.  But the great thing about the game is that you can buy the tables you want, try the others for free, and wait for sales or bundles for the tables you're not sure about.  Its generally a very good system.

After spending a decent amount of time with this, I wholeheartedly recommend it if you're in any way a fan of turn based strategy games, and it's an easy buy if you enjoyed your time with Firaxis' first crack at the XCOM franchise with Enemy Unknown and the exceptional expansion pack Enemy Within.
The first significant change (and it's a big one) that you'll notice is that for a large portion of the missions, you begin concealed. That means that you can discover the enemy, set up your positions, and coordinate an attack before the enemy can react. Those that have played Enemy Unknown/Within should realize just how much this changes things.
However, at the same time, Firaxis has decided to push you to be a bit more aggressive than you may be comfortable with by effectively creating turn limits on a lot of missions be it by having a hard timer before reinforcements arrive (losing your troops in the process if they don't evacuate in time), having an object across the map you have to protect before the enemy destoys, or having a bomb go off etc.  I'm definitely no expert and maybe I was doing it wrong, but I wouldn't be surprised if a lot of people found themselves having to essentially sprint instead of methodically making their ways forward to the objective.
Troops and classes have been given a bit of a makeover, and while they have some significant changes, they will feel inherently familiar to those who have played Enemy Unknown/Within. You still have your shotgun class, your heavy, your medic, and your sniper, but either they've been given some new toys to play with (A sword? Yes please), the respective talent trees associated with each class has been modified as well. For example, the sniper class has a branch that focuses on you being able to leverage your sidearm to devastating effect.
Oh yea, each soldier is fully customizable from colors, to hats, to glasses, and even speech. They went all out here.
The campaign is based around you fighting against your alien oppressors, contacting resistance pockets around the globe, and slowing down the game doom counter known as the Avatar project. On the global map, you will balance obtaining money and troops, saving a local populace from annihilation, protecting yourself from assaults, and launching assaults on highly protected bases where if you're successful, you'll set the doom timer back a couple ticks. There will be hard choices you'll have to make. At points, a prompt will come up where there will be 3 bad things that will have long lasting effects, but you can only choose one of them that you can stop. It's really a, "Well, all 3 suck, but I really don't want that one happening to me so I'll go stop that one from happening and deal with the negative effects of the other two."
I haven't touched any of the official dlc that Firaxis has put out, but at least at first glance it appears that a lot of people think it's overpriced. Given that, I'd wait for a sale. Especially because Firaxis has done this:
Day one Steam Workshop support.
This game has thousands of mods. Some are tweaks to speed up the game animations to you being able to rocking Storm Troopers in your guerilla battle against the aliens. I actually got overwhelmed at the number of options available. I'm the kind of person that goes through the game completely vanilla the first time and then after I saw what the devs wanted the game to be, then I'll start switching it up via mods.
Hopefully Firaxis is working on a full fledged expansion. I'll buy it day one at full price.

The first Lego game I played was the original Star Wars Trilogy.  It was a little rough; don't get me wrong, I had a blast with it, but some of the levels were simply unmanageably long -- sometimes you don't want to play for an hour or two at a time because you can't.  My next foray was with the Harry Potter games.  It was pretty apparent some major upgrades had been made in the gameplay department.
And then came Lego Lord of the Rings, which incorporated not only soundclips from the movies, an open world, and Howard Shore's soundtrack, but also midpoint saves, and a lot of other particularly nice features.  Lego Lord of the Rings was one of two games I bought in 2013 before the Bar Exam (lawyered!) in anticipation of actually having some down time come August.  I loved the game.  I really did.  I was thoroughly impressed with it.  It was just whimsical and fun.
And then Lego The Hobbit comes in and crushes its predecessors in terms of gameplay, the expansiveness of the world, the depth and richness of the map, the side quests, and a pretty spectacular attention to detail.  Traveler's Tales knocked it clear out of the park with this game.  This was everything that impressed me about Lego Lord of the Rings with vast improvements in the graphics department and the fluidity of the gameplay itself.
I have heard there will be DLC for The Battle of the Five Armies.  If this is so, I will absolutely be throwing money at it.
My normal cup of tea involves a gravity gun, hidden blades, lightsabers, s-foils and twin ion engines, and the the Sun On Yee gang.  Lego games are a far departure from these.  Just the same, this is an example of a game studio "getting it right" and really mastering their craft.  This is the culmination of several years' development of the engine and the concept, and I was completely blown away by the result of this fun romp through Middle Earth.

ACU for myself is very much hit and miss. There where points in the game which I really enjoyed, such as the story, and the assassination missions, but there are moments when I just look at it and cant help but feel the game was pushed out the door. You will not get more than 20 hours of enjoyment out of this game!
Graphics!
I played this game roughly 2 months after the release date, in this time I assume that ubisoft have patch most of the FPS issues due to the fact that throughout my 14 hour play session I didnt crash once, and came across around 8 major FPS drops, none of which I really cared about. You do however notice the render issues when synchronizing (I didnt really care though). One thing that truly annoyed me was the models, I really wish more effort was put into this as it gets extremely boring fighting the same 3 people over and over again (yes the police are slighly different, but there is very little conflict with them). Oh I will be fighting the elite swiss guard, to bad they look the exact same as ♥♥♥♥ing patriots........ Other than that the models for elise and Arno look great, along with any other main character.
Story.
Personally I enjoyed the story (I play AC games for the story), the end was very predictable as with all AC games. I didnt enjoy it enough to play through the main story a second time, in saying that AC2 was the only AC game I played twice. I will however go around and collect all the collectables just to expand on the story. I hate all the abstergo stuff, it takes away any immersion you might have had while playing, it was bearable with AC1 to AC3 when there was a sub story to it, but now its just ♥♥♥♥ing special with no point to it. Wish arno would talk less to himself makes him look like a nut job :3
On a side note if your going to set your story in France make the characters have French accents not English ones. There where a bunch of historical things that annoyed me to, but thats just because im a history nerd :P
Gameplay.
Combat is extremely similar to every other AC game, just counter..... I mean parry your way to victory. You dont need to upgrade your weapon once throughout the entire story, or armour for that matter. Parhour is basically the same, very little to improve, except now you can fall from great heights and not die, im sorry but it looks ♥♥♥♥ing stupid when you jump off a 3 story building and dont take any damage. To get the best stuff you have to grind like crazy which is boring in this game, I have a feeling this was done so people would buy the premium currency (terrible buisness practice). The assassination missions are quite enjoyable, you have to think, and create a plan (IKR thinking in a AC game), but it still holds your hand like crazy, and doesnt really allow anything to creative.To put it simply the gameplay is very average, with little to no improvement on previous titles.
Conclusion.
Personally ACU is very average, it just another AC game, nothing ground breaking nothing special just another AC game. I felt ripped off by the $50 price tag I payed for this game, and with the business practices Ubi has been making with the premium currency and the state this game was at launch I really doubt I will be buying another AC game after this one. If your new to the series you will most likely enjoy the game, if your a fan like myself who has played all the games you will just see the same old thing.

FX3 has the same fundamental flaws that FX2 had, but unfortunately, FX2 is no longer available in the store so your choice - insofar as which one to get - has been made for you, for better or for worse.  With that nonsense out of the way, let's talk about Zen's take on pinball.
While there are some genuinely fun tables to be found in the FX library, most of them are either middling or just downright awful.  The latter comprises most of the "classic" tables before Zen started their licensing crusade, and while I would say that's not really a big deal since the licensed tables are generally more entertaining, they also cost a pretty penny.  Worse yet, you can no longer buy individual tables and now have to settle for whole packs as Zen chases the Pinball Arcade model.
The short of it is that most tables suffer from the often-insane physics model that fuels the FX engine.  Tables are lifted higher than real ones and therefore the ball will come careening down at lightning speeds.  While this arguably makes for a more exciting game of pinball, it sometimes makes unreasonable demands of your reflexes.  This also makes any shoulder flippers (or whatever you call them) - which are featured on almost every licensed table - much harder to shoot on certain tables as sometimes the table design just doesn't mesh with the possible ball speeds.  Balls also tend to shoot off at weird angles and go the "wrong way" more often than I would like to see in a digital pinball game.  It also makes real-table tricks like flipper exchanges incredibly difficult to pull off (moreso than a real table, I mean).
All that said, there is quite a lot of fun to be found in FX once you get used to its high-octane underpinnings, but it is ultimately about which table you're playing.  Some tables are incredibly fun to play and make for great time sinks (a couple of the Star Wars ones are excellent, so if you are going to get a pack, I'd start there), but the new levelling and bonus system rubs me the wrong way.  While classic mode for each table allows you to play vanilla, the main meat of the game is a sort of challenge/reward system whereby completing certain objectives on a table unlocks bonuses you can equip for subsequent plays.  These mostly come in the form of point boosts when hitting certain targets, but some allow you to extend combo timeouts and stuff like that.  To me, this amounts fully to cheating, so it's weird that the new version of FX would be centered around it.  Maybe that's just me.
At any rate, the game ultimately remains the same FX we all know and sort of love.  FX3 brings "better" (more dynamic) lighting and texturing to your favorite tables (and some of your unfavorite ones, too), so if you were among the lucky folks who'd been playing FX2 before it got pulled, know that all of your tables port over for free (except South Park, WTF?!), so that's a really nice touch on what has obviously rubbed people the wrong way.  For me, I'm happy to switch to the new engine (running on a GTX1050 so no lag issues like some people are experiencing), but I doubt I'll be buying any table packs.
Ultimately, pinball is pinball and without buying a whole bevy of real tables, digital is your affordable way to play.  To this very day, Big Race USA from 1998 (find on gog) remains the ultimate digital pinball experience and if you're satisfied with just one table, I'd say go get that over anything else.  If you need more table variety, however, I'd recommend Season 1 of Pinball Arcade - you get real licensed tables (Medieval Madness!!!) and while the physics engine is also wonky over there (it actually got worse from the stand-alone console (Wii/360) release, imo), the ball speeds are more to your expectations and the tables are generally far better designed despite some of their ages.  However, on pure challenge and fresh ideas alone, FX3 provides a veritable salad bar full of good stuff and some of that stuff that makes you wonder just who on earth eats that crap?
While the sensibilities of Midway and Bally &c. remain elusive to the Zen table designers, they are the only ones providing fresh and new
content in a world that has largely forgotten about the real thing.  If you can stand the generally-faster speed of the game and the hit-and-miss nature of the tables that are available, and if you can spare the time and the cash to explore a table pack, there's no doubt you'll find something that speaks to you.  If you already own FX2, however, save your HDD space, stay there, enjoy what you have - you probably didn't want those other tables anyway.

Let's not kid ourselves, guys: The progression in this game basically stops after completing the first system and then just repeats itself until the end of the game. The first sword you built that was capable of dealing with Tier 1 enemies is going to have an almost identical version of it in the next crafting tier, as is every other piece of equipment. The enemies being randomized sounds cool and is as far as the sprite-mixing goes, but it really just results in a bunch of nice looking enemies with boring and mixed up attack patterns and pretty much guarantees that the planets in the next system aren't any more difficult outside of a fairly dull stat scaling. This randomness makes the game's progression dull and samey and creates most of the issues that make the game boring to play. Unlike Terraria, there aren't any dangerous and well planned out locations to explore that are tied to the game's progression; If you're lucky, you'll manage to get 6 hours out of it before seeing all the unique content. If you're luckier still, you won't have stuck around after that 6 hours trying in vain to find the cool, limitless content that the developers promised but never delivered on.
Here's to hoping that they fix it. They certainly could, and the game does have potential, but at this point it looks incredibly unlikely.

It's more XCOM, of course. You know what it isn't, though? It isn't as difficult as some people say.
XCOM 1 was a great game with a fantastic atmosphere but way too often the best way you could approach every fight was by slowly crawling through the map, taking overwatch (reaction) shots. This actually does get old after a while and XCOM 2 (much like Invisible Inc, which is also great and you should ALSO play) doesn't have time for that♥♥♥♥♥♥ You will almost always be racing against some time limit. Stressful? Kind of. But by pushing you out of the turtling mindset you start playing like a crazed madman and suddenly discover how much more fun the game can be.
Some tips for your consideration:
- Do you often make mistakes/get unlucky and feel tempted to load a previous save? This sounds crazy, but consider playing Ironman, even if its in Veteran difficulty instead of Commander. I'd wager most people can finish the campaign in that difficulty on their first try, but you'll likely experience -some- tragic loss, which makes victory even sweater.
- Don't worry about soldier upgrades too much! Every class has some great use and most builts work fine, plus you can actually retrain a soldier anyway. Don't be afraid to experiment (I was pleasantly surprised with the gunslinger sharpshooter).
- At some point in the campaign map you'll face an ominous countdown. No, you aren't about to lose the game, you'll be able to push it back. Fight on!

Though similar to twin stick shooters such as Geometry Wars, it's the execution that makes this game different. First off you have no shooting style weapon, instead you have a set of particles strapped to your ship. By using momentum to spin or flick the particles, you use them to destroy the asteroids and enemies that come your way. It's a simple concept in premise, but the game itself is challenging. Between the different enemy types, asteroids that break apart as you hit them, and the ever changing arena, there are lots of ways to fail. Multiple unlockable ships vary the game, where each ship has different abilities and different particles. Also different game modes offer different styles of play. The simple graphics feel like the game was made in the 80's, with a obviously modern physics engine. The music is very synth and gives a great energy to the game. This is a great pick up and play game when you just have some time to kill, but offers enough depth to keep coming back again and again.

I've played over 30 hours of this game, and I have to say it's been a tough 30 hours that I could've spent playing something else. I basically payed 60 bucks for a group of very nice screenshots. I'll be straight, this game is horrible. The things you hear about Ubisoft and AC: Unity are very very true. Honestly, every good thing about AC: Unity is partly a bad thing.
All in all, I suggest you cross Assassin's Creed Unity off your list for potential purchases.
(One more thing-- I have a pretty good PC. Don't think getting yourself something better helps the lag. You'll still have to deal with bugs.)

Is it worth 60$? Not in its current state, no. I'd recommend picking it up on a sale, which is exactly what I did. Was it worth 40$? I'd say yes.
Before purchasing I contacted a few people and the consensus was that it is indeed more stable than it was on release, two months ago.
Admittedly Ubisoft has garnered some good will from me. There have been a few misses. AC Liberation wasn't good. Watch Dogs was underwhelming, and AC3 was a bit of a difficulty spike for the franchise.
Consider the game right before Unity. Black Flag was absolutely wonderful and I recommend it to everyone (Seriously, go play it if you haven't already. Show Ubisoft that we can reward their quality work).
There is the framerate issue which I do find annoying on ocassion. I'd be fine for a while but then all of the sudden the game will stutter and suddenly I'm looking straight into the sky, or completely turned around. During chases, this issue has caused me to start running back into groups of guards I was fleeing from.
But the game seems to be judged primarily on the amount of glitches it has. Yes, it was a very messy release. Yes, it did prove that people need to stop preordering.
However. Is the game fun? Yes, yes it is.
I have 22 hours on it so far, so allow me to set aside the PR misshaps and various glitches and let me tell you about the game itself:
You play as a faceless, nameless gamer. The Assassin order hacks your feed and recruits you into the Brotherhood. I'm not fond of this framing device honestly, because I myself am not really one capable of saving the world. And how we can save the world while playing a game is beyond me, but whatever.
They place you in the memories of Arno whom is essentially Ezio 2.0, which some of you may recall kind of outstayed his welcome when stretched across three games. Arno seems to quickly become a loyal Assassin which is a bit uninteresting when compared to the more colorful Kenway to the last game.
But the game is fairly solid. The combat is a little more balanced this time around. Counter-attacking no longer oneshots enemies but opens them up for a flurry of your own attacks. No longer are we legion-clearing badasses. If you let them, enemies will swarm and murder your Arno regardless of gear. Bullets, also more realistically, will kill you in two hits. If you don't pay attention to your surroundings, the game will punish you for it.
And that is awesome.
Gear has taken a more RPG-like vibe. In previous games, gear only served to add to your health. This time, there are various statistics like detection speed, health, and bonus ammunition pools for your gun and bombs. Each peace has a focus between health bonuses, stealth and ranged and you're free to choose which line you focus on. (I personally go for stealth stuff).
It's interesting but I'm not sure if it's a better system. It all ties back to the fact that enemies will continue to hurt if you let them, as we can't really one-shot people in open combat any longer. That said, once you get a 5-star sword you can mow through enemies - As long as you pay attention!
Multiplayer. It has various levels of function. Most of the time I've tried it, nobody has a mic. The one time I connected with someone, we actually had to connect through steam and I replied to his speech via Uplay (I don't have a mic). This was very clunky because Uplay wouldn't let me make a call without some kind of input device. Or something. I don't know.
The rest of the time, each multiplayer match turns into this madhouse of combat. Without coordination, without any way to talk to these people ingame via text, stealth is thrown out the window. Within seconds of being given control of our characters, inevitably I see my screen blink red and combat has begun with my teammates.
So the promotional videos of all those coordinated attacks? Doesn't happen.
Good idea in theory but I don't believe it's working as intended.
Am I forgetting something? Oh yes. The microtransaction function.
22 hours and I've barely looked at it twice. Complain all you want but it's actually very, very easy to ignore. I still don't even know how to "get" more "Helix" points if I wanted to.
Ultimately, nothing so far has been completely game breaking, which is an improvement from release.
Allow me to sum up with some added notes:
PROS
-Combat is given some more complexity. No longer a powerhouse by Act 2 of the game. Can't one-shot counter. Enemies seem to be aware of this and will take advantage. Forces a player to pay attention (And I love this).
-Gear is varied and fun to mix, match, and experiment with.
-Multiplayer is doable, but with some problems.
-Boss fights are more interesting than punching a fat man to death.
CONS
-Glitches still present, just depends on your level of patience.
-Framerate drops is an issue for absolutely everyone and probably isn't our computers. It's probably on Ubi's end.
-Map is a bit of a spam of icons.
-Multiplayer is doable, but lack of coordination turns every single mission into pure combat and nothing else.
MIXED
-Blue chests can only be opened with some cell phone App. I do not have this capability.
-Microtransactions are easily ignored.
-Arno is fairly forgettable as a protagonist. There are side characters I care more about than him. (Elise, for example).
-Areas have difficulty gates. Normally in this series (And other games), I'd prioritize exploring and nabbing all those towers to open up my map. This got me killed a few times as a fledgling assassin when 5-star enemies started to one-shot me with their spears. I'm not sure how I feel about this, other than "Mixed", thus this section.
Worth 60$? Nah. Worth a sale? Sure!
Beyond the messy launch and bad business practices from Ubisoft, this isn't that bad an installment to this franchise. It just depends on your threshold of patience and how easy you can ignore a few of the problems.

Gameplay, storyline, music and art are the four cornerstones of video games, and Bastion gets all of them right. You'll form a bond with the Narrator almost immediately as he narrates your actions as you progress.
You'll have a variety of unique weapons to choose from, discovered as the game progresses. Unlike many other games, the weapons don't simply get better, they get different. In fact, there's nothing wrong with sticking with your original weapon throughout the entire game, although you're limiting yourself by not trying the different fighting styles the other weapons encourage.
Bastion is a game that you'll remember for a long time, one of those unique experiences you'll fondly remember for years to come after you've mastered it. In a time where downloadable games often mean low prices and low quality, Bastion is a shining example of great things really can come in "small" packages.

Half-Life is one of the most influential games and many of us have played our fair share of it's modifications like the original Counter-Strike and many more. It surely is an important game and many refer to it as the best game ever made, but Half-Life does have it's flaws as well. I'll start off with the positive.
Most of the games at the time didn't have much depth in the story. Mainly, you simply had to run and shoot and the story felt irrelevant, but in Half-Life it was different. The story is quite the usual - an experiment goes wrong and it creates a portal to another planet which allows hostile aliens to go through. Eventhough it seems nothing much, you can always feel that there's more depth put into the story. The pacing is perfect and the world you are playing in is still interesting to look at. The level design is amazing and it does hold up today, even if some of the levels may feel a bit too long. All of the weapons are unique and have use for them. All of them are useful in certain situations. There's also a big variety on how to defeat your enemy.
The multi-player is still being played today and you'll be able to find servers, but I'd suggest looking up servers on internet, since there's a bigger choice. Multi-player is a fast-paced deathmatch which requires a lot of skill and patience. Concept is pretty simple, but actually getting good at it is hard. If there was a game that plays similliar, I would say Quake, but HL can be a bit slower at times. Maps are well designed and it's still a fun experience, but I'd suggest finishing the story first, because it's where the real beauty of the game is.
So, there aren't many things to say about Half-Life's flaws. One of the biggest issues is that the soldiers will most likely hit you most of the time, because they are not designed to miss their shots as much. You have to kill them as fast as possible, just so you won't catch as many bullets. On the other hand, other enemies don't do this. Also the levels drag on too much sometimes. Some of the levels feel too long and it might be a little irritating if you are playing the first time. The levels where you have to jump on platforms aren't something I'd like to play through either, but hey, maybe you enjoy that.
Overall, Half-Life still holds up today despite it's age and I can see why people, including me, still play it and it's mods today. If you can't decide whether you should pick Half-Life or Half-Life: Source, I'd say that you should definitely go for the original. The new gun models, textures etc. doesn't make the game feel balanced. It's like your stuck between an old and a new game. Also, Source version does not have as many mods, so go for the original.

During the game you will play many diffrent charackters, all of them motivated by a personal goal, some of them linked to other charackters. Only 30 seconds to grab my brother and get back to my ship or I will loose them both forever...
This sort of thing is priceless to me and it is this part of the game that I didn't quite expect grabing me like it did. Sure the scenario and the mechanics looked interesting to me at first, but not every game manages to motivate you like this one does. A refreshing title, reminding me a lot of FTL in the sense that both are able to conjure up meaningful stories and complexe gameplay out of seemingly simple mechanics and graphics. Definitly recommended for everyone who likes this sort of thing.

Heat Signature re-ignited my love for gaming. I played 7 hours the first day alone.
It truly encourages creative solutions. And not in the "you can either go in the secret vent, shoot, or backstab the Enemies":
If you don't use guns at enemies, here are some gameplay choices you can make:
1- Enemy infighting is a legitimate tactic.
2- Switch-teleporting between yourself and enemies so they get shot at.
3- Fooling enemies into opening locked doors by making a noise two rooms over then teleporting behind them.
4- Hijacking a bystander ship to destroy your target ship.
5- As an escape, destroying windows/rooms so that it sucks the room's contents into space.
6- Propelling yourself in space using a gun to re-enter a ship through an airlock or a broken room. (I legit managed to do this once in perma-death mode and my mind exploded)
And more.
Sometimes I would get stuck in a very difficult ship, until I devise a duck-tape solution which saves me in the nick of time. On my last successful game, that was the Visitor Teleporter, it's a gadget that lets you teleport anywhere for two seconds then you will go back to your original location, l only needed one charge to alert the guards into opening the last locked door allowing me to slip in, complete the objective, and smash out of a window.
Because of these moments, Heat Signature is really, really worth buying!

If you've never played Xcom, you can start here.
The devs recently added controller support, so this makes for as great a couch strategy game as the first one.
DLC has added a few interesting items to the game, but they're really mostly for fans. On balance, I'd skip the DLC, since you can get similar or better effects out of mods. The biggest addition is the super-alien bosses who pop up in missions and are extremely hard (or impossible) to kill. In practice, they feel more like a 'you're screwed' random element than something that enriches the game. The weird weapons they give you as part of that DLC are a nice early boost, but you can accomplish the same early boost with modded weapons or character classes, and you won't have to worry about the limitations they put on the weapons (like losing them forever if their soldier dies and you can't recover the body, only having one of each, and the fact that their special abilities usually only work once per mission).
The mod community is thriving here, and the ease of modding has really made for a rich set of options. Some people are expanding on the mechanics, maps, and variety of the base game, while others are adding your favorite characters and weapons from other franchises. There's nothing quite like playing through the campaign with the cast of Archer and Futurama. The Long War guys--who worked their asses off to mod Xcom 1 (which wasn't modder-friendly) and greatly expand on the game--have made several additions, here, including more classes, enemies, and weapons. You might as well just grab anything they do right from the get-go.
Xcom 2's biggest change from 1 is the addition of the stealth-phase to some missions, which gives you the option (and allows some soldier classes to maintain) to maneuver around the enemy once you spot them, before deciding to start fighting. This helps fix some of the ambiguity that made Xcom 1 weird to play, especially on higher difficulties and later missions.
This game is good without any mods, but the fact that so many people are making mods for it will mean it will stay fresh and fun for a long time.

Gameplay, storyline, music and art are the four cornerstones of video games, and Bastion gets all of them right. You'll form a bond with the Narrator almost immediately as he narrates your actions as you progress.
You'll have a variety of unique weapons to choose from, discovered as the game progresses. Unlike many other games, the weapons don't simply get better, they get different. In fact, there's nothing wrong with sticking with your original weapon throughout the entire game, although you're limiting yourself by not trying the different fighting styles the other weapons encourage.
Bastion is a game that you'll remember for a long time, one of those unique experiences you'll fondly remember for years to come after you've mastered it. In a time where downloadable games often mean low prices and low quality, Bastion is a shining example of great things really can come in "small" packages.

Half-Life is one of the most influential games and many of us have played our fair share of it's modifications like the original Counter-Strike and many more. It surely is an important game and many refer to it as the best game ever made, but Half-Life does have it's flaws as well. I'll start off with the positive.
Most of the games at the time didn't have much depth in the story. Mainly, you simply had to run and shoot and the story felt irrelevant, but in Half-Life it was different. The story is quite the usual - an experiment goes wrong and it creates a portal to another planet which allows hostile aliens to go through. Eventhough it seems nothing much, you can always feel that there's more depth put into the story. The pacing is perfect and the world you are playing in is still interesting to look at. The level design is amazing and it does hold up today, even if some of the levels may feel a bit too long. All of the weapons are unique and have use for them. All of them are useful in certain situations. There's also a big variety on how to defeat your enemy.
The multi-player is still being played today and you'll be able to find servers, but I'd suggest looking up servers on internet, since there's a bigger choice. Multi-player is a fast-paced deathmatch which requires a lot of skill and patience. Concept is pretty simple, but actually getting good at it is hard. If there was a game that plays similliar, I would say Quake, but HL can be a bit slower at times. Maps are well designed and it's still a fun experience, but I'd suggest finishing the story first, because it's where the real beauty of the game is.
So, there aren't many things to say about Half-Life's flaws. One of the biggest issues is that the soldiers will most likely hit you most of the time, because they are not designed to miss their shots as much. You have to kill them as fast as possible, just so you won't catch as many bullets. On the other hand, other enemies don't do this. Also the levels drag on too much sometimes. Some of the levels feel too long and it might be a little irritating if you are playing the first time. The levels where you have to jump on platforms aren't something I'd like to play through either, but hey, maybe you enjoy that.
Overall, Half-Life still holds up today despite it's age and I can see why people, including me, still play it and it's mods today. If you can't decide whether you should pick Half-Life or Half-Life: Source, I'd say that you should definitely go for the original. The new gun models, textures etc. doesn't make the game feel balanced. It's like your stuck between an old and a new game. Also, Source version does not have as many mods, so go for the original.
Highly recommended.
