I'm not a MOBA or arena fan at all.  Honestly I shy away from PvP in most games, but this one is quite a lot of fun to play.  You can play solo, co-op, or PvP in a capture or skirmish game mode.  Despite the lack of modes, the game hits a home run in my opinion as each of the 31 ships plays and feels different enough to keep me interested in learning them all.  The learning curve can be daunting at times, but once you figure things out like tactics for your ship and which plays off your team the best, things start to get interesting.  It is addictive and graphically beautiful, and the controls work well in maneuvering, shooting, and evading.
Most ships offer upgrades for their various systems and abilities, and these range from a point to point "blink" to cloaking to even commanding a detachment of fighters or bombers that follow your capitol ship and defend or attack based on your orders.  You can buff allies or debuff enemies, heal or recharge, or jump into an attack ship and wreck face.  Choice is yours and you are guarenteed to have fun as long as your team works together.  Losing isn't as much fun, but always take it as a learning experience as to what works and what doesn't.
Has it's issues and poor design choices but the overall feel of the game is just balances it out. Heavily recommended.

The more steam friends you have the better your pool of competitors. I strongly suggest finding an FX3 group on Steam and randomly adding friends - they're a good bunch of people.

This sort of furious gameplay is quite addictive and there are lots of rewards and achievements to earn. The table guides are very thorough which I find helpful because I've always had a problem identifying every single goal in a pinball game.
There's an amazing variety of tables to choose from.  I suggest watching YouTube videos for tables you're considering for purchase.  My goal is to purchase every table, since I have yet to play a table that wasn't entertaining in some way (some tables do entertain me more than others).
Having skimmed other reviews I expected FX3 to run poorly on my gimpy AMD but it runs fine.  I only play with 2 of 4 cores activated (long story):
Windows 10 Home 64-bit
AMD A12-9800 RADEON R7 ~3.8GHz
16 GB RAM

I bought this game a couple of years ago during a steam sale. Even when it was buggy as absolute hell, I loved it. Every update corrupted a save, but added so many more new optimizations and items that I couldn't care less.
Fast forward to now, the game is super polished, fun, and even the unstable version is fairly stable. I haven't lost a world in a long time, and the one I did lose was somehow saved by another update.
The devs for this game work EXTREMELY hard to pump out a good game whilst making their community happy. Early Access on Steam has been getting loads of crap due to some shoddy devs shafting users out of their money on empty promises, but the TerraTech team should be seen as the gold standard for Early Access Devs.
As for performance, you won't get far on the max settings before your computer begs to be mercy killed with a flaming axe, but the 2 graphics settings below Fantastic look just as great, and will spare your computer. The gameplay is based around an ever-growing tech you build from literally the remains of those who dared to face you. The first couple of hours are essentially the same, kill things, make your bot strong enough to take on the Liscense Boss, and so on, but after that gets out of the way, the world becomes yours to explore, die in, fly in, and dirty up to your hearts content.
Buy it.
Edit: Over a year later, the content updates only get better, and the game is looking better than ever. They've also been hard at work implementing storage solutions to help cut down on lag. I'd recommend this game twice over at this point in time.
Edit Edit: Items and features are being added even faster... Beta Branch for life

I don't usually write reviews, but I love this game. You know how sometimes you're just looking for a good, cheap game that you can sink your teeth into right away without having to think too much about it? A game that has an interesting new mechanic and is instantly addictive? This is that game. It takes about five seconds to learn the basics, and then it grabs you--that whole whip-the-mace-at-rocks-and-ships thing.
For those who don't know: Imagine chunks of space junk tethered (by bungie cords) to an agile spaceship. The trick is to, with a single thumbstick, use the ship's momentum and direction to fling those tethered chunks like a mace and pulverize asteroids and enemy ships. (Yes, there is a local, four-player muiltiplayer mode.) It's simply divine.
While it is inspired by arcade classics, it instantly sets itself apart. There's a whole lot of variety here for just a few bucks. This is that game you'll play as your warm-up for a marathon session of some bigger, grander game. Only...you'll probably look up after a few hours and realize that you spent all your time flinging the PARTICLE MACE.
WARNING: Like a lot of folks, I was disappointed about the lack of Steam Controller support. I'm glad I took the time to dig up my old Xbox 360 controller, but this omission is unfortunate.
Still, to quote Doug McKenzie: "...all in all, a good five dollars worth for me and my whole family."

The best terrible game I've ever played.
I've been a fan of Assassin's Creed since the first game, and I've purchased every game since.  I even preordered every game after AC2 - I loved the historical sandbox, I loved the gameplay, and the modern-day story was compelling.
And then there's Unity.
Between the almost completely-absent modern-day story, the unrelateable wooden protagonist, and the completely forgettable support characters (seriously, how did the Marquis de Sade become so boring) you'll find yourself wondering what the hell is going on.  The game takes places in a seriously important period of European history (the French Revolution and the beginning of Napoleon's rise to power) - so why is it that it is just so boring?
But most importantly, there's the bugs.  I have a fairly high-end rig, capable of playing this game at Ultra graphics settings across the board.  So why, then, did it take four patches to make my game play WORSE than it did at release?  Why does it periodically freeze for 5-20 seconds at a time?
The biggest bug affecting me is that after a certain point in the game (I'm not sure which), I lost the ability to obtain new weapons.  I could buy them, upgrade them, use them for a while - but if I changed weapons for ANY reason, any weapons I purchased after the bug took effect locked themselves again.  This required me to purchase those weapons, again, to use them.  If I obtained a weapon from a quest, that weapon became COMPLETELY UNUSABLE.  I cannot equip quest rewards at all.  Period.
Ubisoft has not announced that they are working on a fix, and no further patches have been announced, so it is likely that this bug will persist forever.  And because of this bug, I cannot complete all of the achievements in Dead Kings - meaning this is the first Assassin's Creed game I have ever purchased, that I have not been able to 100% complete, because of a game-breaking bug.
On to gameplay ...
There's a lot to do, while at the same time there's very little of anything INTERESTING to do.  Paris is beautiful and enormous.  But its size belies the complete lack of interaction between Arno and the city itself.  Sure, there's random events - kill these criminals, chase down this thief, throw money to the poor - but these are basically one-offs that take about 5 seconds to do, and have essentially no bearing on anything at all.  The Murder Mysteries are a good change of pace, and I enjoyed them quite a bit.  The Nostradamus Enigmas are also fun, if not frustratingly vague at times.  Almost every other side quest is the same - go to this place, kill this guy/fetch this item, run away.
The much-vaunted multiplayer is fun, if not monotonous.  It can be completed 100% by yourself, which is good because matchmaking is peer-to-peer and laggy, when you can connect at all.
The gameplay is fun, until you realize you can spam smoke bombs and kill everything easily.  After Brotherhood, you'd think that Ubisoft would figure out a way to make enemies respond to smoke bombs intelligently.  The game's AI is garbage, akin to Storm Troopers from Star Wars or an army of red-shirted ensigns from Star Trek.
TL;DR - it's a beautiful, enormous playground - one that's full of broken toys.  The toys that aren't broken are boring.

Half-Life is one of the most influential games and many of us have played our fair share of it's modifications like the original Counter-Strike and many more. It surely is an important game and many refer to it as the best game ever made, but Half-Life does have it's flaws as well. I'll start off with the positive.
Most of the games at the time didn't have much depth in the story. Mainly, you simply had to run and shoot and the story felt irrelevant, but in Half-Life it was different. The story is quite the usual - an experiment goes wrong and it creates a portal to another planet which allows hostile aliens to go through. Eventhough it seems nothing much, you can always feel that there's more depth put into the story. The pacing is perfect and the world you are playing in is still interesting to look at. The level design is amazing and it does hold up today, even if some of the levels may feel a bit too long. All of the weapons are unique and have use for them. All of them are useful in certain situations. There's also a big variety on how to defeat your enemy.
The multi-player is still being played today and you'll be able to find servers, but I'd suggest looking up servers on internet, since there's a bigger choice. Multi-player is a fast-paced deathmatch which requires a lot of skill and patience. Concept is pretty simple, but actually getting good at it is hard. If there was a game that plays similliar, I would say Quake, but HL can be a bit slower at times. Maps are well designed and it's still a fun experience, but I'd suggest finishing the story first, because it's where the real beauty of the game is.
So, there aren't many things to say about Half-Life's flaws. One of the biggest issues is that the soldiers will most likely hit you most of the time, because they are not designed to miss their shots as much. You have to kill them as fast as possible, just so you won't catch as many bullets. On the other hand, other enemies don't do this. Also the levels drag on too much sometimes. Some of the levels feel too long and it might be a little irritating if you are playing the first time. The levels where you have to jump on platforms aren't something I'd like to play through either, but hey, maybe you enjoy that.
Overall, Half-Life still holds up today despite it's age and I can see why people, including me, still play it and it's mods today. If you can't decide whether you should pick Half-Life or Half-Life: Source, I'd say that you should definitely go for the original. The new gun models, textures etc. doesn't make the game feel balanced. It's like your stuck between an old and a new game. Also, Source version does not have as many mods, so go for the original.

Deceptively simple, surprisingly difficult.
Does anyone remember agar.io, that blob-eat-blob multiplayer browser game that became viral somewhere around 2015 and not a lot of people play anymore? Well, Osmos has been there and done that 6 years earlier, except it's single-player, features several game modes instead of just one and is way more beautiful to look at. Nice ambient soundtrack too, if you're into that style of music.
The basic premise is really simple: You are a blob in an enclosed area with a bunch of other blobs. Absorb smaller blobs to become larger, avoid running into larger blobs or else they will absorb you. You win when you manage to become the largest blob in the area. Be frugal with your movements, however, because each thrust comes at the cost of a fraction of your mass. For those of you who remember high school physics, this is all about conservation of momentum. Think of jetpacks in space, except there's no distinction between you and jetpack propellant; you
your jetpack propellant.
Sounds rather easy, huh? Think again!
Hemisphere Games have tried really hard to sell this as a "relaxing" game, and I guess you technically
play it in a relaxed mood... if you're some sort of zen master who can handle one defeat after another with unwavering stoicism. A relaxing game this is not, folks; maybe the first few introductory levels are, but once things start to get serious, it becomes as tense and frustrating as any other hard game you've played. Fast reflexes and quick desicions will become increasingly more vital as you progress. I know it looks pretty casual (hell, it's even
as "Casual") but appearances (and tags) can be deceiving!
Osmos features several types of challenges to keep things interesting. For example, there are levels where all blobs are orbiting around the same mass and making it through requires that you brush up on your orbital mechanics; there are levels where blobs of anti-matter are added to the mix, which add a whole new dimension of danger and opportunity in the game (hint: you can push them away from you and towards a bigger blob in order to shrink it and be able to absorb it later); and there are levels where you are not the only sentient blob in the area, and you'll have to outrun, outsmart and outperform other blobs in order to survive.
Whether or not you'll enjoy Osmos, I cannot say with any certainty. Speaking for myself, I've taken several long breaks from this game but I keep coming back just to beat one more level, so I guess you can say I have a love-hate relationship with it. If you enjoy games that are challenging, go ahead and give this one a shot - it might keep you busy for a long time. ;)

Hacknet is a game about hacking. The game opens with the Hacknet OS booting up with a message from a man named Bit, who says that if you see the message, he’s already dead. He leads you on a quest to start hacking, getting the attention of one hacker group, then a second, all to avenge his death and prevent the distribution of a hacking program.
The story itself is kind of mediocre, but it is serviceable; at its core, it is a story of corporate greed, as well as a revenge story, though by the end of it, it is pretty clear that the whole thing isn’t really as sinister as it appeared at first.
The real core of the story is the hacking – you log into various computers, break through their security mechanisms, and then are lead onto other computers. Spicing things up are timers, various mechanisms you have to bypass, and the various files and passwords and IPs you have to find to lead you on the next leg of your hunt.
Sadly, the game is plagued with poor design decisions. There are various points at which it isn’t clear what you’re supposed to be doing, and you’re left confused, only to find out you needed to hit the “reply” button on an email after breaking into a server to move on – despite the fact that the email wasn’t clear about that. At other times, you have to send them messages, and while this is usually clear (sending them an IP or password), on occasion it is not and ends up being rather frustrating.
Worse (and even more frustrating) are some outright bugs – situations where the game simply does not function like it is supposed to. Beyond there being some lost forevers in the game which are less than obvious, there’s additionally the fact that sometimes the game simply bugs out and won’t let you progress or do various things. You get a “mission incomplete” message when trying to proceed, and there’s simply no clear way around the issue. Indeed, two of the achievements require you to do things which simply don’t function half the time or more, judging by the many frustrated players who had to restart the game time and again to try and get them to work.
The UI itself is a bit obtuse at times as well; several of the hacking programs you use require additional bits of typing to execute, despite the fact that in many cases it literally never matters – it is always exactly the same number you have to punch in. And while it is neat seeing it use actual hackerish commands, ultimately there’s a lot of little pieces which just feel annoying to have to do time and again.
The only real good thing about the game is its aesthetics; which do work pretty well for what it is.
In the end, you aren’t really rewarded for your frustration. The core idea is cute enough, but in the end the game ends up being rather repetitive, and there just isn’t enough variation in the core gameplay. A mediocre story combined with sometimes unclear gating mechanics to make the game advance is just not a winning recipe for a game.
The game seems like a neat idea at first, but it just ends up being more frustrating than enjoyable to play. It isn’t worth your time or your money.

A visually appealing grinde through space combat. Do I recommend it? No. Am I going to keep playing it? Probably, for a little longer.
So Fractured Space is a MOBA like League of Legends or DOTA. For the uninitiated, that means that you work with a small team of other players to capture objectives to earn more minerals which are used to upgrade your ship, which helps you defeat the other team. At the end of the match (which can be anywhere from 10-30 minutes long) you get credits and experience; more for winning. With those credits you can then buy new ships to play as in your future games. You can also use credits to buy new crew and upgrades for your ships.
What you should not expect is any story, character development or interaction. There is no campaign, and no real reason given why we are fighting each other. There is no real end goal, you just play to have some fun.
That said, Fractured Space really teases the other ships available to you. You start out with 3 ships that you own. They don't rotate weekly to let you try the others in battle before buying them. Ships cost roughly 100k, 300k and 600k credits. You earn roughly 10-20k credits per match. Every 2, 4, and 6 PvP matches you play per day will give you some random bonuses. But you're looking at anywhere from 5-10 matches if you want to buy even one of the lower end ships. But, you're also using 40-50k credits per minor upgrade on your ship, and roughly another 125k credits to purchase new crew. Then if you want to 'make' the crew that you've purchased you need DNA (another currency) which you can get through those random drops I mentioned earlier, or you can convert credits into DNA. Or course, you can pay to play but you're either rich or an idiot if that's your plan. Like who wants to pay $10-20 for a skin that only changes the color of your ship and makes your a bigger target?
Besides that, the real problem with this game, and most MOBAs for that matter is that the amount of fun you're going to have is based heavily on the team you get matched up with. If you get stuck with a disorganized, rookie, or juvenile team there isn't much that you're going to be able to do on your own to fix it.

This is not a game I hate. However, much like that TIS-100 game, I was left completely clueless as to how to proceed, though nowhere near as quickly, thanks to an actual tutorial and being able to play a little bit of the game before getting stuck, as well as a help menu listing commands. As a child in the 80s, I spent a fair amount of time using DOS to find files, modify them, etc., and in college, I used UNIX for a semester, scoring an A. There isn't a day that goes by where I don't use a PC, unless something really weird happens, like a blackout. Therefore, I was more than a little surprised when I got so hopelessly dumbfounded by this game. Granted, this game is far classier than TIS-100.
This game actually has music, and it's quite nice, while TIS-100 had none that I found. TIS-100's manual was difficult to understand and quite daunting, while Hacknet is far more user friendly, and really appears to have a story and more purpose to it. That said, the game left me confused and stuck when I came upon a firewall. The game never covered how to deal with firewalls in the tutorial. I tried running a program I had just downloaded from another computer in-game, which let me access one port, but I couldn't access any of the other ports. I used every page of help to look up commands that could help me, and analyzing the firewall brought up a wall of letters and numbers that didn't seem to do anything, and selecting to "solve" the firewall didn't do anything, either. I checked every computer I had access to and found nothing else that could help me.
If I'm stuck this early in, checking a walkthrough or asking for help online will likely lead to me continuing my confused wandering without learning anything within the game itself. I should not have to rely on the Internet to learn how to play a game for fun...
I'm disappointed in the game, but only because I liked what I saw when the game was presenting things in a way that cleverly educates the player, but then it throws you a problem early-game that no amount of searching within the game itself appears to turn up a solution. The point where it figuratively drops you in the deep end of the digital pool with a cyber-anchor tied to your feet is where I lose any ability to appreciate the game beyond that point.
It's also entirely possible I lack the mental faculties to interact with this digital gaming experience in a fulfilling manner. If that's the case, then so be it, but I must represent the "mentally deficient" population and state that I do not recommend this game as a result.

I am seriously digging this game. I got it from the Dec 2016 monthly Humble Bundle. It makes me feel more like a real hacker than real hacking probably would. :P
Seriously though, you get the thrill of breaking into secure computers and digging around finding secrets and reading files -- but without, you know, actually needing to spend years learning how to do it and without actually committing felonies.
It's exciting joining secret hacking groups and being assigned missions. There's a sense of panic when another hacker starts counter-hacking you and messing with your system.
The main issue with this game is also its biggest strength -- and that is that it really is a computer terminal simulator. There are some fancy graphics to make hacking seem a bit more exciting, but ultimately it really is just entering commands in a command prompt and anwering emails. This is what makes it "feel" like real hacking, which is what makes it fun and special to me. But I'm sure some people will be turned off by the fact that the game is mostly reading and typing -- basically a hacking-themed, text-based adventure. Like Zork -- except instead of "enter room" "take scroll" it's "connect 205.34.1.220" "scp scroll.txt". Which, when you think about it, is kinda the same thing. :P
I'm recommending this because I'm having a blast, but just make sure it's the sort of thing you would enjoy before buying it.

Gameplay:
Singleplayer: 8/10
Great concept, slowly increasing difficulty with different tiers, an incredible amount of crafting/cooking recepies, many different items, not only weapons, but also things like instruments (which you really are able to play) or . Each race has its own style of buildings, different advantages.
You are free to decide, if your ship is your base or if you settle on a planet. You can visit villages on planets peacefully or conquer everything - your choice. There is a quest line, but it's not very dominating - you are free to follow it (most of this questline consists of "build *item to summon boss fight*" "fight *boss*" and "go to the next sector"). There are no smaller quest you can get from in villages - but I never missed it. (Yet it could be an improvement).
Also every planet looks different, has different monsters and biomes. After a while, you are able to see the repetitive elements, but you can't expect infinite creativity and 12 billion unique planets.
Multiplayer: 6/10
Coop mode adds even more fun to this game - it's way more entertaning to explore planets and dungeons together and fight boss monsters.
There are many more possible features - and as far as I experienced some problems with servers (a unique game ID per player is still missing), so public games are a risk (griefers can't really be banned), but if you only play with people you know, it's awesome.
Yet the beta state is still visible, but (if you try unstable updates, you see more) there are many improvements. Soon there will be the big announced winter update - maybe there are finally some big (and mostly bug-free) changes.
AI: 4/10
Mostly randomized monsters, people from the different starter races and even a few other races. The monsters are not very smart, not even the bosses, and seem not very intelligent. Same goes for the villagers (or dungeon guards) - you can't have a real RPG-like conversation or get quests because most of them tell you one randomised phrase (of a pool of phrases). There are at least merchants or aggressive bandits every now and then.
Story: 6/10
Every race has an individual backstory which you can explore by finding books in the villages. You start with some information about your own race, the rest is up to you.
Graphics: 9/10
Perfectly fitting cute pixel art design.
Sound: 8/10:
Weapons (bows, guns, swords,...) sound great, monster sounds are fitting, but not extremely unusual.
Music: 9/10:
Perfect background for playing, not too distractive, the transitions are smooth. The only problem is the fight music - sometimes it begins way too late and the fight is already over.
Replay Value: 7/10
You start on a different planet each time and have many things to explore. Yet, you see more repetitive elements and there are no stable changes since many months. Maybe the winter update will change this.
=> 57/90
If you are patient enough to wait for stable updates (or willingly enough to test bugs), this can be a great game for you and you will get lots of fun in an (almost literally) addictive universe.
If not, you should wait until the game leaves the beta state. You will miss lots of development, but also some disappointment when there are (maybe) months without stable changes.
Definitely recommend, but maybe wait for the final release.

When I first got this game, I played it for a few hours, then stopped. I thought nothing of stopping, I thought that it was because I found other games to play, which happens, even with games that are my favorite.

While there seems to be a large amount of customization, it's very lacking, and you find yourself wanting the next part of the game. You want to find that big civilization that will have more to do, but it isn't there. You want the high tech armor and special equipment, the better building blocks and house parts, but they are so far in the distance, with so much tedium in the way, you wonder "Why bother?".
The dungeons and mine shafts have little to nil, enemies go down easily with even the most rudimentary of weaponry, and important items (like food) only drop with VERY specific weapons, thus disallowing you from using the weapons you want. And when I say enemies go down easily, I am not kidding. Let's use an example. On one of the planets I found a laboratory. In that lab were what APPEARED to be heavily armed soldiers and scientists. They said some generic "leave the area" phrases, before I started to kill them. I was wearing no armor, and was carrying a cheap weapon I had found randomly in a chest. I only had to heal myself once.
In short, this game just isn't worth it. You want a nice, open world 2d building game with lots of options? Go with Terraria, the game that this game blatantly ripped off.

I'm going to say this straight, I bought this game day one. I bought it for $60, and bought the season pass for $30. I was excited, plain and simple. I had previously played Fallout 3 on the Xbox and loved it, dabbled in New vegas, and tried the mobile spin off, so I knew what to expect from Fallout. So I can unironically say that I enjoyed the game, issues and all. Does it run well on my computer, no. Was there a pleathora of glitches, yes. Were there gaping holes in the narriative that break immersion (I can't be the only one who heard Travis on Diamond City radio druing one of the flashbacks), absolutely. But all this aside, Fallout 4 is still a decent game.
While the base Fallout 4 game, microtransactions and all are fine, the core experience of being a Fallout game in comparison to the strong pedigree left by the others leaves this entry something to be desired. A classic case of being a good game, but not standing up to the rest of the series.
The gameplay is a cross between RPG and FPS, something that I never knew I needed in my life until I played Fallout 3 for the first time. But this game starts to lean harder on the FPS side, to mixed results. While I do enjoy the smoother combat and the enjoyable weapon and armor upgrade system, the lack of any meaningful dialogue that can effect throughout the rest of the game is apparent. I suppose I understood the complaints a little more by finally finishing New Vegas recently to only now come back to this game and realize what Falllout 4 was missing. But is the game horrible and a slandering of the franchise, no.
Like many stumbling points in other series preceeding Fallout itself, Fallout 4 is simply a misstep from the quality the previous games had. Mario took a dip with games like Sunshine, but came back with masterpieces like Galaxy.

"This is a game about making the best out of a bad situation."
Or as the quote goes. I'm paraphrasing. But it pretty much sets the stage for the entire game. Things will go wrong. Characters will die. On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero. I'm sure you can beat this game without anyone dying. But that's unlikely.
And that's why I love this game. Ever since Fire Emblem instilled the fear of losing a party member forever, no matter how hard it was, I always completed those missions perfect, even if I had to restart and lose hours of play. Even now I save scum on XCom just to make sure my beloved soldiers don't parish. When I set a rule for myself that I'll let soldiers die when it happens, I rarely actually follow through. I think this is a sentiment many can understand.
Then there's Darkest Dungeon. Sometimes, you're unprepared. You cannot simply power through. You cannot outwit. You simply cannot win. You aren't set up for it. Party wipes. You lose progress. You lose items. You waste gold. It feels absolutely awful. And it's not a feeling I get often in games. When I feel awful, it's easy to blame something else, save scum and restart. It's easy to see where I went wrong and correct myself. This game might not even show me in every great detail what I did wrong. It just simply wipes me and leaves me to my own thoughts. Eventually, I may learn, and may delve deeper into better strategies and team combinations. But it's an earned thing.
It's the feeling I got when I defeated a boss in Dark Souls the first time on repeat. Over and over again, I get smashed, I get back up, and I take the good with the heaping amount of bad and I get better. I make the best out of a bad situation.
To anyone reading this who may see other people claim this game is unfair, I'd like to make something very clear. Nothing can be further from the truth. Video games are almost always unfair, and almost always unfair in your favor. Whether by calculation tricks that make you stronger when you're more vulnerable, or simply making the last bullet in a clip 3 times as powerful. This is a game that has nothing like this. This game is probably one of the only fair games I've ever played. The RNG isn't stacked in your favor, it's simply absolute luck. The enemies aren't overpowered, they're just equal to you. The best thing I can tell someone is that whatever you think "making the best out of a bad situation" looks like, it's much worse than you think, and hopefully, when you do make the best of that bad situation, you get that wonderful feeling of reward. "We survived" has never felt so close to "We won".

Fallout 4 was a decent game, I had fun with it, but it lost the soul that Fallout originally had. The game trades away a lot of the RPG mechanics in exchange for main character vocal dialogue, enhanced gunplay, a streamlined experience and tacked on, borderline broken, base building system. Well, fortunately the majority of the issues I had with Fallout 4 were fixed with the incredible modding community this game has. the Nexus has plenty of amazing content that changes this game from an average, streamlined fallout experience, into everything you could have ever wanted this game to be. Tons and tons of weapon, armor, companion, NPC, quest and location mods, retextures, overhauls, you name it. If it weren't for the Nexus, I'd have stopped playing this game at about the 20 hour mark.
Now, on to the part where I explain why I cannot recommend this game in its current state.
SHort answer? Greed, shoddy business practices and unsafe software practices.
Long answer? the DLC we recieved for this game was mediocre at best, with a few exceptions (Far harbour and Nuka world to an extent) People who paid for the Season pass were shafted with addons to the already broken base building system (mods can fix the base building, but still) and two actually decent DLC out of the list, maybe a third if you like building your own robots (Automatron is overall disappointing and underwhelming in content)
The DLC in Fallout 4 is pretty sub-par coming from the company who gave us such gems as "Shivering Isles" and "Operation Anchorage" but I was able to look past it, since I was smart enough to not pay for anything in advance via the season pass (pre-purchasing games taught me that lesson already)
Thats when we get to the real root of the issue and why Fallout 4 currently has a Overwhelmingly negative review
The Creation Club.
The creation club is bethesdas way of saying one or all of these things:
1. "We didn't learn our lesson from the paid mods debacle on Steam"
2. "We think gamers are stupid and will buy whatever bulls*** we shove in their faces as long as its got our name on it"
3. "We don't care about the quality of our products anymore, we just want more money."
4. "We're fine with shooting ourselves in the foot, as long as we can make a quick buck out of it."
to summarize, Bethesda is trying to get players to pay real money for what boils down to dumbed down versions of mods you can already get for free on the Nexus. You'd think that for what they expect you to pay for these mods they'd give you some sort of mini-quest or some enemy to fight to obtain the weapon or armor you paid for, right? Nope, just go to a random area and find it in a box (literally thats all it is). There's also a distinct lack of features for these weapons and armor. Looking at the comparable alternatives from the nexus (which you can get for free btw) these bethesda paid mods have not even half the amount of content that these free nexus mods give you, and Bethesda expects you to pay HOW MUCH???
Yeah, no,♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
As if that matter wasn't bad enough, to add salt into the gaping wound.... Bethesda arbitrarily downloads all of the available paid mods onto your hard drive, regardless of if you paid for any of them or were like me and said "Screw that I'm not touching the creation club" They're on your hard drive anyway behind a paywall, all of them. You don't get to use them or anything, they're just there taking up space serving no other purpose whatsoever. THis is essentially bloatware, and anyone who knows anything about computers knows how potentially dangerous this tactic is, of just having anything uploaded into the creation club arbitrarily download onto your hard drive without your consent. This presents a huge and completely unacceptable security risk to the playerbase.
Therefor, unless Bethesda wises up and realises what an inherently god awful idea this creation club is, I cannot and will not recommend Fallout 4.

Well, meh.
It's clear that it's not Fallout 3. Whatever you say, sometimes, it just doesn't matter. That, to me, is a rush-job that shouldn't have been rushed. Every interaction, and i mean, EVERY interaction, should have had its' own possible outcome that changes the rest of the game. Not a difference in dialogue, then the same events occur. That just makes reloading and trying different dialogues boring and stupid, knowing the same things will happen anyway.
Max building limits is dumb. I know it's a new feature, and they wanted the game to still run smooth, but even when i wasn't hitting the build limit, i would be crashing and freezing. Another rush job, that, since it was new, should not have been rushed.
It's the same engine. It should have been built on a new engine so that it all could have felt new and fresh, but, like before, A rush job that shouldn't have been rushed.
I like it in games where you go to do a single dialogue, like "joking" or "taunting", and different things are said. In Fallout 4, telling dogmeat to "do tricks" just results in him standing up on his Hind legs, EVERY TIME. Again, A rush job that shouldn't have been rushed. That feature was just a waste of data, if people are only going to use it a couple times over it being new, and never using it again because it's just repetitive.
If the engine was new, the DLC's would have been more interesting to play. I owned them on Xbone, not PC. But the engine isn't new. So, it's just the same graphics with the same bland apocalypse colors with different architecture, grinding process and same rewards.
So, all in all, a great new leap into the abyss at first, but soon you realize that it's just a rush-jobbed game built as quick as possible, to sell as fast as possible on hype. It was great day 1. But it took some time for people to find out just that. That,it was all a rush-job.
Mods are the only thing holding this game together right now. But, because too many of them can crash more then just your loads (yes, some aren't tested and can break YOUR WHOLE CLIENT) it's more like, holding this game together by loose strings.
When you poke through all the broken mods and install all the working ones that change the way you knew the vanilla game, it does turn it into a cool game. A bunch of sexy women hangin around, Desert Eagle Handguns, M9 Handguns, Campfire setups, different voice effects for some companions, reskins... It all can make it last just a little while longer.
But, eventually, you're just aimlessly walking around because you are the strongest thing over God Mode and whatnot. The cheats render the cool fair-play mods kinda unintersting.
Then, you just stop playing. Just like that. Interest? Gonza.
I would recommend for those moments in the beginning of the whole journey. Resource management, logistics and the reward for being organized is a rewarding feeling. And, unlike me, IF you like playing it to the very end the fair way, then go ahead! it's a very good game then.

Just finished my first playtrough of the game as a warrior. I ended the game with a nice set of armor with enough of all resistances to facetank most magic, fire and even physical attacks. A lot of poise too, so I could continue swinging my greatsword/greataxe/polesword without getting interrupted by most attacks. Didn't have a shield equipped and rarely utilized the gauntlet. My setup might've made the game quite easy, but I still enjoyed it and intend to replay the game using a different, perhaps more challenging setup.
As a whole, I liked the game. The aesthetic worked for me, and the gameplay felt good. Areas were nice and interconnected and exploring them was rather fun. Lots of stuff to collect and equip while using runes to make them suit your specific needs (Flawless Magic Rune + Flawless Fire Rune in armor helped a lot, as did Higher Luck Runes in my weapons). Ran well enough on the lowest settings at 1920x1200 using an i3-3220, 8 GB of ram and an R9 270 and still looked decent. Familiar controls for someone coming from a souls game using a controller.
Of course I also have some gripes. Too many of the enemies felt tedious to fight and the bosses were quite weak both in design and actual strenght. The game also had a tendency to freeze (UI would still update, but the game itself was frozen) after alt tabbing and opening a browser or using the browser in the Steam overlay. Lost some progress due to that, but nothing major. Audio from the scrolls sometimes got cut mid sentence and the enemies still making noise quite a while after dying sometimes confused me. Screenshake occasionally behaved weirdly (way too much of it on some occasions it seemed). I also hated how Harkyn removed his helmet during the cutscenes, he wasn't that interesting of a character anyways and keeping the helmet on would've been much more aesthetically pleasing.
It did feel like a Souls game in some aspects, but it also heavily reminded me of Darksiders 1. It definitely exceeded my expectations and I think it deserves a higher rating than it currently has on steam (both recent and all reviews are mixed). The GOTY version can be currently had for only 5,99 € (-80%), which in my opinion is an absolute bargain!
Edit: Well, I did play trough the game again (mere hours after first finishing it!) in a sort of speedrun fashion. This time I picked the cleric character and solely focused on faith. Some of the bosses were a bit harder using mainly magic (and a special faith weapon you can get pretty early in the game, shame that there are so few faith-based weapons), but mostly the game was a breeze thanks to the cleric having access to a shield spell that reflects damage, ups your resistances and also heals you! At one point I was mixing heavy and medium armors, but ended the game with a medium armor set, which seemed to provide enough protection, although I wasn't able to poise-tank as well. After this run I'd say the magic in this game is better left to a supportive role and instead focusing on weapons that scale with strenght or agility (which I have yet to try, although I didn't really enjoy playing with the Monk Staff early on).
The fact that the player's actions are reflected in the end cinematic was a nice touch.

If you've never played Xcom, you can start here.
The devs recently added controller support, so this makes for as great a couch strategy game as the first one.
DLC has added a few interesting items to the game, but they're really mostly for fans. On balance, I'd skip the DLC, since you can get similar or better effects out of mods. The biggest addition is the super-alien bosses who pop up in missions and are extremely hard (or impossible) to kill. In practice, they feel more like a 'you're screwed' random element than something that enriches the game. The weird weapons they give you as part of that DLC are a nice early boost, but you can accomplish the same early boost with modded weapons or character classes, and you won't have to worry about the limitations they put on the weapons (like losing them forever if their soldier dies and you can't recover the body, only having one of each, and the fact that their special abilities usually only work once per mission).
The mod community is thriving here, and the ease of modding has really made for a rich set of options. Some people are expanding on the mechanics, maps, and variety of the base game, while others are adding your favorite characters and weapons from other franchises. There's nothing quite like playing through the campaign with the cast of Archer and Futurama. The Long War guys--who worked their asses off to mod Xcom 1 (which wasn't modder-friendly) and greatly expand on the game--have made several additions, here, including more classes, enemies, and weapons. You might as well just grab anything they do right from the get-go.
Xcom 2's biggest change from 1 is the addition of the stealth-phase to some missions, which gives you the option (and allows some soldier classes to maintain) to maneuver around the enemy once you spot them, before deciding to start fighting. This helps fix some of the ambiguity that made Xcom 1 weird to play, especially on higher difficulties and later missions.
This game is good without any mods, but the fact that so many people are making mods for it will mean it will stay fresh and fun for a long time.

Actually Osmos reminds me of old 8-bit games. Mechanically I'd say it's a cross between 'Asteroids', in that you propel yourself across a screen full of obstacles of varying sizes, and your movement is determined by your momentum and thrust; and 'Pacman', in that you consume objects around you, and under the right conditions that includes your enemies; and to tie that all together you lose mass by using it for propulsion and gain it by consuming. Aesthetically Osmos is something else again in that it appears to be a naturalistic universe of single-celled organisms.
About the only problem I have is not with the game itself but with one of the tags. I partly purchased the game because it was tagged as 'relaxing', and whilst it can be a very meditative and patient game at times, a lot of the time you have to act quite quickly because in no time at all the cells in the environment could absorb each other to the point that they're too large for you to consume and you are in danger of being consumed yourself. I certainly felt the pressure at times.
Personally this game isn't really for me and I would prefer playing 'Asteroids' so that I could just fly and maneuver amongst the asteroids without having to worry about time limits or anything actively trying to kill me (besides the odd stupid flying saucer >_>) but this is still a good game and if it sounds like your thing then by all means give it a go! ^_^

Hello everyone, sit down, and let me tell you a story of glitchy Assassins and even more glitchy Templars.
Since the beginning of time, the PC master race has been criticizing consoles for holding PC back from its true gaming potential. Well, here you go PC elitists, a game that can push even the strongest PCs past their breaking points.
Let me start off by saying that Assassin’s Creed Unity is not a perfect game, far from it. It has been plagued by bugs from the beginning, and, lesbehonest, Ubisoft hasn’t done a very stellar job in fixing them.
But all of those minor bugs and glitches are nothing compared to the problem that has rustled the jimmies of many an Assassin, including myself. Performance. ACU is a BEAST to run. Just take a glance at the system requirements and you can tell that it takes some serious GPU power to run this monster. But who gives a crap about system requirements? Let’s talk about benchmarks.
If you’re looking to run ACU at 4K resolutions, don’t. Just… don’t. Not even with dual gtx 970s, with averages of 22 FPS, and an absolutley dreadful a minimum of 5. With 4K out of the question, it’s time to start lowering settings. The same can be said for QHD, with the 970s in SLI almost, but not quite, reaching the coveted 30 FPS minimum. My conclusion? 99.99% of people looking to play ACU will need to do so at 1080p. *gasp*
If you want to read more benchmarks, here’s a good site I found:
Even at 1080p, if you’re looking to run this game on ultra, it will still require some serious GPU heat. I bought ACU thinking that my r9 270 would be able to run it just fine. (I based this assumption upon the fact that I was able to max out Black Flag without any problems whatsoever) I was very, very wrong. I had to lower everything as much as possible and apply the maximum stable overclock I could to even make it playable. So, as any gamer would, I began shopping around for a new video card. Anyways, two-day Amazon Prime shipping and 400 dollars later, I found myself with an r9 290x. Now I can play the game with a minor overclock at high and ultra settings with very few performance problems.
My current rig:
AMD FX-6350
R9 290X
2 x 4GB RAM
6 x 500GB HDD in a raid 0
Windows 8.1
Here’s the truth: ACU requires more much GPU power than any other game at the moment. However, it is also one of the best looking, if not THE best looking game of all time. As long as you don’t pay attention to character’s hair (it’s under a hood most of the time anyways) the graphics of this game will blow you away GUARANTEED.  The reality is, you will need to invest in a quality GPU in order to get to enjoy it’s full potential.
I’m not saying that it isn’t an enjoyable game at low settings, however. It does have its fair share of bugs and glitches, but the core concept of Assassin’s Creed is still enjoyable as hell. The new fighting mechanics are fantastic, previous ACU titles have simply required you to mash mouse 1 when surrounded by 30 enemies and they’d all be dead in a minute. In ACU, even with legendary items and mad skillz, you will die if surrounded by 6 or more enemies, bringing the game back to its stealthy roots. The enjoyment of jumping off buildings and commiting general badassery is still there, now it just requires skill.
In conclusion, ACU is a gorgeous game, although it will take a serious GPU to run it. The game is still enjoyable as hell and is a solid addition to the Assassin’s Creed franchise.

This game was a great idea with very poor followthrough. You learn two or three tricks to bypass security, have to collect the appropriate scripts to defeat each of the half dozen interfaces, and then boom, you're a legendary hacker. It's all text-based with a super basic linuxy command line interface, which I'm sure makes some people feel like they're all h4xx0r... I'm probably being unnecissarily harsh, but I really was shocked at how repetative this game was.
It seemed like there were alot of mechanics that they planned, but never got around to implementing. All that hype about deleting the logs after you access a computer... maybe I missed something, but I couldn't see that it did anything. And the Trap and Forkbombs... were those actually useful somehow? Oh, and it was very easy to make game-breaking mistakes, like deleting a file you were supposed to steal. Alot of silent ways to ruin the game and be unable to recover... hope you didn't save after one of those.
There are alot of fun points. Getting a new script and seeing the new computers you can crack is exciting. The story in the beginning and end of the game are interesting. Also the little easter-eggs of emails and chat snippets were pretty funny. And I'm sure the game does look cool if you let people see you playing it.
My background in embedded sofware may have colored my opinion a bit, but the game felt awfully thin for $10. And from a gameplay perspective, it was awfully rough. Serious programmers should look at TIS-100 instead, although beware: Zacktronics games are not for the faint-hearted, and may feel a little too much like work to the professional programmer.

I'll start off by saying I don't usually write reviews as my account will reflect.  Allow that to bare some weight on this, my one of few reviews.  I write it because I want Fractured Space to be successful, I feel it deserves to be.  You should too.
8 out of 10.  Thats what I would honestly rate Fractured Space at this point.  It has a lot of replayability in the 30+ starships available and each one of them that I have tried (about 15 or so) feels and plays differently than the last.  That is one of the strengths and source of appeal to me; the fact that there doesn't feel to be cookie cutter mechanics and easy-way-outs in the ship design.  Some ships are better at specific roles than others, but each ship has an effective part to play.
The MOBA style gameplay found on 1 of the 2 game modes (with a unique twist in the "Gamma Sector") works for it pretty well, it adds sufficient depth to strategy while the maps themself make positioning and team work a very important factor.  With that said, winning a match against an otherwise stacked team is very possible if they let their guard down.  A single ship has the potential of pulling off a victory if timing and a little luck is on its side.  I think this adds to the games sense of hope when situations seem dire.
This game has been in development since 2014. I got involved in late 2015 as a founder after watching its development and seeing sufficient progress towards solid gameplay.  Since I have got involved, the progress has evolved into something that is fun to play and very much invokes the "easy to learn, hard to master" feeling with a pretty high skill-cap on some roles in specific ships, especially with a team that works together.
Be all that as it may, it is a work in progress and it isn't perfect.  But it is my opinion that its got a lot of potential to be that game everybody has heard of, a lot have played, and many have enjoyed.  It's going to take exposure and player-base to do that and that is why I reccomend that you download and play Fractured Space.  It's free-to-play and there is no pay-to-win.

This game has been one tumultuous ride. I would be remiss to not acknowledge at least that. For that past year,
has been one of my frequently visited sites, for updates, for excitment, for community and for drama, for laughs and fun and what unfortunately most sours the memory, resigned dissapointment.
If you’re reading this and deciding whether or not to purchase, I suggest just this.
If you do all this, you should be in good shape to decide for yourself just what you want from this game. If you want my total opinion, read on.
Despite all the calamity, I had fun with starbound. It's a decent game. I recommend it as another terraria if you're bored of terraria but want terraria still, and you're willing to deal with early access poppycock.
I understand that as an early access, you are not likely to get what you desire, you are not even likely to get what you are promised.
I understand now, because it actually bloody happened. I was young, you know how we are at my age, silly and shiny and dumb. I was enticed by the ritz, the stars, the bounds. I wanted it all. They promised it all.
Many months have passed now, and I’ve still to see what I was promised. And at this point, even if the moment I finish this review I should find a finished Starbound gift basket, filled with apples and condoms and cornish pixies, I would still feel tricked. And I payed good money for that feeling, and damn to you all if I’m not entitled to that emotion considering the circumstances
And I deserved to be tricked. I bought the game before it was finished. I was told things wouldn’t be as they planned it. I knew it was a risk. But like Napoleon, I advanced into Russia with nothing more than high hopes. It doesn’t make me a victim, nor does it make the developers criminals. I think what it does make us is a bunch of retreating French and homeless Russians.
There have been many asservations, many blind white knights and attention mongering whistleblowers. Hell, I’m probably both of those personas. What I think now though, is that this game is one hell of a gamble to buy as is. If you can’t wait for the full title, and you’re a gambling man or woman, I say capitalism ho! Otherwise, come on back once the smoke’s settled.

I definitely recommend...but I find that it goes from being really cool getting to each new area and finding new weapons and stuff to being a total chore. If you're used to FPS games, or games in general, by today's standards, this will take a lot of getting used to. Objectives are not clearly marked and you will often find yourself wandering around trying to figure exactly where you should be going next...which is fine if you're ok with a little exploration. Aiming is weird...it's sort of automatic, but still feels weird compared to newer games. There's no base controller support and aiming/moving with keyboard and mouse just doesn't quite feel right. The character often feels like he's walking on ice. Walking along small ledges and stuff or trying to make some jumps is a total nightmare. You literally cannot see your character's feet so it's also impossible to tell exactly where you are when trying to get around laser sensor things or the radioactive waste until you set off a mine, activate a turret, or start taking damage from the radiation.
Basically, it's a pretty good game, and, as far as I can tell, really set the bar for FPS type games going forward from it, but it also feels really dated and can be really aggravating.

You start off the game like any freemium FPS game online. There's a server tab, a "shop" tab, settings, etc. It's what you expect. Gamewise, it's a blocky Counter-Strike that lets you lay blocks like Jagex's "Ace of Spades". The first game I entered was a blatant rip of Aztec (with a few edits) from CS:GO and all you have to do is have your team reach 500 frags. Now I don't know if I just suck or there are hackers because I noticed many people doing consistent headshots with AKs, snipers, and tons of grenades being thrown. Next game I joined was a "zombie" mode map. Whatever they did with the view range, I do not know - I could not see 10 feet ahead as there was a very black fog. The whole map was covered in camping spots with one entrance where you can wall yourself in (ala block building) until the end of the round.
As far as buying guns goes, I don't understand it. I saw the tab and every gun was blocked by 1) level requirements and 2) a $ currency. I am not sure if it's real life money or ingame. I would be surprised if it was real life as some of those guns are over $1 each. That's way too expensive.
The game just didn't capture my attention or give me enough fun for me to keep on playing so I uninstalled the game. It's still in early access so there's time for it to get better and I hope it does. I like the overall game but still it has a long way to go to be good. If you've played a lego game before you know what to expect somewhat but this was quite a unique experience. The open world really makes you feel like you're going on an adventure with Bilbo and the dwarfs in an almost Skyrim esc. manner. The game is very easy and simple to get through but if you want to 100% the game it is surprisingly difficult. Well dang.
I finally had some free time and thought I might play a bit more Fallout 4, and found it had a 2 GB patch.  Well, I was certainly happy.  I wondered at what all new things they could have added with all that, and I was so pleased that it was all free.  Then I found the truth.  They added the ability for me to give them more money whist chewing up my bandwidth.
Is Creation Club paid mods?  Well, yes, as far as I can tell.  They're mods that Bethesda gives a once over for stability and compatibility.  That once over is nice, but they already dealt with a firestorm over paid mods before and adding a bit of quality control doesn't really help much, and isn't really needed.   I feel like it's paid mods, and the differences they are touting are semantic...except there is one notable difference and I'll get back to that....
Is Creation Club DLC content?  Well, not really.  It's handled seperately from DLCs, requiring a different portal to access.  So, it's more or less just like a collection of curated mods.  Besides, if they WERE DLCs, I'd already have paid for them via the Season Pass...ah...now we're on to something.
So...they're not mods because the idea of paid mods is loathed by the public and already brought them a firestorm of hate.  And they're not DLCs because then they wouldn't make more money off of people who bought the Season Pass.  So, they're a "new thing".  I don't know what's going on in the heads of the Bethesda execs.  I hope it's just a disconnect and unintentional, but it sure looks like an attempt to squeeze money out of pockets while providing virtually nothing.
Net effect, I have to wait for a huge patch that does nothing other than anger me.
As for the game itself, it's pretty good.  It's a bit overpriced, but on sale as a bundle, it's good.  I really liked the main story aside from HUGE plot holes, but as soon as I finished the main story arc I was left wondering what reason I have for doing anything else.  And I can't help but wonder why I walk into a settlement and am instantly accepted as their god king able to change and do anything I like, give orders, destroy homes, force people into any job, etc.  It's neat as a game mechanic, but story-wise, I'm perplexed.
In short (too late):  Should you buy this?  Maybe.  If you've always had fun with Bethesda RPGs and it's a bundle that's on sale, it might be fun.  I wish I could get my money back as a protest for what they're doing now.  But I DID finish the game and had some fun.  Next game, though, they'll have to do a lot to convince me to give it a chance.

If you continue doing this, you will have a veritable MOUNTAIN  of bodies! Well, I mean, they will all be flat, since the game is 2D, but they will be stacked upon one another, and eventually, if you keep doing this, the game crashes. I’m not sure the right way to describe how I feel about XCOM 2. “Guilty pleasure” is probably it, but I’m hung up on the “pleasure” part. This isn’t something I know is stupid that I have fun with, it’s more of something that satisfies some animal desire within me, but leaves me cognitively unsatisfied. This isn’t what I want from games, it doesn’t get me excited, but I also can’t dismiss how deeply hooked it had me. That appeal to your lizard brain can be much more powerful than any affection you have that involves any kind of rationality.
I think its worth recognizing that distinction, because rationality is something we can all share in, but our individual animal hungers cannot quite be communicated through the logic of language. You can’t share that, because there’s nothing there to learn; it’s just a crapshoot if anyone else shares your same dark desires. It’s fine to have them, I just wish people would recognize that within themselves and help draw that line for others better.
We’re all just animals pretending at rationality. It makes things so much easier if we’re at least self aware about that.

As a self-described huge fan of Assassin's Creed, I got very excited about Unity. I watched all the trailers and game play demos, read all the marketing materials produced by Ubisoft, discussed Unity with other gamers, and got my hopes up really high. I pre-ordered and played the game within hours of launch. I agree with what everyone else is saying: what a massive disappointment! Unity just doesn't meet my expectations. I thought it would look better, perform better, and I certainly didn't expect there to be so many bugs on launch. Ubisoft owe us for that.
This is the fourth time I've got very excited about an Ubisoft game over the year leading up to its launch and found that it wasn't what I imagined. When Ubisoft put so much money into marketing to drum up anticipation for their games, and then release those games scaled back and poorly tested, people are still going to go ahead and buy them at launch. It's like Ubisoft just isn't learning a lesson.
Assassin's Creed has been basically exactly the same over the past six or seven games or however many its been (except for little changes here and there; incidentally most of which I didn't like). This sets our expectations about how the game is going to play. When Ubisoft make changes to the game they are betraying those expectations. Even though most the changes they made to Unity were to specifically address previously criticisms, its very hard to learn those new systems after training myself to play Assassin's Creed a certain way, and they're nowhere near perfect.
I'm also majorly disappointed in the performance of the game. At first I thought my computer (that is only three years old!) need upgrading. But then I read that other people, some who apparently have SLI, say it's a bad console port, so now I'm just angry. I don't know much about graphics or game engines aside from what the game developers talk about, but it doesn't look to me like the quality improvements in Unity should justify new expensive hardware that I'd rather not buy. It seems more likely the programmers have done a bad job because they're lazy and apathetic to PC users. I was really looking forward to Next Gen and how it would revolutionise gaming, but now it's here and hasn't changed much of anything except it doesn't work on my PC that was playing the previous Gen perfectly.
I'm still going to go ahead and complete as much of the game as I can though, but that doesn't mean I'm going to enjoy it.
I've been looking at the concept art and leaked screenshots and reading about the next game, Assassin's Creed Victory which will apparently be set in Victorian London. This time it's being developed by Ubisoft Quebec, instead of Ubisoft Montreal who developed Unity, which gives raises my hopes that this time the game will be finished and work properly on launch day. After all our negative feedback about Ubisoft routinely raising our expectations and then letting us down, maybe lessons will be learned.

Jake Solomon's team have found their place as the successors to Side Meier's legacy of brilliant tactical world building.
There are still some technical gripes which persist from the previous instalment, usually around aliens glitching through/seeing through things they shouldn't be able to see through. It can make ironman campaigns unplayable at times, but this is really only applicable to corner cases in hardcore campaigns for only a few players (it's devastating none the less). My issues with this game are purely technical - things that the team have been working well to iron out, and it comes against the backdrop of a spectacularly designed modular map system, a clever new high-octane twist on the original formula and a surprisingly deep set of characters.
Hail the resistance!
