Well, I guess I can call myself lucky I didn't buy any of the tables that didn't make it into FX3. To be fair, I think getting these same licenses yet again for new a version, is an incredible feet. I don't think people appreciate or know how tough it can be to acquire these licenses AND give the products away for free. Then again, I probably wouldn't be intersted, if I was offered to buy the same tables again, which I have in FX2 already. They did remove Pinball FX2 from the store, but if you have it already, you can still download and play FX2 and all the tables you bought. Works for me, leaderboards work too.
EDIT: there's a bug right now, which might cause some tables to display as locked, which you actually own. A restart should fix it.
The engine received a significant overhaul. Lots of dynamic lights, The ball now actually receives lighting and shadowing from the environmant and so does everything else on the table that's moving. Looks veeeeery different and realistic now. Very noticeable on the Ghost Rider table with all the fires and stuff.
Some of you might want to turn the graphics down though. As cool as it looks, all these moving shadows and lighting effects might make the table look... cluttered. It's not a problem for me, but I know people who prefer visual clarity over the cool-factor. Rest assured, turning gfx down helps with that.
There's also a little campaign and challenges now. If you were ever afraid of pinball because of how "competitive" and frustrating it can get sometimes, now's your chance to actually learn the tricks pros use. Some of these tricks even I didn't know about e.g.: the nudge pass - in other pinball games I never had to use it, or it was not the correct way to pass the ball onto the other flipper.
These come with the challenges. E.g. Earn as much score as you can in 5 minutes, or with only a single ball, or try and survive for as long as you can. It's not much different in playstyle, but it adds a little bit to the game.
You can join them and even dynamically create them at the push of a button. They come in different game modes as well.
Leaderboards are unified across platforms (if I understood this correctly). As Steam users we can play against both PS4 and XBOne players.
with cool effects, cool tables, interesting missions. It's not a massive step from Pinball FX2, but it's still a little bit of evolution. They are trying to create a AAA pinball game and evolve the genre a bit by mixing in new gamemodes and special abilities (wizard powers) and stuff.
There's a setting in-game which toggles the licensed muscic on/off for e.g. Star Wars tables. It is off by default, so everyone else might want to turn this on to get the nostalgic music from the movies.
There's now passives and abilities which you can level up through playing, which give you an edge in playing. Some examples are:
Now I wouldn't really have a problem with these, if it wasn't for the fact that you have toacquire and level them up separately for each table. This is massively stupid. If I didn't play the same amount on some table as someone else, I won't get a bonus for e.g landing a skillshot, because he has the same ability on a higher level. Thankfully, you can turn all this garbage off by playing in
mode. It has its own leaderboards as well. I wouldn't be bothered if you couldn't level them up and scale the bonus they give, but you can.
I can definitively see why they were added. They are trying to give new players a little bit of edge, make it easier for them. Attract a wider audience. Pinball might have been big about 20 years ago, but times change.
Don't get me wrong, this is actually some of the most advanced ball physics I've seen in a pinball game. It even simulates ball spin and everything. However, on some tables it is set up to be... too floaty? (looking at you, Avengers table - by far the worst table in this game) It's not a problem with the physics engine, it's a problem with how the table is set up. It's like they have different gravity or different incline set for every table, or the ramps' incline is weird. Luckily, you can change mechanics in the table itself (flipper stiffness, power, springs etc.) using cabinet support, but if you play that way, your table won't be eligible for the leaderboards (which is a good thing, people could cheat with this). You need to request a Cabinet key from the devs (they pass it no problem). I'm guessing they use the key to identify how some people fix various issues with some tables.
There's leagues now. You can do "matchups", where you challenge someone else's score in a league (rank tier). If you beat the score, you get league points. If you are in the TOP 20% by the end of the season (week), you progress into the next tier. It's a bit weird. You get to choose between 3 opponents (easy, medium, hard). You get more points for beating harder ones. As you can imagine it will get a bit grindy - you will have to keep beating the opponents (usually around the same score) to gather the league points to stay in the top 20%. You can stay up there by simply beating the easy opponent over and over again and grinding those league points. However, I imagine there will come a tier, where the median score will be so high, that you won't even be able to beat the easy opponent. If you do have the skill to beat it, it will still be a grind though, because a lot of other people will be able to beat it as well and you gotta stay in the top 20% of the tier.
To top it off, Wizard powers are enabled in this league mode. It's pretty BS. As far as I'm concerned, classic table leaderboards are the way to go for now, if you want to get competitive. Leagues are a good start though. Hopefully they will change it later, to eliminate the grind aspect of it.

Great game. I read the reviews before playing the game and noticed that there were a lot of comparisons with Dark Souls due to the fighting mechanics and the level design which in turn, the majority of them labeled the game as a "Dark Souls rip-off" which makes me believe that many people do not understand the concept of iteration, but allow me to elaborate on this:
0 - Why 0? Well, I need you to know that I have fresh runs through new game+ for both Dark Souls 1 and 2 (Trying to get hooked on 3, but the faster pace is kind of killing it for me) hence, my points will be presented with that information out there.
1 - It is important to note, this game is an RPG, with story and characters, as all other RPGs before Dark Souls. There is an interesting plot with different endings and quite impressive turns here and there.
2 - In terms of mechanics, it takes the base Dark Souls mechanics and iterates on them, adapting the mechanics to mesh with the world presented, hence:
- When rolling, the animation is slower than Dark Souls, but so are the attacks of both you and the enemies, which makes sense to the rules of this universe. You truly feel like Arthas from a Warcraft 3 cinematic, carrying a huge sword with a huge armor set that takes an immeasurable amount of strength to be able to use both, translating into slow but incredibly satisfying swings.
- Talking about swings, every attack, just like the souls series, takes stamina, but the improvement here comes from one small brilliant idea, attack at the right time, don’t spam light and heavy attacks, combine swings at the end of each to have a more effective attack (reduce stamina consumption) and dependent of the weapon, a faster attack (even faster than DS).
- Shields now have a sort of tank position on tower shields which allows you to suck up damage during enemy combos, most useful on boss fights where there will be attack windows after each 2 to 3 hit combos they perform.
- Secret walls are no longer "hit it with a sword" for DS 1 or "Press A" for DS 2; in Lords of the Fallen, sprint with the shield up towards a breakable wall and bash the s*** out of it, it feels great.
- If you plan to go for heavy builds, you will soak damage as a heavy build, basically havel x3.
- Use of runes to improve your armor and weapons instead of "leveling" them, very simple and straight forward.
- Bosses are kind of easy, especially for DS players, but there are challenges (conditions) to complete for special loot.
3 - Level Design in this game is very maze like that can only be achieved with a small map as this game has, with many shortcuts that are quite impressively connected (connect the end game area with the starting area is brilliant)

Why I Hate My Generation
Our generation is the iPod generation, the smart phone generation, the Facebook generation, one that speaks through technology. That is how our voices are heard today: through texts, messages and the internet.
Studies report that  75 percent of teens own cell phones and 87 percent use the Internet. When faced with a room containing strangers, many of us don't even look up from our phones long enough to see the people around us let alone communicate with them.
I am a seventeen year old boy and was unfortunately born into the most dysfunctional generation ever. I sometimes just want to break down and cry. Back in the old days the younger generation actually acted like they wanted to make a difference out in the world. Today what do we have? A bunch of brain-dead teenagers who only care about making differences to their MySpace, Facebook, instagram and twitter pages. When was the last time someone our age held a war protest? When was the last time someone our age organized a clean-up day? When was the last time you had a conversation with someone your age who didn't have a smartphone in their hands?
According to a survey by CTIA: The Wireless Association, 57 percent of teens believe their cell phones have enhanced their lives. The cell phone technology has improved our generation's ability to maintain contact with guardians and family members. However, mostly, I believe technology has let the words of my generation become seemingly meaningless.
It’s all about I me mine and nothing about us we them and yours. Teamwork is dead. No one reads books anymore. No one listens to anything that can be justified as music. Killing and violence fills our media. No one smiles and no one laughs unless it is making fun of another person. It’s just sad. I really wonder where our future is headed. It scares me. I guess there are a few out there who do care about things. There are a few out there who want to make a difference. To those of you like that, may the FORCE BE WITH YOU!!! What this world needs now is love, peace and break from technology.
At the end of the day, we’re all equal, we’re all human and we all deserve equal rights in life. Don’t you think we all deserve happiness? Let’s make that happen. Let’s stop the overuse of social media, let’s stop the degradation of our generation , let’s stop the ever increasing expansion of life destroying technology . Let’s keep our best memories within our bodies rather than sharing them on social media, as the thing you will want most “At the moment of death, when the seed atom in the heart is ruptured, which contains all the experience of the past life in a panoramic picture, the spirit leaves its physical body, taking with it the finer bodies.”

Cold, cruel, dark... how do I describe this game? No, this story? I just hope for one thing, and that is that no one has to ever experience the kind of emotional suffering involved for people in real life with real life decisions like choosing between lives to save or between your own welfare and your children's. No human should have to be forced to make those kinds of decisions. But that is exactly what this game forces you to do. Sure, you can stay silent during conversations, but you'll lose all respect.
I played all five episodes, one each day, and I've just finished the last one. And I feel like I really don't want to play another Season. This game is not hard, it's brutal. I think about things like the apocalypse a lot, like what a world full of the living dead will be like, or a world where only you are alive. This game had me questioning, as I still do, the worth and value of human existence in times of prolonged suffering. Is there hope? Real hope? Or is that simply a mental mechanism to keep going and find a reason, however illogical, to keep living. What is the purpose of life, what are we living for? To raise up children, to just enjoy ourselves, to keep moving towards the inevitability of death? However unreal and farcical you may think a zombie apocalypse is, it acts as a compelling context for life questions.
And not just that. It serves to seek out how we might react in a certain situation. Everyone has different personalities, and I'm sure you'd agree with me when I suggest that in this modern society, it's difficult to really know someone within a few days of meeting them. But when the world goes to absolute sh*t, there is no need for false impressions anymore. You can see people pretty square on. I had my brain in agony deciding, at times, what to say. I found myself trying to protect Clementine as much as I could. I realised her deepest desire was to see her parents, and I kept that in mind. I tried to save whoever I could. I saw people as humans, I saw them beneath their often capricious personalities (Kenny, Larry, Lilly - heh, even me sometimes). I tried to keep a level head all the time, and I guess that goes with my own underlying scepticism of life, held together by vocally agreeing with people who are good by their actions. I defined good as judging people not by what I or even our group needs, but by what the person being judged actually says they need. I could cite several situations, but I note this is a review, for those yet to buy the game.
I'm glad, now looking at the game as a whole, that TellTale didn't do a 'Last of Us'. Not only is this game true to the comic book foundations of TWD, but it meant that more resources can go into making a fantastic decision-based story that feels so real and just draws you into it. Yes, you are not Lee Everett, you don't have his history, his family, or even his words (talking about the choices of dialogue you get), but it's close enough to identifying what kind of a person YOU are, because each dialogue option takes a certain philosophy and moral direction. Mostly, I was consistent, but sometimes, such as with Larry, I blew. I could talk a lot about what this game teaches you, or has taught me, but I must restrain myself, knowing not to let a review become an essay in philosophical thought.
I haven't played anything like this before. It's different, and it's intelligent, and it will make you, yes, force you, to really think about what you say and do.

-Is the game better than Dark Souls? Not as a Souls-like, definitely not.
-Is the game pleasant? It is.
-Biggest Pro: A more accessible, simple Dark Souls, but still challenging.
-Biggest Con: Gets easy after a while, when you have all the OP loot.
-How much is that game worth? In my opinion, I would say that at 20-25$ (CAD) or less, you got yourself a good deal.
-How long is the story? It took me around 15 hours to complete the story, and that was me rushing it, add New Game+(+) to that and it's a bit longer assuming you do finish both NG+'s.
I didn't know what to think when installing the game, my initial thought was ''that game is going to be terrible, a cheap♥♥♥♥♥ dumbed down Dark Souls.''
I was wrong.
LORE & SETTING:
Lords Of The Fallen sings the tale of Harkyn, your typical anti-hero, life-sentenced prisonner that got free'd as a desperate move kinda deal. Badass, fearless, man of a few words, kinda reminds you of God of War's Kratos due to his complete lack of care for imminent danger. Followed by the man who free'd you himself, Kaslo, your typical Hagrid-looking mage, huge beard, long hair, staff, y'know, the usual. So long story short, the peace and silence of the kingdom gets completely broken by the arriving of Rhogars, demon-like creatures sent by a god named Adyr. Harkyn's mission? kill every single one of them, and find a way to stop Adyr from spawning his minions into our realm. During the adventure, Harkyn will have to face stronger foes: the ''Lords'', stronger Rhogars chosen by Adyr himself to stop you. I'll leave it at that.
QUALITY:
Not much to say, there's nothing really ground breaking about the game's quality, but I have to admit that after a while, while walking through the gigantic bridge on the Rhogar realm, I actually took the time to stop and look around for a second and was greeted with a beautfiul scenery. The graphics are good looking, nothing more to say apart from some beautiful particle effects. The sound is ok, the music is very good, but that's to be expected from a Souls-like. The atmosphere is very good but again, to be expected from a Souls-like. The voice acting is...  ''ok'' at best. Very straightforward, but it does the job, it's not cringeworthy at all, so that's good. The game feels a bit more polished than at least the first Dark Souls, it doesn't feel clunky in my opinion, the only annoyingly clunky thing in the game is the lock-in system... it's a bit frustrating, sometimes, to say the least, the camera too, well the camera's good, but there are some specific times like in the Worshipper boss fight when you enter the shrines, where you just can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ some other very specific bits like that occur.
OVERALL DIFFICULTY:
This game isn't as hard as Dark Souls like previously mentionned, (I know what you may be thinking right now, yes the Dark Souls comparisons are annoying, but there's a reason for them and I expect most people to understand very clearly why they're there.) but it IS challenging, there are even alot of moments when the game not only doesn't feel very challenging... But extremely unfair, I mean Dark Souls never really FEELS unfair, just hard, LOTF may sometimes leave you scratching your head out of frustration and confusion. A very common complaint by veteran Souls player are the shielded ennemies,  if you hit an ennemy while he's got his shield up, you'll get staggered and he's most likely going to react accordingly and punish you, so you just roll... Right...? Well no, because by the time the roll animation is done, 90% of the time shielded ennemies will have turned around with their shields back up. So this leaves you with two options: either get a buckler and parry them, or find a weapon that hits so goddamn hard that it overwhelms their poise, and staggers them so you can follow up with a finishing blow. So yeah, doesn't leave much room. Some ennemies might also have some frustrating mechanics, like the ''banshee'' ghosts, who have a spell which reflects damage, and if you hit too hard you'll just end up one shotting yourself. The bosses are ok, they never feel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I'd even be ready to say that while the fights themselves are fun, the bosses feel lackluster, barely intimidating at some point. The game becomes a breeze after a while and that is a problem. I mean you'll still maybe sometimes die, and all that, but not hard enough.
PROS:
+A more simple, accessible, toned-down Dark Souls but still feels at least a bit challenging.
+Combat and movement generally feels fluid, for the most part.
+Nice story, especially at the end, worth getting invested into.
+Nice atmosphere.
+Pleasant graphics.
+At least 15 hours of playtime, more if you add NG+/NG++
+The game just, feels fun, at least it did for me.
CONS:
-Gets way too easy after a while if you build correctly, at some point most bosses and bigger mobs don't really feel THAT threatening, you just end up rushing them and beating them up very fast.
-Some extremely frustrating balance issues and mechanics (like the previously mentionned Shielded ennemies)
-Characters feel very stereotypical and a bit bland.
-Optimization/stability issues. The game MAY crash once or twice in a full playtrough, sometimes at very unfortunate moment.
-Some camera issues there and there.
I give this game a 8/10. Very fun and a good start if you wanna get into Souls-like games without the headache of getting smashed by Dark Souls general roster of ennemies/bosses.

There are many reasons to both like and dislike Fallout 4. However, the reason I'm leaving this negative review is very simple: the microtransactions.
I would just roll my eyes and ignore the microtransaction Creation Club/Paid Mods, but Bethesda made that very difficult as they decided to pre-load the files on my PC. I don't want any of the paid mods nor will I be buying any of them. But apparently, I have to host them on my PC's hard drive regardless.
And then there's the fact that the paid mods crash your game if you use regular mods (like the vast majority of us do). They mess up your game by the simple fact of the matter that they force your mods to load in alphabetical order. As anyone who's ever modded their game knows - that can cause none of them to work at best and an immediate crash to desktop (CTD) at worst.
Plus there's the fact that with every update and if you use the Fallout 4 Script Extender (F4SE), you need to wait for the F4SE team to release a new version of F4SE in order to play your game - meaning you will likely not be able to play your game for several days. For normal update content, this would be perfectly fine and acceptable. However, if it's just to add new files to the Creation Club (and preload them on everyone's systems), that's not acceptable. At all.
Pete Hines said on Twitter that Bethesda isn't forcing the Creation Club on anyone. However, by forcing all of us to download Creation Club BA2 files on our systems, regardless of whether or not we actually purchase them, they ARE forcing the Creation Club on us. It's On-Disc DLC all over again, only this time it's on my actual hard drive instead of a disc. Did Bethesda learn nothing from Horse Armor in Oblivion? Or even from the paid mods through Steam just two years ago? WE DON'T WANT THIS!!!

First off, I buy these games for the Career(story) mode. It's always been my favorite aspect, being able to make your own guy and take him through his career. Well, in this game, you can make your own guy in the physical aspects, but that's about as far as it goes. Because it all has to follow Spike Lee's story mode. Which is...awful. It's nothing but played-out, racial stereotypes, embarrassing dialogue, and an extremely predictable story.
Who thought this type of a Story Mode was a good idea? We play these games because we like to have control of a character, and we like to play actual basketball simulation. Well, you don't get much character control in this one, except for raising your attributes (which takes forever). And between each game, you are expected to watch lengthy, boring cutscenes. You can skip them, but I mean...if you give the slightest bit of a care about the storyline, you'll be lost.
I also don't understand why-- you start out as a star high school player. Then you go on to be a star college player. You can barely miss a shot. It feels like the previous NBA games, you have decent attributes and it's all based on your timing. Then you advance to become an NBA rookie, and...all of your stats basically reset themselves. Every game becomes a struggle, even on "Rookie" mode. And if you play a great game, you still only get enough points to level up a couple meager stats.
If you aren't playing story mode, it's fine. The actual gameplay is great, no complaints there. But this whole story mode, even the idea to involve Spike Lee...it's all just a massive fumble.

Excellent game design all around, but it's not 100% perfect (cue internet rage flame war). I'm not going to count the graphics against the game because due to its age, that just wouldn't be fair. Anyway, it does a lot of things right that so many games today really, really struggle with. For starters, you never feel like you have the whole picture. Throughout the game, you'll meet characters who clearly know more about the situation than you do, and just expect you to go along with their instructions. You feel vulnerable and scared, and every tiny little victory you can find is one you will savor for hours until the next one. This game understands good pacing, and demonstrates the difference between gameplay/level variety (this entire series), and  gameplay/level discord (Halo 3). The gunplay is smooth, vicious, and satisfying, the sound design is (to quote a popular phrase) "hella dope af bruh", and the story, characters, and atmosphere are all intriguing. However, as I said, it's not perfect. Some of the puzzles are a bit misleading (you'll often go into a room designed to look like you're supposed to move a bookcase, when you're actually supposed to pick your nose and wipe it on your♥♥♥♥♥, there's just a little TOO much mystery and vagueness surrounding the game's events, which in turn make the player feel alienated (pun not intended), and sometimes the game decides to reinvent the rules without telling you, and take advantage (it's like everyone deciding to play king of the hill when you think you're still playing tag). Still, at least you won't have to read a book. 8/10.

A normal day turned into a nightmare. A normal man turned into a hero. Valve Software's (Presently, Valve Corporation's), 1998 game, Half-Life, is a masterpiece of gaming that never lets up from start to finish. A masterfully, perfect balance of storyline, pacing, action and atmosphere, don't pass this one up! The premise of the story, sees its protagonist, Seattle, Washington, native, Gordan Freeman, a graduate of MIT and having a Ph.D in theoretical physics on his first day of work at an undisclosed location in the New Mexican desert, known as the Black Mesa Research Facility. On a normal day of work, (wouldn't you know that it had to happen on his first day) devastation ensues when a science experiment goes horribly wrong by his own hand or at least partly by his own hand. He doesn't really know what's going on because everything has happened so very quickly, but all he knows is that he must rise to the occasion. He must take on a sense of responsibility for his own actions and attempt to escape the Black Mesa Research Facility, alive, all the while fighting off dimensional aliens and the military forces that have been sent in to clean up the evidence (mess lol). He also enounters the mysterious, G-Man, along the way. A mysterious and eerie figure with a suit and briefcase. One can only assume that Gordon Freeman, because of being a silent character, is constantly questioning what is going on as a result of his actions. He doesn't know but he does it, anyway. Quite the hero! When the player gets to the end of the game, he finds that there's time for only a bit of relief and none for celebration of actually being able escape the facility and Xen, alive, as the mysterious G-Man offers to either hire on Freeman or offer him "an anticlimax". There's also quite a bit to say about the G-Man but very little at the same time. Whether the G-Man is a person, some sort of an entity or a figment of the imagination brought on by some sort of attempted mind control or experiments (possibly, government-owned), is not, yet, known. Perhaps, the in-game character of G-Man could even be a reflection of his real life counterpart. On the topic of the soundtrack. The entire soundtrack was brilliant and fit extremely well into the entire atmosphere and storyline of the game. My favorite OST from the Half-Life Original Soundtrack, was Sirens in the Distance. Sirens in the Distance encompassed a sense of eerieness, mystery, perseverance, and was a firm reminder that an average person turned hero now has a sense of duty to take responsibility for his own actions, to not only fight for his own survival but little does he know at the time, the fate of the world as well. The OST begins with hearing the sirens blare twice, over and then the music begins to mimic the sirens and it seems to kind of merge with them at the same time, which was a very creative, move. To me, this OST marks the beginning when his present predictament finally sinks in to Gordon and he really begins to wonder if his actions may not be contained solely within the confines of the facility, itself but may have spread to the outside, world as well. What's happening out there? Is it the same that's happening in, here? Could it be worse? These are imporant questions for when we get to the second game, Valve's Half-Life 2 (2004), things start to be brought into a perspective a bit clearer than, before. We now know that the disaster has made a significant spread into the world, outside of the Black Mesa Research Facility, that the predicatament is worse than originally, thought. The brilliantly developed, protagonist, Gordon Freeman is the single greatest video game character in history. What I really love about Gordon Freeman, above all the other traits, is that the player knows quite a bit about him but also really nothing at the same time. His silent demeanor speaks volumes and allows the player to constantly question what is on his mind. We never really know for sure. He is also a humble reminder that one person, one man, can be enough to make a difference in the world. In a way, Gordon Freeman, is us or at the least a reflection. Of what could happen at any given moment when we least expect, it. Would we rise to be the hero? Again, this is a masterful game with a wonderful main character. A transition, from average person to Hero of the moment and eventually of the world, a man who continues his fight for survival against overwhelming odds, regardless of what comes before him, the ability to take responsiblity for one's own actions, etc. There are so very many motifs and without Half-Life, gaming wouldn't be where it is, today. A winner of over 50 game of the year awards and rightfully, so!

Don'Yoku is the reincarnation of the cabinet that sat in the corner of your local dive arcade. You know, the one that gorged itself on the pocket change of the unwary and stubborn; the one that had even the guy with seemingly superhuman coordination and reflexes sweating during the early levels. If you were that guy, Don’Yoku will reveal whether you’ve still “got it.” If you were the bystander who could barely surmount stage one, then Don’Yoku is your chance for redemption. Whatever your goal and whatever the outcome, you’re going to have fun.
This is a brutal but enjoyable game: tough but fair. The first stage mercilessly showers you with bullets. The second? Ditto. The third? Same. The fourth? Guess. The fifth? Good luck getting there. As you make progress, Don’Yoku will pour on the rain in increasingly dense patterns, and you’ll love every minute of it. Controls are just about as tight and responsive as possible, so as much as you might curse the game when death comes (and it will), deep down you’ll know the real reason you keep eating bullets is poor plane placement and/or slow reaction time. Granted, upon first encounter, some patterns will appear impossible to dodge. In these instances, Don’Yoku’s weapon mechanics serve as a buffer. Strategic use of your arsenal can extend your survivalbility by quite a bit.
You are given three planes to choose from, and each comes with a standard machine gun, an energy beam, and a Don’Yoku attack (basically, a bomb). Damaging enemies with the machine gun fills the Don’Yoku counter (i.e. gauge) for the Don'Yoku attack; whereas, the energy beam causes slight slowdown of onscreen action and converts kills to coins for increased score. A huge part of surviving in Don’Yoku involves efficient swapping of the the weaker machine gun and the more powerful beam, as well as juggling Don’Yoku energy stocking with Don'Yoku attack striking. Do this balancing act well and combine it with effective dodging, and your plane can endure a beating.
All in all, great gameplay and cool presentation makes Don'Yoku a must-have for bullet hell aficionados.

Personally I am a big fan of real pinball machines, but those can get really expensive for a regular player and are even more expensive to put into your living room and hard to maintain if anything breaks.
Since you can have lots of fun with just one pack of a few tables and even the free to play table, I can not give this any other rating than a resounding YES! This game is great. Download and have fun. If you are enthusiastic and have money, by all means, spend it here.

I don't normally do reviews, so this is one of the few games that have a definite need for a good, truthful review.
I honestly don't know how, nor do I want to, make a very long, and boring review... so I will keep it short, sweet, and simple.
PARTICLE MACE is a very unique game, with absolutely beautiful gameplay, and style. The concept of the game is simple. Don't let your ship get hit by the meteors, ships, and other enemies around you, while staying inside your designated zone. Around you there are multiple "particles" attached to your ship. Your goal is to move around, and maneuver the particle so that they hit (and destroy) all of those nasty little meteors and what I can only assume are alien ships. The physics in the game are absolutely amazing as well, seeing as all of the particles pretty much revolve around them.
Also, just so that the game does not begin to get boring early on, you have extra ships to unlock, with varying amounts of particles, and speed. Not only are there added ships, but there are also multiple missions that you are assigned or tasked with completing.
This game is absolutely amazing, and most definitely worth those ten dollars!

This is a really fun game that oozes quality in every aspect and imo the best pool game that is currently available on Steam. It also has a strong focus on online multiplayer and it's quick and easy to find a game against someone. [EDIT: Online is pretty dead at the moment, so beware of that before buying]
It has FANTASTIC graphics, easily the best out of any pool game I've ever seen. The depth of field effect in particular is excellent and very visually pleasing. There's real time ball reflections and incredibly detailed textures so much so I swear you can almost feel and smell that fresh pool table cloth ahhhh.
The sound is solid with a good meaty smack when the balls hit each other. There's quite a nice jazz soundtrack with a subtle but convincing crowd ambience and along with the great visuals and lack of UI creates a really engaging atmosphere.
Physics seem good. The balls always behave as I would expect them too. They seem to have a solid realistic weight to them and I haven't noticed any weird quirks. I have on occasion made a ball bounce off the table from whacking it with full force which is to be expected and it is good to see it simulated, rather than having the balls arbitrarily stuck to the table. But don't get me wrong there's no weird floaty aracade physics.
The controls may feel odd at first but with practice it feels intuitive. It supports both controller and mouse and keyboard, although many people have expressed that the mouse and keyboard controls are clunky and awkward to use. I personally use the controller in which you hold the right thumbstick down to distance your cue and slam it forward to hit the ball. It feels very satisfying once you nail it and I think this is about the closest a game has captured what it's really like to hold a cue and hit the ball; there's no arbitary power bar here. I've been an avid pool player in real life for over 20 years and after seeing the screen shots and trailer for Pure Pool I was really looking forward to it coming out.  I was not disappointed.
Pure Pool will no doubt draw many comparisons with the other pool game on Steam, Pool Nation.  I've played a ton of Pool Nation and I think Pool Nation looked cool but was very arcade when you got right down to it. The crazy swerve shots and jumps you could do and were REQUIRED to do for certain challenges were fun but no where near realistic.
Pure Pool is much more grounded in real life.  Your view is locked to what you would see if you were aiming a shot on a real table, aside from the aiming lines of course.  There is no overhead view or birds-eye view of the table.  You can "Stand Up" from your aiming view and walk around the table and move the view about as high as I could go if I was on my tip-toes over the table but that's it.  It feels very real and makes aiming a shot much more difficult.  Long shots the length of the table take skill just like in real pool.
From what I've played of Pure Pool and I'm loving it so far. My only criticism of the game is that it has clearly been designed with a controller in mind. I would highly recommend this game be played with a 360 pad as the keyboard controls are not awful but slightly sluggish when compared to the responsiveness you get with a pad.
I like that the game has strived for realism though. The way you move around the table as you would in real life and your view being is limited, no overhead view, only being able go as high as you could on your tip-toes to survey the table.  It really does feel like real pool.
Like I said, I love it. I'd highly recommend this game. One of the best pool games I've played since the days of Virtual Pool 3. This game is as close to real life pool as I think you will get without buying your own table for the back room.

TLDR:
Lords of the Fallen is a  3.25 / 5
The weapons and equiment are well done, and the gamplay for the most part is pretty good too. However, a mediocre plot, slow movement, and repetitive and frustrating enemies bring this game down a lot. If you're a big fan of these types of games, get this one on sale. I'm still going to reccommend this game because the score is above a 2.5 / 5, but seriously, if you are going to buy this game, GET IT ON SALE.
FULL REVIEW
Gameplay and controls:

For the most part, the gameplay is pretty good. Harkyn controls pretty well, with essentially identical button mapping to a Dark Souls game. As such, movement and attacks have different speeds depending on equipped gear. Heavy gear means slow movement, and ligher gear means quicker movement. There are three different classes you can choose from, which essentially boil down to a ranged class (mage), a tank class (knight) and a quick but deadly class (rogue), as well as different spells to pick at the beginning of the game, either focusing on combat, healing, or distracting enemies. So from what I've said, everything seems pretty good right? Well, not exactly. Here's the thing that brings the gameplay down. HARKYN. MOVES. SO. GODDAM. SLOWLY. It doesn't matter what weapon you use, it doesn't matter what gear you have on, you'll still attack pretty slowly. Of course as I said earlier, the weapons and equipment you use will make you slower or faster when you attack, run or roll, but you'll always feel sluggish. I had to play as the more tankier class just so I could handle the sluggishness and so I felt like there was a reason for being so slow. It's because of this that the gameplay suffers.
(0.75 POINTS)
Narrative:
So here comes the plot of the game. I'm not going to spoil anything just in case any of you are sensitive to that kind of stuff, but it's nothing special in my opinion. Basically, a criminal named Harkyn gets broken out of prison by this monk named Kaslo in order to destroy some otherworldly creatures known as Rhogars, and so begins Harkyns' quest to kill absolutely every Rhogar he sees. There is a fair bit of lore to find in the world in the form of scrolls, who give you a little bit of backstory to the world you're in. As I said, the plot is nothing special, but it's passable.
(0.50 POINTS)
Visuals:
The visuals aren't completely spectacular by today's standards of course since the game is nearly 3 years old, but there are quite a few pretty scenes in the game, most of the alpha effects are pretty well done, especially the fire effects (when fire is coming off of your sword oh man that♥♥♥♥♥♥looks cool), and the lighting effects when in outside areas are really cool too, with a lot of lens flare coming off of the sun (or fires in darker areas). Speaking of darker areas, the game is VERY dark. It's almost horror game dark sometimes where you can't see 3 feet ahead of yourself. There are some areas that are supposed to be super dark (like in the Rhogar dimension) but for the most part, it gets really hard to see in most areas. The animations for the characters are alright. Again, nothing special. Some of the movements that the characters make look particularly still and kinda robotic, which can look a bit weird. Another thing is the textures. The face and hair textures on characters are pretty good as they are, but the look of armour and weapons up close isn't very good. I don't know if they used low resolution assets for the armour or what, but when actually looking at it, ESPECIALLY in cutscenes, it just looks bad. Just to be clear, I have all of the settings set to the max, and it still looks like that.
(0.75 POINTS)
Gear and Weapons:
The weapons and gear are pretty well done for the most part. Most of the armour sets have fun and cool designs and are fun to look at, even if you aren't going to use all of them. The same goes for the weapons. There's quite a few cool weapon designs in this game, my favourite being the PERSISTENCE. A greatsword with burning ash coming off of it. Another cool one is the gauntlet you get pretty early on in the game. It's a magic weapon that Harkyn uses in his left hand instead of a shield. It's pretty cool. Later on in the game, I'd say about 3-4 hours in depending on how much you die, you meet a blacksmith who can upgrade your weapons using runes, which can give your weapons different buffs, like fire, poison, luck, etc. It's pretty average for this kind of game but it's still a nice inclusion. Overall, the weapons and gear are well done.
(1 POINT)
Enemies and Bosses:
Okay. Last thing. In these Dark Souls-esque games some of the most interesting and fun things are the different enemies in and bosses. In Lords of the Fallen, that's only partially true. The enemies, make me want to tear my hair out. And not in a "oh that's just Dark Souls difficulty at it again, once I figure out his attack patterns it will be easy to beat him!" kind of way. At first, yeah. It's fun to fight these enemies and learn their attack patterns. But then the enemies start using sheilds, and that was when fighting them went from fun, to rage inducing. The game turned into a waiting game from that point on, and I HATE WAITING IN GAMES. The combat with them turned into (wait for enemy to attack and open themself up. attack enemy. 46 damage done. rinse and repeat.) most of the enemies later on have lots of hit points too, so you can easily spend up to 5 minutes on one stupid freak with a shield. The worst place this happens though is in the catacombs. Oh man. You're in these narrow hallways and then this ENORMOUS Rhogar shows up and creates a wall that you can't pass, and you can't kill him either, because you can't get around him, you can't dodge roll, and you can't really parry some of these big enemies either. It's the worst. Now speaking of bosses, they aren't really enough to keep me excited for the next area. I kill one, and I'm like "yep, okay time to move on". None of them have any particularly interesting designs either, they're pretty much just bigger versions of the main enemies you fight. You won't find any Gaping Dragon or Nameless King here. So it's because of this I can't give this part of the game a very high score. Sorry guys.
(0.25 POINTS)
OVERALL SCORE:
3.25 / 5

I'll be basing my experiences so far on 100 or so hours with Virtual Pool 4, & VooFoo's previous pool title, Hustle Kings. Keep in mind that some of my issues might have been addressed by the time you've read this review, but I'll try to keep it as current as possible.
Positives:
Very clean visually. Probably the best looking pool title on the market.
Plenty of table customization. Logos/patterns are easily turned off, and there's several colours of cloth available.
The cloth feels closer to the real thing than any other pool sim I've played. I can actually see/feel the backspin grip into it.
Plenty of content to keep you going, especially at the price point.
Fair £/€/$ conversion rate.
Negatives:
I feel the game lacks a bit of cue power. It would be nice to be able to really nail a ball.
The AI can sometimes take too long with each shot, with a weird faux aiming "effect" that just eats up time.
Inverted controls for adding English to the ball/moving the ball - Not a settings issue.
Sometimes, the game just doesn't seem to want to accept inputs, especially when wanting to add English to the ball.
Mouse & Keyboard controls are pretty poor.
Minor graphical issues.
9 ball rules are incomplete (no push-out, 3 fouls, etc).
Overall, I'd recommend it. It will be a very good game once the few little issues it has are ironed out, but right now, just treat it like an unpolished gem - The core is there, and it's very, very good.

This is a game with a good deal of potential but one massive flaw: for people who enjoyed the previous games, this one will be hard as brass balls. It seems as though the devs took complaints that AC IV could be too easy personally and decided to punish us gamers. Counters can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ and checkpoints for memories are few and far between. Each chapter ends in a special mission where you have to infiltrate a location and carry out an assassination. These are quite fun, until you spend 10 to 20 minutes preparing and clearing the area of guards only to be detected and have 50 guards swarm and kill you, sending you back to the start. In fact, there aren't even checkpoints after the assassination but before the escape. This can be positively maddening when coupled with the difficult combat and the controls which, somehow, have gotten worse since AC IV. Die hard fans of the series would love the story as I have played it so far, but even they will have trouble playing past the difficulty (which I should say is not challenging, but arbitrarily difficult) and the numerous glitches that still occurr even over two months since the game's launch, which range from crashes to graphics glitches. In addition to this I must warn that the graphics are still not optimized, and even with my MSI GTX 780ti in a low overclock can be choppy with textures taking a longer time to load than in AC IV. In short, let the buyer beware with this game.

It is with great joy that I can say that this game does still function even so long after its initial release. My only complaint with this game after so many years is that the only way to get it to function properly is to undergo a process that most would never do on their own.
On a Windows 10 operating system, it will likely not function upon launching any of the three versions, declaring that it 'failed to initialize'. To fix the error, you must navigate to your 'Apps & features' page, scroll to the bottom, click on 'Programs and Features' under the Related setting section, and in the resulting menu click on the 'Turn Windows features on or off' button next to the windows shield at the left part of the screen. In the NEXT screen, you must click the drop down menu for 'Legacy Components' and enable DirectPlay. You may need to restart your computer afterwards or take other measures such as running as an administrator or verifying your game cache to get this game to work.
While it pains me that this solution is not properly displayed on the store page directly, there is a solution. Currently, only the efforts of the steam community can ensure that people realize that this solution exists, which is why I deleted a prior negative review. I did so because I ran into the problem and decided to create a negative review in the hopes that someone could diagnose a problem that I could not diagnose myself even after numerous attempts and rooting around steam for a while and missing the correct solution.
I have nothing but praise for the game itself, as the campaign is really quite entertaining, and the 'new'(As this game is quite old) mechanics for the Hometown makes the game nearly infinitely replayable. I purchased this game during the Steam Sale for a very cheap price, but I would gladly pay the full price tag to enjoy this game. Also, play Asian dynasties as it includes all previous content, including the other dlc. I don't honestly know why you would choose to play the basic version unless you absolutely despised teh Asian/Warchief content, which can be safely ignored anyway if you are so inclined.
For those of you who might look at my recorded hours and scoff, I will inform you that I played this game for hundreds of hours from a CD, that being years ago. Also, cheatcodes exist and can be extremely funny. (Especially the giant thingamajig that slaughters everything in its path and has no right to exist in the game's timeline, lul.)

Fallout 4 was a decent game, I had fun with it, but it lost the soul that Fallout originally had. The game trades away a lot of the RPG mechanics in exchange for main character vocal dialogue, enhanced gunplay, a streamlined experience and tacked on, borderline broken, base building system. Well, fortunately the majority of the issues I had with Fallout 4 were fixed with the incredible modding community this game has. the Nexus has plenty of amazing content that changes this game from an average, streamlined fallout experience, into everything you could have ever wanted this game to be. Tons and tons of weapon, armor, companion, NPC, quest and location mods, retextures, overhauls, you name it. If it weren't for the Nexus, I'd have stopped playing this game at about the 20 hour mark.
Now, on to the part where I explain why I cannot recommend this game in its current state.
SHort answer? Greed, shoddy business practices and unsafe software practices.
Long answer? the DLC we recieved for this game was mediocre at best, with a few exceptions (Far harbour and Nuka world to an extent) People who paid for the Season pass were shafted with addons to the already broken base building system (mods can fix the base building, but still) and two actually decent DLC out of the list, maybe a third if you like building your own robots (Automatron is overall disappointing and underwhelming in content)
The DLC in Fallout 4 is pretty sub-par coming from the company who gave us such gems as "Shivering Isles" and "Operation Anchorage" but I was able to look past it, since I was smart enough to not pay for anything in advance via the season pass (pre-purchasing games taught me that lesson already)
Thats when we get to the real root of the issue and why Fallout 4 currently has a Overwhelmingly negative review
The Creation Club.
The creation club is bethesdas way of saying one or all of these things:
1. "We didn't learn our lesson from the paid mods debacle on Steam"
2. "We think gamers are stupid and will buy whatever bulls*** we shove in their faces as long as its got our name on it"
3. "We don't care about the quality of our products anymore, we just want more money."
4. "We're fine with shooting ourselves in the foot, as long as we can make a quick buck out of it."
to summarize, Bethesda is trying to get players to pay real money for what boils down to dumbed down versions of mods you can already get for free on the Nexus. You'd think that for what they expect you to pay for these mods they'd give you some sort of mini-quest or some enemy to fight to obtain the weapon or armor you paid for, right? Nope, just go to a random area and find it in a box (literally thats all it is). There's also a distinct lack of features for these weapons and armor. Looking at the comparable alternatives from the nexus (which you can get for free btw) these bethesda paid mods have not even half the amount of content that these free nexus mods give you, and Bethesda expects you to pay HOW MUCH???
Yeah, no,♥♥♥♥♥♥off.
As if that matter wasn't bad enough, to add salt into the gaping wound.... Bethesda arbitrarily downloads all of the available paid mods onto your hard drive, regardless of if you paid for any of them or were like me and said "Screw that I'm not touching the creation club" They're on your hard drive anyway behind a paywall, all of them. You don't get to use them or anything, they're just there taking up space serving no other purpose whatsoever. THis is essentially bloatware, and anyone who knows anything about computers knows how potentially dangerous this tactic is, of just having anything uploaded into the creation club arbitrarily download onto your hard drive without your consent. This presents a huge and completely unacceptable security risk to the playerbase.
Therefor, unless Bethesda wises up and realises what an inherently god awful idea this creation club is, I cannot and will not recommend Fallout 4.

In Fallout 4, telling dogmeat to "do tricks" just results in him standing up on his Hind legs, EVERY TIME. Again, A rush job that shouldn't have been rushed. A normal day turned into a nightmare. A normal man turned into a hero. Valve Software's (Presently, Valve Corporation's), 1998 game, Half-Life, is a masterpiece of gaming that never lets up from start to finish. A masterfully, perfect balance of storyline, pacing, action and atmosphere, don't pass this one up! The premise of the story, sees its protagonist, Seattle, Washington, native, Gordan Freeman, a graduate of MIT and having a Ph.D in theoretical physics on his first day of work at an undisclosed location in the New Mexican desert, known as the Black Mesa Research Facility. On a normal day of work, (wouldn't you know that it had to happen on his first day) devastation ensues when a science experiment goes horribly wrong by his own hand or at least partly by his own hand. He doesn't really know what's going on because everything has happened so very quickly, but all he knows is that he must rise to the occasion. He must take on a sense of responsibility for his own actions and attempt to escape the Black Mesa Research Facility, alive, all the while fighting off dimensional aliens and the military forces that have been sent in to clean up the evidence (mess lol). He also enounters the mysterious, G-Man, along the way. A mysterious and eerie figure with a suit and briefcase. One can only assume that Gordon Freeman, because of being a silent character, is constantly questioning what is going on as a result of his actions. He doesn't know but he does it, anyway. Quite the hero! When the player gets to the end of the game, he finds that there's time for only a bit of relief and none for celebration of actually being able escape the facility and Xen, alive, as the mysterious G-Man offers to either hire on Freeman or offer him "an anticlimax". There's also quite a bit to say about the G-Man but very little at the same time. Whether the G-Man is a person, some sort of an entity or a figment of the imagination brought on by some sort of attempted mind control or experiments (possibly, government-owned), is not, yet, known. Perhaps, the in-game character of G-Man could even be a reflection of his real life counterpart. On the topic of the soundtrack. The entire soundtrack was brilliant and fit extremely well into the entire atmosphere and storyline of the game. My favorite OST from the Half-Life Original Soundtrack, was Sirens in the Distance. Sirens in the Distance encompassed a sense of eerieness, mystery, perseverance, and was a firm reminder that an average person turned hero now has a sense of duty to take responsibility for his own actions, to not only fight for his own survival but little does he know at the time, the fate of the world as well. The OST begins with hearing the sirens blare twice, over and then the music begins to mimic the sirens and it seems to kind of merge with them at the same time, which was a very creative, move. To me, this OST marks the beginning when his present predictament finally sinks in to Gordon and he really begins to wonder if his actions may not be contained solely within the confines of the facility, itself but may have spread to the outside, world as well. What's happening out there? Is it the same that's happening in, here? Could it be worse? These are imporant questions for when we get to the second game, Valve's Half-Life 2 (2004), things start to be brought into a perspective a bit clearer than, before. We now know that the disaster has made a significant spread into the world, outside of the Black Mesa Research Facility, that the predicatament is worse than originally, thought. The brilliantly developed, protagonist, Gordon Freeman is the single greatest video game character in history. What I really love about Gordon Freeman, above all the other traits, is that the player knows quite a bit about him but also really nothing at the same time. His silent demeanor speaks volumes and allows the player to constantly question what is on his mind. We never really know for sure. He is also a humble reminder that one person, one man, can be enough to make a difference in the world. In a way, Gordon Freeman, is us or at the least a reflection. Of what could happen at any given moment when we least expect, it. Would we rise to be the hero? Again, this is a masterful game with a wonderful main character. A transition, from average person to Hero of the moment and eventually of the world, a man who continues his fight for survival against overwhelming odds, regardless of what comes before him, the ability to take responsiblity for one's own actions, etc. There are so very many motifs and without Half-Life, gaming wouldn't be where it is, today. A winner of over 50 game of the year awards and rightfully, so!

When you had to find your "starter pet" outside randomly on a planet and capture it, I actually got myself a cute dog, I could recapture it and kill it as I please, as long as it was outside my ship. Why remove the freedom?
Why make possibilities limited?

Osmos is based around a fairly simple concept. You are a mote. You propel yourself by shooting out part of your own mass.
You get absorbed by motes larger than you. You absorb motes smaller than you.
On every level, you are attempting to grow much larger.
There is a time control mechanism allowing you to speed up and slow down how quickly time passes. This is essential.
Why you may need to speed up time: You're moving in the correct direction, but very slowly. You could speed yourself up by shooting out more of your mass, but you generally don't want to waste mass doing that.
Why you may need to slow down time:  Sometimes things are moving fast and you need to propel yourself in a very particular direction.
Pros
+ Decent variety of levels. For example:
* Entire map covered with motes and the motes are non-moving. You start in middle and have to carefully maneuver yourself around. Be careful! The pieces you shoot out can hit the other motes and start to move them. These feel a little bit like puzzles.
* Orbits. You and other motes orbit around one or more "Attractor" motes.
* Sentient motes. You have to absorb some motes that have some basic AI.
+ The orbit prediction arc. This arc predicts your orbit around another object.  You can then see if your path matches what you want. The game would've been too hard without it.
Cons
- Can be very frustrating. You may have been playing a level for 10-15 minutes when you lose because of:
* a moment of inattention.
* you realize you've reached an unwinnable state. That one other mote you need to absorb is just a tiny bit bigger than you.  (Note: the game will warn you when the level has reached an unwinnable state. You'll see "Doesn't look good..." at the bottom of the screen. However, that warning is often late.)
Overall
If you're prepared for a lot of frustration, Osmos can be a rewarding game.

Heat Signature is a crazy trip, it can be played with a twitchy temperament like Hotline Miami, or more tactfully like a turn based game, or something in between, or all of the above. Its being compared to Hotline Miami a lot actually, and if you could hijack the slum you just cleared out and take it on joyride and crash into some other randomly generated slum and kick more♥♥♥♥♥their, then yeah, its a lot like Hotline Miami.

This is an amazingly fun quick-to-play Roguelike! I can't really describe the game better than the game already does, but I will say it does meet its expectations 100% in terms of not super-plot heavy, but instead it's the personal "epic" feel of personalized missions.
I bought the game today, and within the first 2 hours, figured out how to wander around complete several missions, including a few medium difficulty missions; accumulated enough cash to fund my "Personalized Mission"- but realized I'm going to need more resources in order to complete it, and was able to locate the Unique Ship to get the special first two week promotional bonus gun "The Everything Gun"... which would lead to my last mission of the night and the one that sums up the fun of the game:
My Hero Casacara was tasked to complete a "Bloodless" mission- to infiltrate a ship, assassinate a target and walk away without killing any other members. It was going to be my first Bloodless mission, but seemed easy. My intel noted it would be a skeleton crew, the Alarm was going to be around 90 seconds to get in and get out if I was spotted, and it was a small ship." Easy-peasy lemon squeezy," my agent thought: "I've already liberated a base; I've got plenty of rare items, and I even have this sweet Unique new gun. Let's take a wrench, my stun gun, and the new gun and get in and out."
Casacara docked onto the skeleton ship a few mins later (docking is still tricky, but I'm getting the hang of it). And a quick recon over the base showed my intel was true: 3 people on the ship: A pilot, a guard by the door, and the target himself. "This is too easy"- I thought to myself. Casacara quickly opened the door, threw the wrench and knocked out the guard. She stepped into the room, and saw the Target was two rooms over and checking his data pads, the pilot was a distance away at the aft of the ship. Her plan was simple- use the new unique Everything Gun to make a distraction, cause the Target to run up, and then bam! Stun and snap his neck. Easy-Peasy.
Casacara shot the everything gun at the wall, causing it to suck up the nearby wrench and fling it at the wall, when the wrench struck the wall- bounced off- and struck Casacara in the face, knocking her out!! I stared dumbstruck as my character was unconcious, the Target heard the ruckus, and sounded the alarm, causing the 90 second timer to countdown before the ship would escape and I'd be out of luck. The target came over to my unconcious agent, grabbed her and started to drag her away- I watched the timer to see if I was going to regain conciousness, while that counter went down to 80 seconds... 79...78... and suddenly the Target opened the airlock and sucked out my Agent into the cold vacuum of space!
I stared stunned, as I lucky had my autopilot on my ship, but I had to quickly fly over to grab my character's body before we ran out of oxygen- and then just as I picked her up, and contemplated my next move- I realized the Alarm countdown was still going- I had less than 60 seconds to complete the mission! Casacara quickly woke up and gunned it to chase after that ship- but she overshot the distance and ended up in it's headlights- The Pilot now seeing my ship, fired rockets and blew out my engines blasting me away from the target. I had to quickly perform evasive manuevers as Casacara and I realized we lost that mission, and my engines were blown out and now I'm on emergency fuel and unsure if I could get back home....
However, I could still see the ship nearby, with it's countdown at 45 seconds. I gritted my teeth- I hadn't failed a mission yet! We punched the engines, burning our fuel as we caught up to the ship. Casacara opened the airlock door and with the counter on 30 seconds now, we came out stun guns blazing and knocked out the Target, who was suprised to see the would-be-assassin that he had thrown out the airlock and whom his pilot had blown out of the sky now returned! It would be the last thing he saw as he was concussed and quickly his neck snapped. I debated taking out the pilot, but realized I had no time! I quickly dashed back into my ship, and then used the remainer of my emergency fuel to drift back towards home base....
It was supposed to be a simple mission- a skeleton crew of 3, and I had done missions with 20+ guards and taken them all out, but I had not expected the unexpected, and the countdown only added to the pressure. It's just one random mission, nothing contributory to the plot- but it was a small tiny moment of awesome!
If those tiny moments in a rogue-like are what you're looking for- this game is perfect for you- if you're looking for a game that's going to give you 100+ hours of plot, dialogue and multiplayer- this is NOT the game for you.
I know I'm hooked though. It's perfect for a casual gamer who wants to play for a few hours, and stop but still feel like they did something and had a good time! I'm looking forwards to the future... and Casacara needs to continue onwards to eventually solve her personalized quest as well.

By and large, most choice-driven games have followed the same formula, inviting you to make your mark in the world by deciding if you want to be “good” or “bad,” and accepting the binary nature of existence. But in the post-apocalyptic world of The Walking Dead, where the titular dead walk the decaying earth, the notion of good and bad is somewhat dated. There’s no “right” when right can mean shooting an innocent child before it can turn into a flesh-eating beast, and there’s no “wrong” when wrong can mean stealing the supplies you need to survive from those just as needy as you. The Walking Dead is the story of the choices you can’t live with, and the choices you can, coming together to create an experience as depressing and pessimistic as it is remarkable and memorable.
The Walking Dead never pretends to be anything less than a cruel, dour analysis of humanity’s downfall. You’re tossed into the cuffs of Lee Everett, a convicted murderer on his way to prison when the first episode begins. In the opening moments, his police escort is sidetracked by the zombie apocalypse, freeing Lee into a world that’s not nearly as comfortable as a jail cell would've been. Soon, he’s joined by the young Clementine, a child left on her own after her parents took a poorly timed vacation and her babysitter contracted a bad case of the flesh munchies. And off into the new, horrible world Lee goes, hoping to find Clementine’s parents despite knowing that they’re likely dead; off to find sanctuary when he doubts one even exists.
In stark contrast to the rest of gaming, The Walking Dead is more focused on what you do than how you do it. There aren’t many traditional puzzles, per se, as much as there are tasks that you’re asked to perform to move the story forward. Menial activities like finding batteries for a radio or starting up a train aren’t all that engaging by themselves, but they serve a very necessary pacing purpose, as well as give you a chance to explore the world a bit and get to know the characters better. If you’re looking to rampage around Georgia popping the heads off of undead monsters, you’re better served by one of the many other zombie games on the market.
Though some might be turned off by this minimization of traditional gameplay, it works well in the context of the game. The effect you have on the world is fairly minimal by design, mixing together Telltale’s point-and-click adventure game style with a smattering of quick-time events and choice-driven dialogue. This amorphous take on gameplay works very well to make you feel like you’re a part of the world, without allowing you to go too far off the rails. But just because you’re not allowed to stray too far off the beaten path, doesn’t mean you don’t have an actual influence--on the contrary, your words and actions actually play an integral part in crafting the world.
Incredibly strong writing and voice-acting give the narrative the spotlight it deserves. The vast majority of the characters you interact with are well-developed, and it’s hard not to feel compassion for even the meanest of the bunch, making you actually care about who you foster relationships with and who you choose to disappoint. What’s more, your actions have an impact not just on the events that you encounter, but in how people treat you. Don’t back up Kenny when his son is accused of being bitten, and he might not have your back a few episodes later when you need him to. Side with Lilly when she’s trying to ration the food, and she might respect you enough to help you in the coming episodes.
Your choices, both large and small, have repercussions, and can change the course of the remaining episodes--even if it’s only a slight shift. Split-second choices made later in the game can rewrite how people react to you regardless of how you’ve treated them up to that point, making each and every action all the more important. Inaction, too, is usually an option, amplified by the inclusion of a timer that makes it possible to completely miss a chance at making a decision, forcing you to sit on the sidelines and watch whatever your indifference hath wrought.
These decisions wouldn't be as emotional if it didn’t feel like there was something on the line, but there is: Clementine. The hopelessness of the world would be infectious if not for her constant optimism, giving you something to fight for. She’s slow to adapt to the fact that good and evil are now meaningless, and her innocence keeps the concept of hope alive in the survivors. More importantly, it makes it harder to justify going against what you think is truly “right,” since you know you’re going to have her big, sad eyes staring up at you. It’s heartbreaking and motivational, inspirational and depressing.
The Walking Dead’s success isn’t in creating a Choose Your Own Adventure game with hundreds of possible outcomes and limitless plotlines. Instead, it reflect the reality of life, reminding you that many of the choices you’re given have predetermined outcomes, and some things simply can’t be changed. And yet, this undermining of everything that makes The Walking Dead unique is arguably its greatest triumph. Despite not always being in control, The Walking Dead makes you feel as though you are. Even though you can’t always save someone from death, you can give it your best try, shaping the person you are. And it’s up to you to decide if it’s worth the effort to change what, in all likelihood, can not be changed.
Sure, you can replay it to see what else would happen, but that won’t change anything. It won’t change that you’re not going to leave The Walking Dead happy. You’ll feel like you made mistakes. You’ll feel like you could have done better, if you gave it another go. At best, you’ll leave without any regrets, knowing that you did the best you could do. The Walking Dead deals in a spectrum of emotion that few other games dare to take on, and it does so with aplomb. It’s utterly triumphant, crafting a narrative that proves the power of the medium by embracing what makes it unique, leading to one of the most memorable gameplay experiences ever created.

Lords of the Fallen isn't a terrible game. The first thing to get out of the way is that there is a heavy Souls influence here, period. That's unavoidable. The issue with Lords of the Fallen is that it didn't do enough to really create an identity of its own. So here you have a game that is undeniably a Dark Souls clone that fails to do many of the things that makes Dark Souls
or memorable.
To make the review short, the reason the game gets bad reviews is because of the combat. Your character's animations feel long, heavy, and drawn-out. It actually feels as if the animations are running at half speed. Enemy attacks always seem to be fluid. Combat never feels graceful, even in light armor. Winning a battle unscathed ultimately comes down to getting the first hit and connecting a lethal combo. Instead of dueling your enemy and exploiting their weakness, you're simply waiting for them to attack so you can step out of the way to land an attack. It's boring, repetitive and predictable.
I completed 2 full areas and killed 2 bosses. Even with such a small sampling of the game, I think I got the gist of it. Get it on sale, if at all.

Hello friends! This game is one of my favorites. I've invested a ton of time into it and still play pretty much every night. Its a swirling melee of a game with plenty of depth to the combat with plenty of strategy and tactics to play with. So if you read no farther then know my opinion is: yes get it and start playing.
This game is also 100% free to play! With absolutely no pay to win involved. Crew and ships as well as alternative load outs can all be purchased with in game earned credits (earned just by playing, which is why you are here right?)
You can use money to speed things along, but mostly money gets you cosmetics. Some of which are really cool and lovingly made. And no ship is truely 'better' than all the others.
The models and graphics in this game are georgous. It plays smoothly and is well optimized. It is still technically under development and so a lot of things have changed since i got here. But honestly it is amazingly polished. And at the time I am writing this things are in a great place.
The balance is solid, with a few ships over preforming and a few under preforming. The thing that really sells this game for me isn't the team play (though I love that) or exciting combat but the unique way good piloting can turn a ship from average to unstoppable and how great tactics and strategy can make or break a team.
I hope you pick this title up and love it the way I do. See you out there.

With the aid of fellow scientist, Gordon Freeman goes around the facility seeking to stop the invading aliens who seem to be teleporting onto Earth. Simultaneously, the military has come to silence all Black Mesa workers in hopes of covering up the castastrophic incident. Traveling through the insides of the facility to the mountain sides to the strange alien world, there is always danger around the corner along with a few puzzles to get around. Even with a variety of weapons to get ahead of others, you may find yourself in a tough situation from time to time. The story behind all this is full of amazement as it goes on to the sequal.
Multi-player is also an enjoyment with several maps to choose from, custom or otherwise. Players can always find an enjoyment when playing against each other whether it be underground with water traps to a bomb testing facility to Homer Simpson's house.
