Zombillie is one of the cheaper titles that I purchased during the 2016/17 Steam Winter sale. I have enjoyed several of Forever Entertainment S.A.’s games in the past. Among these are the Teddy Floppy Ear games and the Frederic music titles. Although these games never feature tremendously high production value they are generally lower-priced indie games that are high on entertainment. Therefore, I was hoping for a title that would be something a little more than just a trading card idle game.
Having previously played Millie, another of Forever Entertainment’s games, I knew to expect a combination of the classics Snake, Centipede and other casual arcade games. Only this time the game had been skinned with the overdone and outplayed zombie stylings.
Therefore, I had somewhat basic hopes for Zombillie before playing. I anticipated a simple, well-designed puzzler with smooth controls and challenging gameplay. I suspected that the game would be able to hold my attention for about an hour while I went on an achievement hunt.
Unfortunately, the expectations that I held for the gameplay failed to materialize to the level that I had hoped. Although the game has been designed for full controller support keyboard play is also enabled. Having spent time with both I found the keyboard the better of the two options. However, both have similar issues. I found that inputs weren’t as responsive as what I would have liked. This was more glaring when using my Xbox One controller than it was in using the keyboard but neither solution was quite satisfactory.
The problem with this issue is that the game requires accurate input to be played at its maximum effectiveness. Having read through other reviews and discussions on the game I have found this to be a relatively common complaint. Therefore, this issue tends to take away from the overall gaming experience.
I found the queues at the beginning of each levels a little too easy to skip. This information is important in educating the player with the necessary information at the beginning of each level. These do not repeat if you accidentally click through them by trying to restart the level. This was a minor source of aggravation.
As has been traditionally the case with Forever Entertainment’s games you’re looking at lower production values. The production values of the game are almost always most apparent in the presentation. Zombillie wouldn’t have looked out of place with games released a decade or more ago.
Therefore, players can expect to find a simple presentation package in regards to both graphics and sound. These are passable for the game at hand, however, there is nothing within the entire presentation package that will be the least bit memorable after you complete the game. In fact, in a number of ways the presentation values of Zombillie really do nothing to persuade gamers to think any differently of cheap zombie skinned games.
I have levied more criticism upon the game than it arguably deserves. For the cost of the game, especially when purchased at the discount price that I paid for it ($0.49 at 90% off), you shouldn’t be expecting very much.
There is a significant amount of content that will delight completionists.  There are almost 100 levels available to be played across 3 completely different environments and there are an additional 2 types of mini-games. This does keep the content relatively fresh and rewarding.
The game contains a significant amount of content. There are almost 100 levels available to be played across 3 completely different environments and there are an additional 2 types of mini-games. Furthermore, there is an in-game store where players can cash in their in-game collectibles for bonuses and tools that will help you progress throughout the game.
Forever Entertainment have always had a reasonable grasp on what their playerbase wants in a Steam game. There is a good set of five Steam trading cards along with 16 Steam achievements. The game utilizes the Steam cloud and leaderboard system and as mentioned previously also offers full controller support.
In this respect, the way it utilizes the advantages of Steam’s available feature list is relatively impressive for a low tiered indie title. Such utilization does nothing but encourage players to purchase games when on sale and as such these practices are to be commended.
Given the price that I paid for the game ($0.49 at 90% off) I’m not disappointed. The fact is that at this price point anything close to an hour’s worth of play is reasonable value. If you’re the type of gamer who purchases cheap trading card games to sell on the cards, you would have found the game to be a bargain at this price point.
However, I would urge you not to purchase the game without it being on sale. The game really doesn’t have enough quality content nor smooth enough gameplay to justify a $4.99 price tag. I suspect that Forever Entertainment would understand this and given the regular discount intervals for the game may even agree. I would argue that games such as Zombillie are made especially for sales and bundles where any reasonable amount of income for the developer-publisher is a win-win situation.
If you’re interested in cheap arcade puzzler’s and the game is on sale, then I would recommend a purchase. You’ll more than likely get your monies worth in this scenario.

Despite putting out a new engine, Pinball FX remains an inferior product.
The idea for this, or at least what they've always said, was to make pinball tables you can't play in reality. The problem with this is it is really used to mask the developers inability to make decent pinball tables. Instead they always rely on ripping off concepts, and individual parts, from classic tables any real life pinball player will immediately notice, and use bad physics which don't feel at all like real pinball, and say it's "magic" (not directly, but rather implied). Some may excuse this due to those tables being created by the legends- arguably the greatest pinball can ever get. I do not make these apologies. This is a bad pinball game- it always has been.
That being said they do somewhat get better, at times, at their own ideas. They reappropriated the concept of a "pinball RPG" (which has been done on real tables, but never to the extent that Zen Studios has created). The one bright side to all this is the newer tables they've put out for Fallout 4, Skyrim and Doom. There are a few other new tables as well that are also recommendable, but the most recommended I can give is those 3 tables. These tables in particular are quite novel, and fun to play utilizing RPG concepts to create an atmosphere of building up a character and going on adventures.
Overall, Pinball FX 3 remains the inferior pinball "simulation." With games like "Pinball Arcade" on the market, which most accurately represents the look and feel of playing an actual arcade pinball machine down to some almost minute details, Pinball FX doesn't stand a chance to even be considered pinball "simulating." Instead it's strengths are in what it originally touted it wanted to be, but never fully realized until fairly recently (within the last few years). If you want pinball simulation stick with "Pinball arcade." Even if you want something pinball can't do in real life 90% of the tables in this game are really really bad- I do not recommend you buy any of them. However, the newer tables (Fallout 4, Skyrim, Doom, An "Alien" table or two, and a few others here and there) really stand out as something interesting and unique in the pinball space. I highly recommend you play free trials of any table before purchasing in this game- as well as heavily thinking it over (I assume they are still bringing over the old ones, if you don't already have them, anyway). Many of them are really really bad even as just digital non realistic pinball. Let's all hope they make more of the ones that have interesting ideas, and new concepts, and less of what they were making for a long time before.
Much like 90% of Pinball FX of the past, most of this review is reappropriated, based on my experience with Pinball FX and Pinball FX 2. I have almost all of the tables they've released up to this point- 90% of which are trash and I'll probably never play again.
Update: After an update today I no longer have 45 of the tables available in this version. They have somehow decided I no longer own these tables I already own and now 15 tables have been taken away from me. Downgrading this now to NOT RECOMMENDED. These devs are shadier by the day. I thought they were trying to improve, but I guess they are not.

Stardew Valley is an amazing game created by a single developer, reminiscent of the old Harvest Moon games. Has a great story which is primarily driven and created by the player themself. The only real large problem other than multiplayer with most people is replayability which can most likely be fixed with mods, or it might not bother you. The game is an absolute gem and the pricing is amazing, getting it on sale is pretty much highway robbery. It get's a glowing recommendation from this random stranger on the internet. Metacritic also gave this game an 89 if you care about that at all.
No, seriously, it's one of the best games I've ever played. In fact I felt it was good enough to throw it in for an award for the steam awards this year. I nominated it for the "The World is Grim Enough Lets Just All Get Along" award. Which the game pretty much meets all criteria except for despite killing slimes and monsters, although that is hardly the focus of the game.
Stardew Valley at it's core is a farming game, that is what it is if you'd stripped all other aspects of the game away, and the game does it very well. With everything from seasons, to seasonal produce, sprinklers, fruits, vegitables, fertilizer, livestock, and everything necessary to make processed goods (mayo, wine, jam, etc.)
While one may initially buy, download, and play the game for it's nostalgia ticklers in reference to the Harvest Moon series (or Story of Seasons it's "offical name") of games. After playing for awhile you'll find it's much more than just a farming game. It's an experience that never ceases to amaze me, from everything to the farming itself, to the stories you uncover from the townspeople intentionally or unintentionally. Honestly, it is incredibly impressive that one dude managed to make this entire game.
Now a serious disclaimer, I have not "finished" the game, I haven't even come remotely close. Even so, the game lacks any concrete story because you as the player are the center of your own story. You're the one who decides what crops to plant, which townsfolk you like and don't like, who you care about more as a romantic partner, are you gay or not, whatever it is you do in this game, you're the one driving the story forward.
Stardew Valley, is the epitome of a chilled out game, it's focus isn't on slaying vast waves of enemy drones with aim to match a stormtroopers. It's to farm, take in the sights, slow down a bit and notice the smaller things in life, and value interaction with people. It's such a nice change of pace that it kinda just unwinds you from the constant bombardment of violence and gun play that you find so often in modern media. Whenever I'm burnt out on FPS's or even just feel overwhelmed from life itself, I'll play some Stardew Valley, because to me, the gameplay is almost theraputic.

Enter a dreamy, minimalist environment where you are a single-celled organism.  You can absorb other organisms smaller than you, but beware any that are larger, as they will consume you.  Your only method of locomotion is to expel mass, propelling you in the opposite direction.  But you must be discerning in your movement, as this will also make you smaller, leaving yourself more vulnerable to attack.  Osmos is a game that rewards patience and thoughtfulness.  Its main draw is not its challenge, though it can be plenty difficult.  Osmos strives to bring you serenity and relaxation.  How well does it succeed?
The game has 3 modes, Ambient, Force, and Sentient.  You can progress through each path independently through harder and harder levels.  This is a great design choice, as the three modes play out completely differently, and allows each player to find their own favorite style of game to play.  Ambient is probably best described as the “base” game.  The main objective is usually to become the biggest mote on the level, or to absorb a certain percentage of the available mass.  Force throws a twist into this formula, bringing gravitational motes that act like stars you and all the other motes will orbit.  Sentient adds other intelligent motes, that will avoid you or try to consume you, depending on how large they are.  After you complete the main levels in each mode, you unlock endless random levels of that type, giving the game great replayability.
The hardest of these, by far, are the Force levels.  You are thrown into an environment that does not behave like a normal 2D plane, like most video games or life in general.  The levels are radial in nature.  You will be forced to develop a working understanding of orbital mechanics.  This guide from the developers is crucial to understanding the effective strategies to complete these levels.  I spent an entire semester in college studying the principles used here, and I still struggle with interpreting the different orbits and planning my moves accordingly.  A huge benefit to the player in any level is the ability to speed up or slow down time.  This allows you to execute maneuvers within tight spaces or time frames.  Very useful for sneaking through two larger motes at just the right angle to capture a smaller one, for instance.
The soundtrack is empty, aetheric, and spacy.  It fits the game very well, as you’ll feel like you’re floating in a void.  The music doesn’t push you ahead or drive you, it is calming and instead allows you to focus on the task at hand.  Grab some headphones and get lost in the game.
The graphics are also beautifully realized.  There’s no way to play this game but at fullscreen, your entire field of vision taken up by these beautiful motes floating through space.  Simple and very easy to understand.  Blue motes you can consume.  Red motes will consume you.  Blue motes with a ring of red just near the edge: those you should be very careful approaching, as they are almost your size.  Can you make contact with it without expelling too much mass in transit and tipping the scale in its favor?
The choice to split up the levels into discrete sections is a welcome one.  I found the Ambient levels to be the easiest, and completed those first.  The Sentient levels required a more aggressive approach, as the other motes would usually be quick to outgrow you and hunt you down.  I feel this went a little against the stated goal of the game, which was to be a source of relaxation and serenity.  Turning down the AI’s aggression a little bit would have helped that.  The Force levels, however, were a constant source of frustration to me.  Often there are not very many motes that you would like to pursue near your initial orbit in these levels, so you will have to do some tricky maneuvering right out of the gate.  Wait too long to make these moves, and the level will coalesce into only a few large motes that you have no chance of absorbing.  This gives these levels an unwelcome sense of urgency that leads to many mistakes, because you are trying to literally learn rocket science.
Osmos is a really interesting game.  A simple ruleset, stunning visuals, and ethereal music give this game a really unique atmosphere that I haven’t seen anywhere else.  While sometimes it can be frustrating or almost unfair, the experience of mastering the laws of physics to grow your mote is truly rewarding.

What a game. I whole heartedly recommend this game, and so far I only have 4 hours and feel it was worth the money, which is the mark of a very good game. The moment that solidifies how good the game is, is when you are almost out of items, and your plan is no longer possible, and in fact there is no plan. You're ready to give up on saving your husband and admitting defeat, surrounded by panicked guards. You realize you haven't a particular item yet, in my case the emergency shield. Well, why not, what's the worst that could happen. You buckle up, pick up your husband, and go for it, and there are no words to describe the joy and tension in the next few seconds, where every single move you make counts. There are no words to describe how amazing it is to discover that you can fire a glitch trap with the everything gun and it will work, or the feeling of being chased by an angry guard on your tail with a wrench and throwing away your husband at the last second in order to put your last shield back on, then shooting the window and catching both your husband and yourself and completeing the mission. This game is full of moments you don't expect to happen that will completely make this game for you, and it is completely personalized so don't expect a review to predict those moments for you.
One suggestion that will likely never be seen but anywho, closure would go a long way in this game. For example, being able to talk to a rescued family member, in a very limited way maybe, seeing a character who is retired playing space golf in the bar with their new family member, seeing a wake in the bar for a deceased friend. Of course these are probably very complicated to pull of, and it's not a make or break things, but it's just a suggestion that would make a really fun exciting game just that little bit more amazing even after the you've completed a personal mission.
In summary, the game is absolutely fantastic and definitely worth the price but the personal missions could be a bit more personal in the long run.

Particle Mace is a small, tight, fun little game. It's a twin-stick-shooter, except you only use one stick, if that makes any sense.
Instead of directional fire from the second stick, you drag "particles" behind you on stretchy tethers (i.e. a "mace), and use the physics model to whip your mace into enemies.
It's a neat mechanic that forces the player to split their focus between dodging enemies and asteroids, and fudgily manipulating the mace to make kills. The physics model is simple but perfect, and never feels arbitrary or mean. There's a classic score-chase mode, and a "mission" mode, which gives the player a selection of interesting goals to meet, which provides a neat way to switch up the gameplay and keep it fresh. There's multiple ships to unlock, which provide further tweaks to how the game plays.
It's not going to be your game of the year, but Particle Mace might be your "interesting diversion of the year that you boot up for five or ten minutes every week".

This game is a such a mixed bag - its three main categories of levels (Ambient, Sentient, and Force) differ immensely in quality.
The Ambient levels strike an almost-perfect balance between relaxing and strategic gameplay, and show off the game's systems at their finest - the Impasse levels, in particular, require a surprising degree of forethought in anticipating chain reactions between cells.
The Sentient levels are just kind of... there. There's nothing particularly bad about them, but they're not interesting - the same strategy of growing as quickly as possible before enemy cells can catch up is generally effective regardless of enemy type. I was relieved that there were less of these stages than the other two main categories, as Osmos' gameplay doesn't seem particularly well suited to competitive action and there wasn't much memorable about them.
The Force levels are just seriously terrible. None of the three categories is enjoyable to play, unless perhaps you have a burning passion for orbital physics and waiting ages for cells to slowly drift into place. I'm not ashamed to say that I didn't finish these.
Overall, though, I enjoyed my time with it and think that it's worth playing for the Ambient stages alone.

Well, lets start by the part that was the most awaited, the mycareer story.
This year, its directed by Spike Lee, and well, lets cut to the point, its hiscareer.
The storyline is EXTREMELY cliché and really doesnt let you make any decision whatsoever in your first year.
People complained in previous years of the voice of the character being too "black"
Well, 2k solved the problem, now you have a black familly regardless of your character (not a big deal, but really it prevents any immersion in the story.)
High school is totally useless, youre just an overpowered player gliding trough 4 games before every college available in the game comes to you and make a speech. (and to my knowledge, there is absolutely no repercussion to the rest of your career)
Then you decide wich college youd like to attend and play for another 4 games making your draft stock rise.
NBA draft comes, you play through some "key" games in your rookie year (8 games exactly) each coming with a cutscene that is as boring and as predictable as it could be.
You dont make ANY choice during your rookie season.
Conclusion on that : they could have featured a movie in the game that you could optionnally watch before starting your career, with the sole purpose of explaining why said career starts on your second season (and thus sparing our precious time)
Then season 2 comes, you now have chosen where you wanted to go during free agency (btw, thats not how NBA contract work but meh.)
the new additions when it comes to off days are interesting, its more entertaining than just playing and spending vc on upgrades/animaitons.
Overall, except for the HORRIBLE rookie movie (its not a season, its literally a movie)
The mycareer mode is actually enjoyable to play and progress through.
Now, the gameplay.
Just like previous year since the new engine, the ball handling feels strange at times. (i.e : way too many bizarre turnovers/lost balls)
The cheesy chasedown block on fastbreak dunks still occurs half of the time.
Animation wise, this year feels really good in term of quality, ive found myself just pausing and watching replays just to see how detailed it was.
The new substitution menu ingame feels odd.
you used to just use the pad to do everything, now you access it with the pad, and then have to do weird joysticks combinations.
Overall, the game is still pretty good, but really that hype around the "spike lee joint" is laughable seeing the big failure that it is.

A game that remains in our hearts even after beating it. They only try to survive without losing humanity, caring for their neighbors, not forgetting about feelings (love, compassion, consolation, trust, caring). The game from the first seconds is already fascinating with its plot. Sometimes it is really difficult to make a certain choice.
The game is definitely worth its money and time spent in it!

I am absolutely not an expert in this kind of game. So, if you want an "expert" opinion, skip this review. But I hope this will be instructive for others who are unfamiliar with the genre....
Key good points:
1) Big spaceships, cruising around trying to work out cunning ways to defeat your enemies.... Yeah, it's meaningless, but it's an appealing idea, it's attractive, it's mentally engaging - basically, big spaceships are cool.
2) The game is free to play, but not pay-to-win. This is awesome. It means you try the whole game for free, and then decide if you want to pay. If you do pay, what you're paying for is not power but variety - for the ability to try out different playstyles (new ships) sooner than you would if you bought them with in-game winnings - and for some cosmetic changes. (Seriously, everyone who plays this should be willing to pay a few bucks. The devs have built a good game, and their business model isn't exploitative; if you can afford a shiny games-spec PC, you can spend five bucks or so. Reward them.)
3) The game is pretty tense. Although it doesn't look fast paced there is a lot to keep an eye on, and I reckon my heart rate is higher playing this than if I play a FPS; but since I mainly play strategy games, maybe it seems more intense to me than it would to action-oriented folks.
4) There is a real challenge trying to work out how to make the most of each ship. First time I tried the new shiny ship I bought (stealth mode - yeah, I am the space ninja!) I got utterly trashed (dead ninja... dead ninja again... embarrassingly dead ninja... and oh **** how did he kill me that fast!), repeatedly; now I seem to have got the hang of the ship - but that probably took 2-4 hours, I can still utterly embarass myself, and I'm sure I have a lot to learn. Now I've just bought a new, big scary looking ship (whoa, it's like and aircraft carrier! cool!) and I have exactly no idea what to do with it (useless aircraft carrier! Hey everyone, come and shoot the big hunk of metal cruising impotently through space!) - I thought I understood (hint: find the game's YouTube chanel - there is a tactical primer for each ship - at least, most of them) but no, I'm useless with it... but give me a few hours....
5) It doesn't seem like there is an uber-ship, and the "expensive" ships aren't necessarily better than the cheap ones. (They probably have the potential to be more effective if played really, really well - but that's the point; the player still needs skill.) In fact, sitting in my shiny stealth ship, the craft I least want to see coming up on the enemy team list is actually one of the starting ships; and the vessel I find I'm most effective with is another of the starting ships. It's a bit like a giant game of rock-paper-scissors, and it takes a while to work out what beats what. So, it's about learning and mastery. There's always something out there that can flatten you, and something that is really vulnerable to you.
Basically it's a really interesting, intelligent, pretty tense game.
But having said that... some negatives:
1) Yeah, there are a few snarky folks on team chat. But fortunately chat seems to be text based (so I don;t have to listen to them) and really, there are very, very few (or so it seems to me - unless I've been very lucky.) So, I think I've seen two people being nasty in PvP (and dude, seriously, I know I'm not very good at this game... but if you're going to go all caps and shout insults at me, at least be less cr*p at it than I am!), and none at all in PvE - in PvE everyone seems really polite and reasonable. Speaking of which...
2) The game says it can be played Solo, PvE or PvP. Yeah... but the devs don't really want you to play solo or PvE. Playing solo strikes me as a great idea - I can indulge my desires to expore the environments and try stupid things and tinker with what's possible without potentially letting anyone down... but if I play solo the game gives me zero rewards. So, OK, lets be friendly and cooperative and play PvE... but no, you get fewer rewards for that than PvP. The devs want you to play PvP, and that's how they incentivize you.
3) Match making can be a bit slow. (Especially if I'm playing Solo. Seriously, who exactly am I waiting for?!)
4) The game is too fast paced to be really thoughtfully strategic like a TBS, and too slow to be an adrenaline-fest. I really enjoy the middle ground, but maybe it isn't for everyone.
5) The game maps can get a bit repetitive. (Oh look, for the third game in a row I've started by jumping to sit behind that big asteroid where if I press W+Space and skim over the top I'll find a trench behind that I can drop into as an ambush location....) Not such a problem if your mainly watching your recharge rates and emphasizing the ship-vs-ship abilities, but if you're playing lighter ships and trying to use cover it feels a bit samey.
But basically.... it's free. Try it. Really, what have you got to lose?

). I know a game without a sense of challenge isn't much of a game, but there's a point where it stops being fun and becomes a headache.
I see a lot of downvotes on the negative reviews here, and I understand why. Osmos is gorgeous and it's easy to appreciate it as something fresh. That said, I simply refuse recommend this game on the grounds that it's unenjoyable because of the difficulty. I'd say your mileage may vary, but honestly, I don't expect it to.
Grab it in a bundle or a sale if you want to give it a go, but be prepared to feel aggravated.

I rate Osmos 4/5. Good...
...but this game can quickly become frustrating and is extremely difficult. Indeed, I remember an old "friendlyware" dos-based lunar lander game I had which sought to have fairly realistic controls. This is harder than that game ever was. In this game you control some sort of microscopic super-organism (I always pretend it's some sort of genetically engineered thing) and generally try to make it become the biggest creature in the petri dish (or microscope slide rather). You control it by ejecting parts of itself out in particular directions. Hence moving makes you smaller. You consume any other creatures (well most other creatures) which are also smaller than you are (bump into them to consume them) to get bigger (In a way it reminds me of that old Mortal Engines young adult book except there it was entire cities, not micro-organisms). The bigger you are the more you need to eject to move or even change direction. This dynamic quickly gets really complicated and challenging because you have to balance your need to move (both to hunt and to avoid danger) with your need to consume. I admit the game is now too hard for me to win (I'd have to be totally obsessed with this game to even try at this point) but despite this I still had a lot of fun getting to this point along the way. This game has peaceful, relaxing music and has a great visual athstetic. This is certainly one of the best, though one of the hardest, puzzle games I have ever played.

I don't understand people. This game is one you play to get your rewards.
If you're those kind of people that spend your money on every game because you don't want to grind or have mostly never played an MMORPG, please stop right now.
This game requires you to earn your gear. Sure you can buy everything you NEED off the mart. But, it doesn't matter. Everyone has the same chance to die. The Pay2Play people are talking about are for those who don't want to play the game, buy the items to make yourself look like a "pro."
This game is fair and exactly as said. A FREE-TO-PLAY, Perma Death, Rogue-like, Bulllet-Hell, MMORPG-like game.
The learning curve may be steep but it is rewarding. Like mostly every game, your goal is to get the best which is a UT set.
UT's cannot be bought.
If you want to think of this as a shop, go ahead.
This is a game that's entirely fair. An optional shop is just included for those that don't earn their items, and like almost every MMORPG, fashion items. The in-game trading is where this game shines as well as raiding dungeons with your friends. Your money can buy extra character slots which is really good if you don't want to make another account for free on their actual website which does the same exact thing because 99.99% of all items are tradeable.
Like almost every MMORPG (again), money is the fast way to get items. Definitely not the safest way. If those people buy their items they are half of the time, wasting their own money. Although I do feel bad for those that lose their items they have bought, they can be easily found again.
I also don't like Kabam for adding so much microtransactions but the game itself has not been hurt. Again, everyone has the same chance to get those items found in the shop besides vanity items, and everyone has the same chance to die. If you think you have the skills to keep your items then go ahead. Just remember bullet hells are unforgiving and there's no way to pay to "win" this game.
*Edit: Definitely give it a try if you don't care that you can die in a game, which is especially a bullet-hell.

Alright I have 107 hours into this game and I have to say I loved it. I've beaten the game on normal diffculty and I am currently attempting it on new game +. The game's atmosphere and narrator are amazing as you've heard. The combat is always tense and each ability, target and kill needs to be planned but even before that a good party with synergies is essential, along with well thought ahead supplies. I do have to agree that at a point in the game it get's to be a grind. This isn't so bad as at this point you should be well aware of enemy attacks, party comp and trinkets but RNG can be bad and it can lead to a failed mission. However, you always need to plan for failure in this game retreat often, camp or heal when needed and bring alot of bandages and antivenom. Alot of reviews i've seen, talk about horrble openings to a dungeon where they lose a hero before there turn but the chances of this happening are slim and with specific skills or classes these circumstances can easily be avoided. One example I can give is a mission I went on, I had the 4 starting heros and had went to a max diffculty medium length quest for the first time. The mission was going smooth until the last fight where I got crit a few times and every party member was at their limit but assuming the quest item i needed was ahead i pressed forward and lost 3 heros to a full on combat room. Now in that room I was crit 5 times but I was at fault because i did not retreat when i should have and i did not bring a good party for the mission as I had no way to protect my squishies. In that situation if I had brought a character with a guard, 2 heals or more damage I would have been fine but I only had one main damage dealer. Final word, this is a great game that takes a lot of planning, strategy and understanding enemy attacks, it is not about picking your best early heros and expecting the same positive results on higher level mission

The short rundown is, it's a SoulsLite game with a somewhat more coherent story than the Souls games. 6/10 for effort.
Combat is reminiscent of other action rpgs like The Surge and uh, Dark Souls. There is barely anything that sets this game apart from its contemporaries in this regard. Once you kill a boss, you get a large soul er I mean a large rune, and you can upgrade your weapons once you meet Andre er I mean The Crafter. There's some boss fights, with some that can be regarded as memorable such as The Guardian or the Worshipper (that spams minions at you). Once you drop these bosses, you also get their signature weapon, so that's a nice treat. Weight, endurance and agility become major factors in combat as what you're wearing can affect how fast you can run or swing your blade. Naturally, enemies are less bogged down by this feature so uh, plan ahead. There is also very little, if any, parrying in this game. You can land some finishers, but the way this works is vague at best and not something you should fool yourself into relying on. Eventually, you also get a Megaman handcannon that you can also block with, so you don't have to mess around to switch with a buckler.
Presentation wise, the game looks pretty good. The map and the gear and enemies look well designed and aesthetically pleasing. The map is relatively much smaller than the average Souls map with parts interconnected with doors you can get around to opening, making going back for items and chests less of a hassle when you unlock shortcuts. Animation wise, it's a bit of 50/50 as blows and strikes feel satisfyingly heavy, but your conversations with NPC look janky with some of the gestures not matching the words. Otherwise, much of the game's satisfaction comes from being able to see all the pretty stuff on the maps and beating fancy looking minions to a pulp.
The story is more straightforward: there is a God-like entity Adyr that humans rebelled against, the result is the handshape mountain. Eventually, your King finds a way to split the "good side" from the "evil side" of men and this old god Adyr isn't having any of it and starts invading the human realm with his demons. As you progress, you take down the Lords that the game is titled after and then learn more about what's really going on.
I bought this game as bundle offsite for a fraction of it's price here, so having paid less I feel like I got my money's worth. The game does great with regards to presentation and storytelling, but isn't exceptional and plays it safe with regards to gameplay and combat.

I think it really boils down to whether you play this game mainly for the MyCareer mode, or whether you play MyGM, MyTeam and so on.  I personally play a lot of MyTeam and MyGM, as well as MyCareer, so the games worth it to me.  The game plays a lot better in my opinion.  It feels a lot smoother (although you need to play with the graphical settings, because it isn't very well optimised), defense feels a lot more realistic making scoring more rewarding.  They've finally fixed the player speed issue where a 90+ speed guard would struggle to drive past really slow big men.  Now you can really feel the speed difference in players, and take full advantage of mismatches.
I play a lot of MyTeam, and now you can design your own logo and import it into the game.  Design your own uniforms, even design your own arena.  It's a brilliant addition.  In MyGM they've even added the ability to re-locate your team.
The MyCareer story has really tainted the game, because it doesn't feel like your career at all.  They've totally alienated anyone who isn't black by using a set storyline, and I'm shocked they've made such a monumental error in all honesty.  Having said that, once you get past the rookie season, there are some really good improvements with the things you can do on off days etc.
Overall I'd recommend it if you enjoy playing all the modes available.  I'd definitely exercise caution if you spend 90% of the time playing MyCareer, though.

[after the 4th patch]
Alrighty....let's see....where do I start...
Assassin's Creed Unity is taking place on the 19th Century French Revolution. We follow a new character Arno Victor Dorion in his quest to find the culprit who murdered his adoptive father. He along with his lover, Elise de la Serre (Elise is for revenge, while Arno is simply doing it for redemption).
[Visual]
This is something that many people will more likely agree. This game is truly beautiful. I appreciate the fact that Ubisoft truly made the game really eye candy. You can go to many other places and see the beauty on the poor and rich side of Paris. Of course, to experience this well, you might have to have a good PC to explore it pretty well. Otherwise, it is just a tease to you.
[Gameplay]
The game seems to play out like a refined version of AC1. The parkouring is smooth, but sometimes a bit buggy. The Combat is actually more difficult than one might think, if fighting a bunch of guards, you might end up using alot of smoke bombs and even with all the medicine you take, it might not be enough and you will more likely die. The new combat also removed the free flow kill streaks and counter kills, instead you parry, attack, or dodge. Fans wanted a more difficult challenge, and so they have it. Now the Fanbase is divided about it. For me, it wasn't bad but it could have been better refined. I believe Ubi was trying to add more realism into the AC series, after all, I don't think its normal for someone to kill 10 guards under 1 minute unless you had explosives. Stealth in this game is possible. It's not really the best stealth feature, but it is possible.
[Missions & Other Objectives]
The Main Missions are pretty well done If I may say. You can enter a building, lure them out, riot, go yolo, sneak under the building, etc. This made the game less repetitive. I cannot say the same for the Side Mission however, they do tend to repeat itself, however it does have some interesting stories behind these missions. Investegation Missions is pretty awesome, you play detective and try to figure out who murdered the person, and you have a variety of people to blame. So choose wisely. The Notredamus Puzzle is the most time consuming unworthy chore I ever done. You pretty much do all these painful riddles just to get a reskin altair costume that is merely cosmetic, I personally think it is not worth it. And finally the helix rifts. They are actually part of the storyline and you are basically just trying to escape that era. It was pretty enjoyable to watch and explore this small linear era, but it wasn't that big of a deal as I thought. The game has chest...BUT WAY too many chests....and some Nomad Chests and Initiate chest that are usually not opened to you unless you use a third party program (AC Initiates and the AC Unity app). There are finally co-op missions which aren't bad, but has little to no communication with ur teammates whatsoever and sometimes you will end up with just one fellow player instead of three.
[Customization & Weapons]
This is the only game in the series that has ALOT of customization for your character. Its really REALLY well done and many people enjoyed having their own attire. The weapons are also pretty cool as well. Some of these attires must be unlocked through missions, chests or through club competitions (which hasn't started yet)
[Story]
I won't lie to you guys, I say this as a true fan of the AC storyline, the story....is the weakest of all the series. I will explain with no spoiler as possible. The story focuses soo much on Arno and Elise that everyone else, including historical figures, was forgetable. And even when it focuses on Arno and Elise, it feels pretty meh. I do admit though, their love story is pretty well made. This is pretty much how the story usually ends up going: Arno kills the target, drain his target's memories to find the next target (there is no last words for the victim unfortunatly), kills the next guy, repeat. I know there is story behind all of it, but there is hardly any backstory for that target, not even the main target hardly had a backstory other than the fact he is a sage (but we knew that from the beginning). The ending was....I have to say...it was pretty cliche....and the Modern Day storyline was little to nonexistant , unfortunatly. I am NOT saying the story was horrible, but it is a weak storyline for an AC game.
[Bugs & Glitches]
This is where the game's experience was killed since its launch. It performed badly. Now we are at Patch 4. I can say that Online was fixed but it still isn't perfect. the Crashes however, I still get that. It really does kill the experience for me along with constant stuttering issues. I was able to run this game at around 45 fps with custom high/ultra high setting so it wasn't entirely bad for me. But I really cannot say the same for others. If you check the forums, you will see that many people can't run this game as well as others (this includes people with good PCs and bad PCs.) I also read reports that as if Patch 4, SLI/Crossfire Users perform worse for them.
[Microtransactions]
This one has no affect to us in gameplay, since this is optional. However, this cannot be ignored either. Putting microtransactions on a Single-player/Co-op game, simply to get items early instead of encouraging players to get them through effort is just....wrong. What bothers me is the price....it ranges from $20 - $100 and the helix credits aren't that much either. This is possibly the worst thing I ever saw in an AC game and this sort of business practice has made Ubisoft look like the new EA.
[Recommend?]
This game does have fun in it and I know you see a thumbs down. The reason is because this game may not run for everyone and to top it all, this game still has major issues that needs to be dealt with and the chances of having that is 50/50. You might be one of the lucky ones to run the game with little to no problems, or be one of those unfortunate enough to have a bad experience, Sooo....If you feel you can run this game and can deal with the issues the game has, by all means get it since it can still prove to be enjoyable, BUT please...get this game during discount, because I personally think this isn't worth the full price. This game isn't simply given by Ubisoft haters, but fans alike as well. Trust me...If a lot of people are complaining less about Uplay and more on Unity, then something went seriously bad for Ubisoft. I really worry for the series now. Personally, this game may have been given a recommendation or just a mere complaint about Uplay launcher if there were little bugs and glitches, or at least a good optimization and better support. The damage has been done and there is no doubt that this game became one of the biggest dissapointment of 2014 (sorry my fellow gamers who do like this game, but as much as I enjoyed some of the gameplay given by this game, would have to agree.)

Fallout 4 is an exploration and looting game with a story added onto it. The exploration is rewarded through interesting conversations and sometimes rare loot, but more often is rewarded through material used for crafting better upgrades for your weapons.
Difficulty is adjustable while you play, but sometimes it feels the game doesn't scale itself well. When you start the game, you are weak and learn to save high powered weapons and the power armor for more difficult fights, but with the carrying capacity limited by weight, it is annoying to have to travel back to pick up the power armor. An example I had was when I was running around having difficulty winning fights with my fairly upgraded pipe rifle. I died several times to grenades, overwhelming weapons fire, or the annoying super mutant suiciders. I got frustrated and lowered the difficulty, but then obtained a combat rifle that killed almost anything in one or two shots. I returned the difficulty and was still breezing through combat. I used that rifle for nearly the entire game, and it wasn't even a legendary modded version.
I still recommend this game, but I will state that I feel it is not as good as fallout 3 or fallout new vegas.

Osmos adds an extra element to the familiar "eat objects smaller than you, avoid those bigger than you" gameplay with challenging physics, requiring the player to manage their inertia and gravity. To propel yourself in a certain direction you must jettison pieces of your blob, which other blobs can absorb and grow in the same manner as you. In early stages the main challenge this brings is the decision of what is and isn't worth chasing- that blob might be bigger than you are by the time you get to it. Later levels add to the difficulty by requiring careful management of where your refuse travels and which order you absorb your foes in, lest you accidentally make another blob too large to ever absorb. Osmos doesn't last for too long, but it's a fun ride while it lasts.

A lot like Hotline Miami, but with a lot of extra bells and whistles. This is a good thing: Where Hotline Miami gets very stale after a while because of limited weapon, enemy and environment variety, HS manages to get around this with a variety of different weapons, enemies with different abilities and a different layout for every ship.
It also allows for a variety of gameplay options: Where Hotline Miami is rather straightforward, HS gives you a toolbox of options to use to attain your goals.
Have to assassinate a target but didn't pay enough attention to the fine print on the contract, leaving you facing an army of guards and automated turrets you don't want to chance fighting your way through? Just remember the location of your target in the ship, undock your pod and go hijack a random other ship with weaker defenses. Then return to your target with your newly acquired ship and pummel the region of the other vessel containing your target with missiles. With a bit of luck, he'll get ejected into deep space out of one of the newly created holes, or get blown to pieces by your anti-ship missiles. But watch out for his ship returning fire or it might just be you who ends up getting shot into the void.
TL;DR
Hotline Miami with tactics instead of reflexes, more depth and more space battles.

I kinda got into pinball (virtual and at my local BeerCade) again in the last months. So when the summer sale came along, I purchased about 4 game packs started playing. I was very impressed with Pinball FX2 though there were definitely issues with the game itself.
The UI was very dated and hard to read. It was hard to setup a game with my three year old son.
The graphics were good, but definitely looked PS3/360 era.
There were odd framerate issues on some tables with full reflections and the action zoom cameras being used.
I still played the heck out of it, but as soon as I heard FX 3 was on the horizon, and the game engine would be upgraded to DX11, I decided to stand back and wait for the release. I'm glad I did.
Almost all the tables got graphical upgrades outside of just using DX11. Mars for example got some texture updates and all the effects look cleaner. Mars also had a zoom in framerate issue, and I run an i7 with an nVidia GTX970. It shouldn't slow down ever, which means it was an issue with older non-optimized FX. Everything is good now, I've cranked up the settings to get it to break and it has not yet.
Another thing is multiplayer. I'm a professional adult with two kids, I can't invite friends over to play some games anymore. Being able to play other people and see how the other side is doing on-line is a fantastic feature. Coupled with the massive UI overhaul, the game has never been easier to navigate.
Anyways, this is a worthwhile update to a already great pinball sim. This makes me want to build a virtual table. I highly recommend anybody into pinball to give it a bash.

The best Hollywood hacking game ever! Alright, so there are like three of those ever, but this is still all kinds of great. The missions here each feel like there's a touch of character, a reason behind them that just passes the threshold of generic gamestory and hits that spot of "I am a hacker at my computer." (Even if you're just ultimate script kiddie.)
Hacknet is an ever evolving experience, constantly throwing you through unexpected hoops and challenges that all manage to make perfect sense in its world while still being completely inside all the mechanics of the game. The best of these are all spoilers and are best when they take you by surprise. The moments of, "I didn't think that could happen!" Followed by, "Of course, that makes perfect sense," then, "but how do I fix this?" All within all the rules you've seen thus far. It's like you're always in control, always the hacker, actually working to hack the hackables.
Oh, and the music is spectacualr. A combination of tailor made electronic-technomancer and artists like Carpenter Brut provide the background to Hacknet and I've never seen better use of mixing. It understands when songs should be quiet, when they should hit you, when to be solem and when to kick you into high gear. Coupled with an incredible UI that proves itself time and time again to make more sense than you thought leaves you more immersed than you can be with real hacking.

Very fun. The concept of the game is simple, you fly around dragging a bunch of weights that are smashed into enemies while trying not to crash into obstacles. No online, but local multiplayer is pretty solid if you've got people around and multiple gamepads. There aren't very many maps, but they're dynamic and faily distinct. The game also slowed down quite a bit in multiplayer as players moved apart and the game had to zoom out. This was on my laptop however, which is nothing close to a powerhouse, but still suggests some optimization issues.
I don't think I'd recommend the game without a controller, I just can't imagine fluidly controlling the ships without one. Fortunately, it's been friendly with all types that I've tried (360 and logitech).
If nothing else, it's great arcade time waster.

tl;dr New features try hard but add little, overall very good though. Minor stability issues.
I get the distinct impression with this game they really wanted to expand on the usual gameplay of the Lego games (don't worry, the usual gameplay is all there still and if you like Lego games you will still like this one).  The addition of materials for crafting probably sounded great in theory, but in practise adding in a requirement to farm items from various sources coupled with terrain that enjoys sending said items spinning off the edges of cliffs was more frustrating than fun. It can be forgiven though because once you complete the storyline you can simply buy resources using your studs.
I thought the way it used the mithril (gold) bricks to actually make stuff was also cool. Initially I thought this would cut down on time spent moving through the character selection screens, but since it takes just as long to select an item, some items refuse to equip if you have other items already equipped and some items repeatedly fail to work consistantly (flails for example), and your character returns to default if you switch to another character.. for the most part it was simply easier to switch characters rather than fight with your items.
The red bricks are scattered around the game in the form of side quests and are indistinguishable from other sidequests making them hard to target. This makes it very hard to prioritise things like multiplier bricks and makes this the first game where I've completed it without hitting the achievements for studs - I actually had to go and grind some purple studs to get that achievement.
The map and mini map are excellent, with the option to zoom in/out and set waypoints for quests/bricks etc. The main quest I'm guessing is based off the film which I haven't gotten around to seeing since I rather loved the book growing up and thus contains a bunch of stuff that wasn't in the original and inexplicably seems to be missing the ending, but it's still fun. The side quests are varied and there are bunches of chained quests which add a sense of continuity. They actually managed to make using the custom characters a part of the game as well which was great as that's a feature I normally entirely ignore.
I've had the most stability problems with this game over all the others I've played. Although it never outright crashed and could always be rescued with a save and quit or eagle trigger I had it repeatedly freeze during travel, during forging when making multiple items and when purchasing new characters. There were also the problems with inventory items and for some reasons some items - most notably flails - simply refusing to work properly on some characters.
Overall though it is very fun and since no loss of progress was included in the problems with it, they are entirely bearable.

TL:DR - Was not worth the £4.00 on sale and I love the dark souls series expecting this to be somewhat similar. Nope, never again am I buying a souls-esque game by deck 13. The game has so much potential and I feel its all been squandered because of really bad game design choices.
I love the dark souls franchise I have played through all 3 games and mostly enjoyed them (I'm looking at you DS2). When I bought this game I had already heard it wasn't that good but I was willing to give it the benefit of the doubt that it had its own flavour which could be interesting to delve into. OH BOY WAS I WRONG.
The game suffers from too many problems that it feels more of a chore to get through than enjoy. A few of these problems include; clunky controls, an awkward camera, terrible and lazily designed bosses, characters I could not give 2 s***s and a f*** about.
Dont get me wrong the game does introduce interesting mechanics such as xp modifiers based on less use of checkpoints and storing your xp so you don't lose it all trying to defeat a boss. But for every good thing that this game produces I can also list two bad things that make the game almost unplayable (note almost as I have beaten the Judge).
I even tried the DLC that I accidentally stumbled upon and it was god awful, aspects like the level design and trash mobs to even the end boss (which in the end is just reskin of a trash mob enemy) are so fundamentally s*** I would rather attempt to suck my own d*** than go through that section again.
Many areas feel repetitive with the same concrete hallways that you'll wander through to the point where I swear I saw the same place twice even though I was in two different locations. The game does however take an awesome page from Dark Souls with shortcuts as surprisingly enough many areas lead back onto themselves and can allow you to choose alternative paths to the same area (you could be more comfortable facing X enemies rather than Y enemies and therefore choose the X path).
Each of the bosses feel uninspired and lack the creativity many other games have. Most are humanoid beings with 1 or 2 melee combos and a ranged attack which can easily be dodged (assuming you went with a lighter build). Some bosses can be easily cheesed with simple tactics, for example with the Annihilator I baited his ranged attack and followed up with sprinting attack -> backed up and repeated. Some bosses also have different phases but the problem is the game points it out to you and as a result you expect the boss to change when it reaches that marker in its health bar.
Speaking of rolling, this game has less rolling directions than Dark Souls 1 which came out 6 years ago. What does this mean you might ask? In these types of games rolling can be a viable way to avoid damage and get around an opponent, in DS1 you can roll in 8 directions (forward, backwards, left, right, and each diagonal variant in between), in DS2 and 3 you can roll in any direction within the 360 degree circle even when in an unlocked camera. Unfortunately LotF only has four rolling directions and you can guess what they are. It severely handicaps players who dont like the sword and board style of play and can make the game infuriating when trying to out maneouver your opponent.
Trash mobs can sometimes be ridiculously powerful to the point where the game's difficulty can spruce up because you didn't expect the next enemy to one shot you and thus causing you to lose a certain amount of progression. This, although a problem, I could deal with because I know not to underestimate any enemy but it surprised me how easily I could die to certain enemies.
All in all it felt awful to fuly play through this damn game but I was hoping the ending would be fulfilling and once again I was wrong. **SPOILER ALERT IF YOU F***ING CARE** Some mountains shift then the game tells you your decisions which in the end mean nothing. If you really want to get into a difficult RPG soulslike game, start with DS2 SotFS because this s*** aint worth your time.

Alright, I gave this game another go after all the patches and that I cooled off, and to be honnest I ended up liking the game much more. In between my first time playing it and my new playthrough, I've done multiple essays, one of which was about the French Revolution, so this made me much more aware of the historical/political events in the game. Reading the database entries made the entire experience feel a little more immersive. Knowing this, the story was more bareable and enjoyable (even if this isn't the better story experience the franchise has to offer). The characters made more sense on my second playthrough.
Gameplay wise, the game didn't improve uppon my first playthrough. I still believe the combat was still somewhat easy (harder than before, but still easy). The AI was still dumb and laughable, same goes to the cover system which is clunky at best. The stealth was a step foward and a step backwards, it improved and worsten on many occasions. The side missions are okay but became a chore after a while so I stopped doing the typical Ubisoft sand box thing. The assassination missions are some of the best in the series, reminding me of the first Assassin's Creed game.
As for the port, it has majorly improved since release but I still do notice some issues: frames still drop in cutscenes for some odd reason and there are still bugs applenty. However it is much, MUCH better than what it was before.
In conclusion, if you like the series, I do somewhat recomend this. I believe it is a step foward and a step backwards for the franchise. Purchasing it during a sale would be optimal, 69.99 CAD $ is far too much.

As someone with a history with Minecraft, I came to this when a friend bought it for me to get me to play with them, expecting a 2D minecraft clone.
Its more then that..
I like to call it a choose your own side scroller..
The crafting mechanics are easy to use, with different stations you can make that allow the creation of different things, but there are no recipies to remember, you can even search and if you have the resources you can make the item..
The space travel option adds an interesting twist with different planets having a range of materials and hostile or passive native life.
Don't think you can settle in easily though..  This game is brutal when you first enter a new tier of planet.   The equipment you start with is barely going to keep you alive if you're very carefull...   But once you get the hanf of things, and build better armor and weapons you'll do just fine.  Then you finish the needed quest paths to gain access to the next tier of star system...  And the gear that let you dominate your old sector .... Well you'll be wanting upgrades all over again..
You'll find colonies, crashed ships and occassional wandering merchants as well as native flora or fauna...
All told what may seem to be mine craft with a 2D 16bit asthetic is a deeply rewarding game of exploration and cration.

The nightly builds show you that development for this game did not end when they got a sizable amount of money unlike some other early access games out there.
If you want a lot of content and replayability now, look somewhere else. If you want to see a game go through quite a number of changes (albeit slow on the stable end), then this early access game can give you that.

I finished all five episodes of The Walking Dead and it was fantastic. This game is the definition of story rich. It has a stable plot with well developed characters that aggrivate you beyond belief yet you hope that they stay alive throughout the entire game. I think the part about TWD that I loved the most was the friendship between Lee (the main character) and Clementine (the little girl he takes care of). Although Lee isn't Clem's biological dad, I can see that he becomes to love her like she's his own daughter, even though this is a video game with graphics that remind me of a comic book. Lee shows the audience that it's so important to be a strong person through tough times and that he would do anything to protect this little girl he met by chance during the start of the zombie apocalypse. There are sad parts that pull at your heart and parts that warms it back up. This game is a must buy and I give it a 9/10. If anything, the one thing I didn't like was at some parts, you have to replay the combat scenes because of how hard they can become. So, 9/10.

This is going to be a positive review, for only one reason - the game's potential. This game could be great; it will be great, tha's a certainty that was established as the devs showed the Starbound community how open and committed they are to this great game.
However, if you're looking to buy and play something amzing RIGHT NOW, grab Terraria. Starbound is what the devs called a 'spiritual sucessor' to Terraria; that is, main gmeplay elements and teh art style are the same in both games. However this game is barely an engine, and if you're looking for something fun and enjoyable I suggest at least waiting for the winter update coming January 2015, if not longer. It's a bit like early Minecraft in that there was stuff to do, but there came a point (very quickly) where the game said 'Ok I'm done now, go build and explore and stuff' and left you to it. This is what Starbound is now.
All in all, do you like trying out indev games and exploring the engine and mechanics of games? This is for you.
Do you like to get a good complete game and play it with some friends, having a good time without bugs and lack of stuff to do? Then wait a year or so.

A lot like Hotline Miami, but with a lot of extra bells and whistles. This is a good thing: Where Hotline Miami gets very stale after a while because of limited weapon, enemy and environment variety, HS manages to get around this with a variety of different weapons, enemies with different abilities and a different layout for every ship.
It also allows for a variety of gameplay options: Where Hotline Miami is rather straightforward, HS gives you a toolbox of options to use to attain your goals.
Have to assassinate a target but didn't pay enough attention to the fine print on the contract, leaving you facing an army of guards and automated turrets you don't want to chance fighting your way through? Just remember the location of your target in the ship, undock your pod and go hijack a random other ship with weaker defenses. Then return to your target with your newly acquired ship and pummel the region of the other vessel containing your target with missiles. With a bit of luck, he'll get ejected into deep space out of one of the newly created holes, or get blown to pieces by your anti-ship missiles. But watch out for his ship returning fire or it might just be you who ends up getting shot into the void.
TL;DR
Hotline Miami with tactics instead of reflexes, more depth and more space battles.

This game is a true example of how you do a sequel.
A brilliant mix and match of turn based strategy on one hand and base and soldier management on the other.  This game evokes the perfect feeling of just wanting to try 1 more mission as you unlock more and more stuff in the base for you to use in combat.  From a mech companion, new soldier ability, new gun and even new psychic abilities.
The story is well written and the pacing is good.  You learn about the world around you as you go along and as your scientists and technicians research new stuff you get about a page worth’s of lore to read if you want.  There is the occasional banter on your home base as well but you can ignore that for the most part.
The game has its bugs of course.  Sometimes the maps feel a little samey even though they are procedural and there have been the occasional AI glitch or graphical glitch but those aren’t a huge issue.
The game boasts modding support and it has a rather powerful set of tools for mod making.  If I can recommend any then go look at the Long War collection of mini mods.  All together they make for a rather fantastic set of mods to greatly expand your game.

Summary: Great entry into the LEGO (Insert Franchise Here) series. Bring a controller.
Travlers Tales is nothing if not consistant. Starting with LEGO Star Wars, they hit on a formula that has served them well for years. The games are the best kind of collet-a-thon: rewarding exploration and the act of collection with useful or fun gameplay changes. That on it's own is delicious cake, but the thick layer of icing on that cake is the worlds they recreate, more or less faithfully, while editing the stories down to rapid-fire, goof-filled cutscenes that neither fail to deliver narritive or get at least one laugh-out-loud moment (average 1 per game). The LEGO Hobbit is no exception, though there are some new sprinkles on the LEGO game cake that make it less of a gameplay rehash than others in the series.
The game is clearly built on whatever engine LEGO Marvel used, and the difference between LEGO LOTR and LEGO Hobbit is astounding. Moving and attacking are fluid, aiming ranged characters is vastly improved (read: it actually works), and non-lego environment's have gotten a graphical update. The "Voice Acting" from LEGO LOTR is back too, though MUCH better integrated into the cutscenes than it was in LOTR.
Gameplay-wise, LEGO Hobbit brings a single twist on the standard LEGO formula that manages to mix things up a bit, and that twist is "Loot". Loot can be one of a few kinds of things that drop when Lego stuff is destroyed: several varities of gems and metals, several varites of food, and several building materials like "Rock". (You will have a lot of rock.) Metals and gems are usually aquired via a little reflex-based mining minigame, the others are aquired simply by destroying lego "stuff" and enemies. You can use this loot to craft items (Like crafting in LOTR, but slightly more involved) or to build larger lego structures at specific points in the world. You can also hord them, like a certain dwarf king, but that wont get you the mithril blocks or crafting patterns.
Other than that, Lego Hobbit doesn't do anything too different. There's also the matter of it missing characters from the LOTR game, which is a bit of dissapointment, especially for the huge ensamble piece that the LOTR universe is. More of a dissapointment is that it only covers the first two Hobbit movies, with the third promised as DLC. While the game certainly stands on it's own, it's a much weaker sell at $30+DLC. If you absolutely can't stand having the story halted 2/3rds in, you might want to wait for the inevitable combo pack.
All in all, LEGO Hobbit is a great addition to the series. It does just enough to keep it from being the same old thing again, while maintaining the polish and humor of the games before it. If you like Lego Games, buy it. If you're tired of them, you'll probably still be bored with this one.
Also, PLAY WITH A CONTROLLER. This game is designed around a controller experience, and is uncomfortable to the point of unplayability without one.

Quick overview, is this a good game?  In my opinion, YES.
Is this a game for everyone?  No, not at all, but I feel many would enjoy it.
Pros:
-Very balanced with regular updates to keep the meta healthy
-Good hud
-All ships are viable, even the cheap ones and starter ships
-Pretty good tutorial for getting down the basics
-The game is very polished and the controls are tight and responsive, it definitely feels like you're managing a big capital ship
-Ships are very unique to each other and come with strengths and weaknesses.
-Game is easy to pick up, hard to master, learning all the ships is important too and the game provides ship hightlights on youtube and how to play them, you can also test any ship you want in the firing range as much as you want, get a feel for how they work, if you want to get that ship, and some insight on what to look out for and counter.
Cons:
-Not enough tools for pinging the map and communicating with your team quickly
-It can be hard to micromange between enemy ships and ally ships when it comes to commanding squadrons and drones or having said things protect or engage another squadron.
-The game is pretty unforgiving to new players, making too many mistakes, especially as a team can make you lose a match fast.
-Grinding for some of the ships can be a nightmare, it's easier just to spend a few dollars on a ship instead of grinding 900k credits for it, and if you're not a founder or someone that bought a pack you only get about 8k per match on average.  Who in the right mind is going to want to grind for over 100 games for one ship?  Luckily there are cheaper options.
-Tutorial doesn't really go in depth on how you have to react to things ahead of time rather than what is currently happening if you're not in a zone.  For example, if an enemy is capping a forward station, and they are about to cap it before you're jumping, DON'T jump to where they are, just jump to base and intercept them since they're obviously going there.  Making a simple mistake like this, can cost your team the game because you have to wait to be able to jump again if you already wasted the return home jump.  Or tricks like, jumping home, followed by a normal jump go off seperate cool downs and can save you 10-20 seconds on response time, which can make all the difference in the world.

Coming from someone who put around 600 hours into 2k15, NBA2k16 is the best and most complete sports game I have ever played. It has it's bugs and issues, but it is the most real to life version of NBA 2k ever.
PROS
-2k did a great job this year of reducing the "cheese" in every way (It is VERY hard to draw charges, run baseline for an easy 2, or pull up for a contested 3 and knock it down for example)
-You feel like you are in complete control of your players much more than last year, mainly because you rarely are ever stuck in animations
-It isn't easy to score. This might sound bad, but this makes the game so much better. As I'm sure some people remember in 2k15, RT+X to the basket or shooting a 3 with any half decent 3pt shooter gave you a free basket.
-Excellent graphics, the best looking sports game I have ever seen.
-Fluid and varied gameplay, overall fun to play with many different modes, difficulties, and playstyles
-Much better connection to servers/lag issues than previous years
-Music/overall atmosphere- pregame/postgame show with Shaq, Ernie, and Kenny is great. The music is a wide variety of genres and cultures, mainly hip-hop and rap however so if you arent into that kind of music you can turn it off
-Lots of settings/options, very customizeable and in some gamemodes you can even adjust gameplay sliders (percentage of 3's going in for example)
-VERY ACCURATE RATINGS. This is so important, because many cards last year had extremely over-boosted ratings, which contributed a lot to the "cheese"
CONS
-Some framerate issues, especially in cutscenes, but I have a 750 ti and I'm doing fine framerate wise with some medium, some high settings
-"BE THE STORY" except all you do in mycareer is follow the exact storyline Spike Lee has laid out for you, rarely being able to ever make your own decisions
-Sometimes the game can be frusturating, players missing wide open shots when it seems like you should make it or things like that
-Lots of bugs unrelated to gameplay, cards having the wrong ratings (Rookie vince carter has the same ratings as the 15+years later vince carter) and other things like that, but im sure these will be fixed
Overall- 9/10, I really recommend this game to anyone who remotely enjoys basketball, I don't watch the NBA all that much but I love me some 2k.

It was worth it - for me, and i hope it would be too for you if you give it more time.
Normally the first thing i do is check the GPU and CPU requirements; if no AMD is listed i would immediately skip it and move on. This one made me pause to take a closer look because it was discounted heavily. After perusing the forum discussions, it was apparent that it had problems with both Nvidia and AMD GPUs, yet some AMD users reported it runs fine so i took a calculated low-risk purchase of it.
Lots of talk about it being clunky and slow. Well it was perceived that way for the most part when i started, being used to immediate response and animations which can be interrupted at will. Well not this one, once clicked you had to follow through so timing of strikes and blocks are crucial and has to be done with a keen eye of the opponent and the other on your energy reserve. Well not one eye here and one eye there really but you need good peripheral vision.
The combat system while being frequently describe as slow is due to 2 things; weight of gear and weapons, AND realistically it takes time to move from one stance to another; there's no luxury of frame skip or time skip where you can switch motion and animation instantly. Remember you expend energy on every motion and quickly mashing buttons will exhaust your hero to the point that
. There's no luxury of time dilation either where everything slows but you. So yeah i think combat is as realistic as it gets.
My bad depleting energy reserves does not disable ability to strike, only to dodge or run. The reason for not being able to move is due to enemy's strong attack; it may stun or stagger thereby causing momentary immobility.
As can be inferred in previous paragraphs, you can probably see that LOTF can be both hard and easy depending on how you play it. Grinding in order to level-up and farming for loot may be required in order to progress. Key points; save energy and mana or as is called in the game 'magic energy'. Patience, don't look for easy kill on the bosses unless you've grinded too much in your backtracking.
Why is this game easy? Ordinary enemies wait for you, they don't hunt you down even when you're well within visual range unless you shoot/strike first. Plus there is an easy stealth mode where you can sneak-up behind an enemy and perform special kills; heavy boots or armor clunky clangs are not taken into account. There is also a rush and bash technique to knock your opponent down or shoot from afar with a range weapon to wear down your enemies or lure it closer for a finishing blow. Bosses need to be handled with good tactics; plus being at the right level helps a lot. Bosses can be really hard until you figure out what works.
So yeah, it's hard, it's easy and there's a lot of farming for loot in the process. There's crafting later in the game that allows you to improve your gear but i haven't reached that stage yet; you need to find an NPC to unlock that feature.
Runs smooth but changing screen resolution for the first time may cause it to cycle modes endlessly while flickering at a fraction of a second. No glitch or crash encountered during play. Only one time it freezes for a few seconds during combat then resumed normally.

There are many reasons to both like and dislike Fallout 4. However, the reason I'm leaving this negative review is very simple: the microtransactions.
I would just roll my eyes and ignore the microtransaction Creation Club/Paid Mods, but Bethesda made that very difficult as they decided to pre-load the files on my PC. I don't want any of the paid mods nor will I be buying any of them. But apparently, I have to host them on my PC's hard drive regardless.
And then there's the fact that the paid mods crash your game if you use regular mods (like the vast majority of us do). They mess up your game by the simple fact of the matter that they force your mods to load in alphabetical order. As anyone who's ever modded their game knows - that can cause none of them to work at best and an immediate crash to desktop (CTD) at worst.
Plus there's the fact that with every update and if you use the Fallout 4 Script Extender (F4SE), you need to wait for the F4SE team to release a new version of F4SE in order to play your game - meaning you will likely not be able to play your game for several days. For normal update content, this would be perfectly fine and acceptable. However, if it's just to add new files to the Creation Club (and preload them on everyone's systems), that's not acceptable. At all.
Pete Hines said on Twitter that Bethesda isn't forcing the Creation Club on anyone. However, by forcing all of us to download Creation Club BA2 files on our systems, regardless of whether or not we actually purchase them, they ARE forcing the Creation Club on us. It's On-Disc DLC all over again, only this time it's on my actual hard drive instead of a disc. Did Bethesda learn nothing from Horse Armor in Oblivion? Or even from the paid mods through Steam just two years ago? WE DON'T WANT THIS!!!
