Heat Signature is a top-down stealth-not-really shooter sort of hybrid.  Gameplay's a bit like Hotline Miami, but with the ability to pause during combat to plan out your moves, aim shots, and whatnot.  It's also a rogue-light-lite, in a sense.  Characters hardly last one hour, whether it's due to you retiring them (once a character does their fair share of missions, their ability to contribute to the main cause depletes), or them dying in some fashion.  It's also rogue-light-lite in the sense that outright 'failure' is hard to accomplish.  Usually getting caught means you're shot out the airlock and start to bleed out to death, and have to catch yourself with your escape/breach pod before you fully die.  You have 30 seconds bleed-out time, period, so the more you get vented, the less time you'll have to live.  Missions are also tend to be hard to fail.  Things won't go to plan, but chances are you probably won't outright fail the mission.
Allow me to provide an example: Enter Babu Polk, on her personal mission for revenge.  To capture the captain that had killed her mother.  Now, personal missions for characters tend to be some of the hardest in the game, and this ship was definitely no slouch.  The guards were armed with personal teleporters that allowed them to investigate suspicious activity instantly, the captains armored with emergency shields and armor plating, and the ships was armed head to toe with sentry guns.  Our hero is equipped with an array of personal teleporters, key-copiers, a self-charging teleporter trap (great for sending guards to space!) and a really heavy hammer.  A heavy armament, well-planned, a simple mission.
The first squad Babu encountered had a captain.  The captain had armor.  The hammer doesn't pierce armor.  I had forgotten this.
The capture target is also armored.  I had also forgotten this.
What follows is a ridiculous chase around the ship in an attempt to knock out the pilot of the vessel before a two minute alarm expired.  Hammers were swung, tossed, teleported back into hand and swung again.  Locked doors were teleported past to knock out the guard that had the keycard and steal it for myself.  Armored guards were lured into traps to jettison them out into space.  Babu herself got shot and vented out the airlock twice in all the commotion.  After tossing or knocking out about 80% of the ship's crew, the caper finally ended when our heroine took to the helm of the ship, flew it to an allied station, entered, sold off everything she had, and bought up a non-lethal, armor-piercing assault rifle to capture the target.
This is the main allure of Heat Signature.  Getting a plan, grabbing tools, and then screwing it up hilariously.  The thing is, screwing things up tends to never be the end of the world.  The game is rather generous with the various gadgets and gizmos it gives you, and all neccessary information is given upfront from mission select: map size, guard/captain modifiers, time limits and alerts.  So while your plan to wait out the guards to access terminals and knock them out one by one may have failed, you probably do have the tools to rewire the sentry guns, a teleporter to jump into the room with the mission-loot, and a gun to shoot the window and launch yourself into space, remote-piloting the pod to pick you up before you run out of breath.
As they say in Dwarf Fortress, losing is fun.  And while you may not lose, per say, things will not go to plan.
And man, is it fun when they don't.

I'm quite a big fan of the LEGO games, mainly for these three reasons: they're highly replayable, enjoyable and casual. Hours of gameplay can easily be put into a single LEGO game for unlocking extra collectables or other LEGO characters among many other things. Just like in other LEGO games,
is an addictive and light-hearted experience that will take hours for LEGO- and Lord of the Rings-fans alike to complete and perfect, but that's also it's main problem just like with any previous LEGO title... it's more or less the same.
The Pros:
·
stays true to the new popular prequel trilogy (The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey, The Hobbit: Desolation of Smaug and the upcoming The Hobbit: There and Back Again) in both story and lore. Just like in LEGO Lord of the Rings you'll play through the three movies (There and Back Again announced to be DLC when the final movie is released) with some added humorous elements, like silly LEGO figurines holding an umbrella above their heads in order to avoid being hit by falling bricks.
· Didn't get a chance to watch the movies? This game will tell you the same story with entertaining LEGO moments and buildable & destructable LEGO constructions to add a ton of extra content without ever forgetting about the story that needs to be told. Don't let that keep you from buying
if you have already watched The Hobbit movies released so far though! I have seen both movies plenty of times (six times each) and I still find this game just as enjoyable if not a bit more entertaining than watching the movies. It adds an open world LEGO experience that stays true to both LEGO-imagination and the same beautiful world we've seen in The Hobbit and the Lord of the Rings trilogy by Peter Jackson.
· There's a ton of stuff to do, like collecting items for crafting (which is an entertaining new addition to the LEGO series), sidequests, replaying missions with certain characters in order to get all the level-specific collectables (for example: Legolas can create a "staircase" of arrows and dwarves can't) or simply running around destroying constructions to collect LEGO studs that will help to fill up your Master Burglar meter. Still...
The Cons:
· That's more or less exactly what we've been doing in the past couple of LEGO games. For those who are not as interrested in the Lord of the Rings universe as I am among many many others, the game(s) can quickly get repetetive and lose their charm. Someone who has played LEGO Marvel Superheroes for example will find lots of simularities. Don't get me wrong, the game offers a lot of content, but if you've spent countless hours collecting every single collectible in any previous LEGO title, I'll doubt you'll want to do the same with
.
The Visuals:
· The visuals are quite simular to LEGO Marvel Superheroes, which is a good thing.
is a combination of LEGO-built structures and normal textures (for example, roads and mountains are not (or not always) made from LEGO bricks). The lighting is gorgeous and the animations are charmingly funny. Overal
is another beautiful addition to the LEGO series.
Final Verdict:
· Hardcore LotR-fans and casual gamers alike will definately enjoy
. With a high replayability and even bigger satisfaction,
is a worthy addition to both the LEGO universe and the Lord of the Rings universe. 9/10.

I entered a beginner level dungeon in the warrens. My party had a vestal, a highwayman, a houndmaster, and a leper.
In my very first encounter in that dungeon I encountered 4 spiders. 2 webbers, 2 spitters.
The first spitter stunned and marked my vestal.
My houndmaster attacked a spitter. It rolled the lowest possible damage which is 6.
My leper used hew. It missed. Twice.
Then these ♥♥♥♥ING SPIDERS BOTH BIT MY MARKED VESTAL AND BOTH GOT A CRIT. FIRST SPITTER CRIT FOR 15 DAMAGE AND GOT A BLIGHT. SECOND SPITTER CRIT FOR 14 DAMAGE AND GOT A BLIGHT. THEN MY VESTAL (with base death resist at 66%, which is 2/3) DIED IMMEDIATELY TO THE FIRST TICK OF BLIGHT. ON THE VERY FIRST ROUND.
I want to like this game. But this 'game' isn't really what you would call a video game in the traditional sense. Apart from a tiny bit of macro (which amounts to getting money, upgrading gear and getting more money) the actual dungeon-crawling part of the game is nothing but a glorified random number generator where the game decides pretty much everything for you. Sure, there are modifiers you could stack to tip the odds a little bit more in your favour, but the variance on every single metric is so high (the ridiculous damage variance in this game can mean that one character can do half of a monster's HP bar in one round, then 100% of it the next. There is no way to control or modify this. If a character says it can do 7-14 damage, there is NOTHING YOU CAN DO to control whether it does 7 or 14 damage this round).
This means that pretty much the entire game you're praying for things beyond your control to go your way. Praying that your healer doesn't get chainstunned into an immediate death. Praying that the enemy stress dealer doesn't dodge 5 attacks in a row. Praying that the turn order (which is loosely decided in order of speed but might as well be completely ♥♥♥♥ing random, enemies slower than you can and will go before you) is in your favour. Praying that you don't miss, and don't lowroll on the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ damage variance of your every attacking move. So many things have to go right for you to get a single successful fight in one single dungeon run in your campaign, and the only thing you can do to impact the outcome of all this is applying some do-nothing buffs and pressing attack while praying.
When you 'play' Darkest Dungeon, you're not playing a game. You're watching a movie, the positive or negative outcome of which is predetermined by the RNG seed generated by your computer. All the buttons you get to press just exist to give you an illusion of control. Don't waste dozens of hours trying to defeat this poorly made game, just watch a B-grade horror movie on the same lovecraftian theme and be done with it. That will save you lots of time, energy, money and anguish.

If you enjoy roguelikes or card battle games, this is pretty much the top of both genres, in my opinion.
Created by current Hearthstone developer Peter Whelan, it was the game that got him noticed and hired by Blizzard.  I've heard the very primitive/silly art in the game was done by his pre-teen daughters.
Don't be put off by the art, this is one of the deepest, most well designed strategy games around.  Similar to other pseudo-random games like FTL, you may be put off in the beginning by "bad luck", but know there are highly talented players who can go on incredible win streaks by optimizing every single decision made in a game.
Classes have mana (blue), action points (green), HP, can get an equipment slot (rather than having to draw and play an Equipment card, you just start with it in play), and have all sorts of different talents with a cooldown based on their class.  Thieves find extra treasure, warriors can duplicate 1 card or go berserk, monks can delete unwanted cards from their deck... there are 4 starting classes and 10 more to unlock, including advanced ones like the professor (steals and keeps cards from a monster's deck) and dragons (can't use shops but can devour monsters whole, and depending on the monster type devoured gets various bonuses and different cards)
Red "attack" cards are played for "free."  Most classes start with the lowly "attack 1" but only certain classes get access to the high attack based cards like Rallying Stroke.  Blue spell cards require mana.  Some classes like the Necromancer steal mana and can start combat with a very high starting mana count, which means they may not need to put different cards that add mana to them before they can finish off opponents.   Other types of casters may want to equip a Staff that deals damage as they gain mana through cards.   Even some "non casters" get access to spells like Blur (half physical damage taken for 1 turn), I had a monk with a very small deck that included 1 Wisdom (Gain 3 mana, draw a card) and 1 Blur and by cycling and drawing could usually draw its entire deck every turn and keep that Blur up the entire fight.
Explore a map and fight 70+ different monster types.  Get to know them, because they all have different strengths, weaknesses, and gimmicks.  Most classes have various abilities that let them explore, scout the map and see which monsters will be easy, which will be hard, and which may be impossible for your particular deck.  A wizard may want to teleport past a particularly nasty magic-immune monster.  Or, it may hatch a plan to try one of the toughest monsters first, use its long cooldown that doubles damage and lowers resistance for 1 turn, (and maybe use Flee if it gets a bad draw).  It may want to fight some medium-difficulty monsters first and time its level ups off of easier monsters to maximize the amount of healing gained.  If it scouts that the final Floor Boss is a Titan, it may want to save money for that Crumble (exile equipment or Prayer card) in a shop to deal with its nasty starting equipment.  If you don't know the last boss is a Titan, you maybe didn't save for the Crumble, and you probably get owned.
There's lots of things to unlock, and there is a system where every game gives you a score.  You can use points from your accumulating score to "buy" achievement unlocks that have been particularly stubborn.

-It's not pay to win. Everything can be unlocked with in game credits, except for ship skins.  Ship skins don't effect performance, so no big deal there.

-People are pretty nice in this game.  Even when I started out and didn't know what I was doing, people were still nice about it.
-Pretty good tutorial mode. You can play solo games to get used to a ship.  You can also fly a ship in a firing range before you buy it.

-Every player makes a difference in the game.  Sometimes I feel like I'm just a bullet sponge, but at least that means my teammates are dealing damage without dying.

Ok
So its been 2 years since the release of starbound onto steam
And i can tell you right away.
If you are a newcomer or a returning player
ALOT has changed since the past 2 years have passed
What is Starbound?
Starbound is a 2D based sandbox game with RPG elements along with a heavy influence on spelunking
The main goal of the game is to repair and upgrade your ship which you escape from earth with due to someone unleashing there hentai folder onto the planet (Im serious)
Along with improving your ship you will also be upgrading many other things.
Such as armor and weapons
Along with your overall performance with you're main tool "The Matter Manipulator"
Will i like Starbound?
If you like terraria or anything similiar to terraia then yes for sure you will.
But it does have some drawbacks
With Terraria being very heavy on the RPG elements with things such as damage boosting items and armor set bonuses that are essential for progression
Starbound has very little in ways of progression.
Not in a bad way at least.
The way you progress in Starbound is in my opinion very linear as it involves you just mineing ores and crafting armor with said ores. But towards the later end gear you will start to require alot more stuff to make armor and weapons. Making it more challenging
Should i get Starbound?
If you have any idea how bad most if not all games that are in beta/alpha with a full price tag on them. You expect them to be bad.
But Starbound is faaaaaaaaaaaaar from that
Starbound is offering alot more with each update and the most recent one which was published has overhauled alot of what starbound player found frustrating or linear to do
Along with this update they also added Steam intergration to the game which in turn adds the steam workshop and steam freind invitation instead of hosting a dedicated server/offline LAN server
My total time clocked on this game would be much higher if there wasent so many other games to play.
But if you want something that is relaxing and easy to play then Starbound is just for you

PARTICLE MACE is an awesome game. It makes a lot of fun and I definitly recommend it, but it's not perfect.
Each time you kill an enemy or asteroid the screen shakes. While this makes every kill very rewarding and is generally nice in arcade mode (try to score as high as possible without dieing), it can be very frustrating in mission mode (do special missions like "survive 30 seconds without killing a foe"). There are missions that require fast and precise play, and the screenshakes make it a lot harder and extremly frustrating.
Another problem with the missions is, that a lot of missions don't synergies with each other. Every time you play mission mode, you are given 3 missions (150 missions in total). Most of the time I was not able to complete all 3 at once because they excluded each other (e.g. "survive 30 seconds without killing a foe" and "kill 8 foes in 30 seconds"). This made mission mode a bit slow and repetitive.
Still, the majority of the game is super awesome! The idea of a bunch of particles as your weapon is great and makes a lot of fun. The music is nice and the game is challanging, but not unfair (except a few missions). Although the graphic is simple, it's not bad.
TL;DR Don't excepct a perfect game, but it's great to play now and then. Recommended.

This game is built on you.
You, the player, take on the role of a nameless protagonist, with the challenge of restoring the world of Caelondia to its formal glory.
In terms of gameplay, it is superb: different options and challenges are available to you making sure one playthrough of the game is never identical to the other. Different weapon combinations, upgrades to choose from, and passive buffs from spirits all contribute to a unique game for you. You also have the option of giving more challenge to yourself by giving buffs to enemies as well, in return for experience.
In terms of plot, those decisions are harder to make. The turning point, the climax of the story, was amazingly well done. The road to said point gave it all the more impact, and seeing the aftermath of your decisions as the credits roll will make you remember how you got there. How will the game begin, play, and end for you? That's your decision.
Try this game, and have fun.

In other words, you're playing this game at its best when you're only making small corrections to your movement instead of big changes, so you're forced to be patient. You can speed up time if you don't want to wait, but this can result in you missing stuff because you aren't observing your movement as carefully. It's an interesting idea but somehow it just isn't very enjoyable once you get to a certain level of difficulty. I found myself at that level within the first few stages. Instead of being motivated to try again, I just got frustrated and quit because each attempt involved lots of patient waiting and observation. It just feels like it's trying to waste my time, and there's better games that give me more enjoyment per second, waiting to be played.

NBA 2k16 is not NEARLY as bad as all of these reviews describe. The two biggest issues being brought up are optimization, and Spike Lee’s “MyCareer” mode.
First of all, if your computer meets the system requirements, you can run all gameplay at a very smooth FPS. I have all graphic settings maxed and can run the game perfectly fine. The stuttering and lag being described in the reviews has ONLY occurred for me during the between-gameplay cutscenes, (introductions, timeouts, ect). While actually in game, everything runs better than ever, with smooth animations and high definition characters. The graphics are by far more superior to any previous installment.
2K decided to take a risk and use Spike Lee to write/direct the MyCareer mode. Like any other movie, Lee’s story centers around one character and his family. While you can make your character look any way you want, the story encourages you to be a young black man. If you don’t want to be black, you don’t have to be. It is not racist like some people say… it is just how the story is meant to be. Throughout 2K games, many people have hoped and wished that eventually they would have the choice to play through High School and College games. NBA 2K16 listened to its fans and delivered on this! Now everyone is complaining because it isn’t good enough… I on the other hand found that it complimented the story in a perfect amount of games (4 high school, 4 college). Between each game, the story progresses. The story itself is actually quite engaging! You feel emotion towards the characters IF you take the time to listen and watch the cut scenes. All in all, it is clear after completing the story (which I have) that Lee put in a lot of time and effort.
Here is the main point I wanted to make about MyCareer. If you absolutely hate what 2K has done by implementing a more complex story, DO NOT WORRY! After your first season in the NBA (you play 8 games your rookie year), the story aspect ends. At this point, you play just like you would in 2K15. Taking on full seasons, talking to the press, signing endorsements, increasing your stats, ect. All of this, along with even more!
With those two issues being pushed aside, there are many positives in NBA 2K16. The music is the best I have heard yet, finally landing on many good & popular tracks. The customization has drastically improved, and all of the best modes are there. 2K will be releasing bug fixes and updates, so all of these negative reviews will hopefully be changing. As for me, I find it the best installment in the series, and have enjoyed every minute I have played so far.

Hemisphere Games is a Canadian developer company that released Osmos back in 2009. They give you the opportunity to control a... well... cell. You need to find other cells that are smaller than you so that you can absorb them and grow bigger. This concept, of course, also means that you need to avoid bigger cells until you are big enough to absorb those, as well. If I remember correctly the criterion on each level is always to become quite big (not necessarily to absorb all the cells on the map).
I like how you need to proper yourself ahead to gain momentum - in the process you are losing matter so you cannot really do this forever as you are gradually becoming smaller. Patience is a virtue!
There are several levels and all are part of 3 major zones - each require you to follow a different playstyle and some of the later levels can be pretty challenging.
The game has an excellent soundtrack full of ambient tracks. They accompany this unique gameplay perfectly. I believe Osmos is one of those indie games that is a must-have.

I must admit I was a little cautious about the new canon for this game coming from Xcom:EU but now it looks like a stroke of genius.  You get to stay rooted in earth based tech at the beginning and the path of discovery that is the core of the game is still intact but with new gear and new takes on familiar enemies.
Apart from quality of life changes such as the LoS indicator when previewing move positions, buttons to make gear and weapons available when equipping soldiers pre-mission etc, there are also new mechanics such as the concealment system allowing you to start a mission on your terms (usually).  The soldier customisation is back and extensively expanded along with upgraded stylised graphics that really bring you into the dystopian version of earth in the not too distant future.
The mission timers that most missions have are not to everyone's tastes but you can mod them out if wanted.  Personally I think they really do add to the game as they are carefully balanced to give you enough time but not too much, assuming you play in an agressive fashion.  If you try to spend your turns doing overwatch creep to try and spring the perfect ambush, yes, you're going to run out of time and pay the price.  Don't do that.  Watch Beaglerush on twitch or youtube to see the sort of approach you need to be taking.
There are still some glitches left, but nothing that I've found to be game breaking so far even on Ironman.
Overall this is a legendary game and well worth your time, unless you really hate turn based games.

Steam needs to update the rating system. This thumbs up/down is just too simplistic. While I do recommend the game for those who never played a hack "sim" before, I get the feeling that some people who are used to Uplink will be disappointed.
Uplink is the only game like this one I've played, and Hacknet is obviously inspired by it, so this is basically a comparison between the 2.
If you played Uplink this will be a walk in the park. Aside from visuals, there's nothing here that Uplink didn't do better back in 2001. With the excepton of a couple of moments, all missions are exactly the same all the way through, so it gets repetitive quite fast.
There's no sense of danger or urgency Uplink gives you. Nobody will come after you, there's no police, companies you hack won't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥ Despite of what the game tells you right at the beggining, there's no need to cover your tracks. In Uplink, everytime you hack into a system it's a race against time. In Hacknet there's nothing like it. Once you block a trace you can spend as much time as you want in any system.
There's no rig upgrades, no rewards, nothing like it. You just complete the mission, get a "thank you" email and move on to the next.
Both games have a story, but Uplink is more of a sandbox. After you get the hang of it you can do whatever you want and follow the story whenever you want. Hacknet, on the other hand, is pretty linear. That's a big dissapointment, specially after a great "wtf do I do now" moment right in the beggining. After that, you get the feeling you're never safe, but unfortunately nothing like that ever happens again. Storywise, Uplink is way more interesting, while Hacknet is cliche and way too simplistic.
That's the main problem with this game. It's way too easy. Uplink is infuriating unforgiven to the player. Once you start to mess with big companies, one small screw up means game over. Add that to the fact that the game is pretty much a roguelike, so it's not like you can go back to a previous save, you have to start all over again. In Hacknet, you don't need to worry about that. Like I said before, there's no need to clean after you. If you get caught, all you need to do is change your ip adress.
Anyway, if you never played a hacking "sim" before, this might be a good place to start. Like Uplink, It's really easy to get into, you don't need to now anything about code to play both games, and they give you a good sense of immersion.
Hacknet has a good concept, but is way too simple for those looking for a challenge. I hope the "Labyrinths" expansion adds more substance to the game.

It's a good time-waster, best played in short bursts (not hours on end). In the game you play a blob, a blob that can absorb other blobs and if you aren't careful, get absorbed yourself (thus losing). It's almost a puzzle game of sorts, or perhaps strategy. You're constantly trying to balance gravity, momentum and mass as you make your way around. Your main way of moving is by expelling mass, shooting out your own 'essence' in order to move in a given direction. This is the crux; balancing how much you'll lose by moving versus how much mass you may absorb, assuming everything goes according to plan. That's the goal in the game, absorb lots of other blobs until your blob is supreme. Easy, right? Wrong, it gets very difficult and chaotic in the later stages of the game. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, you've just got to put all you've learned to task. Some of it is luck, some of it is perfect timing. It's a good game for what it does, elegantly simple.

Let me start out by clarifying why i do not recommend buying the game for PC in its current state:
It's unstable, lacks countless comfort options and knowing 2K, a PC patch won't be out before next year. So just spare yourself some pain, wait for a patch. By then, it's probably on sale aswell.
It's definetely not a bad game, but i feel the lack of competition in this genre (NBA Live anyone?) has led 2K to believe they can just port the console version and be done with it. Bug fixing is not a priority, performance questionable, glitches are common.
So here's my two cents on some topics, I tried to keep it somewhat short. It's not a complete list by any means, just what stuck with me the most.
Gameplay
All that being said, the gameplay has been improved in some areas - and still, there are plenty of issues. Steals and turnovers are happening at an alarming rate (HoF, Simulation), at lower difficulties it still might be frustrating for newer players to drive to the basket, let alone score in the paint without cheesing. Pick and Roll is overly effective and seems to be the only option to get an open shot, so it's basically everyones go-to move in MyCareer. Gets old really quick though.
MyCareer
Well, if you didn't know by now, the decision to bring Spike Lee onboard hasn't been overly popular. I can appreciate the attempt to immerse the player some more, but it just does not work this time around. At all. It feels like a trainwreck, forced and contrary to the intent, immersion breaking. "Oh you're such a big star, let me get you this shoe deal for putting up 7/5/4!" Wow.
The Rookie season spans 8 games, after which you can choose a team, negotiate a contract and finally get to play unhindered by a "Spike Lee Joint". At this point, the game was eventually enjoyable. Slowly building your (this year) extremely ♥♥♥♥♥♥, 55 rated scrub into a more refined player has always been the best part of the game for me. They added the option to spend your off-days playing practices, hanging out with other players, or completing activities for your sponsors, which will net you some VC, an attribute boost or some other gimmicks. Overall, MyCareer sucks for the first part, as soon as you've played through the story it actually gets good. Thank God.

You have to change game to 12 minute quarters if you want any decent stats for your players, and it still takes far too long to play a game. Ontop of that, your players are very emotional, constantly upset about minutes, roles, and performances against other teams. It's pretty much just an emotional simulator, and you have no options to appease the player except to grant their request, deny their request, and if you want to tell them to be patient or wait their time because the player ahead of them is better, you have to use coins that take forever to earn or spend real money on them. When I got this game I expected less of it, the game amused me and resulted to be an interesting arcade game with some physics-based mechanics for the weapons.
Basically, you're a ship that has some particles that you swing to kill your enemies/obstacles, the concept is simple and you get it really fast.
It has some "Mission" kind of campaign thing that gives you different objectives and changes your way of playing, the arcade mode can be relaxing since most if the time you can freely move around without worrying too much about the things that may hit you (unless you're in Asteroid Field difficulty or there are a lot of enemies around).
Pros:
- Simple concept, fast to learn
- Nice music
- Nice achievements (No "open the game"-like achievements)
- Global leaderboards
- Different difficulties, so you can play whatever you want
- Missions change your vision of the way you play
Cons:
- Screen shakes once you hit an enemy (you can crash because of this)
- There is a bug in mission that makes it impossible to beat it
- Way too hard achievements (Get 3001 with the show-off ship, really?)
- No achievements in offline mode
- Maybe a bit expensive
Overall, I would recommend this game if you enjoy arcade games or games that have complex challenges, get it on sale if possible.

This game follows in its predecessor footsteps: a tactical, fun, hard and often slave to the RNG.
If you want to kill aliens by the dozens, make them explode easily, and kill wave after wave of them, go play doom.
On the other hand, if you enjoy fighting with a small squad and having to carefully advance throug maps, discovering aliens at the mos tinopportune moment during your turn, and pray that they will not rampage through your team in mere seconds, this is the game for you.
Driven by a compelling story, following the story from the first opus, if the player had lost (which, lets be honest, happened often) XCOM 2 brings back the the basic mechanics from the first.
The player starts with a small team of 4 rookies, with no special weapons, no training, and most of the time, only high cover to defend it's team member. By plowing through missions smartly, switching members between missions to let them rest and build new stuff, the team expends up to 6, with classes being unlocked by gaining ranks.
I've enjoyed this game very much, even after finishing the first one multiple times. This game keeps all the core mechanics, and changes everything else. New enemies, new classes, new weapons, new technologies.. Everything is different, and yet still the same. And the ever-maddening "difficulty" is still there, sometimes making you want to stop playing altogether.
The AI doesn't get much smarter. The mobs just have more HP, more defense, and there are more of them on the map (and they do get a bit smarter, but do not expect genius-level AI at higher difficulties, or even at end-game).
There is much more to say about the game (characters and weapons cutomisations, mods, new mission types...) but I think I've said the essential (you can ignore everything else during your first playthrough). I highly recommend this game if you want to play a good tactical game with a nice story, and you're ot afraid of getting rip to shreds until you learn how to play smart.

I love this game, I played it a long time ago before it was on steam, but I had fallen out of it due to other things that I had to tend to. After hearing a lot of complaining about it turning into a P2W, I decided to download it again and see how bad things got.
---Before MoP Update---
This game was awesome long ago, hell, it still is in my opinion, but to explain the changes that happened during recent updates and etc. I'll start here. The game used to have a small amount of portals and you were able to enter any of them even as a beginner and get carried through it all. Was that fun? No, no not really. It allowed for easy XP and gear farming and just kinda messed with the game. Now, don't misunderstand, it was still extremely fun doing the shadow dungeons and such, it was a good way to kill time, but it didn't have much of a grind feel to it, and let's be honest, an MMORPG is all about the grinds for gear, ITS NOT SUPPOSED TO BE EASY!
---After the MoP Update---
MoP launched and it introduced a lot of things, it introduced more portals for farming Gems, which are used to increase stats, unlock abilities, and raise your gear level. (Yes, like WoW) and it also introduced, as stated before, gear level, which is what allows you to access certain areas. If your gear doesn't meet the criteria? Guess what, you can't go there, just like I feel it should be. Honestly, I love the new update because it allows more grinding because that's what an MMORPG is all about and considering this doesn't have a story line, I'm pretty sure more grinding is kind of a good thing.
---Overall Review---
I love this game, My hours aren't much via steam but I have somewhere around 800 between steam and the launcher itself, I don't think they screwed the game up, but they definently changed it from how it used to be. It did take a day to get used to the new aspect, but I absolutely love it. The farming is fun, the arena is fun, and so is everything else. Don't think that just because you can buy stuff that it ruined the game, because it did not. Do I recommend this? Hell yes I do. If you have time that you need something to kill it with, this is the game to do it on.

Cygnus Elvashak was a simple man with a tragic past. His sister had been killed by the Glitchers; specifically, by a man named Gio Estralda. With a heart of fire, Elvashak raced to find the best way to exact revenge. And, as luck would have it, he became the main character... For a short while. With his Longblade and Rechargeable High Capacity Stealth Shield, he was ready!
Elvashak amassed a large sum of money through missions of three difficulty types; Easy, Medium, and Hard. With his blade and shield in hand, he managed to gather what almost seemed to be randomized, but useful, loot, such as a Rechargeable Glitch Trap and Quiet Quickfire Gun.
With his money, he paid for intel on his sister's killer. He tracked the man down to the exact ship, but when he boarded, Elvashak was blown away. Literally. A turret shot him and he was thrown out of the airlock.
His breaching pod managed to catch him, however, and bring him back to safety! Elvashak, now being far more careful, found the ship to be much, much larger than any he had encountered before. Try as he might, Elvashak could not overcome the huge amounts of guards and sentry turrets. Taking out six men, Elvashak felt himself thrown into space yet again. Once again catching himself with his remote controlled pod, he boarded for what he knew was the last time. He would make one last effort and, failing that, retreat and try again at another point in time.
Unforeseen by him, however, was the explosion of an engine. The ship was split apart, and he managed to get very, very close to his sister's killer. The ship, on the other hand, was fast approaching its destination. As the countdown ticked away, he decided to retreat. As his pod pulled away, he was blasted by an array of missiles. Barely hitting the proper buttons to keep the pod from breaking the part, he relaxed in his chair.
The day was done, and he would come back another day. That is, he would have. If he hadn't been on emergency fuel.
Try as he might, he could not get the trajectory correct; and once the fuel was out, life support disengaged. After multiple successful missions, liberating a station, and coming so close to avenging his sister's death, Elvashak was left to die from lack of oxygen, his pod drifting away from the known galaxy.
Anyways, that's Heat Signature. Randomized loot, what feels like a personal story each and every time,  and a very intriguing retirement system that I didn't experience with Elvashak. Seems that when your character retires, he goes down as a "Living Legend" and can name one of his items. This item can be found by later characters you make and by your Steam friends! Very interested in trying that out.

As far as unique gaming experiences go (and let's be honest, they're hard to find some days), Hacknet delivers spectacularly. Not your traditional game in any way, Hacknet lets you live out that "1337 hax0r" fantasy most techies have felt at some point in their lives. The game can be a little repetitive at times, and the final third of the game is where it really shines, but the experience as a whole is a lot of fun and prompts you to think in some unexpected ways. No previous command line experience is truly required thanks to the visual interface, but you might understand the workflow a little better if you've worked with a terminal before. Regardless of your experience, definitely give Hacknet a go; it's worth your time.

-poorly optimized

Here are the two things that really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off most, and sorry if its a rant.
1: You can only have one character.  This is the first assassins creed with only one save spot.  I loved going through the campaign and starting fresh, but you cannot do this in ACU.  You can go back and do the missions, but its not the same.  I have all legendary gear, so its easy as can be, and just equipping old gear is not something I should have to do to have fun.  At this point in the game I have beaten the campaign and I'm waiting for the week long club competition to get more legendary stuff, but its boring. Most coop missions have 3 pieces of gear, and upon completion you get one of them at random.  However, almost all the gear you get is terrible, so there is no reason to do coop missions for gear.  The way you get legendary gear is through club competition, which is the stupidest thing I have seen in an assassins creed game.  I now have to wait a whole week for a random piece of legendary gear to be the reward, then I have to win the club competition.  I prefer the payday 2 loot system to this, and for those that do not know the payday 2 loot system, every mission you complete you have a 1/3 chance at getting a randomly selected piece of gear. 140 hours of game time and I still havent gotten something I want. +the time period is well done

Darkest Dungeon is a game that I have a very love/hate relationship with.
It's a very polished title, the graphics being very stylish and capturing the feel of a bleak and corrupted world, the darkness of every lidded eye, staring outward at the shambling unknowables really putting you in the moment when fights kick off and you realize your favourite heroes might not be coming home tonight.
The style is excellent, and props go out to the artist for bringing out the feel of the world. The voiceovers from the deceased relative, while perhaps a bit histrionic, are sharp, and that narration does well to set the mood and slowly unravel the mystery of what dark horrors lie within the aptly named Darkest Dungeon.
Presentation is immaculate, and I find myself enraptured by the style enough to write little snippets of my party's travels after every successful foray with a particular group, expositing into Discord as if a town crier or a woman amongst the party. However, presentation alone does not excuse some of the honestly baffling design decisions made by the people at Red Hook.
Starting with the elephant in the room, the complete reliance on random-number-generation in lieu of actual challenge in many aspects. Traps, quirks, and even special boss enemies, are all dictated entirely by RNG. If a trap is to generate in a hall between the rooms you're travelling, there is no way of knowing, unless RNG also dictates that you successfully scout it beforehand, or it dictates that you find a map marking its location. There is no cue otherwise within the halls to inform you that a party member may simply lose a chunk of their health and gain stress, and very little, if anything, you can do to prevent the damage other than hope the character with the most dodge or trap resistance is the one to trigger it.
Quirks and diseases themselves can also be gained from interactions with enemies or static objects in the world, curios and treasures. To avoid spoilers, I won't give names to anything, but there are several groups of enemies with a projectile attack that can simply stack blight, which is an acidic 'damage-over-time' type attack, or disease, which are negative modifiers to your party members that are permanent unless treated for a lump sum of gold in the hamlet's sanitarium.
Quirks are modifiers to the party members' actions and statistics, of which there are a fair few negative and positive ones. These can be gained upon successful quest completion, or upon interaction with stress relief methods in the hamlet, or upon interaction with treasures and curios within the dungeon halls on an expedition. These can also be treated, or, in the case of positive quirks, locked in and kept, for another fee at the sanitarium. Fresh arrivals to the town, arriving via the stagecoach, will also sport a couple of typically-managable positive and negative quirks by default. Don't get me wrong, I do honestly like the quirk system, but its balance is a bit of a predicament.
Quirks gained after completion of a quest are weighted to be positive or negative depending on the percentage of stress that the party member returned with. Quirks gained whilst adventuring, however, are heavily weighted in the negative direction. Innocuous objects such as a stone relief, a small pool of water, or so much as a bookshelf, are primed to have a negative lasting impact on the hero, sometimes providing them with quirks that can force interaction with other curios, putting them at further risk of harm, even causing them to pocket items they find at times, essentially removing them from the game world. The stealing effect, and the very nature of quirks, are, of course, dictated almost entirely by weighted RNG.
The nature of the negatively-weighted curios teaches the player early on to avoid touching them, even the most innocuous ones, lest they be afflicted with bloodloss, a disease, blight, immense stress, or a negative quirk. It makes the hallways less interesting and overall bland. You learn to avoid touching things, passing up potentially useful items like a map of all the floor traps in the nearby areas, for fear of having one of your heroes crippled with no warning or recompense. The scenario of weighing your chances of getting some nice loot to pay off your supplies spent thus far, or potentially starting a spiral of failure from looking at a bookshelf, while decent in theory, does not stick the landing in practice.
Both friendly and enemy attacks are also RNG-dictated in many aspects. Resisting specific debuffs or statuses, inflicting stun and bleed effects, even certain healing spells, are entirely at the mercy of randomness. It is not uncommon to have an occultist member of your group heal an ally for 0 health and inflict bleed with the same spell, causing considerable damage to the party as a whole as you spend another turn trying to right the situation, missing opportunities to buff or debuff with other occultist casts.
The heavy reliance on RNG, and the overall weight towards negative modifiers, enemy crits, even randomly spawned mini-boss enemies, feels cheap instead of difficult, which is my main problem with a game such as this. I imagine part of the draw for people is the complete randomness that the game has in store, as the world within is painted to be as bleak and unfair as RNG may make the encounters, but I can't help but feel like the 'crushing difficulty' the game is regarded for simply doesn't exist.
The game has overall been very easy thus far, including several semi-successful forays into boss arenas and the downfall of hundreds of monsters before my men, and is only ever broken up when the "+++Monster Surprised" chance of a radiant torch somehow turns on my crew, leaving them surprised and randomly rearranged while the enemy takes two turns in a row to blight my plague doctor through their 60% resist before marking them for death and having the mushroom-shaped man send them to death's door before I'm even given control.
(I have lost several men via this exact course of action, through no fault of my own)
The nature of difficulty is also regarded with near-disdain, and it is more than likely you will continue grinding after successful raids on the Darkest Dungeon itself, due to the nature of the dungeon.
Minor spoilers ahead for a specific gameplay feature.
The absurd reliance on RNG and extreme emphasis on grinding leaves a combination of bad tastes in my mouth that the presentation can't wash away. Surface level, the game is pretty, but taxing, it seems exceedingly challenging, but once you've delved long enough, you begin to realize that the difficulty is merely a die being cast, and that the same quips in the ancestor's brooding voice don't do enough to cover it up. It's almost poetic, the madman's knowledge you gain whilst playing isn't of some serpentine monster that crawled out of the ocean, it's of understanding how little an impact you have.
I will keep playing, however, in hopes that the game somehow turns me, and because the polish and presentation are simply too much to go without. I'm attached to my crew for now, and I hope we can stave off the darkness that seeps from within the estate, but I am not looking forward to when the dice land in such a way to take them from me.

I do reccommend this game, played so far 42 hours and enjoyed most of it. I bought the game about a month or so after it came out, so this review is not based on any of the major glitches, I'm sure for people who bought it on release it was a very different experience for them, but this is judging the game in the state it is currently and around when I bought it. In terms of glitches and bugs and lag, most of that has been fixed, for me and my friends at least. I have a GTX 860M graphics card, which is a "good" but not amazing or great, its just a good gaming graphics card, I play the game on High graphics, w/ some options on Very High, and I run the game at around 40-50 fps, at this range I can rarely notice frame stutter and everything works fine. A lot of people have complained about having this not work w/ a GTX 970, prob. before there were issues w/ it but I can say at least for most people I know w/ a 970, it works great. The glitches are minimum now and don't annoy me too much, yes every now and then you'll see someone walking through a wall, or dancing w/ someone invisible, but it happens not too often and its very minor. One of the things I find annoyying about the game is the pop-in, as it is very easy to notice. Here are the more basic Pros and Cons about the game:
Pros:
-Amazing graphics, even on low or medium
-Ok story, AC4's was better, but this one is still fine
-Large amount of content (lots of missions, Co-Op or Singleplayer)
-New additions to the climbing like being able to control descent
-Open World Co-Op (Very fun to explore the world of Revolutionary Paris w/ a friend)
-Very large map
-Great recreation of revolutionary paris, amazing buildings
-Lots of NPCs give a feeling of realism to the city
-New stealth mechanics
-Compedative Co-Op called Club Competition is interesting, makes you want to do more Co-Op in order to unlock better armor and weapons
-There are goats
Cons:
-Some frame stutters here and there
-The stealth, although new, is somewhat broken
-Pop-in
-Glitchy NPCs
-For me and my friends, we had to Port Foward in order to play Co-Op together, was hoping for some dedicated servers
So overall I give the game an 8.5/10, because even though parts of the game are broken, I still find that the pros greatly outweigh the cons, and I can see myself easily getting my money's worth out of this game. People have been hating on Ubisoft a lot recently but they fail to see some of the amazing achievements they've made, the way they recreate real-world locations is better than any other company, the life they put into cities modern or in history is amazing, whether it is Chicago in Watchdogs or late 1700s Paris in AC Unity. The greatest aspect of their city games are the cities themselves, too many gamers fail to see this.

AC UNITY REVIEW (System: Intel core i7 4790K @ 4 ghz, Gigabyte GTX 970, 16GB DDR3)
Performance:
I've played 40 hours and haven't had a single performance bug. NOT ONE. I'm not lying so "I can get you guys wallet♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; as the people who are crying about this game are saying to silence the positive reviews. I seriously have not had one bug that affected performance. I had 2-3 during a full playtime that were all small objects that didin't render in with textures. OH BOY HOW CAN WE COPE??? I know i'm running a 970 so you may argue that "I don't have to worry about performance" but apparently people with 980's in SLI are having issues so yeah. Anyways I get a solid 50-60 frames which may not be acceptable for you 60fps minimum fanatics out there but it ran smooth as butter for me, If you're having problems then cool, but I'm not suffering at all. I Played the game at 3 pm on day 2 (My internet is slow) so there MAY have been a day 1 patch (idk) but whatever.
Now for the actual game:
Story: This seems to be hit or miss for most people, it's definetly not as engaging as Black Flag's story but it makes sense and dosen't even really have any real-life segments and that's a plus for me as Desmond's story is boring and ACIV's Abstergo office moments pulled me entirely out of the experience. Arno is a decent character, I'm not spoiling anything about the plot besides that there's a kind of predictable ending death but overall it works and story isin't why I buy AC games anyways (Not to say this is not a good story, because it is)
Story = 8/10
Graphics: YES. Like the first scene is actually kind of mediocre and put me off from the game, but once I got into paris it was SHOCK AND AWE. Like, good enough to understand 3GB vram reccomended. Every texture looks amazing, every cobblestone looks unique, the citizens look great, you can see farther than before and even that little house in the distance is totally visitable, the interiors looks amazing due to great Nvidia technologies (sorry AMD) and the game overall is just AMAZING graphically. I can't even explain it. You have to see it.
Graphics = 9/10
Gameplay: This is most different AC yet. Like I mean, theres so much more to do. If I didin't get Far Cry 4 with my 970 I'd have already sunk 80 hours into this. It's just so fun and entertaining. Combat is about 3x harder, any group bigger than 3-4 guys is a challenge, and stealth is a viable option this time. A competent deck-building dungeon-crawler with hillariously bad graphics. Basically a mix of Desktop Dungeons (2013) and the board game Dominion (2008). Though you can't get murdered by a level 10 goat here.
You fight your way through three floors. On each, you encouter monsters (exp/gold) and shops and try to optimize the punching power of your deck. Each class has prefered card types, which causes them to encounter them more often: A priest or monk will find 'prayers', a mage 'spells' and a thief 'actions'.
There is 5 card types:
-the bread and butter 'attack' and deal x damage
-the actions (that require action points) that often are something like 'do something, then draw a card"
-prayers that you play and that get triggered after 1-5 turns
-equipment that give you a permanent ability for the fight (e.g. deal 1 damage for every two attack cards you play; ignore the first 3 damage every turn; ..)
-spells.. from fireball to haste
And thats the elements this surprisingly deep deck builder gets build from.

I'm a big Dark Souls fan, and after beating DS3, I wanted some DS fix. I still had DS2 to complete (which I left for after beating DS3) but instead of going there, The Surge came out. It looked interesting so I got it, beat it and loved it. Since I liked it so much, I said what the heck, I'll give LotF a try, to support Deck 13, and I thought it couldn't be as bad as a lot of reviews say. If it's close to The Surge, I'm all good.
Well, it's definitely close to The Surge fun wise. In fact, I liked it about as much (still giving a slight nudge favoring The Surge). This is a great game reminiscent of the old Severance: The Blade of Darkness and certain parts reminded me of Vampire the Masquerade: Redemption. Both of the oldies I love. Of course, mix in the Dark Souls formula as well, and you have a winner. The gfx are great, the combat is meaty, with a heft and weigth to it, sfx are great, voice acting is solid all around, the story is decent and there's plenty of fun to be had. Spells are useful as well, and there's plenty of options along with the gauntlet to spice up your fighting style. Inventory system and overall user interface is easy to use and understand. Controls are nicely responsive and playing it with an Xbox controller was a blast.
At this point, I haven't noticed any game breaking bugs or crashes, and I've beaten the game once, putting in 26 hours into it (and haven't found all the loot and secrets), so I guess things are nicely patched by now.
If you're looking for a nice DS fix or a great sword & sorcery title, don't pass this up due to mixed reviews.
I'm looking forward to seeing what Deck 13 has next in store for us.

A fun RTS? Definitely.
Better than Age of Empires II? Not necessarily.
Age of Empires III  is a RTS game in the 18th/19th century, featuring Native Americans, European Countries and Asian nations. The recipe is the same as always: Build your town, build units, gather resources, build more units, defeat your enemies. However, they found a few things to spice it up:
- Home Cities, allowing you to seperately level up ingame and overall
- shipements from your home country to gain bonus units, buffs and resources
- no more gathering stations > you get wood / money / food right away
- lots of diverse nations and units, making it possible to have a huge variety of tactics.
The game aged (heh) very well and still looks awesome today. Graphics are very good, same for the physics. The gameplay is very fun, even more if you play multiplayer with friends.
Here is also the only downside - multiplayer requires a seperate login. However, that's not too much of a problem.
Would i recommend the game to others? Yes of course! The campaign will take a good amount of time to finish and the skirmish mode is endless. This game will continue being aweosme until they release Age of Empire IV or equivalent.

Excellent idea to combine walking around a fog of war map with RPG leveling up/items, deck building, and rogue-like. This results in a somewhat original card game- one varied enough to stand out in my bloated collection, although the fantasy theme is basic.

I mean, we are talking about some very bad artwork here, my friends, and very rudimentary backgrounds, text windows, and sprites. Why not use royalty free graphics or invest in some passable images? Why release a game that doesn't even have cute pixels to fool everyone into thinking it is retro? Such a target for critics. That said, I read a comment that the developer now a job with Blizzard, so they must have been impressed with his gameplay, mechanics, and programming, so in many ways the bad graphics got their attention. Kinda like how Stevie Wonder stood out as a singer because he was blind.
Most people will pass because of the lack of graphics, and that is a shame. The upgrading, unlocking skills, and randomization make this a very fun game!

Well I had a high expectations with this game. In the end it is a Souls-like game and I would like expand my experience in this type of games.
So that was a horrible mistake because Lords Of The Fallen has many flaws. Another drawback is the camera work especially in tight spaces. It happens then camera is losing our character and losing our marked aim. To makes matters worse the game has optimization problems, I had a few crash...
The last thing that I don't like is the lack of any inventory of side quests, while in the case of main tasks is not necessary I think that could use the opportunity to view the list of side quests.
Moreover I had a problem with "feeling" the main character that may result from weak dialogue or fine-ground story.
That I said this game is so similar to Dark Souls so the comparison to it is natural. This aspect of LOTF is very weak, has a lower level of difficulty, fewer classes and gear, etc. Generally has a lower quality.
In conclusion, this is a title that will not satisfy hardcore Souls players, but maybe new players will find something for themselves.

Whoever did the character models and armour/weapon design, very well done. Seriously, every piece I found looked great. It's a shame it was let down by nearly every other aspect. I only stuck it out for a couple of hours but there's still plenty of things that showed up and made it a bad experience
Cons:
-Combat is very slow and cumbersome even with the lighter weapons, and there's no animation cancelling, feels overall very clumsy.
-Animation is a bit iffy, they make a point of taking your helmet off for the cutscenes but your face only has basic movements and the mouths aren't synced with the speech.
-Very linear, there's only one actual path, there are technically other paths but they're all just a corrider leading to a room with a chest and some trash mobs that then lead straight back to the main path.
-For a game clearly trying to be a SoulsLike it was very easy, I didn't come close to dying for the first two bosses and any of the mobs between them.
-Not very well thought out, for instance there is a equipment weight system that affects how easily you move but it seems to base it purely off what chest piece you were wearing, so you could equip a 'Heavy' helm, boots, and gauntlets with the biggest weapon and shield you could manage and as long as you wore a 'Light' chest piece you can flip about like an acrobat.
-There is backstabbing/parrying but its inconsistent if you're invulnerable or not during, some attacks hit you and some don't.
-This one is just a pet peeve of mine, but it has the thing where you have to hold a button down for a short time to activate anything, which always sucks anyway but it's especially poorly done here, being quite innacurate and awkward.
-While they look impressive and varied most weapons function much the same as eachother within the same catagory, and there was always a new one with clearly superiour stats so the other are rendered completely worthless within minutes of finding it.
Pros:
-3D Models look amazing
-Hitboxes seem fairly good
-Story could be interesting from the short bit I saw
It really feels like they had a bunch of left over assets from a failed project and stitched them together with an inexperienced team, it's a shame really, if only it had more time and care spent on it it could have been a nice little game.

This game follows in its predecessor footsteps: a tactical, fun, hard and often slave to the RNG.
If you want to kill aliens by the dozens, make them explode easily, and kill wave after wave of them, go play doom.
On the other hand, if you enjoy fighting with a small squad and having to carefully advance throug maps, discovering aliens at the mos tinopportune moment during your turn, and pray that they will not rampage through your team in mere seconds, this is the game for you.
Driven by a compelling story, following the story from the first opus, if the player had lost (which, lets be honest, happened often) XCOM 2 brings back the the basic mechanics from the first.
The player starts with a small team of 4 rookies, with no special weapons, no training, and most of the time, only high cover to defend it's team member. By plowing through missions smartly, switching members between missions to let them rest and build new stuff, the team expends up to 6, with classes being unlocked by gaining ranks.
I've enjoyed this game very much, even after finishing the first one multiple times. This game keeps all the core mechanics, and changes everything else. New enemies, new classes, new weapons, new technologies.. Everything is different, and yet still the same. And the ever-maddening "difficulty" is still there, sometimes making you want to stop playing altogether.
The AI doesn't get much smarter. The mobs just have more HP, more defense, and there are more of them on the map (and they do get a bit smarter, but do not expect genius-level AI at higher difficulties, or even at end-game).
There is much more to say about the game (characters and weapons cutomisations, mods, new mission types...) but I think I've said the essential (you can ignore everything else during your first playthrough). I highly recommend this game if you want to play a good tactical game with a nice story, and you're ot afraid of getting rip to shreds until you learn how to play smart.

But after I spent half an hour with it, when I dominated its psychics mechanics and I understood its scoring system realizing the masterful and completely perfect game design behind it, I became anxious.
I felt my pulse accelerated with each heartbeat sending unconscious signals to my mind. Full of binary coded verses talking about the overwhelming sense of beauty suspended in the abstract and almost ethereal world behind
.
It’s the same sense of accomplishment that you can feel when you meet for the first time a lifetime love, this person who you will spend some of your more pleasant and intimate moments. Sometimes this tempestuous love will induce you to obfuscation, making you to feel a bit dumb about yourself for every bad step taken in your relationship, this meteor that you stupidly crashed while you were concentrated trying to evade a pursuing enemy’s red ship. But then you reconcile with it and the previously induced rage only takes you to a next and much more passionate encounter in which you have a better understanding of every particle in its body, allowing you to achieve a higher score.
Sometimes,

An experience similar to a Sufi whirling dance ritual in which the participants are able to elevate his minds from his bodies through the constant act of swirling with the rhythm of the music.
At other times,
turns into a fast pace and frantic arcade experience with the screen inundated with menacing objects floating in the vastness of space. And you feel inside of a space opera, while you maneuver your ship tracing impossible parables. Creating complex strategies to destroy the enemy ships, trying to not lose the momentum while you increase even more an epic chain of explosions.
It has a perfectly crafted level design, that like Nintendo’s most beloved classics, works on a two-dimensional level of complexity. There is a first layer in the game that makes it instantly pleasant to play only to be absorbed in its universe, being an experience close to meditation and with a main mechanic that is instantly fun. And then comes with its second layer of complexity, because the better you learn its level structure, scoring system and enemies patterns, the more you can improve your runs in a competitive way. In each run you can feel your progress, how you have a better knowledge of the game rules every time. At the end, destroying the enemies becomes an instinctive reflex skill.

Each mode has a completely different layout with a diverse range of challenges that can immensely alter the gameplay. And every layout is in a constant change. And then you have a glorious 150 missions mode that constantly amazes you with new design ideas, new menaces, new rules. This mode exhibits a level of ingenuity in its construction that is on par with the constant sense of surprise and novelty found in each of the levels of

In this game I have :
- stolen KFC's most secret recipe
- read Doom fanfiction
- accessed the computer of a major Naruto fan
- nearly been traced and sent to jail, working relentlessly to avert this under a time limit that slowly painted my screen red, while synthwave was blasting in the background
And many more, but I'm not gonna spoil it all. Super good game.
Pros :
- Sleek interface, easy to use
- Shiny effects and nice atmosphere
- Messing up and getting traced is one of the most intense experiences in recent gaming history
- Objectives are clear, you always know what you have to do even if the mission text doesn't always tell you
- 10/10 soundtrack
- Game uses a terminal, always gonna be a pro for me
Cons :
- Upon viewing certain programs and nodes the framerate will be locked at 30 and 20fps
- Bloom makes it hard to read text and if you deactivate it you lose practically nothing graphics-wise
- Kind of short. 6-7 hours for a first time completion, nice replayability though
- Bypassing proxies is an extremely tedious process, and they're commonplace
- Like Uplink a decade before Hacknet's release, it also tells you early that you have to delete logs so as to not get caught. However, unlike Uplink, if you do leave logs all over the place, absolutely nobody is going to trace you since apparently nobody's ever at their computer
- Hexclock and Notes take an outrageous amount of RAM
- Factions could've been better (Entropy and CSEC anyway), there is no incentive to keep doing missions for them once you have unlocked the story mission by going up the ranks since there is no money to be earned and the other hackers that have been here for way longer than you don't care one Bit (hehe) that they got owned by a script kiddie that entered the faction an hour ago
- [EDIT] I should also mention that the game is way too easy except for some nodes. For instance, if you're about to get traced but you have hacked every port, and then you disconnect and reconnect, the trace will be dropped and you'll be allowed to look at every file without any time constraint. Now, this isn't a con for most people, but it is for me because the moment you know about the point I just made plus the point about the logs, then the difficulty suddenly disappears, and the only moment your hacking skills will be challenged is at the very end of the game in a story mission.
All of these are more or less nitpicks though, the game is a solid 8/10. The team behind Hacknet has expressed a desire to make Hacknet 2, and honestly with Hacknet 1 as a base, I think they could easily create the best hacking game of all time.

When I was younger, I had a lot of fun playing Asteroid for the Atari 2600, now comes along this game. It's a very similar concept and graphical style, but this game adds so much compared to what the Atari, and arcade version had available (even though there were many limitations then). The only difference is, instead of a weapon, you get a mace made out of particles!
There's the arcade mode, which is basically score attack, and is very fun. There's missions, which is by far my favorite. Very challenging, fun, quick, missions that have specific requirements. There's other co-op modes, but I don't have any friends available at the time of writing this review to try it out with, nor do I have a second gamepad.
If you like quick, simple, interesting gameplay this is a great game for you.

You seek a review but our opinion will vary.  Instead, let me tell you a story of four brave adventurers, who came to the Darkest Dungeon; and became changed forever.
The Crusader Yohan. The highwayyman Jex. The man-At-Arms John. And the Vestal Diana.
Into the dungeon these brave companions delved. Encountering darkness and eerie silence. The occupants of this ruin long since diminished.  But it was not without light that the party travelled. Embracing the flames of the torch they would venture forth, slowly moving but with a purposeful quickness. They knew staying here forever was not an option; regardless of how many torches, food, or firewood was held upon their persons.
Their movement soon became fruitful, for it was with great glee they found treasures long since abandoned.  But that happy moment would soon be cut short, for the rattling of bones upon hardened earth could be heard, and it was with an eternal quickness that the undead hordes were upon them.
But the skeletons were easily dispatched and without worry the companions moved forward in a stalwart formation:
The Crusader Yohan, the man-At-Arms John, highwayman Jex, all trailed by the Vestal Diana. They overcame impenetrable barriers of stone and corpses, they braved traps ruthlessly hidden by former patrons, men who even now are too fraught with greed and malice to let their treasures be taken. But then suddenly, the situation changed.... Skeletons were now complemented with human cultists brandishing razor sharp knives and goblets of disease.  Mages in the rear attired with cult like garb, disrupted the companions formation and filled their hearts with dread.  But our brave adventurers pulled through. They estimated they were halfway through to the exit after many challenging encounters, but there was simply no way to be certain. The only option was to camp and rest, for the wounds of the party had become great, and the horrors of the dead and their foul worshippers were starting to overwhelm their bodies and minds. Taxing them to the call of blissful eternity.
Rested and healed, the party of brave adventurers began anew.  Refreshed and healed, the way forward seemed at least to be easier. Unfortunately, it only became harder.  Enraged by the defeat of their brothers, the cult followers began to amass from the woodwork, appearing to have an eye especially for John, the Man-At-Arms. Whether it was due to the strange features of his face, or simply because he would constantly aggravate enemies, taking attacks upon himself and riposting with sheer authority it is hard to say, and though his wounds became greater and greater, Vestal Diana was able to keep him and the party alive with great healing energy. And yet, even though the resolve of John was great, he was not able to withstand the horrors of the dungeon. His resolve faltered for just a moment, his head swimming with pain from a million wounds and the fear of losing to these abominable cultists. His mind slips, his torment comes to the fore, and his selfishness awakens; he steals from the group, he withholds his attacks, he changes formation without warning, and soon enough brave Crusader Yohan succumbs as well. His resolve proving too frail against the horrors of the dungeon; his desire of self-loathing becomes apparent for all to see. The rest of the party soon follows, each overstressed and burdened by the horrors of the enemy; the only one seeming to hold on is Highwayman Jex. But for how long? How long can a thief and being of distrust and shame hold out against the terrors that plague his mind?
Finally, the end of the dungeon appears to be in sight.  The group is barely holding on to their sanity, and John, our brave Man-At-Arms seems to be a Golem straight from our deepest nightmares; for how could a simple mortal still be standing after so many attacks, regardless of how much healing has been administered? Is he even real? These questions begin to plague the group, even as another group of sharp bladed cultists appear; this time with crossbows in the rear.  The fight seems to last for an eternity, but in truth it is perhaps over by the third round.  This time John faces death yet again and spits right into its eye.  And behold, the dungeon is over. Our mission is complete......but there still remains one more path and more door. I see the party and their weariness, I know we should leave and take our spoils, resting in the abbey and the tavern and continuing at a later time, but I insist we press on. "We did not come this far nothing"! I scream. And so we press forward, those final steps clawing at my mind, the doubt increasing, but I quell it deep inside of me, I do not allow it to overcome my resolve.  My mind is fortified, my decision made.  I can see the end.....
And so the final battle commences.  Cultists yet again.  I am not surprised, I simply cannot believe they are brave enough to attack once more.  Some dark master must be guiding their will, for no other force would dare oppose us after all we have faced and brought low.
They come at us with their blades and their magic, and we hold firm.  The battle is in our favor, but all of a sudden Man-At-Arms John is struck with a crossbow bolt, he screams in pain as it clutches his chest with more ferocity than a vice holding a man's head.  He grips his mace and shield resolutely, but his eyes begin to roll into his head; he screams yet again in rage, and instantly he collapses to the floor, our brave Man-At-Arms is gone. Stalwart warrior that he is, his body simply could not bear another hit, but I was filled with too much hubris to recognize this, and he was too proud to voice any weakness.
As John falls, Crusader Yohan gives a cry of religious might, banishing a skeleton that none of us seemed to notice, but he too is instantly struck by the cultists blades.  The death of his friend John, coupled with the stabbing pain of the life quenching cultists attack is too much, and he too falls, his heart giving out, the fear overcoming his mind completely. It is shortly after this that Jex and Diana suffer similar fates. Jex has not the strength to overcome the piercing bolts of a crossbow, and he has long tried to overcome the fear of the dungeon. In his last gasp of life, he attempts to flee but is unable, the coward that hides beneath the surface of his exterior coming to the fore. He too suffers an arrested heart. Diana, without the strength of a warrior or the protection of others quickly falls to the attacks of a mage.  Overcome with agony at the death of the others, realizing there is no way out, she succumbs to fear and paranoia, and also, though it appears ironic at this point, a heart attack.
I wish we had left that dungeon when we had the chance.  When our hearts were heavy with grief but our minds were still burdened with the strength to return to the surface.  Now all by myself, knowing I could not make it out on my own, I too lost hope. I quit my adventure in rage.  Hoping one day to have the strength to try again. But knowing I might never come back the same way again.

Realm of the Mad God is one of the only free to play Bullet Hell MMOs, as we all know. Though, despite being free, what makes this game as good as it is? We'll start with the basics; Gameplay.
Like your average game it has selectable classes, but what makes that special? Well maybe the fact to actually earn new class you have to master another. Take Necromancer for example if you want to master its black magic you must earn Max Level with Priest and Wizard. This all leads back to gameplay showing it has many possibilities of different things to do. However a downfall is upon it. An unfair advantage towards non-steam players. There are class skins, and these can be purchased via steam or traded in-game at a high price. Much like that Steam starts with 5 classes, unlock the browser version where you only start with 1. It leaves less work needed for those who trained hard for those classes, nevertheless leaves a challenge. Another thing however is pay-to-play.
*Sigh* I didn't wanna have to go here but if you want an advantage you'll most likely have to pay. "Oh really cool skin at level 5 and 10!" You reach the level; "That'll be 900 gold please." And what does gold cost? REAL LIFE CURRENCY. I cannot stess enough how much pay-to-play there is. SURE it is free and all and they need profit but it leaves the other currency; fame, in the dust why earn it besides feeding pets and guild functions? On top of skins, wanna change color; GOLD. Wanna new sword for less work; GOLD. I see a strict issue on this part. This all leads back to Steam Advantage however.
Steam is a well known game-user system where people can buy games and play directly from the comfort of their desktops without much hassle. However so much is steam related it is hardly fair for browser players without steam. On the starter classes subject again, instead of wizard you get Archer, Warrior, Rogue, Priest, AND Wizard opposed to the usual Wizard. Now that seems fine and all no big deal right? Wrong. There is more to the Steam part. Steam can allow you to purchase ingame items via steam currency, you can buy gold easier, and so on so forth. Steam makes everything easier putting the browser players to dust. Steam users just have so much more to do is all. Now, what is my overall feel?
Realm of the Mad God's 8-bit graphics makes it have an original taste and feel. The gameplay is fun overall travelling with friends in Bullet Hell motion, and everything is good. There are connection errors and loading errors now and then but it is all good. The Pay-To-Play and Steam advantages drag it down a bit but the gameplay overall is still good. Now overall I place Realm of the Mad God at a staggering; 82/100. However it is suggested!
Yours truly, Bravelyzach.
