It's possible that HackNet is the most fun I've had in a LONG LONG time.    At first, I thought it was a little hokey.. Sort of like how Hollywood movies portray hacking.. And then as the plot develops (closer to the end), everything started to fit into place... The overdone interfaces, the limited options... everything...  slotted together... perfectly..
OK, so this game is pretty much for geeks and programming/unix nerds.  If you've never used a command prompt, and think typing your username into the PSN login is "programming", this ain't for you.   This game relies on an X-Server-like interface, and relies on fast typing, and a fair working knowledge of what a server is, ports, IP Addresses, and so on. Knowing that you can press "up" in a shell window to get to previously typed commands, for instance, can save a lot of typing.. It's that kind of knowledge which comes in handy...
The game presents itself as an X-server interface with a fixed layout (which can be modified in-game!), you just can't drag windows about. You wouldn't want to, anyway.  The layout is perfect for what you need.   There's a "net map" to show your progress, a terminal for typing in commands, and an all-purpose web-browser interface.
You have control of an advanced unix-based OS which has serious MIL-spec hacking software installed on it.  The server comes with an timed message, which asks you to perform 'a favour' for the previous owner of the software...  And from that point on, you're sucked headfirst into the screen, as you probe, hack, and trace your way around the internet.
You're not alone, though.  There's a few groups out there who do this sort of thing every day of the week.  Some of them are REALLY good.  But all of them are using old-gen kit, so while you know next-to-nothing, you're already as powerful as the best of them... With a little training, and some experience, you can be the best Hacker on the 'Net...
The game is about 50% hacking simulation (a-la Hollywood) with flashy graphics, and fast, heart-pounding music to crank up the tension.   You have to 'connect' to a server to inject cracks and exploits onto it.  Once running, you can disconnect from the server and let them run.  As long as you're connected, you're vulnerable to being traced and back-hacked!   But if you disconnect too often or too quickly, you may need to start over.  It's a brilliant device which deviates slightly from accepted terminology, but works great as a game device.    The other 50% of the game is done after you've successfully breached a server.  Your OS filters out all the unnecessary stuff, leaving you with the important bits.. And buried in that dross are gold nuggets.. Usernames, passwords, blackmail material, recipes (sic), saved IRC quotes, and all-important IP addresses to other servers.
Once you hook up with a team of other hackers, you can opt to take on 'contracts' to hack into servers to perform tasks.  Some of them require you to figure out where you have to hack, and might involve chain-hacks of three or four servers.  Each one holds the key (somewhere) to the next (you hope), or might be a dead-end to slow you down....  Who knows? The game randomizes some element each playthrough, so you may never be 100% sure!
As you get better, you may find your current group is pretty small-fry, or doesn't take the sorts of things you want to.. you may want to move up in the world....  But all the time, at the back of your mind... Who was the previous owner of this awesome system?  Am I the only one with it?  who else has it?  Why can I run Windows .EXEs on a *nix box?!?!    Perhaps you'll get to find out....
Partway through the game, there's a mini-easter egg which spawns a nice little side-plot.  You can continue on through without triggering it.. But once you win the game, there's a (sort-of) hint about how to trigger it.. but TBH, just go read the forums.    The side-plot is short, sweet, and switches things up a bit.
I loved the variety in the game.   It's amazing, because (at its core) everything is the same... A circle with an IP address, that exposes ports, and may be protected...  But how you get that circle varies... And what that circle entails varies...   The logs, emails, and text files throughout the game paint a glorious picture (with many spelling mistakes!),  giving you a grand idea of the people at the other end of the pipe.
From the first moment I started this game, I loved every second of it.  When I was away from the PC, I was trying to think   a) how I could solve the puzzle I was stuck at   and  b) how I could get back to the PC to play it...
In-game explanation is fair.  Actually figuring out what you have to do is relatively straightforward:  It generally boils down to executing a particular command to attempt to breach a particular piece of security.   The in-game explanation, however, makes it sound a little more complicated than it is.  Just read it through, and try the commands out.

I've played various iterations of Heat Signature throughout its development; from when it was a very simple wrench-em-up to the crazily-unpredictable-but-very-tactical action game the final product ended up being.
And it's awesome.
There are two things that alleviate Heat Signature from 'great' to 'genius', and incredibly, neither mechanic existed until relatively late in development. They are the pause mechanic, and teleportation items. With these two additions, the game went from a fairly simple top down action game to something incredibly tactical, unpredictable, and truly beautiful.
The premise of Heat Signature is pretty simple: you fly around an area of space in a tiny, weaponless ship that can dock undetected with larger ships. Dock with a ship, and suddenly (and seamlessly) you're onboard, running around with the WASD keys. Ships are procedurally generated and vary in size and difficulty, so each one will play out differently. Both you and the guards onboard have access to a wide variety of guns, grenades, teleporters, and other items and your aim is normally to sneak through the ship and steal something, or assassinate/rescue/capture something.
Sneaking through a ship you've docked with rarely goes to plan, and this is where the excellent pause mechanic comes into play. At any time, you can hit the spacebar, pausing the game. This is essential, as without pausing, firefights in Heat Signature normally last about 0.3 seconds and end up with you bleeding out on the floor. You could play without using the pause function - it might be fun if you thought Hotline: Miami was a bit easy and slow-paced... For the rest of us, pausing the game allows us to breathe, and take stock of the situation. Ok, I just ran into this room and was spotted by four guards with shotguns. Another two guards have just teleported in behind me, there's approximately 136 shotgun pellets about five feet away from my face, and I have no ammo.♥♥♥♥♥♥ However, I do have a visitor teleporter. I use this to temporarily teleport to an adjacent room. The shotgun pellets pass through the empty space I was just occupying and smash into the window behind. It shatters, and all six guards go flying out into space. The window's automatic force-field activates just as the visitor teleporter wears off and I return to my original position. I stick my hands in my space-pockets and walk away, whistling.
Surviving situations that seem unsurvivable is what Heat Signature is all about. Try doing all of the above with another ship firing missiles at the ship you're on, blowing massive chunks out of it (ships are not just procedurally generated, but fully destructable too). It's fun, it's intense, and amid all of the chaos, it carries all of the hallmarks of excellent design that you'd expect from Tom Francis.
Another commendable aspect of the game is the graphics - they are unique and gorgeous, while, most importatly, always staying entirely readable even amidst the most chaotic missions. It's hard to believe they're done by the same artist that did Gunpoint's beautiful pixel art. John Roberts is one hell of a talented person.
Go buy this game, then buy four more copies for your friends, so Tom Francis continues to make more games. They'll probably be about throwing people through large windows, but that's no bad thing.

Downloaded the game on a whim, not expecting much. Overall, the game far exceeded my expectations in almost every category.
I was expecting a realtively simplistic MOBA style game with a few ships and clunky controls. Fortunately, the game is so much better than that.
I'll admit, it does take a few games to get accustomed to the visuals, HUD, controls, and movement, but after you've learned the basics, it becomes extremely engaging.  You really need to play a few matches before judging the game.
Pros:
-impressive graphics
-enaging combat
-variety of ships (30 with different roles/abilities)
-strategic combat (every match feels like a game of tug-of-war and teamplay is critical)
-game duration does not drag onnnn like some MOBAs and the snowball effect is minimalized with GAMMA captures
-F2P model seems fairs...can buy new ships after a day or 2 of quick matches
-Ship movement...some may complain that is too "slow", but it perfectly captures the scope of the battles and the size of the ships you pilot...these are carriers and capital ships, not fighters. You actually have to release/fend off swarms of fighters and bombers as part of the combat.
-AI/Solo macthes are still fun if you just hate other people
Cons:
-No real lore to speak of, but not unusual for the genre
-Stat descriptions/modifiers could be expanded
I'd add more cons, but for what the game is trying to accomplish...there isn't much.
EDIT: Forgot to mention the often overlooked sound design. The ship and space sounds are very good and the voice acting is even pretty solid...the dialogue itself, however, not so much...some lines from the crew are unspeakably bad, even if meant to be funny.

During your time as one of the characters, you can capture outposts by doing several missions involving boarding a spaceship and doing whatever you are ordered to do, this slowly increases a "Liberation" bar, when full you can choose to capture a place. Some places offer gear others offer only mini-missions, think of it as a progress system, you use it to unlock new gear and expand outward.

I really like this game. It's TPP action rpg with really good combat system. You have couple of different weapons to fight with. Each weapon have different speed and range of effect. You can choose Your fightstyle (go for speed and use fast combos and quick movement or go for "tank mode" and 1-2 hits which will end the opponent). There is also some magic, but I didn't focus on it, because mana replenish is much slower than Your stamina (which is needed to make faster attacks and more types than default one). There are some guides on steam or on internet which can really help You out with quests, game mechanics, equipments, statistics etc.).
Side quests are the only thing which I have some issues with. Sometimes when You get quest You do not really know what exactly You need to do. There is no way to even hear the quest again. That is only minor problem anyway.
Game is not long, so after You finish You probably will want to play it again. Even fights with normal mobs can be really spectacular not mention fights with bosses which You have 10 in the game.
It took me almost 80 hours to get all achievements (could be faster, but I made some mistakes and I had to finish game 4 times, not 3).
Graphics are great. Locations are beautiful. Each armor on Your character looks cool. Enemies and bosses are well done.
The only thing I have problem was the lore window which crashed my game twice during my whole play.
Audio is good as well, but could be more music durng the game. Main menu song is just outstanding.
Some hints:
You have few different attacks. Check each weapon how the attacks affects, becuase there are many diffrences between them.
If You plan to play few times with one char then I suggest do not use magic and statistic points from potions till end of first game, because they are also working as lvl up Your char and each enemy will give less exp. After that I suggest to respec and go for 40 luck and You will get lots of such potions from chests where You had special weapons during first walktrough. That's why You can lvl up really high.
To fight with all kinds of ghosts You need weapons with strong magic attacks.
There are three speeds of Your char depends of weight of Your equipment: 0-25%, 25%-75% and 75%-. Each of them are signed with different color.
No more, I could go with is for long.
If You are older player and You know Rune or Blade of Darkness then You will know what kind of game this is. For everyone else just believe me if You like single char action rpg with some more finesse than just spamming one button then this game is for You.

This game is such a breath of fresh air and criminally overlooked. I just found out about it by chance aswell, but boy am I glad I did!
It's a space ARPG within a randomly generated galaxy where AI factions play a 4X game. You can help the different factions, spy on them, sabotage, steal their stuff, try to form alliances or wage war - or just ignore them and go hunt monsters, get loot, improve your ship, trade stuff and become rich. And once this sector is done, for better or for worse, you take your ship and go to the next sector, growing bigger and more powerful each time.
The game world actually feeling dynamic and alive is probably what fascinates me the most about the game, but the fighting, the loot, the diplomatic options, etc. are all very well done aswell.
Highly recommended!

Explore a new sector in space.  Find tons of monsters and aliens.  Explode them all.  Find salvage to upgrade ship (and crew, even). I like how the universe evolves in a galaxy campaign depending on your actions in previous sector.  New subraces popping up or others going extinct.  Some races start to tend to align towards or (more likely) against each other.  But you can still change these trends if you focus on them.
You can do the quests the planets give you or you can ignore them and go fight random monsters and pirates.  Or just go on a rampage against those energy beings that annoyed you in the last sector, seeking to wipe them from the galaxy for good this time.  But when the guild gives you a mission, well, sometimes you just have wipe out your closest allies for the good of the galaxy or the loot.  (Mostly the loot.)

Drox Operative is Soldak Entertainment's space ARPG in which you play the eponymous Drox Operative, a sort of mercenary. You are plopped into a procedurally generated sector where you must achieve any one of a list of victory conditions. Whether you succeed or fail (by producing a loss condition) the sector closes and you start the process again.
The problems start with the foundation. The game is almost entirely created from code recycled from Soldak's older
clones. Added to that old code is a shallow diplomacy system that any player of Civilization will recognize. Some of the phrasing used in diplomacy screens is identical to what can be found in Civilization 4 or 5. I don't think it's wrong to copy ideas, but there's not enough original creativity in the diplomacy system for my taste.
If you're looking for a short game, this is it.

Like most Early Access games, TerraTech has a long way to go before we see a finished product. If you're a fan of Early Access, pre-alpha, alpha, and beta games, and supporting the developers by purchasing a game when it is in these stages of development, then by all means purchase TerraTech. Like any other game, I suggest you watch some Let's Play videos on YouTube, or watch a few Twitch streams to see if it looks like something you'd be interested in.
TerraTech is a game about building bots, or "techs" as they're called. You can build both land-based and flying techs, or a combination of both. The game has wheeled vehicles, from slow and rugged to very fast and fragile. It has hovercraft, conventional flight, and VTOL/STOL. It's up to you how you build your tech. You can also build a base, gather and refine resources, craft objects, as well as sell them (or sell the refined resources).
The price, admittedly, is a little on the high side for a non-AAA game in this stage of development, but not so high that I consider it a deal-breaker. It was on sale recently for 30% off, so if money is tight, I suggest you add it to your wishlist and check your e-mail daily. It's difficult to say what is and what isn't a "fair price" for an Early Access game, since we have no way of knowing what the developer's costs and overhead are. I recently purchased a game on Steam for $5 that I felt could easily have sold for $20. The reason for the low price? It was being developed by one guy, which meant very low overhead. What it really boils down to, I suppose, is "will you get $20 worth of enjoyment from the game?". I think you will. And don't forget, you can always come back to Early Access games 6 months, a year, or two years down the road and play again.
With the price of AAA games still on the rise, it's up to us as gamers to support the independent developers and purchase pre-release games that we think we'll enjoy playing. The more small companies that turn into larger companies, the more competition the huge companies will have, which is always a good thing.

Your decisions are very important. If you make a bad decision, expect the game to make it
clear.
You have the option to run from battles and leave the dungeon.
Just like real life, stress damage is much worse than physical damage. A broken bone will heal with minimal attention. Insanity is not so easy. Do
ignore this.
This game is turn-based. This is extremely important. Giving your enemies as few turns as possible as late as possible is the single most important aspect of combat.
The second most important aspect is target priority. Know the most dangerous targets and stop them from acting however possible.
Grinding will not make the game easier. The stronger your units get, the bigger their ego gets, and they will refuse to accept easier quests.
Everything in both life and in game is uncertain. Plan for this. Do not expect anything to go perfectly and have a plan for when something fails. Because it
fail when you do not.
Every boss will utterly destroy you. The best you can do is to utterly destroy them
.
People
die. Mistakes
be made. Things
go horribly wrong. Stand up and try again. If things aren't looking up, turn back and fight another day. Managing your own stress is just as important as managing your party's.

There is a school of criticism that holds limited experience of a thing as disqualifying: if you don't have a full appreciation of a thing, your opinion is necesarily incomplete, partially-formed, less useful, etc.
Having spent a little less than an hour with Lords of the Fallen, what I have to say about it is without a doubt based on a very incomplete consideration, so make what you will of it.
Between its phoned-in, me-too character and environment designs (which make the second-rate, copy-cat toss-offs of Darksiders look downright creative by comparison) and the fact that it shamlessly and half-assedly apes all of the worst parts of Dark Souls gameplay/control design apparently without realizing what makes DaS fun in the first place, Lords of the Fallen is a complete non-starter.
One could certainly make the argument that my opinion is superficial and, if I had stuck with Lords of the Fallen, I might have found something redeeming about it, but to that I can only say that I have but one life to live, and I have neither the time nor the inclination to embark upon an 80-plus-hour search for some kernel of fun in this mercilessly unoriginal, punishingly cheap-feeling Souls-like/Souls-clone simply to justify my opinion that Lords of the Fallen is an absolutely irredeemable piece of trash.
If you managed to stick with it and you found something you like in this game, good on you.
Me? I refuse to do it.

UPDATE:  Everything I've said below is true, but I've done some research and am forced to change my review to negative.  I purchased an annual pass (which I almost never do...but Fallout is so awesome I couldn't resist) but that apparently DIDN'T include ANY of the new content.  I find that to be questionable business practice at best.  Further, the system downloading content to my PC which I cannot access unless I pay money is also uncool.  Sorry, Bethesda.  Fix this and I'll fix the review (not that they care, but at least I can say it).
I'm seeing a lot of negative reviews recently for Fallout 4 and I figure I needed to add my voice to the fray.  I should start by saying that Fallout 3 and Fallout New Vegas are amongst my all-time favorite games.  Does Fallout 4 live up to those games for intricacy and depth of story?  No, not really.  It is, however, beautifully presented with quality voice acting and music, a good story, and dozens of fascinating characters to meet.  The gameplay ranges from story-driven open-world exploration to settlement building.  It does still contain an embarrassing number of bugs and the settlements you build will sometimes glitch in ways that are frustrating.  My biggest personal complaint about this game is that some of the relationships are more shallow than I'd like (the writers of this game don't seem to put much weight on the impact that children have on their parents or the other way around) and the end of the game's story is more of a whimper than a bang.
This game is, overall, incredibly fun to play with tons of content, an engaging story (even if the end isn't terribly dramatic), and a character building system that lets you play the game the way you want to.  I strongly reccomend it to anyone who likes open-world RPGs in a dystopian post-apocalyptic world with settlement building content.

TL:DR - If you love ARPGs and want to play a very unique interpretation of the genre, buy this game. It is wonderful.
Drox Operative is a highly unique experience which is a rare feat in today's world of games that are immediately familiar and easily described as "Game A" combined with "Game B". Although not flashy, it has heart, creativity, fun, reward, and innovation in spades. The play is direct and simple as is typical for ARPGs but very deep and customizable, and the choices of what equipment to keep and what to trade away goes well beyond simply choosing which bauble has the biggest numbers on it. The best adjective I can use for this game is 'rewarding'. The experience of playing Drox Operative FAR FAR outstrips the moderate price tag that Texas-based Soldak Entertainment is asking for it.
Drox Operative is a true hidden gem that combines 4x space, ARPG, and resource management into a game that is simple to play, hard to master and always evolving because of the choices you make. All of this combines to make a game that feels alive and dangerous in a way that other ARPGs just don't have. It is an unexpected treasure nestled in a hidden corner of a genre that has many fine offerings. The only disappointing thing about this game is that so few people know about it. With wider coverage this game would be legendary.
If you love ARPGs but want something that takes the genre to the next level, play the free demo. Better still, save yourself some time and just buy the game. The galaxy awaits.
Happy gaming,

I want to like this game. I really honestly do. I love the concept. I love flying around in space shooting♥♥♥♥♥♥
But honestly, this game fails on a lot of levels. It just misses the mark in a lot of glaring ways.
1) Scaling: I understand that a "boss" monster is gonna be tough, but when he's got 10x your health/shields/whatever and can do vastly more damage per hit than you can (to the tune of damn near 1shotting you), it just takes the fun out of it for me.
2) Speed: Enemy ships can and will outrun your bullets; missiles i could understand, but bullets ought to be a lot faster than they are. Additionally, enemy ships (even MASSIVE boss ships) are capable of going WAY faster than player ship. They will go ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ across the screen in crazy circles etc. making them unhittable via most weapon types.
3) Energy: It is your enemy. Your ship will be permanently sucking wind. If i had most of my hardpoints dedicated to weapons, was cycling all of them on cooldown, and had no energy regen items installed, i can understand energy problems. That is NOT the case, a single decent laser will suck down as much energy as your whole ship can produce, including several installed energy regen devices. Get used to sucking down energy consumables on cooldown during fights.
4) AI races: They basically all hate each other, and you. War is the default state in each sector. Someone will be mad at you virtually all the time.
5) Victory conditions: Game has great array of victory conditions, several of which are nigh unusable. A diplomatic victory requires you to be allied with multiple AI races, who must be allied with each other. After playing over a dozen sectors, i've only seen 2 computer races allied once, and it didnt last very long before i got drug into the resulting war. Economic victory requires you to accumulate a ♥♥♥♥pile of wealth via quests etc. I've never been more than 1/3 of the way to that victory before the AI races have killed each other off and quests collapse in number. Simplest victories are to kill enough AI race ships/planets to become "feared", or ally with the dominant race and help them kill off everyone else.
Bottom line is that i just dont feel at all like a "hero" in this game. AI ships play by different rules, allowing them to be much stronger than the game allows me to be. Not a very rewarding experience in a game that aims itself at being a fun shooting time waster.

Overall the gameplay is much improved from NBA 2k15(which i put almost 600 hours into) between MYGM, and MyCareer modes. There are more animations and they feel smoother and more realistic. Dribbling and using the right stick to crossover and perform other moves is still very satisfying. The shot meter is back and feels the same helping you to guide shots into the net. Defense even has its own meter that shows how close to the defender you are and how much pressure you are producing on him.  There have been some small control changes since 2k15. Now the face buttons of the controller allow you to perform bounce passes, or lob passes alongside the standard pass. This helps you feel more in control and turn the ball over less. Centers and other big men down low feel more like you are playing their counter parts. Slow, not very good ball handling but big tall bruisers who use their size to their advantage. Defense has been slightly improved and shots are harder to make, as you are less likely to be wide open. This more realistically portrays FG % in the NBA and feels less cheesy online.
Graphics are improved as well, with 2k adding in new body scans. Carmelo Anthony now looks substantially different than Lebron James. As mentioned before animations feel smoother and more realistic. I have experienced some crashing issues when in game and navigating menues. There are also some random glitches in game that detract from the overall experience. For example there is a new feature when your my player is subbed into the game.This feature shows the player you are currently guarding or being guarded by. It shows the players strengths and weaknesses. There is a problem that occurs randomly however when the players strengths/ weaknesses never appear and you are stuck looking at a semi frozen image of the player for 30 seconds. After playing last years version im sure the bugs will still be there months later(none are gamebreaking save for the infrequent crashes, just minor annoyances.)
There is no ability to configure keyboard controls. 2k literally gave no thought to the PC gamer with this port. Crossfire is terrible but with my one AMD r9 270x i am getting 60 FPS with very little stuttering, so i am pleased with the optimization especially over last years version.
There is a wide plethora of game modes in this years game, i have never dabbled in My team because i hate pay to win. But MYGM is fun and feels improved. The real reason i cannot recommend this game at full price is the changes to MYCareer and to be specific the changes directed by Spike Lee. Livin' Da Dream is a joke.You create a character like in past iterations of the gamemode however this time you dont get to choose a nickname because that persona has already been created for you. Spike Lee has dubbed your character Frequency Vibrations or Freq for short, sex toy or porn star either way the name is terrible. The story revolves around your character and his family, you are born into a african-american family with an african-american twin sister. If the story following all this was actually good and well written than maybe i could excuse my white character who looked totally out of place and confused as to why his mom had never told him who his real father was. Honestly its not a big deal, things like this have happened to other races and games in the past and i could get over it, the problem is the story is absolutely terrible. The story revolves around your friend VIctor Van Lier who is supossed to be a bad influence on you and you are warned multiple times by the team owner, your twin sister, and your characters girlfriend who comes out of nowhere sometime in college.
You dont get to make any choices about how your story unfolds besides the choice of High schools (1 of 3) and choice of colleges (1 of 9). The story is so melodramatic, people arguing over your image or multiple refrences to friends and family using you as a meal ticket. Choices of team do not affect the story any. Minor details like your characters celebratory dance "freaking and vibin" as well as interviews of family and friends during the cutscenes do nothing to add anything to the terribly written farse that is Livin' Da Dream.  Spike Lee seems to believe that people from Harlem have the same terrible vernacular that he embodys in his titles. This terrible story mode takes away your rookie season as well, which is something that 2k really seems to enjoy in MYCareer the last two years. You get to play 3 Highschool games where your character is truly OP and 4 college games but not earn any VC for them as well as not be able to change the game lengths. Your character than is forced to be a one and done player and go to the NBA draft with an overall rating of 55, which is terrible. You are heralded as a top 10 draft pick, i went number 7 but the other players selected around that time are 77-78. By design 2k makes you either a terrible player or have to open your wallet just to keep up. Your rookie season is only 8 games (instead of the 82 in a real NBA season) with Spike Lee's terrible 20 minute cutscenes in between. Also you can change the Freq nickname after your rookie season but for some reason announcers/ pre game show will still sometimes refer to you as Freq.
After your rookie season MyCareer returns to its roots allowing you to play any games along the season you would like while also introducing a new days off feature and allowing you to select whether or not to go to a "Live practice" or hang out with teamates/fellow Nba players or go do endorsement deals. This is where MyCareer should have started. "Live Practices are fun and really the draw in this mode is building a character and watching his career progress rather than slated cutscenes of melodrama.
Somewhere along the way this mode lost all its basing in realisim as well because after your first season the team owner realeases you to go into Free Agency where you can choose three teams that have varying levels of interest in your sevices and negotiate Money and minutes. I think Spike Lee tries to rationalize it with your friend Victor causing you to get fired. Honestly though has anyone ever heard of a top 10 pick being dropped because of a friends actions? Spike Lee just took the easy way out as he did with most of the other parts of this mode.
Tldr: Really i cant recommend the game even though gameplay is so much better and graphics improved because of how much the Mycarrer mode has declined. I still find ways to enjoy the game, but get it on deal since this is turning into a yearly cash cow akin to EA's.

I've never really paid much attention to this title, assuming (wrongly) that it was a lesser version of SPAZ. How I wish I had known what a gem this game was sooner! Unfortunatley, Drox Operative is mislabeled as simply being an "action RPG," when in reality it is far more than merely that. This game is actually similar to The Last Federation in some ways; a 4X game that pits you with or against the computer players who are warring against or allying with each other. Half-Life was revolutionary at release and still holds up as one of the best fps games ever made. It has tight controls, an interesting story, an immersive world with gameplay to that perfectly compliments it among the things that makes Half-Life amazing, each of which I will try to go into throughout this review. The first thing I would like to mention that I personally think was a fantastic innovation was completely in game story without a single cutscene that breaks up the gameplay. This draws you into the game, makes you a part of the world that makes you identify with the character and story. You feel like you are Gordon Freeman. You aren't just watching a story play out, you are experiencing it. The NPCs feel to be real people, and you can identify with each one with what position they are in. Even the main character is just a normal scientist put into a tight spot. The next part of Half-Life that is incredible is how cohesive the world is. It is not seperate levels with just moving from one to another, the entire game is one straight line through the world (up to the end) and just advancing farther through the Black Mesa complex and area surrounding it. You are continuously moving throughout the world, and while it is linear it does feel like you are exploring a world instead of being led through it (looking at you Ocarina Of Time). The gameplay doesn't just drop you into the action, you start going on a train ride into Black Mesa and go through everything up to the experiment that sets the game off, but this hidden exposition really deepens just how drastic the scenario is. Now onto the actual gameplay of Half-Life. The guns are varied and you are constantly finding new and interesting weapons as you progress. Shooting feels natural, with realistic recoil and solid aiming and shooting. Each weapon is not just there to be there, they have their own uses that makes each one situational. The enemies that you are fighting have complicated AI that makes fighting each type of enemy its own experience and makes them very difficult and engaging. Enemies do not just sit there and fire, they communicate, they flank, they throw grenades, and more. Shooting is fun and combat is enjoyable. The story is unique and incredibly unexpected as the twists and turns are revealed both directly and through subtle hints. The game does not fall into the same generic story tropes that 65% of fps games seem to. "Bad guy wasn't the real bad guy and he helps you to defeat the true bad guy and it turns out you haven't been the good guy all along" etc etc you know the drill. Half-Life is an engaging and one of a kind fps game that revolutionized the industry when it was released and has continued to be one of the best fps games of all time. Overall, I'd rate Half-Life a 9/10.

Well, a fter a 9 hours journey in the world of virtual hacking, I must say I'm satisfied but also a bit sad it was so short.
At first, I thought it would be a needlessly complicated and boring game but I decided to give it a chance and, boy did I make the right decision. The game was complex enough that anybody without basic computer skills wouldn't stand a chance against this game but it's simplified enough that you don't have to remember dozens of complex commands, you can easily complete a command by pressing TAB, which makes the games less of a chore.
The story is engaging as the death of a known hacker named Bit is slowly revealed to be not a fruit of some accident but something more sinister and you are his last hope of successfully executing plans that might be the difference between corporate digital control and freedom. Along the way, there are contracts to fulfill, ranging from simple information retrieval to adding or removing entries from a death row record and even hacking a suffering patient's pacemaker to give its host a peaceful, painless death. And as you progress, you'll find programs that will help you get inside more secure systems in order to complete the more difficult contracts.
The game is not devoid of humor as you'll find IRC chat logs and other documents inside the devices you hack and some of them are hilarious, such as a guy replacing the word "wand" with "wang" in the first Harry Potter book and has posted some excerpts that are good for a laugh or a guy telling how he stood in front of his nerighbour's burning house, holding a stick with a marshmallow.
The sad thing with these files is they're lacking in variety and often you'll find the same files on different computer, breaking the impression that beyong the machines you're hacking, there are people going about their everyday lives and chatting about different aspects of their lives. As entertaining as they are, once you've read these logs, there's not really anything else worth reading.
Hacknet is pretty linear and all the paths you can take bring you to the same ending. One of the things I found disappointing is, you're never really in much danger, except once, when some other hacked decides to attack you, deleting your UI and forcing you to get out of this mess through terminal. It was a tense moment where I wanted to get back at the guy but none of what I did made the slight difference and once you get out of this mess, there are no other instance where you have to fight off other hackers.
Overall this was a great experience and I would love to play a sequel or at least, an extension, I hope the developper will give us more Hacknet and expand upon all the ideas that were implemented. I wholeheartedly recommend this game for those who like smart, logical experiences and detective games.

Truly amazing game, funny, engaging, and for all types of people who like to solve mysteries and logical puzzles. The story mode can be done under 10 hours, but the game deserves 100% its price.
If you do not have experience in networking, or using computers from command line at all, do not fear. The game introduces you into it gradually and you'll get the trick of it in no time.
If you do (like myself) have experience in networking, or using computers from command line, do not fear either. It feels real, familiar (Unix-like shell), but the "gradually introducing you" is not spoonfeeding you with "type XY to do Z" kind of pop-ups that annoy you. The game has several things "of its own" that you will learn really fast and I saw myself really excited and feeling like I was exploring some kind of distro like BackTrack or Kali Linux and going like "look at the amount of tools we've got!! And they work like a charm, too!"
If you are not a real-life hacker, you'll sure feel like one in here.
I followed the role of a white hat (it aligns with my way of thinking), although some of my in-game actions could qualify enough to be considered "grey". The good thing here is that you have complete freedom to approach and follow the story filling your own role, without the game forcing you into it (or even "presenting" them to you...you have your tools, you decide how to use them and deal with the potential consequences)
The game is full of secrets and jokes to be found here and there (take a look to the IRC logs), the story will keep you immersed from second 0 till the end of it.
Of course the game is not perfect, and I did personally miss some commands, like "cp" (copy files locally), "find" (self explanatory), and some way to create files and edit them beyond using "replace" on them.
I definitely recommend it: 9/10

Darkest Dungeon doesn't speak to everyone, but to those it does, it is absolutely amazing. I will admit at times the game has been extremely punishing. The developers have done a pretty good job about toeing the between just punishing enough and masochistic.
The end game can be quite the grind and I have definitely walked away from the game for months at a time because I was angry about losing high level characters to improbable events. But I always come back in the end. I feel like more than any other game, Darkest Dungeon has taught me about how humans react to extremely stressful environments. Sometimes you fail, but other times "Not this one, not today!"
Positives:
1. The narrator is absolutely amazing. I feel like the narrator was worth the price of admission by himself.
2. The combat is fairly enjoyable, if simple.
3. The game does a good job of encapsulating the challenges of being a hero, instead of making it trivially easy.
Negatives:
1. Sometimes the random number generator is just out to completely screw you. It is part of the experience after all.
2. On the harder difficulties, the grind needed to complete the Darkest Dungeon floors is quite slow. Especially if you happen to lose a vital character (which does happen).
3. A lot of the boss fights are just the same boss fight, but with a more difficult iteration. The early ones are a bit too easy. The later ones aren't really worth beating and can be extremely punishing.
4. Most of the core mechanics are instrinsically quite simple.
Overall, I recommend the game quite highly. Just know ahead of time you're getting into a fairly difficult game. Do take heart- there isn't really a failure state, other than walking away and refusing to play anymore.

Let me preface by saying that I loved playing this game.
That out of the way, this is not the pick-a-path narrative that it advertises itself as.  The characters feel real, the story is engaging, and the voice acting is great.  The graphics are pretty good too, for the style that they are in.
However, you control the DETAILS of the story, not any major changes or outcomes.  You can pick who dies a little sooner or who dies a little later or how much people like you.  But you can't stop anyone from dying when the story decides they die, and you can't really change anything that would be worth changing.
It's fun, but it's not what it's hyped up to be.  If all you care about is story, this is the game for you.
If you want your choices to matter, look elsewhere.  There is only one choice that actually lets you affect the outcome of the game, and that comes on the tail-end of Season 2, and no previous choice you make will influence it in any way.
I understand perfectly that this is mostly due to continuity and technical limitations (IE: there would just be TOO MANY outcomes), but the railroading really hits home when you stop, reload, pick the opposite choice... and the same thing happens.  For every.  Single.  Choice.
I am a fan of this game, but people should know this going in.  And that's why I can't really give it a positive recommendation.

I had to write this at some point. I've put it off for a while, knowing I've a lot to say about this game (and Season 2, but that's a review for another day.) Granted, there are some flaws here and there, but everywhere else bleeds tragedy, warmth, tension, and blood. Lots of blood.
(That's one thing I should mention straight away; In spite of the comic-book aesthetic, this is an 18+ game through and through, so be warned.)
The gameplay, like other Telltale games, rings of ye olde point-and-click adventure games, in terms of puzzles as well as dialogue trees and interactions with other characters. The reason I think this works is because they saw the adventure game's potential for interactive storytelling. It gives you, generally, four dialogue options: taking too long to answer will be taken as silence, which is sometimes your best bet. Characters' opinions of you vary depending on things ranging from how you talk to them in downtime to who you side with when decision have to be made. This creates tension when you have to try to make decisions based on what you think is best for the group rather than who you'd like to side with, which works because all the characters are characterised brilliantly, with even the worst people carrying their own set of virtues, and the best their own flaws. The variety of dialogue choices is open enough to have a degree of choosing how the story weaves, but limited enough to keep it consistent with the protagonist Telltale intended for the story.
And what a protagonist he is. Lee Everett, who escapes (albeit unintentionally) from police custody when the zombie outbreak starts, meets a girl named Clementine, who was hiding in a treehouse when they cross paths. They quickly get together with a diverse group of survivors from all walks of life (it's always like that in zombie fiction, isn't it? I bet there's a group somewhere out there consisting of six left-wing plumbers who don't know how to fare when monsters start breaking down doors.)
As I mentioned, Lee was being sent to prison when the story begins, and from there we learn more about why, making you question at first if he can really be trusted to take care of a little girl. Ultimately, though, he is. Because even though he can't completely escape his past, he's someone capable of compassion, humor, and bravery. Some of the story threads (and, indeed, the choices he makes) begin to show you that he and Clementine can't last forever together, and it all culminates in a- sorry, can't go into details, I don't want to spoil anything. I'll just say that, while the game made me cry twice (that's twice more than any other game), it has a masterful balance of humanity, comedy, pacing, and harrowing moments, in one of my favourite videogame narratives to date.
The action is very straightforward, so I'll make it quick. Going between quick-time events and reflexively aiming the mouse to the big glowing weak spot, the combat is never particularly difficult, but it's paced well enough to keep from growing stale.
The puzzles are the game's weak point, as they're generally about searching environments for that one item you need, then clicking 'use.' While it's not particularly exciting, I wouldn't remove the puzzles the game has, because it's all built into the way the game is paced; removing them would turn the game into one long action scene/drama, bouncing between fighting within the group as to what to do next, and actual fighting with the tenacious zombies (and humans, sometimes.)
Ultimately, this is a story game, designed for people looking for engaging characters rather than engaging gameplay, with mechanics meant for putting you in Lee's blood and tear-stained shoes, instead of bringing visceral crunchy zombie killing (Which I'm sure can be found in countless other games.) The journey this game presents is incredible, thankfully, that is almost guaranteed to move you, scare you, and especially in the case of the ending, leave you breathless.
This game has gotten Telltale Games universal acclaim, countless Game of the Year awards, and the keys to countless franchises for them to go crazy with. They've earned it. An enticing precursor to the developers' future endeavors, and a stunning acheivement in its own right. Oh, and don't worry; Season Two does not disappoint.

I received this game as a gift and to be completely honest I didn't expect to play it as much as I have.
Darkest Dungeon is fairly oblique when it comes to game mechanics, and the tutorial levels + hints/messages are concise at best. This plunges the player into a fairly complex scenario that requires constant adaptation and experimentation to be able to survive, and anyone expecting an easy difficulty curve may be rudely shocked.
Expect a first playthrough to be packed with hard lessons, untimely deaths and a decent dose of frustration. Expect your best planned-out virgin strategies to go down in flames, and your most leveled-up and valued heroes will falter.
BUT the game is not difficult once you learn the systems. It's only difficult if you think that you don't have to put any effort in. Because, like other games touted as being 'difficult' that are on the market at the moment, Darkest Dungeon will punish you for mistakes. Any sloppy/unthinking play will likely be hyper-blasted into last decade, and I'm not just talking about the combat - food, torches, shovels and other supplies need to be considered and weighed up when exploring the dungeons of the Estate and skimping on any of these variables will introduce an extra element of danger.
The only complaint I have is how long it takes to level up individual heroes and the way different level heroes can interact with dungeons. For example, if you have a full roster of maximum-level (or close to max level) heroes and one dies, then recruiting a new hero to replace the fallen character and then levelling them up can be problematic.
Overall though, any problems are minor and given the amount of playtime (at least 30-40 hours, and that's if you already know what you are doing) Darkest Dungeon is a no-brainer for anyone looking for a challenging game with a sh*t-load of depth and character.

I can't really understand the high volume of negative opinions about Darkest Dungeon. It probably comes from gamers who just do not enjoy this kind of games, because it delivers exactly what it promises - you need to think ahead, you need tactical sense to make hard battles manageable, you need to prioritize what you spend your sparse resources on, instead of just spamming all upgrades just to maximize everything you can click on; you need to choose if you risk for the greed sake, or play it relatively safe, but with less resources gained, which will eventually handicap you in the long turn. THINK and MAKE HARD CHOICES - this is main philosophy here.
I have to finish it yet, but I am more interested than I was in the beginning. I like this style, but I think it requires applying certain mindset to make it really enjoyable - perhaps the most important thing that can ruin this game for you is trying to automatically repeat the schemes from other titles; that's mistake.
You won't create one, universal superheroes party winning everything - you need to shuffle heroes and send different teams, with different skills, to different places. This is by design.
You won't loot absolutely everything in each quest - you will be forced to pick what you need most, and ditch the rest - the challenge here is to pick right things which will bolster you in the long run.
You will have your favorite heroes have flaws, negative quirks - so what, nobody is perfect. You can choose to fix them - but it is also choice, it's expensive. Better armour, or curing this annoying Fear of Eldritch? Your choice. Make it now, or later, sending the hero to areas with no such problems for now...
You will be occasionally crippled by bad RNG, but it is FAR less issue than i.e. XCOM - RNG here is far less influencing, and proper strategic and tactical choices are far more important.
To be honest for now there is only one thing that should be changed imo, namely some quest items stacking, as for now 3 vials of some liquid taking 3 inventory slots is needless (it can be easily modded, btw); the rest of inventory is fine and adds this additional layer of making hard choices (like throwing away food for some gems, well let's hope we will come out of here soon! ;)). However, with current design from the economical perspective I find it quite pointless to go to Long runs at all - while going to Short with 1 Antiquarian nets similar loot value, being easier, faster and cheaper overall. Some tweaks to inventory for Long runs could make them viable choice perhaps, but for now they are there only if you want some additional sense of adventure, resource-wise it seems pretty counterproductive due to current inventory loot/system design.
Anyway. A lot of things people keep complain about are part of game design, once you accept this design view, game becomes pretty neat, well-thought and awesome. But if you are playing the game pretending that this is some different game is like entering the soccer stadium and complaining why you can't hold the ball with your hands... seriously, people, devs explained very explicitly what this game is about and delivered exactly the kind of game they promised, it is well designed and achieves what was planned and advertised. Giving negative reviews just because it is not the type of game you would like to play seems pretty unfair.
Perhaps nowadays mainstream pop culture taught us that you do not have to choose and you can have just everything it is out there with as little effort as possible, but with mindset like that just stay away from this title, it's not for you. Otherwise - try it, and you won't regret it, it even shines more, the darker levels you descend...

funnily enough this will be my second review of the game
as my first one was mentioning their last attempt at paid mods.

Creation club is bad idea which will hopefully fall apart once more.
But considering the two gigabyte update that was forced on everyone
I doubt it. I was lucky enough for it not to force me update so my mods are
still functional. Now with that out of the way lets countine to the acutal game.
Fallout 4 is a decent fps with some lite rpg elements and base building.
Though I disliked the story like the other fallout games for the most part you can
and will ignore it.
The biggest cons of the game is the lesser rpg elemets such as
-Dialogue
you now have a mass effect-esque Dialouge "tree" but some how even more simplfied
Everyone has seen the jokes of
yes
no (yes)
sarcastic (yes)
question
And that is because for the most part that is true. The biggest shame is that
outside the dlc you can't really be a bad person. Sure you can kill people
assuming they aren't important for the story and even then there are many people
you can't kill for no real reason.
-Skills and perks are now just perks
this forces you to spend your perk points on some perks everyone will use for most builds
as they are just that much more important for general play. Futhermore perks are generally
pretty boring such as 20/40/60/80/100 damage increases for most wep skills.
some are so pointless you might have it on one character for the mild novelty of it.
But won't ever use it for normal play. Though they do have a hand full of fun perks.
-Rep systerm
You no longer have rep for each town or settlement. Instead you can only become enemies/allies of certain
factions. I imagine this is mostly due to the smaller settlements almost guranteed to be part of the minutemen quests.
Which you get them to join you.
That being said there are some improvements which I'll mention.
+shooting
Supposedly they got help with the shooting mechanics from the doom guys and it really shows
the shooting in the game feels miles better then the ealier games.
+base building
Although the base building is quite rough around the edges with some mods it can become one of the more fun
parts of the game, if your into that sorta thing which I am.
+Armour segments
armour is now made out of pieces such as left leg right arm etc
+armour and wep modding
Not the downloadable kind but instead each weapon or armour segment can be upgraded (assuming you have the correct perks) Which while the mods are generally just x is better then y still a nice addition to the game.
+power armour
Power armour is pretty great in this game not only do they come in segments (like armour) they can be upgraded.
But they also require no training to use ,which some hard core fans will dislike and they now use a power souce known
as fusion cores.
Overall the game is a pretty decent FPS but a poor RPG that can be vastly improved with various mods you can download
online from places like nexus mod.  Though don't use their Mod manager use Mod Organizer it will save you some heart ache.

While Fallout 4 fails to live up to core Fallout standards, it isn't bad as it's own game and it's pretty fun to mod. Mods basically did all the work Bethesda couldn't with this game, ranging from bug fixes to making the game more direct towards Fallout 3 & New Vegas.
The Pros:
Fallout 4 is an outstanding upgrade in terms of graphics and some terms of voice acting. Characters look more human and it moves on from the dull singular pallette that's present in 3 and New Vegas. There's a more realistic feel to the environment and it directs more of the "50's retro future" theme nearly everywhere. The story isn't bad but could've had more directions, unlike Fallout 3 and New Vegas, your character's backstory is already defined, and there's really only four paths throughout the story you're able to take. The main 3 DLCs are also pretty fun, though the workshop expansions feel more like free content than paid content.
The Cons:
: This two gigabyte expansion is the bane of this game's existence. While mods have been a way of expressing creative freedom amongst games, Bethesda seems persistent to capitalize on them even after their last blunder with Steam Worshop. While Fallout 4 still has much to be patched by them, Creation Club is the true extent of them saying "fine, pay us five dollars if you're so damn smart." Putting bug fixes and content to potentially enhance the game the way it should've been behind paywalls, Creation Club is one of the worst business moves i've seen made by a video game company, second to none with Nintendo's cease and desist against a fan game. As much as it is a way to profit off of your content much like TF2's Steam Workshop, paid mods just dont work. Unlike items being accepted and profitted off of in games like CS:GO or TF2, mods are a loose cannon that could be a waste of money as they can potentially crash the game, opens a backend to uploading
people's content from sites like Nexus and allowing profits off of stolen content, and overall a really bad move. If you want my advice, just use Nexus.
The game's challenge threshold is also lowered as many rpg elements have been removed in exchange for shooter elements, and perks can just make you OP as hell now.
My conclusion:
A game beriddled with disappointment towards core Fallout fans only enhanced by it's community, the game itself isn't terrible, but way too straightforward compared to previous fallout games. My advice is get it on sale, dont use Creation Club, and use Nexus if you want mods. Show bethesda we dont want their paid patches, but legitimate delivered patches. Ever played a space strategy game where you have to colonize planets, trade and maintain a diplomatic relationship with other races and take care of your own people while doing so? Ever wondered what it would be like to be that random event that caused citizens to rebel, technology to be sold to your enemy, a race that you would like to be a friend but just won't listen because some element in the game says 'Hell no!'?
Well in this game you can; This is a top-down space shooter, but around the player several computer players are playing out a space strategy game. You can befriend them, you can fight them, you can trade with them, you can support them in their war or colonization efforts, you are a Drox Operative. And the other races know that to have a Drox Operative on your side is the path to victory.
The graphics are great and the player is allowed a reasonable range of customization to make it his/her own. Musical score and sounds a pretty good, as is the general feel of the game. I did have some problems with the keys though, and understanding what the game was about in the first place, but after 15 mins of just diving in head first I found it surprisingly easy to understand. As for the keys, would like a weapon group to be used for weapons; The only weapon that fires when pressing the mouse is weapon no. 1, although in all fairness I haven't been looking for it very hard, its probably in there somewhere.
You can only have 1 ship (per Operative / Save slot ) and it is a persistant ship (and crew), meaning it carries over from one game into the other. A bit confusing is a game being called a 'Sector', which from what I understand is a galaxy, which happens to consist of...sectors...ya... Anywho, you can fully customize your ship to be a fighter, bomber, trader, colony vessel, or any combination you may think of. It grows in class as you grow in experience (and award points to a particular skill) opening more slots in your ship to install equipment in.
All in all an original idea realised; A gem in any original gamers collection.

EDIT 2/8/2015: Okay, so this is my first time actually doing this. I never really do this kind of stuff. Mainly, because I'm lazy or something. But this game♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off so much I had to write it. Okay so here's my overall expirence with this game, and yes, I know that it's in "Early Access":
Survival mode:
So, There is like, 20 players here, that speak russian. The game hasn't even started yet and people are getting trolled appearently. I'm watching people's towers just fall down by 3 people at once. My base was ruined in about 30 seconds. It takes way too many hits to kill just one zombie, and I mean extremely way to many. Oh man does this remind me of Unturned. Versus Mode:
Remember how Battle mode was? They're both the same! The only difference was that Battle mode can go up to 4 teams and Versus goes to 2 teams only. Why? Why create two different game modes just to have a different number of teams? Well, I could actually score points. So I decided to actually play something in this game for once. But then I realised the score limit was 500. EVERY KILL IS 1 POINT. There is absoutely no way we're going to win a 5v5 to 500 points! That's completely insane! Who thought that was a good idea?! The gameplay is the same as Battle, you run in, get shot, they got shot, you get the idea. The maps are very small, boxed up cages and are very limited for movement. You could actually spawn camp if your entire team is at their spawn. But then again, it'll happen to you next. You'll get spawn camped nearly half the match. Want to know the best part? Ugh.), and pretty much EVERYTHING. Anyone who would actually pay about $30 just to win a match is just sad, and they should be ashamed of theirselfs for even buying a single thing from the store. When someone with OP Equipment goes on the other team, you're a dead man. One shot kills will happen ALL THE TIME. YOU WILL NOT ESCAPE AND YOU WILL NOT LIVE. But luckily, whoever this kid was, he was a noob, and he sucked horribly. I tried all the weapons. The M3's range is sooooo short! 20% you won't be able to hit a thing! But as me and my team continued onward and after about what seemed like an hour, we FINALLY won the match. And now it was one of the biggest waste of my time. The game doesn't even say "You win!" or anything, it just teleports everyone to the next level! This game is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥! Just a bunch of medikits and useless stuff that won't make a single difference when you meet someone with a Pay 2 Win deal. Alright, so what's next on the list of crap?
Capture Mode:
I honestly expected some kind of "Capture the Flag" thingy. But instead, you had to capture what I like to call "Areas". The more "Areas" you claim, the more points earn. Wait, is that even how it's supposed to go? Because thank the instructions, giving me useful information. THERE IS NO INSTRUCTIONS, I HAD TO FIGURE IT OUT MYSELF. Anyways, rage aside. By looking at the automap with your eyeholes, you can see what color a certain "Area" as. There are 4 teams, just like Battle. Darkest Dungeon doesn't speak to everyone, but to those it does, it is absolutely amazing. I will admit at times the game has been extremely punishing. The developers have done a pretty good job about toeing the between just punishing enough and masochistic.
The end game can be quite the grind and I have definitely walked away from the game for months at a time because I was angry about losing high level characters to improbable events. But I always come back in the end. I feel like more than any other game, Darkest Dungeon has taught me about how humans react to extremely stressful environments. Sometimes you fail, but other times "Not this one, not today!"
Positives:
1. The narrator is absolutely amazing. I feel like the narrator was worth the price of admission by himself.
2. The combat is fairly enjoyable, if simple.
3. The game does a good job of encapsulating the challenges of being a hero, instead of making it trivially easy.
Negatives:
1. Sometimes the random number generator is just out to completely screw you. It is part of the experience after all.
2. On the harder difficulties, the grind needed to complete the Darkest Dungeon floors is quite slow. Especially if you happen to lose a vital character (which does happen).
3. A lot of the boss fights are just the same boss fight, but with a more difficult iteration. The early ones are a bit too easy. The later ones aren't really worth beating and can be extremely punishing.
4. Most of the core mechanics are instrinsically quite simple.
Overall, I recommend the game quite highly. Just know ahead of time you're getting into a fairly difficult game. Do take heart- there isn't really a failure state, other than walking away and refusing to play anymore.

Disclaimer: I was generously given a free copy of Particle Mace with the understanding that I was expected to review the title after spending some time with it.
Particle Mace was a wonderful surprise; with a blend of asteroid/geometry wars aesthetic and Hammerfight combat, my first session was 3 or 4 hours of “just one more try”.
If you have never played Hammerfight, you’re not missing out on much but that is besides the point. The game controls just like every other twin stick shooter out there but instead of using the other stick to pick a direction to fire, you must master inertia to swing around a handful of tethered particles in order to strike down the enemies. There are several ship variants to unlock and each handle markedly differently but all feel wonderful and responsive to pilot. In addition, there are also many modifiers applied to the the tethers in the “Mission” mode to mix things up a bit.
On the subject of modes, there are 4 total of which I have only dabbled in two of them. I didn’t try out coop or deathmatch but I spent extensive time with the arcade (survival) and mission modes. The arcade has 3 endless difficulties-easy, hard and asteroid only-and they scale remarkably well as time passes and you begin to rack the points up. The mission mode constantly cycles through objectives and conditions to meet and is a blast to work through. Unfortunately, this can get rather frustrating because you may get assigned 3 very conflicting quests at once and they each can hinder the others from being completed. It would be really nice to be able to pass on a mission temporarily when it’s causing trouble. However, Particle Mace is still a blast to play despite this quirk as the Arcade mode provides more than enough challenge and replayability.
I was honestly not expecting much booting it up, but I’m so glad to have discovered this little gem.

I received this game as a gift and to be completely honest I didn't expect to play it as much as I have.
Darkest Dungeon is fairly oblique when it comes to game mechanics, and the tutorial levels + hints/messages are concise at best. This plunges the player into a fairly complex scenario that requires constant adaptation and experimentation to be able to survive, and anyone expecting an easy difficulty curve may be rudely shocked.
Expect a first playthrough to be packed with hard lessons, untimely deaths and a decent dose of frustration. Expect your best planned-out virgin strategies to go down in flames, and your most leveled-up and valued heroes will falter.
BUT the game is not difficult once you learn the systems. It's only difficult if you think that you don't have to put any effort in. Because, like other games touted as being 'difficult' that are on the market at the moment, Darkest Dungeon will punish you for mistakes. Any sloppy/unthinking play will likely be hyper-blasted into last decade, and I'm not just talking about the combat - food, torches, shovels and other supplies need to be considered and weighed up when exploring the dungeons of the Estate and skimping on any of these variables will introduce an extra element of danger.
The only complaint I have is how long it takes to level up individual heroes and the way different level heroes can interact with dungeons. For example, if you have a full roster of maximum-level (or close to max level) heroes and one dies, then recruiting a new hero to replace the fallen character and then levelling them up can be problematic.
Overall though, any problems are minor and given the amount of playtime (at least 30-40 hours, and that's if you already know what you are doing) Darkest Dungeon is a no-brainer for anyone looking for a challenging game with a sh*t-load of depth and character.

I can't really understand the high volume of negative opinions about Darkest Dungeon. It probably comes from gamers who just do not enjoy this kind of games, because it delivers exactly what it promises - you need to think ahead, you need tactical sense to make hard battles manageable, you need to prioritize what you spend your sparse resources on, instead of just spamming all upgrades just to maximize everything you can click on; you need to choose if you risk for the greed sake, or play it relatively safe, but with less resources gained, which will eventually handicap you in the long turn. THINK and MAKE HARD CHOICES - this is main philosophy here.
I have to finish it yet, but I am more interested than I was in the beginning. I like this style, but I think it requires applying certain mindset to make it really enjoyable - perhaps the most important thing that can ruin this game for you is trying to automatically repeat the schemes from other titles; that's mistake.
You won't create one, universal superheroes party winning everything - you need to shuffle heroes and send different teams, with different skills, to different places. This is by design.
You won't loot absolutely everything in each quest - you will be forced to pick what you need most, and ditch the rest - the challenge here is to pick right things which will bolster you in the long run.
You will have your favorite heroes have flaws, negative quirks - so what, nobody is perfect. You can choose to fix them - but it is also choice, it's expensive. Better armour, or curing this annoying Fear of Eldritch? Your choice. Make it now, or later, sending the hero to areas with no such problems for now...
You will be occasionally crippled by bad RNG, but it is FAR less issue than i.e. XCOM - RNG here is far less influencing, and proper strategic and tactical choices are far more important.
To be honest for now there is only one thing that should be changed imo, namely some quest items stacking, as for now 3 vials of some liquid taking 3 inventory slots is needless (it can be easily modded, btw); the rest of inventory is fine and adds this additional layer of making hard choices (like throwing away food for some gems, well let's hope we will come out of here soon! ;)). However, with current design from the economical perspective I find it quite pointless to go to Long runs at all - while going to Short with 1 Antiquarian nets similar loot value, being easier, faster and cheaper overall. Giant Bomb PC Gaming Hub explained it best; "Space Diablo, but with consequences."
===Space Diablo===
The game is an action RPG, that takes place within a 4x RTS Strategy game played by the AI. You are a mercenary in this galaxy, and your mission is to achieve victory in one of the following ways...
By achieveing a Military Victory, by being allied with the last surviving race and destroying all your enemies.
By achieveing a Diplomatic Victory, by uniting all surviving races in a single alliance.
By achieveing an Economic Victory, by accumulating wealth for the Drox Operatives.
By achieveing a Fear victory, by destroying all who stand in your way without mercy.
By achieveing a Legend Victory, by completing assignments and missions given to you by the various races and exploring the galaxy.
And finally by completing any and all assignments offered to you by your commanding officers in the Drox Operative's Guild.
To succeed in these goals, you must travel the cosmos and upgrade your ship as you gain experience and randomly generated loot.
===Consequences===
Here's where the game get's interesting... As stated, there is a 4x RTS Strategy game being played by the AI all around you. You, as a Drox Operative, are able to influence the empires in the Galaxy. You can instigate wars and end wars, you can aid ships and colonies in distress, you can even fight in wars alongside an empire. Everything you do in the game influences the galaxy around you in some way.
===Verdict===
The game is excellent, and highly enjoyable in my opinion. I highly reccomend it if you're looking for a good Sci-Fi RPG. The game is also multi-player, allowing players to work together or against one another, so that's another plus in my book. The game is $19.99 normally, and I've seen the winter sale drop it 50% for it and the expansion.

For all of those complaining about lack of updates/content/whatever, did you not read the "Early Access Game" note? Did you not grasp the fact that you are NOT, in fact, buying a completed product? Do you not understand the meaning of being in open beta? You might want to go look up the meanings of those words before you start crying that you bought Starbound and are not getting the full game as you expected, and if you're too oblivious to know that there are nightly builds and updates that you can opt-in to, too bad.
This game IS indeed being worked on still, it has NOT been "abandoned" as some are saying. Creating and working on games takes a lot of time and effort. The creators of Starbound have lives, too, and shouldn't be expected to sit at their desks 24/7 doing nothing but working on it. If you can't handle that idea, go find a different game to play, preferrably one that's already completed.
As for the actual gameplay experience, this game is addicting. The worlds are fantastic, from peaceful grasslands to scummy swamps, to terrifying lava-covered wastelands. The music is beautiful, soothing, dramatic, and very fitting. Gameplay requires you to adapt and learn; as the planets change, so does their gravity. Jumping, moving, and fighting feels different with each new world you visit. Everything is destructable, so like Terraria and Minecraft, you can make amazing homes and basecamps on any planet you want, and then mark it as your home, so you can always return to it.
I could say even more, but there's a pretty good chance most won't read this far to begin with, so I'll stop here. Starbound is a fun game, and is fully worth the pricetag, AS LONG AS YOU UNDERSTAND THAT YOU ARE BUYING AN OPEN BETA, EARLY ACCESS GAME.

This game doesn't seem like much at first glance, and the screenshots and video did not entice me, but I'm glad I picked this up. Other people described it as diablo in space, and not because of the isometric view. However, unlike any other action RPG or just rpg's in general, this is the first that truly made me attempt to balance my build, and I found keeping my ship balanced and functional a rewarding challenge. There are also a lot of different ways to set everything up, for myself I used a combination of rapid fire lasers, missiles, and fighters while slow boating, and unlike most ARPG's, it's very easy to get overwhelmed. The game is very well balanced and put together from what I've seen so far, and that goes a long ways.
Visually the game can be run in 1080p, which makes a difference, and it can look better than the screenshots, but it won't impress anyone. It doesn't seem to have an ongoing story, but rather takes a sandbox approach with very loose winning conditions, ranging from economic and diplomatic methods to conquering and combat oriented methods. Controls for steering the ship aren't what I would consider intuitive, but they are easy enough to pick up using a mouse and keyboard.
While the game does have a lot of depth with the political system and other functions, they don't overcomplicate the game, and as long as you make conscientious choices on your allies and enemies, the politics can be largely ignored, and the game plays very arcadish. If you pay attention to the politics and the goings on, it almost feels like the major factions are engaged in a basebuilding RTS and you are there to push whichever sides you choose (not like a MOBA though, they will conquer each other, had one faction out of the running very early in my game), and interfere or ignore as you please. As long as you don't need AAA graphics, or story driven plots, this game will give you a lot of enjoyment.

I wish that I had played the demo first; I found this game disappointing.
Based on online, gaming magazine reviews and Youtube reviews, I was expecting something similar to Space Rangers 2: Reboot or a 4 x game like either Star Control or Master of Orion 2. This game is neither of these things.
You are the last of the Drox race, a once mighty Empire that was all but destroyed in a war. You only have one ship, you don't build more and you don't colonize planets. Your goal is to figure out which AI race will emerge as the strongest race and brown-nose them, by doing quests for them. A race might ask you to find a replacement power supply for a planet or smuggle in hand-held weapons, to quell subsequent riots. It sounds more interesting than it actually is, since it is just a case of buying an item from a specific vendor and then transporting it to the specific planet.
Figuring out which race will emerge victorious is not difficult, since you have 100% intelligence gathering, regarding Empire strength. Some races lack social skills, or are fickle, or aggressive. I knew how the second game would play out, after losing the first. The race traits don't change between games, so that will completely kill any longevity.
You spend most of your time flying around, at the speed of a snail, exploring derelict ships, in an attempt to uncover the fog of war. Random ships and races will attack you. Combat consists of spamming the 1 key because the other two weapons in the game are worthless, by comparison. Finding random loot and juggling items was fun in the first game but you figure out how to min / max the game in a couple of hours.
This game was a waste of time and money, to the point that I highly recommend playing the demo or avoiding it altogether. I wish that I could get my money back. Play whatever is the best Space Rangers game out there.
