Played an assload during the beta. It never got old (though it admittedly started to feel a bit easy).
I've been advertising it to friends as "Hotline Miami, but it's a sci-fi roguelike." One hit kills (or knocks out) all targets, one hit takes you down the same way, they throw your body out the airlock, and you have a limited time to remote-control your pod to recover your own body before you suffocate or bleed out or both (harder than it sounds).
It's you against an entire ship, often with 50+ heavily-armed opponents, and you had better abuse every little trick you've got. Throw a knife at someone and teleport it back to your inventory to throw it again. Toss a breach grenade at your feet and swap places with your assassination target on the other side of a wall, then run like hell before you get sucked into space. Or just go full Hotline Miami, dual AP shotguns, and blast your way through the entire crew.
(Or you could, like, sneak around and get the Ghost bonus. But that's haaaard, so...)
Fingers crossed for some modding capability - if there's one complaint I can level against the game, it's that item variety eventually feels a little low, because even though loot is randomly generated, they're all variations of the same 15-20 items. Likewise, even though the enemy ships are randomly generated, there are a pretty limited number of room types. The game's systems feel mirror-polished, but there's a LOT more room for breadth here. Let's hope there's some post-launch support!

I'm 8 hours in and truly enjoying this game.  It's actually been some time since a game sucked me in like this and to be frank I wasn't expecting it at all.  I won the game bidding during the holiday auction so it was free and it was the game I bid on after winning my first choice with the points I had left over. I was so wrong. This game should have been the first choice.   Heck I would have gladly paid for a game of this quality.
Now on to the actual game itself.  The weakest points are the graphics and music.  Having said that , if you are playing an ARPG and expecting top notch graphics I thinjk perhaps you're unfamiliar with the genre.  The music itself is less forgiveable, though with a small publisher/development team I'm glad they focused on gameplay instead.  I can always play my own music in the background and turn off the music in the options, and I do. (A mix of several sci-fi soundtracks currently. )
The gameplay is where this tirle shones.  Its an arpg true but you can navigate with WASD and fire in any arc around your ship. It plays like the winderkind love child of Diablo II and Space, Pirates, and Zombies, and Bounty Hunters.  Another title that's worth a look if you like this sort of thing.  There is a lot of customization available for engines weapons, etc. At first I didn't notice much difference in loadout honestly but as time went on the advantages and disadvantages of each become much more clear as you and your enemies get more powerful.  The expandable inventory if the cargo bay system is also a nice treat and a great way to deal with the looting issue of a full inventory.
The overall metagame is what truly sets this apart though with consequences following your choices of who to help and whom to attack.  I allied early with the Shadow because they were at the time overwhelmingly powerful.  Thought I'd go for a quick win that way.  Well, I alkienated another race by attacking them on behalf of the Shadow and was never able to revcover their trust.  In the end I had to fight a long hard battle and do a LOT of diplomacy as they kept buying off my Shadow allies as I worked toward a Fear victory.  That's right multiple victory conditions exist here from diplomacy (which actually seems relevant for once in a game) to military conquest to  a mercenary route of making so much money that your Drox masters are uber pleased.  You can lose all those ways as well so take a look at victory conditios when you first start.
TLDR:  Great game for ARPG, space opera, and sandbox game fans with unique and engaging systems that are surprisingly deep.  Graphics and audio dated and weak. I'd give it a 7/10 and if they remade this with a AAA budget I'd preorder. Something I never do.

Updated: 8/29/2016
3 months after my initial review, it's time for an update.
Stability issues have been worked out for the most part.  Once in a while I might get a crash, but the game politely asks me if I want to save and submit a bug report and lets me keep playing.
At the heart of it, this game is Mad Max meets Mechwarrior.   The gameplay reminds me of some older DOS games I used to play, and it's a genre that I haven't seen done right in a vehicle game in a while.    A lot of these games had fixed hardpoints, and fixed body types.  TerraTech's building system let's you build pretty much anything the wheels can support.
You initially start out with what's called a "Cab".  You get a starter gun and some wheels, now you're off to rebuild your war machine.  Initially the game starts you off on small, equal opponents.  You pick their parts after defeating them, attatching them and increasing the firepower (and weight) of your vehicle.   Parts come from various manufacturers, each avaliable after leveling up.
Eventually you find the singularity unit, and the store.  Now the real fun begins.  You mine some resources, and make enough to start building a base.  Drop your singularity by some destroyed enemy parts, and it sucks it into your inventory. (I like leading them back to it) The base blocks are very functional, and there is a pretty easy to use conveyor system for moving things to parts of your base.   Several blocks chained together can increase the value of your mined resources by refining them, then using the refined materials to make new blocks that you can sell.
Through refinement or purchase, you gain additional "Ai" units.  (Protip.. Use wheels that keep them slow.) Now you plop one of these on your first creation, and start working on a second, or you can just let the little Ai cabs run around your feet with their pew pew shots.  Your choice.
Good game design has a few elements.  It has to reward the player into playing the game correctly, and Terratech does.  At some point your best car will have slow wheels (so minerals don't drop) a battery to keep a shield and repair bubble charged, and some tractor blocks in a t shape with a generator in the middle.  This way you just have to mine the oil, or knock down a tree to keep your shields charged.  Now you can really start dishing out the damage.
*Pros*
Great concept based on an older genre.  Could easily be called "The most flexible" of this genre
Intuitive gameplay that leads a player towards playing the game right.  Great design.
Great physics and mechanics
*Wishlist*

There's a few elements of the game that I think can be improved:
SCU Unit: It's sort of a minor annoyance to have to move an SCU near parts.  Why not have
each cab with a built in SCU unit?  As long as the cab stays parked for an extended period, it starts collecting parts.  Another side benefit?  Less parts that have to be drawn.
Infinite Deployment Consoles:  The deployment console should always be avaliable.  I usually buy a few before heading into a new area, but I do forget to once in a while.  It would be nice to always have them on hand.  I don't mind paying for them, it's just annoying to drive back to another deploy console to get another pocketful.
Flight:  I don't like the "autoswitch" between modes.   If I have shift held down, then for all intents and purposes I should be in flight mode.
Radar/Flight: I think the Flight radar needs to be more like a jet fighter HUD that gives me a little green "Lock On" triangle overlayed in my viewfield.  When I'm trying to strafe units, the current radar doesn't help me much.
Multiple Unit selection:  Would love to be able to select multiple units/cabs the way you do in most RTS's.
Unit right click context actions:  If I right click a blank area of a map in RTS games, the AI assumes I mean, "Move to this point"  If I have a harvesting unit and right click on a resource, most RTS's know to "Harvest" and if I right click an enemy, it knows to "Attack"
Unit grouping: Assign unit to a group
Hotkeys Hotkeys Hotkeys:
Ctrl-a (Select all visible units)
Left Click + Ctrl (add unit to selection)
Ctrl-Z Undo
Ctrl + 0-9 = assign selected to group
Ctrl + H = Selected Harvest nearest
Ctrl + G = Selected Attack nearest
You get the idea.
Conclusion:  This is one of those early access games where the developers are listening, and coming through on their promises.  I would support this studios next endeavor after Terratech.   If they can ever make this work multiplayer, it's going to be amazing.  Get it now while it's cheap.

Picked it up on humble bundle for 10 dollars and holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ the entertainment value per dollar is impressive. I haven't beaten it quite yet but I couldn't wait to write a review. I have to point out that I saw a alot of complaints about RNG and all I can say is that you have to account for RNG in your planning, its a lot like playing fire emblem on classic. Now on to pros and cons.
Pros
-Very punishing for poor choices and poor planning.
-This game is An excellent example of Murphy's law, you cannot control everything, so if you're someone who is a control freak and want everything to go the way they planned, you might consider looking else where.
-Minimal hand holding.
-Captures that the doom and gloom befitting of the title. The music, the art and the narration of the game makes it such a master piece.
-Various options you can enable or disable to suit your difficulty preference.(Disabling corpses, 100% retreats, etc)
-Variety in party compositions and strategies in conquering dungeons.
Cons
-It does get a little grindy towards the midgame.
-The VERY limited inventory space when you head into the quest limits the amount of loot you come out with. Further adding to the grind(I know its supposed to force you to choose between high utility items and gold/upgrade items, but god damn its annoying)
-Why on earth am I forced to sell the supplies back to the shopkeeper at ripoff prices when I finish a quest? It just adds to the grind.
Even though there are some questionable design decisions, I still really enjoy the game for what it is. There is so much depth to the game that I spend alot of time trying to figure out what builds and strategies I want to use in the game. I feel like a lot of games today are really shallow, or they make the games too easy in order to pander to as much people as possible. All in all, I think darkest Dungeon strikes a nice balance between fun and difficulty.

An interesting spin on the classic game of Asteroids. Your ship has no weapons, but you are dragging a cluster of deadly particles behind your ship. Whirling them around like a mad man is how you defend yourself against the onslaught of deadly enemies and giant smashy space rocks.
Play style is somewhere between casual and hardcore. The game can be played in Single Player or Local Co-Op mode.
Local Co-Op supports up to 4 players, although you will need a controller for each player.
Single Player mode consists of an Easy and Hard Endless mode, an Asteroids mode (no enemies) and 150 objectives in Mission mode. Also includes Leaderboard, Steam Achivements and Trading Cards.
The game is very easy to pick up and play but challenging to master.
It has Controller support for both Xbox and PlayStation game pads, which I highly recommend over using the keyboard.
Lastly it has a pretty awesome music score.

by "They Might Be Giants" as you play.

After playing this long enough and grinding non-stop i figured i'd write this review (Though im very salty right now). The early game is very fun, learning how the hamlet works, how to figure out team compositions, the positives and negatives of every action ETC, wonderful experience. However, once you figure this all out you start the grind. You eventually get your 4-6 heroes to level 3! awesome you can now do the higher level dungeons! But first being a smart person you say to yourself "Let me go ahead and keep leveling other heroes". Eventually you decide to do the higher level dungeons. Well you enter these level 3 dungeons which vary from medium to long, and as you go through you'll notice how the enemies are now more powerful, more health ETC. Well you upgraded your troops so no issue there. Well lets go and through RNG at you. Your whole party just got wiped, easily. After all that grinding you just lost so much... Well it happens. So you rinse and repeat the process.. You lose your high level heroes once again.. You once again repeat the grinding process.. And then you go back into the level 3 dungeon and guess what you're doing great you finally feel confident, last room you have to explore, you scout the halls and see there is one battle in the halls before the last room. BAM! RNG you get a collector he spawns in his minions and you eventually get wiped once again. How many times would you seriously want to grind to have the same RNG kill you? This game is fun, challenging, even has great mechanics, but it is sometimes challenging in the wrong ways. I personally cant go through the grind anymore, If you can then you will enjoy this game.. Maybe im just impatient, or unlucky.
TLDR: This game is RNG and grinding, with some strategy. Waiting for the people you actually want on your roster sucks, It's not fun having RNG give you heroes you do not need on your roster at all. go through a dungeon and die, Manage your money, manage the stress of the roster, and die everytime you feel like you did the right thing. Love the mechanics of the game (Stress, campfire, trinkets, stress relief, curing diseases and negative quirks.). Art work is awesome and the bosses are creative.  if you can get the game for less than the retail price, try it out.. Maybe your luck is better.

Let me make this clear. I love the changes to MyGM and MyLeague, which is the only reason I'm recommending this game. However, if you are intending to make MyCareer the majority of your playing experience...DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. The game is advertised as 'My Story' yet puts you on a linear preplanned story. If it was my story my guy would not have been born in Harlem, he would have attended a different college program, and he would have stayed for more than one year. Spike Lee directing the story ruins whatever immersion I had with the character.
I feel MyCareer has some good moments and ideas. I love the idea of playing high school ball and choosing a college. Yeah there are only 9 choices and I wish there were more, but I understand why with the cost of getting more on board so I don't let that bother me.
What MyCareer did wrong. Only able to spend one year in college; I get it you are supposed to be a superstar but let us decide if we want to stay one more year. Heck make the games challenging enough that we don't win the NCAA tournament giving us the option to stay and try again out of pride. Your skill rating when you join the NBA is a puny 55. This forces you to either play with a crappy player, buy VC with your money, or farm in other modes first. On top of that they kept the grouped together stat increases that NBA 2k15 started, which reduces the variation of play styles I could develop MY player into.
I haven't finished up to the FA period yet, so I can't comment on length of seasons fairly. I do like shorter seasons compared to the older games when you had to play every game, but I don't like them moving away from 2k15's decision to let you pick which games you play.
Overall, if you are looking at this game for the MyPlayer mode...just stick to 2k15 or 2k14 and just watch the cutscenes on YouTube. If you are looking at the MyGM/MyLeague then I say buy it, the improvements are worth it.

There are multiple classes, all in which, you can level up and put gear on. Only problem is those classes cost money now. You can only get free classes when you've gotten a certain point into the game. These points are referred to as mastery. You earn mastery by getting things such as weapons, dragons, mounts, and classes. Problem is. All of those things cost cold hard cash. Mounts can be bought or crafted. Crafting takes mastery, mastery takes money. Want a dragon? Spend money. Want a costume for the class you just bought for 10 dollars? Spend 20 dollars. Wish to get to a point in the game where you are having fun all the time? Not a chance. This game has some of the least satisfying gameplay you might ever see. Kill monsters, get loot. Fun the first 1000 times. If you had gotten this game in December of 2015. I'm pretty much an end game player at this point. Got the second best gear, because I didn't have to pay to get it. Got the coolest mounts and dragons, a class I love and friends I can play with. All these things simply do not make up for the pay to win garbage I sat through for 2 months playing.
I do fully respect Trion for making a game pay to win, though. In the end, a company has to make money, it all boils down to that. It's just a shame to see a promising game go down the drain. All in the course of 3 months.

So, I came into this game when I learned it a Souls-like. You know, hard difficulty, a learning curve that's rather deep, dropping your level up materials, etc. The art is beautiful, the design is GREAT, the enviroments are cold and desolate feeling, like a battle field in the snow. The game runs good and nothing seems terribly out of place. All in all the graphics and the enviroments are great. Which goes to show that a good looking game does not make a FUN looking game.
Again, I got this game when I heard that it's a Souls-like and was hoping that the gameplay would reflect this. The equipment feels more of a Diablo 3 style, where random crud will drop off monsters and all that and you seem to need to get the loot that you desire. Now, my problem is that is it far slower, and much clunkier. I have played for two hours straight and cannot seem to get use to the speed of any of the weapons, understand the timing of attacks made by enemies, ways to counter certain foes. Mind you, I do like more Medium build characters: Able to take a blow but able to dodge out of the path of a swing if need be. But everything I used, from swords to axes, bucklers to tower shields, stark naked to clanking around like a tank, everything was slow! I feel like the game itself was making a laughing stock of me the entire damned time. It's not even like the heavier armors block all that much more damage in the first place!
So, I just need to work strategies according to the enemy, right? Well, that's the thing. I can't think of anything. I am stuck up against the wall of vile, demonic flesh of two tower shield weilding monstrosities and I cannot fathom how to deal with them. Here's a quick break down--
The insane monsters, covered with puss and what not, tend to deflect off your shield if you can block in time. But sometimes - just randomly so - they won't. So you'll go to attack, thinking you've deflected their attack and sent them staggering when WHACK WHACK WHACK! HALF MY HEALTH IS GONE. Fine, okay, keep blocking till they do get staggered. Sometimes, that works. At random though, he will check right through your stamina like I do pizza!
Then you have various demon beings, all human like. Some shoot you with a crossbow, some have a sword and shield, and the biggest (Both figurative and literal) jackasses, the Tower Shield Guys. The Sword and shield ones are okay, you just need to work your way around them to BARELY manage to get a back-attack on them. The Cross bow guys? Block their shot and move in quick to chop 'em up, bash 'em up, whatever. The Tower Shield guys are impossible.
For starters, they don't work like the Sword and Board guys. They are always blocking, and when they're not blocking, you SHOULD be, cause they have so much Poise (The stat that is treated like a HP bar for being staggered), they will barely feel your attack before cutting you right the hell up! And their Tower Shields block nearly all the damage from your attacks. I say nearly all, cause you still do MAYBE 3-5 damage.
"Okay, so circle around and back stab them. They must be slow, right?" Wrong. They follow you on just about a 1 to 1 rate, so you are always face to face with a wall of steel that your sword/axe/mace will just bounce right off of. I've even tried waiting till he attacks, rolling around him and attacking him from behind. But as I said, your character is SLOWER than everything else in the damned area. By the time you've stood up from the attack, he's already turned to you and blocking once more. And that's assuming you're not staggered from an attack, because, since your rolling/doding is so slow, it's unreliable. More than likely, you're still hit, despite dodging over or under his sword, you'll still get staggered, and the battle of repeatition con-fricking-tinues. The only way, and I seriously mean the only way, I have been able to take them out is by using the stupid magic cannon you get at some point, which involves unleashing your magic on him, whick bypasses his shield. With a high magic, maybe you are able to kill him without useing the entire magic bar, but as a Priest character, that happens to me with every single Tower Shield Guy. and I don't want to play like that. That's not fun to me. I've even tried to counter. Is that a thing? Does that work? I don't know, cause I've tried to coutner attacks with every single shield and every single one seems to have some sort of wind-up that takes two second to use, so I've always found myself slapping the LT button in the deepest of prayers that the attack is parried and I am able to attack back but NOPE.
And then the nail in the coffin to me that will keep this game from remaining on the harddrive. I though "okay, shield bashing. That should knock them right out of any blocking they're doing and I should be able to sink my axe in their skull." So I do so. And as though to the sound of angelic chorus sing "HALLELUJAH" I swing, only to find that the shield I just shoved out of my way is ALREADY blocking me once again! WHY!? I've tried this with every weapon, big and small, slow and not-as-slow-cause-come-on-man-is-your-blood-sap-or-something!? I've managed to get MAYBE a couple of hits on them before haing to swing back and hope i have enough time to whip out that magic cannon and blast them apart, which I've already stated, is NOT fun to me.
This feels like a case of what Dark Souls suffers to me, and that is that magic is king and makes the game easy mode. I don't want it easy mode for sure, but I also don't want to spend an hour to try to take out two STRONGER versions of the Tower Shield Guys at the same time.
Screw this noise.

I suppose the idea here is that this is like playing a mercenary in a 4X game, while the AI handles the four x's. In practice this seems to work, there are AI civilizations fighting, colonizing and entering into diplomacy and you can influence and effect things, sabotage races you want to lose, or just join in an all-out fight, pick a side to ally with and destroy their enemies. Easy enough to pick up and there's depth to keep you playing. Its a really good idea, the game has a lot of charm, and when it works is a lot of fun. Diablo-like, this is a point and click shooter with a streamlined leveling system and crate-loads of loot.
The trouble is its as buggy as hell, and at 2+ years old there really shouldn't be such blatant bugs. I keep getting quests to colonize non-existent planets, to destroy non-existent enemies and half the time complete quests I wasn't even set (which is a nice XP boost, sure, but confusing!) Imagine hunting a bounty in Diablo 3 having being told they are in Westmarch Commons. You spend an hour looking for them only to get bored, go elsewhere, and discover the bounty was actually in Desolate Sands.
It looks like the main issue is that the game randomly generates each sandbox sector for you to explore, and simply gets muddled by the amount of random info. being generated. It means a lot of aimless wandering, and wiki visiting to find out where you are actually supposed to be. The other trouble is that it is very easy to win a sector (I hope it gets harder as I level up), I just keep buying victories, paying off the most powerful race to be my ally. I also felt the inventory options were limited, while these can be expanded, even when I had four cargo bays I was leaving a lot of litter spread around the galaxy (never mind the fact that none of the vendors ever have enough money to buy goods from you!) Add to this the fact that there are random wormholes everywhere. They always seem to catapult me to a part of the galaxy well above my current level and seem to be a random 'insta-death' function that you cannot avoid. Finally, I have scoured the options and menus and cannot find any information about how many experience points you have and how many are needed to level up. These are all very minor quibbles, but considering the number of indie Diablo-clones out there that are far more polished (and cheaper, or even free!) these add up to disappointment.
Recommended with caveats and a hope that a future patch fixes some of these issues.

Updated: 8/29/2016
3 months after my initial review, it's time for an update.
Stability issues have been worked out for the most part.  Once in a while I might get a crash, but the game politely asks me if I want to save and submit a bug report and lets me keep playing.
At the heart of it, this game is Mad Max meets Mechwarrior.   The gameplay reminds me of some older DOS games I used to play, and it's a genre that I haven't seen done right in a vehicle game in a while.    A lot of these games had fixed hardpoints, and fixed body types.  TerraTech's building system let's you build pretty much anything the wheels can support.
You initially start out with what's called a "Cab".  You get a starter gun and some wheels, now you're off to rebuild your war machine.  Initially the game starts you off on small, equal opponents.  You pick their parts after defeating them, attatching them and increasing the firepower (and weight) of your vehicle.   Parts come from various manufacturers, each avaliable after leveling up.
Eventually you find the singularity unit, and the store.  Now the real fun begins.  You mine some resources, and make enough to start building a base.  Drop your singularity by some destroyed enemy parts, and it sucks it into your inventory. (I like leading them back to it) The base blocks are very functional, and there is a pretty easy to use conveyor system for moving things to parts of your base.   Several blocks chained together can increase the value of your mined resources by refining them, then using the refined materials to make new blocks that you can sell.
Through refinement or purchase, you gain additional "Ai" units.  (Protip.. Use wheels that keep them slow.) Now you plop one of these on your first creation, and start working on a second, or you can just let the little Ai cabs run around your feet with their pew pew shots.  Your choice.
Good game design has a few elements.  It has to reward the player into playing the game correctly, and Terratech does.  At some point your best car will have slow wheels (so minerals don't drop) a battery to keep a shield and repair bubble charged, and some tractor blocks in a t shape with a generator in the middle.  This way you just have to mine the oil, or knock down a tree to keep your shields charged.  Now you can really start dishing out the damage.
*Pros*
Great concept based on an older genre.  Could easily be called "The most flexible" of this genre
Intuitive gameplay that leads a player towards playing the game right.  Great design.
Great physics and mechanics
*Wishlist*

There's a few elements of the game that I think can be improved:
SCU Unit: It's sort of a minor annoyance to have to move an SCU near parts.  Why not have
each cab with a built in SCU unit?  As long as the cab stays parked for an extended period, it starts collecting parts.  Another side benefit?  Less parts that have to be drawn.
Infinite Deployment Consoles:  The deployment console should always be avaliable.  I usually buy a few before heading into a new area, but I do forget to once in a while.  It would be nice to always have them on hand.  I don't mind paying for them, it's just annoying to drive back to another deploy console to get another pocketful.
Flight:  I don't like the "autoswitch" between modes.   If I have shift held down, then for all intents and purposes I should be in flight mode.
Radar/Flight: I think the Flight radar needs to be more like a jet fighter HUD that gives me a little green "Lock On" triangle overlayed in my viewfield.  When I'm trying to strafe units, the current radar doesn't help me much.
Multiple Unit selection:  Would love to be able to select multiple units/cabs the way you do in most RTS's.
Unit right click context actions:  If I right click a blank area of a map in RTS games, the AI assumes I mean, "Move to this point"  If I have a harvesting unit and right click on a resource, most RTS's know to "Harvest" and if I right click an enemy, it knows to "Attack"
Unit grouping: Assign unit to a group
Hotkeys Hotkeys Hotkeys:
Ctrl-a (Select all visible units)
Left Click + Ctrl (add unit to selection)
Ctrl-Z Undo
Ctrl + 0-9 = assign selected to group
Ctrl + H = Selected Harvest nearest
Ctrl + G = Selected Attack nearest
You get the idea.
Conclusion:  This is one of those early access games where the developers are listening, and coming through on their promises.  I would support this studios next endeavor after Terratech.   If they can ever make this work multiplayer, it's going to be amazing.  Get it now while it's cheap.

This game is like Diablo in space but more amazing. Stages (sectors?) develop organically and your actions have a real effect on how the world's situation plays out. Quests are generated based on NPC factions' evolving needs and your success or failure shape overall who gets to live, die, become powerful, become friends or enemies. There is even a meta-game in that relations and power levels carry over somewhat between sectors in the same galaxy. Factions that start out as sub-races or rebel groups, if they survive enough, can become permanent factions in future stages. Starting factions can become extinct.
Many ways to win a sector, many ways to lose. The game is challenging at higher levels and requires (political) strategy, not just fast clicking. You can freely customize your ship with any parts you meet the reqs for, and share equipment among characters via stash, which gives you great flexibility but also the potential to completely ruin yourself. Building up the ship is fun, but the more expensive your build is the harder it is to pay repair/replace costs when you die; fail enough and a sector can become unwinnable.
This is a great, fun game but its weak graphics and difficult nature may be a turn off to many. I recommend it though for anyone who likes building up a character and testing it against random worlds full of monsters and rival factions.
A short but fun journey fill with stellar art, an amazing soundtrack, and plenty of gameplay depth and challenge.

As someone who tries to keep a look out for new and interesting Card Games on Steam, Harald flew right under my radar for a whole 2 weeks before I discovered it. Buried alive in the plethora of Steam releases of late September, it appears to have bypassed almost everyone else too!
This is a great shame. Because I will say upfront that 'Harald' is an absolute hidden gem of a card game! It's also beautifully presented, highly polished, runs smoothly and is incredibly fun to play!
Although very simple to learn and play. Harald is a game that takes time to master. This may only be a game with 6 card types (7 with the expansion) But do not be fooled. This is a game full of depth, tactics and strategy! Every card has a power and a function, which is in turn tied to the other character cards within the deck. How you play these cards is vitally important throughout every turn. Which can be the difference from winning well, to throwing it all away.
Since all cards are on display at all times, you have to be mindful of what cards your opponent has. Requiring you to adapt accordingly. Turns are very limited though, so you do have to maintain your focus.. Did I also mention this is just Vs a single AI opponent?
That's right. The AI is not a pushover. It will play fairly, but it will also play well just on Normal difficulty. It is very competant, sometimes a rarity for these games. Once you manage to understand all the mechanics of Harald, you will start to beat it, and you will find the nuances that make it tick. It is then you can move upto Hard difficult for a tough yet fair challenge where the AI will punish you for holes in your strategy.
If you want even more of a challenge.. There is also modes against 2 or 3 other AI opponents. Here. the AI does put up an even more interesting fight, and you really do have to attack opponent villages hard and/or get a very strong focus on how you structure your own village. Since there's less turns with more players, Your Council & Village strategy has to be on point and you do have to determine what your strategic focus actually is. A supportive backup plan is usually always necessary as well.
Online Multiplayer is also available here. Allowing you to take a rest from the solid AI and instead having you exploit the impurity of human nature in a 2-4 player format. From what I can tell, since this is actually a mobile port, you can take on iOS and Android users too! Although finding actual human players is hit and miss due to Publisher Asmodee Digital being more interested in focussing their efforts on the less superior Smash Up! and Ticket to Ride: First Journey titles across all formats. Such is their franchise priority.
Also in Harald are basic stats tracking (For self goals), in-game achievements (Not Steam), and the ability to unlock each of the characters from original deck of cards from the physical card game to play as an alternative. Plus you get the Badger/Scholar expansion already built into the game. No additional DLC purchase needed!
So as it stands. Harald is one of the best card games on Steam! Easily beating most of the F2P CCGs that are available, and also being better than a large selection of the premium titles also for sale. For the price point too? You're getting a wonderfully small yet enjoyable game that packs a massively large punch!
Highly Recommended!

Genre: Space Action/Adventure w/ RPG Elements
Personal Rating 7.5/10
Drox Operative is an interesting game in that is has Diablo-esque elements that appear in the forms and grades of loot drops (ie different rarities). You take the role of a Drox operative playing the role of one of several distinct races. Your objective is to win thru several different ways such as an economic victory, diplomacy, military might, etc.
You can set the game to have the play field small (such as a mere handfull of sectors) to very vast with dozens of sectors to explore. You start out in your 'Home' sector where you will encounter your first race. It is benificial to open up trade agreements with all you encounter at first; but as time progresses and lines in the sand are drawn you will want to work to forge an alliance with the most powerful factions.
You gain influence with factions by completing quests for them, protecting their planets and ships from attack and trading w/ them. You also lose influince by trading and associating with enemies of factions. Quests can range from assassinitaion to ferrying supplies. Planets can come under all kinds of pressure, from disease/famine/unrest and riots/zombie appocolypse/etc. Each of these problems requires certain cargo to solve so as you pick up the quest you can search the network on where to find the supplies to deliver.
One neat aspect I likes was the addition of random crew members. they can drop as loot and can be leveled up and assigned to your ship.
The game has difficulty levels from 1-100 so to reach higher levles with your ship you will need to keep starting over in new sectors and set the diff to higher levels. You also can invest points into your command skill which will unlock bigger ships for you. I personally liked it when I was able to install my first Fighter Bay. I recomend doing ths asap because it really helps having them support your ship. And let me mention all the other types of customization, from EMP pulses to computer virus' to fusion and nuclear mines and missles to all kinds of lasers and beams just to name a few. The sky is the limit when it comes to customization.
It's worth it to mention all the different encounter types you can come across, from Rogue Elite Mobs to wandering traders to abandoned ships to Minerable Asteroids and Rogue Comets and space pirates to name a few.
If you like Dungeon Delving (albiet in space) and space exploration and hack and slash button mashing combat, I would recommend giving this a try either for yourself or a 4pack so you and your friends can conquer the stars together.

This game is amazing, and I haven't even gotten to the main storyline yet. There's this sort of adreneline rush while you're trying to hack your way in to someone's server and you only have a limited amount of time. Eventually I found myself rushing even when there wasn't a passive trace against me.
The beginning is rather intense, the tutorial really only gives you the bare bones and I am extremely glad I have a linux background because I went through the entire tutorial not reading it xD (although I found myself wishing I could grep, vim and when I upload I almost typed the entire scp command (scp :/home/[file]) .)
I found myself lost once... trying to remember whe- oh, it was when I had to reply to an email. Yeah, that wasn't explained very well at the beginning, but basically, you do what the email asks and you reply a blank email. The blank reply threw me off and I found myself trying to access things that had firewalls when I obviously had no capability of doing so
The GUI is very helpful for those that aren't used to typing. I noticed that the tab complete didn't seem to work until I hit the tutorial for it, so for those that love pressing tab (like I do) and it doesn't work, don't panic, it comes later.
This game made me realize how vindictive I am; there is this one moment where you get hacked into and the GUI interface gets deleted. After I got back I immediately looked up the IP in my logs, went through the proxy server and then went to another server and deleted everything I could find on both server and proxy >_> probably didn't do anything but I got my GUI file back haha
*tl;dr?
Hacknet requires thinking and a lot of muscle memory which you'll get if you resort to typing out the commands (also pressing up like any linux terminal is a great shortcut) and there's a lot of side things you can do that really help pad the game.
I love going through servers and reading the random forum/irc logs because they're all pretty funny. They aren't neccessarily relevant to the server you're on but it's an interesting little tidbit to read nonetheless.
The music is also nice and subtle with a good beat that has it's highs and lows (I believe the music ingame is in the trailer).
There's a bit of a steep learning curve for people that have never programmed in their life but once you're past that it's a fun and exciting game.

This game, when starting out. Was fun. Emphesis on the was. Starting out in this pay to win minecraft mod is amazingly painstaking. There are multiple classes, all in which, you can level up and put gear on. Only problem is those classes cost money now. You can only get free classes when you've gotten a certain point into the game. These points are referred to as mastery. You earn mastery by getting things such as weapons, dragons, mounts, and classes. Problem is. All of those things cost cold hard cash. Mounts can be bought or crafted. Crafting takes mastery, mastery takes money. Want a dragon? Spend money. Want a costume for the class you just bought for 10 dollars? Spend 20 dollars. Wish to get to a point in the game where you are having fun all the time? Not a chance. This game has some of the least satisfying gameplay you might ever see. Kill monsters, get loot. Fun the first 1000 times. If you had gotten this game in December of 2015. I'm pretty much an end game player at this point. Got the second best gear, because I didn't have to pay to get it. Got the coolest mounts and dragons, a class I love and friends I can play with. All these things simply do not make up for the pay to win garbage I sat through for 2 months playing.
I do fully respect Trion for making a game pay to win, though. In the end, a company has to make money, it all boils down to that. It's just a shame to see a promising game go down the drain. All in the course of 3 months.

So, I came into this game when I learned it a Souls-like. You know, hard difficulty, a learning curve that's rather deep, dropping your level up materials, etc. The art is beautiful, the design is GREAT, the enviroments are cold and desolate feeling, like a battle field in the snow. The game runs good and nothing seems terribly out of place. All in all the graphics and the enviroments are great. Which goes to show that a good looking game does not make a FUN looking game.
Again, I got this game when I heard that it's a Souls-like and was hoping that the gameplay would reflect this. The equipment feels more of a Diablo 3 style, where random crud will drop off monsters and all that and you seem to need to get the loot that you desire. Now, my problem is that is it far slower, and much clunkier. I have played for two hours straight and cannot seem to get use to the speed of any of the weapons, understand the timing of attacks made by enemies, ways to counter certain foes. Mind you, I do like more Medium build characters: Able to take a blow but able to dodge out of the path of a swing if need be. But everything I used, from swords to axes, bucklers to tower shields, stark naked to clanking around like a tank, everything was slow! I feel like the game itself was making a laughing stock of me the entire damned time. It's not even like the heavier armors block all that much more damage in the first place!
So, I just need to work strategies according to the enemy, right? Well, that's the thing. I can't think of anything. I am stuck up against the wall of vile, demonic flesh of two tower shield weilding monstrosities and I cannot fathom how to deal with them. Here's a quick break down--
The insane monsters, covered with puss and what not, tend to deflect off your shield if you can block in time. But sometimes - just randomly so - they won't. So you'll go to attack, thinking you've deflected their attack and sent them staggering when WHACK WHACK WHACK! HALF MY HEALTH IS GONE. Fine, okay, keep blocking till they do get staggered. Sometimes, that works. At random though, he will check right through your stamina like I do pizza!
Then you have various demon beings, all human like. Some shoot you with a crossbow, some have a sword and shield, and the biggest (Both figurative and literal) jackasses, the Tower Shield Guys. The Sword and shield ones are okay, you just need to work your way around them to BARELY manage to get a back-attack on them. The Cross bow guys? Block their shot and move in quick to chop 'em up, bash 'em up, whatever. The Tower Shield guys are impossible.
For starters, they don't work like the Sword and Board guys. They are always blocking, and when they're not blocking, you SHOULD be, cause they have so much Poise (The stat that is treated like a HP bar for being staggered), they will barely feel your attack before cutting you right the hell up! And their Tower Shields block nearly all the damage from your attacks. I say nearly all, cause you still do MAYBE 3-5 damage.
"Okay, so circle around and back stab them. They must be slow, right?" Wrong. They follow you on just about a 1 to 1 rate, so you are always face to face with a wall of steel that your sword/axe/mace will just bounce right off of. I've even tried waiting till he attacks, rolling around him and attacking him from behind. But as I said, your character is SLOWER than everything else in the damned area. By the time you've stood up from the attack, he's already turned to you and blocking once more. And that's assuming you're not staggered from an attack, because, since your rolling/doding is so slow, it's unreliable. More than likely, you're still hit, despite dodging over or under his sword, you'll still get staggered, and the battle of repeatition con-fricking-tinues. The only way, and I seriously mean the only way, I have been able to take them out is by using the stupid magic cannon you get at some point, which involves unleashing your magic on him, whick bypasses his shield. With a high magic, maybe you are able to kill him without useing the entire magic bar, but as a Priest character, that happens to me with every single Tower Shield Guy. and I don't want to play like that. That's not fun to me. I've even tried to counter. Is that a thing? Does that work? I don't know, cause I've tried to coutner attacks with every single shield and every single one seems to have some sort of wind-up that takes two second to use, so I've always found myself slapping the LT button in the deepest of prayers that the attack is parried and I am able to attack back but NOPE.
And then the nail in the coffin to me that will keep this game from remaining on the harddrive. I though "okay, shield bashing. That should knock them right out of any blocking they're doing and I should be able to sink my axe in their skull." So I do so. And as though to the sound of angelic chorus sing "HALLELUJAH" I swing, only to find that the shield I just shoved out of my way is ALREADY blocking me once again! WHY!? I've tried this with every weapon, big and small, slow and not-as-slow-cause-come-on-man-is-your-blood-sap-or-something!? I've managed to get MAYBE a couple of hits on them before haing to swing back and hope i have enough time to whip out that magic cannon and blast them apart, which I've already stated, is NOT fun to me.
This feels like a case of what Dark Souls suffers to me, and that is that magic is king and makes the game easy mode. I don't want it easy mode for sure, but I also don't want to spend an hour to try to take out two STRONGER versions of the Tower Shield Guys at the same time.
Screw this noise.

I've wasted my time.
This game used to be good. Hell, you can tell that by my play time. But now, the game is absolutly ruined by paywall.
I've had a total of 3 accounts, and I made another after a few months.
On my first account I found this game absolutely amazing, then got bored. Next account I did something more, got bored and also put off by paywall they were setting up. And third one was to see how bad it is now. And it sure IS bad. It isn't absolutely terrible, but it's kind of ruined. Here are some reasons why it is bad:
1. Classes
Back in the old days you could buy them with cubits (currency you earn for just playing) but, not only it had been made harder to stack on them, they also made classes purchaseable only with credits (purchaseable with $$$), meaning you would need to spend about 25$ to get all the classes. And if you're going to get a single class unlock without spending money, then have fun grinding 100,000 of markets main currency, flux.
2. Dragons
They changed how you get dragons. Previously, you went to a challenge every hour to get dragon caches which gave dragon souls, and having enough of those gave you a dragon. Now, it's about 3 times harder to get the old dragons, and you would need tons of♥♥♥♥♥♥and dragon coins (rare soul and dragon crafting material) to get a dragon nowadays. So not only it's made a thousand times harder, it's also far less rewarding. Guess whats to buy in the shop? Dragon coins and 10x better dragon caches.
And now the worst of all...
3. Gems
Gems are new, and.... not interesting. Ever since gems were released, a new meta was born: "no gems, no win". Gems are literally the only thing that can give you an actual stat bonus compared to gear. But thats not all! There are "empowered" gems, which obviously are stronger. On top of that you can get max. 3 of those a week. And instead of gems as drops, you get them from... boxes. Boxes = gambling and if gambling = win then you know that something is ♥♥♥♥ed up, especially when you only get a chance to progress three times a week. Games that are luck based are boring and not satysfying at all. Especially if that's the only way to grow stronger. Oh, did I mention you could buy empowered gem boxes with credits?
So yes, this game was absolutely messed up by all the microtransactions. Congratulations, Trion Worlds, you messed up another game in a row.

I'm not sure if making a game almost identical to another game means that you're saying you can do better or that you're so much of a fan of that game that you wouldn't do anything to disrespect it, not even create a different game.
Lords of the Fallen is the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of Dark Souls with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rumored to be Darksiders.
What I mean by it is that while the game is pretty similar to Dark Souls, all the armors in the game look like they are wearing armors themselves.
And when I say "pretty similar" I mean that the game tries to do what Dark Souls does in almost every aspect.
You lose your souls (experience) when you die and enemies respawn. All controller mappings and actions are the same as in Dark Souls, and so on.
There is a slight difference whereas in Dark Souls you could play as a tanky character or an agile assassin with lots of stamina, while in Lords of the Fallen you can choose between being a Russian tank or a German tank, because that is the only playstyle that seems to work well. And every playstyle feels clunky for some reason.
I'm saying "Dark Souls" too much and I'm not really trying to compare the two, but I don't have to try.
There's a loading screen tip where something like "you can't have more than one thing of a type, but you don't need to have that because YOUR STUFF DOES NOT DEGRADE! Ha-ha!".
Seeing that I'd think whoever wrote it was a cocky prick, but I know better than that because I've seen the developers being supportive and helpful on the Steam forums, so they seem like nice guys.
I appreciate the fact that they take and give feedback based on the game in a very humane way, a thing that you don't see so often.
The game doesn't seem to have a very wide variety of environments, it's either inside a castle, outside a castle or the equivalent of both in a demonic world.
I assume that while the programmers were implementing things like the chatting system, the artists have already finished their jobs and went home, then the Darksiders team broke in and started drawing random details over all the existing textures.
Even the chests in the game look like they are the sarcophagus of a very wealthy child pharaoh.
Inside of them you can generally find swords that look like they've been made from Turkish swords sewn and stapled together.
...Well, they actually look quite nice, I enjoyed the different looking and feeling pieces of equipment. Not the equipment selection wheel, though, since I was playing this on a controller and selecting some categories wasn't a pleasure.
Anyway, I think creating this kind of game requires a good deal of effort, and since the devs were able to pull it off, I would've liked to see more of their original ideas in this.
It feels like it's trying too much to accommodate the Dark Souls player. Even the story is presented in a way that lets you figure out what's going on without explaining everything (though I got to the end of the game without knowing or caring too much about it). Although here there are some scrolls that work as audio-logs and record whatever the people who were there were saying or doing at a certain time. And there's that pretty annoying dialogue system that goes nowhere.
It's obvious the game has been worked on and polished, but it somehow has some home-made indie sense to it, like some things were not tested enough.
For instance, you can roll to ignore poison damage.
Or if you get close to an NPC that's programmed to say a certain thing, it's enough to step a nanometer away and look at him again to hear him say the same line over and over.
Boss battles are all right, but I would have liked more variety even so. Pretty much all of them are oversized demonic humans I had no problems dealing with. The first ones I have beaten with a small stick, the next ones with a tree branch and the final ones with the whole tree, but that's all that was different in my fights.
Again, I think the game would have done much better with some original concepts.
Playing felt like once a few minutes the protagonist and I were standing at a table and he was saying: "Hey, remember that thing from Dark Souls? Well here it is again with a different hat and clunkier"
At the end of the game there's a thing where you can see how you did in certain parts of it and what decisions you've made. I liked that. It was interesting to see how my actions affected the development of the story. There's a New Game+ mode, so if you want to see all the things that change, there's an option to continue playing.
Overall, there might have been a bit of things I didn't mention, and I know I have pretty much highlighted the game's negative aspects, but that can be a good thing if you're interested in the game, because everything I didn't mention was fine. So give it a try if you're good with all these.
I enjoyed it despite its flaws, I think it was fun, though I'm not sure if playing Lords of the Fallen without having played Dark Souls first could give someone a taste for this kind of game play and style.
I also wonder if the game would have existed without the Souls games.
I'm sure it would have existed without Darksiders, it would have probably been a better game as well.
It's pretty all right even if not compared to other games.
That, or I am just suffering from an illness which makes me appreciate or at least not hate any game that resembles a certain game that I love.

Fractured Space is inoffensive but not particularly compelling.
In Fractured Space, you control a capital ship as part of a 5v5 fleet and push down two lanes to try to control territory to gain resources.  Controlling the opposite side of a lane allows you to warp to the enemy base, which you can capture to end the game.  An arena in the middle of the map periodically opens and provokes a team fight for ever increasing benefits to the team that captures it.
Combat is a relatively simple affair.  Ships have a rapid firing and generally shorter ranged gun, a slower firing and generally longer ranged gun, and very slowly firing, even longer ranged, and frequently debuff-applying missiles.  You'll unload these into an enemy while tapping the point defense button whenever missiles come at you.
Combat is further complicated by cover, special abilities, and armor.  Cover is simple enough- get behind a rock and things on the other side mostly can't hit you.  Ships also have somewhat directional armor that becomes extremely directional when a facing takes enough damage to blow the armor off, causing dramatically increased damage to that facing.  These two factors give you reason to reposition during combat, while sluggish ship handling keeps the game from being exceptionally twitchy.
On the ability front, ships have two special abilities.  Generally, one normal ability and one deployable such as a buoy with an aura or deployable small craft.  These give you access to things like healing, speed boosts, teleports, improved enemy detection (range and behind cover), damage mitigation, etc.
Overall, there's very little about Fractured Space I dislike, but it just doesn't feel that interesting.
Ship roles and special abilities don't feel particularly strong and distinct, the way they are in better MOBAs.  Ships have roles- defense, offense, support, but for the most part they feel like they're all big blocks of HP and DPS rather than the strongly flavored roles that make up a traditional MOBA.  Winning fights generally feels like a matter of picking engagements where your side has more ships present, and there's little of the excitement of a good snipe, initiation, or well-aimed skillshot that makes being on the wrong end of even an even fight in a MOBA a tense affair.
Over the course of the game your ship will gradually level up, and every several levels you can choose if you want to get a stronger boost to attack, defense, or "utility".  (abilities and sensor range)  Again, however, this doesn't feel impactful in the way that better MOBAs do, where you obtain new skills and significant upgrades to your skills, and items or traits that significantly modify how you play.

Strategic positioning is possibly the strongest aspect of the game, but even then it's 90% just a back and fourth battle for control of mines which will gradually give you an edge by determining the rate at which you level up.  In a lane, you're always capable of jumping home to your base or over to the teamfight arena so you're rarely that badly out of position- mostly, you just need to stick together when pushing a lane because flying from your entry point to the opposite side of the lane takes time.  Only the decision to attack the enemy base- especially the decision to sacrifice the team fight arena to try to decapitate the enemy- feels particularly impactful.
I don't dislike Fractured Space at all- I'd probably give it three stars on a five star scale.  Even while writing this, I mildly feel the urge to re-install it and play another round, because I like spaceships, like MOBAs, and like competitive games.  If you're thinking of trying it out, I'd do so- it's F2P, after all, and I didn't find it obnoxious so after three or so hours of playing it.
At the end of writing this, though, I'm not going to go back because there are both better MOBAs and better space or naval combat games out there.  Fractured Space straddles ship combat and MOBA gameplay, but only provides a little bit of the excitement of either.

First I will start off with saying I'm not a HUGE NBA fan. I've played 2k15 and some of the older NBA live games over the years. I bought 2k16 because I wanted an updated version of 2k15.
Overall it seems like people want to complain about the MyCareer mode. I don't understand what everyones complaints are. Yea it is a little odd I made a white guy with a black twin sister. But I found it more funny haha than annoying. In fact, I found 2k15 to be worse since it was almost impossible to make a white guy that didn't have black features and to top it all off they forced your voice to be black as well. So in reality why didn't people complain about that in 2k15? Cause it didn't matter, just like this doesn't matter.
Ignore the peopel who think the MyCareer mode is only about this story. The story is actually a very SHORT part of MyCareer mode. It only last around 15 games. You do Highschoo, then College, then your Rookie year. After that, it doesn't matter where you got drafted, where you went to school, or what your nickname is. You can change ALL of those settings after the rookie year. Think of the story as a cool intro to the mode and also 15 games to learn the controls without having any negative impact on your character. It doesn't matter how bad you play at all in those games, you will get the same result.
As for the game overall I give it a 8/10. It does basketball well. The passing is improved from last year. I don't have my guy dropping passes into the other teams middle when trying to pass behind me. The control stick seems more responsive on changes to dunks and layups. The graphics are hot. I play on everything maxed, with 100fps all the time, and can see the sweat coming off the guys perfectly. Best of all, I can use my DS4 controller, without DS4tools, and keep the xbox icons. Last year, it defaulted to 1,2,3,4 buttons instead of the icons, making it hard to know which button was what.
If you liked 2k15, get this. It's improved and fun. Even the review sites are giving it a 7 or 8. The only people complaining are those who can't get over the intro to the story mode.

I come from a long background with AOE1 and 2, so by comparison, this game was an overwhelming disappointment. The game is, for one, not easy to just pick up and learn. The traditional control scheme of gathering resources while building cities and armies is skewed, removing a large part of resources and troop-building altogether. Most of your income is transported from the 'homeland' to you over the course of a match, which makes sense from a colonial standpoint, but makes games painfully slow, leaves you feeling significantly less in-control of your empire, and narrows down the game into 2-3 playstyles regardless of your civilization choice. And while the game's visuals are nice, the scaling up of buildings and units alongside the 3D view leaves the maps feeling much smaller and minimizes the emphasis on careful exploration that was a landmark of previous games.
AOE3 is, essentially, not reminiscient of its predecessors in any way, and can hardly be called a continuation/conclusion of the franchise: The fact that AOE2 is STILL getting support and new, regular DLCs today while this game is largely left in the dust, speaks to how few gamers made the transition.

A very cautious 'YES'. I'm starting to see that tired trend of caving into the lowest common denominator, with the introduction of the SCU (Storage Containment Unit) Block. It has infinite storage for tech parts, and it completely makes base building, infrastructure management, and design decisions pointless. Before you had to make room on your tech if you wanted to bring pieces back to the vender to sell, an create specialized Techs to help you salvage parts from destroyed Techs. But now, you just plop the SCU down, it sucks up all the pieces, and then you plop it back on your Tech and drive back to the vender and sell it all.
It's completely undermined the progression system, resulting in a game that is becoming way too easy.
I only hope the SCU is just a stand-in for something in the works (something with limited space, preferably), or that it becomes an end-game item.

Development is slow but steady on this possible future classic, although there are occasional big leaps to fix bugs or quickly implement a new idea.  Has elements from sandbox and vehicular combat games of the past but is definately its own thing.  You could sum it up best like this: "Craft and scavenge the parts to build your own mobile battle legos".  The dev team seems to really want to produce something unique and quickly accessible to a large audience.  Their steaming a lot (which I can't watch, unfortuantely) and seem really active in the official site forums.  I hate crafting in most games but I actually enjoy it in Terratech.  The recipies aren't overly complex and is once you get a handle on buildling automated production (ala Factorio but for now a lot simpler) you'll be making credits like a madman.  The game already includes the groundwork for creating fleets of AI controlled allies but its in the very early stages.  There's also the large shadow of performance issues.  The large game world is randomly generated and simulated on your PC, and pretty much in real time from what I can tell.  Once its starts getting pretty populated you WILL notice.  Nevetheless, Terratech has a ridiculous amount of potential.  My single biggest complaint is that the R&D chamber isn't part of the base early access game.  R&D is a playground where all the content is available for testing and building utterly ridiculous things, ala Minecraft's creative mode.  It also costs half of what the base game does.  This creates a paywall that slows down player testing and therefore development.  Payload Studios seriously needs to consider bundling this zero-day DLC into the game.

Fractured Space is inoffensive but not particularly compelling.
In Fractured Space, you control a capital ship as part of a 5v5 fleet and push down two lanes to try to control territory to gain resources.  Controlling the opposite side of a lane allows you to warp to the enemy base, which you can capture to end the game.  An arena in the middle of the map periodically opens and provokes a team fight for ever increasing benefits to the team that captures it.
Combat is a relatively simple affair.  Ships have a rapid firing and generally shorter ranged gun, a slower firing and generally longer ranged gun, and very slowly firing, even longer ranged, and frequently debuff-applying missiles.  You'll unload these into an enemy while tapping the point defense button whenever missiles come at you.
Combat is further complicated by cover, special abilities, and armor.  Cover is simple enough- get behind a rock and things on the other side mostly can't hit you.  Ships also have somewhat directional armor that becomes extremely directional when a facing takes enough damage to blow the armor off, causing dramatically increased damage to that facing.  These two factors give you reason to reposition during combat, while sluggish ship handling keeps the game from being exceptionally twitchy.
On the ability front, ships have two special abilities.  Generally, one normal ability and one deployable such as a buoy with an aura or deployable small craft.  These give you access to things like healing, speed boosts, teleports, improved enemy detection (range and behind cover), damage mitigation, etc.
Overall, there's very little about Fractured Space I dislike, but it just doesn't feel that interesting.
Ship roles and special abilities don't feel particularly strong and distinct, the way they are in better MOBAs.  Ships have roles- defense, offense, support, but for the most part they feel like they're all big blocks of HP and DPS rather than the strongly flavored roles that make up a traditional MOBA.  Winning fights generally feels like a matter of picking engagements where your side has more ships present, and there's little of the excitement of a good snipe, initiation, or well-aimed skillshot that makes being on the wrong end of even an even fight in a MOBA a tense affair.
Over the course of the game your ship will gradually level up, and every several levels you can choose if you want to get a stronger boost to attack, defense, or "utility".  (abilities and sensor range)  Again, however, this doesn't feel impactful in the way that better MOBAs do, where you obtain new skills and significant upgrades to your skills, and items or traits that significantly modify how you play.

Strategic positioning is possibly the strongest aspect of the game, but even then it's 90% just a back and fourth battle for control of mines which will gradually give you an edge by determining the rate at which you level up.  In a lane, you're always capable of jumping home to your base or over to the teamfight arena so you're rarely that badly out of position- mostly, you just need to stick together when pushing a lane because flying from your entry point to the opposite side of the lane takes time.  Only the decision to attack the enemy base- especially the decision to sacrifice the team fight arena to try to decapitate the enemy- feels particularly impactful.
I don't dislike Fractured Space at all- I'd probably give it three stars on a five star scale.  Even while writing this, I mildly feel the urge to re-install it and play another round, because I like spaceships, like MOBAs, and like competitive games.  If you're thinking of trying it out, I'd do so- it's F2P, after all, and I didn't find it obnoxious so after three or so hours of playing it.
At the end of writing this, though, I'm not going to go back because there are both better MOBAs and better space or naval combat games out there.  Fractured Space straddles ship combat and MOBA gameplay, but only provides a little bit of the excitement of either.

So far I've only played single player for this game.
A very distinct and creative title. To me it seemed like an updated version of Astroids. You destroy rocks and enemies through the use of a destructive tether (the mace). The tether responds to any small movement you make. Find enough room to fly your "ship" in a cricle, and it'll cause the tether to gain speed and momentum; this makes for an efficient destructive force that any astroid and red triangle would tremble by. There are 150 Missions ranging from pure point accumuluation to not destroying anything at all within a certain amount of time. It sounds and looks easier than it is. The hectic nature of the game means random chance is a bigger factor than skill. Certain moments cause needless difficulty such as a the camera shaking after a nice chain of kills.
There are several "ships" each with its own unique movement and weight. Heavier ships are slower and may hold larger particles on its tether. There are no levels, the game area changes after completing missions. You have 3 missions to complete at any one time. One area might be designed for one of those missions, but you can still complete the others in the same area. This also causes difficulty, as you might end up with a mission that was meant for an easier area, but since you've progressed past it, you'll just have to somehow finish it in a more diffcult settings. Finally; great soundtrack that works well with the visuals.
The suggested retail is $5.00. I purchased this on sale, I personally would not get it at the full price, but I'm tight with my cash. It may be be worth it to some if you're in the market for this sort of game. It is only 5 bucks!

Overall, it's a repetitive, but very visually and aurally satisfying, clicker/visual novel game. The best features are meant for multiplayer. You're warned to wipe logs early in the game, but logs are useless since there isnt anyone to read them (I stopped clearing them about halfway). Many of the features (like "forkbomb" and the trap functionality of the shells) are completely useless without multiplayer. There are no enemy hackers (save one, who is a major story character and only attempts to hack you once). The world is not alive. It is essentially a visual novel treasure hunt, where you go from one node to the next, doing the same things over and over with the incentive to just finish the game. The story and storytelling arent even good enough to justify it being this way. Maybe when it has multiplayer, itll be worth playing. Overall, the feeling of urgency isn't there like it would be if you were playing a game like slavehack.
When it gets multiplayer, if the multiplayer works correctly, it could well be one of the funnest and most exciting hacking games ever. Until then, unless you think the idea of writing commands instead of doing the same exact thing with a mouse is a good experience, I would probably just get uplink.
Also, if you're reading this review devs, Duckman should be expanded on. He's easily the best character in the game. Thanks Duckfam, you unsung hero.

Fractured Space is a game about driving your gigantic Spaceship into epic 5v5 team Battles on vast maps, with Sectors of up to 100 Kilometers Length. There are currently 33 Ships available to play. Where they are split into 3 Manufacturers, wich each boast their own distinctive Artstyle and unique Systems.
Games can be played in the two currently available Gamemodes "Conquest" and "Frontline", where the first feels somewhat like a good old MOBA and the latter like a fast King of the Hill match with base-Capture elements.
Ships can manouver almost completely free, though you are unable to roll and only limited tilting is possible. Though this goes to ensure that certain ships can function the way they were designed and combat gets more challenging. More on that later.
Movement between sectors is achieved via a "Phase-Relocation", also called Jump, wich keeps both your orientation and momentum.
Fractured Space features a very high depth of mechanics, wich might not jump your thought immediatly and will require some getting used to. Such as the concept of Armor and breaking Armor causing you to take increased Damage from enemy fire.
Fractured Space, due to its high depth, delivers lots of potential for very tactical play and thus has huge potential to become an E-Sport in the future.
Here are my, personal, Scores for the Game:
Graphics: 9/10  The Unreal Engine delivers again! And so do the Art-Devs from Edgecase games! Beatifull looks!
Sound: Solid 8/10 Despite the usual "No Sound in Space" thing, Fractured Space features a really immersive Soundscape!
Depth: 9/10 In terms of Depth, Fractured Space beats most MMOSA's ive yet seen. May be a bit to much for the casual Player.
Character Design: 9/10 The Ships you play feel very very Unique, and become so even more with Loadouts and Crew.
Gameplay: 7/10 Gameplay is a bit unintuitive at times, but a well done Tutorial helps with the tremedous depth of the Game.
Now, do I recommend Fractured Space?
HELL YEAH!
Its one of the most revolutionary Space-Shooters ive ever seen and the Unreal Engine makes it just SO nice to play and look good. The Game is fair and balanced. No cheaters to bee seen since the game started.
There is payed content to the game, but this completely restricts itself to Skins, giving you the cool looks but nothing else. While you can also buy "Credit Boosters" to simply get your next ship faster.
That being said, a more expensive ship doesnt mean you will have an easier time. Having a newer, more expensive ship gives you absolutely no advantages over other people.
Now there are some players i defenitly don't recomment to touch Fractured Space, because the game takes quite some effort to be successful in. So just quickly Jumping in for the pure Ownage will likely not work out.

Drox Operative is an excellent and unique ARPG, well worth your money.
The Good:
-Unique character development
-Extensive variety of builds and ships, you can do pretty much anything you can come up with, and succeed.
-Random area generation, each playthrough is different.
-Built in mechanics to encourage you to play each round differently, without penalizing you for playing the way you want to play. (For example, the Drox guild will issue you a quest to save one race, destroy another, protect a specific alliance, etc, and you earn extra rewards for compliance.)
-The graphics are no where near as bad as the screenshots would lead you to believe.
-Easy to respec, making it almost imposible to permanently screw up a character.
-Fun factor: this is one of those games where you look up and realize hours have dissapeared, and your wife is standing behind you nagging.
The Bad:
-Learning curve can be a bit steep, with spikes in difficulty.
-Drox Guild quests can often encourage you to do the Exact opposite of what you've been working towards.
-Easy to screw up a character, forcing you to respec.

The game is beautiful. Music, voice acting, graphics - it's all superb. But it's not a good strategy game.
And make no mistake, it is a strategy game. There's all that RPG fluff that tricks you into thinking it's about character progression, combat and exploration. But it's not. It's about balancing money, maintaining the right character roster. You build a machine and learn the rules on the way. You learn that you need good resting places, that's easy to see. Then you see that you need many spare characters for when someone from your rooster can't go for the next mission. Then you learn a good party composition. Then you learn which items do you need for specific dungeons. Then you create parties for cracking specific bosses. And then maybe you'll think about what to do in dungeons themselves, the ones that take 95% of the game time - but it's not necessary. Almost everything is decided before you venture into dungeon and the dungeon itself shows you  mistakes you've made during preparation.
It's more like Football Manager than RPG. There's lots of downtime: even though dungeons have a spooky atmosphere they are really not that important themselves. Random numbers may screw you but the big picture is rarely affected. It is somewhat similar to Total War games: if you play singleplayer than this battle engine is only needed when you want to minimise your losses or inflict maximum losses on enemy in an already lost battle. Everything is won or lost on a strategic map - and in DD it's all decided in hamlet.
The worst thing is not even that downtime but the grind. Even when you learn everything there's to learn about the game (except probably how the Darkest Dungeon itself works) you still have to grind. For ages. It may look like your goal is to reach maximum level with a band of characters to go into the final dungeon, but no, you need lots of those characters, you need to upgrade everything, you'll have to spend time on raising new characters while your veterans are resting. It drags on and on without any real decisions. It becomes a boring clicker with micromanagement.
Still fun for first several hours. Turn-based horror. Then the magic quickly fades.

Darkest Dungeon is one of the best designed, most well-balanced games I have ever played. Gameplay focuses on taking a squad of heroes through relatively simple dungeons, and managing your town in between missions. You choose 4 heroes from a wide array of classes, and further customize them by gear and abilities. This game obviously got a huge benefit from its long stay in Early Access- all of the classes are useful and you really have to think carefully about how you organize your squad. A strategy that steamrolls one tier of dungeons may utterly fail at the next tier, so you constantly need to fine tune and readjust. The fact that death is permanent adds real tension.
I was also very impressed by the aesthetics. The graphics are simple 2D sprites with limited animation, but clever use of sound effects and camera work makes them very appealing. The voice work is top notch, one of the best I can think of in any game.
The biggest complaint I see about this game is people claiming its "RNG dependent". I did not find this to be the case at all. Part of the game is the gamble of pushing your beaten-down team through the end of a dungeon for a big payout, or conceding defeat and slinking off to fight another day. If you play too aggressively,  you will lose heroes. If you play with strategy, the RNG is totally tractable, I never felt robbed or cheated by the game- just the opposite in fact, I found it very rewarding to overcome such a challenge. I strongly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys tactics and strategy.

After the critically-acclaimed Age of Empires 2 was released and the expansion of Conquerors was extremely well received, Age of Empires III was bound to happen. And it did in 2009. Moving away from the Conquistador era, AoE III takes places around the 1700's when Settlers began to populate the American continent.
For starters, the graphics changed from the sprites used in AoE II to a tridimensionally rendered objects in AoE III and that made it extremely unpopular for some, as the hardware necessities the software needed were not average. But all in all, the graphical performance of AoE III was extremely well done and on par with other RTS games of the era. Unfortunately, the RTS gaming era was about to end, with AoE III marking a significant decrease in interest the gamers had in this type of games.
What was it? One wonders. The gameplay was extremely similar, and yet the charm AoE II had was somehow missing. The AI was not extremely hard and the games had all kinds of countries to be chosen from.
The expansions made AoE III a bit better, with the return of ancient civilizations being an option just like in the Conquerors expansion. Unfortunately this made a small impact to the decreasing interest in this RTS.
However, it still is a fun game to play. In 2017 it is a game that doesn't require extreme processing power and it is graphically pretty.
The investment is well done nowadays.
If you feel a little nostalgic and want to play one of the last RTS games of the era,
Buy it, play it and don't regret it.

Well, I bought this game for approximately nothing, but it was worth a tenfold more. It's similar to titles such as Grid Wars and Geometry wars – contrary to those titles, however, it requires not only precise use of the mouse to navigate through hostile space, but also understanding of the ships' and enemies' behavior.
The game offers a very smooth gameplay (its CPU usage is relatively low). It has a very nice, well-fitting, ambient soundtrack. The backstory is gripping. And last but not least – it can notably pride itself in having the best controller remapping in the history of gaming.
It does have a number of drawbacks, though – namely:
• a console window is shown when the game is starting;
• you cannot change variables governing the game's behavior (at least not in-game);
• Alt + F4 does not work.
Still, it is a fun game to spend some evenings with!

This is a very interesting little adventure platformer in space!  Don't let the simple graphics deceive you.  It is not a very hard game, but it is a quite satisfying platforming experience.
It has all the hallmarks, collecting different weapons, fighting bosses, travel to different worlds, even some understand action.
There are even little elements you don't find elsewhere, like the weapon kickback.  The baddies seek you out, rather than all following simple patterns.
Light challenge and I do with the boss fights were a little harder, as the final boss difficulty curves way up in comparison...I think the only real issue is knowing where to go next is not always made clean, but that is the open nature of the game.
10 locations...12 weapons to collect...power ups!  What for can you ask for at this price?!?  When it is on sale, like Steam Winter Sale, you can get it super cheap ;)
ACHIEVEMENTS:  Mostly straight forward with a few you have to pay attention to :)
